Fe 3 O 4 NPs also possess a high surface area and can directly interact with bacterial cell membranes. Metal ions exhibit a propensity to bind with thiol (-SH), amino (-NH), and carboxyl (-COOH) groups of proteins, including enzymes, leading to their inactivation or partial inhibition. 50 Additionally, IONPs were found to suppress expressions of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in antibiotic-resistant bacteria typically encountered in clinical settings. 49 Mechanistic insights suggest that IONPs disrupt the function of F0/F1-ATPase, impeding H+ flow across membranes and altering the redox potential. 51 Such antimicrobial actions attributed to IONPs are consistent across various studies and are shared by other metal oxide NPs. 52 Moreover, NPs with smaller dimensions were implicated in inhibiting DNA replication through inactivating topoisomerases. 53 Electron microscopic studies indicated direct interaction of Fe 2 O 3 NPs with cell walls of Escherichia coli ( E. coli ). 54 IONPs can penetrate the cytoplasm, accumulate, induce vacuole formation, and disrupt cell walls.

Fe 3 O 4 IONPs exhibit distinct antimicrobial mechanisms, particularly effective against gram-negative bacteria due to their ability to concentrate between the outer and inner membranes of bacterial cell walls. 55 This concentration is facilitated by the binding of Fe 3 O 4 IONPs to the formate hydrogen lyase (FHL) complex in the inner membrane, enhancing their antimicrobial efficacy against these bacteria. 51 The bactericidal and antibiofilm activities of Fe 3 O 4 IONPs are well-documented. For instance, positively charged and neutral IONPs significantly reduce Streptococcus mutans biofilms more effectively than negatively charged IONPs, likely due to better electrostatic interactions with the bacterial cell surface. 56 Moreover, Fe 3 O 4 IONPs coated with oleic acid prevented biofilm formation by S. aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa , suggesting that surface modifications can enhance the antibiofilm properties of these NPs. 57 The physicochemical characteristics of IONPs, including surface charge, hydrophobicity, and a high surface area-to-volume ratio, facilitate their adsorption onto and penetration into bacterial biofilms, disrupting the biofilm matrix and impairing bacterial communication and survival. 58

Beyond the intrinsic oxidative, membrane-disruptive, and antibiofilm effects described above, recent magnetic nanoplatforms increasingly exploit the simultaneous generation of thermal, mechanical, and catalytic stresses. These mechanisms are closely interconnected because the same Fe 3 O 4 -based platform can produce heat under an alternating magnetic field, undergo field-driven displacement or rotation, and catalyze ROS formation through iron-mediated reactions. Luo et al developed hyaluronic acid-coated MnFe 2 O 4 nanoparticles that combined magnetic hyperthermia with quorum-sensing interference. 59 Downregulation of agrA, agrC , and hld weakened bacterial stress responses, improved nanoparticle penetration, and enhanced treatment in an implant-associated infection model. Mesoporous Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticles loaded with IR-820 similarly combined AMF-induced heating with photodynamic ROS generation, resulting in improved biofilm disruption and bacterial clearance in infected wound and subcutaneous abscess models. 60 These approaches illustrate how modulation of the biofilm microenvironment can enhance magnetothermal efficacy without relying exclusively on high bulk temperatures.

Compared to traditional magnetothermal damage, magnetomechanical systems exploit field-driven torque, oscillation, or rotation ( Figure 3 ). Šavli et al used anisotropic iron oxide nanochains under a rotating magnetic field to remove more than 90% of selected Gram-negative biofilms, although the principal outcome was physical detachment rather than bacterial killing. 61 By comparison, Fe 3 O 4 @polydopamine nanospears concentrated mechanical stress at the bacterial envelope, producing membrane puncture and enhanced S. aureus killing when combined with localized heating. 62 These findings demonstrate that particle geometry and field mode determine whether magnetic actuation primarily causes matrix disruption, bacterial dispersal, or irreversible membrane injury. Fe 3 O 4 -based platforms may also function as magnetically responsive nanozymes ( Figure 3 ). He et al showed that magnetic stimulation enhanced the peroxidase-like activity of iron oxide nanoparticles, indicating that localized magnetic energy can accelerate catalytic reactions without a pronounced increase in bulk temperature. 63 Ma et al translated this principle into a magneto-nanozyme platform in which magnetic assembly, AMF heating, and multivalent-iron catalysis promoted EPS degradation and ROS-mediated bacterial killing in a mouse skin-infection model. 64 Copper-doped magnetic vortex nanorings further integrated magnetic hyperthermia, Cu-mediated chemodynamic therapy, and photothermal activation, producing near-complete elimination of E. coli and S. aureus under low-H 2 O 2 conditions. 65 Positively charged Fe 3 O 4 @Polyethyleneimine nanoparticles likewise accumulated within S. aureus biofilms and generated combined thermal, mechanical, and oxidative stress under AMF exposure. 66

Furthermore, SPIONs have reported to establish multimodal mechanism with optical, catalytic, and immune-directed platforms and to identify the relative advantages and limitations of each approach. Koç et al combined aminolevulinic acid-loaded SPIONs with photothermal and photodynamic activation, producing 3–6-log reductions in Pseudomonas aeruginosa , 2–4-log reductions in Staphylococcus epidermidis , and up to a 13-log reduction in P. aeruginosa biofilms; however, light penetration and oxygen dependence may restrict application to deep infections. Ma et al developed an electromagnetically actuated magneto-nanozyme that integrated magnetic heating, mechanical biofilm disruption, and iron-mediated ROS generation, achieving 99.99% antibacterial efficacy in an MRSA-infected wound model while maintaining the treatment temperature at approximately 45 °C. 64 Host-directed platforms provide a complementary strategy: a STING-adjuvanted P. aeruginosa outer-membrane-vesicle nanoparticle vaccine completely protected mice from lethal pneumonia at an antigen dose of 0.01 μg and reduced pulmonary bacterial burden by approximately 2 log units, 67 whereas infection-responsive macrophage-targeted nanoparticles enhanced intracellular vancomycin delivery, ROS generation, bacterial clearance, and wound healing. 68 Compared with these platforms, SPIONs offer deep magnetic-field penetration, remote activation, potential MRI guidance, and the capacity to integrate magnetothermal, magnetomechanical, catalytic, and drug-delivery functions. Their principal advantage therefore lies in providing a localized and externally controlled multimodal platform.

## Synthesis Techniques

Fe 3 O 4 NPs, owing to their unique size-dependent properties, have been applied across diverse fields; therefore, it is pivotal to understand fabrication methods to tailor these NPs to specific uses. Generally, Fe 3 O 4 NPs are synthesized by two major routes: a top-down approach and a bottom-up approach. The top-down approach involves mechanical fractionation of bulk materials into smaller particles, achieved through techniques like milling or laser ablation. While effective, these methods may limit control over the particle size and shape. In contrast, the bottom-up approach builds NPs from molecular or atomic precursors. It encompasses both chemical and biological routes. Chemical methods utilize organic solvents as reaction media, allowing precise control over the size, composition, and surface properties. Examples include sol-gel synthesis and hydrothermal methods. Biological methods, on the other hand, leverage living organisms or their components. Green synthesis approaches minimize environmental impacts, making them attractive for sustainable NP production. Challenges include standardization, reproducibility, and optimization. Recent research focused on hybrid approaches, combining top-down and bottom-up methods. As we unravel the intricacies of these techniques, we pave the way for transformative applications in medicine, energy, and materials science.

### Physical Approaches

#### Ball Milling

Ball milling is a dominant method for the physical synthesis of Fe 3 O 4 NPs. This technique utilizes the principles of impact and attrition to achieve solid-state size reduction, transforming iron precursors into refined NPs. The process employs a rotating cylindrical chamber filled with micron-sized grinding media, which mechanically fractures the precursor materials into NPs. The incorporation of solvents or excess salts can improve the milling efficiency and prevent agglomeration of the synthesized NPs. 69 The ball mill process is described in Figure 3 . Notably, advancements in ball milling have enabled the synthesis of magnetic catalysts, such as Cu/Fe/Fe 3 O 4 , through applying an auxiliary electromagnetic field during the milling process. It was established that the ball milling process plays a critical role in determining the morphology and electromagnetic absorption properties of the resulting NPs. 70 , 71

#### Laser Ablation

Laser ablation has emerged as an alternative to ball milling for MNP synthesis. 72 This technique places the solid material below a thin sheet through which laser irradiation is applied from the top as illustrated in ( Figure 4 ). This technique offers precise control over particle properties but suffers from limitations like low production rates and polydispersity. 73 Unlike ball milling, laser ablation is simpler and requires no temperature or pressure adjustments. The laser power can be tailored to achieve the desired NP characteristics. For instance, the effects of laser power and solvent choice on Fe 3 O 4 /Au NP properties using neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser ablation highlight the potential for optimizing laser ablation parameters to address its limitations and facile NP synthesis. 74 Figure 4 Illustration of the underlying mechanisms of the ball mill and laser ablation methods of synthesis. #### Sonolysis

The sonolysis method, which utilizes ultrasonic waves to induce acoustic cavitation, is an efficacious technique for synthesizing Fe 3 O 4 NPs. This process entails dissolving iron salts, such as FeCl 2 or FeCl 3 , in an appropriate solvent, followed by ultrasonic irradiation. 75 The implosive collapse of cavitation bubbles generates extreme localized temperatures and pressures, facilitating the nucleation and growth of Fe 3 O 4 NPs. Critical factors influencing NP properties include the precursor concentration, pH, irradiation duration, and presence of surfactants. 76 This method allows precise control over the NP size, shape, and surface characteristics, making it highly suitable for biomedical applications. 77

### Chemical Approaches

#### Coprecipitation

First deployed in 1981 by Massart et al, coprecipitation remains a gold standard in the industry due to its simplicity, ease, and efficacy. 78 It uses the principle of the alkalization of metals, using homogeneous solutions containing the ions to be mixed and precipitated. Upon the addition of anions and a change in the pH, the desired NPs are precipitated, which are then washed and magnetically separated. The coprecipitation methos is well described in Figure 5 . Coprecipitation offers a robust and versatile approach for synthesizing NPs with well-defined homogenous properties. This technique relies on a well-orchestrated sequence of two critical stages: nucleation and growth. During nucleation, a rapid yet crucial event, precursor ions assemble in a supersaturated reaction medium to form minute, stable clusters. 79 , 80 This initial particle formation, driven by the thermodynamic instability of the supersaturated state, lays the foundation for the final NP characteristics. The subsequent growth stage, typically slower and more controlled, involves the diffusion of dissolved precursor species from the bulk solution towards the existing NPs, leading to a gradual increase in their size.

Crucially, the success of this method hinges on the meticulous control of reaction parameters. The molar ratio of the starting salts and the solution pH (8–14) play pivotal roles in influencing the rates of both nucleation and growth. 81 These parameters ultimately dictate the final morphology and size distribution (monodispersed nature) of the synthesized NPs. 29 For instance, studies suggested that a judicious selection of the molar ratio can promote the formation of specific crystal phases within the NPs. Additionally, the influence of temperature on the coprecipitation process cannot be overlooked. Elevated temperatures (above 80 ° C) were reported to be particularly beneficial for synthesis, potentially by enhancing the diffusion kinetics of precursor species and promoting the formation of well-defined morphologies. 82

Several modifications have been made to the coprecipitation method referred to as modified coprecipitation methods. They involve the addition of different surfactants or stabilizers making IONPs more adaptable and versatile. For instance, the addition of polyethylene glycol (PEG) 4000, not only improved the antibacterial activities against E. coli and S. aureus but also prevented the agglomeration by reducing the particle size from 17 to 12.2 nm. 83 Similarly other stabilizers like chitosan 84 and glycol chitosan, 85 and polysaccharides like dextran and sucrose 86 were also deployed to enhance the stability as well as evaluate the antibacterial performance giving an edge to surfactant-coated NPs compared to traditional ones. Furthermore, utilizing the coprecipitation route of synthesis, various antibacterial drugs were also loaded onto Fe 3 O 4 NPs, delivering a synergistic antibacterial effect with hyperthermia. For example, Al-Jabari et al synthesized Fe 3 O 4 @SiO 2 NPs and loaded levofloxacin to test it against a panel of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria by an agar-well diffusion method. Similarly, antibacterial drugs like streptomycin 87 and ampicillin 88 were also adsorbed onto the surface of functionalized IONPs, making them an advanced nanocarrier for antibacterial drug delivery.

#### Hydrothermal Method

Hydrothermal methods, or solvothermal synthesis, have emerged as an effective way to synthesize Fe 3 O 4 NPs due to their versatility and controllability. 89–92 These techniques exploit the unique properties of water at elevated temperatures and pressures. Under such conditions, water exhibits enhanced reactivity, facilitating the dissolution of iron precursors (eg, FeCl 2 , FeCl 3 , Fe(NO 3 ) 3 , or Fe 2 O 3 ) and accelerates overall reaction kinetics. Furthermore, high pressures in the system further promote this effect fostering the formation of well-defined Fe 3 O 4 crystals. 93 , 94 However some researchers also used solvents like triethylene glycol to synthesize advanced NPs of Fe 3 O 4 and CuFe 2 O 4 resulting in NPs with higher magnetism curves and hyperthermia. 95 The hydrothermal synthesis process involves a well-defined sequence, as shown in Figure 6 . First, iron precursors are dissolved in deionized water, and the solution is sealed within a Teflon-lined autoclave. The autoclave subjects it to high temperatures (typically 150–300 °C) and elevated pressures for a predetermined time in a closed environment. Finally, the Fe 3 O 4 NPs are separated and dried using magnetic separation or centrifugation. Figure 6 Hydrothermal route of synthesis of superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles. Created with BioRender.com. A diagram of nanoparticle synthesis via hydrothermal method.

This approach offers several advantages including simplicity, scalability due to readily available equipment and precursors, and the ability to tailor the size, morphology, and crystallinity of the NPs through meticulous control of reaction parameters (temperature, pressure, and reaction time). 96–98 Additionally, the use of water as the solvent and a closed autoclave system minimizes contamination, leading to high-purity Fe 3 O 4 NPs. However, precise control over NP characteristics necessitates careful optimization of reaction conditions, and operating at high pressures and temperatures demands robust equipment and strict adherence to safety protocols.

Various researchers have deployed the hydrothermal-based synthesis of Fe 3 O 4 for the development of nanomaterials in the domains of antibacterial and anticancer therapeutics. For example, Wei et al synthesized iron oxide-based Fe 3 O 4 @MoS 2 -Ag NPs using hydrothermal synthesis with a recoverable peroxidase-like effect resulting into antibacterial activities. 99 Jabir et al synthesized PEG-coated Fe 3 O 4 @PEG NPs to induce an apoptotic effect against cancer. The PEG coating not only stabilized and reduced the average particle size from 9–20 to 5–12 nm but also was twofold more cytotoxic towards the AMJ13 breast cancer cell line with respective 50% inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) values of 36.53 and 18.23 mmol. 100 Similarly hyaluronic acid used to prepare Fe 3 O 4 @HA NPs delivered a cytotoxic effect by selectively targeting overexpressed cluster of differentiation 44 (CD44) cells. 101 Such modifications also improved the hyperthermic effect by increasing the intrinsic power loss up to 25 times.

#### Microemulsions

Microemulsion method is a versatile technique for synthesizing Fe 3 O 4 NPs, that utilizes thermodynamically stable mixtures of water, oil, and surfactants to create nanoscale reaction environments. In this method, iron salts such as FeCl 2 or FeCl 3 are dissolved in the aqueous phase, while the oil phase typically contains a hydrocarbon solvent. 102 Surfactants stabilize the interface between the water and oil phases, forming microemulsions. Upon mixing, reduction and nucleation of Fe 3 O 4 occur within confined microemulsion droplets, allowing for controlled NP growth. The resultant Fe 3 O 4 NPs exhibit uniform size and shape due to the constrained reaction environment. Critical parameters influencing synthesis include the type and concentration of surfactants, water-to-oil ratio, and reaction temperature. 103 Post-synthesis, NPs are recovered through magnetic separation or centrifugation, followed by washing. This method enables precise control over NP characteristics, making it suitable for biomedical and catalytic applications.

#### Green Synthesis

The green synthesis of Fe 3 O 4 NPs represents a sustainable and environmentally friendly approach that utilizes natural plant extracts as reducing and stabilizing agents. This methodology presents several advantages over traditional chemical synthesis techniques, such as lower environmental impacts, cost-efficiency, and enhanced biocompatibility of the resulting NPs. 104–109 The synthesis process generally involves the following steps. Initially, plant extracts are prepared by boiling plant materials (leaves, seeds, or bark) to extract bioactive compounds. Subsequently, the plant extract is mixed with an aqueous solution of an iron precursor, commonly FeCl 3 or FeSO 4 . The bioactive compounds in the extract, which include polyphenols, flavonoids, and other antioxidants, serve as reducing agents, converting Fe 3+ ions to Fe 3 O 4 NPs. 110 Concurrently, these compounds act as capping agents, stabilizing the NPs and preventing agglomeration. 111 The NPs are then purified by centrifugation, followed by washing with distilled water and ethanol to ensure high purity. Finally, the purified NPs are collected and dried for further use.

The principal advantages of green synthesis include its simplicity, scalability, and the utilization of non-toxic, renewable resources. 111–113 This approach circumvents the use of hazardous chemicals, thereby reducing environmental pollution and associated health risks. Moreover, the biocompatibility of green-synthesized NPs makes them particularly suitable for antibacterial applications. The antibacterial efficacy of green-synthesized Fe 3 O 4 NPs has been rigorously validated in multiple studies, demonstrating their potential in biomedical applications. For instance, Dhavale et al employed an extract from Sphagneticola trilobata to synthesize IONPs, which exhibited zones of inhibition ranging from 12 to 18 mm against various pathogenic bacteria. 105 This significant antibacterial activity underscores the potential of these NPs in combating bacterial infections. Similarly, Majid et al utilized a Phoenix dactylifera seed extract for the green synthesis of Fe 3 O 4 NPs, achieving a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 6 µg/mL against pathogenic bacteria, highlighting their strong antibacterial properties suitable for infection control and therapeutic applications. ## Biocompatibility

IONPs are renowned for their exceptional biocompatibility and biodegradability. However, their safety depends strongly on particle size, surface chemistry, dose, administration route, and exposure duration. After systemic administration, SPIONs rapidly acquire a plasma-protein corona and are preferentially sequestered by the mononuclear phagocyte system, particularly Kupffer cells in the liver and macrophages in the spleen. Subsequent endosomal–lysosomal degradation releases Fe 2+ /Fe 3+ , which can enter physiological ferritin, transferrin, and hemosiderin pools; however, clearance may require days to weeks and can be delayed by aggregation, dense coatings, repeated dosing, or high tissue burden.

For example, an intravenous injection of 0.8 mg/kg body weight of γ-Fe 2 O 4 NPs did not adversely impact the weight gain of rats or induce apoptosis in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). 134 Following injection, these NPs were observed in the lungs, liver, and kidneys, but not in the brain or heart. Moreover, a substantial amount of the NPs was eliminated in the urine within 72 h. Generally, IONPs exhibit low or no cytotoxic effects on cell cultures. Coatings such as polyethyleneimine, dimercaptosuccinate, or citrate applied to IONPs did not adversely affect primary rat cerebellar cortex astrocytes or cultured murine astrocytes. 135 Similarly, IONPs conjugated with PEG-phospholipids (WFION) did not impact the viability of the B16 F10 cell line at concentrations of up to 0.75 mg Fe/mL. 136 Fe 3 O 4 NPs were shown to have a bacteriostatic effect without causing hemolysis. In some cases, IONPs can enhance caspase-3-dependent apoptosis, generate ROS, cause membrane damage, and alter the cytoskeleton in HUVECs, 137 although those cytotoxic effects generally occur at much higher concentrations than those needed for their antimicrobial properties.

Several experimental studies indicate that the antibacterial benefit of SPION-mediated hyperthermia must be interpreted together with its effects on mammalian cells and surrounding tissues. Kim et al showed that antibody-conjugated magnetic nanoparticles could localize heating within Staphylococcus aureus -infected wounds, reduce bacterial burden, and accelerate wound closure without detectable damage to adjacent tissue, suggesting that pathogen targeting can improve the therapeutic window. 138 Nguyen et al achieved only a modest temperature increase of approximately 5 °C in Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms, yet this was sufficient to promote biofilm dispersal and enhance gentamicin activity, supporting the use of mild hyperthermia rather than direct thermal ablation. 45 Similarly, Almutairi et al reported that ferumoxytol-mediated heating combined with ciprofloxacin reduced S. aureus and P. aeruginosa burdens while producing limited systemic temperature elevation, indicating that localized treatment may preserve host tissue when the thermal dose is carefully controlled. 139 Nevertheless, SPION toxicity is strongly formulation-dependent. Mesoporous and polyethyleneimine-functionalized Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticles can improve bacterial adhesion and biofilm penetration, but their positive surface charge may also increase interactions with erythrocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and other mammalian membranes, potentially causing membrane disruption, oxidative stress, inflammation, or hemolysis. 66 Ma et al maintained infected wounds near 45 °C and achieved high antibacterial efficacy through combined heating and catalytic ROS generation, whereas higher temperatures are more likely to damage regenerating tissue. 64 This concern is particularly relevant to the microfiber system reported by Ansari et al, in which exposures above 50 °C enhanced MRSA killing but may compromise fibroblast viability, angiogenesis, collagen deposition, and wound repair. 21 Magnetotactic bacteria-mediated targeting likewise improved bacterial attachment and killing, but biological carriers introduce additional considerations related to immunogenicity and inflammatory responses. 140 Overall, SPIONs are not inherently selective for bacteria over mammalian cells; their apparent biocompatibility depends on local administration, surface coating, particle dose, AMF intensity, exposure duration, and the resulting thermal profile. 141 , 142 From an antibacterial perspective, the most clinically realistic strategy is therefore to use mild, localized hyperthermia to sensitize biofilms and resistant bacteria to antibiotics or catalytic treatment while avoiding temperatures and nanoparticle concentrations that induce host-cell injury.

## Application of Magnetic Hyperthermia-Based IONPs as Antibacterial Agents

Iron oxide-based magnetic hyperthermia is emerging as a highly promising approach in contemporary therapeutic modalities. Figure 7 illustrates the various theragnostic applications of magnetic hyperthermia as an antibacterial treatment strategy. Magnetic hyperthermia enables spatially confined energy deposition, while the associated temperature increase can weaken the extracellular polymeric substance matrix, increase bacterial membrane permeability, and facilitate antimicrobial penetration into biofilms. Distinct from the studies discussed above, Nickel et al (2020) evaluated shape-selected iron oxide nanoparticles loaded with cetyltrimethylammonium bromide and demonstrated that magnetic transport enhanced nanoparticle penetration through robust methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus biofilms. 143 Their findings further showed that nanoparticle morphology and surface charge strongly influenced the delivery of the biocide to bacteria located within deeper biofilm regions. For magnetically targeted antibiotic delivery, Geilich et al (2017) developed SPION-containing polymersomes coencapsulating methicillin, which penetrated approximately 20-μm-thick Staphylococcus epidermidis biofilms under an externally applied magnetic field. 144 Confocal microscopy demonstrated loading-dependent bacterial killing, while SPION incorporation simultaneously increased the magnetic responsiveness and MRI relaxivity of the nanocarriers, supporting their potential use as theragnostic antibacterial systems. A related thermoresponsive mesoporous silica nano system employed surface-decorated SPIONs to generate localized heat and trigger the opening of antibiotic-loaded pores. Exposure of Escherichia coli biofilms to 200 μg mL −1 of the nanocarrier under a 202 kHz and 30 mT alternating magnetic field produced an approximately 4-log 10 reduction in viable bacterial counts, illustrating the combination of magnetic hyperthermia and controlled antibiotic release represented in the schematic (Álvarez et al, 2022). 145 Implant-associated infection control has also been demonstrated using a silk-fibroin-stabilized Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticle coating applied to titanium surfaces. Magnetically induced detachment of the coating physically removed adherent biofilm and enhanced antibiotic efficacy by up to 100-fold in vitro and in a rat subcutaneous implant model, highlighting a mechanically assisted strategy for protecting implanted medical devices (Quan et al, 2024). 146 For dental applications, Fe 3 O 4 /BiVO 4 photoactive microrobot swarms were magnetically navigated across titanium implant surfaces, where their collective mechanical motion and light-triggered reactive oxygen species generation disrupted established biofilm colonies (Mayorga-Martinez et al, 2022). 147 MRI-compatible magnetic nanocarriers additionally provide a theranostic route by combining field-directed accumulation, therapeutic delivery, anatomical localization, and treatment monitoring within a single platform, as demonstrated by the SPION-containing polymersomes reported by Geilich et al (2017). 144 Magnetic resonance-guided mild hyperthermia has also been used to trigger localized ciprofloxacin release at approximately 42 °C in an infected-tissue model; however, this system employed low-temperature-sensitive liposomes activated by magnetic resonance-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound rather than SPION-mediated magnetic heating (Wardlow et al, 2016). 148 Collectively, these findings support the central concept illustrated in the figure that SPION-based systems can integrate externally controlled physical activation, deep biofilm penetration, antimicrobial delivery, implant protection, and diagnostic imaging within a multifunctional antibacterial strategy. ## Clinical Translation and Regulatory Pathways for SPION-Based Magnetothermal Antibacterial Therapy

Clinical translation of SPIONs is most advanced in diagnostic imaging, iron replacement, sentinel-lymph-node mapping, and oncological hyperthermia, whereas antibacterial magnetic hyperthermia remains at an early stage. The clearest registered antibacterial precedent is NCT06110494 , a completed randomized Phase 4 study in 44 patients with apical periodontitis that repurposed ferumoxytol with H 2 O 2 as a topical root-canal nanozyme; however, its activity relied on catalytic ROS generation rather than AMF-induced heating. 155 Other registered studies, including NCT07224464 and NCT04316091 , investigate SPION-mediated magnetic treatment in advanced solid tumors and osteosarcoma, respectively, 156 , 157 and therefore provide relevant experience in nanoparticle dosing, magnetic-field delivery, thermal monitoring, acute safety, and long-term follow-up without establishing antibacterial efficacy. The patent landscape summarized in Table 3 further reflects expanding technological interest in magnetic hyperthermia systems, catalytic nanozymes, antibiofilm coatings, implant-associated platforms, and multifunctional SPION formulations, although patent protection demonstrates technical novelty rather than clinical effectiveness or regulatory readiness. Translation is further complicated by the likely classification of SPION hyperthermia as a drug–device combination product, requiring integrated assessment of nanoparticle composition and manufacture, magnetic-field generation, treatment control, and biological performance. The FDA-approved Magtrace/Sentimag system provides an important regulatory precedent for clinical use of an iron oxide–device combination, but its diagnostic indication cannot be directly extrapolated to antibacterial therapy. Accordingly, the principal translational barriers remain the absence of dedicated antibacterial AMF trials, harmonized thermal and microbiological endpoints, and validated manufacturing and safety standards. ## Challenges and Prospects

The development and application of IONPs in combating bacterial infections present several challenges. One of the primary challenges is the rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant bacterial strains, which limits the efficacy of conventional antibiotics and necessitates alternative therapeutic strategies such as IONPs. 163 Ensuring consistent quality and reproducibility in IONP synthesis remains difficult due to variations in methods that affect their size, shape, and antibacterial properties. 163 , 164 Additionally, while IONPs exhibit minimal cytotoxicity to mammalian cells, comprehensive in vivo studies are required to fully understand their long-term biocompatibility and potential side effects. 165 , 166 Regulatory hurdles also pose a significant barrier, as the approval process for new nanomaterials is complex and time-consuming, requiring extensive safety and efficacy testing. 167 Furthermore, scaling up the production of IONPs in a cost-effective manner is challenging, and the environmental implications of large-scale production and disposal need careful assessment to prevent ecological harm. 164 Despite these challenges, the prospects for IONPs are promising. Advanced synthesis techniques, such as hybrid approaches combining top-down and bottom-up methods, can enhance the quality and functionality of IONPs. 163 , 166 , 168 IONPs engineered for targeted drug delivery have the potential to deliver antibiotics and other therapeutic agents directly to infection sites, increasing treatment efficacies and reducing side effects. 166 The development of multifunctional NPs with simultaneous antibacterial, imaging, and therapeutic capabilities could revolutionize the treatment of bacterial infections. 169 , 170 Rigorous clinical trials are necessary to validate the safety and effectiveness of IONPs in humans, paving the way for their integration into standard medical practice. 171 , 172 Moreover, the application of IONPs in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine holds promise for enhancing wound healing and repairing damaged tissues. 169 , 171 Beyond medical applications, IONPs could be utilized in environmental cleanup processes, such as removing bacterial contaminants from water sources, highlighting their versatility. Increased collaboration between academia, industry, and regulatory bodies, coupled with substantial funding, can accelerate the development and deployment of IONPs as next-generation antimicrobial agents, address global health issues and advance the field of nanotechnology.

## Conclusion

SPIONs represent a promising platform for the localized treatment of antibiotic-resistant and biofilm-associated infections because they combine remotely activated magnetic heating with catalytic, mechanical, drug-delivery, and imaging functions. The therapeutic performance is determined by the coupled effects of particle size, morphology, crystallinity, magnetic anisotropy, oxidation state, surface chemistry, aggregation, nanoparticle concentration, and alternating magnetic field conditions. These parameters govern specific absorption rate, intrinsic loss power, biofilm penetration, bacterial association, reactive oxygen species generation, and host-cell compatibility. Importantly, SPION-mediated treatment need not rely exclusively on high-temperature ablation. Mild hyperthermia can destabilize extracellular polymeric substances, increase membrane permeability, enhance antibiotic diffusion, promote biofilm dispersal, and amplify nanozyme-mediated oxidative stress while reducing injury to surrounding tissue. Multifunctional systems incorporating magneto-mechanical actuation, quorum-sensing interference, photodynamic therapy, thermoresponsive drug release, and implant coatings further expand the antibacterial potential of SPIONs. Nevertheless, translation remains limited by formulation variability, heterogeneous tissue accumulation, nonuniform thermal dosing, incomplete mechanistic resolution, inconsistent microbiological endpoints, and uncertainties concerning biodistribution, biodegradation, and long-term toxicity. Future progress will require quality-by-design manufacturing, standardized magnetic and thermal characterization, spatially resolved dosimetry, clinically relevant polymicrobial models, and integrated evaluation of antibacterial efficacy and host response. These advances could establish SPION-mediated magnetic hyperthermia as an effective adjunct for chronic wounds, dental infections, abscesses, and implant-associated biofilms.

# Nanoparticle-Based Therapeutic Strategies for Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy: Preclinical Advances, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives

## Abstract
Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is a major contributor to heart failure and is characterized by complex molecular mechanisms involving transcriptional and epigenetic regulation, signal transduction, metabolic remodeling, inflammatory responses, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Although conventional pharmaceutical treatments may alleviate the progression of cardiac hypertrophy, their clinical effectiveness is limited by poor cardiac selectivity, systemic side effects, and limited efficacy in reverseing pathological remodeling. Recently, nanoparticle-based strategies have emerged as a promising therapeutic approach for cardiac hypertrophy owing to their ability to enhance cardiac-targeted drug delivery, enable controlled or stimuli-responsive drug release, and reduce off-target toxicity through improved biodistribution. This review systematically summarizes the design strategies of nanoparticle-based therapies for pathological cardiac hypertrophy, including material platforms such as inorganic, organic, and biomimetic nanoparticles, key delivery strategies such as passive targeting, active targeting, biomimetic targeting, and stimulus-responsive release, and administration routes including intravenous, intraperitoneal, intradermal, inhalation, and oral administration. In addition, this review provides a comprehensive summary of the preclinical applications of the above strategies in the fields of gene and epigenetic regulation, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic treatments. Finally, this review analyzes the challenges in clinical translation on the basis of critical issues, including long-term biosafety, insufficient targeting efficacy, large-scale production, and appropriate administration routes.

## Keywords
pathological cardiac hypertrophy; nanomedicine; targeted drug delivery; stimuli-responsive release; precision therapy

## Introduction

Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is a detrimental cardiac remodeling process triggered by various pathological stimuli, including persistent pressure or volume overload, abnormal activation of the neurohumoral system, and myocardial ischemia and hypoxia, as well as genetic abnormalities such as storage disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy ( Figure 1 ). 1 The key features of cardiac hypertrophy include an elevated volume of cardiomyocytes, alteration of the extracellular matrix, and compromised cardiac contraction and relaxation capabilities. 2 Pathological cardiac hypertrophy has been observed in various cardiovascular diseases and typically results in severe consequences, including heart failure, arrhythmia, and even sudden death. 3–5 According to the report from the American Heart Association in 2023, cardiovascular diseases remain one of the leading causes of death in the United States and globally, imposing a heavy burden on public health and the healthcare system. 6 Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is the predominant structural remodeling of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and affects approximately 10–20% of the general adult population worldwide, 7 with the prevalence increasing to 36–41% among patients with hypertension. 8 LVH is an independent predictor of adverse cardiovascular outcomes. A prospective study demonstrated that the risk factor-adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for sudden death was 2.16 in LVH patients compared with those without LVH. 9 In addition, a meta-analysis reported that LVH was associated with a 2.16-fold higher risk of non-fatal cardiovascular events and a 2.58-fold higher risk of cardiovascular mortality. 10 Figure 1 Etiology of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and the therapeutic potential of nanoparticle-based treatments (created with BioRender.com). Cardiac hypertrophy arises from diverse stimuli such as pressure overload, neurohumoral activation, and genetic mutations and can progress to heart failure. Traditional treatments offer low cost and an established safety profile but are limited by side effects and inadequate reversal of hypertrophy. Nanoparticle-based treatments enable targeted delivery, stimuli-responsive release, and potential reversal of remodeling, but their high cost and preclinical status remain major translational hurdles. A diagram illustrating the causes and treatments of pathological hypertrophy. The top section lists causes: pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis), volume overload (aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation), neurohumoral factors (angiotensin II, catecholamine), ischemia/hypoxia (myocardial infarction, COPD), storage diseases (glycogen, misfolded protein) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (MYH7, MYBPC3). An arrow points from these causes to pathological hypertrophy, depicted with a heart image, leading to heart failure. Below, two treatment options are shown. Traditional treatments have advantages: low cost, established safety profile and limitations: side effects, limited reversibility. Nanoparticle-based treatments offer advantages: targeted delivery, stimuli-responsive release, potential to reverse hypertrophy and limitations: costly, preclinical stage. A diagram of pathological hypertrophy causes and treatments, showing progression to heart failure. Abbreviations : COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; MYH7, myosin heavy chain 7; MYBPC3, myosin binding protein C3.

Pathological cardiac hypertrophy can be categorized into concentric and eccentric hypertrophy. Concentric hypertrophy typically occurs in response to pressure overload and is characterized by increased ventricular wall thickness and decreased chamber size. Eccentric hypertrophy is more common in response to volume overload and is characterized by dilatation of the ventricular chamber and thinning of the wall. 1 The concentric hypertrophy induced by pressure overload preferentially involves activation of signaling pathways such as mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), calcineurin, and β-arrestin-2, as well as more severe cardiac fibrosis and cardiomyocyte death. 11 , 12 Eccentric hypertrophy due to volume overload preferentially involves activation of signaling pathways, including protein kinase B (Akt) and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), with less fibrosis and apoptosis and more evident angiogenesis. 12 In conclusion, the two phenotypes of cardiac hypertrophy exhibit distinct patterns of preferentially activated pathways, indicating that anti-hypertrophic therapies may target the underlying signaling pathways based on their unique phenotypes.

Traditional treatments for pathological cardiac hypertrophy mainly include β-blockers, calcium channel antagonists, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors, and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. 13 Despite their low cost and established safety profile, these pharmacological therapies often lack cardiac specificity, and the systemic side effects cannot be ignored. Depending on the specific category of the drugs, systemic adverse side effects mainly include hypotension, bradycardia, electrolyte disturbances, and urinary tract infections. 14 , 15 Importantly, current pharmacological therapies mainly relieve hemodynamic overload and neurohormonal activation rather than directly regulating the molecular mechanisms underlying pathological cardiac hypertrophy. As a result, their ability to reverse established pathological cardiac remodeling remains limited. Moreover, the small-molecule drugs also exhibit limited intrinsic cardiac specificity. 16 The cellular uptake occurs predominantly via passive diffusion across biological membranes in a non-selective manner. Consequently, cardiac distribution is largely governed by regional perfusion rather than active uptake by cardiomyocytes. Furthermore, cardiac delivery of conventional pharmaceuticals is impeded by various pharmacokinetic hurdles, including hepatic first-pass metabolism following oral administration and fast systemic clearance caused by short plasma half-lives, consequently limiting local bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. 17 Moreover, surgical and device therapies including aortic valve replacement surgery 18 , 19 and left ventricular assist device therapy 20 , 21 are often used to correct hemodynamic abnormalities and relieve cardiac hypertrophy. However, they are only applicable to patients with specific indications and have difficulty intervening in pathological cardiac hypertrophy at the molecular level. Hence, the development of new treatments for cardiac hypertrophy is an urgent issue.

Nanoparticle-based therapies have recently emerged as a novel therapeutic method for cardiac hypertrophy. Many therapeutic agents, such as small molecule medications, 22 nucleic acids, 23 proteins, 24 and peptides, 25 can be delivered by nanoparticles. In addition, by achieving cardiac targeting and exhibiting controlled release in diseased regions, nanoparticles may enhance drug accumulation while reducing systemic side effects. Figure 1 illustrates the principal etiologies of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and compares traditional treatments with nanoparticle-based treatments. It highlights the key advantages of nanoparticle-based treatments, including targeted drug delivery, stimuli-responsive release, and the potential to reverse cardiac hypertrophy.

In addition to enhancing the efficiency of targeted drug delivery, the nanoparticle-based delivery systems can also overcome the limitations of free drugs by controlling the drug release behaviors and optimizing the drug exposure characteristics. 26 The free drugs generally lack the protection and drug release regulation mechanisms, and many therapeutic agents have a limited systemic half-life due to the rapid distribution, metabolism, and clearance. 27 Therefore, the plasma drug concentrations usually peak shortly after administration and subsequently decrease, which makes it difficult to maintain the therapeutic concentrations over time and increases the risk of adverse effects associated with peak drug concentrations. 28 Conversely, nanoparticle-based delivery systems can protect therapeutic agents through drug encapsulation, structural engineering, and surface modification strategies, thus enabling controlled drug release. 29 As conceptually illustrated in Figure 2 , under ideal design conditions, nanoparticle-based systems can transform the rapid release profile of free drugs to a slower and sustained release profile. 29 Thus, the plasma concentration-time profile can be theoretically shifted from the sharp peak and rapid decline observed with free drugs to a more stable exposure pattern with reduced peak concentrations, slow elimination, and prolonged maintenance within the therapeutic window. 30 This modulation not only reduces the risk of toxicity associated with peak concentrations but also enables sustained drug exposure within the therapeutic range, thereby improving therapeutic efficacy and enhancing the overall safety profile. Figure 2 Theoretical schematic of nanoparticle-based controlled drug release and its potential impact on therapeutic efficacy and safety (created with BioRender.com). This is an idealized conceptual model of controlled drug release using nanoparticles. Compared with free drugs, which show rapid release and a sharp peak in plasma drug concentration followed by rapid decline, nanoparticle-based delivery systems can offer a slower and more sustained drug release profile under optimized design conditions. Hence, the plasma concentration-time profile is characterized by lower peak drug concentrations, prolonged maintenance within the therapeutic window, and a more gradual decline in drug concentration. Controlled drug release from nanoparticles has the potential to improve therapeutic efficacy and the overall safety profile by minimizing burst release and peak concentration-associated toxicity while maintaining sustained therapeutic drug exposure. A line graph showing cumulative drug release over time for free drug and nanoparticle-based delivery. The free drug shows rapid release reaching 100 percent quickly, while nanoparticle-based delivery shows a slower, sustained release. Another graph depicts drug concentration in plasma over time. The free drug shows a sharp peak exceeding the toxicity threshold, followed by a rapid decline. Nanoparticle-based delivery maintains concentration within the therapeutic window, showing a gradual decline. Icons illustrate free drug characteristics: burst release, shorter circulation time, higher toxicity risk. Nanoparticles show controlled release, prolonged circulation, improved safety profile. Two graphs compare free drug and nanoparticle-based delivery in drug release and plasma concentration over time.

Nonetheless, the nanoparticle-based delivery system is still facing significant challenges in the treatment of pathological cardiac hypertrophy. Firstly, the long-term biosafety of nanoparticles remains unclear, largely because most nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies are still at the preclinical stage and lack sufficient long-term clinical safety data. Their potential toxicity and long-term accumulation are particularly concerning. 31 , 32 Secondly, hypertrophic myocardium lacks the typical enhanced permeability and retention effects, 33 , 34 as well as the formation of a protein corona, 35 limiting the efficient accumulation of nanoparticles in the cardiac tissue. Thirdly, the large-scale production of nanoparticles is limited by significant batch-to-batch variations, 36 complex and costly preparation processes, 37 and the absence of quality control standards. In addition, the administration route of nanoparticles is mainly intravenous injection. Long-term and repeated administration may reduce patient compliance. Alternative routes such as oral administration and inhalation still need to be further verified.

Despite the existence of multiple publications addressing the molecular mechanisms of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and the development of nanoparticle-based delivery systems, a comprehensive summary that integrates both aspects remains rather scarce. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in nanoparticle-based delivery systems, with a particular focus on material platforms, targeting strategies, stimuli-responsive drug release, and preclinical applications.

## The Molecular and Cellular Mechanisms of Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy

As a crucial pathological process underlying various cardiovascular disorders, pathological cardiac hypertrophy is driven by highly complex molecular and cellular mechanisms. 1 Figure 3 illustrates the key pathological mechanisms that contribute to cardiac hypertrophy, including fetal gene reactivation, 38 , 39 activation of hypertrophic signal transduction pathways, 2 metabolic remodeling, 40 inflammatory responses, 41 , 42 and extracellular matrix remodeling. 43 Moreover, nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies were also described in Figure 3 , including gene and epigenetic nanotherapy, anti-oxidative nanotherapy, anti-inflammatory nanotherapy, and anti-fibrotic nanotherapy. By precisely intervening in specific pathological processes, nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies offer the potential to alleviate pathological cardiac hypertrophy at the molecular level, providing new strategies and directions for the treatment of pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 25 , 44 , 45 Figure 3 Key mechanisms of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies (created with BioRender.com). Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is regulated by multiple mechanisms, including transcription and epigenetic regulation, signal transduction, metabolic remodeling, inflammation, and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Additionally, nanoparticle-based therapies mainly include gene and epigenetic nanotherapy, anti-oxidative nanotherapy, anti-inflammatory nanotherapy, and anti-fibrotic nanotherapy. Horizontal arrows indicate cellular transitions. Upward and downward arrows indicate increased and decreased levels of the corresponding molecules, respectively. Cross symbols denote inhibition of pathological processes. Bidirectional arrows indicate crosstalk and reciprocal interactions among these pathological mechanisms. The diagram illustrates pathological cardiac remodeling and nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies. Central to the image is ′Pathological cardiac remodeling′. Surrounding it are sections: ′Transcription and epigenetic regulation′ with ′Fetal gene reactivation′; ′Signal transduction′ with ′NFAT′, ′MAPK′, ′PI3K/AKT/mTORC1′, ′TGF-beta1/SMAD′; ′Metabolic remodeling′ showing ′Mitochondrial dysfunction′, ′FAO′, ′Glycolysis′; ′Inflammation′ with ′IL-6′, ′IL-1beta′, ′TNF-alpha′; ′ECM remodeling′ with ′Fibroblasts′, ′Collagen I/III′. Anti-fibrotic nanotherapy shows ′Quiescent fibroblasts′ to ′Activated fibroblasts′. Anti-inflammatory nanotherapy shows ′M1 macrophages′ to ′M2 macrophages′, ′TNF-alpha′, ′IL-1beta′, ′IL-6′. Anti-oxidative nanotherapy includes ′ROS scavenging′, ′Mitochondrial repair′. Gene and epigenetic nanotherapy lists ′plasmid DNA′, ′miRNA′, ′siRNA′. Arrows indicate processes and interactions. Diagram of pathological cardiac remodeling and nanoparticle therapies. Abbreviations : ECM, extracellular matrix; NFAT, nuclear factor of activated T cells; MAPK, mitogen-activated protein kinase; PI3K/AKT/mTORC1: phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1; TGF-β1/SMAD: transforming growth factor-beta 1/suppressor of mothers against decapentaplegic; ROS, reactive oxygen species; FAO, fatty acid oxidation; IL-1β, interleukin-1 beta; IL-6, interleukin-6; TNF-α, tumor necrosis factor-alpha.

### Transcription and Epigenetic Regulation

Transcription and epigenetic regulation contribute to the gene expression alterations in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. Among them, one of the most typical alterations is fetal gene reactivation, including Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP), Brain Natriuretic Peptide (BNP), and Beta-Myosin Heavy Chain (β-MHC). 38 , 39 Nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) is recognized as a significant transcription factor in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 46 Calcium signal-dependent calcineurin induces the dephosphorylation of NFAT, promoting its translocation into the nucleus and triggering the transcription of downstream target genes, including hypertrophy-related genes and fetal genes. 47 , 48 Given its central role in pathological hypertrophy and its relatively well-characterized regulatory mechanism, the NFAT pathway represents an attractive candidate for targeted therapeutic intervention. Additionally, myocyte enhancer factor 2 (MEF2) functions as a central node in multiple signaling pathway networks, and MEF2 promotes the transcription of hypertrophy-associated genes by synergy with NFAT and GATA4. 49 MEF2 acetylation is essential for the activation of hypertrophy-related gene expression, while class IIa histone deacetylases (HDACs) suppress MEF2 activity. 50 Blocking MEF2 acetylation is a highly promising target for nanoparticle-based therapies in reversing cardiac hypertrophy. 50 Another essential transcription factor, GATA binding protein 4 (GATA4), is highly expressed in cardiomyocytes. Accumulating evidence indicates that GATA4 is indispensable in the reactivation of fetal genes in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 51 , 52 However, GATA4 also contributes to the survival of cardiomyocytes and the maintenance of normal cardiac function. 53 Inhibition of GATA4 may cause potential safety challenges. In contrast to the aforementioned pro-hypertrophic transcription factors (NFAT, MEF2, and GATA4), forkhead box protein O1 (FOXO1) exerts context-dependent effects on hypertrophic remodeling by regulating stress adaptation and metabolic homeostasis. Moderate FOXO1 activity generally exerts anti-hypertrophic effects, while sustained FOXO1 activation may promote cardiac hypertrophy. 54 Therefore, therapeutic modulation of FOXO1 may require precise control of its activation intensity and duration rather than complete inhibition. Collectively, NFAT- and MEF2-associated networks may represent promising targets for nanoparticle-based therapies, whereas GATA4 and FOXO1 may require more selective and spatiotemporally controlled delivery to enhance efficacy and reduce off-target effects.

Alongside transcription factor-mediated regulation, the role of epigenetic regulation cannot be overlooked. In pathological cardiac hypertrophy, histone modifications such as acetylation, methylation, lactylation, and ubiquitination are involved in regulating hypertrophy-related gene expression. 55–58 Among these modifications, histone acetylation has drawn particular interest owing to its recognition by epigenetic reader proteins, such as bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4), which governs enhancer activity and drives hypertrophic gene transcription. 59 For instance, the BRD4 inhibitor JQ1 has shown anti-hypertrophic effects in preclinical models, providing a rationale for the development of BRD4-targeted nanoparticle-based strategies. 22 Moreover, DNA methylation has been extensively investigated for its role in regulating hypertrophy-related gene expression and contributing to the progression of cardiac hypertrophy. 60 , 61 However, therapeutic modulation of DNA methylation is still challenging, because DNA methylation patterns influence broad genomic programs beyond hypertrophy-associated pathways. 62 Therefore, precise and disease-specific control of DNA methylation is a major challenge for nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, non-coding RNA is an important post-transcriptional and epigenetic regulatory factor in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 63 Among them, microRNAs (miRNAs) mainly bind with the 3’ non-translated region of target mRNAs, inhibiting the translation or promoting the degradation of mRNA, thereby regulating the expression of genes related to hypertrophy. 64 , 65 Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) act as miRNA sponges through the competitive endogenous RNA (ceRNA) mechanism, regulating the expression of downstream genes. 66 Due to their ability to precisely regulate disease-associated gene networks through specific molecular interactions, miRNAs and lncRNAs provide promising potential for nanoparticle-based therapies. 67

Nanoparticle-based therapies have been employed to modulate the lncRNA/miRNA regulatory network and have demonstrated therapeutic effects in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. For example, neutrophil membrane-coated mesoporous silica nanoparticles have been applied to deliver siRNA of lncRNA AAB, a known sponge of miR-30b-5p. In a rat model of cardiac hypertrophy, this nanoparticle was given via intravenous injection at a dose of 50 nM siRNA per rat, once every two days over a four-week treatment period. As a result, miR-30b-5p activity was restored, which suppressed ferroptosis in cardiac microvascular endothelial cells and ultimately alleviated the hypertrophic phenotype. 67 Furthermore, the above nanoparticles integrate precise targeting, excellent biocompatibility, and biodegradability, thereby providing an effective and safe platform for therapeutic delivery. 67

### Signal Transduction

A number of signal transduction pathways contribute to pathological cardiac hypertrophy, with the NFAT, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) pathway, and MAPK pathways being regarded as the major signaling pathways. 13 , 68 Persistent pathological stimulation results in a prolonged elevation of intracellular calcium concentrations in cardiomyocytes, consequently activating calcineurin. Activated calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT, facilitating its translocation into the nucleus and directly promoting the reactivation of hypertrophy-related genes and fetal genes. 47 , 48 The NFAT pathway connects pathological signaling to hypertrophic gene transcription and has well-characterized regulatory mechanisms, which makes it a promising target for nanoparticle-based interventions. Additionally, the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) pathway is another central regulator of pathological cardiac hypertrophy. Under pathological stress, PI3K activation results in phosphorylation and activation of AKT, which therefore activates mTORC1 signaling. Activated mTORC1 subsequently phosphorylates downstream effectors, including ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1), which enhances protein synthesis and promotes cardiomyocyte growth, ultimately leading to pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 69 , 70 The PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway is a direct regulator of cardiomyocyte growth and a potential therapeutic target. However, its broad involvement in systemic physiological growth and metabolism across multiple tissues poses a challenge to the design of selective and spatiotemporally controlled delivery strategies of nanoparticles for therapeutic efficacy with minimal off-target effect. 71 Moreover, the MAPK pathway mainly consists of three main pathways, including extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), p38, and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK). 72 The MAPK signaling system facilitates cardiac hypertrophy by regulating cardiomyocyte proliferation, apoptosis, and the expression of hypertrophic genes. 73 However, its involvement in diverse physiological and pathological processes may complicate selective therapeutic targeting and raise concerns about pathway-wide inhibition. 74

### Metabolic Remodeling and Mitochondrial Dysfunction

Metabolic remodeling is a hallmark of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and an important basis for the decline of cardiac function. 1 Metabolic remodeling in pathological cardiac hypertrophy is defined by alterations in substrate use patterns. The capacity for oxidation of the fatty acids is reduced, whereas the extent of glycolysis is relatively increased. 75 This switch of metabolism is similar to the cardiac fetal metabolic phenotype and is called fetal-type metabolism. 76 Glycolysis is less efficient in energy transformation than fatty acid oxidation, which may contribute to the imbalance of energy supply and demand. 40

Mitochondrial dysfunction is another characteristic of metabolic remodeling. Chronic pathological stimulation impairs the efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production by dysregulation of mitochondrial autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis, 77 and imbalance in mitochondrial fusion and fission. 78 Metabolic remodeling and mitochondrial dysfunction synergistically contribute to excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). 79 Excessive ROS not only aggravates mitochondrial injury but also acts as signaling molecules to activate hypertrophic-related signaling pathways, thus forming a vicious cycle to accelerate pathological cardiac remodeling. 80

To break this vicious cycle, nanoparticle-based antioxidant delivery has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. For example, a ROS-responsive nanoparticle encapsulated with the death receptor 5 fusion protein (sDR5-Fc) was given intravenously in rats (200 μL/dose, twice weekly for 14 days, specific drug loading not provided). This approach permitted sDR5-Fc release and ROS scavenging at the site of myocardial infarction, thereby lowering infarct size, attenuating fibrosis, and inhibiting cardiac hypertrophy. 81

### Inflammation

Previous studies showed that the expression levels of pro-inflammatory factors were increased in hypertrophic cardiac tissue, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). 41 , 42 Pro-inflammatory factors are generated not just by immune cells but also by cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts. 82 These cytokines increase the expression of genes associated with cardiac hypertrophy directly via the activation of signaling pathways such as nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) and MAPK. 83 , 84 Particularly, macrophages are key mediators in cardiac remodeling, 85 and they secrete pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic mediators, thereby linking cardiac inflammation to hypertrophic remodeling. 86 , 87 Collectively, inflammatory factors work in synergy with immune cells to accelerate the progression of pathological cardiac hypertrophy.

### Extracellular Matrix Remodeling and Fibrosis

Continuous pathogenic stimulation causes excessive deposition and cross-linking of collagen, particularly type I and type III collagen, 88 , 89 which enhances cardiac stiffness, diminishes cardiac compliance, and promotes diastolic dysfunction. 90 Cardiac fibroblasts are the primary effector cells in extracellular matrix remodeling. Under pathological stimulation, resting fibroblasts activate and differentiate into α-smooth muscle actin-expressing myofibroblasts, which synthesize and secrete large amounts of ECM proteins, continuously driving myocardial fibrosis and maladaptive remodeling. 43 The above pathological process is principally regulated by the transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1)/suppressor of mothers against decapentaplegic (Smad) signaling pathway. The expression level of TGF-β1 is proven to be upregulated in the hypertrophic myocardium. Upon ligand binding, TGF-β receptors phosphorylate and activate Smad2/3, which form a complex with Smad4 and translocate to the nucleus. This leads to increased transcription of genes associated with cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. 91 In addition to excessive ECM production, an imbalance between matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs) further disrupts ECM homeostasis, contributing to abnormal matrix turnover and structural disorganization. 92

Nanoparticle‑mediated delivery of antifibrotic agents has demonstrated considerable potential in reducing ECM remodeling and fibrosis. For instance, engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) loaded with the TGF‑β1 receptor inhibitor GW788388 were administered via tail vein injection at 100 μg of EVs every 3 days for a total of four doses in an isoproterenol‑induced mouse model of cardiac fibrosis. This system effectively suppressed fibroblast activation and attenuated collagen deposition. 93

## Design Strategies of Nanoparticles in Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy

### Biological Barriers of Nanoparticle Delivery in Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy

The therapeutic efficacy of nanoparticle-based therapies for pathological cardiac hypertrophy depends not only on the biological activity of the therapeutic agents but also on the efficiency of their delivery to the myocardium. After systemic administration, the nanoparticles undergo a series of processes that impact the delivery efficiency, including impaired vascular extravasation, 44 the formation of protein corona, 35 and in vivo clearance 30 ( Figure 4A ). These factors influence the circulation time and the efficiency of cardiac accumulation of the nanoparticles. A major obstacle to nanoparticle accumulation in hypertrophic myocardium is the lack of tumor-like vascular remodeling. Cardiac hypertrophy is characterized by an imbalance between angiogenesis and cardiomyocyte proliferation, 94 resulting in microvascular rarefaction and endothelial dysfunction. 95 , 96 As opposed to tumors, which are characterized by aberrant angiogenesis, defective vascular architecture, and impaired lymphatic drainage that contribute to the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, 97 pathological cardiac hypertrophy generally lacks such tumor-like remodeling. Therefore, the typical EPR effect is unlikely to be observed in cardiac hypertrophy, 98 which may lead to impaired vascular extravasation. However, the absence of a typical EPR effect does not imply an unchanged vascular permeability. Endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory activation, and microvascular remodeling in pathological cardiac hypertrophy also contribute to altered vascular permeability. 99 , 100 However, these permeability changes are usually less pronounced and less predictable than the classical tumor-associated EPR effect, resulting in insufficient accumulation of nanoparticles. 101 Additionally, the fast blood flow, dense extracellular matrix, and continuous mechanical contraction of the heart are all obstacles to the accumulation and retention of nanoparticles. 102

In addition, protein corona formation may influence the cardiac targeting efficiency of nanoparticles. 35 Nanoparticles adsorb plasma proteins in the circulation, forming a protein corona composed of a stable hard corona and a dynamic soft corona, which subsequently influences their cellular recognition, endocytic pathways, and biodistribution in vivo. 103 The protein corona can partially shield the targeting ligands on the nanoparticle surface, thus decreasing their accessibility to cell membrane receptors and attenuating specific cellular uptake. 104 Furthermore, variations in nanoparticle physicochemical properties may lead to differences in the abundance of adsorbed proteins and protein corona composition, thereby influencing downstream biological effects. 105 For instance, the protein corona formed by lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) is abundant in apolipoprotein E, which facilitates receptor-mediated uptake through lipoprotein receptors, particularly in the liver. 106 Importantly, by modifying the lipid composition of LNPs, the composition of the protein corona can be altered, hence affecting its selectivity for particular organs, 107 which may provide a potential strategy for improving cardiac targeting. Without the modification of protein repulsion coating, the surface chemical properties of inorganic nanoparticles make them more likely to adsorb immunoglobulins, complement, and fibrinogen. 108 These proteins can accelerate the immune clearance of nanoparticles through complement activation and Fc receptor-mediated phagocytosis, 109 thereby limiting targeted delivery efficiency. Moreover, biomimetic nanoparticles may inhibit non-specific protein adsorption, reduce the shielding effect of the protein corona on surface-targeting ligands, and preserve the recognition capability of these ligands toward target cell receptors. 110 Therefore, rational engineering of nanoparticle properties and modulation of protein corona formation may improve the efficiency of cardiac targeting delivery.

Systemic clearance is a critical factor influencing the delivery efficacy of nanoparticles. Premature clearance may reduce circulation time and limit nanoparticle accumulation in the myocardium. 30 After systemic administration, nanoparticles are mainly cleared from the blood circulation by the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS), particularly by Kupffer cells in the liver and macrophages in the spleen, which recognize opsonins, such as immunoglobulins and complement proteins adsorbed on the surface of the nanoparticles, and remove them through phagocytosis. 111 It is worth noting that liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) also play a significant role in the hepatic clearance of nanoparticles. The fenestrations of LSECs have a size-selective filtering function, limiting the trans-sinusoidal passage of nanoparticles larger than approximately 100 nm. The retained particles are subsequently cleared through endocytosis mediated by scavenger receptors, including Stabilin-1, Stabilin-2, and mannose receptors. 112 , 113 Furthermore, glomerular filtration represents an additional size-dependent clearance pathway, as nanoparticles with hydrodynamic diameters below approximately 5.5 nm can traverse the glomerular filtration barrier and subsequently undergo urinary excretion. 114 Overall, The clearance process of nanoparticles is mainly determined by their physicochemical properties, including particle size, surface charges, and surface chemical characteristics. 30 Generally speaking, nanoparticles with larger particle size and positively charged surfaces are more likely to adsorb plasma proteins and undergo opsonization, thereby facilitating MPS-mediated recognition and phagocytic clearance. 115 In contrast, neutral, hydrophilic, or protein-adsorption-resistant surface modifications can reduce the formation of non-specific protein corona, minimize immune system recognition, and prolong circulation time. 116 , 117 Premature clearance reduces circulation time and limits cardiac accumulation, whereas insufficient clearance of nanoparticles may lead to prolonged tissue accumulation and potential toxicity. Therefore, balancing prolonged systemic circulation with safe and efficient clearance represents a key challenge for advancing nanoparticle-based therapies toward clinical translation.

To overcome these barriers, nanoparticle-based systems have been designed using several complementary strategies, including material platform selection, targeted functionalization, and stimuli-responsive release strategies, which will be discussed in the following sections. Figure 4 showed the design strategies of nanoparticles in pathological cardiac hypertrophy, including the classifications of nanoparticle platforms, targeting strategies, and stimuli-responsive release strategies.

Based on the material composition and characteristics, nanoparticles for the treatment of pathological cardiac hypertrophy can be broadly divided into inorganic nanoparticles, organic nanoparticles, and biomimetic nanoparticles 44 , 45 , 118 ( Figure 4B ).
