### SPNs Loaded with Functional Materials (Without Traditional Drugs)

Beyond passive ROS scavenging, engineered nanozymes can function as “messengers” that actively reprogram the inflammatory microenvironment. Jia et al 97 designed a messenger nanozyme system that not only catalytically eliminates ROS but also modulates macrophage polarization and suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokine cascades, thereby disrupting the self-sustaining loop of oxidative stress and inflammation in RA. This paradigm illustrates how functional nanomaterials can serve as therapeutic entities in their own right, independent of traditional drug payloads.

Simón-Vázquez et al 98 reported the encapsulation of palmitate dexamethasone (DXP) into PLGA-PEG nanoparticles (DXP-NPs). The lipophilic nature of DXP facilitates its incorporation into the hydrophobic core of PLGA-PEG, achieving a drug loading capacity of 7.5%. Through the action of in vivo enzymes, DXP is gradually released and hydrolyzed into dexamethasone (DXM). DXM exerts its anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting transcription factors such as NF-κB and AP-1, thereby blocking the MAPK signaling pathway and reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. The targeted delivery via DXP-NPs enhances the local concentration of DXM at inflammatory sites, improving anti-inflammatory efficacy. This approach prolongs the plasma half-life of DXM and reduces its distribution in non-target organs. In both ex vivo and in vivo experiments, DXP-NPs demonstrated superior therapeutic effects compared to free dexamethasone sodium phosphate (DSP), optimizing the pharmacokinetic profile and therapeutic outcome of the drug. In addition to prodrug modification strategies, optimizing the internal structure of nanocarriers is also an important research direction.

Chlorogenic acid (CA), despite its known therapeutic potential in RA—mediated by inhibiting NF-κB and activating Nrf-2 pathways—it suffers from poor stability, a short half-life, and rapid in vivo clearance; meanwhile, conventional liposomal drug delivery systems suffer from inherent drawbacks such as prone to in vivo drug leakage, insufficient targeting capability, and poor stability. Therefore, Lin et al developed a novel alginate nanogel-embedded liposome system (LSHNPs) to address critical challenges in RA treatment. 99 This nanosystem features a distinctive internal structural design: a Ca 2 ⁺-crosslinked three-dimensional alginate network was incorporated into the internal aqueous phase of liposomes. Significantly, this modification enhanced particle rigidity by 2.6-fold without compromising the liposome’s surface properties (eg, PEGylation), thereby endowing LSHNPs with superior resistance to serum protein adsorption, enhanced tolerance to blood flow shear stress, and reduced drug leakage. Their results demonstrated that LSHNPs exhibited exceptional targeting ability and therapeutic efficacy in the arthritic microenvironment. Their optimized rigidity significantly promoted active endocytosis by inflammatory macrophages, and by regulating protein corona composition—specifically increasing apolipoprotein E (ApoE)/albumin adsorption while decreasing fibrinogen adsorption—LSHNPs extended in vivo blood circulation time by 2-fold. Upon intracellular entry, the internal gel network enabled sustained release of CA, which subsequently inhibited ROS production and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor-α [TNF-α], interleukin-6 [IL-6]) via the NF-κB/Nrf-2 pathway. This mechanism effectively reversed macrophage M1 polarization and alleviated inflammatory infiltration. In a rat model of RA, LSHNPs completely suppressed joint swelling and significantly improved histopathological scores, thereby demonstrating excellent therapeutic efficacy.

Therapeutic specificity can be enhanced through synergistic designs combining pH responsiveness with targeted modifications. A representative example is folate-modified carboxymethyl chitosan nanopolymers (SCNP), which also utilize pH-sensitive drug release within the acidic inflammatory microenvironment. 100 This synergistically inhibits the NF-κB/NLRP3 pathway, effectively modulating the inflammatory microenvironment and alleviating RA symptoms. To address the complex inflammatory microenvironment of RA, another targeted nanoplatform (MPMAF) was developed. This platform utilizes folate (FA) to target folate receptors on M1 macrophages, enabling specific drug accumulation at inflammatory sites. This platform demonstrated triple therapeutic effects: it releases loaded drugs such as MTX to suppress pro-inflammatory cytokine production (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and promotes macrophage polarization from M1 to M2 type, thereby reducing inflammatory infiltration. Simultaneously, it leverages the inherent antioxidant properties of the carrier material (PDA) to directly scavenge excess ROS at the lesion site (eg, O 2 − , ·OH), mitigating oxidative stress-induced joint damage. Finally, the loaded drugs also directly suppress the expression of key osteoclast differentiation genes (NFATc1, c-Fos), collectively reducing bone erosion.

Building on the concept of MMP-responsive polymer deshielding, a recent study developed MMP-sensitive macrophage-targeted nanoparticles (CoQ10-NPs) comprising an MMP-2/9-cleavable PEG–peptide–phosphatidylethanolamine (PEG-pp-PE) copolymer and phosphatidylserine (PS). 101 When the molar ratio of the polymer to PS was 50:50, the CoQ10 loading was approximately 9.7%. The CoQ10-loaded nanoparticles had a particle size of less than 200 nm and a zeta potential of approximately −40 mV, and exhibited sustained drug release under simulated sedimentation conditions at 37 °C. Under normal physiological conditions, the PEG corona shielded the PS “eat-me” signal, minimizing nonspecific phagocytosis. Upon exposure to MMP-2/9 in the RA synovium, the peptide linker was enzymatically cleaved, leading to PEG deshielding and PS exposure, which triggered selective uptake by macrophages. The cellular uptake in RAW264.7 cells was 3.5-fold higher in the presence of MMPs than in their absence, and more than 13-fold higher than in fibroblasts, underscoring the exquisite macrophage selectivity of this enzyme-responsive design. The CoQ10-loaded NPs significantly inhibited pro-inflammatory cytokine production (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) while enhancing anti-inflammatory IL-10 secretion.

Wang et al developed an inflammatory stimulus‑responsive hyaluronic acid–triglycerol monostearate polymersome (HTDD) for the co‑delivery of 2‑DG (a glycolysis inhibitor) and dexamethasone to treat RA. 102 The polymersomes were assembled from HA (5 kDa) conjugated with TGMS via a pH‑sensitive PBA linker, forming amphiphilic conjugates that self‑assembled into vesicular structures by thin‑film hydration (size ~178.6 nm, zeta potential –16.8 mV). Hydrophilic 2‑DG was encapsulated in the aqueous core, while hydrophobic Dex was embedded in the bilayer membrane, with encapsulation efficiencies of 12.3% and 72.5%, respectively. The system acts through a triple mechanism: ① 2‑DG inhibits glycolysis (downregulating 11 glycolytic genes including Hk3 and Eno1), cutting off the energy supply to inflammatory cells; ② Dex suppresses the NF‑κB pathway and counteracts 2‑DG‑induced ROS elevation, synergistically breaking the “inflammation–glycolysis” positive feedback loop; ③ HA mediates CD44‑targeted delivery to multiple inflammatory cell types, while acidic pH and overexpressed MMPs trigger polymersome disassembly and synchronous drug release (cumulative release increased from <40% at pH 7.4 to >70% at pH 5.5 + MMPs over 48 h). Compared with free drug combinations or monotherapies, HTDD significantly prolonged the half‑life and AUC of Dex, achieved ~3‑fold higher drug accumulation in inflamed joints versus normal joints, reduced arthritis scores in the AIA model, decreased CD4⁺ T‑cell and M1 macrophage infiltration, increased Treg proportions, and improved synovial pathology without hepatorenal toxicity. However, the drug loading capacity of 2-DG is only 1.2%, and its hydrophilic drug-loading capacity is severely insufficient, which affects clinical feasibility and the volume of administration. Data on long-term degradation behavior are lacking (only 48 hours in vitro); future efforts should focus on optimizing the structure-function relationship of the material, enhancing its hydrophilic drug-loading capacity, and establishing long-term toxicological evaluations.

## Structure–Property–Function Relationships of Smart Polymer Nanoparticles

The therapeutic efficacy of SPNs in RA is governed not only by their stimulus-responsive functionality but also by fundamental physicochemical parameters—including polymer composition, molecular weight, architecture, degradability, and surface chemistry—that collectively determine targeting efficiency, drug release kinetics, and biological performance. A critical understanding of these structure–property–function relationships is essential for the rational design of next-generation nanomedicines.

### Polymer Composition and Molecular Weight

The chemical identity and molecular weight (MW) of the constituent polymers dictate the hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance, self-assembly behavior, and drug compatibility of SPNs. For instance, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), the most widely used synthetic polyester in RA nanomedicine, exhibits degradation rates that scale inversely with lactide content and MW: PLGA 50:50 degrades within 1–2 months, whereas 85:15 formulations persist for 5–6 months. 103 This tunability allows precise matching of release profiles to disease chronology. Higher-MW PLGA chains entangle more extensively, reducing initial burst release and extending the duration of therapeutic exposure. 104 Conversely, low-MW chitosan (eg, <50 kDa) enhances mucoadhesion and transcytosis across inflamed synovial membranes but may compromise structural integrity during systemic transit. The optimal MW thus represents a trade-off between circulation stability and tissue penetration.

### Polymer Architecture: Dendrimers versus Hyperbranched Polymers

The branching architecture of polymers profoundly influences drug payload capacity, release kinetics, and manufacturing scalability. Dendrimers, with their perfectly branched, monodisperse structures, offer precisely defined multivalency and high surface functional group density, enabling conjugation of multiple targeting ligands and drug molecules per particle. 105 However, their stepwise synthesis is labor-intensive and costly. Hyperbranched polymers (HBPs), by contrast, are synthesized in a single-pot reaction and possess imperfect branching with greater conformational flexibility. 106 Comparative studies using methylprednisolone as a model drug revealed that HBPs achieved higher drug payloads and faster intracellular release due to reduced steric crowding and enhanced lysosomal enzyme accessibility. 107 Theoretically, HBP micelles also exhibit lower critical micelle concentrations and superior stability under dilution compared to dendrimer analogs, making them attractive for in vivo applications. For RA therapy, this architectural distinction is clinically relevant: dendrimers excel in applications requiring precise ligand spacing (eg, multivalent folate targeting), whereas HBPs are preferable for high-loading, cost-sensitive formulations.

### Degradability and Drug Release Kinetics

Biodegradability is a double-edged sword in RA nanomedicine. While rapid degradation ensures clearance and minimizes foreign-body reactions, premature disassembly before reaching the synovium undermines therapeutic efficacy. PLGA degrades via bulk or surface hydrolysis of ester bonds, producing lactic and glycolic acids that are metabolized through the Krebs cycle; however, the acidic microenvironment generated during degradation can paradoxically exacerbate local inflammation if buffering strategies are not implemented. Natural polymers such as chitosan and hyaluronic acid degrade enzymatically (eg, via lysozyme or hyaluronidase), offering release profiles that are more closely coupled to the inflammatory milieu. 108 The incorporation of stimuli-cleavable linkers—such as disulfide bonds for GSH-responsive release or MMP-cleavable peptides for enzyme-triggered activation—further decouples systemic stability from site-specific payload liberation, as detailed in subsequent sections.

### Surface Chemistry and the Protein Corona

Upon intravenous administration, SPNs instantaneously adsorb plasma proteins to form a “protein corona” that constitutes the true biological identity of the particle. The composition of this corona—enriched in opsonins (eg, immunoglobulins, complement factors) versus dysopsonins (eg, albumin, apolipoproteins)—determines macrophage recognition, circulation half-life, and biodistribution. 109 Surface PEGylation remains the gold standard for minimizing protein fouling and extending circulation. However, the stealth effect is not binary but depends critically on PEG grafting density and chain conformation. At low densities, PEG adopts a “mushroom” conformation (Flory radius R<sub> ≥ inter-graft distance D), providing limited steric protection. Only when PEG transitions to a “brush” conformation (R<sub>/D > 1) or, optimally, a “dense brush” regime (L > 2R<sub>, where L is the layer thickness) does effective suppression of macrophage uptake and protein adsorption occur. 110 , 111

### Nanoparticle Size, Shape, and Charge

These geometric and electrostatic parameters collectively govern vascular extravasation, tissue penetration, and cellular internalization. Particles <50 nm undergo rapid renal filtration, whereas those >200 nm are preferentially sequestered by hepatic Kupffer cells; the optimal size window for RA targeting via the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect and subsequent macrophage uptake lies between 100–200 nm. 112 Shape exerts equally profound effects: rod-like or filamentous particles exhibit prolonged circulation and reduced macrophage internalization compared to spherical counterparts of equivalent volume, owing to impaired recognition by actin-driven phagocytosis machinery. 113 Surface charge modulates both protein corona composition and direct electrostatic interactions with cell membranes. Cationic nanoparticles (ζ-potential > +30 mV) adsorb negatively charged plasma proteins (eg, albumin) and exhibit enhanced uptake by negatively charged macrophage membranes but suffer from rapid opsonization and hemolytic toxicity. Anionic or near-neutral surfaces (ζ ~ −10 to +10 mV) minimize nonspecific interactions while preserving colloidal stability. 114

### Nanoparticle Rigidity and Mechanical Properties

An emerging yet critical parameter is nanoparticle elasticity, which influences protein corona formation, cellular uptake mechanisms, and circulation lifetime. Soft, deformable nanoparticles (eg, conventional liposomes) can traverse biological hydrogels and tight endothelial junctions more readily but are prone to disassembly under hemodynamic shear stress. Rigid nanoparticles, conversely, resist deformation and maintain structural integrity but may be recognized as “foreign bodies” by mechanosensitive phagocytic receptors. 115 In the context of RA, Lin et al 99 engineered alginate nanogel-embedded liposomes (LSHNPs) in which internal Ca 2 ⁺-crosslinked alginate networks increased particle rigidity by 2.6-fold without altering surface PEGylation. This optimized rigidity promoted active endocytosis by inflammatory macrophages, altered protein corona composition (increasing ApoE/albumin adsorption while decreasing fibrinogen), and extended blood circulation time by 2-fold—directly translating to enhanced arthritic joint accumulation and therapeutic efficacy. These findings underscore that mechanical properties must be co-optimized with chemical functionality in SPN design.

## Comparison of Nanomedicine for RA

### Intra-SPN Comparative Analysis

Among the systems reviewed, Chen et al 60 and Kumar et al 73 adopted single-drug strategies (MTX), achieving targeted therapy through GSH- or pH-triggered release. In contrast, Negi et al 75 designed a dual-drug co-delivery system comprising MTX-LPHNPs and ACE-NLCs, acting synergistically via intravenous and transdermal routes. The theoretical advantage of dual-drug strategies lies in simultaneous blockade of distinct pathological pathways (MTX inhibits immune cell proliferation; ACE suppresses COX-2/PGE 2 ), yielding synergistic anti-inflammatory effects. However, this comes at the cost of significantly increased formulation complexity—two distinct nanocarriers must be separately optimized for particle size, release kinetics, and stability, with risks of drug–drug interactions. Single-drug systems offer streamlined synthetic routes and superior batch-to-batch consistency but may be insufficient to address the multi-pathway complexity of RA. Most systems reviewed herein rely on passive accumulation via the EPR effect (eg, Chen et al)[ 60 ] However, MPS clearance eliminates 40–50% of nanoparticles within hours. Active targeting strategies substantially improve upon this limitation: Kumar et al 73 (folate-modified MFGCN) and Siddiqui et al 92 (FA-LEF-NPs) achieve 3–4-fold improved MTX delivery efficiency via folate–FR-β binding; Xu et al 94 (M-M@I) and Xie et al 81 (MACP siTNF-α NPs) employ macrophage membrane coating, leveraging native surface receptors (eg, LFA-1, CXCR2, SR-B1) for inflammatory homing with targeting efficiencies rivaling or exceeding chemical ligand modification. Nevertheless, active targeting introduces risks of immunogenicity and manufacturing complexity.

### SPNs versus Other Nanocarriers

Different types of nanocarriers possess distinct advantages and disadvantages and exhibit differentiated application prospects in the clinical translation of targeted therapy for RA. Liposomes and solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) represent the most clinically mature nanocarriers, featuring excellent biocompatibility, scalable manufacturing capability, efficient metabolic clearance through natural lipid degradation pathways, and mild inflammatory responses. However, they are commonly plagued by low drug loading capacity, drug leakage during storage, and poor stability in serum environments. Relevant comparative studies have verified that polymer-based delivery systems, in contrast to rapidly releasing lipid formulations, enable sustained and slow drug release, thereby prolonging therapeutic duration and improving joint protection effects. 116 SPNs compensate for many limitations of lipid carriers due to their superior structural integrity, precisely tunable degradation rates, and versatile surface functionalization for multiple modifications. Nevertheless, acidic byproducts such as lactic acid generated during SPN degradation may exacerbate local inflammation without adequate buffering treatment. Compared with SPNs, inorganic nanoparticles including gold, iron oxide, silica, and quantum dots exhibit unique photothermal conversion, magnetic targeting, and multimodal imaging functions that cannot be achieved by pure organic polymer carriers. However, these inorganic materials lack established in vivo biodegradation pathways, tend to accumulate long-term in organs such as the liver and spleen, and present unresolved toxicological risks, severely hindering their clinical translation. 117 , 118 Biomimetic vesicle carriers represented by exosomes and cell membrane-coated nanoparticles inherit natural cellular structures, possessing outstanding biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, and inherent inflammatory homing capability, which enables inflammation-targeted drug delivery without hepatotoxicity. 119 Even so, their large-scale clinical applications are bottlenecked by low isolation yield, high batch-to-batch heterogeneity, imperfect quality control systems, and inherently limited cargo-loading efficiency. Overall, SPNs demonstrate unique application merits attributed to their highly flexible chemical design and programmable stimulus-responsive performance.

## Theranostic Polymer Nanoparticles for Imaging-Guided RA Therapy

Beyond conventional drug delivery, an emerging frontier in RA nanomedicine is the integration of diagnostic imaging with therapeutic intervention—theranostics—to enable real-time monitoring of disease progression, drug distribution, and treatment response. Chen et al 120 pioneered this approach by engineering tocilizumab-conjugated polymer nanoparticles for NIR-II photoacoustic-imaging-guided therapy of RA. These polymeric nanoprobes enabled high-resolution visualization of swollen cartilage and synovial tissue in CIA models, allowing noninvasive tracking of disease development while simultaneously delivering anti-IL-6R therapy. Similarly, Xiao et al developed endogenous melanin nanoparticles (MNPs) conjugated with cyclic RGD peptide (MNP-PEG-RGD) as a photoacoustic imaging (PAI) contrast agent. In RA mouse models, this nanoplatform actively targeted αvβ3 integrins within 1 h post-injection, with signal intensity remarkably increased in arthritic joints—enabling earlier diagnosis than conventional imaging modalities. Critically, the platform permitted dynamic monitoring of etanercept therapeutic efficacy by PAI, with histological validation confirming correlation between imaging signals and disease regression. 121 Gandhi and Shende 122 further advanced this paradigm with anti-CD64 antibody-conjugated PLGA nanoparticles co-loaded with methotrexate and gold nanoparticles, creating a multimodal theranostic system that combines macrophage-targeted chemotherapy with CT imaging capabilities for traceable, targeted RA therapy. These theranostic polymer systems address a critical unmet need in RA management: the ability to noninvasively assess synovial inflammation heterogeneity, verify nanoparticle accumulation at inflamed sites, and adapt therapeutic regimens based on real-time imaging feedback.

## Challenges

Within the field of RA treatment, precision modulation strategies represented by SPNs offer a novel paradigm to overcome the limitations of traditional therapies by targeting pathological pathways through multidimensional approaches ( Table 1 ): At the macrophage level, SPNs leverage precise targeting capabilities to suppress macrophage overactivation, promote their polarization toward the M2 anti-inflammatory phenotype, and eliminate abnormally activated cells. This approach disrupts the macrophage-centric inflammatory network at its source, effectively halting the propagation of inflammation in RA. At the FLS level, SPNs leverage the responsive characteristics of the RA synovial microenvironment to specifically inhibit abnormal FLS proliferation, migration, and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion. This reduces synovial hyperplasia and joint tissue erosion, mitigating the progression of structural damage in RA. At the level of regulating macrophage-fibroblast synergy, SPNs reshape their signaling interactions (eg, by blocking pro-inflammatory cytokine-mediated positive feedback loops), breaking the vicious cycle of “macrophage pro-inflammation → FLS activation.” This approach curbs RA progression by disrupting intercellular collaboration. Finally, at the microenvironmental level, SPNs leverage RA lesion characteristics like acidity and high ROS levels to achieve drug-responsive release. Simultaneously, they modulate inflammatory cytokine levels and clear oxidative stress byproducts, optimizing the local synovial immune microenvironment to create favorable conditions for cellular function recovery. The integration of these four synergistic regulatory approaches constitutes a “multi-targeted, precision-based” therapeutic paradigm for RA. This approach enhances drug concentration at the lesion site while reducing systemic toxicity, thereby effectively counteracting the multifaceted pathological complexity of RA.

Despite their significant potential in basic research and animal studies for RA treatment, their clinical translation remains challenging. There is significant inter-individual heterogeneity among RA patients, encompassing pathophysiology, immune responses, metabolic pathways, and genetic background, which makes it difficult for the same treatment plans to be effective for all individuals. For instance, some patients respond well to conventional DMARDs such as MTX, whereas others show no response. Currently available biomarkers, such as rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-CCP antibodies, lack sufficient sensitivity and specificity for predicting treatment response and stratifying disease subtypes, thereby hindering the achievement of true precision stratification and personalized therapy. 123 Moreover, RA patients often present with multiple comorbidities (eg, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, osteoporosis), which may influence drug selection and dosage adjustment. 124 Meanwhile, SPNs face three core challenges in transitioning from laboratory research to clinical application: manufacturing, clinical safety, and patient acceptance. In production, the challenge lies in achieving large-scale, low-cost standardized manufacturing to ensure consistent nanoparticle size and targeting properties across batches. Regarding safety, while animal studies have yielded promising results, long-term human use requires extended follow-up periods to assess potential issues such as immune rejection or organ accumulation. Patient acceptance presents another concern, as current SPN delivery methods primarily involve intravenous or intra-articular injections. Intravenous administration may cause puncture pain and infection risks, while intra-articular injections require specialized medical personnel and frequent dosing, leading to reduced patient compliance. Although we have outlined the diverse design strategies and underlying mechanisms of SPNs for RA, we should examine the gap between preclinical efficacy and clinical translational potential. This critical discussion unfolds across the following interrelated dimensions: the mechanistic basis of carrier design, comparative performance of competing platforms, biological and manufacturing barriers to translation, and the limitations of current preclinical models. The “smartness” of SPNs—operationalized through stimulus-cleavable linkers and conformation-switchable moieties—confers theoretical precision, yet each responsive modality entails inherent compromises. pH-responsive systems exploit the reliably acidic RA synovium (pH 6.0–6.8), but acidic microenvironments are not pathognomonic to RA, raising concerns about off-target release in tumors or ischemic tissues. ROS-responsive platforms capitalize on the marked oxidative burst in inflamed joints, yet ROS is a ubiquitous secondary messenger in numerous physiological processes, potentially compromising specificity. GSH-responsive disulfide chemistry benefits from dramatic intracellular/extracellular concentration gradients, but inter-patient variability in synovial GSH levels and the risk of premature systemic cleavage remain practical challenges. Enzyme-responsive systems (eg, MMP-2/9-cleavable linkers) offer arguably the highest disease specificity; nevertheless, enzyme activity fluctuates with disease stage and individual patient protease profiles, complicating predictable dosing. 125 Multi-stimuli-responsive platforms have emerged as the most promising strategy to enhance release fidelity, but at the cost of increased synthetic complexity and batch-to-batch variability. 126 These trade-offs underscore that “smartness” is not an absolute attribute but a design parameter that must be optimized against specificity, scalability, and regulatory feasibility. When evaluated against alternative nanomedicine platforms, SPNs occupy a distinctive but not universally superior niche. In a landmark head-to-head comparison, Quan et al 116 demonstrated that polymeric micelles and HPMA copolymer prodrugs, with their sustained-release characteristics, outperformed liposomes in joint protection in AIA rats. Lipid-based carriers generally exhibit milder inflammatory responses and efficient metabolic clearance, yet they suffer from lower drug loading capacity, drug leakage during storage, and limited stability in serum. Inorganic nanoparticles (gold, iron oxide, silica) provide unique imaging and photothermal functionalities, but their clinical translation is severely hampered by long-term biopersistence, potential organ accumulation, and the absence of established biodegradation pathways—concerns that have precluded FDA approval for chronic inflammatory indications. Exosomes and biomimetic vesicles confer exceptional biocompatibility and intrinsic homing capabilities, but isolation yields are low, batch heterogeneity is high, and quality control standards remain immature. Lipid–polymer hybrid nanoparticles (LPHNs) integrate the strengths of both classes, demonstrating 27% higher cellular uptake, 30% lower cytotoxicity, and 34% greater therapeutic efficacy than single-component counterparts. 127 Yet their multi-step synthesis increases manufacturing costs and complicates regulatory approval. The optimal therapeutic strategy, therefore, involves not the supremacy of a single platform but the judicious matching of carrier properties to specific clinical scenarios—acute versus chronic inflammation, monotherapy versus combination therapy, and systemic versus intra-articular administration.

The translational trajectory of SPNs for RA is contingent upon resolving a quartet of interdependent challenges that span from bench synthesis to bedside administration. First, pharmacokinetic behavior is governed by the instantaneous formation of a protein corona upon intravascular entry: hydrophobic surfaces recruit opsonins (IgGs, complement, fibrinogen) that flag particles for rapid RES sequestration in the liver and spleen, whereas PEGylated or hydrophilic surfaces generate a stealth corona enriched in dysopsonins such as ApoA-I, prolonging circulation. Quantitatively, nanoparticles of ~100 nm exhibit an optimal balance, avoiding renal filtration (<6 nm) and splenic trapping (>200 nm), while intermediate elasticity (~10 2 –10 3 kPa) further enhances ApoA-I adsorption and extends half-life. Across diverse compounds, intravenous nanoformulations consistently elevate AUC by a median of ~38-fold and prolong half-life up to 5-fold compared to conventional formulations. 128 Yet, the EPR effect in inflamed joints remains heterogeneous, and 40–50% of intravenously administered particles are cleared by hepatic and splenic macrophages within hours, limiting joint bioavailability.

Second, these pharmacokinetic realities impose stringent demands on manufacturing reproducibility. Batch-to-batch variability in particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), drug encapsulation efficiency, and surface ligand density remains a major hurdle for polymeric nanoparticles, necessitating iterative optimization of solvent removal and lyophilization steps. While microfluidic continuous-flow synthesis offers superior reproducibility and scalability compared with conventional batch methods—achieving coefficient of variation in particle size below 5% at kilogram-per-hour scales 129 —the transition from laboratory (μg–mg) to clinical (100 g/d) and industrial (1 kg/d) production rates requires parallelization, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling, and quality-by-design (QbD) frameworks incorporating process analytical technology (PAT) and real-time release testing (RTRT). 130 Sterilization without compromising particle integrity—particularly for temperature-sensitive polymeric matrices—further complicates GMP compliance.

Third, long-term safety profiles present formidable obstacles. Biodegradable polymers such as PLGA degrade into glycolic and lactic acids that are metabolized via the Krebs cycle, yet acidic byproducts may inadvertently activate inflammatory cascades in the chronically inflamed joint microenvironment. More critically, repeated administration of PEGylated nanoparticles elicits anti-PEG antibodies (APAs) in a substantial fraction of patients—including those with pre-existing APAs from cosmetic or pharmaceutical exposure—triggering the accelerated blood clearance (ABC) phenomenon upon subsequent doses. APAs bind to PEGylated carriers, activate complement, and reduce circulation time and therapeutic efficacy, while also predisposing to hypersensitivity reactions ranging from urticaria to anaphylaxis. Strategies to mitigate APA formation include fast-shedding PEG-lipids, terminal group substitution (eg, hydroxyl-PEG), and alternative stealth polymers such as poly(2-oxazoline), polyglycerol, and zwitterionic materials that evade immunogenicity entirely. 131 Beyond PEG immunogenicity, cationic polymer residues (eg, PEI, chitosan derivatives) can activate complement and induce cytotoxicity, whereas non-degradable inorganic cores accumulate in RES organs and raise chronic toxicity concerns. 132

Fourth, addressing these multifaceted challenges necessitates a paradigm shift toward intelligent, data-driven design. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms are revolutionizing nanomedicine development by enabling high-throughput polymer screening, predicting structure–activity relationships, and optimizing drug release kinetics based on large experimental datasets. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) and reinforcement learning can design polymeric scaffolds and nanoparticle surface chemistries that maximize endothelial uptake while minimizing immune clearance. ML-driven analysis of multi-omics datasets further offers a transformative framework for precision-engineered therapies customized to patient-specific immunogenetic profiles, potentially stratifying patients based on baseline anti-PEG antibody levels or synovial microenvironment signatures. Integration of automated microfluidic platforms with AI-driven process optimization may substantially enhance production consistency and quality control, bridging the gap between preclinical promise and clinical reality. 133 Ultimately, the convergence of mechanistic pharmacokinetic understanding, GMP-compliant scalable manufacturing, proactive immunogenicity mitigation, and AI-guided personalized design will determine whether SPNs transition from promising preclinical constructs to standard-of-care therapeutics for rheumatoid arthritis.

It is worth noting that the therapeutic mechanisms reviewed herein predominantly derive from collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) and adjuvant-induced arthritis (AIA) models, yet these experimental systems exhibit fundamental disparities with human RA that constrain their predictive validity. CIA, the most widely employed model, requires both T-cell and B-cell responses to autologous type II collagen and reproduces synovitis, pannus formation, and progressive bone erosion, making it the benchmark for preclinical efficacy testing. However, CIA develops rapidly over weeks rather than the chronic, relapsing-remitting course characteristic of human RA, and critically, CIA mice and rats lack anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs)—the serological hallmark and key pathogenic driver in approximately 70% of human RA patients. 134 This absence of ACPA-mediated immunity fundamentally alters the immunological landscape, rendering CIA inadequate for evaluating therapies targeting citrullination pathways or ACPA-producing B-cell subsets. AIA, induced by complete Freund’s adjuvant, is even more problematic: it is self-limiting, typically resolving within a few weeks, and is now recognized as a more appropriate model for reactive arthritis than for RA due to divergent histological and immunological features. The acute, monophasic inflammation of AIA fails to capture the sustained synovial hyperplasia, tertiary lymphoid neogenesis, and adaptive immune dysregulation that define human disease chronology. 135 Furthermore, both CIA and AIA rely on artificial immunization protocols that bypass the genetic and environmental risk factors (eg, HLA-DRB1 shared epitope, smoking, microbiome) implicated in human RA pathogenesis, and neither model adequately recapitulates the systemic comorbidity burden—cardiovascular, metabolic, and psychological—that profoundly impacts patient outcomes. Emerging alternatives such as the K/BxN serum-transfer model (autoantibody-driven), pristane-induced arthritis (PIA, T-cell-mediated), and humanized mouse models engrafted with patient-derived immune cells offer incremental improvements in face validity, yet each introduces its own limitations: K/BxN overemphasizes humoral mechanisms at the expense of cellular immunity, PIA exhibits limited antibody involvement, and humanized models remain technically demanding, expensive, and incompletely engrafted. 135 Collectively, these translational gaps contribute to the well-documented attrition of nanomedicine candidates from preclinical promise to clinical failure. Future SPN development for RA must therefore incorporate multi-model validation—spanning at least two distinct species and pathogenic mechanisms—alongside human ex vivo synovial tissue assays and organ-on-chip platforms that preserve the three-dimensional architecture and cellular heterogeneity of the rheumatoid joint, thereby bridging the chasm between rodent efficacy and human therapeutic benefit.

## Conclusion and Outlook

Despite impressive preclinical efficacy, SPNs face substantial translational barriers. CIA/AIA models lack ACPAs and fail to recapitulate human disease chronology. The EPR effect in human joints is weaker and more heterogeneous than in rodents, with 40–50% of intravenously administered nanoparticles cleared by RES organs within hours. Manufacturing scale-up remains constrained by batch variability and sterilization challenges. 128 , 130 Safety concerns include PLGA degradation byproducts, anti-PEG antibody-mediated ABC phenomenon, and uncertain long-term fate of non-degradable components. While SPNs demonstrate targeted accumulation, stimulus-responsive release, and macrophage repolarization in rodents, clinical translation remains nascent. Clinically, however, the field remains in early phases: while liposomal prednisolone and PEGylated biologics have achieved regulatory approval for RA, these are not stimulus-responsive systems in the sense reviewed here. No Phase III data for intelligent polymeric nanocarriers in RA yet exist, and the few SPN platforms entering early-stage trials remain preliminary. Near-term (2025–2030): validate in large-animal models and human synovial organ-on-chip platforms; 136 deploy AI-driven formulation optimization. Mid-term (2030–2035): Phase I/II trials with imaging-guided dosing and multi-omics patient stratification. Long-term (2035+): personalized adaptive nanomedicine integrating microenvironment profiling, immunogenicity screening, and real-time therapeutic monitoring. 137

In summary, SPNs represent a paradigm shift from empirical dosing to intelligent, microenvironment-adaptive therapy for RA. Yet realizing this potential demands that the field move beyond demonstrative efficacy in rodent models toward mechanistically grounded, safety-focused, and clinically validated research. Only through candid acknowledgment of current limitations and systematic execution of this translational roadmap can SPNs transit from promising laboratory constructs to transformative clinical therapeutics for rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Engineering Small Extracellular Vesicles for Colon-Targeted Delivery: Microenvironment-Responsive Design, Therapeutic Mechanisms, and Clinical Translation
abstract: Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are endogenous lipid-bilayer nanovesicles that combine cargo protection, biological membrane compatibility, and modifiable surface recognition. For colon-targeted delivery, their value depends on engineering them to withstand gastric acidity and proteolysis, negotiate the mucus barrier, and respond to colon-specific cues, including the distal gastrointestinal pH profile, microbiota-derived enzymes, inflammatory reactive oxygen species, and lesion-associated receptors such as integrins, CD44, and folate receptors. This review critically compares sEVs with conventional colon-targeted drug delivery systems and summarizes sEV biogenesis, cargo sorting, isolation, characterization, exogenous and endogenous loading, surface engineering, and passive, active, and stimuli-responsive targeting strategies. Therapeutic applications are evaluated in inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer, with attention to epithelial barrier restoration, immune regulation, macrophage polarization, apoptosis, tumor-microenvironment remodeling, and emerging intestinal indications such as irritable bowel syndrome. Recent clinical trials, Good Manufacturing Practice requirements, potency and release specifications, safety assessment, and regulatory uncertainties are also discussed. A disease- and route-oriented decision framework is proposed to connect cargo properties, administration route, target-cell biology, manufacturing feasibility, and clinically meaningful endpoints. Although engineered sEVs remain investigational and no therapeutic product has achieved full regulatory approval, integration of microfluidic manufacturing, organ-on-chip validation, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and image-guided precision delivery may improve reproducibility and translational readiness.

# Engineering Small Extracellular Vesicles for Colon-Targeted Delivery: Microenvironment-Responsive Design, Therapeutic Mechanisms, and Clinical Translation

## Abstract
Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are endogenous lipid-bilayer nanovesicles that combine cargo protection, biological membrane compatibility, and modifiable surface recognition. For colon-targeted delivery, their value depends on engineering them to withstand gastric acidity and proteolysis, negotiate the mucus barrier, and respond to colon-specific cues, including the distal gastrointestinal pH profile, microbiota-derived enzymes, inflammatory reactive oxygen species, and lesion-associated receptors such as integrins, CD44, and folate receptors. This review critically compares sEVs with conventional colon-targeted drug delivery systems and summarizes sEV biogenesis, cargo sorting, isolation, characterization, exogenous and endogenous loading, surface engineering, and passive, active, and stimuli-responsive targeting strategies. Therapeutic applications are evaluated in inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer, with attention to epithelial barrier restoration, immune regulation, macrophage polarization, apoptosis, tumor-microenvironment remodeling, and emerging intestinal indications such as irritable bowel syndrome. Recent clinical trials, Good Manufacturing Practice requirements, potency and release specifications, safety assessment, and regulatory uncertainties are also discussed. A disease- and route-oriented decision framework is proposed to connect cargo properties, administration route, target-cell biology, manufacturing feasibility, and clinically meaningful endpoints. Although engineered sEVs remain investigational and no therapeutic product has achieved full regulatory approval, integration of microfluidic manufacturing, organ-on-chip validation, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and image-guided precision delivery may improve reproducibility and translational readiness.

## Keywords
small extracellular vesicles; sEVs; colon-targeted delivery; inflammatory bowel disease; IBD; colorectal cancer; CRC; irritable bowel syndrome; IBS; engineering strategies

## Introduction

Colonic disorders encompass inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), colorectal cancer (CRC), functional conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and infectious colitis. IBD is characterized by recurrent mucosal inflammation, epithelial barrier disruption, dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, and microbial dysbiosis; persistent inflammation can promote fibrosis and colitis-associated neoplasia. CRC develops through progressive genetic and epigenetic alterations within a complex tumor microenvironment containing epithelial, stromal, vascular, immune, and microbial components. Although IBS lacks the destructive mucosal pathology typical of IBD, altered barrier function, visceral hypersensitivity, immune activation, and microbiota-derived metabolites may contribute to selected subgroups. Infectious colitis adds pathogen- and toxin-mediated injury to the mucus layer and tight junctions, intense innate-cell recruitment, and, for some organisms, intracellular or biofilm-associated reservoirs that restrict effective drug exposure. 1 , 2 These distinct disease mechanisms require delivery systems that can protect therapeutics during gastrointestinal transit while differentiating the healthy colon from inflamed or malignant tissue. Conventional immunosuppressants, biologics, chemotherapeutics, and antibiotics can be effective, but durable responses may be limited by disease heterogeneity, resistance, systemic exposure, and off-target toxicity. 3–6

Oral administration is attractive for colon-targeted therapy because it is non-invasive and generally compatible with long-term patient use. 7 However, cargoes must survive gastric acidity, digestive enzymes, variable intestinal transit, and the mucus barrier before achieving adequate colonic exposure. 8–11 Conventional colon-targeted drug delivery systems (CTDDS), including pH-dependent coatings, time-controlled multiparticulates, microbiota-degradable polysaccharides, liposomes, and polymeric nanoparticles, can improve regional release and are supported by comparatively mature manufacturing processes. 9–16 However, their clinical utility is constrained by fundamental drawbacks. 17 pH- and time-dependent systems are susceptible to premature release due to inter-patient variability in gastrointestinal transit and luminal pH. 18 Microbiota-degradable matrices rely on disease-sensitive enzyme activity, which becomes unreliable in dysbiosis. Many synthetic nanomaterials, particularly non-biodegradable or slowly degradable polymers, raise persistent concerns regarding long-term accumulation and material-associated toxicity. 17 , 19 , 20

By contrast, small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) offer a biologically derived alternative. Their native lipid bilayer protects labile proteins and nucleic acids during gastrointestinal transit, supports cellular uptake, and can be functionally modified without replacing the biological membrane. 21–23 Food- and plant-derived vesicles are particularly attractive for oral use. 24 Edible plant materials provide broad, renewable, and widely accessible sources with practical scale-up potential. Several plant-derived preparations resist gastric acid, digestive enzymes, and intestinal degradation sufficiently to preserve cargo during oral transit. Their native lipids, RNAs, proteins, and phytochemicals may also provide intrinsic anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and microbiota-modulating activity. 25 , 26 These advantages are preparation- and source-dependent rather than universal, but they support sEVs as a versatile biological platform for oral colon delivery. 27

These same abnormalities also serve as mechanistic entry points for engineered sEVs, enabling cell-level delivery beyond the regional release offered by conventional CTDDS. 28 In IBD, tight-junction disruption, increased mucosal permeability, altered mucus, activated macrophages and neutrophils, oxidative stress, matrix metalloproteinase activity, and dysbiosis create both access points and lesion-responsive triggers for regional release coupled to barrier repair and immune modulation. 29 In CRC, overexpression of receptors such as CD44, A33, EpCAM, and the folate receptor, together with abnormal vasculature, extracellular-matrix remodeling, acidity, oxidative stress, and immunosuppressive stromal and myeloid compartments, can support ligand-mediated uptake, responsive release, intracellular gene or cytotoxic delivery, and tumor-immune microenvironment remodeling. 30 The native lipid membrane and cargo-protective properties of sEVs therefore make them particularly suited to linking disease-associated signals with cell-level delivery rather than serving only as passive regional carriers. Infection presents a complementary rationale: pathogen- and toxin-induced barrier damage, intense innate-cell recruitment, and intracellular or biofilm-associated reservoirs can favor local delivery of antimicrobial or host-directed cargo together with barrier repair and immunomodulation. 24

The colon provides several engineering opportunities. The distal gastrointestinal pH profile can trigger dissolution of enteric coatings, whereas pectinase, azoreductase, nitroreductase, and other microbiota-derived enzymes can activate degradable matrices. 14–16 , 42 , 43 Mucus thickness and composition, epithelial permeability, local reactive oxygen species, and matrix metalloproteinases differ between healthy and diseased tissue and can be exploited for mucoadhesive, mucus-penetrating, inflammation-responsive, or enzyme-cleavable designs. At the cellular level, receptors such as integrin α4β7 in intestinal inflammation, and CD44, folate receptor, A33 antigen, EGFR, and selected integrins in CRC, offer opportunities for ligand-directed uptake 44–48 Because each signal is variable and rarely disease-exclusive, robust colon targeting is more likely to require layered design—regional protection, lesion recognition, and intracellular release—rather than reliance on a single trigger.

Recent reviews have separately examined extracellular-vesicle engineering across multiple physiological barriers, 23 plant-derived vesicle-like nanoparticles for oral ulcerative-colitis therapy, 25 and mesenchymal stem/stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicles in inflammatory bowel disease. 29 , 49 Taken together, these reviews do not provide a unified colon-specific engineering framework that links gastrointestinal regional barriers and triggers—including pH, transit time, mucus, microbiota-derived enzymes, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)—to surface and cargo engineering, disease-specific target-cell biology in IBD versus CRC, administration route, manufacturability, and clinical-regulatory readiness. The distinctive aim of the present review is therefore not simply to catalogue sEV engineering methods, but to organize them into a disease- and route-oriented decision framework for colon-targeted delivery. Important unresolved questions include how sEVs terminology and source heterogeneity should be standardized; which targeting strategy is most appropriate for a given disease, cargo, and route; how microbiome variability alters release and response; which potency assays predict clinical benefit; and whether added engineering complexity produces sufficient benefit to justify scale-up and cost. Accordingly, this review critically synthesizes sEVs biology, preparation and characterization, cargo loading, surface engineering, colon-specific targeting and responsive release, microbiome interactions, disease mechanisms, clinical evidence, and regulatory considerations. Comparative tables and a rational design matrix are used to identify trade-offs and to provide a practical roadmap for development of safe, reproducible, and clinically relevant colon-targeted sEV systems ( Figure 1 ). ## Overview of sEVs

### Biogenesis, Molecular Composition, and Functional Mechanisms of sEVs

Extracellular vesicles comprise heterogeneous lipid-bilayer particles released by cells. Operationally, the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles recommends describing vesicles by physical characteristics, biochemical composition, or experimental source when endosomal origin has not been directly demonstrated. Exosomes are generated as intraluminal vesicles within multivesicular bodies and are released after fusion with the plasma membrane, whereas microvesicles arise predominantly by outward budding of the plasma membrane; apoptotic bodies are generated during programmed cell death. 50–52 Because common isolation methods do not completely separate these populations, the operational term “sEVs” is used throughout this review for particles within the small-size range unless biogenesis has been established.

sEVs biogenesis and cargo sorting involve endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT)-dependent machinery, ESCRT-independent lipid pathways, tetraspanins, Rab GTPases, and SNARE proteins. 53 Cargo selection is not random: RNA-binding proteins, sequence motifs, post-translational modifications, membrane microdomains, and donor-cell state influence enrichment of proteins, lipids, messenger RNAs, microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and DNA fragments. 54 , 55 The membrane is enriched in cholesterol, sphingomyelin, ceramide, and proteins including CD9, CD63, CD81, Alix, and TSG101, although marker abundance varies by source and preparation. Recipient cells internalize sEVs through clathrin- or caveolin-dependent endocytosis, macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, receptor-ligand binding, or direct membrane fusion. Subsequent endosomal escape or lysosomal processing determines whether cargo reaches the cytosol and remains functional. 56–59

### Comparison of sEV Isolation and Purification Technologies

Preparation of therapeutic sEVs is a multistep process rather than a single isolation step. A concise workflow comprises: selection and qualification of the donor source; controlled cell or biological-fluid collection; removal of cells, debris, and large vesicles; enrichment by ultracentrifugation, filtration, size-exclusion chromatography, precipitation, immunoaffinity, or microfluidics; orthogonal characterization of particle number, size, morphology, markers, purity, and biological activity; cargo loading or surface engineering; removal of unincorporated reagents; sterile formulation; and stability testing. Since high recovery, high purity, preserved functionality, throughput, and scalability are seldom achieved simultaneously, the choice of methods should be carefully aligned with the intended application ( Table 2 and Figure 2 ). Beyond the isolation protocol, storage buffer, temperature, freeze-thaw exposure, and sample concentration are additional critical variables that substantially influence sEV recovery and potency. 41 , Ultracentrifugation (100,000–150,000 g) remains one of the most widely used methods for bulk sEV enrichment because it can process relatively large sample volumes using well-established workflows. 84 However, it is time-consuming, requires specialized equipment, and high shear forces can damage vesicles, while co-pelleted protein aggregates limit purity. 85 , 86 By comparison, size-based methods (ultrafiltration and size-exclusion chromatography) offer milder conditions—especially SEC, which preserves vesicle integrity—but neither fully removes similarly sized lipoproteins, and SEC suffers from low throughput and diluted eluates. 87–89 Polymer precipitation (eg, PEG) is even simpler and faster, ideal for small volumes, yet it yields the lowest purity because reagents co-precipitate abundant proteins and lipoproteins, and residual polymers interfere with downstream assays. 90 Stimuli-responsive polymers have emerged to improve purity and recovery but remain laboratory-stage. 91

Immunoaffinity capture can provide high-purity, subset-selective isolation by targeting exosomal surface markers (CD63, CD81, EpCAM), making it uniquely suited for diagnostic applications requiring origin discrimination. 92 In contrast, its high cost, limited capture capacity, potential elution-induced activity loss, and restriction to marker-positive subsets hinder large-scale use. Microfluidic technologies integrate multiple principles (immunoaffinity, size, acoustics, dielectrophoresis) on miniaturized chips, enabling automated, low-consumption isolation directly from whole blood with preserved bioactivity. 79 , 80 , 93 While microfluidics holds great promise for clinical diagnostics and point-of-care testing, its processing throughput remains lower than ultracentrifugation or precipitation, and scale-up poses significant engineering challenges—mirroring the scalability limitations of immunoaffinity but offering greater flexibility in sample type and labeling options.

Advances in kits and novel platforms have aimed to bridge the gap between purity, speed, and scalability. Early kits like ExoQuick (polymer precipitation) prioritized speed, whereas Qiagen’s membrane affinity improved reproducibility for GMP compliance, and MagCapture enabled clinical throughput via magnetic beads. Newer designs such as Exodisc integrate filtration for efficient urine processing; ultrathin membranes support continuous low-cost production; ExoSearch offers closed-loop analysis; and iKnife uses AI to optimize parameters and reduce variability. 94 , 95 None of these emerging techniques, however, completely resolve all trade-offs between purity, yield, vesicle integrity, and throughput—highlighting the need for method selection based on specific research or production goals.

In summary, sEVs isolation requires trade-offs among purity, yield, throughput, and vesicle integrity. No single method is optimal for all applications. Future development should prioritize scalable, standardized isolation systems that preserve structural and functional integrity and are compatible with clinical translation.

### Key Technologies for sEV Characterization

Although substantial progress has been achieved in sEV isolation and purification, preparations may still contain proteins, lipoproteins, nucleic-acid complexes, or other vesicles that confound biological interpretation and reduce therapeutic consistency. Comprehensive characterization and quality control are therefore essential. 52 sEV characterization should address at least three domains: particle concentration and size, morphology, and biochemical identity. No single technique provides complete characterization; orthogonal methods are therefore required to verify vesicle identity ( Table 3 ). Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA), Tunable Resistive Pulse Sensing (TRPS), and Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) are commonly employed to quantify the particle concentration and size distribution of sEVs in the sample, representing the most fundamental and initial step in sEV characterization. 96–98 Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and cryo-electron microscopy can visualize vesicular morphology. Conventional dehydration-based electron microscopy often produces cup-shaped profiles, which should be interpreted as preparation-related artifacts rather than the native morphology of sEVs in solution. Morphology should therefore be evaluated together with complementary methods such as cryo-electron microscopy or liquid-phase AFM. 99 , 100 It should be noted that different characterization methods and equipment may lead to differences in detection results. Therefore, accurate characterization of individual sEVs typically necessitates the integration of at least two complementary methodologies for validation. 52

Commonly utilized markers for exosomal surface identification encompass tetraspanin proteins (eg, CD9, CD63, and CD81) and late endosome-associated proteins (eg, Tsg101 and Alix). 101 ISEV guidance recommends assessing multiple complementary positive markers together with source-appropriate negative or contaminant markers rather than relying on a fixed universal marker panel. 102 Accordingly, transmembrane proteins (eg, CD9, CD63, and CD81) and cytosolic EV-associated proteins (eg, ALIX and TSG101) should be assessed alongside source-appropriate negative or contaminant markers to support EV identity and preparation purity. 103 , 104

Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) has emerged as a powerful complementary tool for sEV characterization, offering unique advantages beyond conventional techniques. Unlike ensemble methods such as NTA or DLS, AFM enables label-free, high-resolution imaging of individual sEVs under near-physiological conditions (eg, liquid environment), preserving their native morphology and mechanical properties. 105 AFM provides three-dimensional topographic images with sub-nanometer vertical resolution, directly revealing the size, height, and surface ultrastructure of sEVs. More importantly, it simultaneously quantifies nanomechanical parameters such as Young’s modulus, adhesion force, and deformation, allowing discrimination of sEVs subpopulations based on their biophysical signatures. 106 In contrast to the “cup-shaped” or “biconcave” artifacts commonly observed under dried TEM/SEM conditions, AFM in liquid typically visualizes spherical or disk-like sEVs with intact membranes.

Nano-flow cytometry (NanoFCM) has emerged as a powerful complementary tool for sEV characterization, offering distinct advantages over ensemble methods such as DLS. Unlike DLS, NanoFCM enables direct, label-free detection of individual sEVs at the single-particle level, resolving particles as small as 40 nm with high sizing resolution covering the entire sEV size range of 40–200. 107 It simultaneously quantifies particle size, concentration, and biochemical properties such as surface markers at rates up to 10,000 particles per minute, providing statistically robust data from as little as 1 μL of sample. 108 In contrast to the population-averaged outputs of conventional techniques, NanoFCM resolves sEVs subpopulations based on both physical size and molecular signatures, revealing heterogeneity that is otherwise masked. While AFM delivers three-dimensional topography and nanomechanics of individual sEVs, NanoFCM offers high-throughput, multiparameter analysis of sEV populations. 109 Due to the inherent variability among different characterization platforms, the integration of NanoFCM with at least one orthogonal method (eg, AFM for structural details, NTA for cross-validation) is strongly recommended to ensure accurate and comprehensive sEV profiling. 110

In summary, existing isolation and characterization technologies provide a strong research foundation, but cross-platform variability, incomplete impurity removal, and limited process standardization remain major barriers to industrial-scale manufacturing. Donor-cell physiology must also be controlled because hypoxia, three-dimensional culture, senescence, inflammation, and other stressors can alter sEVs yield and cargo composition; such conditioning may improve a desired function but can also introduce unintended biological activity. 111 Future development should prioritize scalable, closed, and standardized processes that preserve structural integrity and demonstrate consistent potency.

## Drug Loading Strategies for Engineered sEVs

A key advantage of sEVs as drug-delivery vehicles is their ability to protect and transport small molecules, proteins, and nucleic acids. However, efficient incorporation into the lumen or membrane remains technically challenging. Current approaches can be classified as post-isolation loading through physicochemical membrane perturbation and pre-isolation loading by engineering donor cells to package cargo during biogenesis ( Figure 2 and Table 4 ). ### Physicochemical Methods: Exogenous Loading via Membrane Perturbation

Physicochemical methods mainly use physical fields or chemical reagents to transiently alter the permeability of the exosomal lipid bilayer, allowing therapeutic molecules in the sEVs suspension to cross the membrane into the lumen. The core design principle of this paradigm is the precise control of reversible membrane rearrangement, with the goal of improving loading efficiency while minimizing irreversible damage to the intrinsic structure (eg, surface targeting proteins) and function of sEVs. 126

Electroporation is one of the most widely used physical loading techniques. It works by applying high-voltage electrical pulses to transiently generate hydrophilic nanopores in the lipid bilayer of cells or vesicles, providing a diffusion pathway for charged molecules (such as siRNA, miRNA, or certain small-molecule chemotherapeutic drugs) in the surrounding medium. After the pulse ceases, the fluidity of the lipid bilayer enables spontaneous rearrangement and pore repair, thereby entrapping the drug inside. 127 This technique is particularly effective for nucleic acid loading, with reported siRNA loading efficiencies exceeding 30% in some studies. 128 Nevertheless, the critical design parameters include optimization of buffer ionic strength and electrical pulse conditions to avoid nucleic acid aggregation or irreversible fusion and rupture of exosomal membranes caused by excessive electric fields. For instance, by optimizing electroporation parameters, doxorubicin has been successfully loaded into sEVs on the surface of intraocular lenses, effectively inhibiting the proliferation of lens epithelial cells. 129 In colon-targeted applications, researchers employed electroporation to load CX5461 into extracellular vesicles derived from Sophora japonica flowers, achieving a loading efficiency of 23%. In a DSS-induced colitis mouse model, these engineered sEVs significantly promoted an anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotypic polarization of macrophages in colonic tissues and effectively repaired the intestinal barrier function. 130

Sonication and extrusion represent another category of loading strategies that rely on mechanical shear forces. Sonication increases membrane permeability via transient cavitation-induced disturbances, while extrusion forces sEVs through nanoporous membranes with smaller pore sizes smaller than the sEVs diameter; the intense mechanical shear and deformation cause temporary membrane disruption, followed by re-sealing, thus encapsulating drugs from the surrounding medium. 131 In the context of colorectal cancer treatment research, 5-fluorouracil was loaded into milk-derived sEVs via sonication, yielding a drug loading efficiency of 37.65%. 132 This formulation exhibited no obvious toxicity in Caco-2 cell uptake assays when compared with the saponin method. Studies have shown that extrusion significantly improves loading efficiency for large proteins (eg, catalase) compared with simple co-incubation. 133 The extrusion method generally achieves a loading efficiency of 20–40% for macromolecular proteins, which is 2.45 times higher than that obtained with the simple co-incubation method. 134 However, an inherent drawback is that mechanical forces may alter sEVs size or cause surface protein shedding, requiring a balance between loading efficiency and vesicle integrity. 135

In addition, chemical-assisted approaches such as saponin treatment and freeze–thaw cycles are commonly employed. As a surfactant, saponin increases lipid bilayer fluidity by extracting membrane cholesterol, facilitating the entry of macromolecules. 136 Studies have demonstrated that the saponin-assisted approach elevates the loading efficiency of catalase from 4.9% ± 0.5% (achieved by conventional incubation) to 18.5% ± 1.3%, but rigorous elimination of residual saponin is necessary to prevent cytotoxicity. 123 Freeze–thaw cycles mechanically disrupt and reorganize membrane structures through repeated ice crystal formation and melting. For instance, the freeze-thaw method enables successful construction of sEVs–nanoliposome hybrids that retain the key characteristics of exosomal proteins, lipid membranes, and encapsulated drugs. 137 , 138 Although these methods are operationally simple, they often require rigorous removal of chemical reagents or carry the risk of vesicle aggregation and size enlargement, limiting their use in clinical translation settings that demand high purity and homogeneity. 139

### Genetic Engineering Methods: Endogenous Loading via Donor Cell Modification

In contrast to physicochemical methods, genetic engineering shifts the loading process from in vitro to in situ by genetically modifying donor cells to naturally sort therapeutic cargo into sEVs during their biogenesis. 140 A major advantage of this paradigm is that it maximally preserves the native structure and biological activity of sEVs, making it especially suitable for the delivery of proteins and complex nucleic acid drugs.

The fusion protein strategy is a classic approach for endogenous loading of protein drugs. Its design principle involves genetically fusing the protein of interest to highly abundant exosomal membrane proteins (eg, lysosome-associated membrane protein 2b (Lamp2b) or tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81) 141 When expressed in donor cells, the fusion protein is naturally enriched in the exosomal membrane during biogenesis. Using this principle, researchers fused the rabies virus glycoprotein-derived targeting peptide RVG with Lamp2b, achieving active targeting of sEVs to the central nervous system. 114 , 142 Furthermore, fusing soluble proteins to the cytoplasmic domains of these membrane proteins, or using viral proteins with efficient sorting signals (eg, the pX protein of HAV), can also efficiently package target proteins into the exosomal lumen. 143

Nucleic acid-binding protein-mediated loading is tailored for nucleic acid drugs such as miRNAs, siRNAs, or mRNAs. Researchers fuse specific RNA-binding proteins (eg, HuR, MS2 coat protein) to exosomal membrane proteins (eg, CD9), while introducing corresponding binding motifs (eg, AU-rich elements or MS2 stem-loops) into the target RNA. 144 When co-expressed in donor cells, the target RNA is efficiently recruited into sEVs via protein-RNA interactions. For example, the CD9-HuR system for loading miRNA inhibitors has demonstrated effective target gene silencing in both in vitro and in vivo models. 145

Light- or chemically induced protein-protein interactions represent more sophisticated pre-loading strategies. For example, the EXPLORs technology uses the heterodimerization of the photosensitive proteins CRY2 and CIBN under blue light illumination to achieve controllable recruitment of target proteins into sEVs at specific time points. 146 Such “on-demand loading” provides a powerful tool for studying the biological functions of proteins at specific stages and developing spatiotemporally controllable protein delivery systems.

In summary, physicochemical methods are simple and universal, suitable for rapid loading of small molecules and selected nucleic acids but require caution regarding vesicle integrity. Genetic engineering approaches, despite higher technical barriers and longer processing times, may preserve vesicle structure while enabling more controlled cargo incorporation, but they also add manufacturing and regulatory complexity. 147 Continued optimization of both strategy classes will be important for translational development.

## Colon-Targeting Strategies of Engineered sEVs

### Regional Localization Based on Physiological Barrier Differences (Passive Targeting)

The unique physiological environment of the colon provides a natural basis for the regional localization and site-specific release of engineered sEVs. 25 The core design principle of passive targeting is to construct sEVs delivery systems that can remain stable during upper gastrointestinal transit and achieve “on-demand unlocking” specifically in the colonic microenvironment, thereby realizing route protection, colonic localization, and responsive release in an integrated manner ( Figure 3 ).
