Mechanistically, colon-specific targeting can be viewed as a four-step sequence: (1) protect sEVs from gastric acid, digestive enzymes, and premature small-intestinal release; (2) trigger regional exposure using distal-GI pH or microbiota-derived enzymes; (3) increase contact with the diseased mucosa through controlled mucoadhesion or mucus penetration; and (4) add lesion-selective recognition or activation using inflammatory signals or cell-surface receptors. Regional release alone therefore does not guarantee disease specificity; retention, epithelial access, and lesion-triggered activation must be considered together.

#### pH-Responsive Passive Targeting and Release

pH-responsive delivery is among the most established passive approaches, but gastrointestinal pH is dynamic and disease-dependent rather than a fixed sequence of values. The stomach is strongly acidic, the small intestine is generally near neutral, and the distal ileum/colon may become neutral to mildly alkaline; active IBD, diet, transit, and concomitant medication can shift these profiles. 42 Consequently, pH-sensitive coatings should be validated under biorelevant ranges and, where possible, combined with a second trigger. 148 , 149

One strategy encapsulates sEVs within pH-responsive polymer matrices. Mesenchymal stromal cell-derived sEVs have been incorporated into alginate microspheres, coated with gelatin, and protected by Eudragit® FS 30 D (a methacrylic acid-methyl methacrylate copolymer) to limit release in the upper gastrointestinal tract. Dissolution of the enteric layer at higher intestinal pH enabled preferential colonic release and improved anti-inflammatory activity in experimental colitis. 150 , 151

An alternative approach employs layer-by-layer coating with pH-sensitive polymers. Human placental mesenchymal stem cell-derived sEVs coated with N-(2-hydroxypropyl)-3-trimethylammonium chitosan chloride (HTCC) and oxidized konjac glucomannan (OKGM) exhibited resistance to gastrointestinal degradation and enabled targeted release in inflamed colons, where the slightly alkaline colonic pH triggers coating dissociation and subsequent sEVs release. 152

#### Enzyme-Responsive Passive Targeting and Release

The colonic microbiota provides diverse enzymatic activities, including glycosidases and polysaccharidases, as well as azoreductases and nitroreductases, that are scarce in the upper gastrointestinal tract and can serve as biological triggers for colonic release. 43

Pectin resists human gastric and small-intestinal digestion but can be cleaved by microbiota-derived pectinases, making it a useful component of enzyme-responsive matrices. 14 , 153 Pectin-calcium hydrogels have been explored for sEVs encapsulation, with approximately 70% greater release in enzyme-containing simulated colonic fluid than in enzyme-free medium. 154 Beyond sEVs-specific formulations, studies on conventional CTDDS have also shown that pectin source, degree of esterification, coating architecture, and microbial activity materially influence release. 14 , 15 These findings are relevant to sEVs formulations because dysbiosis or reduced bacterial diversity may weaken single enzyme-dependent triggers; time/pH or pH/enzyme combinations can provide redundancy. 16

#### Time-Dependent and Transit-Aware Passive Targeting

Time-dependent systems use a programmed lag phase generated by coating hydration, swelling, erosion, or rupture to delay sEV release until the dosage form is expected to reach the distal ileum or colon. 155 Their targeting mechanism is temporal rather than tissue specific because release is governed primarily by coating kinetics and an assumed small intestinal transit window. However, gastric emptying and small intestinal transit vary substantially among individuals and may be further altered by intestinal inflammation, motility disturbances, and IBD-associated lesions. 156–158 Consequently, timing alone may lead to premature release or release after the intended site has already been passed. Transit-aware timing should therefore be used as a secondary safeguard in combination with elements that respond to pH, microbial enzymes, mucus properties, or inflammatory signals. 152 These systems should also be evaluated under fed, fasted, and disease-relevant transit conditions, with direct confirmation of the release location whenever feasible. 159

#### pH/Enzyme Dual-Responsive Passive Systems

Single-response mechanisms may fail because pH, transit time, microbial composition, and enzymatic activity differ across individuals and disease states. Dual-responsive platforms therefore combine independent triggers to improve release reliability. For example, a functionalized chitosan/HP-β-cyclodextrin hydrogel combined pH- and enzyme-sensitive elements for two-stage oral delivery of plant-derived nanovesicles and kaempferol in experimental ulcerative colitis, achieving greater release under simulated colonic conditions than under upper-gastrointestinal conditions. 160 , 161 The additional complexity, however, must be justified by reproducible manufacturing and a demonstrable improvement over simpler formulations.

#### Mucus-Interactive and Inflamed-Mucosa Retention

The colonic mucus layer is both a barrier and a potential retention site. 162 Mucoadhesive cationic or polysaccharide coatings can increase residence time through electrostatic and hydrogen-bond interactions, whereas hydrophilic or near-neutral surfaces can reduce nonspecific mucin binding and favor penetration toward the epithelium. 25 In active IBD, mucus composition, thickness, and barrier integrity are altered; consequently, a design optimized for healthy mucus may either become trapped superficially or cross too rapidly. Colon targeting therefore requires an explicit balance between retention and penetration, validated under disease-relevant mucus conditions rather than buffer alone. 13 , 163

#### Inflammation-Responsive Regional Targeting

Inflamed colonic lesions exhibit higher oxidative stress, increased matrix-metalloproteinase activity, and disrupted epithelial barriers. 164 , 165 These features can be used as regional activation mechanisms by incorporating ROS-cleavable materials, MMP-cleavable linkers, or inflammation-responsive surface elements that expose targeting ligands or release cargo preferentially within diseased mucosa. 166 This strategy differs from pH- or microbiota-dependent release because the trigger is linked to inflammatory pathology rather than colon location alone.

### Active Navigation Based on Receptor–Ligand Recognition

Passive localization solves the problem of “release in the colonic region” but cannot distinguish between “healthy colon” and “diseased colon”. The core of active targeting strategies is to equip sEVs with the ability to recognize specific markers on diseased cells, thereby achieving precise localization at the “specific address” level. According to the manner of ligand anchoring on the membrane, active targeting strategies can be further divided into genetic engineering and chemical modification methods.

#### Genetic Engineering: Display of Targeting Ligands Using Scaffold Proteins

Genetic engineering modifies donor cells so that the sEVs they secrete naturally display targeting ligands on their surface. The key advantage of this paradigm is that it maximally preserves the integrity and native topological structure of the exosomal membrane. 167

The Lamp2b scaffold system is the most widely used genetic engineering platform. Lamp2b is a type I transmembrane protein with an N-terminal domain extending outside the exosomal membrane and a C-terminus located inside the lumen, allowing the N-terminus to serve as a fusion display site for exogenous ligands. 168 This design was first applied by Alvarez-Erviti et al to display the rabies virus glycoprotein-derived peptide RVG, achieving targeted delivery of siRNA to the mouse brain. 114

In the field of colon targeting, researchers have used this strategy to display arginine-glycine-aspartate (RGD) peptides on the sEV surface. RGD peptides specifically recognize integrins αvβ3/αvβ5, which are highly expressed in colon cancer cells and tumor neovascular endothelial cells. 46 RGD-engineered sEVs co-deliver miR-21 inhibitors and 5-fluorouracil, significantly enhancing the therapeutic efficacy against colon cancer by targeting and suppressing drug resistance-related genes. 47 Similarly, anti-A33 antibody-engineered sEVs enable the specific delivery of doxorubicin to colorectal cancer cells overexpressing the A33 antigen. 48

CAP-sEVs represent a recent extension of the Lamp2b display strategy. Inspired by the evolution of adeno-associated virus capsid proteins, researchers fused functional peptides responsible for blood-brain barrier crossing and brain parenchyma targeting (including nuclear localization signals, endosomal escape signals, and two surface-exposed loop regions) from the AAV9 capsid in tandem to the N-terminus of Lamp2b, constructing a CAP-Lamp2b fusion protein. 169 After displaying these CAP peptides on sEVs derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, intravenous injection achieved transgene expression throughout the brain, with delivery efficiency increased by more than 20-fold compared with the control group and significantly reduced liver distribution. 170 Although developed for brain rather than colon delivery, this study illustrates how multivalent peptide modules can be displayed on sEVs; colon-specific candidates would require independent screening and validation.

#### Chemical Modification: Ligand Display Based on Lipid Anchoring and Covalent Conjugation

Chemical modification directly conjugates targeting ligands onto the surface of isolated and purified sEVs. Its advantage lies in being unrestricted by the modifiability of donor cells, making it suitable for sEVs from various sources.

The DSPE-PEG lipid anchoring system is a classical strategy that uses the FDA-approved pharmaceutical excipient DSPE (1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine) to anchor ligands onto the exosomal membrane. The hydrophobic double chains of DSPE can spontaneously insert into the exosomal lipid bilayer, while the hydrophilic PEG chain extends outside the membrane, with its terminus able to link various targeting molecules. 171 Kim et al anchored aminoethyl anisamide, a high-affinity ligand for sigma receptors, onto macrophage sEV surfaces via DSPE-PEG, achieving targeted delivery of paclitaxel to lung metastases and markedly improving therapeutic efficacy. 172

A cholesterol-anchored RNA nanostructure provides a well-defined strategy for post-isolation ligand display on EVs. Positioning membrane-anchoring cholesterol at the tail of a three-way-junction RNA construct promotes its insertion into the vesicle membrane while exposing folate or RNA aptamers on the outer surface. In a primary study, folate-displaying EVs loaded with survivin siRNA inhibited tumor growth in a patient-derived colorectal cancer xenograft model, supporting the feasibility of combining cholesterol-mediated membrane anchoring with folate-receptor-directed delivery. 173

The DBCO (dibenzocyclooctyne) click chemistry platform is a widely used bioorthogonal approach for chemical modification. DBCO can undergo strain-promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition with azide groups under physiological conditions without copper catalysts. The mildness and efficiency of this bioorthogonal reaction make it particularly suitable for the modification of sensitive biological nanoparticles. 174 In brain targeting studies, researchers conjugated mitochondria-targeting ligands to brain-derived sEV surfaces using the DBCO-SPAAC reaction, successfully preserving the morphological integrity and endocytic dynamics of sEVs. 175 In colon targeting applications, this strategy can be used to controllably conjugate colon cancer-specific aptamers (such as AS1411 and EpCAM aptamers) onto sEV surfaces.

The combination of metabolic glycoengineering and DBCO click chemistry provides another modular route for sEVs modification. 176 Researchers added tetraacetylated N-azidoacetyl-D-mannosamine to the donor cell culture system, allowing cells to integrate azide groups into the glycan chains of surface glycoproteins during metabolic processes. 177 Subsequently, fluorescent dyes or targeting ligands were conjugated to the secreted sEV surfaces via DBCO click chemistry. 178 This tandem strategy of “endogenous labeling + exogenous conjugation” avoids in vitro membrane perturbation and enables efficient and specific sEVs labeling and tracking.

### Chemical Biology-Mediated Programmed Anchoring

Although genetic engineering and chemical modification have been widely used for sEVs targeting engineering, both have inherent limitations: genetic engineering relies on the modifiability of donor cells and cannot be applied to sEVs from isolated clinical samples; chemical modification often lacks site specificity and may mask key functional domains on the sEV surface. 179 Chemical biology hybrid strategies have emerged accordingly, with the core design principle of integrating the advantages of different technologies to achieve efficient and controllable ligand display while maintaining site specificity. 180

For instance, the sialyltransferase CSTII was utilized to install 9-N 3 -Neu5Ac onto the glycan chains on the surface of sEVs, followed by DBCO-based click chemistry to conjugate biotin or fluorescent probes, thereby enabling the engineering of sEVs derived from various cell types, including A549, PC3, and COLO-1 cells. 181

Additionally, Sortase-mediated site-specific ligation represents a representative example of this paradigm. Sortase A is a transpeptidase derived from Staphylococcus aureus that recognizes the LPXTG motif and catalyzes the formation of an amide bond with oligoglycine (GGG). 182 Zhang et al applied this enzymatic tool to the functional modification of milk-derived sEVs. They first synthesized an NH 2 -GG-PEG2000-DSPE molecule bearing diglycine, which was inserted into the exosomal membrane via hydrophobic DSPE anchoring. Next, Sortase A and the EGFR nanobody 7D12 carrying the LPETG motif were added to the system. 183 Sortase A specifically recognized the LPETG motif of the nanobody and covalently linked it to the GG group on the membrane, thereby achieving site-specific display of the nanobody on the sEV surface. Doxorubicin loading experiments showed that 7D12-functionalized sEVs specifically killed EGFR-overexpressing tumor cells, while exhibiting significantly reduced toxicity toward EGFR-negative cells. 184

This chemo-enzymatic hybrid strategy offers three potential advantages: (1) Sortase-catalyzed ligation is site-selective and may preserve ligand activity; (2) the reaction conditions are comparatively mild and can limit membrane disruption; and (3) the modular PEG-DSPE anchoring and LPXTG-ligand components facilitate systematic ligand substitution and screening. These advantages should nevertheless be confirmed for each vesicle source and ligand through structural, functional, and stability assays.

This platform may be adaptable to colon-targeted sEVs by coupling validated LPXTG-tagged ligands against accessible lesion-associated receptors, such as integrin α4β7, CD98, or CD206. However, receptor specificity, ligand orientation, conjugation efficiency, product stability, and in vivo off-target distribution must be demonstrated before the approach can be considered broadly transferable.

### Comparative Selection of Surface-Engineering Strategies

Surface engineering spans genetically encoded peptide or protein display, lipid insertion, antibody or aptamer conjugation, glycoengineering, copper-free click chemistry, enzymatic ligation, membrane fusion, and receptor-directed hybrid systems. 167 , 171 Genetic display offers controlled topology and stable inheritance from donor cells but requires a modifiable production cell and may reduce yield. Lipid anchoring is rapid and source-agnostic but can exchange or desorb in biological fluids. Covalent antibody and aptamer conjugation can increase affinity, yet random coupling may mask binding domains or alter membrane proteins. Glycoengineering and bioorthogonal click chemistry provide modularity and site selectivity, whereas membrane fusion can combine the loading capacity of synthetic particles with biological membranes but introduces compositional and regulatory complexity. 174–184 A rational choice should therefore consider target abundance and accessibility, ligand internalization, receptor heterogeneity, administration route, product stability, analytical measurability, and manufacturing cost rather than targeting affinity alone.

### Bidirectional Interactions Between Engineered sEVs and the Gut Microbiome

The gut microbiome is both a targeting variable and a potential therapeutic mediator. Microbiota-derived enzymes can activate pectin-, dextran-, azo-, or polysaccharide-based carriers, but antibiotic exposure, diet, inflammation, and inter-individual dysbiosis can alter the timing and completeness of release. 43 Conversely, plant-, food-, mammalian-, or microbial-derived vesicles may change bacterial abundance, metabolite production, epithelial signaling, and mucosal immunity. 25 , 163 , 185 For example, nanovesicle-associated interventions have been reported to alter microbial composition and metabolites while improving experimental colitis or CRC endpoints; 186 however, causality is often difficult to separate from reduced inflammation itself. 187

Microbial membrane vesicles also participate in host-microbiota communication by carrying proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and microbe-associated molecular patterns across mucus and epithelial barriers. 188 Depending on microbial origin and dose, these vesicles may support barrier homeostasis, facilitate immune education, or amplify inflammation and tumor-promoting signaling. 189 , 190 Engineered sEVs development should therefore measure microbiome-dependent variability rather than treating the microbiota solely as a release switch. Recommended studies include antibiotic or gnotobiotic controls, longitudinal metagenomics and metabolomics, fecal transfer or defined-consortium experiments when causal claims are made, and assessment of how the formulation itself changes microbial ecology.

## Responsive Release Strategies of Engineered sEVs

The precise spatiotemporal control of drug release at the target site represents the ultimate goal of any drug delivery system. Although surface engineering endows sEVs with the ability to recognize and bind to diseased cells, therapeutic cargoes must ultimately be released in a biologically active form to exert their pharmacological effects. To better evaluate the targeting efficiency of engineered sEVs, a systematic evaluation system is required, including in vitro binding, in vivo distribution, targeting specificity, and functional efficacy ( Table 5 ). Premature drug leakage during systemic circulation or gastrointestinal transit not only reduces therapeutic efficacy but also increases the risk of off-target toxicity. 25 Conversely, inefficient release even after reaching the target site renders even the most sophisticated targeting strategies ineffective. Therefore, engineering of sEVs with stimuli-responsive release mechanisms has emerged as a key frontier in the development of next-generation colon-targeted therapies. The colonic environment provides multiple endogenous signals for responsive release, including pH, microbiota-derived enzymes, reactive oxygen species, matrix metalloproteinases, and disease-associated metabolic changes. 148 , 163 , 191 None is perfectly specific or constant. This section therefore evaluates not only representative designs but also the biological variability, analytical requirements, and failure modes associated with each trigger.

### Single Physiological Signal-Responsive Systems

#### Reactive Oxygen Species-Responsive Release

Both inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer are characterized by significantly elevated levels of reactive oxygen species in the lesional microenvironment. 191 In inflamed colonic mucosa, infiltrating immune cells-particularly neutrophils and macrophages-generate large amounts of superoxide anions and hydrogen peroxide via respiratory burst. 192 This pathological ROS accumulation not only drives tissue damage but can also serve as a disease-specific trigger for drug release.

One strategy involves directly loading ROS scavengers into sEVs. Regulatory T cell-derived sEVs loaded with cerium oxide nanoparticles were developed as bifunctional antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents for IBD treatment. 193 Cerium oxide nanoparticles possess potent ROS-scavenging properties due to their unique autocatalytic redox activity cycling between Ce 3+ and Ce 4+ oxidation states. In both TNF-α-stimulated cellular models and DSS-induced mouse colitis models, exo@nCeO effectively reduced ROS levels in intestinal epithelial cells, maintained intestinal barrier integrity, and hindered IBD progression. 194 In this formulation, sEVs serve as carriers for ROS-scavenging nanozymes, coupling vesicle delivery with antioxidant activity at inflamed sites.

### Dual and Multi-Responsive Systems

Although single stimulus-responsive systems offer improved selectivity over non-responsive formulations, they remain vulnerable to inter-individual physiological variations and fluctuations in disease states. For example, colonic pH varies significantly among individuals and may be altered in disease states such as active IBD. Similarly, microbial enzymatic activity is influenced by diet, medication use, and disease-associated dysbiosis. 195 To overcome these limitations, researchers have increasingly focused on developing dual or multi-responsive systems that integrate two or more trigger mechanisms, thereby enhancing targeting precision and release reliability.

A representative example is the ROS/enzyme dual-responsive oral drug delivery system developed for colorectal cancer therapy. This system is designed to respond to both elevated ROS levels characteristic of CRC and overexpressed β-mannanase in colorectal tissues. The design comprises two hierarchical components: (1) ROS-responsive prodrug micelles composed of methoxy polyethylene glycol and mesalazine linked via a thioether bond cleavable under oxidative conditions; (2) konjac glucomannan (KGM) microspheres encapsulating curcumin-loaded prodrug micelles, which can be specifically degraded by colonic β-mannanase. Following oral administration, the KGM shell is first degraded by β-mannanase in the colon, releasing the curcumin-loaded prodrug micelles. Subsequently, exposure to the high-ROS tumor microenvironment triggers thioether bond cleavage and site-specific drug release. 185 In azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS)-induced CRC mice, this dual-responsive system significantly improved survival rates, suppressed tumor growth, reduced inflammatory cytokine expression, and restored near-normal gut microbiota composition.

Similarly, a functionalized chitosan/HP-β-CD hydrogel platform combining pH-sensitive and enzyme-sensitive elements has been developed for the synergistic “two-stage” oral delivery of sEVs and kaempferol in ulcerative colitis therapy. 196 This dual-responsive system achieved over 85% drug release within 48 hours in simulated colonic environments, significantly outperforming single-responsive systems.

### Enzyme-Cleavable Activated Smart Delivery Systems

A particularly sophisticated class of responsive systems involves the use of enzyme-cleavable linkers to tether therapeutic or targeting moieties to the sEV surface, enabling programmed activation in the diseased microenvironment. We term this design concept “programmable anchoring”, which combines the targeting specificity of surface engineering with the release control of stimuli-responsive chemistry.

In the context of intestinal inflammation, a representative example of this paradigm comes from recent work on reprogrammed Treg cell-derived sEVs. Researchers engineered sEVs to deliver the antioxidant trace element selenium for IBD therapy, with one key innovation: synthetic mitochondria-targeting peptide SS-31 was modified on sEVs via a peptide linker designed to be specifically cleaved by matrix metalloproteinases significantly upregulated in inflammatory lesions. 164 This design achieves spatiotemporally controlled activation via a two-step process: (1) engineered sEVs home to inflamed intestinal tissues, then (2) elevated MMP activity cleaves the peptide linker, releasing the SS-31 peptide and enabling its mitochondria-targeting function. The resulting system precisely scavenges excess mitochondrial ROS in inflamed intestinal regions, prevents PANoptosis-a coordinated form of programmed cell death encompassing pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis-and restores intestinal barrier integrity. This represents a paradigm in which sEVs act not merely as passive carriers but as actively unlocked vehicles whose full therapeutic potential is unleashed only upon encountering disease-specific enzymatic activity.

### Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Barrier Repair and Immune Rebalancing

In IBD models, therapeutic sEVs exert their effects through several interconnected mechanisms. Within the intestinal epithelium, uptake of sEVs enhances tight-junction and adherens-junction protein expression, stimulates mucin production, reduces epithelial apoptosis and PANoptosis, and facilitates wound healing and barrier restoration. 49 , 130 , 151 , 152 In the immune compartment, sEV cargo suppresses NF-κB and related pro-inflammatory pathways, lowers levels of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), promotes macrophage polarization from a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, and rebalances the Th17/Treg axis. 164 , 193 , 194 Additionally, antioxidant payloads can mitigate both mitochondrial and cytosolic oxidative stress. 164 , 194 However, these mechanisms should not be generalized across different sEV preparations: their activity is critically dependent on donor cell source, cargo composition, dosage, administration route, and disease stage. Moreover, anti-inflammatory effects observed in acute murine colitis models do not, by themselves, predict durable mucosal healing in human patients. 197

### Colorectal Cancer: Cytotoxic Delivery and Tumor-Microenvironment Remodeling

In CRC, engineered sEVs are being used to increase intratumoral delivery of chemotherapy, small interfering RNA, microRNA modulators, and proteins. 198–201 Proposed effects include induction of apoptosis, reversal of drug resistance, suppression of proliferation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, inhibition of angiogenesis, macrophage or dendritic-cell reprogramming, and enhancement of antitumor T-cell responses. 47 , 184 , 185 , 198 , 201–203 Ligand-directed systems targeting A33, integrins, folate receptors, EGFR, or aptamer-defined antigens can improve cellular uptake, whereas combination with immune-checkpoint blockade may help remodel an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. 48 , 183 , 184 , 200 , 202 , 204 Such combinations should be benchmarked against both free-cargo and checkpoint-inhibitor controls, because increased immune-cell infiltration alone does not establish improved checkpoint responsiveness. A critical counterpoint is that tumor- or stromal-cell-derived sEVs may carry pro-angiogenic, pro-metastatic, or immunosuppressive cargo. 205 Source qualification and comprehensive molecular profiling are therefore essential, and therapeutic benefit must be separated from possible parent-cell-derived tumor-promoting signals. ### A Rational Design Framework

The preferred design should be selected from the clinical problem backward. Oral regional delivery favors acid protection and pH/enzyme-responsive release; inflamed-mucosa retention may require charge, mucus interaction, or inflammation-responsive ligands; cell-specific intracellular delivery requires an internalizing receptor and an endosomal-escape strategy; systemic CRC delivery requires control of mononuclear-phagocyte sequestration and off-tumor receptor expression. 10 , 11 , 43 , 87 , 107 , 112 Cargo stability, dose, product heterogeneity, assayability, route-related patient burden, and manufacturing cost must be considered concurrently. 211 Table 7 summarizes a decision matrix linking design objective, strategy, disease context, principal limitation, and translational priority. ## Clinical Translation of sEVs as Drug Carriers: Current Status and Future Perspectives

Clinical investigation of extracellular-vesicle products has expanded rapidly, but engineered therapeutic sEVs remain at an early translational stage. 202 , 212 , 213 No engineered sEV therapeutic dosage form has received full regulatory approval. 120 , 214 Products that have reached clinical use are primarily diagnostic assays, whereas therapeutic candidates remain investigational. 202 , 215 This distinction is important because analytical validation of an sEVs biomarker test does not establish manufacturing feasibility, dose reproducibility, or clinical efficacy for a therapeutic product. 120 , 212 , 214

### Clinical Trial Landscape

Most registered extracellular-vesicle studies evaluate naturally derived preparations, biomarkers, or unmodified products, whereas comparatively few investigate actively engineered therapeutic delivery systems. 120 , 213 A systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 clinical reports found generally acceptable short-term safety across heterogeneous indications and preparations, but small samples, variable manufacturing, and inconsistent outcome reporting preclude broad conclusions regarding efficacy or class-wide safety. 214 These limitations reinforce the need for product-specific dose, biodistribution, potency, and long-term follow-up data.

Diagnostic assays based on extracellular-vesicle-associated biomarkers have progressed faster than therapeutic products. The ExoDx Prostate IntelliScore urine assay illustrates the clinical translation of an extracellular-vesicle-associated molecular test. 215 This diagnostic precedent supports the feasibility of standardized sample handling and analytical validation, but it should not be interpreted as validation of therapeutic sEVs manufacturing, dosing, or efficacy.

### Clinical Trials of sEVs in Intestinal Diseases

For intestinal disorders, registered studies have evaluated natural or engineered sEVs preparations in IBD, CRC, IBS, and postoperative complications ( Table 8 ). Most are early-phase, small, open-label, or exploratory, and several have uncertain or terminated recruitment status. For ulcerative colitis, a registry study of orally administered whey-protein milk-derived sEVs ( NCT06755021 ) evaluates disease activity, fecal calprotectin, and quality of life, but its recruitment status requires confirmation. A separate Phase I study of intravenous bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicles ( NCT05176366 ) was terminated because of enrollment challenges; it therefore does not provide efficacy evidence.

Phase I studies of intravenous or locally injected bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicles for refractory Crohn’s disease and perianal fistulas ( NCT05130983 , NCT05836883 ) were also terminated because of enrollment challenges. These outcomes illustrate that trial feasibility, route burden, eligibility criteria, and access to competing therapies are important translational constraints in addition to product biology.

A Phase I registry record describes intraperitoneal administration of human placental mesenchymal stromal cell-derived exosomes for preventing postoperative anastomotic leakage after low anterior resection for rectal cancer ( NCT06536712 ). The study remains listed as not yet recruiting, although its estimated study dates have passed. It should therefore be regarded as an unverified or potentially outdated registry entry rather than a completed study, and no conclusion regarding clinical benefit can be drawn.

Plant- and food-derived vesicles are attractive for oral delivery because of potential availability and lower production cost. Ginger-derived vesicles with or without curcumin ( NCT04879810 ) have been registered for IBD, plant vesicle-conjugated curcumin has been investigated in colon cancer ( NCT01294072 ), and milk-derived vesicles have been explored for dose tolerability relevant to IBS/IBD. Public registry information is incomplete for several studies, and particle dose, product identity, and results should be interpreted cautiously.

### Translational Evidence and Current Limitations

Despite growing clinical interest, several interconnected challenges impede the regulatory approval and widespread adoption of sEV-based therapeutics.

First, biodistribution and targeting efficiency remain suboptimal. Intravenous sEVs are predominantly sequestered by the mononuclear phagocyte system (liver, spleen, lungs), resulting in low accumulation in colon lesions. 32 Orally delivered sEVs must overcome gastric acid, enzymatic degradation, and mucus barriers, which severely reduce bioavailability. 12 , 13

Second, scalable and standardized production under GMP conditions is limited by low yield, high cost, and lack of unified isolation protocols. 36 , 216 The inherent heterogeneity of sEVs further complicates quality control and batch-to-batch consistency. 37

Third, regulatory uncertainty persists. The FDA, EMA, and other agencies have not established specific guidelines for engineered sEVs therapeutics, leading to ambiguity in manufacturing standards, nonclinical evaluation, and clinical trial design. 38 , 202

### Key Scientific and Translational Challenges

To accelerate translation, future research should focus on four priorities: (1) Develop closed automated bioreactors and high-throughput isolation technologies for GMP-grade production. 22 , 36 (2) Establish unified quality control standards covering particle size, concentration, surface markers, loading efficiency, purity, and safety. 39 , 52 (3) Optimize colon-targeting and microenvironment-responsive design to enhance lesion-specific accumulation and therapeutic efficacy. 25 , 120 (4) Promote regulatory harmonization and launch well-designed Phase I/II trials dedicated to engineered sEVs for colon diseases. 38 , 202

## Challenges and Prospects

Engineered sEVs provide a versatile platform for colon-targeted therapy, but added biological functionality is accompanied by source heterogeneity, analytical uncertainty, manufacturing complexity, and regulatory burden. Future progress will depend less on adding isolated engineering features and more on demonstrating that each feature improves a clinically relevant outcome relative to a simpler comparator.

### Production, Quality Control, and Drug Loading: Current Bottlenecks and Emerging Solutions

Large-scale sEV production remains constrained by donor-cell productivity, media requirements, purification losses, and cost. No universal isolation method simultaneously maximizes yield, purity, integrity, and throughput. 38 , 40 , 60 Closed bioreactors, tangential-flow filtration, scalable chromatography, microfluidic or acoustofluidic process analytics, and standardized storage can improve reproducibility, but each process change requires comparability testing. 38 , 40 , 41 , 60 Process analytical technology should monitor cell health, particle output, impurities, and functional potency rather than particle count alone. 213

For a clinical candidate, release specifications should be product- and mechanism-specific and should define acceptance criteria for identity, particle concentration and size distribution, vesicle-associated markers, purity and process-related impurities, cargo content or loading, sterility and microbial safety, residual reagents, and a potency assay linked to the proposed mechanism of action.

Low loading efficiency and limited cargo capacity remain central bottlenecks. 113 Electroporation, sonication, extrusion, and membrane fusion can increase loading but may alter size, aggregation, membrane proteins, or cargo activity. 123 , 128 Donor-cell engineering can improve endogenous loading and product uniformity but lengthens development and raises genetic and regulatory complexity. 144–147 Hybrid sEV–liposome or sEV–lipid nanoparticle systemsmay combine biological recognition with higher loading capacity, although their composition and mechanism must be defined as a new product rather than assumed to retain all advantages of either parent platform. 23 , 126 , 137 , 138 , 217

### Targeting Specificity, in vivo Fate, and Safety

Achieving colon or lesion specificity while avoiding off-organ uptake is critical. Orally administered sEVs must survive gastrointestinal transit and negotiate mucus, whereas intravenously administered sEVs are frequently sequestered by the liver, spleen, and lungs. 32 , 217 Receptor expression is heterogeneous and may also occur in healthy tissues; increased binding in vitro therefore does not guarantee favorable biodistribution in vivo. 23 , 34 Targeting claims should be supported by quantitative tissue distribution, receptor-blocking controls, non-targeted vesicle controls, and dose-normalized functional outcomes. 23 , 213 , 217

For oral delivery, gastrointestinal and intracellular stability are both important. Akkermansia muciniphila membrane vesicles have been reported to promote active mucus penetration through mucin degradation. Following uptake by tumor cells, these vesicles bypassed the conventional endosomal–lysosomal route through Golgi-to-endoplasmic-reticulum trafficking, thereby increasing endoplasmic-reticulum accumulation of siRNA and improving gene silencing in a mouse colorectal cancer model. 218 Stimuli-responsive sEVs that sense pH, ROS, or enzymes in inflamed colon represent a key direction. More directly relevant sEV-based systems have used protective multilayer or hydrogel coatings for oral colon delivery. For example, layer-by-layer-coated exosomes showed improved gastrointestinal protection and colonic delivery in experimental colitis, while galactose-modified, IL-10-carrying sEVs enclosed within a chitosan–alginate coating combined gastrointestinal protection, colonic release, and macrophage-directed delivery. 152 , 219

Although many sEVs preparations are less immunogenic than synthetic or cellular therapies, safety cannot be inferred from endogenous origin alone. 52 , 101 , 220 Source cells may contribute oncogenic, pro-angiogenic, immunosuppressive, infectious, or alloimmune signals; engineering can introduce residual reagents, neoepitopes, altered biodistribution, or unexpected uptake. 101 , 111 , 220 , 221 Safety assessment should cover source-cell qualification, genomic and proteomic cargo, biodistribution, persistence, immunogenicity, thrombogenicity, tumorigenicity, reproductive risk when relevant, and dose-dependent toxicity. 101 Multi-omics and functional assays should be interpreted together because molecular profiling alone does not establish biological safety.

### Regulatory Pathways and Integrated Therapeutic Applications

Regulatory frameworks for engineered sEVs therapeutics are still evolving. 221 , 222 Product definition, manufacturing control, potency, comparability, and long-term safety must be resolved through collaboration among regulators, academia, clinicians, and industry. 223 Clinical development should begin with mechanistically justified, analytically well-defined products rather than highly complex constructs whose active components cannot be measured. 224 Early trials should prioritize safety, dose, pharmacodynamics, feasibility, and informative biomarkers before efficacy claims are expanded. 225

Engineered sEVs may support combination therapy and theranostics by co-delivering drugs, nucleic acids, immune modulators, or imaging probes. In CRC, this could complement immune-checkpoint blockade or chemotherapy; in IBD, it could combine mucosal repair with pathway-specific immune regulation. Image-guided tracking may help connect gastrointestinal transit and tissue exposure with pharmacodynamic response. However, each additional component increases analytical, toxicological, and manufacturing requirements, and combination products should be benchmarked against the individual components and current standard of care. 226

### AI-Enabled Engineering and Precision Translation

Artificial intelligence and machine learning could assist ligand screening, cargo-sequence selection, formulation optimization, image-based particle analysis, process control, and prediction of biodistribution or immunogenicity. 227–229 These models require curated, interoperable datasets with negative results, batch metadata, and external validation; otherwise, algorithmic optimization may reproduce laboratory-specific bias. Digital twins that integrate gastrointestinal physiology, disease state, microbial composition, and formulation properties could support virtual dose and release simulations, 230 but they should complement rather than replace experimental pharmacology.

Organ-on-chip and gut-on-chip systems can incorporate flow, mucus, epithelium, immune cells, microbiota, and patient-derived tissues to test penetration, release, barrier effects, and toxicity under more realistic conditions than static monolayers. 231–233 Coupling these models with microfluidic manufacturing and multimodal imaging may enable rapid iteration between product design and biological validation. 234 , 235 In the longer term, patient stratification by receptor expression, inflammatory state, microbiome function, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers may support personalized sEV therapy; clinical adoption will nevertheless require simple, scalable products and prospective evidence that personalization improves outcomes. 236 , 237

## Conclusions

Engineered sEVs combine a natural lipid bilayer, cargo protection, cellular uptake, and programmable modification of their surfaces and cargo. These features make them suitable for overcoming the sequential barriers encountered during oral delivery to the colon. Within a single system, they can provide protection during gastrointestinal transit, regional release, recognition of diseased tissue, delivery into target cells, and biological signaling. Nanovesicles derived from edible plants further expand this design space because their sources are abundant, renewable, and potentially scalable. Several preparations tolerate gastrointestinal conditions and contain components that suppress inflammation, reduce oxidative stress, or regulate the intestinal microbiota. However, these properties depend on the source and preparation method. The most immediate opportunities lie in applications with clearly defined mechanisms, including restoration of epithelial barrier integrity and immune homeostasis in IBD and targeted delivery of cytotoxic or immunomodulatory agents in CRC.

Clinical translation now depends on resolving three priorities. First, heterogeneity among sources and uncertainty in potency require nomenclature that identifies the source, benchmarks for composition, and potency assays tied to mechanisms of action. Second, variable yield and product instability require closed production systems that comply with good manufacturing practice. Tangential-flow filtration followed by size-exclusion chromatography may be used where appropriate, together with controls during production and protective formulations or lyophilization. Third, limited knowledge of biodistribution, safety over extended periods, and clinical efficacy requires quantitative fate studies, organoids and microphysiological intestinal models that reproduce relevant diseases, and early clinical trials that include pharmacodynamic measures and outcomes meaningful to patients. A development framework that integrates the route of administration, disease context, cargo, mechanism of action, and manufacturing requirements will therefore be essential. Progress in these related areas could convert promising vesicle biology into reproducible and clinically useful sEV products for delivery to the colon.

figure_captions: Figure 1 Integrated workflow for engineered sEVs in colon-targeted therapy. The central vesicle illustrates representative engineering features, including cluster of differentiation 44 (CD44)- and folate-receptor targeting and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive elements. The upper-right module shows density-gradient centrifugation, size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), microfluidic devices, and tangential-flow filtration (TFF) for separation. The lower-right module shows freeze–thaw cycling, extrusion, transfection, electroporation, co-incubation, and sonication for cargo loading. The lower-left module depicts modulation of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK; ERK1/2, JNK, and p38), and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB; IκB-α, p65, and p50) signaling. The clinical module lists inflammation, quality of life, gut microbiota, and intestinal epithelial integrity as representative evaluation domains. Solid arrows denote process flow or activation, whereas blunt-ended lines denote inhibition; dashed outlines group conceptual modules, and bold labels identify the principal workflow modules.

Figure 2 Isolation, loading, and surface modification of sEVs. Conditioned cell-culture medium, blood, and plant fluid are clarified, concentrated, and purified by size-exclusion chromatography, polymer precipitation, immunoaffinity, or microfluidics. Endogenous transfection or co-incubation loads messenger RNA or CRISPR-Cas9 cargo; freeze–thaw, electroporation, extrusion, or sonication provides exogenous loading. CP05 or aptamers attach small interfering RNA or other cargo to the surface. Arrows show sequence; dashed boxes group modules; the plus sign indicates combination of vesicles with ligands or cargo, and bold labels denote the principal technical modules. CP05, exosome-binding peptide CP05.

Figure 3 Passive and active colon targeting of engineered sEVs. Passive localization uses pH-responsive enteric polymers or microbiota enzyme-sensitive coatings to protect vesicles during upper gastrointestinal transit and trigger colonic release. Active targeting uses aptamers, folate ligands, antibodies, mannose, or liposome–sEV membrane hybridization for lesion- or cell-specific recognition. Orange dashed lines separate passive and active engineering. Blue arrows denote coating, delivery, or assembly; the large downward blue arrow in the active-targeting panel indicates liposome–sEV membrane hybridization. Bold labels identify the two targeting paradigms.

Figure 4 Representative therapeutic mechanisms of engineered sEVs in IBD and CRC. From left to right: (1) sEVs-mediated delivery of microRNA-23a-3p (miR-23a-3p) to colonic epithelial cells; (2) repression of tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (TNFR1) mRNA and downstream nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling; (3) effects in the IBD immune microenvironment, including increased mucin 2 (MUC2), zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1), and occludin, modulation of macrophage and neutrophil activity, restoration of the T helper 17 (Th17)/regulatory T-cell (Treg) balance, increased interleukin-10 (IL-10) and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), and reduced tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-17A (IL-17A), and myeloperoxidase (MPO); and (4) effects in the CRC tumor microenvironment, including increased apoptosis, reduced epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), tumor-associated macrophage (TAM)/dendritic-cell (DC) remodeling, antitumor immunity, and reduced angiogenesis. Conventional arrows indicate cargo delivery or signaling flow; upward and downward arrows indicate increases and decreases, respectively; T-bars indicate inhibition. The pathways are representative and may vary with vesicle source, cargo, and disease model; bold labels denote major biological modules. NEVs, Bifidobacterium longum NSP001-derived extracellular vesicles; TME, tumor microenvironment.

title: cRGD-Targeted Nanoparticles Co-Loaded with Ag, Quercetin and PD-L1 siRNA with Combined Antibacterial and Immunotherapeutic Functions Against Fusobacterium nucleatum -Associated Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
abstract:
### Introduction

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis, and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) colonization further aggravates tumor progression, immunosuppression and therapeutic resistance. Conventional monotherapies are limited by insufficient tumor targeting, rapid drug clearance and failure to reverse immune suppression. Here, we fabricated cRGD-modified nanoparticles (Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L) for co-delivery of AgNPs, quercetin (QUE) and PD-L1 siRNA (siP).

### Methods

The morphology, particle size, surface metal elements, drug content and QUE entrapment efficiency of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L were obtained using particle size analysis, SEM, inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) and HPLC. We further detected cellular uptake, in vitro drug release, cytotoxicity, intracellular reactive oxygen species level, PD-L1 gene silencing efficiency and in vitro anti-Fn activity. Pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of Ag and QUE were analyzed by ICP-OES and LC-MS/MS, and in vivo antitumor efficacy and biosafety were tested in Fn-colonized orthotopic 4T1 tumor mice.

### Results

Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L exhibited uniform spherical morphology (195.87± 15.96 nm) with high encapsulation of QUE. cRGD modification enhanced Ag/QUE cellular uptake in 4T1 cells, with pH-responsive release accelerated under tumor acidic conditions. The nanoparticles exhibited selective tumor cytotoxicity, induced oxidative stress, downregulated PD-L1 mRNA, and exerted potent anti-Fn activity in vitro. Pharmacokinetics revealed increased AUC 0-t and reduced clearance compared with free drugs, and cRGD modification promoted tumor accumulation and retention of drugs. In vivo preliminary experiments proved the Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L formulation suppressed tumor growth with a tumor inhibition rate of 45%, and effectively modulated the tumor immune microenvironment: it increased tumor-infiltrating CD3⁺CD4⁺ T cells, reduced PD-L1⁺CD11c⁺ dendritic cells, and decreased the proportions of immunosuppressive Tregs and MDSCs. Hematoxylin-eosin staining and serum liver-kidney biochemistry confirmed no obvious systemic toxicity.

### Conclusion

Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L serves as a multimodal nanoplatform for Fn -associated TNBC with combined in vitro antibacterial, gene silencing and in vivo antitumor immunomodulatory effects, showing great potential for future translational research.

In vivo preliminary experiments proved the Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L formulation suppressed tumor growth with a tumor inhibition rate of 45%, and effectively modulated the tumor immune microenvironment: it increased tumor-infiltrating CD3⁺CD4⁺ T cells, reduced PD-L1⁺CD11c⁺ dendritic cells, and decreased the proportions of immunosuppressive Tregs and MDSCs. Hematoxylin-eosin staining and serum liver-kidney biochemistry confirmed no obvious systemic toxicity.

### Conclusion

Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L serves as a multimodal nanoplatform for Fn -associated TNBC with combined in vitro antibacterial, gene silencing and in vivo antitumor immunomodulatory effects, showing great potential for future translational research.

## Keywords
silver nanoparticles; PD-L1 siRNA; Fusobacterium nucleatum; breast cancer; quercetin; combined therapy

## Introduction

Breast cancer remains the most prevalent malignant tumor and leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women worldwide, among which triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) represents the most aggressive subtype with high metastasis, strong drug resistance, and extremely poor prognosis due to the lack of effective therapeutic targets. Clinical mainstream strategies including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy are severely limited by poor tumor specificity, rapid drug clearance, off-target toxicity, and high recurrence risk, failing to meet the clinical demand for precise and efficient treatment of TNBC. 1 In recent years, emerging evidence has confirmed that tumor-associated microbiota, especially Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), is highly enriched in breast cancer tissues and plays a critical oncogenic role. 2 Fn colonizes in tumor parenchyma, remodels the tumor microenvironment (TME) into an immunosuppressive niche, inhibits cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, accelerates tumor proliferation and distant metastasis, and further reduces the sensitivity of TNBC to conventional therapy, which has become a new key target for breast cancer treatment. 3 Therefore, the development of a novel therapeutic platform that can simultaneously kill tumor cells, reverse immunosuppression, and eliminate tumor-resident Fn is of great significance to break through the treatment dilemma of TNBC.

Combination therapy has become a core strategy for cancer treatment, which exerts synergistic antitumor effects through multi-target and multi-mechanism intervention, reduces toxic side effects, and overcomes the limitations of single-drug therapy. 4 In our previous study, we constructed a lipid-coated silver nanoparticle (AgNP)-single-stranded DNA (ssDNA)-graphene quantum dot (GQDs) delivery system, which achieved favorable antitumor efficacy against cervical cancer and enabled real-time fluorescence imaging tracking owing to the excellent optical properties of GQDs. 5 Inspired by multi-modal combination therapy and tumor bacteria-targeted strategies, we further optimized this delivery system by introducing GQDs as a fluorescent tracking module and structural stabilizer to construct a stable AgNP-GQDs composite core. To endow the carrier with multifunctions of bacteriostasis, tumor growth suppression and immune checkpoint blockade, we incorporated natural flavonoid quercetin (QUE) and PD-L1 siRNA (siP) into cyclic arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (cRGD)-functionalized AgNP-GQDs-cored nanoparticles for synchronous co-delivery.

In summary, we designed a novel targeted nanoparticle Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L for the co-delivery of AgNPs, QUE, and siP. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the physicochemical properties, in vitro performance, in vivo pharmacokinetics, antitumor efficacy, and biosafety of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L, and explore its synergistic therapeutic mechanism against TNBC, so as to provide a novel and effective multi-functional targeted strategy for the clinical treatment of TNBC.

### Synthesis of AgNPs

Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were prepared via a redox method using polyallylamine hydrochloride (PAH) as the reducing agent. Briefly, PAH and AgNO 3 solutions were prepared at concentrations of 0.03 M and 8×10 −3 M, respectively. Under ice‑water bath at 0 °C and 900 rpm stirring, AgNO 3 solution was slowly added dropwise to PAH solution. The reaction was kept in the dark for 15 min.

After the reaction, the resulting solution was divided into two portions. One portion was dialyzed in a 3.5 kDa dialysis bag for 4 h to remove unreacted reagents, and the purified AgNPs obtained were used as the control group in subsequent in vitro and in vivo assays, and stored at 4 °C. Particle size and zeta potential of the dialyzed AgNPs were measured using a Malvern particle size analyzer (Nano ZS90, Malvern, UK).

The other portion of freshly prepared AgNPs was used directly for the preparation of the final Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L without intermediate dialysis.

### Synthesis of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L

One milliliter of the as-synthesized AgNPs solution (without intermediate dialysis) was mixed with 20 μL of 100 μM citrate solution (adjusted to acidic pH) and incubated at 37 °C for 5 min. Then 5 μL of 100 μM PD-L1 siRNA (siP) was added and incubated for another 5 min. Subsequently, 167 μL of 1 mg/mL graphene quantum dots (GQDs) solution was slowly added dropwise into the above mixture, and incubated at 37 °C with 200 r/min stirring for 30 min to form siP-loaded Ag@GQDs cores (Ag@GQDs/siP).

To prepare Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, ethanol injection method was applied. Lipid materials including DSPE-PEG1000-PAMAM, DSPE-PEG2000 and DSPE-PEG3400-cRGD with a molar ratio of 1:3.5:0.3 were mixed with QUE at a lipid‑to‑drug ratio (total phospholipids: QUE) of 20:1 in ethanol solution. This solution was slowly injected into the Ag@GQDs/siP core solution under 800 rpm stirring, and reacted at 50 °C for 30 min. Finally, the mixture was transferred into a dialysis bag (Mw: 3.5 kDa) and dialyzed for 4 h to obtain the final targeted nanoparticle Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L. To prepare Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, the same procedure was followed, with the addition of DSPE-PEG3400-cRGD replaced by DSPE-PEG2000 in the total phospholipids. Ag@GQDs/QUE-sis-L was prepared by replacing siP with an equal amount of scrambled siRNA (sis) in accordance with the aforementioned procedures of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L.

For the preparation of various control formulations, all operations were performed in accordance with the aforementioned procedures of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L with corresponding adjustments: Ag@GQDs/siP-c-L was prepared without the addition of QUE, Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L was prepared without siP, Ag@GQDs-c-L was prepared without the addition of siP and QUE.

Ag@GQDs/siP-L was prepared in accordance with the aforementioned procedures of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L without QUE, Ag@GQDs/QUE-L was prepared without any siRNA, Ag@GQDs/L was prepared without siP and QUE.

#### Silver Content Determination

The silver content of the samples was determined using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) (700ES, Varian, USA). Briefly, the samples were completely digested by nitric acid and diluted to volume with 1% nitric acid until analysis. 7 The instrument parameters were set with a radio frequency power of 1.0 kW, the plasma gas flow rate was set to 15 L/min, the auxiliary gas flow rate was controlled at 1.5 L/min, the nebulizer gas pressure was maintained at 200 kPa, the rotational speed of the peristaltic pump was tuned to 15 rpm, and the sample introduction rate was kept at 1 mL/min. The instrument dwell time for each test sample was set to 30s. Each sample was analyzed in triplicate, and the final results were calculated using the average of the three replicate measurements.

#### Gel Retardation Assay

The siRNA loading in Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was evaluated using agarose gel electrophoresis. The suspension was added to the pre-prepared siRNA solution at different N:P ratios (1:1, 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 5:1, 6:1, 7:1 and 8:1). The N:P ratio is defined as the molar ratio of nitrogen atoms from the amine groups of the cationic lipid DSPE-PEG1000-PAMAM in the formulation to phosphorus atoms in the phosphate backbone of siRNA. The mixture was then loaded into the wells of a precast 1.2% agarose gel supplemented with SYBR Safe dye (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Free siP (20 μmol/L) was used as a positive control, while Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L without siP addition served as a blank control. Electrophoresis was conducted and visualized using an Invitrogen E-Gel Power Snap Electrophoresis Device (ThermoFisher Scientific) at a constant voltage of 65 V for 30 min.

#### Cell Uptake

4T1 cells were seeded in 6-well plates at 1×10 6 cells/well and incubated for 8 h. After washing, cells were treated with various Ag-containing and QUE-cotaining formulations, including AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L with an Ag concentration of 3 µg/mL, as well as Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L and QUE suspension with a QUE concentration of 2 µg/mL.

After incubation for 2, 5, 10, and 15 min, the drug-containing medium was removed, and cells were washed three times with serum-free medium again. Cells at each time point were collected and divided into two aliquots. One part was digested with aqua regia, and the digested solution was diluted to 5 mL with 1% nitric acid for silver content determination by ICP-OES. The other part was treated with acetonitrile, centrifuged at 12,000 r/min for 10 min at 4 °C to remove protein precipitates, and the supernatant was collected and analyzed by liquid chromatograph-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for QUE content with the following analysis condition.

### Cell Viability

The cytotoxicity of AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L against 4T1 and NIH3T3 cells was evaluated using the CCK-8 assay. Briefly, cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 2×10 4 cells per well and cultured overnight for adherence. Cells were then treated with serial dilutions of these Ag-containing formulations with Ag concentrations of 37.5, 18.75, 9.37, 4.68, 2.34, 1.17, 0.58, 0.29 µg/mL for 12 h. According to the manufacturer’s instruction, 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent was added to each well and incubated for another 2 h. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured by an M200 PRO microplate reader (Tecan, Switzerland). Cell viability was calculated relative to the untreated control group, and the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 5 0 ) was determined using GraphPad Prism software (Version 10).

### Intracellular Reactive Oxygen Species Detection

The intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) level in 4T1 cells treated with Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was detected by the Reactive Oxygen Species Assay Kit (Beyotime Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) using 2′,7′-Dichlorofluorescin diacetate (DCFH-DA) as the fluorescent probe. Briefly, 4T1 cells were seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 2×10 6 cells/well and incubated for 12 h. Then cell culture medium was removed. Diluted DCFH-DA (10μmol/L) was added and incubated for 20 minutes in a 37°C-cell incubator. Then the medium was replaced with fresh medium containing AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-c-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L at a final concentration of 1 μg/mL, while the control group received an equal volume of serum-free medium. After 2 h incubation, cells were washed and harvested. Intracellular fluorescence intensity was measured at an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and emission wavelength of 525 nm using a M200 PRO microplate reader (Tecan, Switzerland).

### Gene Silencing Assay

4T1 cells in logarithmic growth phase were seeded into 24-well plates at a density of 1×10 5 cells per well and cultured in complete medium containing 10% FBS overnight. After washing twice with PBS, cells were divided into five groups: blank group (untreated), free siP group, empty nanocarrier group (siP-free nanoparticles at the same particle concentration, Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L), Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L group, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L group. All siRNA-containing groups were dosed at an equivalent final siRNA concentration of 20 nM. After 4 h of transfection incubation, the drug-containing medium was aspirated, cells were rinsed once with pre-warmed PBS, and fresh complete medium was added to continue culture. At 48 h after the initial administration, total cellular RNA was extracted using a commercial RNA extraction kit (Yeasen Biotechnology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.) following the manufacturer’s protocol., and equal amounts of total RNA were reverse-transcribed into cDNA following the protocol of the HiFiScript cDNA Synthesis Kit. Quantitative real-time PCR was then performed using Hieff ® qPCR SYBR Master Mix on a real-time PCR system, with β-actin as the endogenous reference gene. The relative expression level of PD-L1 mRNA was calculated via the 2 −ΔΔCT method. 8 All experiments were carried out in three independent replicates.

### Antibacterial Assay

The in vitro antibacterial activity of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L against Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) was evaluated by using colony counting assay. Fn in the logarithmic growth phase was adjusted to a concentration of 3×10 8 CFU/mL in anaerobic broth. Serial dilutions of AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L were prepared in anaerobic medium (concentration of Ag at 50 μg/mL), using PBS solution as negative control, and then mixed with an equal volume of the above bacterial suspension in tubes, followed by anaerobic incubation at 37 °C for 4 h.

For quantitative analysis, 100 μL of each culture suspension was collected, gradient-diluted, and spread on Colombia blood agar plates supplemented with 5% defibrinated sheep blood. After continuous anaerobic incubation at 37 °C for 48 h, the number of colonies on each plate was counted, and the bacterial survival rate and inhibition rate were calculated accordingly. All experiments were performed in triplicate under strict anaerobic conditions (80% N 2 , 10% H 2 , 10% CO 2 ).

### Pharmacokinetic Evaluation

Nine Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly divided into three groups: QUE suspension, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L. After fasting for 12 h before the experiment, the corresponding formulation was administered to each group via tail vein injections at a dose normalized to 3.0 mg/kg for QUE. Blood samples (around 500 μL) were gathered from the retro-orbital venous plexus at scheduled time points: 0.017, 0.083, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24, and 48 h post-injection. Collected blood was immediately transferred into heparin-coated tubes, followed by centrifugation at 2000 rpm for 15 min under 4 °C to obtain plasma. For sample pretreatment, 50 μL plasma was mixed with 30 ng Kaempferol (purity≥98%) in 150 μL acetonitrile for protein precipitation. After vortex blending for 5 min and centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, the supernatant was collected and subjected to liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) (QTRAP ® 4500, AB Sciex, USA) for analysis. Pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated by fitting the concentration-time data using PK solver software (version 2.0).

### LC-MS/MS Analysis of QUE

#### Chromatographic Conditions

Chromatographic separation was performed on a ZORBAX Eclipse XDB-C18 column (2.1×50 mm, 5 μm) maintained at 40 °C. The mobile phase consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and acetonitrile (B) at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min, with an injection volume of 5 μL. Gradient elution was carried out as follows: 0.00–1.00 min, 5% B; 1.00–2.00 min, 5–20% B; 2.00–3.00 min, 20–80% B; 3.00–3.50 min, 80–95% B; 4.00–4.50 min, 95–5% B; 4.50–5.50 min, 5% B.

#### Mass Spectrometric Conditions

Mass spectrometry was operated in electrospray ionization (ESI) negative mode with multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). The ion spray voltage was set to 4500 V; curtain gas, nebulizing gas, and auxiliary gas were all nitrogen, at 25 psi, 55 psi, and 55 psi, respectively. The nebulization temperature was 550 °C, declustering potential (DP) was 100 V, and collision energy (CE) was 30 eV.

The MRM transitions were m/z 301.0→150.7 for QUE (DP: −116.94 V; CE: −28.20 eV) and m/z 284.9→184.8 for kaempferol (internal standard, DP: −132.01 V; CE: −36.90 eV).

### Tissue Distribution

When the tumor volume of mice reached approximately 300 mm 3 , BALB/c mice were randomly divided into the Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-c-L groups as experimental groups, with the same concentration of AgNPs and QUE-suspension as the control group. Each formulation was administered to each group via tail vein injections at a dose of 3.0 mg/kg for QUE. All tail vein injection procedures were performed under isoflurane inhalation anesthesia. Mice were induced with 3–5% isoflurane in 100% oxygen at a flow rate of 1 L/min in an induction chamber, and anesthesia was maintained at 1.5–2% isoflurane during the operation. The depth of anesthesia was confirmed by the loss of the pedal withdrawal reflex to ensure the comfort of animals.

Mice were humanely euthanized at 0.5, 6, and 24 h after injection. Then the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys, and tumor tissues were excised. After rinsing, drying, and weighing, the tissue samples were sectioned. ICP-OES was used to measure the Ag content in the major organs and tumors as aforementioned. LC-MS/MS was used to detect QUE content in the major organs and tumors as aforementioned. For quantitative analysis, tissue Ag and QUE levels were further normalized relative to their corresponding free formulations (free AgNPs and free QUE suspension, respectively) to compare the tissue distribution performance of Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-c-L.

Female BALB/c mice were used to establish orthotopic 4T1 breast cancer models colonized with Fn. Briefly, 1×10 6 4T1 cells suspension was inoculated into the mammary fat pad of mice, and a round, white, raised bleb on the mammary surface confirmed successful in-situ retention of cells. Tumor volume was measured, and the experiment was initiated when tumor volume reached 80–100 mm 3 .

Tumor volume was calculated by measuring the longest diameter (D) and shortest diameter (L) with a vernier caliper, using the following formula: \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage[substack]{amsmath} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage[mathscr]{eucal} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \DeclareFontFamily{T1}{linotext}{} \DeclareFontShape{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} {linotext }{} \DeclareSymbolFont{linotext}{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} \DeclareSymbolFontAlphabet{\mathLINOTEXT}{linotext} \begin{document}$${\mathrm{V }} = {\mathrm{ D}} \times {{\mathrm{L}}^2}/2$$\end{document}

Tumor-bearing mice were randomly divided into nine groups: bacteria-colonized model group, AgNPs group, QUE suspension group, Ag@GQDs/L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-sis-L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L group, and Paclitaxel (PTX) Injection group. ### Hematoxylin and Eosin Staining

The heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and tumor tissues were collected and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, dehydrated, embedded in paraffin, and cut into 5 μm sections. For hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, sections were dewaxed and rehydrated, stained with hematoxylin for 5 min, differentiated in 1% hydrochloric acid-ethanol for 15s, blued in running tap water for 2 min, counterstained with eosin for 1 min, then dehydrated, cleared and mounted with neutral balsam. Histopathological observation and image acquisition were performed using a DM2500 biological microscope (Leica Microsystems, Shanghai, China).

### Biochemical Parameter Measurement

Four hundred microliters of blood were collected from the orbital venous plexus of the mice, which was centrifuged later. The serum level of liver function indicators (alkaline Phosphatase [ALP] and aspartate aminotransferase [AST]), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine (CRE-L) were detected by an automatic analyzer (7100, Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan).

### Statistical Analyses

All quantitative measurements were presented as means±standard deviations (SD). For comparisons among experimental groups, Shapiro–Wilk test and combined Bartlett/Brown-Forsythe tests were performed to verify residual normality and variance homogeneity prior to variance analysis. Hierarchical ANOVA and matched multiple comparison tests (Tukey’s HSD or Dunnett’s T3) were applied for intergroup pairwise comparisons, whereas two-way ANOVA was utilized for datasets involving two independent variables, with corresponding pairwise comparisons conducted as needed. p <0.05 considered statistically significant.

## Results

### Characterization of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L

As shown in Figure 1A , the synthesized AgNPs were spherical with relatively uniform size, forming a dense, closely packed assembly. When the cores were entrapped in multi-functional phospholipids and co-loaded with QUE, the morphology of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L maintained the spherical or nearly spherical shape. The particle size of the AgNPs was around 50 nm. The well-distributed particle size of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L (about 200 nm) was assumed to come from the coating of lipid membrane ( Figure 1A ), with Ag and QUE content were determined. Figure 1 ( A ) Physicochemical characterization of AgNPs and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L including particle size, polydispersity index, zeta potential, drug content and the entrapment efficiency (EE%) of QUE (n=3); ( B ) Representative SEM images and corresponding EDS elemental analysis of AgNPs and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L; ( C ) Agarose gel electrophoresis assay for siRNA condensation capacity of Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L at gradient N:P ratios (Lane 1–8: N:P at 1:1; 2:1; 3:1; 4:1; 5:1; 6:1; 7:1; 8:1; Lane 9: free siP as positive control; Lane 10: Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L without siP as negative control). Composite: table, SEM micrographs, EDS plots, agarose gel (lanes M, 1-10).

The surface elemental composition of AgNPs and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was analyzed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) point analysis coupled with SEM ( Figure 1B ). As shown in Figure 1B , the primary element in bare AgNPs was silver (Ag), with a mass fraction of 42.18%, accompanied by minor carbon (C, 30.35%) signals. In contrast, the Ag content of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was drastically reduced to 6.07%, while carbon (C) became the dominant element (51.45%).

The siRNA condensation and loading efficiency of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L were evaluated by agarose gel electrophoresis, with the results depicted in Figure 1C . Free siP served as the positive control, exhibiting a distinct electrophoretic band. The blank control (Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L without siP) showed no visible band, verifying that the vector itself did not interfere with siRNA detection. As the N:P ratio increased from 1:1 to 8:1, the migration of siRNA was gradually retarded. At lower N:P ratios (1:1), residual siRNA bands remained detectable, indicating incomplete complexation between siP and the Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L vector. No visible free siRNA bands are detected on the gel when the N:P ratio is≥2:1. In the in vivo physiological environment, serum proteins, salt ion fluctuations and pH changes can weaken the electrostatic binding between the carrier and siRNA. 10 On the other hand, an excessively high N:P ratio might result in overly strong positive surface charge of the particles, bringing about extra cytotoxicity and non-specific adsorption issues. 11 Therefore, N:P ratio at 6:1 as the final preparation condition was selected for subsequent in vitro and in vivo biological evaluations.

### In vitro Release of QUE and Ag

The in vitro release behavior of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L nanoformulation was investigated under different pH conditions to evaluate its tumor microenvironment-responsive properties. As in Figure 2B , Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L exhibited excellent pH-sensitive release behavior: in the simulated normal physiological environment (pH 7.4), the release of both Ag and QUE was notably sustained, with cumulative release rates of 29.4% and 41.9% at 24 h, respectively, indicating favorable stability in the blood circulation; in contrast, under the acidic tumor microenvironment (pH 5.0), the release rates of both components were significantly accelerated, with cumulative release rates exceeding 60% at 24 h (66.6% for Ag and 62.5% for QUE, respectively).

For silver release, both zero-order and Higuchi models yielded better fitting performance than the first-order model at both pH conditions ( Figure 2C ). At neutral pH, the Higuchi model showed slightly higher goodness-of-fit than the zero-order model. For QUE release, the optimal fitting model varied with pH. The Higuchi model achieved the best correlation under acidic condition, while the first-order kinetic model showed the highest fitting degree at pH 7.4.

### ROS Detection

ROS, as natural byproducts of cellular aerobic metabolism, play critical roles in cell signal transduction and homeostasis maintenance, while abnormally elevated ROS levels can trigger oxidative damage and induce cell apoptosis. 12 To verify the ROS-inducing capacity, the blank control group, AgNPs group, QUE-free control group (Ag@GQDs/siP-c-L), and final target formulation group (Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L) were selected for ROS detection ( Figure 3B ). Compared with the blank control group, the intracellular ROS level in the AgNPs-treated group only slightly increased by approximately 8.6%, which may be attributed to the low cellular uptake efficiency of Ag nanoparticles or insufficient intracellular catalytic activity. In contrast, treatment with Ag@GQDs/siP-c-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L significantly elevated intracellular ROS levels to 2.27-fold and 2.24-fold that of the blank group, respectively.

### In vitro PD-L1 Gene Silencing Efficiency

Real-time qPCR was performed to evaluate the PD-L1 gene silencing efficiency of different siRNA-loaded nanoformulations. As shown in Figure 3C , free naked siP barely downregulated PD-L1 mRNA expression in 4T1 cells, with no statistically significant difference compared with the blank group. Both nanoformulations containing siP significantly reduced PD-L1 mRNA levels, which was significantly superior to the free siP group.

### In vitro Antibacterial Activity

The in vitro antibacterial activities of silver-containing formulations against F. nucleatum were evaluated under equal silver content, with PBS as the negative control, and the colony counting results are presented in Figure 3D . The PBS group exhibited dense and vigorous bacterial growth, with a colony count of (2650 ± 455) per dish. All silver-containing formulations exerted varying degrees of bactericidal effects. Free AgNPs showed moderate antibacterial activity with an inhibition rate of 52.3% ( p <0.001). After encapsulation, the Ag@GQDs/siP-L group further decreased the colony count to (596 ± 53) per dish with an inhibition rate of 77.5%, which was significantly stronger than that of free AgNPs. With the co-loading of quercetin, the Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L groups achieved the optimal bactericidal performance, showing an extremely significant difference from the PBS group ( p <0.0001). The cRGD-functionalized Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L group maintained similar antibacterial activity, compared with its non-targeted counterpart.

### Immunity Indicators

Flow cytometric analysis was performed to characterize the alterations of immune cell infiltration in tumor tissues of Fn-colonized 4T1 breast cancer mice ( Figure 8 ).
