### Liver and Kidney Function Biomarkers

Serum AST, ALP, BUN and CRE-L were detected to assess hepatic and renal function, with results shown in Figure 9B . AST reflects hepatocyte integrity, ALP indicates biliary function, and BUN/CRE-L represent glomerular filtration capacity.

The model group showed slightly elevated AST beyond the normal range, suggesting mild hepatic stress induced by tumor burden, while ALP remained normal. Free AgNPs and QUE suspension further increased AST levels but did not cause abnormal ALP elevation, indicating hepatocyte-dominant liver injury without biliary involvement. All nanoformulations maintained the four indicators within or close to the normal range. Notably, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L restored AST to the normal interval, with all parameters meeting the normal reference standard.

## Discussion

To tackle Fn -induced immune suppression and refractory TNBC progression, multifunctional modules were integrated into Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L, with complementary therapeutic advantages. In this system, AgNP serve as dual-functional therapeutic agents with two core biological activities. On the one hand, AgNPs induce tumor cell apoptosis by triggering excessive ROS production and destroying mitochondrial homeostasis, exerting direct and potent anti-tumor cytotoxicity. 7 , 13 On the other hand, AgNPs possess broad-spectrum and highly efficient antibacterial activity, which has been systematically confirmed as a powerful antibacterial agent against bacteria, fungi, and viruses; this antibacterial effect is the primary functional component for eliminating tumor-resident Fn, interrupting bacteria-mediated tumor promotion and immune suppression. 14

Immune checkpoint blockade therapy targeting PD-L1 has revolutionized cancer treatment, 15 , 16 but monoclonal antibody (mAb) drugs are limited by large molecular weight, poor tumor tissue penetration, difficulty in effectively interacting with intracellular PD-L1, and low efficacy in “cold” immunosuppressive tumors like TNBC. 17 PD-L1 siRNA can specifically silence PD-L1 gene expression through RNA interference, directly blocking the transcription and translation of PD-L1, overcome the delivery defects of mAbs, and reactivating T-cell-mediated antitumor immune responses. 18 Moreover, siP possesses the distinct advantages of small molecular size, easy synthesis, and low cost, making it an ideal alternative to PD-L1 antibodies. 18–20 However, the easy degradation, low cell membrane permeability, and off-target risk of siRNA severely restrict its clinical application. 21 , 22 Therefore, we applied siP instead of ssDNA in the cores to bridge the AgNPs and GQDs through π–π interactions and exhibit a silencing effect. Considering the poor stability of siRNA, we used safe and biodegradable lipids to coat the cores and achieve precise, targeted delivery to tumor cells.

QUE, a natural flavonoid, induces immunogenic cell death (ICD) of tumor cells, promotes the exposure of calreticulin and release of HMGB1, regulates the immune TME, and enhances immune cell infiltration, thereby synergizing with immune therapy. 23–25 Our previously work has also verified the ICD-inducing effect of QUE. 26 Nevertheless, the clinical application of QUE is severely limited by its poor water solubility, low bioavailability, and lack of tumor-targeting ability. 27 To overcome this bottleneck, nanotechnology-based delivery systems (such as liposomes and polymer micelles) have emerged as key strategies for optimizing the application of quercetin. 28–30 Furthermore, cRGD specifically binds to integrin αvβ3, which is highly overexpressed on tumor cells and tumor vascular endothelial cells, 31 endowing nanocarriers with active tumor-targeting ability, enhancing drug accumulation at tumor sites, and improving therapeutic efficacy while reducing systemic toxicity. 32 , 33

Lipid-based nanocarriers represent a highly translatable platform for breast cancer therapy, with proven advantages in improving drug solubility, enhancing tumor accumulation and enabling multi-drug co-delivery. 34 Accumulating studies have validated the synergistic antitumor effect of QUE combined with PD-L1 blockade, either as free drug plus anti-PD-1 antibody or as peptide-loaded nanosystems, providing a solid biological rationale for this combinatorial strategy. 35 , 36 However, existing modalities mainly rely on protein- or peptide-level PD-L1 inhibitors, and lipid-based nanoplatforms co-delivering quercetin with PD-L1 siRNA for gene-level silencing in breast cancer remain rarely reported. Our lipid-coated silver-cored nanoplatform thus offers a novel delivery paradigm for quercetin-based combinational immunotherapy against breast cancer.

The Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was fabricated via the ethanol injection method and characterized by SEM-EDS, agarose gel retardation, cellular uptake and in vitro release evaluation. The remarkable increase in carbon content and the significant decrease in silver content confirmed that the AgNPs were effectively encapsulated by the phospholipid-based organic materials. This bilayer structure could prevent silver ion leakage and improves systemic circulation stability, 37 while providing with a loading capability for lipophilic quercetin and anionic PD-L1 siRNA, achieving synchronous delivery of cargos with disparate physicochemical properties. In terms of colloidal stability, the nanocarrier relies on a synergistic stabilization mechanism of electrostatic repulsion and lipid bilayer-derived steric hindrance, rather than depending solely on high surface charge. This rational design avoids massive non-specific serum protein adsorption and accelerated in vivo reticuloendothelial clearance caused by excessively high positive charge. 38 An optimal N:P ratio of 6:1 enables full electrostatic condensation of siRNA, guaranteeing nucleic acid encapsulation efficiency and anti-nuclease protection.

This enhanced cellular uptake could be ascribed to the cRGD peptide, which specifically recognizes and binds with high affinity to integrin αvβ3 receptors overexpressed on tumor cell surfaces, thereby effectively triggering receptor-mediated endocytosis and markedly accelerating the internalization of the nanoformulation. 32 The final intracellular level of nanoparticles is essentially determined by a dynamic balance between inward endocytosis and outward exocytosis processes. 39 , 40 Such active targeting driven by cRGD-integrin binding significantly elevates the internalization rate and allows fast intracellular accumulation of the active payload, showing a clear advantage over non-targeted formulations that depend on passive diffusion and non-specific adsorption for cellular entry. It is worth noting that αvβ3 integrin receptors follow a rapid recycling pathway after ligand-triggered endocytosis, which in turn shapes the intracellular retention profile of targeted nanoparticles. 41

Furthermore, the nanoformulation exhibits typical tumor microenvironment-triggered pH-responsive release profiles. Sustained slow drug release was shown under neutral physiological media, which maintains structural stability during blood circulation and reduces off-target drug leakage to healthy organs. However, relative rapid cargo release occurs in acidic tumor environment. It is helpful for elevating local tumor therapeutic concentrations. 42 In fact, PAMAM dendrimers in the lipids might modulate pH-responsive release via the proton sponge effect. At pH 5.0, tertiary amine protonation in PAMAM induces osmotic swelling, disrupting the phospholipid bilayer internally and boosting drugs release with lipid headgroup protonation. 43 Release kinetic modeling further reveals differentiated release mechanisms for Ag and QUE. Ag release is co-governed by lipid matrix erosion and Fickian diffusion, with zero-order and Higuchi models showing optimal goodness-of-fit under both pH conditions; the slightly superior fitting of the Higuchi model at neutral pH indicates diffusion plays a more dominant role when the bilayer remains structurally intact. For lipophilic QUE solubilized in the bilayer, release follows first-order diffusion kinetics at pH 7.4, a classic feature of encapsulated hydrophobic drugs driven by concentration gradients, while acidic conditions disrupt lipid packing and shift the release pattern toward matrix-diffusion dominance, resulting in the best fit with the Higuchi model at pH 5.0. The increased release rate constant under acidic conditions quantitatively confirms the pH-accelerated release capacity of the formulation.

As for cell toxicity of Ag-based nanoparticles, the preferential toxicity toward 4T1 cancer cells over NIH3T3 normal fibroblasts. The cytotoxic effect of silver nanoparticles relies on a “Trojan horse” mechanism: once internalized into cells mainly through endocytic pathways, the particles localize to lysosomes, and the acidic lysosomal environment promotes the dissolution of silver ions, which in turn disrupt cellular redox homeostasis and drive apoptotic cell death. 44 In addition, tumor cells carry an intrinsically labile intracellular redox state with persistently raised baseline oxidative load, making them substantially more vulnerable to cytotoxic and oxidative damage driven by silver ions. Normal fibroblasts, by contrast, are furnished with a more well-buffered antioxidant protective system that can effectively counteract moderate oxidative insult from silver exposure and sustain intact cellular physiology and viability. 45 In parallel, the higher IC 5 0 values of all nanoformulations relative to free AgNPs might come from the fact that the outer GQDs shell and lipid bilayer function as diffusional barriers that slow the rapid extracellular release of Ag⁺, and shifts in particle surface properties can further modulate cellular internalization kinetics, which together result in diminished acute cytotoxicity over the 12 h treatment period. 46

The improved intracellular delivery enables the nanoformulations to trigger cellular oxidative stress more effectively. AgNPs slowly release Ag⁺, which binds to sulfhydryl groups of mitochondrial respiratory chain proteins, interferes with electron transfer and causes electron leakage to generate superoxide anions, initiating a ROS cascade that converts H 2 O 2 into hydroxyl radicals. 47 , 48 Unmodified AgNPs are prone to aggregation and have low cellular uptake efficiency, 49 , 50 resulting in limited ROS elevation. 51 As a redox modulator with dual antioxidant-pro-oxidant properties, 24 , 52 QUE could promote oxidative stress via multiple pathways: auto-oxidation to produce semi-quinone radicals and other ROS, depletion of intracellular antioxidants such as glutathione, and disruption of the mitochondrial respiratory chain to trigger electron leakage. 53 With lipid coating and cRGD modification, the cellular uptake of the composite nanoformulations is significantly enhanced, allowing more Ag and QUE to enter cells and accumulate around organelles. However, the dual redox property of QUE may counteract partial Ag-induced oxidative stress at the tested concentration, suggesting that the redox regulation of this nano-system is affected by multiple factors and still requires further in-depth investigation.

In parallel, the nanosystem effectively delivers siRNA into cells to mediate PD-L1 gene silencing. RT-PCR results show that free siRNA barely downregulates PD-L1 mRNA due to poor stability and membrane permeability, while both siRNA-loaded nanoformulations induce significant knockdown, confirming the delivery advantage of nanoparticle encapsulation, however, no significant difference in silencing efficiency was observed between these two formulations, likely because prolonged static incubation allows sufficient non-specific endocytosis of the non-targeted group, weakening the in vitro advantage of cRGD active targeting. Meanwhile, the siRNA-free blank nanocarrier, Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L, caused no obvious PD-L1 downregulation, indicating the silencing effect stems from specific siRNA knockdown rather than non-specific carrier regulation.

Beyond direct tumor cell killing via oxidative stress, the antibacterial activity of the system is core to the synergistic effect of nanocarrier optimization and active components. Although bare AgNPs can disrupt bacterial membrane integrity by releasing Ag⁺ and induce ROS to damage bacterial DNA, 51 their inherent tendency to aggregate limited the effective contact area with bacteria, 49 , 54 showing moderate antibacterial activity. After modification with lipid bilayers, and PEG, the nanocarrier not only effectively improved the colloidal stability and dispersibility of AgNPs, 55 avoiding activity loss caused by aggregation, but also enhanced the adsorption capacity to negatively charged bacterial cell walls through surface charge regulation, facilitating efficient penetration and sustained release of Ag⁺ and prolonging the antibacterial duration. The incorporation of QUE achieved an elevation in antibacterial efficacy, since QUE itself was reported to exert antibacterial effects by disrupting bacterial membrane permeability, inhibiting key metabolic enzyme activities, and depleting intracellular antioxidants (eg, glutathione). 56 , 57 As for the similar antibacterial activity of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L with its corresponding unmodified counterparts, it may be attributed to the steric hindrance and hydrophilic barrier introduced by the long-chain PEG3400 during cRGD conjugation, 58 which moderately weakened the direct contact efficiency between nanoparticles and bacteria. However, it should be emphasized that cRGD is designed to target integrin αvβ3 receptors highly expressed on tumor cells. Its targeting modification enables specific accumulation in tumor tissues in vivo, which can compensate for the slight difference in in vitro antibacterial activity through local high concentrations in tumors. Notably, the antibacterial performance of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was only characterized at the in vitro level in the current work; its actual bacterial regulatory effect within the tumor microenvironment and its direct contribution to the in vivo antitumor efficacy will be further elucidated.

The pharmacokinetic and biodistribution results systematically validate the in vivo delivery advantages of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L. The elevated systemic exposure and reduced clearance of nanoformulations stem from the protective effect of the phospholipid bilayer and PEGylated surface structure. Lipid encapsulation isolates active components from direct contact with blood components. The hydrophilic PEG shell forms a steric barrier on the particle surface, reducing opsonin adsorption and RES recognition, 59 thereby elevating the AUC values. The reduced Vz further verifies that nanocarriers retain most payloads in the systemic circulation, rather than allowing extensive non-specific diffusion into peripheral tissues. The further improved pharmacokinetic parameters of the cRGD-modified formulation prove that cRGD peptide conjugation does not compromise the long-circulating property of the nanocarrier. Instead, the enhanced surface hydrophilicity and particle stability further reduce clearance by the reticuloendothelial system (RES), leading to higher systemic drug exposure. In terms of tissue distribution, it confirmed that nanocarrier modification and cRGD active targeting strategy could effectively optimize the in vivo distribution of Ag and QUE, among which Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L had the optimal tumor targeting performance, mainly due to the synergy of active and passive targeting. The cRGD peptide could specifically bind to αvβ3 integrin highly expressed on tumor cells, mediating the active recognition, internalization and retention of the formulation at tumor sites. The nanocarrier composed of GQDs, phospholipid layer and PEG endowed the formulation with long-circulating properties, which not only prolonged the residence time in systemic circulation, but also realized passive drug enrichment through the EPR effect of tumor tissues, laying a foundation for continuous drug supply to tumors. Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L only achieved passive targeting through the EPR effect, with significantly lower tumor drug enrichment efficiency than the cRGD-modified group. Without carrier protection and targeting ability, these formulations were easily recognized and phagocytosed by the RES system or presented non-specific distribution, mainly accumulating in normal organs such as spleen, liver and lung, resulting in extremely low tumor delivery efficiency and high toxicity risk to normal organs.

Besides of targeted delivery, direct tumoricidal action and bacterial clearance, the superior in vivo antitumor efficacy of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L also stems from immune microenvironment remodeling. The elevated CD3 + CD4 + helper T cell infiltration demonstrates effective activation of T-cell-mediated immunity, arising from the combined effects of quercetin-triggered ICD, 60 PD-L1 siRNA-mediated checkpoint blockade, and Ag-driven intratumoral Fn elimination to remove bacteria-derived immunosuppressive signals that block T cell recruitment, collectively boosting CD4 + T cell infiltration and helper function.

Notably, the Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L did not induce significant numerical expansion of CD8⁺ T cells. Instead, the detected decreased PD-L1⁺CD11c⁺ population of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L mainly reflects the altered antigen presentation state of tumor-infiltrating conventional dendritic cells in vivo. Together with the effectively silence of PD-L1 expression on tumor cells by the delivered PD-L1 siRNA of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L in vitro, the PD-L1 downregulation on both tumor cells and dendritic cells is expected to block the PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitory axis, thereby potentially reversing T cell exhaustion and reinvigorating the antitumor effector function of pre-existing CD8⁺ T cells. 61 , 62 Furthermore, the targeted formulation markedly reduced the proportions of two core immunosuppressive cell populations in the tumor microenvironment, CD4 + CD25 + Foxp3 + Tregs and CD11b + Gr-1 + MDSCs. Tregs suppress effector T cell activity by secreting inhibitory cytokines, while MDSCs block T cell activation and promote immune escape through metabolic interference and oxidative stress. 63 The decline of these two subsets confirms that Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.

The H&E histopathological and serum biochemical results are consistent, verifying the safety of the targeted co-delivery system. The reduced systemic toxicity of nanoformulations mainly derives from three structural advantages: the PEGylated shell decreases reticuloendothelial phagocytosis, pH-responsive release avoids premature drug leakage in circulation, and cRGD-mediated active targeting redirects most payloads to tumor sites, thus lowering off-target exposure in normal tissues. The combined effects of EPR-based passive accumulation, multi-component synergistic tumoricidal action, PD-L1 silencing-mediated immune activation and cRGD-amplified local drug concentration collectively contribute to the extensive tumor necrosis.

## Conclusions

In summary, we constructed a cRGD-modified Ag@GQDs-based co-delivery nanoplatform co-loaded with quercetin and PD-L1 siRNA for Fn-associated triple-negative breast cancer therapy. With favorable physicochemical properties and pH-responsive release characteristics, the nanoplatform achieves prolonged systemic circulation and preferential tumor accumulation through the combination of the EPR effect and cRGD-mediated active targeting. In vitro, it exhibits selective tumoricidal activity via oxidative stress, strong bactericidal efficacy against Fn, and efficient PD-L1 gene silencing in tumor cells. In vivo, the formulation delivers robust antitumor efficacy, effectively remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by boosting CD4⁺ T cell infiltration, downregulating PD-L1 on tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells, and reducing immunosuppressive Treg and MDSC populations, while maintaining negligible systemic toxicity and favorable biocompatibility. Deeper synergistic mechanisms, including the actual antibacterial performance within the complex tumor microenvironment and the specific functional recovery of CD8⁺ T cells, still require further comprehensive validation to advance its translational application potential. Collectively, this multifunctional nanoplatform offers a promising strategy for the precise treatment of bacteria-associated tumors.
conclusions: In summary, we constructed a cRGD-modified Ag@GQDs-based co-delivery nanoplatform co-loaded with quercetin and PD-L1 siRNA for Fn-associated triple-negative breast cancer therapy. With favorable physicochemical properties and pH-responsive release characteristics, the nanoplatform achieves prolonged systemic circulation and preferential tumor accumulation through the combination of the EPR effect and cRGD-mediated active targeting. In vitro, it exhibits selective tumoricidal activity via oxidative stress, strong bactericidal efficacy against Fn, and efficient PD-L1 gene silencing in tumor cells. In vivo, the formulation delivers robust antitumor efficacy, effectively remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by boosting CD4⁺ T cell infiltration, downregulating PD-L1 on tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells, and reducing immunosuppressive Treg and MDSC populations, while maintaining negligible systemic toxicity and favorable biocompatibility. Deeper synergistic mechanisms, including the actual antibacterial performance within the complex tumor microenvironment and the specific functional recovery of CD8⁺ T cells, still require further comprehensive validation to advance its translational application potential. Collectively, this multifunctional nanoplatform offers a promising strategy for the precise treatment of bacteria-associated tumors.

title: Ex vivo Evaluation of Live-MB2 and CX-2 Biotic Strains on Inflammatory and Barrier-Related Biomarkers in a Human Skin Atopic Dermatitis–Like Model

### Objective

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by epidermal barrier disruption and immune dysregulation. Live-MB2 and CX-2 were used in an ex vivo human skin AD-like model, which provides a biologically relevant platform for assessing cosmetic ingredients targeting AD-like features.

### Methods

An AD-like condition was induced in ex vivo human skin explants by repeated tape stripping followed by 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene stimulation. Skin tissues were treated with Live-MB2 or CX-2 via topical or dermal exposure. Epidermal thickness, IgE, and filaggrin levels were evaluated using hematoxylin and eosin, immunofluorescence, and Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay analyses.

Topical application of Live-MB2 and CX-2 significantly reduced epidermal thickness compared with AD-induced controls. IgE levels were significantly reduced, while filaggrin expression indicated a marked increase, indicating barrier recovery. No treatment-related tissue damage was observed.

Live-MB2 and CX-2 showed favorable effects on inflammatory and barrier-related parameters in an ex vivo human skin AD-like model, supporting their potential application as cosmetic ingredients for sensitive and atopic-prone skin.

# Ex vivo Evaluation of Live-MB2 and CX-2 Biotic Strains on Inflammatory and Barrier-Related Biomarkers in a Human Skin Atopic Dermatitis–Like Model

## Abstract
### Objective

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by epidermal barrier disruption and immune dysregulation. Live-MB2 and CX-2 were used in an ex vivo human skin AD-like model, which provides a biologically relevant platform for assessing cosmetic ingredients targeting AD-like features.

### Methods

An AD-like condition was induced in ex vivo human skin explants by repeated tape stripping followed by 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene stimulation. Skin tissues were treated with Live-MB2 or CX-2 via topical or dermal exposure. Epidermal thickness, IgE, and filaggrin levels were evaluated using hematoxylin and eosin, immunofluorescence, and Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay analyses.

### Results

Topical application of Live-MB2 and CX-2 significantly reduced epidermal thickness compared with AD-induced controls. IgE levels were significantly reduced, while filaggrin expression indicated a marked increase, indicating barrier recovery. No treatment-related tissue damage was observed.

### Conclusion

Live-MB2 and CX-2 showed favorable effects on inflammatory and barrier-related parameters in an ex vivo human skin AD-like model, supporting their potential application as cosmetic ingredients for sensitive and atopic-prone skin.

## Keywords
Ex vivo human skin; atopic dermatitis; live biotics; skin barrier; filaggrin; cosmetic ingredients

## Introduction

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a multifactorial inflammatory skin disorder involving epidermal barrier impairment, immune imbalance, and environmental triggers. 1 , 2 The pathogenesis of AD is largely explained by defects in epidermal barrier function and immune system dysregulation. Notably, mutations and reduced expression of the epidermal barrier protein filaggrin (FLG) decrease the stratum corneum’s water-retention capacity and increase trans epidermal water loss. 3 This weakening of the physical barrier facilitates the penetration of allergens and pathogens into the epidermis, thereby triggering an “outside-in” pathogenesis that induces Th2-skewed immune responses and excessive immunoglobulin E (IgE) production. 2 In addition to epidermal barrier disruption, AD is strongly associated with type 2 immune inflammation. Key cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, and IL-31, along with epithelial mediators including thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), contribute to pruritus, inflammation, and further deterioration of skin barrier function. 4 , 5

Recent studies have shown that the skin of patients with AD exhibits a severe reduction in microbial diversity. In particular, the overgrowth of Staphylococcus aureus is closely associated with epidermal barrier damage and the exacerbation of inflammation. 6–8 Consequently, topical application of probiotics to restore the skin microbiome and modulate inflammation has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. Topical probiotics and microbiome-based ingredients contribute to suppressing harmful bacteria by secreting antimicrobial peptides and regulating the innate immune responses of the epidermis. 9

While many topical microbiome interventions currently rely on non-viable bacterial lysates or postbiotics, these inactive derivatives lack the dynamic ability to colonize, continuously secrete active metabolites, and engage in active host-microbe cross-talk. 10 , 11 Therefore, there is a critical need to investigate the direct immunomodulatory and barrier-restoring effects of viable live biotics on human skin. 12–14

Conventional in vitro models using keratinocytes provide mechanistic insights but lack the structural complexity of human skin. 15 Compared with conventional two-dimensional keratinocyte models, an ex vivo human skin model preserves native tissue architecture and epidermal-dermal interactions, thereby providing a more biologically relevant platform for evaluating inflammatory and barrier-related changes in human skin. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the effects of two candidate live biotic strains, Live-MB2 ( Epidermidibacterium keratini ; previously referred to as EPI-7) and CX-2 ( Streptococcus thermophilus ), on inflammatory and barrier-related parameters using an ex vivo human skin AD-like model. 16 , 17 Live-MB2 is a skin-derived strain isolated from the human skin microbiome and reported to be more prevalent in younger individuals, with potential relevance to skin homeostasis and microbiome-associated skin function. 18 CX-2 is a skin-associated strain with reported potential to support dermal recovery, barrier function, and sensitive-skin normalization. 19 Ultimately, we aimed to evaluate their potential application as cosmetic ingredients for sensitive and atopic-prone skin.

## Methods

### Human Skin Explants

Human skin explants were obtained from the Korea Biomedical Research Institute (KBI) under the approval of the Institutional Review Board (IRB No. 2023–0247 and 2023–0210). Korean females (ages 35, 48, 48, 49 years old) were collected from surgical discards with written informed consent in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant national bioethics regulations. Subcutaneous fat was removed, and the skin was sectioned using biopsy punches before culture. The ex vivo skin explants were maintained in a sterile culture system at 37 °C in a 5% CO 2 humidified incubator, as previously described in established models. The tissues were placed on Transwell ® inserts (Corning Inc., Corning, NY, USA) with the epidermal surface exposed to air to reproduce the physiological air–liquid interface of human skin. The culture medium was replaced every 48 hours.

### Induction of AD-Like Condition in Human Skin Explants

To mimic the structural and immunological characteristics of AD ex vivo, an acute AD-like inflammatory state was induced using a combination of mechanical and chemical barrier disruption. After allowing the human skin explants to equilibrate in an air-liquid interface culture for 24 hours, the stratum corneum was mechanically disrupted by repeated tape stripping (30 consecutive times) using standard adhesive discs (D-Squame; CuDerm Co., Dallas, TX, USA). Immediately following the mechanical disruption, the skin explants were topically stimulated with 0.001% 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene dissolved in an appropriate vehicle (eg, acetone and olive oil, 3:1 v/v) to induce a robust allergic inflammatory response. The explants were then incubated at 37°C in a 5% CO 2 humidified atmosphere. This short-term induction protocol, followed by a 48-hour treatment period, was designed to model an acute rather than chronic AD-like response.

### Treatment with Live Biotics

E. keratini Live-MB2 and S. thermophilus CX-2 strains were obtained from the COSMAX Microbiome Bank (Seongnam, South Korea) and had been previously identified by 16S rRNA sequencing. For inoculum preparation, a single colony grown on an agar plate was inoculated into seed culture medium, followed by a 1% secondary inoculation and further cultivation. Live-MB2 and CX-2 were cultured into Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB; MB Cell, Seoul, South Korea) and de Man, Rogosa and Sharpe broth (MRS broth; MB Cell), respectively, and cultured at 37°C for 48 hours. Following incubation, the bacterial cells were harvested by centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 3 minutes. The supernatants were carefully discarded, and the remaining cell pellets were washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to remove any residual culture media. The washed bacterial cells were then resuspended in PBS for subsequent ex vivo experiments. Bacterial concentration was determined by serial dilution plating (10 −3 , 10 −4 , and 10 −5 ), and CFU/mL was calculated using plates within the countable colony range. Following acute AD induction, Live-MB2 and CX-2 were applied to the skin explants either by topical (epidermal) application or by dermal exposure via the culture medium at a designated concentration for each treatment group. The explants were cultured for an additional 48 hours prior to harvest.

### Experimental Design

Skin explants obtained from four independent donors were allocated across all experimental conditions after induction of an acute AD-like state. A total of 11 experimental groups were established: an untreated control (without AD-like induction), a negative control (with AD-like induction), three vehicle-control groups, three Live-MB2 treatment groups, and three CX-2 treatment groups. For each strain, treatment conditions comprised 1×10 6 CFU/mL applied via the dermal-side culture medium, 1×10 3 CFU/mL applied via the dermal-side culture medium, and 1×10 6 CFU/mL applied topically to the epidermal surface, with corresponding vehicle-control conditions. Each donor contributed one skin punch to each of the 11 groups; therefore, each experimental group contained four explants (n = 4 biological replicates, one explant per donor). This donor-matched allocation ensured that tissues from all four donors were represented across all experimental conditions and minimized donor-dependent bias.

### Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) Staining

To assess morphological changes and epidermal thickness, the harvested tissue samples were immediately fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 hours and embedded in paraffin blocks. The blocks were sectioned into 4–5 μm thick slices using a microtome. After deparaffinization and rehydration, the sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) according to standard protocols. Histological images were captured using a light microscope (original magnification×100). Epidermal thickness was quantitatively measured from the granular layer to the basal layer using image analysis software (ImageJ; National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA). For each explant, measurements were obtained from three randomly selected fields, and the mean value was used for analysis.

### Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) for IgE and FLG Quantification

To quantify specific protein levels, the skin tissues were homogenized in RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with a protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatants were collected. Total protein concentration was determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit. The levels of IgE and FLG in the tissue lysates were then measured using commercially available human-specific ELISA kits strictly following the manufacturer’s instructions. The optical density was read at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Each sample was assayed in duplicate, and the mean value was used for analysis. The mean of the duplicate wells was treated as a single technical measurement for each donor-derived explant. For IgE quantification, one donor-derived sample produced no detectable signal and was therefore excluded from the IgE analysis, resulting in n = 3 biological replicates for this endpoint; all other endpoints included n = 4 biological replicates.

### Immunofluorescence (IF) Staining

For the spatial localization and expression analysis of FLG, tissue sections were deparaffinized and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval using a citrate buffer (pH 6.0). Sections were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin for 1 hour at room temperature to prevent non-specific binding. Subsequently, the sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with a primary antibody targeting human FLG. After washing, sections were incubated with a fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibody for 1 hour in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole. Fluorescence images were obtained using a fluorescence microscope (original magnification ×100). For each explant, three representative fields were analyzed under identical imaging conditions, and the mean signal intensity was used for analysis.

### Statistical Analysis

Unless otherwise specified, analyses were performed using four independent biological replicates (n = 4; one explant per donor per experimental condition). The IgE analysis included three biological replicates (n = 3) because one donor-derived sample yielded no detectable signal. Quantitative data are expressed as the mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). The normal distribution of the data was assessed, and statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance followed by an appropriate post-hoc test (Tukey’s or Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test) or paired Student’s t -test for two-group comparisons. A two-sided p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results

### Tissue Safety and Epidermal Thickness

No treatment-related tissue damage was observed, indicating the safety of the live biotics on human tissue ( Figure 1 ). In the AD-induced control group, epidermal thickness increased markedly to 112.27 μm compared with 56.87 μm in the untreated control group. However, this AD-induced hyperproliferation was significantly reduced following topical application of 41.15% in the Live-MB2 (epidermal thickness, 66.07 μm) and 47.42% in the CX-2 group (59.04 μm) compared with the AD-induced control group, restoring the tissue closer to a normal state ( Figure 2 ). Figure 1 Representative histological images and skin safety evaluation in an ex vivo atopic-like skin model. Cross-sections of human skin explants from a 35-year-old South Korean female donor were visualized via H&E staining (original magnification × 100). (1) Untreated control (without atopy induction); (2) Negative control (with atopy induction); (3–5) Vehicle-treated groups; (6–8) Live-MB2 treated groups; (9–11) CX-2 treated groups. Symbols indicate the presence (+) or absence (−) of the listed condition or treatment. Scale bar = 100 μm. Live-MB2 and CX-2 groups are tested at 1 by 10 superscript 6 CFU/mL (1 percent live biotics) and 1 by 10 superscript 3 CFU/mL (0.001 percent live biotics) with high dermal, medium dermal, or topical epidermal application. Each row includes an H&E stained micrograph of skin cross-sections. The untreated control shows normal histology, while the negative control displays thicker epidermis due to atopy induction. ## Discussion

### Key Findings

This study evaluated the effects of novel probiotic ingredients, including Live-MB2 and CX-2, utilizing an ex vivo human skin AD-like model. Live-MB2 and CX-2 treatment was not associated with tissue damage. Epidermal thickness was significantly reduced in both topically treated groups. IgE protein expression significantly reduced in both the topically treated Live-MB2 and CX-2 groups compared to AD-induced control group. FLG protein expression significantly recovered in the topical CX-2 group. The novelty of the present study lies in the evaluation of these two candidates live biotic strains in a human ex vivo AD-like skin model that preserves native tissue architecture and epidermal–dermal interactions. These findings suggest that Live-MB2 and CX-2 may contribute to barrier-repairing and anti-inflammatory functions, without evidence of overt tissue damage under the present experimental conditions.

### Plausible Underlying Mechanisms

The reduction in epidermal thickness and the enhancement of FLG expression observed in this study suggest that Live-MB2 and CX-2 may contribute to barrier-related improvement in AD-like skin. A pathological hallmark of AD is the overexpression of Th2 cytokines (eg, IL-4, IL-13), which inhibits the synthesis of FLG in the epidermis, thereby contributing to barrier dysfunction and inflammation. 20–22 The decreasing trend in IgE levels and the recovery of FLG expression, particularly in the topical CX-2 group, suggest that live biotic treatment may influence processes associated with barrier impairment and inflammatory dysregulation in AD-like skin, although the underlying molecular mechanisms were not directly examined in the present study. 4

The observed reductions in epidermal thickness and the enhancement of FLG expression further support the potential relevance of both Live-MB2 and CX-2 to barrier-related changes in AD-like skin. Topically applied live biotics may interact with keratinocytes at the skin surface to induce local immune tolerance or stimulate the production of essential skin barrier proteins. 23 , 24 In this regard, previous studies reported that metabolites and antimicrobial peptides secreted by skin commensal bacteria inhibit inflammatory microbes and protect the physical barrier. 6 , 25 , 26 These findings are consistent with previous reports on the efficacy of topical microbiome modulators.

### Comparisons with Previous Studies

This study utilized an ex vivo model to evaluate probiotic ingredients. Compared with conventional 2D in vitro keratinocyte cultures, the ex vivo human skin model provides a more physiologically relevant platform by preserving native tissue architecture and epidermal–dermal interactions. 16 , 17 Within this experimental context, the observed effects of Live-MB2 and CX-2 support their potential relevance to barrier-related and inflammatory changes in AD-like skin.

Although conventional immunosuppressive therapies, including topical corticosteroids, are widely used in AD management, the present findings should be interpreted cautiously because this study was performed in an ex vivo model without a positive control or direct mechanistic analyses. 27 , 28 Accordingly, Live-MB2 and CX-2 may be considered candidate live biotic ingredients with potential relevance to skin barrier- and inflammation-related applications, rather than established therapeutic alternatives at this stage. The observed restoration of epidermal barrier-related readouts by CX-2 and Live-MB2, together with the absence of overt tissue damage under the present experimental conditions, supports their potential relevance to microbiome-based approaches for AD-like skin. 4 Beyond their mechanistic benefits, the direct topical application of live biotics represents a complementary strategy from transient symptom management to proactive skin ecosystem restoration. 13 , 14 Because viable strains like Live-MB2 and CX-2 can continuously secrete functional metabolites and dynamically engage in host-microbe cross-talk, they could offer sustained barrier-enhancing efficacy compared to non-viable postbiotics. 29 Practically, these findings underscore the high industrial and medical applicability of live biotics as next-generation dermo cosmetics (cosmeceuticals) and adjunctive treatments in clinical dermatology for sensitive and atopic-prone skin. 30

### Strengths and Limitations

There are several limitations to our study. First, donor-to-donor variation inherent to ex vivo human skin AD-like models may introduce variability in outcomes attributable to intrinsic genetic differences across donated skin tissues. 31 In particular, donor-specific characteristics such as sex, age, and ethnicity represent important variables that should be carefully considered in future investigations to elucidate differential immune responses in the skin. 31 , 32 In this study, tissue samples were collected from four donors of varying ages, with deliberate emphasis placed on ensuring donor diversity. Nevertheless, further studies incorporating a larger donor cohort will be required to comprehensively assess the potential confounding influence of sex and ethnicity on the observed outcomes. In addition, no positive control, such as an established AD treatment or a previously validated probiotic/postbiotic formulation, was included in the present study; therefore, the relative efficacy of Live-MB2 and CX-2 could not be determined. Second, the immune responses observed in ex vivo human skin AD-like models are inherently limited in their ability to reflect in vivo conditions, particularly because these systems lack systemic immune responses, circulating immune cells, vascular components, and long-term microbiome interactions that are relevant to AD pathophysiology. 31 Moreover, the current study primarily evaluated phenotypic endpoints, including epidermal thickness, IgE, and FLG-related readouts, and did not directly assess key AD-associated inflammatory mediators such as IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, TSLP, or related signaling mechanisms. Future investigations employing randomized controlled trials in in vivo settings would be warranted to further validate and extend the explanatory power of the findings reported in the present study. 33 Although the strains used in this study had been previously identified by 16S rRNA sequencing, no additional sequencing was performed immediately before the experiment. In addition, viability was not re-confirmed immediately prior to tissue application, and stability during the experimental period was not separately evaluated.

Despite these limitations, our study has important strengths. This study provides the first comprehensive ex vivo assessment of the effects of two novel live biotics, Live-MB2 and CX-2, on AD-induced skin. While conventional in vitro models utilizing keratinocytes offer valuable mechanistic insights, they inherently lack the cellular complexity of intact human skin. 15 Accordingly, the present findings should be interpreted as preliminary ex vivo evidence supporting the potential of these strains in skin barrier- and inflammation-related applications. Our findings serve as a foundational ex vivo evidence base to inform the development of candidate active ingredients for medical-grade skincare applications.

## Conclusion

Live-MB2 and CX-2 demonstrated promising effects on inflammatory- and barrier-related parameters in an ex vivo human skin AD-like model. These findings provide preliminary ex vivo evidence supporting the potential of live biotics as microbiome-based candidate active ingredients for sensitive and atopic-prone skin. In particular, the observed changes in epidermal thickness, IgE, and FLG-related readouts support the further evaluation of these strains in skin barrier- and inflammation-related applications. This study also highlights the value of ex vivo human skin models as biologically relevant platforms for the preclinical assessment of candidate microbiome-based ingredients. Further in vivo and clinical studies are warranted to confirm their long-term efficacy, safety, and clinical relevance.

title: Non‐Invasively Quantitative Raman Imaging for Calculation of Lymphatic Transport Kinetics of Micelles in Mice
abstract: Raman spectroscopy based on surface enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) has received great interest in biological and medical applications owing to its high specificity and sensitivity. However, a reliable and quantitative SERS analysis in vivo is a great challenge since SERS is affected by the unevenly distributed field enhancement in hot spots of nanoparticle substrate and unpredictable nanoparticle aggregation in the complex biological environment. Here, we present non‐invasively quantitative Raman imaging through stacking‐induced intermolecular charge transfer‐enhanced Raman scattering (SICTERS) without relying on substrate. Based on the Raman imaging with SICTERS micelles, a quantitative method is established to accurately calculate the concentration of micelles in draining lymph nodes (DLNs) following subcutaneous administration. A physiologically based pharmacokinetic model is generated to fit the concentration‐time curve of the SICTERS micelles in DLNs (R 2 > 0.99), which calculates the pharmacokinetic parameters of the lymphatic transport of micelles with different sizes and surface charges. The optimized SICTERS micelles loading ovalbumin (OVA) as model antigen exhibits significant anti‐tumor effect in mice bearing B16‐OVA melanoma following vaccination. This study demonstrates a quantitative in vivo Raman imaging platform based on SICTERS for image‐based pharmacokinetic modeling of micellar transport in lymphatics.

# Non‐Invasively Quantitative Raman Imaging for Calculation of Lymphatic Transport Kinetics of Micelles in Mice

## Abstract
Raman spectroscopy based on surface enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) has received great interest in biological and medical applications owing to its high specificity and sensitivity. However, a reliable and quantitative SERS analysis in vivo is a great challenge since SERS is affected by the unevenly distributed field enhancement in hot spots of nanoparticle substrate and unpredictable nanoparticle aggregation in the complex biological environment. Here, we present non‐invasively quantitative Raman imaging through stacking‐induced intermolecular charge transfer‐enhanced Raman scattering (SICTERS) without relying on substrate. Based on the Raman imaging with SICTERS micelles, a quantitative method is established to accurately calculate the concentration of micelles in draining lymph nodes (DLNs) following subcutaneous administration. A physiologically based pharmacokinetic model is generated to fit the concentration‐time curve of the SICTERS micelles in DLNs (R 2 > 0.99), which calculates the pharmacokinetic parameters of the lymphatic transport of micelles with different sizes and surface charges. The optimized SICTERS micelles loading ovalbumin (OVA) as model antigen exhibits significant anti‐tumor effect in mice bearing B16‐OVA melanoma following vaccination. This study demonstrates a quantitative in vivo Raman imaging platform based on SICTERS for image‐based pharmacokinetic modeling of micellar transport in lymphatics.

## Keywords
lymphatic transport; non‐invasive Raman imaging; pharmacokinetic model; quantitative analysis; vaccine

## Introduction

Raman imaging has advantages of high specificity and low susceptibility to photobleaching, showing great potentials for biomedical application [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ]. By using the surface enhanced Raman scattering (SERS), small Raman molecules are adsorbed onto inorganic Au or Ag substrate whose Raman scattering signal can be remarkably amplified [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. However, the quantitative SERS remains a great challenge. Due to the inherently near‐field phenomenon of SERS, the overall Raman signals are determined by coherent collective electron oscillations, the so‐called localized surface plasmon resonances, which induce enhanced electromagnetic fields (hot spots) surrounding the metallic nanostructure. The field enhancement in the hot spots may vary by several orders of magnitude depending on the local structure like nanoparticle size [ 9 ], shape [ 9 , 10 ], crystal face [ 11 ], surface roughness [ 12 ], dispersing state [ 13 ], and interparticle spacing [ 14 , 15 ], even if the Raman molecules are uniformly distributed on the metal surface [ 16 , 17 ]. Moreover, the uncontrollable aggregation of nanoparticles resulted in the random distribution of hot spots with subsequent signal heterogeneity [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ]. Through the incorporation of Raman internal standard, a reliable and direct quantitative SERS analysis has been achieved in vitro [ 23 ]. Nevertheless, the much more complex biological environment in vivo causes nanoparticles to produce unpredictable nano distance and surface deformation, resulting in fluctuations in Raman signal [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ]. To date, in vivo quantitative SERS imaging has not been accomplished.

Recently, we have reported the stacking‐induced charge transfer‐enhanced Raman scattering (SICTERS), which can enhance the Raman scattering signal of small molecules by self‐stacking without relying on an external metal substrate [ 28 , 29 ]. Compared with the traditional SERS gold nanoprobe, the Raman scattering cross‐section per SICTERS nanoparticle is 1350 times higher [ 28 ]. A side‐by‐side comparison of in vivo imaging between SICTERS nanoparticles with 4‐nitrobenzenethiol (4‐NBT)‐labeled gap‐enhanced Raman tags (Au GERTs) has been performed [ 28 ]. The intradermal injection of Au GERTs at a dose of 80 µg of Au does not yield transdermal Raman signals in axillary lymph nodes (ALNs), while the injection of the SICTERS nanoparticles at a dose of 20 µg SICTERS molecules offers noninvasive transdermal imaging of ALNs. Besides, unlike SERS dependent on the hot spots formed by local metal structure and the distribution patterns of Raman molecules onto metal surface, the SICTERS molecules stack in the core of the micellar structure through nano‐assembly. The particle size of SICTERS nanoparticles does not cause changes in the intermolecular distance of BBT stacks, or not interfere with the Raman signal [ 28 ], which provides a rationale for in vivo quantitative analysis of SICTERS.

Vaccines play a pivotal role in preventing and controlling human infectious diseases and cancer [ 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ]. The SICTERS nanoprobes offer non‐invasive and highly sensitive Raman imaging of lymphatic drainage in mice, which has not been achieved by SERS [ 28 ]. However, there is a lack of an approach to quantitative analysis of nanoparticle transport from lymphatic vessels to lymph nodes based on real‐time Raman imaging and their pharmacokinetic modeling and calculation.

Here, we use 1,2‐distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphoethanolamine‐polyethyleneimine (DSPE‐PEG‐PEI) to encapsulate SICTERS molecule 4,7‐bis(4‐(2‐ethylhexyl)thiophen‐2‐yl)benzobis [ c ] [1,2,5] thiadiazole (BBT) to prepare micelles for non‐invasively continuous Raman imaging of their lymphatic transport following subcutaneous injection into the footpad of mice. A standard curve is established by the quantitative method, that calculates the concentration of SICTERS micelles in the popliteal lymph node (PLN), afferent lymphatic vessel (ALV), or efferent lymphatic vessel (ELV) of mice based on the SICTERS images. The accuracy of the calculated concentration in PLN based on the Raman imaging is verified by the concentration directly measured through tissue extraction. The concentration‐time curve of SICTERS micelles in PLN is acquired to calculate C max and area under the curve (AUC). Moreover, we generate a physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to calculate pharmacokinetics, including influx rate constant k a and efflux rate constant k b (Figure 1 ). Four types of micelles with different particle sizes and surface charges were compared to demonstrate differences in pharmacokinetics. Lastly, the optimized SICTERS micelles loading antigen ovalbumin (OVA) as micellar vaccines significantly inhibit the growth of B16‐OVA melanoma in mice.

## Results

### Quantitative Analysis of SICTERS Micelles in Lymphatics Through Non‐Invasive Raman Imaging

Four types of SICTERS micelles were prepared. DSPE‐PEG‐PEI was used to encapsulate BBT for preparing PEI‐100 micelles and PEI‐170 micelles with average diameters of 97 and 168 nm, and average zeta potentials of 11.47 and 9.97 mV, respectively (Figures 2a and S1 ). The negatively charged COOH micelles were prepared using 1,2‐distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphoethanolamine‐N‐[carboxy (polyethylene glycol)] (DSPE‐PEG‐COOH) to encapsulate BBT, characterized by an average zeta potential of ‐32 mV. The PEI‐100 micelles were further used to prepare micellar vaccines through electrostatic adsorption of antigen OVA and adjuvant oligodeoxynucleotides containing CpG motifs (CpG) (Figure S1 ). When the ratio of DSPE‐PEG‐PEI to total lipid was 0.3, the optimal micellar vaccines were obtained with OVA and CpG encapsulation efficiency of 52.15% and 51.53%, respectively, and an average zeta potential of −1.5 mV close to neutral (Figure S1 ). Both COOH micelles and micellar vaccines had an average diameter of 100 nm. The raw Raman spectrum of PEI‐100 micelle showed characteristic peaks at 894 cm − 1 and 1264 cm − 1 with a gradually increasing fluorescence background. After baseline correction, the Raman shifts of both peaks remained unchanged, the Raman peak intensity variation relative to the baseline at 894 cm − 1 was merely 0.6% compared with the raw spectrum (Figure S2 ), indicating that the fluorescence background did not significantly influence the Raman shift or intensity of the characteristic peak at 894 cm − 1 . The Raman spectra of all SICTERS micelles showed characteristic peaks at 894 and 1264 cm −1 with similar signal‐to‐noise ratios (Figures 2b and S3 ). The Raman intensity (894 cm −1 ) of all the micelles showed a good linear relationship with BBT concentration.

The PLNs and their draining lymphatic vessels are located under the mouse leg skin and on the surface of superficial muscle tissue at a depth of approximately 0.3–0.5 mm [ 34 , 35 ]. Based on such anatomic structure, a quantitatively analytical method was developed through which a capillary glass tube containing different concentrations of PEI‐100 micelles was covered with depilated mouse leg skin (Figure 2c ). Raman imaging of the micelles in the glass was performed from the top of the skin excited at 785 nm (Figure 2d,e ). At a concentration ranging from 0.1875 to 3 mg/g of BBT, the Raman intensity of the micelles showed a good linear relationship with their concentrations (R 2 = 0.9980, Figure 2f ). After subcutaneous injection of PEI‐100 micelles into the mouse footpad, the maximum penetration depth of SICTERS Raman imaging was 2.0 mm by covering exposed PLNs with various pieces of porcine skin slices, demonstrating the ability of non‐invasive Raman imaging of superficial lymphatic structures in mice (Figure S4 ). To calculate the concentrations in vivo, the mice were divided into 3 groups, non‐invasive Raman imaging was conducted at 15 min, 1 h, and 4 h post subcutaneous injection of PEI‐100 micelles into the mouse footpad, respectively. The images clearly delineated the location and morphology of PLNs and lymphatic vessels with a high signal‐to‐noise ratio (Figure 2g ). The average value of Raman intensity (894 cm −1 ) of all the pixels in the circled PLN area in Figure 2g was substituted into the standard curve in Figure 2f to obtain the calculated BBT concentrations. To verify the accuracy of the calculated values, the PLNs of mice following the imaging at each time point post injection were collected. BBT were extracted from the PLN homogenate, whose actual concentrations were measured by fluorescence analysis. The results confirmed that the calculated BBT concentrations in PLN were consistent with the actual concentrations (Figure 2h ). Besides, the minimum injection dose of SICTERS micelles for the non‐invasively quantitative analysis of PLN was 25 µg of BBT (Figure S5 ).

### Continuously Quantitative Imaging and Non‐Compartmental Analysis of Lymphatic Transport of SICTERS Micelles

We then performed continuous Raman imaging to track the lymphatic transport of different SICTERS micelles in mice (Figures 3a,b and S6–S16 ). The Raman intensity of pixels that exceeded the sensitivity (15 a.u.) in the location of lymphatic vessels or lymph nodes was circled to calculate the average intensity. These average values were used to calculate the concentrations of BBT based on the standard curve in Figure 2f to obtain the concentration‐time curve of PLN, ALV, and ELV using non‐compartment model, respectively (Figure 3c–e ). Compared with PEI‐100 micelles, PEI‐170 micelles with larger particle size exhibited significantly lower C max and reduced AUC values in PLN, ALV, and ELV, indicating less lymphatic transport for larger‐sized micelles (Figures 3c–e and S17 ). With similar particle sizes, the negatively charged COOH micelles showed significantly higher C max and AUC in PLN and ALV than the positively charged PEI‐100 micelles, respectively, suggesting that a negatively surface charge facilitates lymphatic transport of micelles (Figures 3c,d and S18–S20 ). The micellar vaccines following loading the antigen and adjuvant did not significantly change C max and AUC in PLN or ALV compared with PEI‐100 micelles (Figures 3c,d and S18–S20 ). During continuous Raman imaging, the skin surface temperature increased from 32.1°C to 33.9°C (Figure S21a ), which complies with clinical safety standards for contact optical imaging systems (< 43°C) [ 36 , 37 ]. After 240 min of the entire imaging study, the mouse skin, PLNs, ALVs, and ELVs were collected for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, respectively (Figure S21b ). The epidermal and dermal morphology of skin tissue remained intact without obvious inflammatory infiltration, necrosis, or tissue damage. PLNs, ALVs, or ELVs did not show evident histologic damage or inflammatory response. Next, we evaluated the photostability of SICTERS micelle after repeated Raman imaging (Figure S22a ). The Raman intensity at 894 cm − 1 maintained 97.5%–99% (Figure S22b ), suggesting that repeated Raman imaging did not substantially affect quantitative signal readout. UV–vis absorption (Figure S22c ) and fluorescence spectra (Figure S22d ) were nearly unchanged, indicating minimal photodegradation under the experimental conditions [ 38 ]. Moreover, SICTERS micelles did not show significant changes in particle sizes (Figure S22e ), and the structure was relatively intact (Figure S22f ).

### Pharmacokinetics of SICTERS Micellar Lymphatic Transport via PBPK Model

Thanks to the valves in lymphatic vessels, the drainage of lymph fluid from ALV to PLN and then to ELV is unidirectional [ 39 , 40 ]. Assuming the amount of SICTERS micelles in PLN ( X ) follows the first‐order rate (linear) process, a PBPK model is generated considering PLN as one single compartment (Figure 4a ). The rate of change of X in PLN (d X /d t ) conforms to the differential Equation ( 1 ): (1) d X d t = k a X a − k b X k a and k b indicate the influx rate constant from ALV and efflux rate constant to ELV, respectively (Figure 4a ). Through formula derivation and calculation (see Supporting Information ), the kinetic Equation ( 2 ) for lymphatic transport is obtained, where C is the concentration of SICTERS micelles in PLN and A is a constant. (2) C = A e − k b t − e − k a t

The data of concentrations over time (Figure 3c ) of all different micelles were well fitted with this kinetic model, evidenced by that the R 2 values analyzed through least‐squares curve fitting algorithms of three mice were all above 0.99 (Figures 4b and S6–S16 ). The t max , C max , and AUC values of PLN were calculated without significant difference between using this PBPK model and by the non‐compartmental model above, further validating the feasibility of the PBPK model (Figure S23 ). The kinetic results revealed k a > k b , supporting the observation that the lymphatic transport of SICTERS micelles in ALVs was faster than that in ELVs (Figures 4 and S24 ). Compared with PEI‐100 micelles, the lager‐sized PEI‐170 micelles showed significantly lower C max and AUC in PLN attributed to quicker influx of smaller t 1/2(a) value and slower efflux of larger t 1/2(b) value (Figure 4c ). These results demonstrated that the particle size had a pronounced impact on all the investigated pharmacokinetic parameters. However, with the same particle size of about 100 nm, the micellar surface charge did not significantly affect k a and k b , but influenced C max and AUC (Figure S24 ). Compared with the PEI‐100 micelles, the negatively charged COOH micelles exhibited significantly higher C max and AUC, respectively. Whereas, the micellar vaccines of nearly neutral surface charge showed similar pharmacokinetic profiles with the PEI‐100 micelles, indicating that loading antigens and adjuvants did not significantly affect the lymphatic transport.

### The Anti‐Tumor Immune Effect of Micellar Vaccines

Micellar vaccines were immunized into mice bearing B16‐OVA melanoma according to the regimen shown in Figure 5a . The micellar vaccines significantly prolonged the median survival time of the tumor‐bearing mice (33 days) compared with the OVA & CpG solution group (26 days) (Figures 5b and S25 ). The immune cells in PLNs, spleen, or tumor of mice following different treatments were subjected to flow cytometric analysis (Figure S26 ). Compared with the OVA & CpG solution, the micellar vaccines significantly induced the activation and antigen presentation of dendritic cells (DCs) in PLNs (Figures 5c and S27 ). Moreover, the micellar vaccines increased the proportion of CD4 + T cells and CD8 + T cells in PLNs and spleen, promoting the secretion of interferon‐γ (IFN‐γ) and granzyme B (GranB), respectively (Figures 5d–f , S27 and S28 ). The micellar vaccines also significantly promoted the maturation and activation of DCs and the infiltration of CD8 + T cells in tumors, respectively (Figure S29 ). In the micellar vaccine group, the mouse body weights (Figure S30 ), organ coefficients (Figure S31 ), hematologic analysis indicators, and liver and kidney function indicators (Table S2 ) were all within normal ranges. The results of histopathological analysis by H&E staining did not show significant pathologic changes in major organs (Figure S32 ), preliminary confirming biocompatibility and biosafety of the micellar vaccines.

## Discussion

The penetration depth of SICTERS imaging (2.0 mm) is superior to that of many reported SERS‐based Raman imaging (Table S3 ). SICTERS Raman imaging exhibits superior performance in quantitative analysis in vivo that SERS may not achieve [ 28 ]. SERS relies on the strong localized surface plasmon resonance generated on the surface of metal nanoparticles such as gold and silver. Moreover, the SERS effect usually depends on the random aggregation state of nanoparticles [ 16 , 17 ]. When Raman reporter molecules are close to the hotspot regions, their Raman signals are dramatically amplified [ 41 , 42 ]. However, due to the assembly of nanoparticles and the influence of the biological environment, the hotspots are distributed unevenly. In practical applications, biological fluids, proteins, and ions can influence the distribution and number of the hotspots, leading to poor signal reproducibility and unstable quantitative correlations [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 26 ]. In contrast, SICTERS performs through electron charge transfer processes induced by the intermolecular stacking of Raman reporter molecules themselves, which does not require metal nanostructures. In the aggregated state through nano‐assembly, the molecules stack in the core of the nanoparticles or micelles, leading to more uniform and stable signal gain. Moreover, the size, surface charge, and surface adsorption of the micelles do not affect the aggregation of BBT molecules within the micellar core, thus resulting in relatively consistent Raman signals and making them comparable (Figure S3 ). The structure of molecular assembly provides a theoretical basis for the consistency and reproducibility of SICTERS imaging and precise quantitative analysis in vivo.

Fluorescence imaging has been widely adopted for in vivo biodistribution and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) tracking due to its high sensitivity, rapid imaging capability, and relatively deep tissue penetration [ 43 , 44 , 45 ]. The near‐infrared window II (NIR‐II) fluorescent lymphatic mapping was first pioneered using carbon nanotube‐derived probes [ 46 ]. Highly bright NIR‐II fluorophores were further developed for high‐resolution visualization of lymphatic vessels and sentinel lymph nodes [ 47 ]. However, for quantitative analysis in vivo, fluorescence intensity may not accurately reflect the intact LNPs, as fluorescence signal may be derived from dissociated or free fluorophores rather than nanoparticle‐associated labels [ 48 , 49 ]. In a complex biological environment, the dissociation, leakage, or metabolic cleavage of fluorophores from nanocarriers leads to signals that misrepresent the actual LNP distribution [ 50 ]. Second, the fluorophores are susceptible to quenching and photobleaching under prolonged excitation, severely compromising long‐term continuous monitoring [ 51 , 52 ]. Yet, to the best of our knowledge, fluorescence imaging has not been reported for quantitative pharmacokinetic modeling of lymphatic transport kinetics of LNPs.

Comparatively, the SICTERS Raman signal depends on the intermolecular stacking of BBT molecules within the micellar core. Once the micellar structure is disrupted, the ordered molecular stacking collapses and the Raman signal disappears [ 28 ]. Thus, the SICTERS signal reports the concentration of intact micelles. Second, Raman scattering is inherently resistant to photobleaching and quenching, enabling stable long‐term acquisition [ 1 , 53 ]. However, compared with fluorescence imaging, Raman imaging is constrained by limited penetration depth, which is advantageous primarily in superficial layers and transparent tissues [ 41 ]. Moreover, because Raman imaging requires point‐by‐point acquisition of Raman signals, its imaging speed is much slower than that of fluorescence imaging [ 54 , 55 ]. In recent years, the development of high‐penetration Raman microscope [ 56 , 57 ] and high‐speed Raman instrument [ 58 , 59 ] is expected to further broaden the applications of SICTERS in quantitative in vivo Raman imaging, extending beyond quantification of lymphatic transport. Furthermore, fluorescence imaging enables high‐sensitivity whole‐body visualization of LNP biodistribution, while Raman‐based SICTERS provides quantitative pharmacokinetic modeling of lymphatic transport. The two imaging modalities are highly complementary for integrated in vivo analysis of nanoparticle dynamics.

Inter‐individual variability in Raman imaging mainly arises from differences in skin thickness, tissue hydration, lipid/protein composition, lymphatic anatomy, thereby affecting signal intensity and spatial distribution [ 1 , 40 ]. Our method used a skin‐covered quantification approach that mimicked the in vivo optical barrier to reduce errors caused by tissue attenuation mismatch [ 60 ]. Although our method improved the reliability of quantitative in vivo comparisons, it cannot fully eliminate biological heterogeneity. Future studies should employ larger study cohorts alongside mixed‐effects statistical models to separate biological variability from measurement variability [ 61 ]. Besides, Raman imaging combined with ultrasound imaging could provide anatomical depth correction and improve the accuracy of concentration estimation in heterogeneous tissues [ 62 ].

The efficacy of vaccines hinges upon the targeted delivery of antigens to lymph nodes to elicit sufficiently protective and therapeutic immune response [ 63 , 64 , 65 , 66 , 67 ]. Real‐time tracking of lymphatic transport of vaccines and analysis of their transport kinetics are imperative to evaluate and optimize the lymph node‐targeted delivery of vaccines, especially various nanovaccines [ 68 ]. A three‐compartment pharmacokinetic model has been generated to describe the transport efficiency of nanoparticles from tissues into lymphatic vessels [ 69 ]. However, quantitative analysis of nanoparticle transport from lymphatic vessels to lymph nodes based on real‐time imaging and their pharmacokinetic modeling and calculation has not yet been reported.

Here, we employ the first‐order kinetics of PBPK modeling to fit the concentration‐time curves of different micelles in DLNs with satisfactory fitting outcomes (Figure 4 ). The micelles with smaller particle size and higher negative surface charge exhibit greater accumulation (AUC), which is consistent with previous reports [ 70 , 71 , 72 ]. The micelles with smaller diameters and higher negative surface charges are more likely to enter the lymphatic circulation from the interstitial space and are more readily transported along with the lymphatic fluid [ 73 , 74 ]. Beyond the extent of transport, the PBPK model partitions the lymphatic system into well‐defined structural compartments (e.g., ALV, PLN, and ELV) and analyzes the dynamic concentrations of micelles in these regions, respectively. As a result, the key parameters, including C max , t max , t 1/2(a) , t 1/2(b) , k a, and k b have been obtained to provide guidance for the precise design of the lymph node‐targeted delivery of nanovaccines (Figure 4 ). Our results demonstrate that the micellar vaccine with optimized lymph node‐targeting ability exhibits significant antitumor efficacy in a murine tumor model (Figure 5 ). The efficient transport to lymph nodes promotes the intranodal enrichment of antigens and adjuvants, further enhancing the DC‐mediated antigen presentation and the T cell‐mediated cytotoxic immune activity [ 75 ].

This study demonstrates a quantitative in vivo Raman imaging platform based on SICTERS for image‐based pharmacokinetic modeling of micellar transport in lymphatics in animals. Nevertheless, there remain substantial gaps before its clinical translation and practical application. The thickness of human skin significantly varies across anatomical sites. Human skin, including epidermis and dermis exhibits variable thickness, mainly ranging from 1 to 2.2 mm [ 76 , 77 ]. High‐frequency ultrasound and optical coherence tomography studies have demonstrated that the skin thickness in the inguinal region of adults is 1.1–2.2 mm, while in the axillary region it is 1.0–1.8 mm [ 78 , 79 ]. The cutaneous lymphatic plexus originates in the dermal papillary layer at a depth of only 0.3–0.8 mm. Whereas collecting lymphatic vessels are typically located in the superficial subcutaneous fat at depths of approximately 1–2 mm [ 80 ]. Inguinal superficial lymph nodes are located within subcutaneous tissue below the inguinal ligament. Ultrasound measurements indicate that some superficial lymph nodes are located at depths < 2 mm in certain individuals [ 81 ].

In humans, vaccines are normally administered into the deltoid muscle, and the primary lymphatic drainage is directed to the axillary lymph node [ 39 ]. These axillary lymph nodes are typically located several millimeters to centimeters beneath the skin surface depending on body habitus [ 82 ]. Axillary level I lymph nodes (low axillary lymph nodes) are within a range of 1–2 mm below the skin surface, particularly sentinel lymph nodes located near the lateral border of the pectoralis major muscle [ 83 ]. Accordingly, a penetration depth of approximately 2 mm achieved by SICTERS imaging may be used for imaging dermal lymphatic plexuses and partial superficial axillary lymph nodes. However, this technique under current imaging condition may be insufficient to visualize human lymph nodes located at depths more than 2 mm.

Clinically deployed Raman spectroscopy systems are mainly fiber‐optic‐probe‐based configurations designed for in vivo or intraoperative point measurements [ 84 ]. Representative Raman spectroscopy systems include fiber‐optic endoscopic systems that have demonstrated feasibility for real‐time diagnosis of gastrointestinal and epithelial cancers [ 85 ]. Handheld or intraoperative Raman probes have been used for neurosurgical margin assessment and dermatological imaging [ 86 ]. In our study, the Raman imaging system is a preclinical Raman confocal microscopy (Renishaw inVia system). The setup includes a 785 nm diode laser excitation source, a Raman microscope equipped with objectives, and a thermoelectrically cooled charged coupled device (CCD) for spectral acquisition. This configuration allows spatially resolved Raman imaging with step sizes down to the micrometer scale, enabling mapping of nanoparticle distribution in murine lymphatic tissues. While this instrument shares fundamental optical principles with clinically used fiber‐optic Raman probes, this preclinical imaging system has not yet been optimized for clinical application. Future clinical translation would require integration into sterilizable handheld or endoscopic probes, enhanced photon collection efficiency via optimized fiber bundles and transmission optics, and validation in large‐scale human cohorts [ 87 ].

Polymeric micelles such as PEI‐based or amphiphilic self‐assembled systems have been extensively investigated with favorable translational potential when administered at low doses with biodegradable or renally/hepatically excretable components [ 88 ]. However, clinical translation of micellar Raman probes requires comprehensive evaluation of reproducibility, batch‐to‐batch consistency, pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, long‐term toxicity, and clearance pathways (hepatic and/or renal). Moreover, Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance for nanomedicine emphasizes systematic Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) toxicology studies and scalable Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) manufacturing processes prior to human application [ 89 , 90 ].

## Conclusion

In summary, we developed a non‐invasive Raman imaging for quantitative analysis of micellar lymphatic transport based on SICTERS. Such a quantitative Raman imaging method achieved accurate measurement of dynamic micellar concentrations in lymphatics over time. A PBPK model was developed to calculate the pharmacokinetics of micellar lymphatic transport with different particle sizes and surface charges. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report to use non‐invasively quantitative Raman imaging for PBPK modeling and calculation of lymphatic transport of nanoparticles that opens an avenue for Raman image‐based design and evaluation of lymph node‐targeted nanovaccines and delivery systems.

The solvents were purchased from Titan. 1,2‐Distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphoethanolamine‐Polyethylene Glycol (DSPE‐PEG 2000 ) was purchased from AVT Pharmaceutical Tech Co., Ltd. 1,2‐distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphoethanolamine‐polyethyleneimine (DSPE‐PEG 2000 ‐PEI 1800 ) was purchased from SUNLipo NanoTech Co., Ltd. 1,2‐distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphoethanolamine‐N‐[carboxy (polyethylene glycol)] (DSPE‐PEG 2000 ‐COOH) was purchased from Yusiyi Pharmaceutical Technology Co., Ltd.
