# Platelet Lysate-Based Biomaterials for Regenerative Tissue Engineering: A Comprehensive Review

## Abstract
Platelet lysate (PL), enriched with growth factors, cytokines, and proteins, exhibits strong regenerative potential, positioning it as a promising bioactive agent in tissue engineering (TE). This review systematically summarizes the research progress, applications, and mechanisms of PL-loaded biomaterials in TE. PL-integrated carriers, including hydrogels, scaffolds, and nanoparticles, transform labile liquid PL into stable, tunable platforms that retain its capacities to promote cell proliferation, angiogenesis, immunomodulation, and tissue repair, while enabling spatiotemporal control of efficacy. These composites have demonstrated significant outcomes in wound healing, bone and cartilage repair, neural regeneration, and ocular disease treatment. Critical limitations are addressed, including unstandardized PL preparation, potential immune and metabolic risks, short half-life of active factors, and slow clinical translation. Proposed solutions encompass unified production guidelines, optimized carrier-based sustained-release systems, and large-scale clinical trials. Future research should prioritize interdisciplinary collaboration to enhance precision and translatability, establishing PL-based systems as core modular platforms in regenerative medicine.

## Keywords
platelet lysate; biomaterials; tissue engineering; tissue repair; nanoparticles

## Introduction

Tissue engineering (TE) is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on repairing, replacing, regenerating, or enhancing tissue and organ function through the integration of cells, growth factors (GFs), and scaffolding materials. 1 The primary objective is to address tissue defects or organ failure by reconstructing or replicating the structure and function of native tissues through biomaterial design and modulation of cellular behavior. The three core components of tissue engineering are cells, biomaterials, and bioactive molecules. 1 Interactions among these elements provides the foundation for tissue regeneration. Biomaterials constitute a fundamental component of TE and serve multiple roles, including providing structural support, facilitating cell adhesion, promoting cell proliferation and differentiation, and regulating the tissue microenvironment. 1 , 2 Despite substantial advances in the integration of TE and biomaterials, notable challenges remain.

Platelet lysate (PL), derived from platelet-rich plasma (PRP), is a biological preparation obtained by lysing platelets to release their intracellular contents. 3–5 PL preparations are free of intact cells, thereby reducing immunogenic risk, and are enriched with a wide range of GFs, cytokines, chemokines, and other bioactive proteins. 3 PRP is typically prepared using methods such as the buffy coat method, PRP centrifugation protocols, and platelet anticoagulation techniques. Subsequently, platelet GFs and other bioactive substances are released through methods such as repeated freeze–thaw cycles, sonication, direct activation, or solvent–detergent (S/D) treatment. The selected preparation method markedly influences protein content and composition. 6 Compared with PRP, PL overcomes several limitations. For example, it exhibits reduced temperature sensitivity, can be cryopreserved for extended periods, and generally contains higher concentrations of GFs. In addition, PL offers advantages for non-autologous applications and reduces patient-to-patient variability. Nevertheless, substantial variability persists in platelet and GF concentrations among PL preparations due to differences in preparation protocols and donor characteristics. 7 , 8 As a platelet-derived product, PL has therefore been increasingly used in recent years to promote tissue proliferation, repair, and healing. In addition to soluble growth factors, PL also contains a substantial population of extracellular vesicles (EVs), which are naturally released from platelets during the lysis process and represent an integral component of PL. 9 These EVs are enriched with a diverse repertoire of bioactive molecules—including proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids such as microRNAs—through which they mediate intercellular communication and contribute to the regenerative, anti‑inflammatory, and pro‑angiogenic activities of PL. 10 Notably, PL‑derived EVs have been shown to enhance angiogenesis through miR‑126, modulate immune responses, and promote tissue repair in various preclinical models. 10 As cell‑free nanoscale vectors, PL‑EVs are increasingly recognized as key bioactive effectors that may complement or even potentiate the functions of soluble factors in PL, offering new opportunities for targeted therapeutic applications. 9

PL has demonstrated notable efficacy in both basic research and clinical applications. In basic research, human platelet lysate (hPL) has become a widely adopted supplement for mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) culture. Compared with fetal bovine serum (FBS), hPL significantly enhances MSC proliferation and expansion efficiency. 11 Studies have shown that bioactive molecules, including proteins and nucleic acids carried by PL-derived vesicles, mediate intercellular signaling and play a key role in tissue repair and regeneration. 12 For example, Platelet-Derived Extracellular Vesicles (PL-Evs) exhibit osteogenic properties comparable to those of whole PL. 12 In clinical settings, hPL is favored because of its human origin and favorable safety profile. hPL has been investigated for the treatment of various conditions, including spinal cord injury, osteoarthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease. 13 PL promotes wound healing through GF release and the stimulation of angiogenesis and cell proliferation. 14 In joint regeneration therapies, PL enhances the functional capacity of synovial fluid–derived MSCs (SF-MSCs) and promotes their differentiation toward cartilage and bone lineages. 15 Moreover, the combination of hPL with nanomaterials has given rise to emerging strategies for the development of nano-based exosome systems, further expanding the potential clinical applications of PL-based therapies. 13

Among platelet-derived products, PRP and platelet-poor plasma (PPP) are the two most extensively studied categories. PRP is a liquid-phase platelet concentrate obtained by differential centrifugation and contains active platelets and a variable leukocyte content. 16 PPP was used as the supernatant and contained the fewest platelets and the lowest concentration of growth factors. In contrast, PL is prepared by physically or chemically disrupting the platelet membrane, releasing the entire intracellular cargo, including growth factors, cytokines, and extracellular vesicles, into cell-free products. 17 This basic difference in preparation leads to several key distinctions. First, PL is cell-free, which reduces immunological risk and reduces pathogens, whereas PRP contains viable platelets that require careful handling. 17 Secondly, PL is less sensitive to temperature than PRP and can be cryopreserved and stored for a long time. 18 Third, PL from multiple donors can be combined to achieve consistency between batches, whereas autologous PRP preparations differ significantly between individuals. 19 Fourth, it has been shown that PL contains significantly higher concentrations of certain growth factors, such as FGF and egf, compared to activated PRP. 18 Fifth, the growth factors in the PRP supernatant are mainly involved in wound repair and healing, whereas the growth factors in PL are mainly involved in tissue repair and anti-inflammatory effects. Functionally, PPP had higher concentrations of certain cytokines, such as IL-1α, VEGF, and TGF-α, compared to PRP, although its overall growth factor content was still lower than that of PL. 18 While PRP remains the most extensively studied platelet derivative in clinical practice, PL has emerged as a promising alternative for regenerative tissue engineering, especially when standardized, reproducible, and off-the-shelf products are required. 20

The combination of PL with biopolymer carriers has shown considerable promise in tissue engineering. Early studies demonstrated that PL incorporation can enhance the physical properties of carrier materials. For example, poly(L-lactide) and aldehyde-functionalized cellulose nanocrystals (a-CNCs) can form freeze gels through covalent cross-linking, generating elastic, interconnected porous network structures capable of withstanding elevated mechanical stress. 21 Combining PL with biopolymer materials can also enable the sustained release of GFs, thereby prolonging their therapeutic effects. 22 For example, gelatin–hydroxypropyl starch (Gtn–HPA) hydrogels loaded with PL have been shown to achieve sustained release of platelet-derived growth factor-BB (PDGF-BB). 22 Certain carriers can further protect the bioactive components of PL. Chitosan/dodecyl hydroxy octadecanoate (CS/DHO) thermosensitive scaffolds, for example, significantly accelerate PL release under acidic conditions while preserving bioactivity. 23 In addition, PL–biopolymer composites have been reported to exhibit antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties. A PL–CNC cryogel demonstrated hemostatic performance comparable to that of commercial hemostatic sponges in vivo, while also exhibiting antibacterial activity. 21 PL combined with biopolymer materials generally demonstrates favorable biocompatibility and controlled degradability. For example, PL incorporated into Gtn–HPA hydrogels exhibited good biocompatibility and degradability in bone reconstruction studies. 22 Consequently, PL-loaded biomaterials have attracted increasing attention for tissue repair applications, including wound healing, 24 , 25 bone regeneration, 26–28 nerve repair, 5 dental repair, 29 ocular diseases, 30 , 31 and oral diseases. 32

Owing to its safety profile, stability, and multifunctional biological activity, PL is expected to support broader applications across diverse disease areas. This review summarizes the bioactive components of PL, including GFs, proteins, and trace elements, and outlines their roles in inflammation modulation, immune regulatory, anti-fibrotic responses, and tissue repair. The use of PL in combination with bioactive material carriers, such as hydrogels, aerogels, cryogels, microspheres, electrospun membranes, nanofiber membranes, nanoparticles, and scaffolds, is discussed in the context of wound healing, bone repair, nerve repair, dental repair, ocular diseases, oral diseases, and related applications ( Figure 1 ). This review provides a consolidated overview and perspective on current research directions and emerging application trends of PL-loaded biomaterials in tissue engineering. Figure 1 Schematic overview of platelet lysate-based regenerative systems for tissue engineering. Platelet lysate contains multiple growth factors, proteins, trace elements, and other components. By loading it into gel-based carriers, scaffold-based carriers, nanoparticles, and other delivery systems, it holds significant application potential across diverse fields including wound healing, bone tissue repair, nerve regeneration, ocular diseases and dental regeneration. The PL bioactive core includes neuroprotective effect, fibroblast, angiogenesis, macrophage transition and immunomodulation. Growth factors (GFs) like PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF, EGF and FGF are shown. Applications include skin (hydrogel dressing PL), nerve (PL-loaded nanoparticles), oral cavity (pulp regeneration, periodontal regeneration, oral mucosal healing), bone (targeted regeneration) and eye (thermoresponsive smart gel).

## Active Components and Major Functions of PL in Tissue Engineering

The active components of PL, including GFs, cytokines, chemokines, structural proteins, matrix components, and other bioactive substances, play a critical role in tissue repair. 33 Among these components, GFs are central to the regulation and coordination of the repair process. Figure 2 summarizes the active components and major functions of PL in tissue engineering. Figure 2 Active components and major functions of PL in tissue engineering. PL encompasses a diverse array of growth factors, proteins, and trace elements. These components act independently or synergistically to mediate anti-inflammatory activity, immune regulation, anti-fibrotic effects, and tissue repair. Image created with Biorender.com. A diagram illustrating the active components and functions of PL in tissue engineering. The diagram illustrates the active components and major functions of PL in tissue engineering, divided into sections: Anti-inflammation, Immune adjustment, Tissue repair and Anti-fibrosis. The central circle contains proteins, GFs and trace elements labeled PL. Anti-inflammation includes inhibiting pro-inflammatory responses with NF-kB and MAPK and promoting anti-inflammatory responses with L-carnitine ceramide. Immune adjustment shows cytokines IL-13, TGF-beta, IL-4, IL-10 and polarization of macrophages M1 and M2. Tissue repair involves cell proliferation and differentiation, angiogenesis and rebuilding the microenvironment with ECM. Anti-fibrosis includes intracellular pathways like PKC and mTORC2 and factors like VEGF and IGF affecting scar tissue. Each section highlights specific processes and pathways involved in tissue engineering.

### Impact of Preparation Protocols on PL Bioactivity and Batch-to-Batch Reproducibility

The clinical translation and regulatory approval of hPL still face a core obstacle, namely, the inconsistency of manufacturing methods. This lack of standardization runs through every link from the starting material to the final product, which profoundly affects the comparability, repeatability and regulatory acceptability of products.

The preparation protocol of PL directly determines the biological activity, safety and interbatch consistency of the lysates, and the interbatch repeatability is the core bottleneck that currently restricts its clinical transformation and large-scale application. Existing studies generally point out that a large number of published studies lack sufficient methodological detail, making it difficult for third parties to replicate experiments. Therefore, systematic comparison of the advantages and disadvantages of different lysis methods (repeated freeze-thaw, ultrasonic treatment, chemical activation) is of great practical significance for the establishment of standardized production processes. 34

Repeated freeze-thaw is currently the most widely used method for PL. 34 The principle is that the platelet membrane structure is destroyed by ice crystal formation and osmotic pressure changes, and the contained growth factors are released. It is easy to operate, requires no special equipment, and is suitable for laboratory-scale preparation. The introduction of exogenous chemical reagents was avoided to reduce the risk of contamination. Good integration with plasma removal processes - studies have shown that secondary centrifugation combined with repeated freezing-thawing (usually more than three times) effectively lyses platelets and releases high levels of TGF-β1. 34 The compatibility of the subsequent freeze-drying treatment is good: the freeze-thawed lysates can be further freeze-dried and stored, and remain stable for at least three months at room temperature. 34 Its disadvantages are also clear, such as the interbatch repeatability is significantly affected by freeze-thaw rate, temperature gradient, freeze-thaw times and other parameters. Ice crystal formation may cause mechanical damage to some sensitive growth factors. Operational differences between laboratories contributed to the poor comparability of results.

Sonication uses the cavitation effect to produce local high temperature and high pressure, which breaks the cell membrane. This method has not been systematically evaluated as an independent method in the existing literature. This method has high lysis efficiency and short processing time. The degree of lysis can be quantitatively controlled by adjusting the ultrasonic power and time. The limitation is that heat and free radicals generated by ultrasound may lead to degeneration or inactivation of growth factors. Moreover, the probe type ultrasound may introduce metal particle pollution. At present, there is a lack of consensus on standardized parameters, and it is difficult to compare the results between different studies.

Chemical activation uses specific reagents to induce platelet activation or direct lysis of the cell membrane. The lysis conditions were mild and caused little damage to the growth factor structure. And can achieve large-scale industrial production. 34 The degree of cleavage is also relatively controllable. But because of the introduction of exogenous chemicals, additional purification steps are required. Residual chemical agents may pose cytotoxicity and biosafety risks. Compatibility with freeze-dried preservation and gamma-ray sterilization processes needs to be verified. Overall, it increases process complexity and cost. 34

The value of platelet lysate as a cell culture additive and regenerative medicine therapeutic agent has been widely recognized, 35 , 36 but its inherent inter-donor variability is still a key bottleneck restricting the stability of product quality. Natural differences in platelet counts, growth factor content, cytokine profiles, and overall biologic activity among individual donors, 37 have given rise to standardized strategies to “average out” these differences by mixing multiple donor sources. The effectiveness of the mixed strategy is based on the statistical law - when enough independent donor samples are pooled, the effect of extreme values is diluted and the consistency of the product is improved. 35 , 36

PL production does not follow uniform standards, and the methods used by different laboratories and institutions vary significantly. 38 The differences are reflected in many technical links: the number of freeze-thaw cycles, the method of fibrin removal, and whether to inactivate pathogens. Notably, the number of freeze-thaw cycles had a direct effect on growth factor release from hPL. 39 A scopling review revealed a worrying current situation: of the studies directly comparing hPL with FBS for artificial blood cell culture, most lacked sufficient methodological detail for replication by third parties. 39 However, the important implication of the 2025 multinational multicenter study is that by following uniform standard operating procedures, it is possible to produce hPL of consistent quality across different facilities, and the standardization effect of this approach even exceeds the impact of differences in starting materials. 36

### GFs in PL

GFs represent the most important active components of PL for tissue repair. Major GFs present in PL include platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), insulin-like growth factor (IGF), epidermal growth factor (EGF), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β). 26 These factors promote tissue repair through multiple mechanisms, including activation of cell proliferation and migration, stimulation of angiogenesis, and remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM). 40 , 41 The short half-life of GFs during wound healing substantially limits their clinical effectiveness. 33 Synergistic interactions among GFs in tissue engineering have been reported. 42 For example, combined IGF and PDGF treatment exhibits partial synergy and induces complex, time-dependent biological responses. 42 Despite these advancements, few studies have systematically examined GF synergism. Whether distinct GFs dominate at specific stages of repair or differ in importance across tissue types remains an open question that warrants further investigation. The regenerative efficacy of PL arises from the coordinated actions of its three major bioactive component classes—GFs, functional proteins, and trace elements. ### Proteins in PL

PL contains a wide range of proteins that contribute to its therapeutic effects. 63 , 64 These proteins include fibrinogen, fibronectin, platelet-reactive protein 1 (PRP-1), antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), extracellular matrix–related proteins, and cell signaling regulatory proteins. 35 , 63–67 Collectively, these proteins regulate inflammation, angiogenesis, ECM remodeling, intracellular signaling, and neuroprotection. 35 , 64 , 67 Fibrinogen participates in blood clot formation and provides a temporary matrix that supports cell migration during early wound repair. 68 Fibronectin promotes cell adhesion and spreading, which are essential for effective wound healing. 69 PRP-1, despite its antiangiogenic activity, counterbalances the proangiogenic effects of VEGF and FGF-2, thereby contributing to controlled vascularization during tissue regeneration. 70 AMPs inhibit pathogenic microorganisms and reduce infection risk through antimicrobial and immunomodulatory mechanisms. 71–73 Current research increasingly focuses on incorporating these proteins into hydrogel-based systems to improve stability, reduce cytotoxicity, and enhance healing outcomes. 74 For example, incorporation of ε-polylysine (ε-PL) into cellulose/γ-polyglutamic acid composites increases elastic modulus and promotes healing of large or infected wounds. 75 Proteins in PL also regulate ECM organization through matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which mediate ECM degradation and remodeling to support tissue repair and regeneration. 35 In addition, cell cycle–related proteins present in PL, including CDK1 and PLK1, regulate cell cycle progression and support cell proliferation during tissue regeneration. 35

### Trace Elements in PL

PL contains trace elements that contribute to tissue repair, including calcium and zinc. These components promote cell proliferation, differentiation, and angiogenesis through synergistic actions and play important roles in bone tissue regeneration, vascular repair, and wound healing. 76–78 Trace elements such as zinc promote DNA synthesis and the proliferation of fibroblasts and mesenchymal stromal cells by regulating calcium channel activity and GF-related signaling pathways. 79 , 80 Zinc deficiency significantly inhibits PDGF-induced calcium influx, thereby impairing cell division. Zinc also exhibits antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. 81 , 82 Synergistic effects between trace elements and GFs have been reported. For example, zinc and PDGF act cooperatively to promote osteogenic differentiation. 83 , 84 Trace elements that contribute to mineralization and structural support, such as calcium, further promote tissue recovery, as demonstrated by enhanced bone regeneration and vascularization. 76 , 85 Other trace elements, including magnesium, are frequently incorporated into biomaterials together with zinc. 86 , 87 These elements are hypothesized to regulate cellular metabolism and mineralization processes; however, direct experimental evidence remains limited. 88 Existing studies indicate that trace elements exert multifaceted effects, including synergy with GFs, modulation of the local microenvironment, and contributions to material performance, highlighting their potential relevance in tissue engineering applications.

### Anti-Inflammation Properties of PL in Tissue Engineering

The anti-inflammatory activity of PL involves multiple mechanisms. A central mechanism is the suppression of pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, including nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways, which regulate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. 89–91 PL also promotes macrophage polarization from the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. 92 , 93 For example, in cartilage repair, PL recruits and induces M2 macrophages through the release of mediators such as sphingosine-1-phosphate, thereby attenuating inflammation. 93 PL further enhances the production of anti-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-10 (IL-10), which counteracts pro-inflammatory responses and supports inflammation resolution. 91 The close coupling between anti-inflammatory activity and tissue repair is reflected in the controlled release of GFs such as VEGF and PDGF, which are stored in distinct α-granules and selectively released upon platelet activation. 91 , 94 For example, platelets stimulated by interleukin-17A upregulate VEGF and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), promoting angiogenesis and endothelial cell proliferation, while concomitantly suppressing IL-10, a cytokine with potential anti-angiogenic effects. 94 The anti‑inflammatory effects of PL are also mediated by its EVs, which are integral components naturally released from platelets during lysis. These EVs transport lipid mediators—including L‑carnitine and ceramides—that regulate apoptosis and modulate regulatory T‑cell function. 95

### Immune Regulation of PL in Tissue Engineering

PL exhibits diverse immunomodulatory effects in tissue engineering applications. 96–98 These effects are primarily mediated through regulation of immune cell proliferation and function. Bone marrow–derived mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) cultured with PL significantly suppress the proliferation of T cells and natural killer (NK) cells, thereby modulating immune responses. 99 PL also promotes macrophage polarization toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype by regulating macrophage activation states. 98 In addition, PL influences the activity of other immune cell populations. MSCs cultured in PL transmit immunoregulatory signals through the secretion of EVs, which inhibit the activation of neutrophils and monocytes and contribute to the attenuation of inflammatory responses. 100 MSCs expanded in PL display phenotypes associated with immune regulation, characterized by high expression of mesenchymal markers such as CD90 and CD44 and low expression of immune-associated markers, including CD45 and major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC II). This phenotype indicates low immunogenicity and strong immunoregulatory capacity. 101 In tissue engineering, these immunomodulatory properties support a range of applications. Culturing MSCs in PL has been shown to enhance bone regeneration while reducing implant rejection, highlighting its value in regenerative strategies that require immune compatibility. 97 , 101

### Anti-Fibrosis Properties of PL in Tissue Engineering

PL demonstrates pronounced anti-fibrotic effects that are particularly relevant to tissue engineering applications. 102 , 103 One key mechanism involves regulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. 104 For example, adipose-derived stem cell (ASC) sheets cultured with hPL exhibit enhanced anti-fibrotic effects in both in vitro and in vivo models, effectively inhibiting excessive collagen and fibronectin deposition and thereby alleviating tissue fibrosis. 104 PL also modulates fibrosis by regulating inflammatory signaling, including upregulation of anti-inflammatory genes and downregulation of pro-inflammatory genes, which collectively suppress fibrotic progression. 105 In addition, PL inhibits transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1)–induced myofibroblast differentiation and reduces α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) expression. These effects have been demonstrated in fibrosis models of multiple tissues, including the cornea, lung, and intestine. 105–107 Consistent with these findings, PL has shown therapeutic potential in fibrotic disorders such as corneal fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis, and intestinal fibrosis. 106 , 108 , 109 These observations indicate that PL exerts anti-fibrotic activity through coordinated regulation of ECM deposition, inflammation, and myofibroblast transformation.

### Tissue Repair Properties of PL in Tissue Engineering

PL promotes tissue repair and regeneration through multiple complementary mechanisms. It contains a broad spectrum of GFs that stimulate the proliferation and differentiation of fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and MSCs, thereby accelerating wound healing and tissue regeneration. 110 In addition, PL-derived GFs optimize the repair microenvironment by modulating inflammatory responses. IGF-1 and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), for example, promote angiogenesis while suppressing inflammation and fibrosis, creating conditions favorable for tissue repair. 41 , 110 PL also markedly enhances neovascularization through the release of VEGF and PDGF. 110 In experimental settings, PL is widely used as a supplement for MSC culture. Its rich content of GFs and nutrients supports stem cell expansion, preserves functional properties, and enhances differentiation toward target lineages. 111 , 112 These characteristics enable PL to be combined with a variety of biomaterials to generate functional tissue engineering constructs. 113 , 114 For example, incorporation of PL into hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogels improves cell adhesion and proliferation while enabling controlled GF release. 115 Collectively, these properties position PL as a versatile biological component that supports tissue repair through coordinated cellular, molecular, and microenvironmental regulation.

## PL-Loaded Carriers to Enhance Tissue Repair Performance

PL has been widely used in regenerative medicine and tissue engineering because of its high content of growth factors and bioactive molecules. Its clinical application, however, remains limited by several factors, including rapid degradation, short release duration, and insufficient mechanical strength. 23 To address these limitations, PL is commonly incorporated into carrier systems to achieve stable loading, controlled release, and localized delivery. Existing PL carriers are mainly classified as gel-based carriers, scaffold-based carriers, and nanoparticle carriers.

### Gels

Gel-based carriers are functional materials widely applied in drug delivery and tissue engineering. When loaded with PL, these carriers exhibit sustained-release behavior, good biocompatibility, and mechanical support capabilities. 116–118 The high water content and tunable mechanical properties of hydrogels make them suitable carriers for drugs and growth factors. 119 Aerogels have also attracted increasing interest because of their structural stability and ease of handling and have become a focus of recent research. 120 Cryogels loaded with PL have demonstrated broad application potential in tissue engineering, bone repair, and hemostasis because of their biological activity, biocompatibility, and multifunctional characteristics. 121

Hydrogels can be categorized according to preparation methods, material sources, and functional characteristics. This section focuses on PL-loaded hydrogels classified by functional properties. Based on their roles in PL delivery, hydrogels are categorized as self-lubricating, sustained-release, thermosensitive, and mechanically reinforced systems. Self-lubricating hydrogels are designed to maintain lubricity and reduce friction during use. 122 , 123 Poly(N-acryloylpropanamide) (PNAAA) hydrogels, for example, exhibit self-lubricating behavior that mimics synovial fluid and provides long-term lubrication. 92 Peng Zhang et al demonstrated that PNAAA@PL effectively promotes osteoarthritis treatment. Sustained-release hydrogels form three-dimensional network structures through physical or chemical cross-linking, enabling encapsulation of PL-derived growth factors and controlled release. 124 Release behavior is mainly governed by material composition, cross-linking strategy, and PL loading concentration. 116 Keratin hydrogels allow precise regulation of growth factor release by adjusting PL content, 117 while chitosan hydrogels reinforced with nanocrystalline cellulose (NCC) significantly prolong release through physical encapsulation of PL. 116 Thermosensitive hydrogels undergo a sol–gel transition at physiological temperature. 125 Implantation of sPL-loaded thermosensitive hydrogels into necrotic regions has been shown to markedly accelerate bone repair and regeneration in avascular necrosis of the femoral head. 126 The physicochemical properties and biocompatibility of gel-based carriers can be tailored by adjusting matrix composition. 127 , 128 Mechanical performance can be enhanced by modifying cross-linking density, polymer concentration, or incorporating reinforcing components. 116 For example, NCC prepared from kenaf bast fibers by acid hydrolysis exhibits a high specific surface area and favorable mechanical properties. Physical incorporation of NCC into a chitosan matrix produces a chitosan–NCC composite hydrogel with improved mechanical strength. 116 Notably, hydrogel carriers may integrate multiple functional characteristics simultaneously, enabling more precise and effective tissue repair strategies. 124

Aerogels are ultralight solid materials with three-dimensional nanoporous structures that exhibit high loading capacity, stability, controllable release behavior, and good biocompatibility. Fahd Tibourtine et al developed dried, porous aerogels derived from PL hydrogels. 120 Following supercritical carbon dioxide drying, the three-dimensional fibrous network structure of the aerogel is effectively preserved. 129 This interconnected porous architecture enables rapid absorption of surrounding body fluids. 130 The hardness of aerogels is markedly higher than that of hydrogels. Dehydration reduces material viscosity, thereby avoiding the deformation and surface adhesion commonly associated with hydrogels due to their high water content. 131 These features improve handling during surgical procedures and implantation. Aerogels can be stably stored at room temperature for several months. 132 Their overall porosity is significantly higher than that of oven-dried hydrogels. 133 Even after 24 months of storage, aerogels retain approximately 90% of cell metabolic activity, comparable to freshly prepared samples. 120 In the dry state, aerogels are convenient for transportation and long-term storage and can be readily used after rehydration, overcoming limitations related to on-site preparation and short storage life of hydrogels. 134 Notably, aerogels exhibit broad adaptability for multi-tissue repair. By combining high mechanical strength, sustained release of bioactive factors, and strong cell-supporting capacity, aerogels show promise for applications in skin, bone, and cartilage regeneration. 135 , 136 Despite these advantages, aerogels exhibit increased rigidity compared with hydrogel carriers and may develop cracks under high compressive stress. 120

To date, reported PL-loaded cryogels include PL/oxidized dextran (OD) cryogels, PL–cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) cryogels, PL/OD porous cryogels, and cryoprecipitate fibrin (CF) plasma cryogels. 21 , 121 , 137 , 138 Based on preparation strategies, these cryogels can be classified as biomineralized cryogels, temperature-controlled cryogels, and chemically cross-linked cryogels. Biomineralized cryogels are composite materials fabricated using biomimetic mineralization approaches, in which inorganic minerals, such as hydroxyapatite, are integrated with organic polymer matrices, including gelatin, chitosan, or alginate, to generate scaffolds with three-dimensional porous structures. 121 , 139 Şükran Şeker et al successfully synthesized biomimetic mineralized PL/OD cryogels that exhibit porous architectures, favorable mechanical properties, and good biocompatibility. After PL loading, these cryogels promote adhesion, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation of human osteoblasts. 121 Temperature-controlled cryogels are prepared by precisely regulating temperature and duration during freezing and cross-linking. These cryogels exhibit gradient porosity and defined morphologies, making them suitable for drug delivery and tissue engineering applications. 140 Cryogels formed from gelatin and PL show tunable release behavior and are well suited for long-acting drug delivery systems. 140 Chemically cross-linked cryogels are produced by introducing chemical cross-linkers during PL cryogel fabrication, which markedly enhances mechanical strength, elasticity, and fatigue resistance. 141 , 142 For example, PL–CNC cryogels are covalently cross-linked through reactions between aldehyde-functionalized cellulose nanocrystals (α-CNCs) and PL. These cryogels exhibit improved mechanical properties and hemostatic performance. 21 PL cryogels combined with α-CNCs rapidly absorb blood while releasing bioactive molecules that regulate the wound healing microenvironment. In animal models, PL–CNC cryogels demonstrate hemostatic efficacy comparable to commercial hemostatic materials while inducing normal tissue responses. 21

In addition to the aforementioned carriers, several emerging hydrogel systems show potential for combination with PL to further enhance tissue repair and regeneration. Amphoteric ionized hydrogels are composed of amphoteric ionic monomers carrying both positive and negative charges 143 and exhibit unique hydrophilicity and stain resistance. 143 , 144 These properties can be tailored for applications such as wound repair, where they maintain a moist environment conducive to tissue regeneration while avoiding adverse effects associated with conventional dressings. 145 Double-network hydrogels represent another promising class of materials. Formed by interpenetrating two polymer networks, these hydrogels display high mechanical strength, self-healing capacity, tissue adhesion, and biocompatibility. 146 Combining PRP with double-network hydrogels addresses several limitations of PRP alone. For example, hydrogels based on hyaluronic acid (HA) and ε-polylysine (ε-PLL) enable sustained GF release through macroporous barrier effects, thereby prolonging PRP activity and enhancing therapeutic outcomes. 146

### Scaffolds

Scaffold carriers are a fundamental component of tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. They provide a three-dimensional environment for cell growth and play a guiding role in tissue formation and regeneration. Based on material properties and fabrication strategies, PL-loaded scaffold carriers can be broadly classified as natural polymer–based scaffolds, synthetic polymer–based scaffolds, composite scaffolds, gel-based scaffolds, and nanofiber-based scaffolds. 147 Representative scaffold types and PL incorporation approaches are further outlined in this section.

Natural polymer–based scaffolds have attracted considerable interest because of their favorable biocompatibility, degradability, and biomimetic characteristics. These scaffolds are composed of natural polymers such as collagen, silk fibroin, hyaluronic acid, and chitosan, which closely resemble the ECM microenvironment. 148 As a result, they provide a suitable three-dimensional architecture for cell attachment, proliferation, and tissue regeneration. 148 Natural polymer scaffolds support cell adhesion and angiogenesis and exhibit excellent biocompatibility. 149 For example, in a diabetic mouse model, a fibrin/polyether urethane bilayer scaffold loaded with PL using an electrospinning–spraying technique significantly accelerated wound healing. 57

Synthetic polymer scaffolds are engineered matrices fabricated through chemical or physical processes and are widely used in tissue engineering, drug delivery, and biomedical research. Their primary role is to provide structural support that mimics key aspects of the ECM, thereby supporting cell growth, differentiation, and drug delivery. 150 When loaded with PL, synthetic polymer scaffolds offer tunable mechanical strength and controlled degradability and are often combined with natural polymers to enhance bioactivity. PCL/gelatin–PVA/chitosan composite nanofibers with an average diameter of 454 ± 257 nm, for example, exhibited high hydrophilicity, with water absorption rates of 222–250%, and tensile strength of 3.71 MPa after loading with 5% PL. These properties support their application in epidermal wound healing. 151

Composite scaffolds combine synthetic and natural materials, thereby integrating mechanical robustness with biological functionality. Compared with single-material synthetic scaffolds, composite systems exhibit improved bioactivity, degradability, and tissue regenerative capacity. 152–154 These scaffolds have demonstrated strong performance in tissue engineering, drug delivery, and regenerative medicine. Inorganic components, such as calcium phosphate salts, impart osteoinductive properties, and their combination with PL further enhances bone regeneration. For example, three-dimensional printed biphasic calcium phosphate (BCP) scaffolds loaded with PL and gelatin methacrylate (GelMA) significantly promoted proliferation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and upregulated vascularization-related gene expression, indicating suitability for bone tissue engineering applications. 153

Gel-based scaffolds are widely applied in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine because of their good biocompatibility, tunable mechanical properties, and capacity to create biomimetic microenvironments. Preparation methods include photo-crosslinking, chemical cross-linking, freeze-drying, and three-dimensional printing, among others. 155–158 When loaded with PL, gel-based scaffolds exhibit adjustable mechanical performance, high biological activity, and functional scalability, supporting applications in tissue engineering, drug screening, and wound repair. Mechanical properties of PL-loaded gel scaffolds, such as HUgel, can be precisely tuned by incorporating aldehyde-functionalized CNCs (a-CNCs). 159 PL retains high biological activity after incorporation into gel scaffolds. In a fish skin–derived GelMA scaffold, co-loading of PL and ASCs considerably enhances cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and wound healing. 160 Functional scalability of gel-based scaffolds is further reflected in their responsiveness to electrical stimulation. Skeletal muscle tissue encapsulated within PL-loaded nanocomposite hydrogel scaffolds generates contractile forces upon electrical stimulation, indicating potential applications in functional muscle modeling, drug testing, and regenerative medicine. 159 Because of these properties, gel-based scaffolds are particularly suitable for cartilage repair and regeneration. Hyaluronic acid–tyramine (HA–TA) hydrogel scaffolds loaded with PL continuously release sphingosine-1-phosphate and proteins, inducing macrophage polarization toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype and establishing a localized anti-inflammatory microenvironment. 93 In addition, PL-loaded HA–TA hydrogel scaffolds promote differentiation of MSCs into chondrocytes, leading to the formation of hyaline cartilage–like matrices. 119

Nanofiber-based scaffolds have emerged as advanced platforms in tissue engineering because of their structural resemblance to the extracellular matrix, tunable physicochemical properties, and multifunctionality. These characteristics arise from diverse fabrication techniques, including electrospinning, spraying, supercritical fluid processing, three-dimensional printing, sacrificial fiber methods, biomolecular cross-linking, in situ synthesis, and surface functionalization. 161–165 Integration of PL further enhances scaffold performance, resulting in high tensile strength, elasticity, improved cell proliferation and differentiation, and antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activities. Hybrid nanofiber scaffolds demonstrate superior tensile strength and elasticity, supporting applications in mechanically dynamic tissues such as skin and cardiac patches. 151 , 166 PL-loaded nanofiber scaffolds promote fibroblast adhesion, proliferation, and random orientation, which are essential for wound contraction and re-epithelialization. 167 In addition, cerium nanoparticle–modified polycaprolactone (PCL)/poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) scaffolds combined with PL exhibit broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against Streptococcus mutans and Staphylococcus aureus , an important property for preventing chronic wound infections. 168 At present, PL-integrated nanofiber scaffolds are primarily applied in wound healing and myocardial repair. For example, PCL/gelatin–polyvinyl alcohol/chitosan (PCL/GEL–PVA/CS) composite scaffolds loaded with 5% PL exhibit high hydrophilicity, mechanical strength, and antibacterial activity, supporting epidermal regeneration. 151 Cardiac patches require both elasticity and bioactivity. PL-loaded gelatin/chondroitin sulfate (G/CS) scaffolds preferentially promote proliferation of immature cardiomyocytes, enhance endothelial cell adhesion, and facilitate vascularization, indicating suitability for myocardial repair applications. 166

### Nanoparticles

Direct application of PL often leads to poor dispersion and limited stability. 169 To overcome these limitations, a range of nanoparticle-based carriers has been developed to enhance PL stability and targeting efficiency. Nanoparticle carriers are nanoscale delivery systems with diverse structures and functions, and their design requires careful consideration of material properties, targeting strategies, and intended clinical applications. In tissue engineering, nanoparticles are frequently combined with other carrier systems to optimize PL delivery. Based on material composition, nanoparticle carriers are commonly classified as organic nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, inorganic nanoparticles, and biological nanoparticles. 118 , 170–172

Organic nanoparticles are nanoscale structures formed from natural or synthetic organic molecules through self-assembly or chemical synthesis. Unlike inorganic or hybrid systems, their core components are composed exclusively of organic materials, without the involvement of metals or mineral supports. 173 PL-loaded organic nanoparticles exhibit good biocompatibility, safety, and stability, supporting broad biomedical applications. For example, chitosan nanoparticles loaded with PL (PL–CS NPs) have been reported to improve in vitro fertilization outcomes and early embryo development in a mouse model of cyclophosphamide-induced premature ovarian insufficiency. 174

Polymeric nanoparticles are nanoscale carrier systems fabricated from polymeric materials. Variations in structure and composition confer a wide range of physicochemical properties and functional behaviors. 175 Applications of PL-loaded polymeric nanoparticles are often integrated with gel-based carrier systems. 118 Hydrogels containing nanoparticles provide a semi-enclosed microenvironment that supports wound healing. Studies using fibroblast cultures and murine wound models have shown that thermoresponsive hydrogels loaded with PLGA nanoparticles carrying PL promote faster tissue regeneration than free PL, highlighting their potential as effective wound treatment systems. 118

Inorganic nanoparticles offer high specific surface area and loading capacity. 176 In addition to their role as delivery vehicles, PL-loaded inorganic nanoparticles provide additional functional benefits, including synergistic modulation of inflammatory responses and oxidative stress. Cerium oxide nanoparticles (CeO 2 NPs), for example, possess mixed Ce 3 ⁺/Ce 4 ⁺ valence states that enable enzyme-mimetic redox activity. 177 Valence cycling on the nanoparticle surface generates reactive species capable of disrupting microbial membranes, contributing to antibacterial effects. 178 A composite system combining CeO 2 NPs and PL within a HA hydrogel matrix exhibits synergistic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and tissue repair–promoting activities, demonstrating therapeutic potential for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment with good biocompatibility and sustained efficacy. 179 Through surface modification and composite design, inorganic nanoparticles can markedly enhance PL delivery efficiency. 171

Biological nanoparticles are nanoscale entities produced by living systems or synthesized using biological approaches and are characterized by high biocompatibility, low toxicity, and intrinsic targeting properties. 180 These systems include exosomes, EVs, virus-like particles (VLPs), and nanoparticles derived from plants or microorganisms. 181 Research on PL-loaded biological nanoparticle carriers, particularly exosome-based systems, remains at an early stage. Available studies indicate that biogenic nanoparticles represent promising candidates for PL delivery, although systematic classification and functional evaluation of these carriers remain limited.

### Comparative Analysis and Synergistic Integration of Carrier Systems

In the previous sections, each type of PL carrier system has been systematically introduced. It is now necessary to investigate how these vectors compare to each other and, more importantly, how they can be synergistically integrated to overcome their respective limitations. This section provides a comparative analysis of vector types and clarifies their complementary relationships, followed by a decision-making framework that links vector selection to specific tissue engineering applications.

In complex tissue regeneration applications, it is often difficult for a single carrier to simultaneously meet the multiple requirements of mechanical support, biological activity, controlled release, and immune regulation. Therefore, multi-carrier recombination strategy has become a hot research direction. The combination strategy of hydrogel combined with nanoparticles has been widely studied. The core synergy logic is that nanoparticles can improve the dispersion of PL in the hydrogel, retain the initial gelation ability of the hydrogel, and achieve long-term PL release. 169 For example, PLGA nanoparticles loaded with PL were incorporated into Pluronic F-127 thermo-sensitive hydrogel to achieve stepwise release of PL and faster tissue regeneration than free PL in vivo experiments. 118 Scaffold combined with hydrogel carrier can complement each other to achieve the dual function of “structural support + biological activity”. At present, 3D printed bone scaffold is the most common application. The combination of nanoparticles and scaffolds can endow the scaffold with biological activity or drug-delivery functions, and nanoparticles can regulate the degradation rate of the scaffold and induce mineralization. The integration of nanoparticles, hydrogels, and scaffolds into a unified system represents the most advanced strategy for PL-based biomaterial design, enabling the simultaneous achievement of structural integrity, controlled bioactive release, and enhanced biological functionality. The integration of nanoparticles, hydrogels, and scaffolds into a unified system represents a state of the art strategy for PL-based biomaterials design. A landmark study by Zhao et al systematically characterized alginate dialdehyde -gelatin hydrogels supplemented with mesoporous bioactive glass nanoparticles and hPL for 3D (biological) printing applications. 182 The ADA-GEL hydrogel combines the biocompatibility and biodegradability of natural biomaterials with the cross-linking advantage of dialdehyde-modified alginate, making it a promising candidate for bioink. However, achieving balanced properties that simultaneously meet degradation rate, printability, and biological functional requirements remains challenging. The tripartite integration strategy represents a paradigm shift in PL-based biomaterial design toward a multifunctional platform tailored for specific tissue engineering applications. 182

Based on the current evidence, the selection of vector should be based on the following core considerations. First, the target tissue type and mechanical requirements need to be considered. Is it a load-bearing site? For load-bearing sites, scaffolds/hybrid construction carriers are preferred, 183 and for soft tissues, hydrogels are optional. 184 Secondly, the delivery factor species and release kinetics are required. This includes whether rapid release or sustained release is required? Need a single factor or multiple factors? Hydrogel is the choice for sustained release, 184 and the composite system of particle + hydrogel can be considered for the synergy of multiple factors. 185 Third, the regulatory requirements of immune microenvironment should also be considered. If desired, carriers with immunomodulatory functions should be selected, or antioxidant components should be introduced. 186 Fourth, cell load and delivery requirements need to be considered. Hydrogels have advantages in loading cells, 124 and the scaffold + hydrogel composite can meet both cell delivery and mechanical support. 183 Fifth, storage stability and clinical translation convenience are also worthy of attention. For example, nanoparticles such as PL-GNPs have the advantage of long-term storage, 187 and the autologous source of PL/PRP has the convenience of clinical translation. 188 Finally, fabrication feasibility and cost are also considered in the choice of carrier. Process complexity and scale production difficulty should be considered. Currently, hydrogel preparation is relatively simple, 184 while nanoparticle and microfluidic processing are highly demanding. 187 Although the scaffold-hydrogel-nanoparticle three-dimensional delivery system has shown great application potential, current research is still mainly based on preclinical animal models. 189

The comparative analysis and decision framework presented above establish clear links between carrier properties and the specific demands of different target tissues. Building on this foundation, the following chapter systematically reviews the application of PL-based biomaterials across various tissue types—skin, bone, nerve, ocular tissues, and dental/oral tissues—with explicit attention to how carrier selection influences therapeutic outcomes in each context”.

Chronic wounds and complex tissue defects are commonly associated with persistent inflammation, insufficient angiogenesis, and impaired cell migration. 167 Conventional treatments, including autologous skin transplantation, face constraints related to donor availability and the risk of immune rejection. 190 Single GFs are expensive and exhibit short biological half-lives, limiting their therapeutic effectiveness. 191 These limitations have driven the development of alternative strategies that combine biocompatibility, regenerative activity, and controlled release. ### Wound Healing

Wound healing is a highly coordinated biological process that involves sequential phases, including inflammation, cell proliferation, neovascularization, and tissue remodeling. Owing to its multitarget regulatory capacity and favorable safety profile, PL has emerged as a promising biological agent for trauma repair. 227 The mechanisms by which PL promotes wound healing mainly include stimulation of cell proliferation and migration, regulation of oxidative stress and autophagy, antibacterial and immunomodulatory actions, and enhancement of matrix remodeling and angiogenesis. 57 , 194 , 228 , 229

PL effectively promotes cell proliferation and migration. Activation of the ERK1/2 and p38 signaling pathways accelerates keratinocyte migration and enhances the collagen-synthesizing capacity of fibroblasts. 228 PL also regulates oxidative stress and autophagy. In a diabetic wound model, PL–hyaluronic acid gel inhibited excessive autophagy by reducing Beclin-1 and LC3 expression while upregulating p62. At the same time, superoxide dismutase activity increased, reactive oxygen species accumulation decreased, and the oxidative stress microenvironment was alleviated. 194 In addition, PL exhibits bactericidal and immunomodulatory properties. Complement proteins and plasma components within PL exert direct antibacterial activity against common wound pathogens, including Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli . 229 PL also attenuates inflammatory responses by inhibiting the TLR4/NF-κB pathway, thereby promoting macrophage polarization toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype. 230 PL further contributes to matrix remodeling and angiogenesis. Sustained release of TGF-β and PDGF stimulates fibroblasts to secrete collagen III and elastin, 57 while vascular endothelial cells are induced to form tubular structures, collectively supporting neovascularization and tissue repair. 24

In wound healing research, PL is frequently incorporated into a range of polymeric carriers, including hydrogels, scaffolds, nanoparticles, and composite materials. These carriers act synergistically with PL to promote healing through multiple mechanisms, such as regulation of oxidative stress, enhancement of cell migration, and improvement of antibacterial activity. When combined with PL, scaffold-based carriers provide several functional advantages in wound repair, including mechanical support, increased hydrophilicity, and optimized sustained-release and antibacterial performance. 151 , 231 For example, in electrospun nanofiber scaffolds, polycaprolactone (PCL) and gelatin contribute mechanical support, whereas polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) improves hydrophilicity. 151 In 3D-printed bilayer scaffolds, polylactic acid (PLA)/chitosan (CS) composites optimize PL release kinetics and antibacterial efficacy. 231 Hydrogel-based carriers integrated with PL exhibit sustained-release capacity, moisture retention, and high water absorption during wound healing. 116 In an animal study, PL-loaded hydrogels demonstrated sustained release efficiency and biocompatibility, thereby promoting angiogenesis and skin regeneration to accelerate wound healing 192 ( Figure 3 ). For example, the CS–NCC hydrogel exhibits a swelling ratio exceeding 1000% and a moisture retention capacity of 60–90%. 232 As a nanofiller, NCC enables a PL release flux of 0.165 mg/cm 2 /h, thereby prolonging the bioactivity of growth factors. 232 Nanoparticles are commonly combined with other carriers and offer additional advantages in wound repair due to their particle-specific properties. In murine models, PLGA nanoparticles combined with PL accelerate tissue repair by establishing a microenvironment favorable for wound recovery. 118 Some nanoparticles, such as silver nanoparticles, release Ag⁺ ions and exert bactericidal effects, conferring anti-infective activity during wound healing. 233 Based on these carrier functionalities, customized composite systems can be designed to better meet the complex requirements of wound repair. Owing to the synergistic actions of multiple growth factors in PL and advances in carrier design, including nanofibers and hydrogels, PL shows considerable potential for clinical application in the treatment of chronic and diabetic wounds, burns, full-thickness skin defects, and oral mucosal repair. For example, hyaluronic acid–PL gel promoted collagen deposition and keratinocyte migration through regulation of the ULK1 and p62 pathways, achieving a diabetic wound closure rate of 92.4% within 14 days. 234 In a clinical trial, autologous hPL demonstrated safety and efficacy in healing chronic DFUs, outperforming autologous PPP. 196 In burn models, PL-cultured adipose-derived stem cell sheets regulated by CCL5 enhanced angiogenesis and orderly collagen deposition, with significantly faster wound closure than the fetal bovine serum control group. 24 Another study demonstrated that cord blood PL gel degraded more slowly than peripheral blood PL (5.28% vs 9.55%) and similarly promoted oral mucosal fibroblast proliferation and wound closure. 235

### Bone Repair

PL has emerged as a highly promising biological agent in bone repair due to its abundant growth factors, safety profile, and cost-effectiveness. During bone regeneration, PL promotes cell proliferation, enhances differentiation, facilitates angiogenesis, and modulates inflammation. 153 , 236 , 237

PL remarkably promotes osteoblast and MSC proliferation. Resting osteoblasts treated with PL re-enter the proliferation cycle through activation of ERK and Akt signaling, inducing Cyclin D1 expression and Rb phosphorylation. 236 PL also preserves osteogenic differentiation potential. In 3D culture systems, PL upregulates osteogenesis-related genes, namely RUNX2, OSX, COL1, by 2–3-fold and increases alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity by 2–10-fold. 237 Angiogenic GFs in PL, such as VEGF, promote endothelial cell migration and vascular formation, supporting nutrient delivery critical for bone tissue engineering. 153 PL transiently induces a moderate inflammatory response, which is beneficial for initiating repair. 236

PL-loaded carriers for bone repair include scaffold-based, hydrogel-based, and composite systems. These carriers enhance osteogenesis, vascularization, and antibacterial activity while providing structural biomimicry, bioactivity, and mechanical support. 85 , 153 , 205 , 237 Scaffold-based carriers loaded with PL promote proliferation and osteogenic differentiation while inhibiting bacterial biofilm formation, 85 a key advantage in infectious bone defects. 205 Hydrogel carriers provide long-term efficacy due to sustained-release and cytocompatibility. 238 Composite carriers allow tailored multifunctionality; for instance, biomimetic mineralized CNC scaffolds provide elasticity, pro-angiogenic potential, and bioactivity. 237 PL-loaded carriers enable the multifunctional synergy of osteogenesis, vascularization, and antibacterial activity in bone repair, with core mechanisms encompassing growth-factor–controlled release, cellular behavior modulation, and biomimetic material design. Consequently, composite carriers represent a pivotal research focus in bone tissue repair.

Carrier selection is largely dictated by disease etiology. For infected bone defects, scaffolds loaded with both PL and antibiotics can deliver simultaneous antibacterial and regenerative effects. 205 Mechanical strength, antibacterial activity, and sustained release are critical requirements. Composite carriers such as gelatin-based hydrogels (Gtn-HPA) and calcium phosphate cement have become focal points. Gtn-HPA allows sustained release of PDGF-BB and is suitable for large bone defects. 22 Calcium phosphate cement loaded with PL and doxycycline provides both antibacterial activity and biocompatibility. 205 In a clinical trial, PL demonstrated a significant positive impact on the clinical treatment of delayed fracture healing and nonunion. 58 Currently, exosomes serve as natural nanocarriers carrier of concentrating GFs within PL. Through surface modification, they enable targeted delivery. For instance, PL-exo-alendronate (ALN) can reverse the inhibitory effects of glucocorticoids on osteogenesis and angiogenesis by delivering GFs 203 ( Figure 4 ). ### Neural Repair

PL is rich in neurotrophic factors, including BDNF, GDNF, and NGF, which are essential for neural repair. 110 , 218 It can substitute for fetal bovine serum (FBS), mitigating biosafety risks associated with animal-derived products. The key mechanisms of PL-mediated neural repair include enhancing stem cell neurotrophic potential, optimizing the regenerative microenvironment, and promoting synchronized angiogenesis and neurogenesis. 110 , 217 , 219

PL enhances the neurotrophic properties of stem cells. ADSCs cultured with PL exhibit increased expression of NGF and BDNF while maintaining low expression of Schwann cell marker S100B, indicating retention of stem cell characteristics alongside enhanced neurotrophic capability 217 ( Figure 5 ). Combining hPL with biomaterials further optimizes the neural microenvironment; for instance, laminin (LN) combined with hPL stimulates BDNF secretion, enhancing neuron-matrix interactions. 219 Angiogenic factors in PL, such as VEGF, indirectly support nerve regeneration by improving local blood supply. 110 In animal models of severe peripheral nerve defects, vascularization in nerve conduits seeded with hPL-treated ADSCs matched that of autologous nerve grafts. 216 Figure 5 PL promotes the neurotrophic potential of ADSCs while preserving stemness. HPL-ASCs were more neurotrophic than SC-ASCs. PL carriers for nerve repair include hydrogels and nerve conduits. Hydrogels provide biocompatibility and sustained-release functionality. When incorporated into nerve conduits, they form three-dimensional scaffolds that support stem cell survival and promote nerve regeneration. For example, LN-derived peptide (IKVAV) functionalized hydrogels combined with polycaprolactone (PCL) conduits support cell survival and enhance regeneration. 216 Nerve guidance conduits (NGCs) are biomimetic scaffolds designed for peripheral nerve repair; they exhibit favorable biodegradability, mechanical stability, and biocompatibility. 239 hPL-loaded NGCs, such as PCL conduits combined with Biogelx-IKVAV hydrogel, mimic the neural extracellular matrix while providing structural support. 216

Clinically, PL primarily functions to enhance ADSC neurotrophic potential, replacing FBS to avoid xenogeneic immune reactions. 218 Animal studies demonstrate that PL-cultured ADSCs can regenerate critical-length nerve defects, and delayed administration of such cells remains feasible, highlighting PL’s translational potential in neural repair. 216 , 240

### Eye Disease

PL serves as a potent biogenic agent for refractory ocular surface diseases, leveraging its multi-target repair capacity. Its therapeutic mechanisms include promoting cell proliferation, angiogenesis, anti-inflammatory activity, immune regulation, and tissue repair. 225 , 241 , 242

PL is enriched with growth factors such as EGF, TGF-β, and PDGF, which directly stimulate corneal epithelial cell migration and proliferation, accelerating defect healing. 225 Additional components, including VEGF and fibronectin, optimize the corneal microenvironment, support tissue remodeling, and promote vascularization. 241 Cord blood platelet lysate (CB-PL) demonstrates immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory effects, reducing IFN-γ production in NK, NKT, and T cells, thereby mitigating chronic inflammatory damage on the ocular surface. 242

In ophthalmic applications, PL is primarily delivered via ophthalmic drops and nanoparticles. Ophthalmic drops offer targeted delivery, high patient compliance, and compatibility with combination therapies. PL-loaded drops maintain stable physicochemical properties and consistent growth factor concentrations. Clinical studies show significant efficacy of PL drops in severe ocular surface disease, including GVHD-related conditions. 221 Nanoparticle carriers, such as liposomal formulations, enhance sustained release and bioavailability of PL-derived growth factors. 243 According to reports, researchers have developed an ocular wound chamber that, when combined with PL, demonstrates an effect of promoting corneal repair in guinea pig models 226 ( Figure 6 ). Preclinical and clinical evaluations confirm both efficacy and safety. In refractory corneal ulcers, unresponsive to conventional treatment, the complete healing rate with umbilical cord blood PL eye drops (UCB-PL) ranges from 50% to 71%, with no adverse effects observed. 225 During corneal burn repair or post-transplantation, PL reduces inflammatory responses, accelerates epithelialization, and mitigates transplant rejection. In dry eye disease, PL replenishes tear components and is especially effective in moderate to severe cases with corneal epithelial injury. 222

### Dental and Oral Regeneration

As a natural reservoir of autologous GFs, PL and its derivatives have demonstrated significant application prospects in the treatment of oral diseases and dental tissue restoration. Ranging from periodontal regeneration to bone defect repair, from pulp regeneration to peri‑implant tissue healing, these bioactive materials promote multiple biological processes—including cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix mineralization—thereby offering effective solutions for oral tissue regeneration. 244

Pulp regeneration represents a core application of PL, which serves as a xeno‑free substitute for fetal bovine serum (FBS) in the expansion of dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) and stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED). Moreover, PL is frequently integrated with carrier systems such as hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogels to construct bioactive scaffolds that support pulp/dentin regeneration. 4 In the context of periodontal regeneration, research has primarily focused on a bilayered system: a PL‑based construct applied to the root surface to promote periodontal ligament regeneration, combined with PL‑loaded calcium phosphate cement/microspheres to facilitate alveolar bone repair. Additionally, PL‑derived Evs combined with HA‑based biomaterials have shown promising potential for periodontal applications. 245 PL has also been widely incorporated into scaffold materials—including calcium phosphate cements and gelatin hydrogels—as a source of bioactive factors for alveolar bone defect repair and vertical bone augmentation. 22

Oral mucosal wound healing represents another growing area of PL application, where PL gels are used primarily to promote fibroblast proliferation and differentiation in the treatment of oral ulcers. 235 A comparative study demonstrated that both cord blood‑derived PL (CB‑PL) and peripheral blood‑derived PL (PB‑PL) gels significantly enhanced oral mucosal fibroblast proliferation and wound closure, with CB‑PL showing comparable efficacy to PB‑PL. 235 Furthermore, clinical evidence suggests that PL‑based gels may alleviate pain associated with oral mucosal lesions. 246

PL also has some research potential in craniofacial tissue engineering. For example, PL can promote the proliferation and angiogenesis of DPSCs by activating SOCE, which can be used as a cell supplement for the survival and differentiation of DPSCs and further applied to the repair and regeneration of peripheral nerve injury. 247 A novel animal-free alginate-fibrin-PL hydrogel bead was developed for embedding human periodontal ligament stem cells (hPDLSCs) for dental and craniofacial regeneration. 248

## Limitations and Future Perspectives

Despite substantial progress, translating PL-based biomaterials from bench to bedside faces critical challenges. This section proposes five priority research areas with actionable directions and timelines.

### Standardization of PL Preparation and Characterization

A unified standard for the production of hPL is lacking. Preparation protocols vary substantially across laboratories, including differences in freeze–thaw cycles, centrifugation conditions, and platelet sources. These variations lead to marked fluctuations in performance, including GF concentrations and cell proliferation efficacy. 39 In addition, some studies incompletely report key parameters, such as platelet concentration and activator type, further limiting comparability across studies. 39 Therefore, establishing internationally harmonized guidelines for hPL production is essential. 39 Critical parameters, including platelet enrichment methods and sterilization thresholds, should be clearly defined. The dose–response relationships between these parameters and cellular functions also require validation through multicenter studies. 39

Actionable directions: (1) Establish minimum release criteria (2026–2028): Define specifications for growth factor concentrations, protein content, pathogen safety, and functional potency assays. Multinational studies have already demonstrated the feasibility of standardized hPL production across multiple centers when unified protocols are followed. 36 (2) Develop reference materials (2027–2029): Create internationally recognized reference PL batches to enable cross-laboratory calibration. (3) Adopt standardized reporting checklists (immediate): Implement minimum reporting guidelines for PL preparation parameters (donor pooling, lysis method, storage conditions, quality control) to reduce product bias and improve comparability, aligning with ISBT Working Party recommendations.

Timeline: 2026–2029.

### Potential Risks Associated with Metabolic and Immune Modulation

PL‑based therapies carry inherent risks related to metabolic and immune regulation. Under stress conditions such as exposure to high palmitate concentrations, MSCs cultured with hPL retain immunosuppressive phenotypes but exhibit increased susceptibility to metabolic dysregulation, potentially compromising efficacy in patients with metabolic disorders. 249 Residual platelet microparticles or inflammatory mediators in PL may also trigger unintended immune responses. 249

Actionable directions: (1) Standardized GMP‑grade production and quality control (2026–2028): Adherence to GMP protocols improves batch consistency. 249 Functional validation of each batch prior to release ensures compliance with predefined specifications. 249 (2) Component removal for specific therapeutic priorities (2026–2028): Manufacturing processes should be optimized according to therapeutic priorities—whether cell expansion or immune regulation. For contexts where immunomodulation is the primary goal, fibrinogen depletion may enhance MSC immunomodulatory properties, though complete removal may reduce proliferative support. 250 (3) Exploration of non‑traditional PL sources (2026–2029): Fibrinogen‑depleted hPL (f‑hPL) obtained from residual platelets and plasma in leukocyte filters demonstrates efficient MSC expansion with superior performance to commercial hPL and FBS. Future studies should validate the safety and efficacy of f‑hPL across additional applications.

Timeline: 2026–2029.

### Integration with Emerging Technologies

PL’s potential can be amplified through integration with 3D bioprinting, smart biomaterials, and personalized medicine, though these remain at proof-of-concept stage.

Actionable directions:

(1) Develop PL-based bioinks with tunable mechanical properties and printability (2026–2028); 251 (2) Engineer stimuli-responsive PL carriers for on-demand growth factor release (2027–2029); (3) Optimize multi-component carrier systems (hydrogel–nanoparticle–scaffold) for synergistic effects (2026–2028); (4) Explore patient-specific PL formulations for personalized medicine (2027–2030).

Timeline: 2026–2030.

### Clinical Translation and Regulatory Pathways

Clinical translation is constrained by the absence of robust dose–response and potency assays, and uncertainty regarding optimal dosing regimens. Recent regulatory progress—including Japan’s PMDA issuing a Material Qualification Certificate for GMP-grade hPL—demonstrates feasibility.

Actionable directions:

(1) Develop functional potency assays correlating PL composition with biological activity (2026–2028); (2) Establish a stepwise clinical evaluation framework for each application area (2026–2030); (3) Achieve regulatory alignment among FDA, EMA, and WHO on quality and safety criteria (2026–2029).

Timeline: 2026–2030.

### Comparative Effectiveness and Health Economics

Limited comparative data exist between PL-based therapies and current standards of care. hPL may offer cost-effectiveness through superior performance at lower concentrations (as low as 0.75% hPL vs 10% FBS).

Actionable directions

(1) Conduct head-to-head randomized trials comparing PL with PRP, FBS-based products, and synthetic alternatives (2027–2030); (2) Perform health economic assessments considering reduced animal product usage, standardization, and off-the-shelf availability (2027–2029); (3) Establish long-term patient registries for real-world evidence (2028–2032).

Timeline: 2027–2032.

In conclusion, while PL-based biomaterials hold tremendous promise for regenerative tissue engineering, realizing their full therapeutic potential requires coordinated, multidisciplinary efforts across academia, industry, and regulatory bodies. The priorities and timelines outlined above provide a roadmap for advancing the field toward clinically validated, commercially available therapies.

## Conclusions

This review consolidates the current evidence, research advances, and applications of PL-loaded biomaterials in TE, highlighting both limitations and potential solutions. The principal advantage of these biomaterials lies in combining PL’s potent regenerative activity with the structural and functional benefits of engineered scaffolds, transforming liquid, labile PL into stable, tunable, and biocompatible therapeutic platforms. These composites maintain PL’s capacity to promote cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and immunomodulation while enabling spatiotemporal control of efficacy through the carrier matrix, offering broad potential for regenerating bone, cartilage, skin, and skeletal muscle, as well as treating degenerative conditions such as osteoarthritis.

PL application in TE is evolving from simple growth factor delivery toward multifunctional, personalized bioactive scaffolds. Future research will require interdisciplinary collaboration across materials science, molecular and cellular biology, and clinical medicine. Key priorities include elucidating interactions between PL components and host microenvironments, standardizing scalable production, and optimizing clinical translation. With the integration of 3D bioprinting and personalized therapeutic strategies, PL-based systems are progressing toward higher precision and translatability, positioning them as central modular platforms in regenerative medicine.
conclusions:
This review consolidates the current evidence, research advances, and applications of PL-loaded biomaterials in TE, highlighting both limitations and potential solutions. The principal advantage of these biomaterials lies in combining PL’s potent regenerative activity with the structural and functional benefits of engineered scaffolds, transforming liquid, labile PL into stable, tunable, and biocompatible therapeutic platforms. These composites maintain PL’s capacity to promote cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and immunomodulation while enabling spatiotemporal control of efficacy through the carrier matrix, offering broad potential for regenerating bone, cartilage, skin, and skeletal muscle, as well as treating degenerative conditions such as osteoarthritis.

PL application in TE is evolving from simple growth factor delivery toward multifunctional, personalized bioactive scaffolds. Future research will require interdisciplinary collaboration across materials science, molecular and cellular biology, and clinical medicine. Key priorities include elucidating interactions between PL components and host microenvironments, standardizing scalable production, and optimizing clinical translation. With the integration of 3D bioprinting and personalized therapeutic strategies, PL-based systems are progressing toward higher precision and translatability, positioning them as central modular platforms in regenerative medicine.
