# Bone Marrow Immunometabolic Remodeling in Osteoporosis: From Systemic Risk Factors to Precision Intervention

## Abstract
Osteoporosis has traditionally been viewed as a bone remodeling disorder characterized by excessive bone resorption and inadequate bone formation. However, this paradigm does not fully explain its systemic heterogeneity, persistent progression, or variable therapeutic responses. This review reconceptualizes osteoporosis as a systemic remodeling disorder driven by immunometabolic dysregulation within the bone marrow microenvironment. Upstream risk factors, including estrogen deficiency, inflammaging, gut microbiota dysbiosis, lipid dysmetabolism, and chronic low-grade inflammation, do not act solely on terminal osteoblasts or osteoclasts; instead, they are hierarchically translated within the marrow niche. These perturbations reshape hematopoietic lineage commitment, redirect Bone Marrow Mesenchymal Stem Cells(BMSC) osteogenic-adipogenic fate, promote pathological marrow adipose tissue expansion, and establish a pro-inflammatory, osteoclastogenic milieu through T helper 17 (Th17)/regulatory T (Treg) imbalance, monocyte/macrophage remodeling, inflammasome activation, and osteoclast metabolic reprogramming. Consequently, the marrow niche shifts from an osteogenesis-supportive state toward a self-reinforcing pathological ecosystem marked by enhanced resorption, impaired formation, and marrow adiposity. We further discuss emerging strategies involving microecological remodeling, immune phenotype correction, metabolic checkpoint modulation, BMSC fate regulation, and biomaterial-based niche repair. Importantly, the current evidence base is derived predominantly from postmenopausal osteoporosis and ovariectomized animal models, whereas validation across other osteoporosis subtypes and in prospective human studies remains limited. Accordingly, the broader applicability of this immunometabolic framework should be regarded as an emerging hypothesis requiring further clinical validation. Nevertheless, it may provide a conceptual basis for understanding osteoporosis heterogeneity and developing subtype-stratified precision interventions beyond conventional anti-resorptive and anabolic therapies.

## Keywords
osteoporosis; immunometabolic dysregulation; bone marrow niche; precision therapy

## Introduction

Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by reduced bone mass, deterioration of bone microarchitecture, and increased skeletal fragility. 1 Its major clinical consequences include increased susceptibility to fragility fractures, progressive functional impairment, and a substantial burden of long-term disability. 2 With accelerating population aging, osteoporosis has emerged as a critical public health challenge with profound medical and socioeconomic implications. Current therapeutic strategies still rely primarily on antiresorptive and bone-forming agents. 3 Bisphosphonates, denosumab, parathyroid hormone analogues, and sclerostin-targeting agents have demonstrated established efficacy in improving bone mineral density and reducing fracture risk. 4 Nevertheless, clinical practice reveals several unresolved limitations, including marked interindividual heterogeneity in treatment response, concerns regarding long-term medication safety, suboptimal adherence, rebound phenomena after drug discontinuation, and insufficient whole-course disease management. 5 These unmet challenges suggest that, although contemporary therapeutic paradigms are clinically effective, they do not fully address the fundamental pathophysiological drivers underlying the persistent progression of osteoporosis.

The osteoblast-osteoclast imbalance model has long served as a central paradigm for understanding the pathogenesis of osteoporosis. 6 This classical framework has established a fundamental basis for interpreting abnormal bone remodeling; however, its explanatory capacity does not fully encompass the systemic complexity of the disease. Crucially, systemic factors distant from bone tissue itself, including menopause, aging, gut microbiota dysbiosis, lipid metabolic disorders, and chronic low-grade inflammation, can exert profound effects on skeletal outcomes, yet these effects cannot be fully explained by dysfunction of terminal bone cells alone. 7–11 Therefore, advancing osteoporosis research does not require rejection of the established remodeling theory, but rather its extension through a complementary systems-level framework. Such a framework should integrate the continuous hierarchical linkages among systemic risk factors, local microenvironmental reprogramming, and downstream dysfunction of bone remodeling effectors.

Based on recent advances in osteoimmunology and immunometabolism, osteoporosis may be more appropriately conceptualized as a systemic disorder in which upstream risk factors are translated through the bone marrow immunometabolic microenvironment into imbalance within the bone remodeling effector layer. 8 , 12 , 13 Within this framework, estrogen deficiency, inflammaging, aberrant microbiota-derived metabolic signals, and lipid metabolic dysregulation do not directly dictate bone loss. 14–16 Rather, they first reprogram the signal-processing state of the marrow niche, thereby altering immune lineage commitment, mesenchymal cell differentiation fate, local inflammatory tone, and metabolic buffering capacity. 12 , 14–16 These changes ultimately sustain pathological osteoclastogenesis and attenuate osteogenesis, leading to persistent remodeling imbalance. Consequently, the bone marrow microenvironment should no longer be viewed merely as a passive structural background in which bone cells reside, but as a critical intermediary layer that connects systemic perturbations with terminal skeletal phenotypes.

Unlike previous osteoimmunology reviews that have primarily focused on individual immune cell populations, inflammatory mediators, or immune-bone cell interactions, the present review places the bone marrow immunometabolic microenvironment at the center of a hierarchical disease framework. Specifically, we integrate systemic endocrine, aging-related, microbial, and metabolic disturbances with marrow niche reprogramming and downstream bone-remodeling dysfunction through a “systemic risk factor-marrow niche-effector” axis. This perspective extends conventional osteoimmunology by incorporating metabolic reprogramming, hematopoietic lineage remodeling, bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (BMSC) fate decisions, bone marrow adiposity, and niche-directed therapeutic strategies into a unified framework, thereby shifting the emphasis from cataloguing individual osteoimmune mechanisms toward understanding how systemic signals are integrated and amplified within the marrow microenvironment.

This conceptual framework is currently supported primarily by mechanistic studies, animal models, and population-based associative evidence. Although much of the current evidence derives from postmenopausal osteoporosis and ovariectomy models, the proposed framework may offer a broader conceptual basis for understanding osteoporosis subtypes in which endocrine deficiency, aging, inflammation, microbial dysbiosis, and metabolic disturbances converge at the bone marrow niche. While this evidence base has substantially advanced our understanding of osteoporosis heterogeneity and persistent progression, its clinical translation pathway remains under development. Accordingly, this review examines immunometabolic imbalance in osteoporosis across four integrated dimensions: first, we summarize how systemic risk factors initiate bone marrow microenvironmental reprogramming; second, we analyze how the bone marrow immunometabolic microenvironment mediates signal translation; third, we clarify how key immune cell networks and metabolic programs drive bone remodeling imbalance; and finally, we evaluate emerging precision intervention strategies. Through this structured analysis, we aim to provide a conceptual foundation for integrating osteoporosis pathogenesis and developing stratified therapeutic paradigms ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 Overall immunometabolic framework of osteoporosis: from systemic risk factors to bone marrow microenvironment remodeling and bone remodeling imbalance. This schematic illustrates the proposed immunometabolic framework of osteoporosis. Upstream systemic risk factors, including estrogen deficiency, aging/inflammaging, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and lipid-glucose metabolic disturbances, are not assumed to act directly and exclusively on terminal osteoblasts or osteoclasts. Instead, these perturbations are integrated and translated within the bone marrow immunometabolic microenvironment. This reprogrammed niche reshapes hematopoietic lineage output, BMSC osteogenic-adipogenic fate decisions, bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) expansion, local inflammatory tone, and metabolic buffering capacity. These changes further drive Th17/Treg imbalance, inflammatory monocyte/macrophage remodeling, osteoclast glycolytic reprogramming, inflammasome activation, and impaired osteogenesis. Ultimately, the marrow niche shifts from an osteogenesis-supportive state toward a pro-inflammatory and osteoclastogenic ecosystem, resulting in enhanced bone resorption, suppressed bone formation, marrow adiposity, skeletal fragility, and persistent osteoporosis progression. Source: Created by the authors based on the literature discussed and cited in the manuscript. The figure was not generated using generative AI tools. The diagram illustrates the immunometabolic framework of osteoporosis across four sections. Section A, titled ′Upstream risk factors′, includes estrogen deficiency, inflammaging, gut dysbiosis and lipid-glucose dysmetabolism, each with specific effects like RANKL/OPG imbalance and oxidative stress. Section B, ′Bone marrow niche as a signal integration and translation hub′, shows HSPC myeloid skewing, BMSC fate deviation, BMAT expansion, inflammatory amplification and metabolic buffering failure, with self-reinforcing loops. Section C, ′Network and metabolic program remodeling′, details immune network remodeling with Th17/Treg imbalance, monocyte/macrophage activation and osteoimmune amplification, alongside metabolic program remodeling with osteoclast glycolysis, NLRP3 activation and lipotoxic suppression of osteogenesis. Section D, ′Terminal skeletal outcomes′, shows enhanced resorption, impaired formation and marrow adiposity leading to persistent bone remodeling imbalance and osteoporosis progression. Future directions include microecological remodeling, immune phenotype correction, metabolic checkpoint modulation and BMSC/BMAT niche reconstruction. ## Literature Search Strategy

A structured literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE (Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online), Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library, with the search updated through May 10, 2026. Search terms were organized around the major conceptual domains of this review and included combinations of osteoporosis-related terms (“osteoporosis”, “postmenopausal osteoporosis”, “age-related osteoporosis”, “glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis”, and “bone loss”) with terms related to the bone marrow niche and osteoimmunology (“bone marrow microenvironment”, “bone marrow niche”, “osteoimmunology”, “T helper 17 (Th17) cells”, “regulatory T (Treg) cells”, “macrophage”, “monocyte”, “osteoclast”, “bone marrow adipose tissue”, and “mesenchymal stromal cells”) and immunometabolic regulation (“immunometabolism”, “metabolic reprogramming”, “glycolysis”, “mitochondrial metabolism”, “lipid metabolism”, “gut microbiota”, “short-chain fatty acids”, and “inflammasome”). Boolean operators were used as appropriate to combine disease-, cell-, and mechanism-related terms.

Peer-reviewed English-language studies relevant to osteoporosis-associated immune and metabolic remodeling were considered, including original clinical and preclinical studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and high-quality mechanistic investigations. Priority was given to recent studies directly addressing the proposed systemic risk factor-bone marrow immunometabolic niche-bone remodeling framework, particularly evidence from postmenopausal osteoporosis, human cohorts, and ovariectomized animal models. Older landmark studies were retained when necessary to establish fundamental biological concepts or trace the development of key mechanisms. Studies with limited relevance to osteoporosis, insufficient mechanistic or clinical information, substantial duplication of previously included evidence, or inadequate information for interpretation were excluded. Because this article is a narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis, literature selection was guided by scientific relevance, methodological quality, and contribution to the proposed conceptual framework rather than by formal quantitative evidence synthesis.

## Upstream Triggers of Immunometabolic Imbalance

### Estrogen Deficiency: The Immunometabolic Origin of Postmenopausal Osteoporosis

Estrogen deficiency first disrupts the coupling between osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and osteoblast-mediated bone formation, thereby shifting postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMOP) from a primarily endocrine disturbance toward a persistent failure of bone homeostasis. Under physiological conditions, estrogen maintains signaling equilibrium among osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts through estrogen receptors. 17 It restrains activation of the receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL)/receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB (RANK)-nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB)-nuclear factor of activated T cells 1 (NFATc1) axis, limiting osteoclast differentiation and survival, while sustaining Wnt/β-catenin, runt-related transcription factor 2 (Runx2), and Osterix signaling to support osteoblast differentiation, matrix synthesis, and mineralization. 8 , 18 , 19 Following menopause, increased osteocyte- and osteoblast-derived RANKL, relative Osteoprotegerin (OPG) insufficiency, and an elevated RANKL/OPG ratio collectively amplify osteoclastogenesis. 20 , 21 At the same time, diminished estrogen-mediated protection aggravates oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cellular senescence, thereby compromising osteoblast activity and weakening compensatory bone formation. 12 , 22 , 23 Evidence from ovariectomy models further supports this bidirectional remodeling defect, characterized by Wnt/β-catenin downregulation, reduced osteogenic transcription factors, and NF-κB/NFATc1-driven osteoclastogenic activation. 24–26 Thus, estrogen deficiency fractures the coupled triad of enhanced resorption, impaired formation, and dysregulated osteocyte control, initiating broader disruption of the bone marrow microenvironment through immune and metabolic dysregulation.

A second consequence of estrogen deficiency is the remodeling of bone marrow immune ecology, in which immune cells shift from homeostatic regulators to pro-resorptive inflammatory effectors. T lymphocytes play a central role in this process by releasing Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-17A (IL-17A). 27 TNF-α synergistically enhances RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis, whereas IL-17A stimulates RANKL expression in osteoblasts and bone marrow stromal cells, thereby reinforcing osteoclastogenic signaling. 28–30 Disruption of the Th17/Treg balance further intensifies this inflammatory cascade: Th17 expansion promotes IL-17-mediated bone resorption, while insufficient Treg function weakens immune restraint on osteoclast differentiation. 31 , 32 Beyond T cells, monocytes/macrophages, dendritic cells, and B cells also participate in this pathological network. 33 Under inflammatory stress and metabolic reprogramming, macrophages preferentially acquire an M1-like phenotype and secrete TNF-α, Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and Interleukin-6 (IL-6), further amplifying RANKL expression and osteoclast differentiation. 33–35 Therefore, estrogen deficiency does not act only through direct effects on bone cells; rather, it transduces endocrine decline into sustained low-grade inflammation, making immune cells both responders to estrogen loss and amplifiers of bone-destructive signaling.

Moreover, estrogen deficiency extends skeletal injury through disruption of the gut-immune-bone-metabolism axis. Postmenopausal estrogen decline is associated with reduced gut microbial diversity, impaired intestinal barrier integrity, and systemic low-grade inflammation. 7 , 11 , 36 Once the intestinal barrier is compromised, bacterial components can translocate into the circulation, activate Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/NF-κB signaling, increase TNF-α and IL-6 production, and thereby strengthen the osteoclastogenic niche within bone marrow. 13 , 37 Altered microbial metabolites provide another mechanistic bridge between estrogen deficiency and skeletal metabolic dysfunction. Insufficient butyrate production may impair Treg differentiation, weaken immune tolerance, and enhance inflammatory bone resorption. 38 , 39 In parallel, disturbances in tryptophan metabolism, bile acid metabolism, lipid handling, and insulin sensitivity may influence the osteogenic/adipogenic fate of BMSCs through aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ), and related pathways, further limiting bone-forming capacity. 40–44 Therefore, estrogen deficiency should be understood as the most representative multi-axis origin of imbalance in postmenopausal osteoporosis: it begins with the disruption of bone remodeling coupling, is amplified by bone marrow immune inflammation, and further aggravates bone microenvironmental damage through intestinal dysbiosis and systemic metabolic abnormalities, ultimately promoting bone loss, microarchitectural deterioration, and skeletal fragility.

### Aging and Inflammaging: Systemic Amplifiers of Osteoporotic Bone Loss

Aging represents an active deterioration of immune homeostasis, metabolic resilience, and tissue repair capacity. In osteoporosis, its significance extends beyond bone loss itself and lies in its ability to induce chronic low-grade inflammation, or inflammaging, which maintains the bone marrow microenvironment in a pro-inflammatory, oxidative, and metabolically maladaptive state. 14 , 45 Unlike the early remodeling imbalance triggered by estrogen deficiency, aging progressively weakens compensatory mechanisms. 46–48 Senescent cells and bone marrow adipocytes continuously release senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors, including IL-6, TNF-α, interleukin-8 (IL-8), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), thereby stimulating osteoclastogenic pathways. 49 Meanwhile, the reparative capacity of BMSCs and osteoblasts becomes blunted, making bone formation increasingly unable to counteract enhanced resorption. 50 , 51 Thus, aging acts as a systemic amplifier of bone loss, converting potentially compensable remodeling disturbances into progressive degeneration of the bone marrow microenvironment.

Immunologically, inflammaging reprograms bone marrow immune cells and establishes an osteoclast-permissive inflammatory niche. Macrophages preferentially polarize toward an M1-like phenotype, releasing TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 and promoting osteoclastogenesis through NF-κB, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and NFATc1 signaling. 52 Persistent antigen exposure, gut-derived inflammatory stimuli, and damage-associated molecular patterns may further induce trained immunity-like changes in myeloid cells, heightening their inflammatory responses upon restimulation. 53–55 Adaptive immunity is also remodeled: reduced Treg abundance or impaired Treg function weakens anti-inflammatory and osteoclast-inhibitory control, 56 whereas Th17 expansion and IL-17 production enhance RANKL expression in osteoblasts and bone marrow stromal cells. 29 B cells and dendritic cells may further contribute by modulating the RANKL/OPG balance and inflammatory mediator production. 57 , 58 Collectively, aging shifts immune regulation from dynamic homeostasis toward sustained pro-resorptive activation.

Metabolically, aging amplifies bone loss by reducing cellular plasticity within the bone marrow. Mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)/sirtuin activity, and AMPK/mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) imbalance impair BMSC osteogenic differentiation while favoring adipogenic commitment. 59–62 Increased bone marrow adiposity further releases adipokines and inflammatory mediators that suppress osteogenic repair. 63 Under bioenergetic stress, osteoblasts exhibit reduced Runx2 and Osterix expression, impaired matrix synthesis, and weakened mineralization capacity. 64–66 In contrast, osteoclasts can enhance glycolytic and mitochondrial metabolism in response to inflammatory stimulation, meeting the energetic demands of fusion, acidification, and bone resorption. 67 This metabolic asymmetry between constrained osteogenesis and adaptive osteoclast metabolism progressively biases remodeling toward net bone loss. Aging further drives bone marrow adiposity and compromises gut barrier integrity, collectively exacerbating inflammatory and metabolic stress within the skeletal niche. 63 , 68

Therefore, postmenopausal osteoporosis and age-related osteoporosis are best viewed as overlapping rather than entirely separate entities. Estrogen deficiency preferentially initiates remodeling imbalance, whereas aging sustains and amplifies it through inflammaging, immune rigidity, mitochondrial dysfunction, adipogenic drift, and gut-axis disturbance. This distinction helps separate endocrine initiation from age-related reinforcement without implying that either process acts in isolation.

### Gut Microbiota Dysbiosis: Immunometabolic Integration in Postmenopausal Osteoporosis

Gut microbiota dysbiosis constitutes a pivotal immunometabolic interface in PMOP, integrating intestinal ecology with systemic immunity, microbial metabolism, estrogen homeostasis, and skeletal remodeling. 7 , 69 , 70 Clinical and preclinical evidence suggests that alterations in the gut microbiota are associated with PMOP and may provide therapeutically actionable targets within the gut-bone axis. 71–73 Consequently, the significance of dysbiosis extends beyond local microbial imbalance; it functions as a systemic nexus through which endocrine decline, aging-related inflammation, metabolic derangement, and bone marrow niche reprogramming converge.

First, gut barrier compromise and microbial translocation provide an important route by which dysbiosis amplifies bone loss. Estrogen deficiency and aging can impair epithelial tight junctions and mucosal barrier integrity, allowing microbial products such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to enter the circulation. 74 , 75 Circulating LPS activates TLR4/myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88)/NF-κB signaling in monocytes/macrophages, marrow stromal cells, and other bone marrow-resident cells, thereby inducing the release of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. 76 These inflammatory mediators enhance osteoclast precursor recruitment, fusion, and differentiation, while also promoting RANKL expression in osteoblast-lineage cells and bone marrow stromal cells. This process establishes a self-reinforcing pathological axis linking barrier failure, systemic low-grade inflammation, and bone marrow osteoclast predominance. Thus, the intestinal barrier is not a passive bystander in PMOP, but a potential inflammatory gateway through which gut-derived signals reshape the skeletal microenvironment.

Second, insufficient production of microbial metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), compromises bone-protective immunometabolic signaling. SCFAs, especially butyrate and propionate, are produced primarily by fiber-fermenting bacteria and contribute to skeletal homeostasis through G protein-coupled receptor activation, histone deacetylase regulation, and cellular metabolic reprogramming. 77 , 78 These metabolites promote Treg differentiation, suppress excessive inflammatory responses, and support osteoblast function and BMSC osteogenic potential. 79–81 When butyrate-producing bacteria decline or SCFA production becomes insufficient, anti-inflammatory immune restraint is weakened, inflammasome activation may persist, and the metabolic buffering capacity of marrow cells is reduced. 38 , 82 Consequently, SCFA depletion reflects both diminished microbial metabolic signaling and impaired osteogenic support.

Third, Th17/Treg disequilibrium is a central mediator through which gut dysbiosis reprograms skeletal immunity toward osteoclastogenesis. A balanced microbiota contributes to intestinal and peripheral immune tolerance, whereas dysbiosis promotes Th17 expansion and impairs Treg function, shifting immune regulation toward inflammatory activation. 83 IL-17 released by Th17 cells upregulates RANKL expression in osteoblasts, mesenchymal stromal cells, and immune cells, and synergizes with TNF-α and IL-6 to potentiate osteoclastogenesis. 84 Conversely, Treg cells suppress osteoclast differentiation through anti-inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-10 (IL-10) and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) and may also support bone formation-related signaling. 39 , 85 Thus, dysbiosis does not simply elevate isolated cytokines; rather, it drives coordinated immune polarization toward a pro-resorptive state, with RANKL acting as a molecular bridge between immune activation and bone loss.

Finally, gut microbiota alterations form a bidirectional pathological loop with estrogen metabolism. Certain intestinal bacteria express β-glucuronidase and sulfatase, affecting estrogen deconjugation and enterohepatic recirculation and thereby systemic estrogen availability. After menopause, dysbiosis may impair this regulatory capacity, while estrogen deficiency can further disrupt barrier integrity, microbial composition, and immune tolerance. This reciprocal interaction can sustain a feed-forward cycle of hypoestrogenism, dysbiosis, inflammatory-metabolic activation, and accelerated bone loss.

### Abnormal Lipid Metabolism and Bone Marrow Adipose Tissue Expansion: Critical Drivers of Bone Marrow Microenvironment Remodeling

Bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) expansion constitutes an immunometabolic event of considerable pathological relevance in postmenopausal osteoporosis. Its essence transcends passive “fat filling” following bone loss and instead represents active remodeling of the bone marrow microenvironment. 86 BMAT shares the same niche with osteoblasts, osteoclasts, BMSCs, and immune cells; 87 therefore, its expansion can directly alter local intercellular communication and the balance of bone remodeling. Previous studies have shown that bone loss in PMOP and ovariectomized animal models is often accompanied by abnormal marrow fat accumulation, while BMAT, as an endocrine tissue, can regulate skeletal metabolism through adipokines and cytokines. 88 , 89 Relevant reviews published in 2024 have further emphasized that BMAT is an important regulator of bone homeostasis, that its expansion is closely associated with bone loss and fracture risk, and that it may represent a potential target for the prevention and treatment of PMOP. 90 Consequently, BMAT expansion should be understood as an important sign of the transition of the bone marrow microenvironment from an “osteogenic-supportive” state toward an “adipogenic, inflammatory, and osteoclast-dominant” state.

The pathological impact of BMAT is largely shaped by alterations in its secretory and metabolic profiles. Bone marrow adipocytes release adipokines, including leptin and adiponectin, as well as inflammatory mediators such as IL-6. 91–93 Under physiological conditions, certain adipokines contribute to energy homeostasis and skeletal maintenance. 86 However, in the context of estrogen deficiency, aging, and lipid dysmetabolism, BMAT is more likely to transition toward a pro-inflammatory endocrine phenotype. 93 Excess saturated free fatty acids and lipid metabolic imbalance can activate macrophages and other immune cells, thereby amplifying cytokine production and osteoclastogenic signaling. 94 , 95 Concurrently, BMAT-derived lipid stress may impair adjacent BMSCs and osteoblasts through oxidative damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and senescence-associated secretory phenotypes. 96 Thus, BMAT functionally couples lipid dysregulation with local inflammation, osteoblast suppression, and osteoclast activation.

BMAT expansion also reflects a systemic shift in BMSC lineage commitment. As common precursors of osteoblasts and marrow adipocytes, BMSCs undergo transcriptional reprogramming under concurrent estrogen deficiency, aging, oxidative stress, and lipotoxic stress: adipogenic drivers, including PPARγ and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein α (C/EBPα), become activated, whereas osteogenic pathways and transcriptional regulators, including Wnt/β-catenin, Runx2, and Osterix, are relatively suppressed. 43 , 60 , 97 This fate shift diverts BMSC differentiation toward adipogenesis at the expense of osteogenesis. Consequently, expanded marrow adiposity releases lipids, adipokines, chemokines, and inflammatory mediators that simultaneously compromise osteogenic repair and reinforce osteoclastogenic activity. Saturated fatty acid accumulation, lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial damage further exacerbate ROS production, induce cellular senescence, and impair osteoblast matrix synthesis and mineralization. Thus, the pathological significance of lipid dysmetabolism in PMOP extends beyond marrow fat accumulation, as it drives a self-perpetuating cycle of metabolic disturbance, BMAT expansion, osteogenic suppression, inflammatory activation, and enhanced osteoclastogenesis ( Figure 2 ). ## Immunometabolic Regulation of the Bone Marrow Microenvironment: Mediating Systemic Risk Factors in Bone Remodeling Imbalance

### Bone Marrow Microenvironment: The Central Integration Hub for Systemic Osteoporotic Signaling

Osteoporosis is not a linear pathological process in which distal risk factors act directly on osteoblasts or osteoclasts; rather, it is a systemic disorder in which upstream signals must be integrated, translated, and amplified through the bone marrow niche. This hierarchical organization arises from the central role of the bone marrow as an active multicellular ecosystem where bone metabolism, hematopoietic activity, immune regulation, and lipid homeostasis converge. 12 Accordingly, the bone marrow microenvironment serves as a major integrative hub capable of sensing systemic endocrine, inflammatory, and metabolic perturbations associated with estrogen deficiency, inflammaging, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and lipid metabolic abnormalities. 98 These signals first engage hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, perivascular cells, immune cell populations, and bone marrow adipocytes. 47 Through receptor recognition, intercellular crosstalk, metabolic coupling, and epigenetic remodeling under sustained stimulation, they reshape myeloid differentiation bias, weaken osteogenic support capacity, increase local inflammatory tone, and expand the availability of osteoclast precursors. 99–101 Together, these interactions position the marrow niche as the site where systemic perturbations are converted into persistent pro-osteoclastogenic and osteogenesis-suppressive outputs that contribute to skeletal fragility and disease heterogeneity.

### Constitutive Basis of the Bone Marrow Niche: Hematopoietic Stem/Progenitor Cells (HSPCs), BMSCs, BMAT, and Immune Networks

The functional capacity of the marrow niche emerges from coordinated interactions among HSPCs, BMSCs, BMAT, and resident immune cells. HSPCs govern the supply of immune lineages, maintaining myeloid-lymphoid balance under homeostatic conditions but becoming prone to myeloid skewing during stress or inflammaging. 102 , 103 This shift expands the monocyte reservoir and provides a cellular basis for the subsequent accumulation of macrophages and osteoclast precursors. BMSCs serve as the central hub for osteogenic-adipogenic fate determination, and their significance extends beyond their role as osteoblast precursors. 104 Rather, they help determine the direction of marrow regeneration. Persistent estrogen deficiency, oxidative stress, and inflammatory burden promote the transition of BMSCs from osteogenic toward adipogenic differentiation, thereby depleting osteogenic progenitor supply and remodeling the local hematopoietic and immune niches through paracrine signaling. 43 , 60 BMAT expansion represents an active metabolic regulator rather than a passive accompaniment of bone loss. 105 Through adipokine and cytokine secretion, altered lipid substrate availability, and space-occupying effects, BMAT continuously reprograms the marrow niche toward an inflammation-permissive and adipogenesis-favoring microenvironment. 106–108 Meanwhile, macrophages, T cells, B cells, and monocytes constitute the direct effector layer of local inflammatory and osteoimmune tone. 109 , 110 Through cell-cell contact and soluble mediators, these immune cells convert upstream stimuli into pro-osteoclastogenic and osteogenesis-suppressive signals. This functional specialization defines the operational hierarchy of the bone marrow niche: HSPCs determine immune lineage supply, BMSCs dictate regenerative fate, BMAT establishes the metabolic background, and immune networks govern inflammatory output. Through continuous cross-talk, these four components collectively transform the bone marrow into a signal-integrating and pathology-amplifying niche capable of converting systemic danger cues into persistent remodeling imbalance.

### Signal Translation: Remodeling the Bone Marrow into a Pro-Osteoclastogenic and Hypo-Osteogenic State

Signal translation within the marrow involves inflammatory, metabolic, hormonal and aging-related, and lipid-derived inputs that reshape hematopoietic, immune, and stromal responses. Inflammatory inputs constitute a major initiating route in this process. After intestinal barrier compromise, LPS and other pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) enter the circulation and activate Toll-like receptor (TLR)/MyD88-dependent pathways within the bone marrow, triggering inflammatory cascades, stress myelopoiesis, and myeloid expansion. 111–113 This enlarges monocyte/macrophage reservoirs and osteoclast precursor pools, establishing an osteoclast-permissive niche. 114 , 115 Under persistent stimulation, epigenetic remodeling may further maintain pro-inflammatory genes in an accessible chromatin state, thereby stabilizing pathological output and prolonging marrow inflammation. 116 Metabolic mediators, in turn, calibrate the immunometabolic buffering capacity of the marrow niche. Short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, and bile acids should not be viewed as isolated circulating molecules, but as biologically interpretable signals within the bone marrow. SCFAs help sustain Treg homeostasis, restrain excessive inflammation, and preserve an osteogenesis-supportive microenvironment, whereas the tryptophan-AhR and bile acid-farnesoid X receptor (FXR)/Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5) axes modulate T-cell differentiation, macrophage polarization, and local metabolic equilibrium. 41 , 77 , 82 , 117 Hormonal and aging-related inputs further reset marrow response thresholds. Estrogen withdrawal increases the susceptibility of the bone marrow to inflammatory activation, while inflammaging stabilizes this abnormal state through chronic low-grade inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, immune rigidity, and immunometabolic maladaptation. 113 , 118 , 119 These mechanisms help explain the persistent progression and limited reversibility of postmenopausal and age-related osteoporosis. Finally, lipid dysregulation reshapes the differentiation landscape of the bone marrow. Abnormal lipid loading affects bone-lineage cells and remodels macrophage activation, T-cell metabolism, and BMSC fate commitment, shifting the marrow environment toward adipogenesis and inflammation. 120 , 121 Concurrent bone marrow steatosis further suppresses osteogenic support through lipotoxicity, adipokine secretion, hypoxic stress, and space-occupying effects. 122 , 123 Thus, the central mechanism of osteoporosis lies not simply in the direct targeting of osteoblasts or osteoclasts by upstream risk factors, but in the remodeling of marrow signal interpretation, through which inflammatory, metabolic, and regenerative cues are converted into persistent remodeling imbalance and skeletal fragility.

### Bone Marrow Immunometabolic Imbalance: Determinant of Remodeling Outcomes

Chronic exposure of the bone marrow microenvironment to inflammatory, metabolic, and aging-related signals drives a series of coupled niche phenotypes, including sustained inflammatory burden, enhanced HSPC myeloid skewing, reduced Treg-mediated buffering capacity, impaired BMSC osteogenic potential, and pathological BMAT expansion. 12 These interconnected alterations do not occur in isolation; rather, they collectively reprogram how the bone marrow transmits regulatory signals to bone homeostatic effectors. Myeloid skewing expands monocyte/macrophage reservoirs and osteoclast precursor pools, while heightened local inflammatory tone continuously reinforces a pro-osteoclastogenic cytokine milieu. 124 , 125 Concurrently, compromised BMSC osteogenic capacity, enhanced adipogenic commitment, and impaired supportive matrix function weaken the osteoblast-supportive environment, making bone formation increasingly unable to compensate for bone resorption. The resulting outcome is therefore not merely increased osteoclast activity or reduced osteoblast function, but a persistent failure of formation-resorption coupling, through which bone remodeling shifts from dynamic equilibrium toward a self-sustaining negative balance. Thus, the immunometabolically imbalanced bone marrow niche should not be regarded as an accessory pathological feature, but as a proximal determinant of terminal skeletal abnormalities. This microenvironmental failure provides the pathological scaffold upon which adaptive immune imbalance, dysfunction of the monocyte/macrophage effector layer, and rigidified metabolic programs are progressively amplified, jointly accelerating the progression of osteoporosis.

Together, these coupled niche changes establish the cellular and metabolic conditions that favor persistent remodeling imbalance. The following sections therefore focus on the downstream effector programs that emerge from this altered niche-adaptive immune polarization, monocyte/macrophage remodeling, and maladaptive metabolic reprogramming-and on how these processes directly influence osteoclast and osteoblast function ( Figure 3 ). ## Key Immune Cell Networks in Osteoporosis

### Th17/Treg Imbalance: A Central Axis of Adaptive Immunity

The Th17/Treg imbalance represents a pivotal adaptive immune mechanism linking gut microbiota dysbiosis, estrogen withdrawal, and skeletal immunopathology in PMOP. Its significance extends beyond a simple opposition between pro-inflammatory Th17 cells and immunosuppressive Treg cells; rather, it functions as a critical translational interface that converts distal intestinal perturbations and endocrine fluctuations into localized osteoclast predominance within the bone marrow. 126 Current evidence suggests that this axis is a major immunological nexus within the gut-bone axis, functionally connecting intestinal ecological disruption, adaptive immune deviation, and pathological bone remodeling. 127

Gut microbiota dysbiosis can initiate Th17/Treg disequilibrium through three interrelated mechanisms. First, increased intestinal permeability facilitates the translocation of microbial components, including lipopolysaccharide, which activates dendritic cells and monocytes/macrophages and promotes the release of Th17-polarizing cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1β, and interleukin-23 (IL-23). 111 , 128 Second, depletion of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, may impair forkhead box P3-positive (FoxP3+) Treg differentiation and weaken immune tolerance. 82 Third, disrupted tryptophan metabolism may disturb aryl hydrocarbon receptor-related signaling, further destabilizing Th17/Treg homeostasis. 129 Although preclinical models have shown that specific bacterial communities and metabolites can influence Th17 or Treg polarization, these findings should be interpreted primarily as mechanistic clues rather than direct clinical conclusions for PMOP. Importantly, intestinal dysregulation can transmit inflammatory pressure to the bone marrow microenvironment through this adaptive immune axis.

Estrogen deficiency further consolidates this immune deviation by disrupting mucosal barrier integrity, immune tolerance, and T-cell homeostasis. After menopause, estrogen withdrawal increases intestinal permeability, promotes microbiota-dependent inflammation, and facilitates the expansion or marrow recruitment of Th17 cells and TNF-α-producing lymphocytes. Experimental evidence indicates that gut-derived Th17 cells and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-positive T cells can migrate to the bone marrow, elevate local IL-17 and TNF levels, stimulate RANKL expression, and promote bone loss. 29 , 130 These findings suggest that estrogen deficiency-induced skeletal deterioration is not driven solely by local skeletal mechanisms, but may also involve a multi-organ pathway comprising intestinal immune activation, T-cell trafficking, and enhanced osteoclastogenic signaling within the marrow.

Within the bone marrow, Th17/Treg imbalance ultimately determines whether pro-osteoclastogenic signaling is persistently amplified. Th17-derived IL-17 induces RANKL expression in osteoblasts, stromal cells, and immune cells, while synergizing with TNF-α and IL-6 to activate NF-κB/NFATc1 pathways that support osteoclast precursor differentiation, fusion, and survival. Conversely, reduced Treg abundance or function weakens FoxP3-associated immune restraint and diminishes osteoclast suppression mediated by interleukin-4 (IL-4), TGF-β, and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4). 131–133 As a result, the marrow microenvironment loses critical brakes on inflammatory RANKL signaling and bone resorption. The Th17/Treg axis therefore functions as an executive interface through which gut-derived and endocrine disturbances are translated into sustained osteoclastogenic pressure.

### Monocyte Subsets and Osteoclast Precursor Remodeling: From Quantitative Shifts to Lineage Imbalance

Traditional osteoimmunology has long regarded monocytes as a major precursor reservoir for osteoclastogenesis. Under stimulation by macrophage colony-stimulating factor and RANKL, monocytes undergo recruitment, differentiation, fusion, and maturation to form bone-resorbing osteoclasts. 134 This model helps explain enhanced bone resorption in PMOP, particularly under estrogen deficiency, inflammatory activation, and RANKL/OPG imbalance. However, it often treats monocytes as a relatively homogeneous precursor population, which cannot fully account for the clinical heterogeneity in bone resorption severity, disease progression, and treatment response among patients with PMOP.

Single-cell transcriptomics is reshaping this view by showing that PMOP-related myeloid pathology involves remodeling of monocyte subset composition and functional architecture rather than merely global changes in monocyte abundance or average gene expression. Bone marrow single-cell analyses have identified distinct cluster of differentiation 14-positive (CD14+) monocyte clusters, among which cluster 7, marked by Fc gamma receptor IIIa (FCGR3A)/cluster of differentiation 16 (CD16), is expanded in PMOP and enriched in inflammatory, immune-response, and osteoclast differentiation pathways. In contrast, cluster 1 shows an opposite tendency and appears to represent a more primitive-like, less osteoclastogenic subset. 135 These findings shift the focus from whether total monocytes are increased to which subsets expand, which are depleted, and which are positioned closer to the osteoclast lineage.

Mechanistically, estrogen withdrawal, inflammaging, and gut-derived inflammatory stimuli may translate systemic risk factors into osteoclast precursor predominance by reshaping monocyte subset behavior. Increased TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and LPS levels heighten monocyte sensitivity to marrow microenvironmental cues, while chemokine axes such as C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2)/C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) may recruit inflammatory monocytes to endosteal surfaces and active remodeling sites. 136–138 Abnormal lactate metabolism, lipid metabolism, and oxidative stress may further promote subset-specific metabolic reprogramming, enhancing monocyte survival, migration, and osteoclastogenic capacity. 139–141 Importantly, single-cell analyses reveals that cluster 7 appears to exhibit active interactions with other marrow cells through major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II) and interleukin-16 (IL-16)/cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4)-related signaling, suggesting that pathogenic monocyte subsets function not only as osteoclast precursors but also as inflammatory signal relays that reset marrow immune communication and lower the threshold for osteoclast differentiation. 135

Consequently, monocyte abnormalities in PMOP should be conceptualized as myeloid lineage remodeling rather than simple quantitative change. Osteoclast predominance may depend on the recalibrated balance between primitive-like, inflammatory-like, CD16+-like, and pre-osteoclast-like subsets, particularly the transition from cluster 1-like states toward cluster 7-like osteoclast-primed phenotypes. Further delineation of their surface markers, metabolic dependencies, and intercellular communication networks is needed to determine which subsets represent stable disease drivers rather than context-dependent states.

### Macrophage Polarization and Bone Microenvironment Homeostasis: Inflammation Regulators and Repair Coordinators

Macrophage polarization constitutes a pivotal regulatory process within the bone marrow immune microenvironment, but its role should not be reduced to a simplistic binary opposition between “pro-inflammatory M1” and “anti-inflammatory M2” phenotypes. The M1/M2 paradigm provides a useful framework for understanding the basic functional differentiation of macrophages in osteoporosis: M1-like macrophages typically release TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and other pro-inflammatory mediators that amplify inflammation and osteoclastogenesis, whereas M2-like macrophages are more closely associated with inflammation resolution, angiogenesis, matrix remodeling, and osteogenic repair. 121 , 142 However, bone marrow macrophages in vivo do not exist as fixed phenotypes; rather, they are dynamically shaped by estrogen levels, aging, gut-derived LPS, lipid metabolic dysregulation, hypoxia, and local cellular crosstalk, thereby exhibiting a continuous spectrum of functional states. Recent single-cell and disease-specific macrophage studies suggest that although the M1/M2 classification has explanatory value, it is insufficient to fully capture macrophage heterogeneity and stage-dependent functions within complex disease microenvironments. 143 Consequently, when discussing macrophage polarization in postmenopausal osteoporosis, the focus should not be limited to labeling macrophages as “pro-inflammatory” or “reparative”, but should instead address whether macrophage functional states can shift the bone marrow microenvironment from persistent inflammation toward effective osteogenic restoration.

Macrophages play a fundamental role in determining whether bone remodeling maintains coupling equilibrium by simultaneously modulating osteoclastogenic and osteogenic pathways. On the pro-osteoclastogenic side, M1-like macrophages release inflammatory mediators, including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, which enhance RANKL/RANK/NF-κB/NFATc1 signaling and thereby promote osteoclast precursor recruitment, fusion, and maturation. 110 Concurrently, these inflammatory mediators, together with macrophage-derived reactive oxygen species, may impair mitochondrial function in osteoblasts and suppress osteogenesis-related programs, including Runx2, Osterix, and type I collagen expression, resulting in insufficient compensatory bone formation. 144 Conversely, appropriate M2-like polarization supports osteogenic repair by promoting inflammation resolution, angiogenesis, matrix remodeling, and BMSC osteogenic differentiation through TGF-β, bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-related signaling, angiogenic factors, and exosomal contents. 145 , 146 Thus, macrophages may function either as amplifiers of inflammatory bone resorption or as coordinators of osteogenic repair, depending on their functional state and local microenvironmental cues. Importantly, this functional plasticity is not fixed but is mechanistically governed by macrophage metabolic programming, which provides the basis for the immunometabolic regulation discussed in the following section.

### B Cells and Other Immune Components: Complementary Regulators of the Bone-Immune Network

Beyond the Th17/Treg axis and the monocyte-macrophage system, B lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and neutrophils constitute a complementary amplification layer within the osteoimmune network of PMOP. Although they are not usually the primary initiators of bone loss, these cells contribute to sustaining osteoclast predominance by modulating the RANKL/OPG balance, amplifying chronic low-grade inflammation, and reshaping bone marrow immune homeostasis. B cells exhibit context-dependent duality in skeletal metabolism. Under physiological conditions, they produce osteoprotegerin and restrain excessive RANKL/RANK-mediated osteoclastogenesis. 147 However, under estrogen deficiency, aging, or inflammatory stimulation, B cells may shift toward RANKL expression and secrete granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, thereby promoting osteoclast precursor expansion and neutrophil-related inflammatory responses. 148–150 Regulatory B-cell subsets may counteract this process through IL-10- and TGF-β-mediated immune suppression. 151 Dendritic cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity by presenting antigens and releasing IL-6, interleukin-12 (IL-12), and IL-23 in response to microbial products, damage-associated signals, and inflammatory mediators, thereby enhancing Th17/IL-17 polarization and the RANKL pathway. 133 Neutrophils mainly participate in the execution and propagation of chronic inflammation through altered chemotaxis, reactive oxygen species production, protease activity, and neutrophil extracellular trap formation. 152 Under specific conditions, they may also promote osteoclastogenesis through RANKL-related and TLR4-dependent mechanisms. 153 Collectively, these immune cells form a self-reinforcing network that consolidates endocrine- and senescence-driven osteoclast dominance, supporting the view of PMOP as a multicellular osteoimmunometabolic disorder requiring integrated therapeutic targeting.

## Immunometabolic Reprogramming: A Critical Layer Determining Bone Cell Fate

Expanding on the immune cell networks described above, this section examines how metabolic programs and microbial metabolites sustain, amplify, or redirect immune and bone-cell phenotypes within the osteoporotic marrow niche.

### Metabolic Reprogramming in Osteoclasts: Metabolic Permissiveness Transcending Signal-Driven Paradigms

Osteoclastogenesis requires not only canonical pro-resorptive signaling through the RANKL/RANK, NF-κB, MAPK, and NFATc1 pathways, but also a metabolically permissive state characterized by glycolytic rewiring and adaptive mitochondrial remodeling. Mature osteoclasts are highly energy-demanding effector cells, and their differentiation, fusion, actin ring formation, ruffled border development, proton pump activation, and lacunar acidification require sustained energy supply and substrate redistribution. 154 Therefore, osteoclast predominance in PMOP should not be interpreted merely as a consequence of increased RANKL expression or inflammatory cytokine stimulation. Rather, it reflects coordinated activation between pro-osteoclastogenic signaling and energy metabolic programs. Only when osteoclast precursors acquire enhanced glycolytic flux, mitochondrial adaptation, and remodeled metabolic intermediates can inflammatory and RANKL signals be efficiently translated into sustained bone-resorptive function.

A pivotal 2024 study provides important mechanistic support for this concept by showing that RANK signaling upregulates protein arginine methyltransferase 6 (PRMT6), thereby promoting a metabolic shift from fatty acid oxidation toward glycolysis in osteoclasts. 155 , 156 Conversely, Prmt6 deletion reduced hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α)-mediated glycolysis, enhanced fatty acid oxidation, and inhibited osteoclast differentiation and bone loss in ovariectomized models. Mechanistically, PRMT6 regulates asymmetric histone H3 arginine 2 (H3R2) dimethylation and modifies the epigenetic status of promoter regions of fatty acid oxidation-related genes, including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (Ppard), acyl-CoA oxidase 3 (Acox3), and carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (Cpt1a). This epigenetic regulation suppresses oxidative lipid utilization and favors a glycolysis-dependent state that supports rapid osteoclast differentiation and functional execution. These findings support PRMT6 as a metabolic checkpoint linking RANK signaling with epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming.

The biological significance of glycolytic rewiring extends beyond adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production. Under RANKL stimulation, osteoclast precursors exhibit increased glucose uptake, upregulated glycolytic enzyme expression, and enhanced lactate production, collectively supporting cytoskeletal reorganization, cell fusion, and extracellular acidification. 157 Glycolytic metabolites may further promote osteoclast maturation through HIF-1α stabilization, lactate transport, and local microenvironmental acidification. 158 , 159 However, osteoclasts do not depend exclusively on glycolysis. Mitochondrial metabolism, including the tricarboxylic acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and mitochondrial dynamics, remains important for sustained resorptive activity, particularly during membrane remodeling, resorption surface formation, and ion pump function. 140 , 160 , 161 Thus, osteoclast metabolic reprogramming should be understood as a staged and functionally adaptive shift in substrate utilization rather than a complete replacement of mitochondrial metabolism by glycolysis.

These findings extend RANKL-centered models by introducing metabolic permission as a necessary component of osteoclast activation. Osteoclasts therefore integrate inflammatory and epigenetic signals with stage-dependent glycolytic and mitochondrial programs rather than relying on a single dominant metabolic pathway. PRMT6, HIF-1α, lactate handling, fatty acid oxidation, and mitochondrial adaptation together define candidate metabolic checkpoints whose therapeutic relevance is considered in Therapeutic Strategies Based on Immunometabolic Remodeling .

### Macrophage Immunometabolism: Sustained Inflammatory Phenotypes and Immunometabolic Memory

Macrophage immunometabolism principally governs macrophage functional polarization and represents a critical mechanistic link between chronic low-grade inflammation and bone degeneration. In PMOP, estrogen deficiency, aging, gut-derived LPS, lipid dysmetabolism, and persistent low-grade inflammation collectively shift bone marrow macrophages from oxidative metabolic homeostasis toward glycolysis-dominant inflammatory states. This metabolic reprogramming does not merely accompany M1-like activation; rather, it sustains cytokine production, enhances inflammasome responsiveness, and prolongs an osteoclast-supportive inflammatory niche. 162–164 Thus, macrophage immunometabolism provides a mechanistic explanation for why inflammatory bone resorption can persist after the initial endocrine, microbial, or metabolic insults have been established.

Metabolites such as citrate and itaconate further reveal the plasticity of macrophage phenotypes. A 2024 study on citrate-functionalized scaffolds suggested that exogenous citrate can regulate macrophage polarization through metabolic modulation, thereby helping to maintain bone homeostasis in the context of osteoporosis. 165 This finding supports the view that metabolites are not merely energy substrates, but also regulatory signals capable of reshaping immune phenotypes. Importantly, the role of citrate in inflammatory metabolism is context-dependent. In pro-inflammatory macrophages, mitochondrial citrate efflux can provide substrates for lipid synthesis, acetylation modifications, and inflammatory mediator production. 166 , 167 Conversely, under conditions of controlled material-based delivery or metabolic regulation, exogenous citrate may promote reparative macrophage transitions by influencing glycolytic flux and tricarboxylic acid cycle activity. 165 , 168 In contrast, the immune-responsive gene 1 (IRG1)/itaconate axis functions as an endogenous inflammatory braking system. IRG1 catalyzes itaconate production, and itaconate constrains excessive inflammatory responses through regulation of oxidative stress, activation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)-related signaling, and inhibition of inflammasome activation. 169–171 Supporting evidence has shown that IRG1 deficiency aggravates ovariectomy-induced bone loss and enhances osteoclastogenesis, with the underlying mechanism associated with amplified NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activation. 172

The NLRP3 inflammasome serves as a key execution node through which macrophage immunometabolism amplifies inflammatory bone loss. Enhanced glycolysis, mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species accumulation, lipid dysmetabolism, and LPS/TLR4 signaling can collectively promote NLRP3 assembly and activation, thereby triggering caspase-1-dependent maturation and release of IL-1β and interleukin-18 (IL-18). 163 , 173–175 IL-1β not only potentiates the responsiveness of pre-osteoclasts to RANKL, but also synergizes with TNF-α, IL-6, and other mediators to activate NF-κB/NFATc1 pathways, accelerating osteoclast differentiation, fusion, and bone resorption. 137 , 176 As noted in recent reviews on the NLRP3 inflammasome and osteoporosis, excessive inflammasome activation may disrupt the balance between bone repair and bone remodeling through osteoimmune signaling, extrinsic stress responses, and intercellular communication. 177

Together, these findings place macrophage immunometabolism at the intersection of metabolic switching, loss of metabolite-mediated inflammatory restraint, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and potentiated osteoclastogenesis. The key mechanistic implication is that macrophage inflammatory output depends on metabolic state and metabolite context, providing a basis for the checkpoint-oriented interventions discussed in Therapeutic Strategies Based on Immunometabolic Remodeling .

### BMSC Fate Shift: The Osteogenic-Adipogenic Imbalance in Postmenopausal Osteoporosis

BMSC fate deviation represents a fundamental mechanism underlying the coexistence of impaired osteogenesis and BMAT expansion in postmenopausal osteoporosis. Under estrogen deficiency, aging, chronic inflammation, and metabolic stress, BMSCs undergo pathological lineage competition between osteogenic and adipogenic programs. 43 Physiologically, Wnt/β-catenin, BMP/Smad, Runx2, and Osterix signaling promote osteoblastogenesis, whereas PPARγ and C/EBPα drive adipogenic commitment. 178 When the marrow microenvironment becomes inflammatory, oxidative, and lipotoxic, osteogenic signaling is progressively suppressed, while adipogenic programs become dominant, resulting in reduced bone formation and BMAT accumulation. 60

Disrupted lipid metabolism provides direct molecular substrates and signaling pressure for this fate shift. Excess free fatty acids, cholesterol, and lipid-derived molecules can inhibit BMSC osteogenic differentiation through lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress, while enhancing PPARγ-dependent adipogenic programming. 60 , 179 , 180 Lipid abnormalities may also modulate macrophage activity and promote inflammatory cytokine release, including IL-6 and TNF-α, thereby further reinforcing a pro-adipogenic and anti-osteogenic marrow environment. 181 Thus, lipid dysmetabolism should not be regarded merely as a concomitant metabolic change in PMOP, but as an active driver of BMSC lineage deviation.

Chronic inflammation further consolidates pathological commitment through transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 activate NF-κB, Janus kinase (JAK)/signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT), and MAPK pathways, suppressing Wnt/β-catenin- and Runx2/Osterix-related osteogenic programs while promoting ROS accumulation and cellular senescence. 60 , 182–185 In parallel, inflammatory cues may reduce osteogenic gene accessibilitythrough enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2)-mediated trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me3), deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) methylation, and non-coding ribonucleic acid (RNA) regulation, thereby durably impairing BMSC osteogenic plasticity under persistent inflammatory-lipotoxic stress. 186

BMAT expansion then establishes a self-perpetuating steatotic niche through endocrine and paracrine signaling. Marrow adipocyte-derived adipokines, free fatty acids, IL-6, and TNF-α can inhibit BMSC osteogenesis, promote inflammatory macrophage polarization, and enhance osteoclastogenesis. 181 , 187 , 188 More importantly, BMAT enlargement indicates that more BMSCs are locked into adipogenic trajectories, reducing the osteoblast precursor pool and creating a vicious cycle of BMSC adipogenic shift, BMAT expansion, lipotoxic inflammation, and further osteogenic suppression. 188 , 189

Consequently, insufficient bone formation and pathological adipogenesis in PMOP are not parallel phenomena, but interconnected outcomes of dysregulated fate determination within a shared progenitor pool. BMSC fate deviation therefore represents a pathogenic hub integrating endocrine withdrawal, lipid dysmetabolism, inflammatory signaling, epigenetic remodeling, and BMAT accumulation.

### Microbial Metabolites: Gut-to-Bone Signal Transducers

Microbial metabolites should be regarded not as passive biomarkers, but as active gut-to-bone signaling mediators that translate intestinal ecological dynamics into skeletal outcomes. SCFAs, including acetate, propionate, and butyrate, are generated by gut microbiota through dietary fiber fermentation and can regulate immune responses, endocrine metabolism, and the bone marrow microenvironment. 77 , 190 Current evidence suggests that gut microbiota dysbiosis is clinically associated with PMOP, supporting the possibility that microbiota-derived metabolites may serve as therapeutic entry points for abnormal bone metabolism. 72

The central significance of SCFAs lies in their dual regulation of immune homeostasis and bone cell metabolism. Butyrate and propionate promote Treg-mediated immune tolerance through histone deacetylase inhibition, G protein-coupled receptor activation, and modulation of T-cell differentiation, while restraining Th17 responses, macrophage activation, and inflammasome-related inflammation. 38 , 191 As inflammatory pressure decreases, RANKL expression, NF-κB/NFATc1 signaling, and osteoclastogenic propensity are correspondingly attenuated. Meanwhile, SCFAs may enhance oxidative stress resistance, energy metabolic adaptation, and osteogenic differentiation in osteoblasts and bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells, suggesting that they function not only as anti-inflammatory mediators but also as pro-repair metabolic signals. 192 , 193 Animal studies further indicate that SCFA supplementation or high-fiber diets can preserve bone mass under estrogen-deficient or inflammatory conditions. 77

Beyond SCFAs, tryptophan metabolites and bile acids also contribute to skeletal immunometabolic regulation. Indole-derived tryptophan metabolites can modulate Th17/Treg balance, mucosal barrier integrity, and inflammatory responses through aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling. 41 , 194 , 195 Secondary bile acids may influence macrophage inflammatory activity, energy metabolism, and osteogenesis-related pathways through farnesoid X receptor and Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 activation. 196–198 Although the evidence for these metabolites remains less mature than that for SCFAs, together they suggest that gut microbiota communicate with the bone marrow through a coordinated metabolic language involving gut-bone and gut-brain communication axes.

Thus, microbial metabolites act as functional signal converters linking gut ecology with skeletal homeostasis. SCFA depletion reflects a loss of anti-inflammatory buffering, immune tolerance, and osteogenic support, whereas abnormal tryptophan metabolite and bile acid profiles may further aggravate immune inflammation and metabolic maladaptation. These metabolite-dependent effects provide the mechanistic basis for the microecological interventions discussed in Therapeutic Strategies Based on Immunometabolic Remodeling .

## Therapeutic Strategies Based on Immunometabolic Remodeling

At present, osteoporosis treatment remains primarily based on anti-resorptive and osteoanabolic strategies. Bisphosphonates, RANKL inhibitors, and bone-forming agents have demonstrated clear efficacy in increasing bone mineral density and reducing fracture risk, and they continue to constitute the clinical cornerstone of disease management. 199 These therapies remain essential but primarily modify osteoclast or osteoblast activity and incompletely address upstream niche abnormalities such as immune dysregulation, BMAT expansion, and BMSC fate deviation. The following subsections therefore examine microecological, immunophenotypic, and metabolic-checkpoint strategies as potential adjuncts to—not replacements for—established anti-resorptive and osteoanabolic treatment.

### Microecological Remodeling: Therapeutic Leverage via Gut-Bone Axis Modulation

Microecological intervention represents a distinct therapeutic dimension in postmenopausal osteoporosis, extending beyond simple bacterial supplementation toward upstream remodeling of the gut-immune-metabolism-bone axis. Estrogen deficiency and aging reduce microbial diversity, impair intestinal barrier integrity, increase systemic exposure to gut-derived inflammatory signals such as lipopolysaccharide, and diminish protective metabolites, particularly SCFAs. 73 , 200 These changes promote Th17/Treg imbalance, pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization, elevated RANKL/OPG signaling, and impaired osteogenic metabolism, indicating that microecological therapy should be viewed as a strategy to restore barrier function, optimize microbial metabolite output, attenuate chronic low-grade inflammation, and redirect bone marrow immunity toward an anti-inflammatory, osteogenesis-supportive state. Among current approaches, probiotics, especially Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains, are the most extensively studied. Their value lies not merely in increasing selected taxa, but in strengthening tight junctions, reducing intestinal and marrow inflammation, rebalancing Treg/Th17 responses, enhancing SCFA production, and modulating distal bone resorption signals; 39 , 201–203 however, these effects are strongly strain-specific, underscoring the need to move beyond taxonomic description toward validation of “strain-metabolite-immunophenotype-bone outcome” pathways. Prebiotics and dietary modulation act at the substrate level by promoting SCFA-producing bacteria and sustaining acetate, propionate, and butyrate generation, thereby enhancing immune tolerance, suppressing inflammasome activation, reducing osteoclast precursor responsiveness to RANKL, and improving the metabolic fitness of BMSCs and osteoblasts. 39 , 77 , 192 , 204 In this sense, they function less as nutritional supplements than as forms of ecological niche engineering. Fecal microbiota transplantation offers a more direct means of reconstructing ecological balance and has shown osteoprotective effects in experimental models, although clinical translation remains limited by donor variability, engraftment stability, safety, and patient selection. 71 , 205 Engineered bacteria and targeted metabolite delivery may further enable precision modulation, but at present are better regarded as mechanistic and delivery platforms than mature therapeutic options. 206 , 207 Overall, microecological strategies are most appropriately positioned as adjunctive approaches that optimize the marrow immunometabolic background rather than replace established anti-resorptive or anabolic therapies.

### Immune Cell Phenotype Correction: Transitioning from Anti-Inflammation to Metabolic Reprogramming

Immune phenotype correction represents a strategic therapeutic approach for immunometabolic intervention in osteoporosis, aiming not at broad immunosuppression but at redirecting pathological immunity toward homeostasis and osteogenic support. In osteoporosis, immune dysregulation involves T cells, B cells, monocytes/macrophages, and cytokine networks that exacerbate osteoclastogenesis through RANKL/OPG imbalance and pro-inflammatory mediators, including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-17, while simultaneously impairing osteoblast function. 208 Effective correction therefore requires reconstruction of the bone marrow immune ecology rather than isolated anti-inflammatory targeting. Key strategies include Th17/Treg rebalancing, macrophage polarization control, and restriction of pathogenic monocytes. Th17/Treg rebalancing counteracts adaptive immune dysfunction by restoring immune tolerance and attenuating IL-23/IL-17 axis overactivation, potentially through regulation of gut-derived metabolites, vitamin D/vitamin D receptor (VDR) signaling, or anti-inflammatory microenvironmental remodeling. Macrophage polarization control leverages innate immune plasticity by shifting pro-inflammatory M1-like phenotypes, characterized by TNF-α and IL-1β release, toward reparative M2-like states associated with angiogenesis, matrix remodeling, and osteogenic support. 121 , 209 Importantly, this strategy is not aimed merely at suppressing inflammation; rather, it seeks to promote metabolic reprogramming by reshaping the glycolysis/oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) balance, regulating itaconate metabolism, activating Nrf2 signaling, and modulating inflammasome activity. Emerging single-cell evidence suggests that PMOP may involve selective expansion of highly osteoclastogenic monocyte subsets rather than uniform monocytic alteration, supporting precision interventions that limit their chemotactic homing, inflammatory communication, RANKL sensitivity, and terminal differentiation. 210 Collectively, these approaches shift PMOP management from bone resorption inhibition toward bone marrow immune ecology restoration, establishing an immunophenotypic foundation for integrating anti-RANKL biologics, anti-inflammatory agents, metabolic modulators, and anabolic therapies within future precision treatment frameworks.

### Metabolic Checkpoint Intervention: Emerging Precision Paradigms in Osteoporosis Management

Metabolic checkpoint intervention represents an emerging precision strategy that complements conventional anti-resorptive and osteoanabolic therapies by reprogramming the bone immunometabolic microenvironment. This paradigm recognizes that pathological bone loss is driven not only by aberrant signaling but also by metabolic permissibility, sustained by glycolytic rewiring, altered fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial stress, inflammasome activation, and metabolite feedback within osteoclasts, macrophages, and marrow immune cells. 155 , 211–213 Several metabolic nodes provide potential intervention opportunities. PRMT6 links RANK signaling to osteoclast glycolytic reprogramming through epigenetic regulation, whereas its inhibition may disrupt osteoclast bioenergetic dependence and attenuate ovariectomy-induced bone loss. 155 The IRG1/itaconate axis functions as an endogenous inflammatory-metabolic buffer; impaired activity may amplify NLRP3 inflammasome activation and osteoclastogenesis, while itaconate derivatives show preclinical potential for suppressing pathological bone turnover. 170 , 171 , 214 NLRP3 itself serves as a key hub converting estrogen deficiency, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and lipid dysmetabolism into IL-1β/IL-18 release, enhanced RANKL responsiveness, and NF-κB/NFATc1-driven osteoclast differentiation. 215 , 216 Thus, NLRP3 inhibition may help decouple chronic inflammation from excessive bone resorption. In parallel, citrate-based biomaterials offer a localized strategy for niche reconstruction by modulating macrophage glycolysis/OXPHOS balance, inflammatory responses, and osteogenic support within bone defects or implant sites, thereby reducing the uncertainty associated with systemic metabolic intervention. 165 , 217 Collectively, PRMT6 targeting, IRG1/itaconate restoration, NLRP3 inhibition, and citrate delivery illustrate a therapeutic shift from terminal bone cell modulation toward upstream immunometabolic program remodeling. Although these approaches remain mainly at mechanistic, preclinical, or biomaterial-translation stages, they provide a rational foundation for integrating metabolic checkpoint modulation with established anti-resorptive, anti-inflammatory, and anabolic strategies in future precision frameworks for osteoporosis ( Figure 4 ).
