# Enhancing the Safety of Nanoparticles in Medicine: Highlights of Progress and Critical Objectives

## Abstract
Nanoparticles have transformed drug delivery, imaging, vaccination, and precision therapeutics, but their clinical translation remains constrained by safety profiles that are inseparable from material design, biological identity, host factors, and manufacturing. This review critically evaluates recent progress, persistent limitations, and priority objectives for safer nanomedicine. Unlike reviews organized primarily by material class or isolated toxicology endpoints, we integrate physicochemical determinants, protein corona formation, immune recognition, organ disposition, preclinical models, chemistry-manufacturing-controls (CMC), regulatory expectations, disease context, and patient heterogeneity into a translational safety-by-design framework. We distinguish clinically established risk-mitigation strategies from emerging approaches and examine why apparently favorable preclinical performance may fail to predict human safety. Particular attention is given to complement activation, repeat-dose immunogenicity, long-term retention, blood-brain barrier delivery, oncology and inflammatory disease, assay interference, quantitative biodistribution, and scale-up. Artificial intelligence, physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling, multi-omics, organ-on-chip systems, imaging, and digital-twin concepts are evaluated as emerging tools for predictive safety, while their present validation limitations are emphasized. Overall, the evidence supports early integration of efficacy, mechanistic toxicology, CMC, and patient-specific risk rather than downstream safety testing alone. Harmonized characterization, clinically relevant models, long-term fate studies, and lifecycle surveillance remain central priorities for the next generation of nanomedicines.

## Keywords
nanoparticle safety; nanotoxicology; biological interactions; immunotoxicity; translational nanomedicine

## Introduction

Nanoparticles have become one of the most influential enabling technologies in modern medicine because they allow therapeutic and diagnostic agents to be formulated, protected, transported, and presented to biological systems in ways that are not achievable with conventional molecular dosage forms alone. 1–4 By controlling size, shape, composition, deformability, surface chemistry, and interfacial behavior, nanoparticle-based systems can modify solubility, circulation half-life, tissue distribution, intracellular trafficking, and release kinetics, thereby widening the therapeutic index of potent but otherwise limited payloads. 1 , 2 These advantages are not merely conceptual. Over the past three decades, nanomedicine has generated clinically used liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, polymer conjugates, protein nanoparticles, iron-carbohydrate nanocolloids, and nanocrystal formulations that have altered standards of care in oncology, infectious disease, metabolic disorders, vaccination, imaging, and supportive care. 2 , 5 , 6 The field therefore occupies a distinctive translational position: unlike many platform technologies that remain largely aspirational, nanoparticle systems have already demonstrated that nanoscale engineering can produce regulatory approvals, industrial adoption, and measurable patient benefit. 2 , 3 , 5 , 6

The clinical promise of nanoparticles in medicine arises from a convergence of pharmacologic and biologic principles. First, nanoparticles can rescue otherwise unmanageable active pharmaceutical ingredients by increasing apparent solubility, improving chemical stability, reducing premature metabolism, and limiting nonspecific exposure. 1 , 2 Second, they can decouple systemic exposure from target exposure by altering biodistribution and organ partitioning, which is particularly relevant for cytotoxic drugs, nucleic acids, immunomodulators, radionuclides, and imaging agents. 1–4 Third, they permit multifunctionality: the same carrier can integrate stealth properties, targeting ligands, triggered-release mechanisms, imaging labels, and immune-modulating features. Fourth, nanoparticles can be designed to engage biological transport processes at several scales, including vascular extravasation, lymphatic trafficking, endocytosis, endosomal escape, and interstitial penetration. 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 In principle, these capabilities support a transition from passive formulation science toward programmable therapeutic systems that are matched to the pathophysiology of specific diseases and even to the heterogeneity of individual patients. 3 , 4 , 7

This promise has been especially visible in cancer. Nanoparticles were embraced in oncology because they offered solutions to several chronic limitations of anticancer pharmacology: poor aqueous solubility, dose-limiting systemic toxicity, low tumor selectivity, and the need to combine multiple agents with incompatible physicochemical properties. 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 Clinically approved systems such as PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin and albumin-bound paclitaxel showed that nanoparticle reformulation could reduce selected toxicities, change infusion behavior, improve tolerability, and create viable commercial products. 3 , 4 , 7 More recently, the success of lipid nanoparticle-enabled nucleic acid delivery, including globally deployed mRNA vaccines, has expanded the perceived scope of nanomedicine beyond oncology and has demonstrated that nanoparticle systems can support rapid manufacturing scale-up, cold-chain distribution, and worldwide clinical deployment. 2 , 6 This broadening of indication space matters for safety because it shifts the field from relatively controlled specialist settings toward larger, more heterogeneous patient populations, repeated dosing paradigms, preventive applications, and combinations with biologics, devices, and immunotherapies. 2 , 6 , 9

Yet the same features that confer therapeutic opportunity also create safety complexity. Nanoparticles are not simply small versions of conventional formulations. Their clinical behavior is governed by emergent properties produced by the coupling of material composition, nanoscale architecture, colloidal stability, interfacial adsorption, dynamic restructuring in biological fluids, and interaction with immune and clearance systems. 1 , 6 , 9–14 Accordingly, nanoparticle safety cannot be reduced to the toxicology of the free drug or the bulk material alone. The relevant hazard profile is a system-level property of the entire nanoscale construct, including its excipients, degradation products, adsorbed biomolecular corona, process-related impurities, storage-dependent transformations, and dose- and route-specific biological interactions. 6 , 9–11 This principle is now well recognized in translational nanomedicine, but it remains imperfectly implemented in discovery pipelines, where efficacy-oriented optimization often still precedes robust mechanistic safety evaluation. 5 , 6 , 10

Safety has therefore become the central barrier to translation not because nanoparticle systems are uniformly unsafe, but because their risk profiles are frequently difficult to predict, compare, standardize, and regulate across platforms. 5 , 6 , 10 The problem is compounded by the historical mismatch between the sophistication of nanoparticle engineering and the maturity of the corresponding safety science. A formulation can be exquisitely optimized for encapsulation efficiency, targeting ligand density, or stimulus-responsive release, yet still fail clinically because of unanticipated complement activation, infusion reactions, altered pharmacokinetics after repeat dosing, off-target accumulation in mononuclear phagocyte system organs, unexpected degradation behavior, assay interference, manufacturing drift, or poor reproducibility across scales. 5 , 6 , 9–14 Translation is further constrained by the reality that preclinical models often overestimate delivery performance and underestimate safety liabilities, particularly when tumor biology, vascular permeability, immune competence, protein composition, and sex- or ancestry-related host variables diverge from those in the intended human population. 7–9 , 11 , 12 , 15

A major conceptual advance in the field has been the recognition that nanoparticle safety and efficacy are inseparable. The traditional translational paradigm treated safety primarily as a downstream gatekeeping exercise that follows proof-of-concept efficacy. In nanomedicine, however, the material features that determine efficacy often also determine toxicity. For example, increasing circulation time through PEGylation can improve exposure and enable tumor accumulation or extrahepatic delivery, but it can also influence anti-PEG immunogenicity, complement activation, and accelerated blood clearance on repeat administration. 13 , 14 , 16 Enhancing cellular uptake by increasing cationic character may improve transfection or endosomal escape, yet at the same time increase membrane disruption, protein adsorption, hemolytic potential, and innate immune activation. 9 , 10 Optimizing size for tissue penetration may change renal clearance thresholds, hepatosplenic sequestration, or placental transfer. Similarly, pursuing multifunctionality through ligand decoration, image-enabling components, or responsive coatings can intensify compositional complexity, increase batch-to-batch variability, and complicate analytical comparability, thereby widening both regulatory uncertainty and toxicologic ambiguity. 5 , 6 , 8 , 10 , 11

This tight coupling is especially important in cancer nanomedicine, where early enthusiasm was strongly shaped by the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect. The EPR framework provided an appealing mechanistic basis for selective tumor delivery, and it helped justify extensive investment in passively targeted nanoparticles. 3 , 4 , 8 , 15 However, subsequent work has shown that EPR is highly heterogeneous across tumor types, anatomical sites, disease stages, and individual patients; moreover, the magnitude and clinical utility of passive accumulation in human solid tumors are often much less predictable than in rodent xenograft models. 8 , 15 This does not negate the value of nanoparticles in oncology, but it changes the safety discussion in a fundamental way. When tumor delivery is variable and often modest, the balance between intended and unintended exposure becomes more dependent on systemic disposition, immune recognition, stromal barriers, vascular physiology, and patient selection. In other words, safety cannot be considered independently of delivery realism. A nanoparticle that performs well in a permissive animal model may expose patients primarily through liver, spleen, blood, or infusion-related pathways rather than through therapeutically meaningful tumor deposition. 7 , 8 , 15

A second major realization is that the biological identity of a nanoparticle is not fixed at the time of manufacture. Once introduced into blood or other biological fluids, nanoparticles rapidly acquire a biomolecular corona composed of proteins, lipids, metabolites, and other macromolecules. 11 , 12 This adsorbed layer can profoundly alter colloidal stability, opsonization, immune recognition, cell-surface interactions, trafficking, and clearance. As a result, the in vivo behavior of a nominally identical formulation may vary across species, disease states, and patient subpopulations as a function of the surrounding biological milieu. 11 , 12 The translational implications are substantial. Protein corona composition is influenced by methodological factors such as sample preparation and analytical workflow, but also by patient-specific variables including inflammation, sex, ancestry, hormonal state, metabolic status, and comorbidities. 11 , 12 Safety assessment that ignores these dynamic interfaces risks both false reassurance and poor reproducibility. The growing emphasis on corona standardization and patient-dependent corona biology represents one of the clearest examples of the field moving from descriptive nanotoxicology toward mechanistically informed translational safety science. 11 , 12

Immunological interactions remain among the most consequential and incompletely resolved safety issues in nanomedicine. Nanoparticles can engage complement pathways, coagulation cascades, platelets, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells, and pattern-recognition systems in ways that depend on composition, curvature, surface charge, PEG density, impurity burden, and aggregation state. 9 , 13 , 14 These responses can manifest as cytokine release, altered innate and adaptive immunity, changes in biodistribution, or acute infusion reactions. Complement activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA) is a paradigmatic concern for liposomes and certain other lipid-based or colloidal products, because it demonstrates how a nanoparticle can trigger clinically relevant reactions that are neither classical IgE-mediated allergy nor easily predicted by conventional toxicology alone. 13 The persistence of this issue across decades of liposomal development underscores a broader lesson: in nanomedicine, safety barriers are not always exotic or late-stage; some are recurrent, mechanistically understandable, and therefore potentially preventable if incorporated early into platform design and translational testing. 9 , 13 , 14

Repeat dosing introduces an additional layer of complexity. Many therapeutic contexts require chronic or cyclical administration, yet repeated exposure can change nanoparticle disposition through adaptive immune responses, altered corona formation, saturation or priming of clearance pathways, and anti-carrier antibodies. 14 , 16 Anti-PEG immunity has become the most widely discussed example, reflecting the extensive use of PEG in liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, protein conjugates, and other long-circulating systems. 14 , 16 Although PEG remains an important technology, its benefits are now understood to coexist with liabilities related to pre-existing antibodies, de novo antibody induction, accelerated blood clearance, and potential hypersensitivity. 14 , 16 This tension is highly instructive for the broader field. It illustrates that excipients once considered largely inert may become critical determinants of clinical performance and safety when deployed repeatedly, at scale, and in immunologically diverse populations. Thus, contemporary nanoparticle safety evaluation must consider not only acute tolerability but also immunologic memory, sequence effects, and the consequences of prior exposure to structurally related materials. 9 , 14 , 16

In parallel with biologic complexity, the chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) dimension of nanoparticle safety has assumed increasing importance. For many nanomedicines, critical quality attributes extend beyond the conventional identity-purity-potency triad to include size distribution, morphology, lamellarity, drug localization, surface composition, corona susceptibility, aggregation tendency, residual solvents, endotoxin burden, free versus encapsulated payload, and time-dependent instability during storage or handling. 6 , 10 Minor shifts in these variables can alter biodistribution, immunoreactivity, or release kinetics enough to change clinical safety. As nanomedicine products become more complex, developers increasingly rely on advanced analytical technologies, orthogonal characterization, and platform-specific comparability strategies. 6 , 10 The importance of this evolution cannot be overstated. Translation failures are often attributed to biology, but a substantial fraction of safety uncertainty arises upstream from insufficiently controlled material definition or from the inability to show that the material used in pivotal studies is analytically and functionally comparable to the material manufactured at larger scale. 6 , 10 In this sense, nanoparticle safety is not only a toxicology problem; it is also a materials science, process engineering, and regulatory science problem. 5 , 6 , 10

Encouragingly, the field has made real progress. First, there is now broad consensus that nanosafety must be integrated into design rather than appended after optimization. 5 , 6 , 9 ,10 Second, clinically informative case studies, especially from liposomes, albumin nanoparticles, LNPs, and iron-based nanocolloids, have clarified which properties are most consequential for tolerability and regulatory acceptability. 2 , 5 , 6 , 13 Third, translational frameworks have shifted toward more realistic disease models, improved bioanalytical methods, and stronger emphasis on patient stratification, imaging-based pharmacology, and mechanism-aware trial design. 3 , 5 , 7 , 8 Fourth, reproducibility efforts are beginning to address long-standing heterogeneity in corona analysis, material characterization, and interlaboratory comparability. 6 , 11 Finally, the recent industrial and regulatory maturation of nucleic acid nanomedicines has strengthened the notion that scalable, clinically acceptable nanoparticle platforms can be developed when platform engineering, process control, analytical depth, and risk assessment evolve together. 2 , 6 , 9 The central challenge now is to convert these lessons from isolated successes into generalizable translational principles.

The next phase of the field therefore depends less on proving that nanoparticles can work and more on demonstrating when, why, and in whom they can work safely. This requires moving beyond generalized claims of “biocompatibility” toward mechanistic, indication-specific, and patient-aware safety definitions. It also requires distinguishing platform-intrinsic hazards from modifiable design liabilities; separating transient, manageable on-target effects from unpredictable off-target reactions; and recognizing that successful translation often rests on selecting the right clinical problem for a given nanoparticle architecture rather than forcing a versatile platform into biologically incompatible settings. 3 , 5 , 7 , 8 Particularly in oncology, future progress will likely depend on aligning carrier design with realistic delivery constraints, measurable biomarkers of accumulation or response, and combination strategies that justify the added complexity of nanoscale formulations. 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 , 15 More broadly, the field must address chronic exposure, special populations, immunogenic memory, degradation fate, and long-term organ retention with the same rigor that it has historically applied to short-term efficacy.

Against this background, the present review examines the safety of nanoparticles in medicine from a translational perspective. Its purpose is not to restate the generic advantages of nanomedicine, but to critically assess what has been learned from approved products, clinical candidates, mechanistic safety studies, and emerging analytical frameworks. The review is organized around three overarching questions. First, what genuine progress has been made in understanding and mitigating the safety liabilities of medical nanoparticles? Second, which limitations remain unresolved despite technological and regulatory advances? Third, what critical objectives should guide the next generation of safer, more clinically reliable nanomedicines? By focusing on the interface between physicochemical design, biological identity, immunological reactivity, manufacturing control, and patient heterogeneity, this review argues that nanoparticle safety should be treated not as a late-stage hurdle, but as the organizing principle of clinically meaningful nanomedicine development. 5 , 6 , 9–14

More specifically, the review highlights progress in platform characterization, standardization of nanosafety-relevant assays, improved recognition of immune-mediated adverse events, deeper understanding of protein corona biology, and growing appreciation of the mismatch between permissive preclinical models and heterogeneous human disease. 6 , 8–12 , 15 At the same time, it addresses persistent limitations: insufficient mechanistic comparability between formulations, incomplete prediction of infusion and repeat-dose toxicities, inadequate representation of susceptible populations, underdeveloped strategies for long-term fate assessment, and the continuing tendency to frame translational failure primarily as a delivery problem rather than as a coupled delivery-safety problem. 5 , 6 , 8–16 The future priorities emerging from this analysis include safe-by-design formulation paradigms, clinically relevant exposure models, patient-stratified evaluation, integrated CMC-toxicology frameworks, and prospective use of biomarkers and imaging to identify the patients most likely to achieve benefit without disproportionate risk. 3 , 5–8 , 11 , 12 , 15 In this sense, enhancing nanoparticle safety is not a defensive or restrictive agenda. On the contrary, it is the most direct route to making nanomedicine more precise, more reproducible, and more clinically transformative. To preserve a translational rather than purely descriptive focus, the literature considered in this narrative synthesis was prioritized according to clinical relevance, mechanistic contribution to nanosafety, regulatory or manufacturing significance, and the ability to clarify reproducibility, patient heterogeneity, long-term fate, or clinically important failure modes. Recent peer-reviewed studies were emphasized while landmark earlier work was retained when it remains foundational. The distinctive contribution of the present review is therefore the integration of physicochemical design, biological identity, host response, preclinical evidence, CMC, regulation, and patient context into a single safety-by-design continuum rather than the treatment of these domains as independent topics. 6 , 10 , 11 , 17–19

## Nanoparticles in Medicine: Classes and Biomedical Uses

Nanoparticles used in medicine comprise a structurally diverse family of materials whose biomedical behavior is determined not only by core composition but also by size, shape, surface chemistry, colloidal stability, protein adsorption, degradation kinetics, and cargo-release behavior. From a translational perspective, it is useful to organize them into broad material classes—lipid-based, polymeric, metallic and metal oxide, silica-based, carbon-based, and hybrid nanomaterials—because each class brings a distinct combination of advantages, limitations, manufacturing constraints, and safety considerations. Although these categories often overlap in practice, especially in multifunctional theranostic platforms, they remain conceptually valuable for understanding how nanomaterial design governs biomedical use in drug delivery, imaging, vaccines, and oncology. 2 , 3 , 20 The current clinical and preclinical landscape further shows that no single nanoparticle class is universally optimal; instead, platform selection must be aligned with the physicochemical requirements of the payload, the biological barriers of the target tissue, the intended route of administration, and the level of multifunctionality required for the therapeutic objective. 2 , 21 , 22

### Lipid-Based Nanoparticles

Lipid-based nanoparticles are the most clinically mature and commercially visible class of nanomedicines. Their central importance reflects a favorable convergence of biocompatibility, formulation flexibility, scalable manufacturing, and the capacity to encapsulate a wide spectrum of payloads ranging from hydrophobic small molecules to fragile nucleic acids. This category includes classical liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs), nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), nanoemulsions, niosomes in broader colloidal discussions, and, most prominently in current translational medicine, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) designed for RNA and other nucleic acid delivery. 2 , 20 , 23 , 24 Across these subclasses, lipids serve not merely as inert carriers but as functional structural elements that determine membrane fusion behavior, endosomal escape, circulation half-life, storage stability, and cell-type selectivity. 20 , 23

The biomedical utility of lipid-based nanoparticles arises from their amphiphilic organization. Liposomes and related vesicular systems can accommodate hydrophilic cargo in aqueous cores and hydrophobic compounds within bilayers, enabling unusually broad formulation versatility. SLNs and NLCs, by contrast, exploit solid or mixed solid–liquid lipid matrices to stabilize loaded agents and modulate release kinetics. Contemporary LNPs for nucleic acid delivery rely on multicomponent formulations that typically include an ionizable lipid, a phospholipid, cholesterol, and a PEG-lipid. The ionizable lipid is especially important because it permits low-to-neutral surface charge under physiological conditions while acquiring positive charge in acidic endosomes, thereby facilitating endosomal escape and intracellular payload release. 20 , 23 , 25 This structure–function logic has become foundational in modern nanomedicine, particularly after the successful deployment of LNP-enabled mRNA vaccines and the broader expansion of RNA therapeutics. 20 , 25 , 26

A major strength of lipid-based nanoparticles is their capacity to improve the pharmacology of otherwise problematic drugs. Lipid encapsulation can increase the apparent solubility of poorly water-soluble compounds, shield labile cargos from hydrolysis or enzymatic degradation, reduce premature systemic exposure, and alter tissue distribution in ways that improve tolerability or efficacy. In oncology, these effects have been exploited to reformulate cytotoxic agents with the goal of reducing off-target toxicity and modifying biodistribution. In nucleic acid therapeutics, lipid nanocarriers protect RNA from extracellular nuclease degradation and promote intracellular delivery, thereby converting a highly unstable macromolecule into a clinically viable platform. 2 , 23 , 25 , 26 The translational significance of this class is therefore not limited to one disease area; instead, lipid-based systems have become enabling technologies across infectious disease, oncology, inflammatory disease, and regenerative medicine. 2 , 20 , 26

Liposomes remain the archetypal lipid nanocarrier and continue to be highly relevant because they illustrate the central design principles of lipid-based drug delivery. Their bilayer architecture permits passive loading, active loading, ligand functionalization, and tuning of rigidity or fusogenicity through lipid composition. The historical success of liposomal formulations demonstrated that nanoscale lipid engineering could translate into approved medicinal products, but the platform has also revealed enduring constraints such as limited loading for some cargo classes, leakage during storage, uptake by the mononuclear phagocyte system, complement activation, and modest target-site delivery in many solid tumors. 2 , 3 , 27 These issues have not displaced liposomes from the field; rather, they have driven increasingly sophisticated lipid selection, PEG-lipid optimization, surface decoration, and trigger-responsive designs.

SLNs and NLCs were developed partly to address some of the limitations associated with conventional emulsions and liposomes, especially in relation to physical stability and sustained release. Their solid or partially solid lipid matrices can enhance drug retention and improve formulation robustness, while their use of physiologically acceptable lipids supports broad interest in oral, topical, pulmonary, and parenteral applications. Recent literature continues to emphasize their suitability for antibacterial agents, chemotherapeutics, nucleic acids, and phytoconstituents, as well as their relative manufacturing simplicity and biocompatibility. 24 Nevertheless, SLNs and related systems are not free of constraints. Drug expulsion during storage, polymorphic lipid transitions, limited loading of certain molecules, and scale-sensitive process variability remain important formulation concerns. 24

The most transformative recent development in lipid nanotechnology has been the rise of LNPs for nucleic acid delivery. These systems differ from classical liposomes in both compositional philosophy and functional purpose. Rather than serving mainly as passive vesicles, LNPs are typically engineered as dynamic condensed assemblies in which the ionizable lipid plays a decisive role in nucleic acid complexation, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal disruption. Their success in clinically deployed mRNA vaccines and siRNA therapeutics has established LNPs as one of the clearest demonstrations that nanoparticle platforms can achieve industrial-scale manufacturing, regulatory acceptance, and global medical impact. 20 , 23 , 25 , 26 At the same time, this success has intensified scrutiny of their immunological and toxicological profiles, including the influence of ionizable lipid chemistry, PEG-lipid immunogenicity, reactogenicity, biodistribution to liver and spleen, and the consequences of repeated administration. 25 , 28

Beyond vaccines and RNA therapeutics, lipid-based nanoparticles are being intensively developed for cancer immunotherapy. Their ability to deliver mRNA, immunostimulatory molecules, tumor antigens, adjuvants, and combination payloads makes them attractive tools for engineering the cancer-immunity cycle. They can be designed to target antigen-presenting cells, modulate tumor-associated myeloid compartments, or support in situ vaccination strategies. In this context, lipid nanoparticles are not simply drug carriers; they are immunopharmacologic devices whose composition can shape innate sensing, antigen expression kinetics, and the spatial pattern of immune activation. 26 , 29 This is one reason why lipid-based nanocarriers occupy a central position in both prophylactic and therapeutic vaccine design.

Lipid-based nanoparticles also contribute substantially to theranostics and imaging, although they are often less intrinsically image-active than metallic or silica-based systems. Their value in this domain comes from their ability to co-load imaging probes and therapeutic agents or to encapsulate radionuclides, fluorophores, MRI-active species, or contrast enhancers together with drugs or nucleic acids. Such combinations enable image-guided drug delivery, biodistribution tracking, and pharmacodynamic readouts. In cancer, lipid-based theranostic systems are being developed to merge molecular imaging with targeted or immune-mediated intervention, though translational success still depends on solving the same core issues of circulation behavior, tumor penetration, and reproducible manufacturability that affect therapeutic-only systems. 17 , 28

Overall, lipid-based nanoparticles represent the most advanced and versatile nanomedicine class currently available. Their success derives from a balance of biological compatibility and engineering adaptability that is difficult to match. However, their maturation has also clarified an essential lesson for the broader field: clinical usability depends not only on elegant nanoparticle design but also on deep control over lipid composition, interfacial behavior, immune compatibility, storage stability, and scalable process reproducibility. 2 , 20 , 23 , 25 , 28

### Polymeric Nanoparticles

Polymeric nanoparticles form one of the broadest and most adaptable classes of nanocarriers in medicine. Unlike lipid systems, whose behavior is largely dictated by supramolecular assembly of amphiphilic molecules, polymeric nanoparticles are built from covalent macromolecular frameworks that can be tuned with exceptional precision in relation to molecular weight, block architecture, degradability, hydrophobicity, charge density, glass transition behavior, and functional group distribution. As a result, polymeric platforms occupy a central place in nanomedicine for applications requiring controlled release, structural durability, ligand-mediated targeting, co-delivery of multiple payload classes, or stimulus-responsive behavior. 21 , 30

This category includes nanospheres, nanocapsules, polymeric micelles, dendritic structures, polymersomes, polyplexes, nanogels, and a wide range of biodegradable or semi-degradable constructs derived from materials such as PLGA, PLA, PCL, chitosan, alginate, PEG-containing copolymers, poly(amino acid)s, and synthetic cationic polymers. Their most important translational advantage is modularity. By altering polymer composition and architecture, investigators can engineer drug-loading mode, release kinetics, degradation rate, surface charge, hydrodynamic size, and interactions with serum proteins and cellular membranes. 21 , 30 This tunability makes polymeric nanoparticles particularly attractive for difficult biomedical tasks such as intracellular macromolecule delivery, local depot formation, BBB-oriented transport strategies, and sequential or combination therapy.

A defining biomedical strength of polymeric nanoparticles is their capacity for sustained and programmable release. Encapsulated drugs can be dispersed throughout polymer matrices, trapped in cores, conjugated by cleavable linkers, or incorporated into responsive compartments that degrade or swell in specific microenvironments. Compared with many lipid formulations, polymeric systems often provide stronger control over release over timescales ranging from hours to weeks. This is especially valuable for anticancer drugs, anti-inflammatory agents, antimicrobials, and growth factors whose therapeutic activity depends on maintaining a defined exposure profile rather than achieving a sharp transient peak. 21 , 30 Polymeric nanocarriers have therefore become major candidates for improving therapeutic index through spatiotemporal control of drug exposure.

The diversity of polymeric nanoparticle behavior also supports extensive surface bioengineering. Ligands, peptides, antibodies, cell-membrane mimics, stealth coatings, and environmentally responsive motifs can be introduced either during polymer synthesis or after nanoparticle formation. Such modification strategies are widely used to promote receptor-mediated uptake, evade rapid clearance, enhance mucosal penetration, cross biological barriers, or create disease-microenvironment sensitivity. 30 This is particularly relevant in oncology, where polymeric nanoparticles are often designed not only to carry cytotoxic agents but also to navigate a series of biological barriers including blood circulation, stromal transport, tumor cell binding, endosomal escape, and intracellular organelle access.

Polymeric nanoparticles are also highly relevant for nucleic acid delivery. Although LNPs currently dominate the clinical landscape of RNA therapeutics, polymer-based platforms remain scientifically important because they offer alternative mechanisms of cargo condensation, protection, endosomal escape, and sustained intracellular release. Cationic polymers and block copolymers can complex DNA, mRNA, siRNA, miRNA, or gene-editing cargos into polyplexes or hybrid assemblies. In principle, these systems can reduce some limitations of lipid carriers and provide prolonged expression or tissue-selective targeting. In practice, however, polymeric nucleic acid delivery faces substantial translational hurdles, especially regarding toxicity associated with cationic charge, variable unpackaging, and manufacturing reproducibility. 21 , 30 Even so, the field continues to develop lower-toxicity biodegradable cationic polymers and highly engineered poly(amino acid) systems that may become important in future generations of precision nanomedicine.

In cancer therapy, polymeric nanoparticles are especially attractive for combination regimens. Their matrix-based or micellar organization can support co-encapsulation of hydrophobic drugs, hydrophilic adjuvants, immunomodulators, photosensitizers, and imaging probes, allowing rational synchronization of release or hierarchical delivery. Such designs are conceptually appealing because they align with the increasingly multidimensional character of oncology, where effective therapy often requires simultaneous modulation of tumor cells, vasculature, stroma, and immune compartments. 21 , 29 , 30 Polymeric nanocarriers can therefore function not only as passive drug depots but as integrated treatment systems capable of coordinating several therapeutic mechanisms.

Another important area of application is vaccination and immunoengineering. Polymeric nanoparticles can protect antigens and nucleic acids, enhance uptake by antigen-presenting cells, and permit controlled release of adjuvants or immune modulators. Relative to lipids, some polymeric platforms offer stronger structural stability and longer retention in lymphoid tissues or mucosal environments. They also enable elaborate design of degradation-triggered antigen presentation and cytokine programming. These features have supported growing interest in polymer-based nanovaccines for infectious disease and cancer, as well as hybrid lipid–polymer strategies intended to combine the immunological and manufacturing strengths of both classes. 27

Despite their versatility, polymeric nanoparticles face persistent translational limitations. Their synthesis is often more chemically complex than that of lipid-based systems, and this complexity can create burdens in characterization, batch reproducibility, impurity control, and regulatory comparability. Residual solvents, monomers, catalysts, and broad molecular-weight distributions may influence safety or performance. Furthermore, while cationic and highly functionalized polymers may excel in vitro, they frequently encounter in vivo obstacles related to protein adsorption, hepatic sequestration, complement activation, limited penetration, or unexpected toxicity. 17 , 21 , 30 These issues have not diminished the scientific value of polymeric nanomedicine, but they have highlighted the need for platform choices that are realistic from both a biological and CMC standpoint.

From a biomedical perspective, polymeric nanoparticles are most compelling when a therapeutic problem truly requires what polymers uniquely offer: sustained release, structural persistence, advanced responsiveness, or multistage functionality. Their future importance will likely remain high in local delivery, implant-associated systems, immunomodulation, combination therapy, and disease settings where kinetic control is more important than simple encapsulation. In this sense, polymeric nanoparticles complement rather than compete directly with lipid systems, broadening the design space of nanomedicine by offering a macromolecular toolkit for precision control over nanoparticle fate and payload behavior. 21 , 27 , 30 The major nanoparticle classes and their medical applications are summarized in Figure 1 . ### Metallic and Metal Oxide Nanoparticles

Metallic and metal oxide nanoparticles are distinguished from organic nanocarriers by their intrinsic physicochemical functionalities. Their appeal in medicine is not primarily based on cargo encapsulation alone, but on properties such as plasmonic behavior, magnetism, catalytic activity, X-ray attenuation, redox reactivity, and high electron density. These features make them uniquely attractive for imaging, externally triggered therapy, photothermal therapy, magnetic targeting, radiosensitization, antimicrobial applications, and multimodal theranostics. 22 , 31 , 32 Gold, silver, iron oxide, titanium dioxide, zinc oxide, copper oxide, cerium oxide, and other related materials represent the best-studied members of this class.

Gold nanoparticles are among the most extensively investigated metallic systems because of their relative chemical inertness, facile surface functionalization, tunable shape-dependent optical properties, and compatibility with photothermal and imaging applications. Nanorods, nanospheres, nanoshells, and other anisotropic gold structures can absorb or scatter light in ways that support optical imaging, photothermal ablation, and image-guided therapy. In oncology, this has motivated development of gold-based systems for tumor visualization, thermal destruction, radiosensitization, and combination treatment strategies. 33 Their surface can also be readily conjugated with drugs, peptides, antibodies, nucleic acids, and diagnostic labels, allowing flexible construction of multifunctional theranostic systems.

Silver nanoparticles, although historically prominent in antimicrobial applications, have also attracted biomedical attention in wound care, anti-infective coatings, and selected anticancer strategies. However, their strong bioactivity is coupled to concerns about oxidative stress, ion release, and off-target toxicity, which have limited their direct translational momentum relative to gold and iron oxide systems. 31 More broadly, the biomedical role of metallic nanoparticles cannot be separated from metal-specific toxicology. Surface oxidation, ion dissolution, catalytic ROS production, and interactions with proteins and membranes may all drive adverse effects. As a result, the same properties that make metallic nanoparticles attractive for therapy often complicate their biocompatibility profile. 31 , 34

Metal oxide nanoparticles broaden the field further by introducing functionalities associated with magnetism, semiconductor behavior, catalytic activity, or redox buffering. Among them, iron oxide nanoparticles are the most clinically and translationally important. Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) and related systems have been intensively studied for MRI contrast, magnetic hyperthermia, magnetic guidance, drug delivery, cell tracking, and multimodal imaging. Their external-field responsiveness offers a distinctive route to spatial control: they can be visualized by MRI, heated under alternating magnetic fields, or directed by magnetic gradients under selected conditions. 32 , 35 These features position iron oxide systems at the intersection of imaging and therapy more clearly than most organic nanoparticles.

The promise of iron oxide nanoparticles in medicine lies in their multifunctionality. They can act as imaging agents by altering local magnetic relaxation, as carriers by adsorbing or conjugating drugs, and as therapeutic effectors through hyperthermia or magnetically assisted localization. In cancer and cardiovascular applications, they have been explored as platforms for lesion imaging, local heating, plaque targeting, and cell trafficking studies. 32 Their biomedical translation, however, depends heavily on core size, crystallinity, aggregation state, surface coating, and degradation behavior. Surface functionalization with polymers, silica, lipids, or biomolecules is often necessary to improve colloidal stability, reduce aggregation, and modulate protein corona formation. 32 , 35

At the same time, iron oxide nanomedicine provides a strong example of the inseparability of utility and safety. Although iron is a biologically familiar element, iron oxide nanoparticles are not inherently benign in every formulation context. Their biodistribution, lysosomal processing, oxidative stress potential, macrophage uptake, and possible long-term tissue persistence must be evaluated carefully. Recent analyses emphasize that cytotoxicity and systemic effects are highly dependent on dose, coating chemistry, particle size, aggregation, and degradation kinetics rather than on composition alone. 35 This principle also applies across the broader family of metallic and metal oxide systems.

A major biomedical use of metallic and metal oxide nanoparticles is theranostics. Because many of these materials are intrinsically image-active or energy-responsive, they are unusually well suited to platforms that combine diagnosis and therapy in one construct. Gold nanoparticles can support optical or CT imaging while enabling photothermal treatment; iron oxide nanoparticles can function in MRI and hyperthermia; titanium dioxide and related systems may be used in photodynamic or catalytic strategies; and radiolabeled metallic cores can support SPECT or PET imaging together with drug or radionuclide therapy. 22 , 28 , 31–33 In this class, theranostics is not an added layer but often a native consequence of material choice.

Another area of strong interest is radiosensitization and image-guided oncology. High-atomic-number metallic nanoparticles can amplify radiation effects or enhance imaging contrast, thereby supporting strategies that aim to improve locoregional tumor control while reducing exposure to surrounding tissue. Such concepts remain attractive, but they also illustrate the gap between mechanistic promise and clinical translation. Achieving sufficient, reproducible intratumoral accumulation in patients remains difficult, and the systemic safety profile of repeated or high-dose administration can be challenging to define. 17 , 22 , 31

In summary, metallic and metal oxide nanoparticles occupy a critical but more safety-sensitive branch of nanomedicine. Their greatest value lies where intrinsic material functionality is essential—magnetic imaging, hyperthermia, plasmonic treatment, catalytic therapy, high-contrast imaging, or multimodal theranostics. Where simpler carrier functions suffice, they may offer less favorable risk–benefit balance than lipid or polymeric systems. Their future clinical role will therefore depend on disciplined indication matching, robust surface engineering, and precise control of degradation, retention, and host response. 22 , 31 , 34 , 35

### Silica-Based, Carbon-Based, and Hybrid Nanomaterials

Silica-based nanomaterials, especially mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs), occupy a distinctive niche in nanomedicine because they combine inorganic structural stability with highly tunable porosity and surface chemistry. Their large surface area, adjustable pore size, high loading capacity, and amenability to functionalization make them attractive for drug delivery, gene delivery, imaging, and theranostics. Unlike many dense inorganic nanoparticles, MSNs are especially valued as cargo-hosting frameworks, since their pores can be engineered to load therapeutic agents while external surfaces are modified for targeting, stealth, or stimulus-responsive gating. 36 , 37 This combination of structural regularity and chemical adaptability has made MSNs one of the most sophisticated scaffold platforms in nanomedicine research.

The biomedical logic of silica nanoparticles is closely linked to controlled release. Drugs can be physically entrapped in mesopores, linked through cleavable chemistries, or retained by molecular gates that open in response to pH, redox state, enzymes, heat, or light. As a result, silica systems are often discussed as model platforms for precision release engineering. Their utility extends to chemotherapy, antimicrobial delivery, gene transfer, tissue engineering, and regenerative medicine. 36 In oncology, MSNs have been especially attractive because they allow co-delivery of multiple agents, high drug loading, and the possibility of integrating imaging elements into the silica matrix or surface.

Surface and matrix modification are central to the medical use of silica nanoparticles. Functional groups, polymers, biomolecules, dyes, radionuclides, and metal species can be introduced either onto the surface or directly into the silica framework, producing particles with enhanced stability, bioactivity, degradability, or imaging capability. Recent work on in situ modified MSNs highlights how such hybridization can generate theranostic systems that preserve drug-loading capacity while adding diagnostic or responsive functions. 37 These strategies also reveal one of the broader strengths of silica: it is an unusually versatile “bridge material” that can combine the precision of inorganic synthesis with the functionality of organic or metallic add-ons.

Nevertheless, silica-based nanomedicine also faces well-recognized translational obstacles. Biocompatibility and biodegradation are not uniform across all silica formulations. Toxicity depends on particle size, porosity, shape, silanol density, dose, route, and surface modification. Colloidal stability and aggregation behavior may change dramatically in biological fluids, and organ retention remains a relevant concern for some formulations. 36 Thus, although silica nanoparticles are often presented as highly adaptable, their translational success depends on careful optimization of degradability and surface reactivity alongside therapeutic performance.

Carbon-based nanomaterials represent another broad and functionally rich class that includes carbon nanotubes, graphene and graphene oxide, fullerenes, nanodiamonds, carbon dots, graphene quantum dots, and carbon nano-onions. Their biomedical appeal arises from high surface area, unique mechanical and electrical properties, strong π–π interactions, tunable optical behavior, and, for some subclasses, photothermal or fluorescent characteristics. 38–40 Carbon nanomaterials have been investigated for drug delivery, biosensing, tissue engineering, imaging, gene delivery, photothermal therapy, and cancer theranostics.

One of the most important biomedical advantages of carbon nanomaterials is their exceptional surface engineering potential. Aromatic drugs can adsorb through π–π stacking, polymers can improve dispersibility, and ligands can be attached for targeting or immune modulation. Nanodiamonds and carbon dots, in particular, have drawn attention for relatively favorable biocompatibility profiles compared with some earlier carbon nanostructures, while graphene derivatives and nanotubes continue to offer powerful optical and thermal functionalities. 38–40 In cancer, carbon-based systems are especially attractive for photothermal therapy, fluorescence-enabled imaging, and multifunctional delivery constructs.

At the same time, carbon nanomedicine has historically been restrained by concerns about biodistribution, persistence, inflammation, oxidative stress, and structure-dependent toxicity. These concerns are particularly pronounced for fibrous or poorly degradable forms such as certain carbon nanotubes, where aspect ratio, residual catalysts, aggregation, and surface defects can profoundly influence biological response. 38 , 39 Surface functionalization can reduce some of these liabilities, improve aqueous dispersibility, and enhance biocompatibility, but it does not eliminate the need for rigorous, structure-specific safety evaluation. As a result, carbon-based nanomaterials remain scientifically powerful but less clinically mature than lipid systems.

Hybrid nanomaterials are increasingly important because they reflect the recognition that no single material class perfectly satisfies all biomedical requirements. Hybridization can combine the encapsulation efficiency and biocompatibility of lipids, the kinetic control of polymers, and the imaging or magnetic functionality of inorganic cores. Examples include lipid–polymer hybrid nanoparticles, silica–metal composites, polymer-coated iron oxide systems, metal nanoparticle–hydrogel constructs, and other composite architectures. 27 , 37 , 41 The rationale is straightforward: by integrating complementary materials, one can seek simultaneous control over loading, stability, targeting, imaging, and triggered release.

In cancer theranostics, hybrid nanoparticles are especially attractive because they enable concurrent treatment and visualization. A lipid or polymer shell may improve circulation and payload capacity, while an inorganic core provides imaging contrast or energy conversion. Similarly, mesoporous silica frameworks may be combined with magnetic or fluorescent elements to create image-guided delivery systems. 28 , 37 , 41 Hybrid systems can therefore be viewed as convergence platforms, bringing together otherwise separate functionalities into single nanoscale constructs.

However, hybridization also increases complexity. Each added component can alter manufacturing reproducibility, interfacial behavior, degradation pathways, regulatory classification, and safety uncertainty. For this reason, hybrid nanomaterials exemplify both the promise and the translational burden of advanced nanomedicine. Their future clinical relevance will depend on showing that the added complexity yields a meaningful biomedical advantage rather than merely an attractive materials-science concept. 17 , 27 , 41 Biomimetic and cell-membrane-coated nanoparticles deserve separate translational consideration because their biological interface is intentionally derived from cells or extracellular structures rather than from a wholly synthetic coating. Membranes from erythrocytes, platelets, leukocytes, tumor cells, and other sources can confer immune camouflage or disease-relevant adhesion properties, but these advantages introduce distinct safety and CMC liabilities, including source variability, membrane-protein heterogeneity, residual biological material, pathogen-control requirements, difficult purification, and scale-dependent reproducibility. Consequently, biomimicry should not be equated automatically with improved safety; clinically meaningful benefit depends on demonstrating that the biological coating remains compositionally controlled and functionally reproducible across batches. 42–44

### Current Applications in Drug Delivery, Imaging, Theranostics, Vaccines, Oncology, and Inflammation

Across material classes, drug delivery remains the dominant biomedical application of nanoparticles. The most consistent and clinically relevant contribution of nanocarriers is their ability to modify the disposition of active agents in ways that conventional formulations often cannot achieve. By increasing apparent solubility, protecting labile cargos from chemical or enzymatic degradation, reducing premature clearance, altering tissue exposure, and enabling controlled or triggered release, nanoparticles can substantially reshape pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. 2 , 20–22 , 36 Lipid-based systems are currently the strongest clinically in this area, particularly for nucleic acids and reformulated small molecules, whereas polymeric carriers remain especially valuable when sustained release, matrix-controlled delivery, or environmentally responsive behavior is required. 20 , 21 , 27 Inorganic and silica-based systems contribute where drug carriage can be integrated with imaging, catalytic activity, or externally triggered functions. 22 , 28 , 33 , 36 , 37 The practical implication is that “drug delivery” should not be treated as a single therapeutic category, but rather as a set of distinct functions requiring different nanoparticle solutions depending on payload chemistry, route of administration, target tissue architecture, and the biological barriers that must be overcome.

Imaging is another major use domain, particularly for inorganic, metal oxide, and hybrid platforms. Iron oxide nanoparticles have been widely studied and used in MRI-related applications; gold and other high-atomic-number materials support CT, optical, and photoacoustic strategies; radiolabeled nanoparticles enable nuclear imaging; and silica-, lipid-, or polymer-based carriers can be engineered to transport fluorophores, contrast agents, or radionuclides. 28 , 32 , 33 , 35 , 37 The attraction of nanoparticle-based imaging lies not only in signal enhancement, but also in the possibility of modulating circulation time, improving lesion-to-background ratios, and enabling multimodal readouts within a single platform. 17 , 28 , 37 However, successful translation in imaging depends on more than the generation of contrast. It requires reproducible biodistribution, predictable clearance, low nonspecific retention, and a clear diagnostic advantage over established imaging agents and workflows. 17 , 28 In this sense, imageability alone is insufficient; the platform must produce clinically useful information without creating disproportionate complexity or retention-related safety concerns.

Theranostics has emerged as one of the defining conceptual themes of nanomedicine because it seeks to unite therapeutic and diagnostic functions within the same nanoscale construct. Metallic, metal oxide, silica-based, and hybrid nanoparticles are especially attractive for theranostic applications because they can intrinsically support imaging, local heating, catalytic action, magnetic responsiveness, or radionuclide incorporation while simultaneously carrying drugs, nucleic acids, or immune-active agents. 17 , 22 , 28 , 37 , 41 In oncology, theranostic nanoparticles are often framed as tools for precision medicine because they offer the possibility of noninvasively identifying patients most likely to benefit, guiding intervention, and monitoring treatment response in real time. 3 , 17 , 28 , 37 Similar logic is increasingly being extended to inflammatory disease, where theranostic platforms may help visualize inflammatory burden, identify active lesions, and coordinate local treatment delivery. 22 , 37 Nevertheless, the translational bar for theranostics remains high. The diagnostic component must provide information that is genuinely actionable, and the therapeutic component must justify the platform’s added material, regulatory, and manufacturing complexity. 17 , 28 , 37 , 41

Vaccines constitute one of the clearest modern success stories of nanomedicine. Nanoparticles can protect antigens or nucleic acids, improve uptake by antigen-presenting cells, shape innate immune activation, and facilitate trafficking to lymphoid tissues. 26 , 27 , 29 Lipid nanoparticles have become the leading example because they transformed mRNA from a fragile biological intermediate into a clinically deployable vaccine modality with global public-health impact. 26 , 27 At the same time, polymeric nanoparticles and lipid–polymer hybrid systems are receiving growing attention in cancer vaccine design because they can co-deliver antigens, adjuvants, cytokine regulators, and immune-modulating payloads in a synchronized manner. 26–28 In these settings, nanoparticle composition does not merely determine pharmacokinetics; it becomes part of the immunological architecture of the vaccine itself, influencing antigen presentation, innate sensing, and the quality and magnitude of adaptive immune responses. 26–28 This dual role—as both carrier and immunological modulator—helps explain why nanoparticle vaccines are among the most translationally successful and biologically sophisticated applications of nanomedicine.

Oncology remains the largest and most conceptually fertile field for nanoparticle application. Nearly every major nanoparticle class has been investigated in cancer drug delivery, molecular imaging, immunotherapy, photothermal therapy, hyperthermia, radiotherapy enhancement, gene delivery, or multimodal theranostics. 3 , 17 , 22 , 29 , 33 This dominance reflects both need and opportunity. Cancer therapy frequently relies on highly potent agents with narrow therapeutic windows, while tumors themselves are biologically heterogeneous, anatomically diverse, and difficult to access selectively. 3 , 17 Nanoparticles are therefore attractive because they promise to improve tolerability, concentrate treatment at disease sites, and enable rational combinations of imaging, cytotoxicity, and immune modulation. 3 , 17 , 22 , 29 However, oncology has also exposed the limits of nanomedicine more clearly than any other field. The heterogeneity of nanoparticle delivery in human tumors, the variability of the EPR effect, and the persistent gap between impressive preclinical accumulation and modest clinical benefit have all demonstrated that tumor targeting is often less predictable than originally anticipated. 3 , 17 Accordingly, the value of cancer nanomedicine increasingly rests not on idealized assumptions of selective tumor homing, but on whether the platform can meaningfully improve the therapeutic index in real clinical contexts.

Inflammation has emerged as another major and increasingly important application area for nanomedicine. Inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, psoriasis, neuroinflammatory disorders, and inflammation-associated tissue injury, are attractive targets for nanoparticles because they often involve dysregulated vascular permeability, activated immune-cell populations, oxidative stress, altered pH, enzyme-rich microenvironments, and tissue-specific inflammatory mediators. 22 , 23 , 25 , 36 , 37 These disease-associated features create opportunities for selective accumulation, triggered release, and cell-specific immune modulation that are difficult to achieve with conventional systemic therapies. 22 , 23 , 25 Nanoparticles are especially valuable in this context because many anti-inflammatory drugs are limited by poor tissue selectivity, off-target immunosuppression, metabolic toxicity, or the need for frequent administration. By improving local retention, protecting sensitive biologics or nucleic acids, and enabling delivery to macrophages, dendritic cells, endothelial cells, or inflamed epithelium, nanoparticle systems may reduce systemic exposure while enhancing therapeutic activity at the site of disease. 22 , 23 , 25 , 36 , 37

Within inflammatory medicine, nanoparticle applications are highly diverse. In inflammatory bowel disease, nanoparticles have been developed to cross mucus barriers, accumulate in inflamed intestinal tissue, and release corticosteroids, biologics, antioxidants, or RNA-based therapeutics in response to pH, ROS, or enzymatic triggers. 25 In atherosclerosis, nanocarriers are being investigated for targeting vascular inflammation, macrophage-rich plaques, and endothelial dysfunction, with the goal of reducing systemic drug exposure while stabilizing high-risk lesions. 22 , 23 In autoimmune and chronic inflammatory disorders, polymeric, lipidic, and hybrid nanoparticles are being explored as vehicles for tolerogenic therapies, cytokine modulation, antigen-specific immune reprogramming, and selective suppression of pathogenic immune-cell populations. 22 , 23 , 36 These applications are particularly important because they broaden the role of nanomedicine beyond cancer and infectious disease into chronic immunological conditions, where long-term safety, repeat-dose compatibility, and immune-specific precision are especially critical.

At the same time, inflammatory applications illustrate a fundamental challenge in nanomedicine: the same inflammatory microenvironments that can be exploited for targeting may also alter nanoparticle behavior in unpredictable ways. Changes in plasma proteins, cytokine profiles, endothelial permeability, phagocyte activation, and tissue architecture can modify protein corona formation, organ distribution, immune recognition, and clearance. 22 , 23 Thus, inflammation is not simply a therapeutic target; it is also a biological state that can reshape the safety and efficacy of the nanoparticle itself. This makes inflammatory nanomedicine particularly important from a translational and safety perspective, because it requires the field to account for disease-conditioned biology rather than assuming that nanoparticle behavior in healthy or simplified preclinical models will translate directly to inflamed human tissues. 22 , 23 , 25

The present state of nanoparticle medicine is therefore characterized by marked asymmetry. Some applications—notably lipid nanoparticle delivery of nucleic acids, vaccine technologies, and selected reformulations of established drugs—have demonstrated clear clinical impact. 2 , 20 , 26 , 27 Others, including many tumor-targeting, theranostic, and multifunctional hybrid constructs, remain scientifically compelling but clinically less established. 3 , 17 , 22 , 28 , 37 , 41 This unevenness should not be interpreted as failure. Rather, it indicates that different biomedical applications impose very different translational demands. Platforms that succeed in vaccines may not be optimal for solid tumor penetration; systems that excel in imaging may not provide the safest chronic exposure profile; and hybrid constructs that appear ideal in mechanistic studies may prove unnecessarily complex for routine manufacturing, regulatory evaluation, or long-term clinical use. 2 , 3 , 17 , 22 , 28 The same principle applies to inflammatory disease, where a platform that successfully exploits local inflammatory cues must still demonstrate acceptable repeat-dose tolerability and minimal unintended immune perturbation. 22 , 23 , 25
