## What “Safety” Means in Nanomedicine

In nanomedicine, the term safety cannot be reduced to the simple absence of overt toxicity. For conventional small-molecule drugs, safety assessment is already multidimensional, encompassing dose-limiting toxicity, organ-specific adverse effects, tolerability, exposure margins, patient susceptibility, and manufacturing control. In nanomedicine, these considerations become more complex because the product is not only a pharmacologically active ingredient but also a structured material system whose clinical behavior depends on emergent properties such as size distribution, morphology, surface chemistry, corona formation, colloidal stability, degradability, impurity profile, and process-dependent heterogeneity. 6 , 10 , 46 , 47 As a consequence, the safety of a nanomedicine is not fully captured by the toxicology of the encapsulated drug, the bulk composition of the carrier, or even the nominal formulation recipe. Rather, safety is a composite property that arises from the interaction between material design, biological context, patient susceptibility, and manufacturing consistency. 6 , 10 , 45–47

This broader framing has become increasingly important as nanomedicine has matured from a field centered on proof-of-concept delivery systems to one that includes marketed products, complex generic formulations, nucleic acid carriers, combination theranostics, and increasingly patient-specific platforms. Regulatory and translational literature now recognizes that nanoscale products require integrated evaluation of physicochemical characterization, biological interactions, immune effects, biodistribution, degradation fate, and critical quality attributes because relatively modest shifts in these parameters can alter both efficacy and toxicity. 6 , 46–48 The meaning of safety in nanomedicine is therefore necessarily layered. It includes whether a product is biocompatible enough to perform its intended function without unacceptable host disturbance, whether it is biosafe across relevant exposure scenarios and populations, whether it is tolerable at clinically useful dose schedules, whether its acute and chronic risks are understood, whether local and systemic toxicities are acceptably controlled, and whether product quality can be manufactured reproducibly enough that the clinical safety profile remains stable across batches and over time. 6 , 10 , 45–48

### Distinction Between Biocompatibility, Biosafety, and Tolerability

A persistent problem in the nanomedicine literature is the interchangeable use of the terms biocompatibility, biosafety, and tolerability, even though they are not synonymous. The distinction matters because conceptual imprecision often leads to weak claims about clinical readiness. In many preclinical studies, nanoparticles are described as “biocompatible” merely because they preserve short-term cell viability in one or two in vitro assays. However, such evidence is insufficient to support broader claims of safety, much less clinical suitability. 9 , 10 , 45

Biocompatibility is best understood as a context-dependent property describing the ability of a material system to perform its intended medical function with an acceptable host response in a specific application. 9 , 45 This definition is inherently relational. A nanomaterial is not universally biocompatible in the abstract; it may be acceptably biocompatible for one route, tissue, exposure duration, or indication and not for another. A formulation that is acceptable as a locally administered imaging probe may not be acceptable as a chronically dosed intravenous therapeutic. Likewise, a degree of transient immune stimulation that is useful in a vaccine may be undesirable in gene replacement therapy. In nanomedicine, biocompatibility therefore includes not only the absence of gross cytotoxicity, but also the compatibility of the nanoparticle with blood components, immune cells, complement pathways, endothelial interfaces, reticuloendothelial clearance systems, and relevant target tissues. 9 , 13 , 45

Biosafety is broader. It refers to the overall safety profile of a nanomaterial or nanomedicine across relevant biological systems, exposure conditions, and time scales, including hazard identification, dose-response behavior, organ disposition, degradation fate, immunotoxicity, genotoxicity where relevant, reproductive considerations where relevant, and environmental or occupational implications when appropriate. 10 , 45 , 49 In the biomedical context, biosafety extends beyond whether the product functions without immediate damage; it asks whether the full range of foreseeable biological risks has been adequately characterized and controlled. For nanomedicines, this broader view is particularly necessary because nanoscale materials may undergo dynamic transformations in vivo, including aggregation, protein corona remodeling, dissolution, biodegradation, or redistribution after repeated administration. 10 , 45 , 47 A product may appear biocompatible in a narrow assay but still raise biosafety concerns if it accumulates chronically in the liver or spleen, alters innate immunity, or produces toxic degradation products after prolonged exposure. 10 , 35 , 45 , 49

Tolerability, by contrast, is a clinical term centered on the degree to which adverse effects can be endured by patients at therapeutically relevant exposures. 50 Tolerability does not imply absence of biologic perturbation. A nanomedicine can be nontrivially reactogenic, immunostimulatory, or organ-active yet still be considered clinically tolerable if adverse effects are transient, manageable, reversible, dose-dependent, and justified by benefit. This distinction is especially important in oncology and vaccinology. Liposomal doxorubicin, for example, may improve tolerability relative to conventional doxorubicin for selected toxicities without eliminating toxicity altogether; similarly, lipid nanoparticle-enabled mRNA vaccines may be clinically acceptable despite transient local and systemic reactogenicity. 50 Tolerability therefore operates at the interface of safety and therapeutic utility. It is inseparable from dose, schedule, route, indication, alternatives, and patient preference.

These three concepts overlap but should be kept distinct in a rigorous review. Biocompatibility concerns the appropriateness of the host response in a given use context. Biosafety concerns the broader hazard and risk profile across biologic systems and exposure scenarios. Tolerability concerns the practical clinical acceptability of adverse effects at useful doses. The distinction is not semantic. It has methodological consequences. Biocompatibility is often probed through hemocompatibility, cytocompatibility, complement activation, protein corona behavior, cell uptake, and tissue-response studies. 9 , 13 , 45 Biosafety requires a larger framework that may include biodistribution, repeated-dose toxicology, degradation studies, immunotoxicity, chronic retention analysis, and quality-related risk assessment. 10 , 35 , 47 , 49 Tolerability ultimately depends on clinical data or clinically meaningful translational proxies, because it asks whether patients can receive the product under realistic treatment conditions. 50

In nanomedicine, failures often arise precisely because these domains are conflated. A nanoparticle platform may look favorable in vitro and be labeled “biocompatible,” yet later prove poorly biosafe because of complement activation-related pseudoallergy, anti-PEG immune responses, or accumulation-driven chronic toxicity. 13 , 51 , 52 Alternatively, a platform may have acceptable biosafety margins but poor tolerability if infusion reactions, fever, fatigue, or local inflammatory effects prevent repeated administration at therapeutic doses. A careful review must therefore treat safety terminology as mechanistic and translationally consequential, not merely descriptive.

### Acute versus Chronic Toxicity

Another essential dimension of nanomedicine safety is the distinction between acute and chronic toxicity. This distinction is familiar in toxicology, but it is especially important for nanoparticles because many nanomaterials produce early and late adverse effects through different mechanisms. Acute toxicity typically refers to harmful effects occurring shortly after administration or exposure, often ranging from minutes to days. In nanomedicine, acute toxicity may include infusion reactions, complement activation, cytokine release, vascular effects, hemolysis, thrombogenicity, acute hepatic or renal injury, neurobehavioral effects in selected systems, or local tissue irritation at the administration site. 11 , 13 , 51 , 52 Such effects may be strongly influenced by the particle’s surface properties, aggregation state, endotoxin burden, residual solvents, injection rate, and first-contact interactions with blood and immune systems. 10 , 13 , 47

Among the best-recognized acute safety phenomena in nanomedicine is complement activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA), which has been described for liposomes and other intravenously administered nanoparticulate systems. 13 , 52 CARPA illustrates why nanomedicine safety cannot rely only on conventional assumptions about excipient inertness or classical IgE-mediated hypersensitivity. Complement activation can trigger cardiopulmonary and systemic symptoms that are acute, clinically significant, and not readily predicted by standard cytotoxicity assays. 13 , 52 This phenomenon is particularly instructive because it demonstrates that a nanomedicine may show acceptable cellular viability in vitro yet still produce clinically meaningful acute intolerance through blood-facing immune mechanisms.

Chronic toxicity, by contrast, refers to adverse effects that emerge or persist after repeated administration or long-term retention, often over weeks to months or longer. In nanomedicine, chronic toxicity is especially relevant for inorganic nanoparticles, slowly degradable systems, repeated-dose lipid or polymer carriers, depot formulations, and products intended for long-term diseases rather than one-time or short-course use. 10 , 35 , 49 The mechanisms involved may include persistent organ accumulation, macrophage overloading, lysosomal stress, ongoing oxidative injury, prolonged inflammatory signaling, fibrosis, adaptive immune sensitization, endocrine or reproductive interference in selected materials, and long-term changes in organ function. 35 , 49 Importantly, chronic risk is not limited to overt pathology. Even moderate but persistent perturbation of immune homeostasis, hepatic processing, or splenic architecture may matter if repeated administration is required over months or years.

The distinction between acute and chronic toxicity has direct implications for study design. Acute studies emphasize early clinical chemistry, infusion reaction monitoring, blood compatibility, innate immune readouts, and immediate histopathology. Chronic studies require repeated-dose protocols, recovery cohorts, toxicokinetic interpretation, delayed histopathology, long-term biodistribution analysis, and often more detailed material fate characterization. 10 , 35 , 49 For nanomedicines, chronic studies are especially challenging because the material itself may change over time in vivo. Particles may dissolve, shed coatings, exchange corona components, degrade into small molecules or ions, or redistribute among tissues. Thus, chronic toxicity assessment must consider not only the original nanoparticle but also its transformation products and evolving biological identity. 10 , 45 , 49

The acute–chronic distinction is also clinically important because the same product can be acceptable in one context and unacceptable in another depending on dosing pattern. A nanomedicine with manageable acute infusion reactions may still be clinically useful for short-course cancer therapy, whereas the same liability could be problematic for repeated administration in chronic inflammatory disease. Conversely, a formulation with minimal acute reactogenicity may still prove unsuitable if chronic hepatic retention, splenic accumulation, or anti-carrier antibody formation limits long-term use. 35 , 51 Anti-PEG responses and accelerated blood clearance exemplify this issue: they may not dominate first-dose safety yet become highly relevant under repeated exposure. 51

In a rigorous safety framework, acute and chronic toxicity should therefore be treated as related but distinct domains. Acute toxicity concerns immediate biological incompatibilities and first-exposure hazards. Chronic toxicity concerns long-term burden, repeated-dose adaptation, retention, and delayed injury. Nanomedicine development frequently underemphasizes the latter, particularly when early proof-of-concept efficacy is prioritized. Yet for many advanced nanoparticle systems, chronic safety may be the more decisive translational barrier.

### Local versus Systemic Adverse Effects

Nanomedicine safety must also distinguish between local and systemic adverse effects, because the route of administration and spatial distribution of nanoparticles strongly shape the risk profile. This distinction is not merely anatomical. It reflects different mechanisms of injury, different biomarkers, and different clinical management strategies.

Local adverse effects occur at or near the site of administration or deposition. Depending on route, these may include injection-site inflammation, tissue necrosis, endothelial irritation, pain, edema, local complement activation, pulmonary irritation after inhalation, mucosal damage after intranasal or oral exposure, ocular irritation, or local neural injury in central nervous system applications. 10 , 45 , 50 For implant-associated or locally retained nanoparticle systems, local safety may additionally involve granulomatous reactions, foreign-body responses, fibrosis, altered wound healing, and chronic inflammatory infiltration. In many cases, local effects are driven by high regional concentration, surface reactivity, osmotic or surfactant-related effects, pH shifts, or direct membrane interactions. A nanoparticle may therefore be systemically acceptable yet locally problematic if it creates irritancy or persistent inflammatory signaling at the administration site. 45 , 50

Local safety has special importance in nanomedicine because nanoparticles are often deliberately designed for site-specific retention. Intratumoral, intranasal, pulmonary, ocular, transdermal, intra-articular, and implantable nanoformulations all exploit regional delivery to improve efficacy or reduce systemic exposure. However, reducing systemic exposure does not guarantee safety if the price is concentrated local toxicity. For example, cationic or highly adhesive nanocarriers may enhance mucosal retention yet damage epithelial barriers; photothermal or catalytic nanoparticles may achieve local tumor destruction yet also injure surrounding healthy tissue if energy deposition is poorly controlled. 45 , 50 Thus, local safety must be assessed in relation to the intended tissue microenvironment and the concentration-time profile actually experienced at that site.

Systemic adverse effects involve effects beyond the administration site, arising through circulation, organ distribution, immune activation, or secondary mediator release. In nanomedicine, systemic toxicity often centers on blood–material interactions, hepatosplenic sequestration, renal handling where applicable, immune activation, endocrine perturbation in selected cases, or off-target accumulation in organs such as liver, spleen, lung, kidney, heart, or brain. 10 , 35 , 45 , 49 Systemic effects may be pharmacologic, carrier-related, or interaction-mediated. A formulation may cause systemic toxicity because the encapsulated drug is released too quickly, because the nanoparticle activates complement or cytokine pathways, because degradation products are toxic, or because long-circulating particles accumulate in immune or filtration organs.

The local-versus-systemic distinction also helps clarify why route matters so strongly in nanomedicine. Intravenous products face immediate blood compatibility and systemic distribution challenges, making complement activation, hemolysis, coagulation effects, and organ uptake central concerns. 13 , 52 Inhaled nanoparticles require careful evaluation of local pulmonary inflammation but may also produce systemic immunologic or cardiovascular effects if translocation occurs. Intramuscular vaccine nanoparticles are often judged partly by local reactogenicity, yet systemic fever, malaise, or cytokine-mediated symptoms are also central to tolerability. 50 Oral nanoparticles confront local gastrointestinal barrier interactions and microbiome-related issues, but systemic absorption and hepatic first-pass exposure remain relevant for those that are bioavailable.

In practice, local and systemic effects frequently interact. Local tissue injury can generate systemic inflammatory mediators; conversely, systemic immune priming can intensify local reactions on repeat dosing. This is particularly relevant for nanomedicines that are immunologically active by design or by consequence. A review article on nanosafety should therefore avoid treating local and systemic toxicity as mutually exclusive compartments. They are analytically distinct but biologically coupled.

For translational evaluation, local adverse effects require route-specific models, tissue histology, barrier-function assays, and exposure-aware regional pharmacology. Systemic adverse effects require biodistribution analysis, organ toxicology, hematology, complement and cytokine profiling, repeated-dose studies, and mechanistic understanding of nanoparticle fate. 10 , 13 , 35 , 45 , 47 , 49 A robust safety framework must integrate both scales, because clinical failure can result from either one.

### Patient-Level, Product-Level, and Manufacturing-Level Safety Considerations

Perhaps the most important modern insight in nanomedicine safety is that risk cannot be understood solely at the level of the material. Safety is produced jointly by the patient, the product, and the manufacturing process. These three levels are analytically separable but clinically inseparable.

#### Patient-Level Safety

At the patient level, nanomedicine safety depends on host biology. Protein corona formation, complement activity, macrophage function, prior immune exposure, vascular permeability, inflammatory status, sex, age, ancestry, metabolic disease, organ impairment, co-medications, and disease-specific pathophysiology may all alter nanoparticle disposition and toxicity. 11 , 45 This makes nanomedicine fundamentally different from any simplistic idea of one-size-fits-all biomaterial compatibility. A formulation may behave differently in healthy volunteers, cancer patients, immunocompromised individuals, or patients with chronic liver disease because the biological environment that the nanoparticle encounters is different. 11 , 45

Protein corona research has been especially important in demonstrating this point. Once introduced into biological fluids, nanoparticles acquire adsorbed biomolecular layers that alter their effective biological identity. Recent multicenter work has emphasized the need for standardization in corona characterization precisely because small methodological and biological differences can alter interpretation and reproducibility. 11 From a patient-level safety perspective, the protein corona is not just a mechanistic curiosity; it is one route by which individual physiology can reshape clearance, immune recognition, cell targeting, and toxicity. Similarly, immunotoxicity reviews have emphasized that susceptible populations may respond differently to the same nanomaterial, particularly when pre-existing inflammatory or immune dysregulation is present. 9

Patient-level safety therefore includes questions such as these: Which patients are at increased risk of infusion reactions? Does prior exposure to PEG-containing products modify risk? Will liver dysfunction change nanoparticle clearance? Does tumor-associated inflammation alter complement activation or macrophage sequestration? Are pediatric, geriatric, or pregnant populations expected to handle the material differently? These are not peripheral considerations. They are central to precision safety assessment in nanomedicine.

#### Product-Level Safety

At the product level, safety depends on the complete nanoparticle construct rather than any single ingredient. Relevant properties include composition, size distribution, morphology, surface charge, ligand density, encapsulation efficiency, release kinetics, aggregation tendency, endotoxin burden, degradation profile, and biological interaction signatures such as hemocompatibility or complement activation. 6 , 46 , 47 These are often treated as critical quality attributes (CQAs) because they influence in vivo exposure, efficacy, and toxicity. 6 , 46 In nanomedicine, product-level safety is thus deeply intertwined with analytical characterization.

The literature on therapeutic nanomedicines has repeatedly emphasized that inadequate definition of CQAs undermines both translational development and safety evaluation. 6 , 46 , 47 A nanoparticle is not safe merely because its intended composition is acceptable; it must also have the right distribution of actual properties, and those properties must remain stable during storage, handling, and administration. Batch heterogeneity matters because a small fraction of larger aggregates, free drug, unstable particles, or impurity-rich species may disproportionately affect safety. Likewise, release behavior is not simply a performance parameter; it is a safety parameter because rapid leakage or altered dissolution can increase off-target exposure. 6

Product-level safety also includes immunological interface properties that are often missed in simplistic screening workflows. Hemolysis, platelet interaction, complement activation, cytokine induction, and uptake by mononuclear phagocyte system cells may all be product-specific consequences of nanoscale design. 9 , 13 , 52 This is why quality control in nanomedicine cannot stop at size and zeta potential; it must aim to identify clinically consequential material behaviors.

#### Manufacturing-Level Safety

At the manufacturing level, safety depends on whether the process reproducibly produces material with the intended CQAs and impurity profile. This level is sometimes underestimated in academic nanomedicine, yet it is central to clinical translation. Manufacturing variables such as raw material purity, mixing conditions, solvent removal, sterilization method, filtration, lyophilization, container closure, and storage conditions can alter size, aggregation, encapsulation, free-drug fraction, oxidation status, endotoxin contamination, and long-term stability. 6 , 46–48 These changes may not be obvious from nominal composition alone, but they can materially alter safety.

Regulatory and industry-oriented analyses now emphasize that nanomedicines demand especially strong integration of CMC, preclinical characterization, and risk-based development because formulation-process interactions are often more consequential than for conventional small molecules. 6 , 47 , 48 This is particularly evident for complex products and follow-on nanomedicines, where demonstrating sameness or bioequivalence can be difficult precisely because clinically relevant CQAs may be incompletely defined or hard to measure. 46 , 48 Manufacturing-level safety is therefore not only about preventing contamination or gross batch failure. It is about ensuring that the product reaching patients is sufficiently comparable, predictable, and stable that prior safety knowledge remains valid.

An important implication follows: manufacturing inconsistency can become a safety issue even when the nominal formulation is well designed. A clinically tolerable nanoparticle platform can become unsafe if process drift changes particle size distribution, free payload levels, complement-activating impurities, or degradation behavior. Thus, manufacturing control is not downstream of safety; it is one of its determinants.

### An Integrated Definition of Safety in Nanomedicine

Taken together, these distinctions show that safety in nanomedicine is best understood as a multiscale translational property. It includes: The appropriateness of the host response to the material in a defined use context, which relates to biocompatibility; 9 , 45 The broader hazard and risk profile across exposure conditions, which relates to biosafety; 10 , 45 , 49 The practical clinical acceptability of adverse effects at useful doses, which relates to tolerability; 50 The separation of immediate first-exposure hazards from repeated-dose and long-term risks, which relates to acute versus chronic toxicity; 13 , 35 , 49 , 51 , 52 The distinction between administration-site injury and body-wide adverse outcomes, which relates to local versus systemic effects; 10 , 45 , 50 and the interaction among patient biology, product attributes, and manufacturing reproducibility, which collectively determine real-world safety. 6 , 11 , 45–48

## Determinants of Nanoparticle Toxicity

Nanoparticle toxicity is not a fixed property of a material name or platform label. It is an emergent consequence of physicochemical design, biological transformation, dose context, and manufacturing-dependent variability. In nanomedicine, toxic responses arise not only from the intrinsic chemistry of a nanoparticle core, but also from how particle dimensions influence cellular uptake, how surface chemistry reshapes protein adsorption, how colloidal instability changes effective dose, how degradation products behave in tissues, and how route and schedule determine which biological barriers and clearance systems are engaged. For this reason, the toxicology of nanoparticles must be understood as determinant-based rather than composition-only. The key determinants consistently identified across translational nanomedicine and nanosafety literature include size, shape and aspect ratio, surface charge and surface chemistry, core composition, biomolecular corona formation, aggregation and colloidal stability, degradation behavior, and the exposure variables of dose, route, and administration schedule. 6 , 10 , 20 , 31 , 53 These determinants do not operate independently. Instead, they interact to govern the most clinically relevant mechanisms of nanosafety failure, including hemocompatibility problems, complement activation, inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress, lysosomal injury, organ accumulation, chronic retention, and changes in biodistribution after repeated exposure. 9 , 10 , 20 , 31 , 53

A central implication follows from this framework: the same nanoparticle class may range from clinically useful to toxic depending on how these determinants are configured. A lipid nanoparticle that is near-neutral, biodegradable, and well-controlled in size may be clinically acceptable, whereas a closely related formulation with altered ionizable lipid chemistry, broader size distribution, or greater aggregate burden may display a substantially different inflammatory or biodistribution profile. 6 , 20 Likewise, a metallic nanoparticle may be useful when surface-engineered for imaging or externally triggered therapy, yet become problematic if dissolution, persistence, or aspect ratio lead to oxidative or chronic tissue injury. 31 , 49 The purpose of this section is therefore not merely to list determinants, but to explain how each variable shapes toxicity in translationally meaningful ways. An additional mechanistic layer is that these safety-relevant attributes are themselves products of synthesis and formulation. Precursor ratio, solvent and surfactant selection, nucleation or self-assembly conditions, polymer molecular weight, lipid composition, mixing and shear, purification, surface-conjugation chemistry, and storage conditions can alter size distribution, morphology, surface charge, ligand density, residual impurities, free-payload fraction, aggregation tendency, and degradation kinetics. Thus, synthesis is not upstream of toxicology in a purely technical sense; it is an upstream determinant of the material state that the biological system actually encounters. This explains why nanoparticles with the same nominal composition can produce different biological outcomes when manufactured by different routes or under different process conditions. 21 , 31 , 37 , 46 , 54 The coupled physicochemical determinants that shape nanoparticle safety are summarized in Figure 2 . ### Size, Shape, and Aspect Ratio

Particle size is one of the most influential determinants of nanoparticle toxicity because it affects nearly every stage of biological interaction, including diffusion, vascular behavior, cellular uptake, endocytic route, intracellular trafficking, renal filtration, reticuloendothelial sequestration, and degradation kinetics. Smaller nanoparticles generally possess a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio, which increases interfacial reactivity and can amplify adsorption of biomolecules, catalytic activity, membrane interaction, and generation of reactive oxygen species in susceptible material systems. 34 , 53 This does not mean that smaller particles are always more toxic, but it does mean that decreasing size often changes the effective biological dose and the mode of tissue interaction. In medicinal systems, small changes within the nanometer range can shift whether particles circulate, extravasate, accumulate in liver or spleen, enter cells efficiently, or are cleared more rapidly. 34 , 35 , 53

Size also affects dose normalization, a frequently underappreciated toxicologic issue. Nanoparticles can be dosed by mass, particle number, surface area, drug content, or active ingredient concentration, and these measures are not equivalent. Two formulations with the same mass concentration but different sizes may present very different total surface area and particle number to cells or organs, thereby producing different biological effects even when nominal dose appears identical. This is one reason why in vitro-to-in vivo comparisons and cross-study toxicity claims are often difficult to interpret in the nanomedicine literature. 53 In practice, smaller particles may penetrate more effectively into tissues or intracellular compartments, while larger particles may remain more confined to vascular or phagocytic pathways. Toxicity can therefore shift from diffusely cellular to predominantly organ-sequestration-driven depending on size regime. 35 , 53

Shape and aspect ratio are equally important but historically less standardized than size in preclinical safety workflows. Spherical particles are often used as default systems because they are easier to produce and characterize, but many nanomaterials used in medicine or investigated for biomedical purposes are rods, tubes, disks, plates, worm-like micelles, or other anisotropic structures. Such geometries can profoundly alter margination in blood flow, membrane wrapping dynamics, phagocytic recognition, endosomal processing, and mechanical interaction with tissues. 53 , 56 High-aspect-ratio nanomaterials are especially important toxicologically because elongated geometries may prolong cellular interaction, frustrate phagocytosis, or increase local membrane stress. These concerns are most strongly associated with fibrous or rigid inorganic materials, but the principle extends more broadly: geometry influences biological handling, and biological handling influences toxicity. 53 , 56

In translational nanomedicine, the toxicologic significance of shape is often mediated through uptake kinetics and intracellular fate. Cells do not internalize rods, spheres, and plate-like particles identically. Differences in membrane wrapping energy and contact orientation can alter uptake rate and subcellular trafficking, which in turn can change lysosomal burden, autophagic stress, and inflammatory signaling. For immune cells, geometry may also alter the balance between rapid clearance and prolonged surface interaction, affecting cytokine release and clearance organ burden. 53 , 56 Shape therefore influences not only whether a nanoparticle enters cells, but how it is sensed and processed once internalized.

Aspect ratio also matters at the organ level. Long or rigid particles may be retained differently in pulmonary or reticuloendothelial tissues than compact isotropic nanoparticles, and they may degrade more slowly if enzymatic or hydrolytic access is geometry-limited. This distinction is especially relevant when evaluating chronic toxicity or retention of inorganic systems. Accordingly, size and shape must be considered together rather than separately. A 50 nm sphere and a 50 nm × 500 nm rod may share one nominal dimension, but their biological exposure signatures and toxicologic consequences are likely to be very different. 35 , 53 , 56

From a safety perspective, the key principle is that particle dimensions determine not only access to therapeutic targets, but also access to vulnerable biological interfaces. Optimizing size and shape for efficacy without parallel safety evaluation is therefore inadequate. In nanomedicine, dimensional design is always a toxicologic decision as well as a delivery decision. 10 , 53

### Surface Charge and Surface Chemistry

Surface charge is one of the most direct determinants of nanoparticle interaction with biological systems because it governs electrostatic attraction and repulsion with membranes, proteins, glycocalyx-rich surfaces, extracellular matrix components, and blood constituents. Highly cationic nanoparticles often show efficient cellular uptake and endosomal escape in vitro because mammalian cell membranes are generally net negative. However, this apparent delivery advantage is frequently accompanied by increased nonspecific protein adsorption, membrane disruption, hemolysis, platelet interaction, complement activation, and inflammatory signaling in vivo. 9 , 20 , 57 For this reason, strongly cationic surface character is commonly associated with greater acute toxicity risk, particularly after intravenous administration. 9 , 20

Near-neutral or modestly negative surfaces are often better tolerated in systemic delivery because they reduce some electrostatic injury and may slow opsonization, but these effects are context-dependent rather than absolute. A near-neutral nanoparticle can still be immunoreactive if its interfacial chemistry, hydrophobicity, ligand density, or impurity profile promotes complement activation or unfavorable protein corona formation. 9 , 20 , 58 This is especially relevant to lipid nanoparticles, where the distinction between permanently cationic and ionizable lipids has become translationally decisive. Ionizable lipids allow particles to remain less charged at physiologic pH yet acquire positive charge in acidic endosomal compartments, thus separating systemic tolerability from intracellular delivery function more effectively than older permanently cationic systems. 20

Surface chemistry extends beyond net charge and includes hydrophobicity, steric shielding, functional group identity, ligand presentation, polymer coatings, roughness, and chemical reactivity at the interface. These factors shape the first-contact biology of nanoparticles by determining how plasma proteins adsorb, whether opsonins dominate the surface, how complement pathways are engaged, and how cells interpret the material. 20 , 58 , 59 Poly(ethylene glycol), zwitterionic coatings, polysaccharides, cell membrane-derived layers, and biomimetic ligands have all been used to reduce rapid clearance or mitigate immune recognition. Yet no coating is universally protective. PEGylation, for example, can extend circulation and improve colloidal stability, but anti-PEG antibodies and accelerated blood clearance have become well-recognized liabilities in some contexts, particularly under repeated exposure. 14 , 51

Surface chemistry also determines whether the nanoparticle is bioinert, biointeractive, or bioactive. A surface bearing targeting ligands, catalytic motifs, redox-active groups, or pH-responsive functionalities may be advantageous for efficacy, but each added function can also increase toxicologic uncertainty. Ligands may alter off-target binding; responsive groups may destabilize unexpectedly in blood; hydrophobic patches may intensify protein adsorption; and reactive groups may disturb membranes or activate innate immune pathways. 10 , 58 In this sense, increasing surface sophistication often increases the burden of safety proof.

An important translational point is that surface properties are not static after administration. Adsorption of proteins, lipids, and metabolites can partially or completely mask the designed interface, producing a new biological surface that may differ sharply from the manufactured one. Thus, the toxicity implications of surface charge and chemistry must be evaluated not only in formulation buffer but also in biologically relevant media and, ideally, across patient-relevant conditions. 11 , 58 , 59 Surface engineering remains one of the most powerful tools for reducing nanoparticle toxicity, but it is only effective when assessed under realistic exposure conditions.

### Composition and Core Material

Core composition remains a foundational determinant of nanoparticle toxicity because it governs intrinsic chemical reactivity, degradability, persistence, dissolution products, density, magnetic or optical properties, and the likelihood of chronic retention. Organic carriers such as lipid-based and many biodegradable polymeric nanoparticles are often favored clinically because they are more readily metabolized or cleared and are generally associated with more familiar pharmaceutical excipients. Even within these classes, however, toxicity depends on the specific lipid, polymer, linker, stabilizer, and impurity profile rather than on broad category labels alone. 6 , 10 , 20 For example, the inflammatory profile of lipid nanoparticles depends strongly on ionizable lipid chemistry, helper lipid composition, PEG-lipid content, and degradation pathways, while polymeric systems may vary substantially depending on cationic charge density, hydrolysis rate, and residual synthetic byproducts. 6 , 20

Inorganic cores introduce different toxicologic considerations. Metallic and metal oxide nanoparticles are often attractive because of their intrinsic optical, magnetic, catalytic, or radiologic properties, but these same features may increase risk of oxidative stress, ion release, or prolonged organ retention. Gold nanoparticles are often considered relatively inert chemically, yet their toxicology still depends on size, shape, coating, and clearance behavior. Silver nanoparticles may release biologically active ions and generate oxidative injury under some conditions. Iron oxide systems offer magnetic functionality and can be clinically useful, but chronic tissue handling, macrophage processing, and dose-dependent oxidative effects remain relevant safety considerations. 31 , 35 , 49 Metal oxides such as titanium dioxide, zinc oxide, cerium oxide, and copper oxide can be particularly sensitive to redox context, dissolution, and photo- or catalytically mediated reactivity, all of which affect their toxicity profile. 31 , 49

Silica-based and carbon-based materials illustrate that “nonmetallic” does not mean toxicologically simple. Mesoporous silica nanoparticles are attractive because of their pore architecture and drug-loading capacity, but their safety depends on particle size, porosity, silanol density, degradation kinetics, and surface modification. Recent translational reviews emphasize that biosafety and clinical potential of mesoporous silica systems are strongly tied to how degradable and surface-stabilized they are in relevant biological environments. 45 Carbon-based materials, meanwhile, present a wide toxicologic spectrum ranging from comparatively favorable profiles for some carbon dots or nanodiamonds to more difficult concerns for rigid or fibrous forms such as certain nanotubes. In these systems, aspect ratio, residual catalysts, surface defects, and persistence can dominate toxicologic behavior. 31

Composition is also inseparable from degradation fate. A nanoparticle may appear acceptable initially but become problematic if its breakdown products are bioactive, acidic, oxidizing, poorly excretable, or immunogenic. Conversely, a material with moderate short-term reactivity may still be clinically acceptable if it degrades rapidly into well-tolerated metabolites. The crucial issue is not only what the nanoparticle is made of, but what it becomes after circulation, uptake, lysosomal processing, oxidation, hydrolysis, or enzymatic attack. 10 , 31 , 45 , 49 This is especially important in chronic dosing or depot settings, where accumulated transformation products can contribute to long-term toxicity.

Thus, composition and core material should be treated as necessary but incomplete descriptors of nanosafety. They set the boundaries of possible behavior, but actual toxicity emerges only when composition is interpreted together with interface properties, colloidal behavior, and exposure context. 10 , 20 , 31 , 53

### Protein Corona Formation

Protein corona formation is one of the most consequential determinants of nanoparticle toxicity because it alters the biological identity of nanoparticles immediately after exposure to blood or other biological fluids. Once a nanoparticle enters a biological environment, proteins and other biomolecules adsorb to its surface, creating a dynamic corona that can reshape cellular uptake, immune recognition, complement activation, colloidal stability, organ distribution, and degradation. 11 , 58 , 59 In practical terms, the cells and tissues of the body do not “see” the pristine manufactured nanoparticle; they encounter a biologically transformed object whose interface reflects both material design and the surrounding biological milieu. 11 , 58

The toxicologic importance of the corona lies in its capacity to alter both hazard and dose delivery. Adsorption of specific plasma proteins may promote opsonization and macrophage uptake, thereby increasing liver and spleen burden while reducing access to intended target tissues. Alternatively, a corona may partially shield reactive surfaces and reduce direct membrane damage. In some cases, targeting ligands are masked by the corona, lowering efficacy without necessarily reducing systemic exposure, thereby shifting the benefit-risk balance unfavorably. 11 , 58 Corona composition can also affect complement activation and cytokine responses, making it directly relevant to infusion reactions and immunotoxicity. 9 , 58

A crucial translational development has been the recognition that corona formation is not only particle-specific but also patient-specific. Recent work emphasizes that sex, inflammatory status, disease state, metabolic phenotype, and other host variables can influence corona composition and therefore alter nanoparticle behavior among patient populations. 11 , 59 This has major implications for safety: a formulation that performs acceptably in healthy donor serum may behave differently in oncology, inflammatory disease, or critical care settings where the circulating proteome is altered. Protein corona formation is therefore one of the clearest mechanisms by which patient-level biology modifies product-level toxicity.

The corona is also methodologically challenging. Its composition depends on incubation conditions, dilution, shear, separation method, analytical workflow, and time scale. A recent multicenter study specifically addressed the need to standardize protein corona characterization in nanomedicine in order to improve reproducibility and data homogeneity across laboratories. 11 This need for standardization is not merely academic. Without robust and comparable corona analysis, toxicologic interpretation remains vulnerable to artifacts and poor cross-study comparability. In other words, protein corona science is now central to both mechanism and method in nanosafety.

From a toxicology perspective, protein corona formation should not be viewed as a secondary modifier but as a primary determinant of biological response. It links material properties to immune recognition, biodistribution, and patient heterogeneity, and it is therefore essential to any credible account of why apparently similar nanoparticles can show different safety profiles in practice. 11 , 58 , 59

### Aggregation, Colloidal Stability, and Degradation Behavior

Aggregation and colloidal instability are major determinants of nanoparticle toxicity because they change the effective size, surface presentation, dose distribution, and clearance behavior of the administered material. Nanoparticles that aggregate in formulation, during storage, upon dilution, or after contact with biological fluids may no longer behave as intended. Aggregates can alter vascular passage, increase local deposition, intensify macrophage uptake, change sedimentation in in vitro assays, and modify the extent of protein adsorption or complement activation. 10 , 20 , 55 In extreme cases, aggregation can transform an otherwise acceptable nanosystem into one that produces embolic risk, infusion reactions, or highly variable organ exposure. 10 , 55

Colloidal stability is therefore both a pharmaceutical quality issue and a toxicologic issue. Stable dispersions maintain a more predictable relationship between administered dose and biological exposure, whereas unstable dispersions introduce time-dependent heterogeneity. This matters especially for intravenous products, where even short-lived changes after injection can alter first-pass interactions with blood, lung, liver, and spleen. In vitro, instability may also generate misleading toxicity readouts because sedimented or aggregated particles can expose adherent cells to far higher local concentrations than intended. 55 Thus, colloidal behavior must be interpreted under the relevant physicochemical environment, including ionic strength, protein content, pH, and shear conditions.

Degradation behavior is closely linked to colloidal stability but conceptually distinct. A nanoparticle may remain colloidally dispersed while undergoing chemical or structural degradation, or it may aggregate as a consequence of degradation-related surface changes. Degradation can be beneficial when it leads to clearance of the material and controlled release of payload, but it can also introduce new safety liabilities if intermediate or final products are reactive, acidic, inflammatory, or poorly excreted. 31 , 45 For biodegradable polymers, degradation rate influences local microenvironment and release kinetics. For lipid nanoparticles, hydrolysis or oxidation can alter potency, immunogenicity, and membrane interaction. For inorganic particles, dissolution may reduce persistence but also generate ions with distinct biological activity. 31 , 35 , 49

Chronic toxicity is often shaped by the balance between persistence and degradability. Reviews of inorganic nanoparticle delivery systems emphasize that subchronic and chronic toxicity depend heavily on how long particles or their products remain in tissues and whether clearance pathways are efficient. 35 Similarly, analyses of inorganic nanomaterials and mesoporous silica systems identify stability, biodegradation, and long-term fate as central translational bottlenecks because retention in liver, spleen, or other organs may convert short-term tolerability into long-term concern. 45 , 60 Thus, neither “stable” nor “degradable” is inherently safer; what matters is whether the time course and products of degradation are compatible with the intended dose and exposure duration.

A robust nanosafety framework therefore evaluates aggregation and degradation not as isolated physicochemical descriptors but as in vivo fate determinants. They determine what form of the material the body actually experiences over time, and that form may differ substantially from the product originally characterized in formulation buffer. 10 , 20 , 45 , 55

### Dose, Exposure Route, and Administration Schedule

Dose remains a central determinant of toxicity in nanomedicine, but it is more complex than in many conventional pharmacologic settings because the relevant dose metric may differ depending on mechanism. Mass dose alone may not capture biologically relevant exposure when particle number, surface area, or free versus encapsulated fraction change between formulations. 53 For some toxic effects, such as oxidative stress or membrane interaction, surface area may correlate more closely with biological burden than mass. For others, particle number or total delivered active ingredient may be more informative. This complexity does not abolish dose-response relationships; it means that nanomedicine toxicology must choose dose metrics carefully and interpret them mechanistically. 53

The route of exposure or administration fundamentally shapes which toxicities are most likely. Intravenous administration immediately exposes nanoparticles to blood components, making hemocompatibility, complement activation, coagulation effects, and organ sequestration especially important. 9 , 51 Inhaled nanoparticles must be evaluated for pulmonary deposition, epithelial injury, macrophage burden, and possible systemic translocation. Oral exposure introduces gastrointestinal barriers, enzymatic conditions, and microbiome interactions, while intramuscular or subcutaneous administration raises questions about local reactogenicity, lymphatic trafficking, and depot persistence. 10 , 53 , 61 Thus, a nanoparticle cannot be classified as safe or unsafe independent of route; the route determines which interfaces are challenged first and which organs define early exposure.

Administration schedule adds another layer. Single-dose toxicity may differ substantially from repeated-dose toxicity because of accumulation, adaptive immune responses, changing protein corona patterns, or altered clearance after prior exposure. This is particularly relevant for PEGylated or other long-circulating systems, where repeated administration can provoke anti-carrier antibodies and accelerated blood clearance, thereby modifying both exposure and safety over time. 14 , 51 Repeated dosing may also overwhelm clearance pathways or create chronic low-grade inflammation even when first-dose tolerability appears acceptable. 35 Accordingly, schedule should be treated as a toxicity determinant in its own right rather than merely a dosing convenience.

Infusion rate and administration method can also alter acute toxicity. Complement-mediated reactions or local concentration spikes may be influenced by how rapidly a formulation enters systemic circulation. Likewise, bolus versus slow infusion can change peak nanoparticle concentration at blood-facing interfaces, potentially modifying acute cardiopulmonary or immune effects. 9 , 51 These practical considerations are especially important in clinically deployed nanomedicines, where administration protocols are part of the safety profile rather than external to it.

Taken together, dose, route, and schedule define the exposure architecture of a nanomedicine. They determine not just how much material reaches the body, but how fast, in what form, through which barrier, and how often. Because nanoparticle toxicity is often interface-dependent and time-dependent, these exposure variables are as important as the nanoparticle’s intrinsic physicochemical properties. 10 , 35 , 53 , 61

### Integrative View: Toxicity as a Systems Property

The determinants discussed above are often presented in separate categories, but translationally they operate as a system. Size influences corona formation; corona formation reshapes surface charge effects; surface chemistry alters aggregation; aggregation changes effective size and clearance; composition determines degradation products; route and schedule determine which of these properties matter most in vivo. For example, a cationic, small, biodegradable nanoparticle may show potent cellular uptake but also strong protein adsorption and acute inflammatory reactivity after intravenous dosing. The same core material, reformulated to alter surface chemistry and schedule, may become substantially safer without any change in therapeutic payload. 9 , 10 , 20 , 53 Likewise, an inorganic nanoparticle with useful imaging properties may be clinically acceptable at low dose for intermittent imaging but not for chronic therapeutic use if retention and long-term tissue burden become limiting. 31 , 35 , 49

This systems view is increasingly reflected in modern nanomedicine development. Recent translational analyses emphasize that safety cannot be inferred from one property at a time, nor from simplified in vitro screens alone. Instead, determinants must be evaluated in combination and under realistic biological conditions, including attention to patient-dependent corona biology, immune profiling, critical quality attributes, and repeated-dose fate. 6 , 10 , 11 , 20 The practical consequence is that nanoparticle toxicity should be managed through safe-by-design integration: selecting size, geometry, chemistry, and exposure parameters not only for efficacy but also for predictable interaction with blood, tissues, and clearance systems.

In this sense, determinants of toxicity are not merely risks to be catalogued after formulation. They are design variables that define whether a nanoparticle platform is likely to become a viable medicine. Nanomedicine succeeds when these variables are engineered as a coherent biological system rather than as isolated material features. 6 , 10 , 20 , 53

## Biological Interactions That Govern Safety

The safety of nanomedicines is determined not only by their nominal physicochemical properties but by the biological interactions that occur immediately after administration and continue throughout circulation, cellular uptake, tissue deposition, degradation, and clearance. 34 , 52 , 62–70 In practical terms, the body does not respond to a nanoparticle as a static material. It responds to a dynamic entity that encounters blood proteins, immune cells, endothelial barriers, phagocytic organs, intracellular trafficking machinery, oxidative pathways, and tissue-specific clearance systems. 34 , 52 , 62–70 These interactions govern whether a nanoparticle remains clinically tolerable, triggers acute immune or hemolytic toxicity, accumulates silently in the mononuclear phagocyte system, or produces delayed organ injury after repeated dosing. 34 , 52 , 62–70 For this reason, nanosafety must be understood as a consequence of nano–bio interactions rather than as a simple extension of conventional drug toxicology. 34 , 52 , 62–70 This section reviews the key biological interactions that most directly shape the safety profile of medical nanoparticles: blood compatibility, immune recognition and complement activation, mononuclear phagocyte system uptake, cellular internalization and intracellular trafficking, oxidative stress and downstream injury pathways, and organ accumulation with long-term retention. 34 , 52 , 62–70 The causal sequence linking biointerface formation, immune recognition, biodistribution, intracellular injury, clearance, and persistence is summarized in Figure 3 .
