### Blood Compatibility and Hemocompatibility

Blood compatibility is one of the earliest and most consequential determinants of nanomedicine safety because blood is either the first compartment encountered after intravenous administration or the gateway through which nanoparticles administered by other routes eventually reach systemic tissues. 63 , 64 Once in blood, nanoparticles interact with erythrocytes, platelets, leukocytes, plasma proteins, endothelial surfaces, and the coagulation and complement systems. 52 , 63–65 These interactions may alter membrane integrity, induce hemolysis, activate platelets, perturb coagulation, trigger leukocyte activation, or reshape the protein corona in ways that influence subsequent biodistribution and immune clearance. 52 , 63–65 Reviews of nanomedicine hemocompatibility consistently emphasize that these effects are not peripheral screening concerns but central translational determinants, especially for systems intended for intravenous use. 63 , 64

Hemocompatibility is broader than hemolysis alone. 63 , 64 A nanoparticle can be nonhemolytic yet still be incompatible with blood if it promotes platelet aggregation, shortens coagulation times, activates leukocytes, or alters red-cell deformability. 63 , 64 Likewise, normal results in a single blood assay do not establish global compatibility because different blood constituents respond through distinct mechanisms. 63 , 64 The most clinically relevant evaluation therefore includes erythrocyte integrity, platelet behavior, coagulation pathways, leukocyte activation, plasma protein adsorption, and, where relevant, endothelial interaction. 63 , 64 This breadth is essential because nanomedicines may fail clinically through acute blood-mediated events long before classic organ toxicities emerge. 52 , 63 , 64

The protein corona is also central to hemocompatibility. 64–66 Plasma proteins adsorb to nanoparticles within seconds and can either buffer or amplify blood-facing toxicity. 65 , 66 Corona formation may mask reactive surfaces and reduce direct membrane damage, but it may also enrich opsonins or complement proteins that increase leukocyte activation and clearance. 52 , 65 , 66 Accordingly, blood compatibility is not simply an intrinsic property of the pristine formulation; it is a property of the nanoparticle as transformed in blood. 64–66 This is one reason why thorough hemocompatibility testing under biologically relevant conditions is so strongly emphasized in translational nanosafety literature. 52 , 63–66

### Immune Recognition and Complement Activation

Immune recognition is one of the defining biological challenges of nanomedicine. 52 , 65 , 66 Even when nanoparticles are engineered to be long-circulating or “stealth,” they are still subject to surveillance by innate immune systems that interpret particulate structures, adsorbed proteins, repeated surface motifs, and damaged-self signals. 52 , 65 , 66 Complement activation is especially important because it can occur rapidly in blood and produce clinically meaningful infusion reactions, inflammatory symptoms, vascular effects, and accelerated clearance. 52 , 65 Complement proteins that bind nanoparticles may also function as opsonins, thereby linking acute immune activation to downstream phagocytic uptake. 52 , 65 , 67

Complement activation-related pseudoallergy, or CARPA, remains one of the best-characterized immune safety phenomena in nanomedicine. 52 It is particularly relevant to liposomes and other intravenously administered nanoparticulate systems and illustrates that clinically significant hypersensitivity-like reactions can arise through non-IgE-mediated innate pathways. 52 This has two major implications. First, conventional assumptions about excipient inertness are insufficient for nanomedicine 47 . Second, standard cytotoxicity assays are poor predictors of some of the most clinically relevant acute reactions. 52 CARPA therefore serves as a model for why nanosafety must include mechanistic immune assessment rather than relying primarily on general toxicity screening. 52

Immune recognition also extends beyond complement. 52 , 65 , 66 Protein corona composition can alter how nanoparticles are perceived by monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, and other innate cells. 65 , 66 Protocol-focused reviews note that complement proteins in the corona can generate both opsonins such as C3b and inflammatory mediators such as C3a and C5a, thereby coupling surface adsorption to phagocytosis and inflammatory signaling. 65 More recent work has also shown that inflammatory disease states can reshape nanoparticle corona composition and shift innate immune activation profiles through pathways including TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling. 65 , 66 This is highly relevant to translational safety because it means that immune recognition is not only product-dependent but also disease-dependent. 65 , 66

Repeated exposure introduces additional immune complexity. 52 , 65 PEGylated systems can prolong circulation and reduce some early opsonization, but anti-PEG antibodies may arise from prior environmental or pharmaceutical exposure and can accelerate blood clearance or increase immune reactivity after repeat dosing. 52 This phenomenon is clinically important because it changes both safety and efficacy over time. 52 A nanomedicine may be acceptable on first administration but behave differently after immunologic priming. 52 In this sense, immune recognition is not a static barrier but a dynamic interaction shaped by exposure history. 52 , 65 , 66

### Mononuclear Phagocyte System Uptake

The mononuclear phagocyte system, or MPS, is a dominant determinant of nanoparticle safety and disposition after systemic administration. 66–68 It includes resident macrophages in organs such as liver and spleen, circulating monocytes, dendritic cells, and related phagocytic populations. 66 , 67 Rapid recognition and uptake by the MPS limits nanoparticle circulation time and strongly influences the distribution of both carrier and cargo. 66–68 This is often discussed mainly as a delivery barrier, but it is equally a safety determinant because MPS uptake governs which organs receive the highest off-target exposure and where chronic retention or inflammatory burden may develop. 66–68

Recent analyses have summarized this issue clearly: rapid uptake by the MPS significantly hampers nanoparticle efficacy, many particles have circulation half-lives of only minutes, and less than 1% of the injected dose reaches intended target tissue in many settings. 67 , 68 The MPS is a primary barrier after intravenous administration, and serum protein coating drives recognition by MPS cells through multiple receptors. 65–68 From a safety perspective, these findings matter because liver and spleen become the major recipients of systemic nanoparticle burden. 67 , 68 Quantitative meta-analysis of biodistribution datasets likewise shows that, after intravenous administration, nanoparticles typically accumulate most strongly in liver and spleen, with much lower deposition in most other tissues. 68

This MPS bias has several safety consequences. 66–68 It can protect other organs from exposure, but it can also create chronic burdens in phagocytic tissues, alter macrophage function, and increase the importance of degradation fate within lysosomal compartments. 66–68 For nanoparticles intended for repeated administration, MPS uptake may also produce cumulative exposure patterns that are not evident from first-dose studies. 66–68 As a result, MPS interaction should be viewed not merely as an efficacy obstacle but as a core axis of nanosafety, especially for inorganic or slowly degradable materials. 66–68

### Cellular Internalization and Intracellular Trafficking

Cellular internalization is a prerequisite for the activity of many nanomedicines, but it is also a major determinant of toxicity. 62 , 69 Nanoparticles generally do not diffuse freely across plasma membranes and instead enter cells through endocytic pathways. 69 The uptake route, uptake rate, and ultimate intracellular destination affect whether the material is recycled, degraded, trapped in endosomes or lysosomes, released into the cytosol, or delivered to sensitive organelles such as mitochondria or nuclei. 62 , 69 Major reviews on intracellular trafficking emphasize that the entry pathway and intracellular localization of nanoparticles are key determinants of both biomedical function and cytotoxicity. 62 , 69

This relationship matters because intracellular trafficking governs exposure at the subcellular level. 62 , 69 Endosomal and lysosomal sequestration can be beneficial when degradative release is intended, but it can also create local acidification-related instability, lysosomal membrane stress, and prolonged intracellular retention. 62 , 69 Cytosolic escape may be essential for nucleic acid therapeutics, yet the membrane-disruptive strategies used to achieve it can increase toxicity. 62 , 69 Similarly, trafficking to mitochondria or prolonged association with endomembrane systems can intensify reactive oxygen species generation or apoptotic signaling. 62 , 69 Thus, the question is not simply whether cells take up nanoparticles, but how they process them after uptake. 62 , 69

Physicochemical features such as size, shape, charge, and surface chemistry strongly affect uptake pathways and downstream safety. 62 , 69 The intracellular-trafficking literature notes that these variables influence internalization mechanism and biological function; therefore, optimizing intracellular delivery without considering toxicity is not feasible. 62 , 69 In nanomedicine, a delivery gain achieved through more aggressive uptake may be offset by greater membrane damage, lysosomal overload, or inflammatory signaling. 62 , 69 Intracellular trafficking is therefore one of the clearest sites where efficacy and safety are mechanistically inseparable. 62 , 69 Mechanistically, nanoparticle internalization can involve clathrin-mediated or caveolae-associated endocytosis, macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and receptor-mediated uptake, with the dominant route depending on particle properties, cell phenotype, ligand presentation, and the adsorbed biomolecular corona. Receptor-mediated uptake may increase selectivity when ligand density and receptor accessibility are appropriate, whereas highly cationic or membrane-active designs can increase nonspecific adsorption and uptake at the cost of membrane injury. Because endocytic route influences endosomal maturation, lysosomal exposure, recycling, and the probability of cytosolic escape, apparently similar uptake levels can lead to very different efficacy and toxicity profiles. 62 , 69

### Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, Genotoxicity, and Apoptosis

Oxidative stress and inflammation are among the most common convergent mechanisms of nanoparticle-induced injury. 34 , 62 , 70 Reviews of metal nanoparticles note that interactions with DNA, proteins, mitochondria, and other cellular structures can trigger reactive oxygen species production, mitochondrial dysfunction, altered ATP levels, lysosomal changes, membrane impairment, and apoptosis. 34 Although these findings are often discussed in the context of metallic nanoparticles, the broader principle extends across nanomedicine: ROS generation and inflammatory signaling are frequent downstream consequences of unfavorable nano–bio interactions. 34 , 62 , 70

Inflammation can emerge through several routes, including complement activation, inflammasome engagement, macrophage activation, damage-associated molecular signaling, and oxidative injury. 34 , 52 , 62 , 65 Once initiated, inflammatory pathways may amplify local tissue toxicity, alter vascular permeability, recruit immune cells, and reshape corona composition or phagocytic uptake. 34 , 62 , 65 , 66 This creates feedback loops in which early oxidative or membrane stress leads to broader inflammatory injury. 34 , 62 , 70 Such mechanisms are especially important for particles that persist intracellularly, undergo redox cycling, or accumulate in phagocytic organs. 34 , 62 , 68 , 70

Genotoxicity is a more specialized but important safety endpoint. 62 , 70 It may arise directly through interaction of nanoparticles or released ions with DNA-associated structures, or indirectly through oxidative stress, inflammation, and interference with chromatin regulation. 34 , 62 , 70 Updated reviews on silica nanoparticles conclude that these materials can damage genetic material at the base, DNA-molecular, and chromosomal levels and that oxidative stress is a major mechanism underlying these effects. 70 The same work also emphasizes epigenetic alterations, including changes in DNA methylation, miRNA expression, histone modification, and chromatin remodeling. 70 These findings matter translationally because persistent sublethal genomic stress can be relevant even when overt cytotoxicity is limited. 62 , 70 A robust genotoxicity evaluation should therefore combine complementary endpoints rather than infer DNA injury from oxidative stress alone. Depending on the material and intended exposure, relevant approaches include the alkaline comet assay for DNA strand breaks, micronucleus testing for chromosomal damage or loss, gamma-H2AX-based assessment of DNA double-strand-break signaling, and chromosome-aberration or related cytogenetic assays. Nanoparticle-specific controls remain essential because adsorption, optical interference, sedimentation, or secondary inflammatory effects can complicate interpretation, particularly when a single assay is used in isolation. 62 , 70 , 71

Apoptosis often appears as a downstream outcome of oxidative stress, organelle injury, and inflammatory signaling. 34 , 62 , 70 In nanomedicine this may be therapeutically desirable in tumor cells but problematic in healthy tissues. 34 , 62 The safety challenge is therefore context-dependent: the same pathway can be beneficial when restricted to target cells and harmful when triggered systemically or in clearance organs. 34 , 62 , 70 This duality reinforces a broader principle of nanosafety: a biologic mechanism cannot be labeled simply as good or bad without considering where, when, and in which cells it occurs. 34 , 62 , 70

### Organ Accumulation and Long-Term Retention

Organ accumulation and long-term retention are critical determinants of chronic nanoparticle safety. 62 , 66–68 Quantitative biodistribution analysis indicates that, after intravenous administration, liver and spleen are typically the principal sites of nanoparticle accumulation, with kidneys, lungs, and tumors generally receiving much smaller fractions on average. 67 , 68 This is not only a pharmacokinetic observation; it is a safety map. 67 , 68 It identifies the organs most likely to experience chronic exposure, macrophage burden, degradation product release, and delayed inflammatory or fibrotic effects. 62 , 67 , 68

Long-term safety depends on whether accumulated particles are efficiently degraded and cleared or instead persist in tissues. 62 , 67 , 68 Reviews of inorganic nanoparticle toxicity emphasize that subchronic and chronic outcomes are strongly shaped by retention time, organ-specific processing, and the biological activity of degradation products. 62 For magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles, recent reviews highlight that toxicity is highly dependent on coating chemistry, aggregation, dose, and degradation kinetics rather than on core composition alone. 62 This illustrates a general rule: chronic safety is determined by the fate of the particle within organs, not just by the identity of the starting material. 62 , 67 , 68

Long-term retention also has immunological implications. 62 , 66–68 Persistent particles in liver, spleen, or other tissues may sustain low-grade inflammation, alter macrophage phenotype, or create organ-specific stress that is not obvious in short-term studies. 62 , 66–68 This is one reason why acute tolerability cannot be taken as evidence of chronic safety. 62 , 67 , 68 In nanomedicine, clearance kinetics and tissue persistence are as important as immediate blood compatibility. 52 , 62–64 A formulation that is well tolerated on first administration may still be unsuitable for chronic use if it accumulates progressively in phagocytic organs or generates slowly cleared transformation products. 62 , 67 , 68

### Integrative Perspective

These biological interactions are best understood as a connected safety network rather than independent checkpoints. 34 , 52 , 62–70 Blood compatibility affects corona formation and complement activation. 52 , 63–66 Complement activation and opsonization accelerate MPS uptake. 52 , 65–68 MPS uptake determines organ accumulation and intracellular lysosomal burden. 62 , 66–68 Intracellular trafficking influences oxidative stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and potentially genotoxicity. 34 , 62 , 69 , 70 Long-term retention feeds back into chronic immune and tissue responses. 62 , 67 , 68 The safety of a nanoparticle therefore emerges from the sequence and coupling of these interactions across time and biological scale. 34 , 52 , 62–70

For translational nanomedicine, the practical conclusion is clear: safety cannot be inferred from one assay, one organ, or one time point. 34 , 52 , 62–70 It must be evaluated through an integrated framework that links blood-facing behavior, immune recognition, phagocytic clearance, intracellular fate, stress-response pathways, and long-term tissue disposition. 34 , 52 , 62–70 This is the level at which “biocompatibility” becomes clinically meaningful. 34 , 52 , 62–70

## Organ-Specific Safety Concerns

Organ-specific toxicology is a decisive component of nanomedicine safety because nanoparticles rarely distribute uniformly after administration. 67 , 68 , 72–82 Instead, their disposition is shaped by vascular architecture, endothelial permeability, protein corona composition, macrophage surveillance, renal filtration constraints, and tissue-specific clearance pathways. 67 , 68 , 75–77 As a result, particular organs repeatedly emerge as dominant sinks or vulnerable interfaces, especially the liver, spleen, kidney, lung, brain, cardiovascular system, and reproductive tissues. 67 , 68 , 72–82 This matters translationally because a nanomedicine may appear systemically tolerable while still imposing clinically relevant burdens on one or more organ systems through sequestration, prolonged retention, local inflammatory signaling, endothelial injury, or organ-specific accumulation of carrier degradation products. 67 , 68 , 72–82 Modern biodistribution analyses show that after intravenous administration, nanoparticles accumulate predominantly in liver and spleen, with far lower fractions generally reaching most other tissues, reinforcing that organ safety is inseparable from disposition biology. 67 , 68

### Liver and Spleen Sequestration

The liver and spleen are the principal organs of nanoparticle sequestration after systemic administration because they contain dense populations of phagocytic cells and highly specialized vascular structures that favor particle capture. 67 , 68 In the liver, Kupffer cells, sinusoidal endothelial cells, and, in some settings, hepatocytes participate in nanoparticle uptake. 67 , 68 In the spleen, macrophage-rich red pulp and filtration architecture contribute to retention of circulating particulate material. 67 , 68 This pattern is so consistent that it is best regarded as a default biodistribution outcome for many intravenously administered nanomedicines rather than as an exception. 67 , 68 Recent analyses emphasize that rapid uptake by the mononuclear phagocyte system remains a primary barrier after intravenous administration, while quantitative biodistribution studies identify liver and spleen as the dominant recipients of systemic nanoparticle dose. 67 , 68

From a safety perspective, hepatosplenic sequestration is not merely an efficacy limitation. 67 , 68 It is also the main determinant of chronic off-target exposure for many nanomedicines. 67 , 68 Accumulation in Kupffer cells and splenic macrophages can alter innate immune tone, sustain low-grade inflammatory signaling, and create organ-specific burdens that become more pronounced under repeated dosing. 67 , 68 , 82 For biodegradable platforms, the liver and spleen are often where degradation and metabolite release primarily occur. 67 , 68 For inorganic or slowly degradable particles, these organs may become sites of long-term persistence, lysosomal storage stress, oxidative injury, or fibrosis-related concern. 67 , 68 , 82 Reviews of inorganic nanoparticle toxicity consistently identify liver and spleen burden as central to subchronic and chronic safety evaluation. 67 , 68 , 82

The translational meaning of hepatosplenic uptake is context-dependent. 67 , 68 In some applications, such as liver-directed RNA therapeutics, hepatic accumulation is partly advantageous. 67 , 68 However, even then, the distinction between therapeutic hepatocyte delivery and nontarget sequestration by Kupffer cells or splenic macrophages remains crucial. 67 , 68 A formulation that reaches the liver is not necessarily reaching the intended hepatic cell type in a safe or efficacious way. 67 , 68 Therefore, liver and spleen safety assessment should include not only bulk organ accumulation but also cell-specific localization, inflammatory readouts, histopathology, and the fate of degradation products over time. 67 , 68 , 82

### Renal Clearance and Nephrotoxicity

The kidney occupies a dual role in nanomedicine safety: it is both a potential clearance route and a potential toxicity target. 75–77 Renal elimination is generally desirable for nanoparticles or degradation products that are sufficiently small and appropriately surface-engineered, because efficient urinary excretion can reduce long-term accumulation in liver and spleen. 75 , 76 Classical work on nanoparticle renal filtration showed that ultrasmall nanostructures can undergo rapid urinary clearance when hydrodynamic properties fall within the renal filtration window, and subsequent reviews have emphasized that size, shape, surface charge, and protein adsorption all influence renal passage. 75 , 76

However, renal clearance is not synonymous with renal safety. 75–77 Nanoparticles or released components that enter the kidney may interact with glomerular structures, proximal tubular cells, podocytes, mesangial cells, or renal endothelial compartments. 75 , 77 Comprehensive toxicology reviews conclude that nanoparticles can produce nephrotoxic effects at both tubular and glomerular levels through mechanisms including oxidative stress, mitochondrial injury, cytoskeletal disruption, and inflammatory signaling. 75 , 77 These risks are especially relevant when particles accumulate intracellularly in renal epithelia or when repeated dosing is used in patients with impaired kidney function, where clearance may be reduced and retention increased. 75–77

The kidney also introduces a safety paradox in nanomedicine design. 75–77 Features that favor renal clearance, such as very small size or specific surface properties, may reduce chronic systemic retention but can simultaneously increase direct renal exposure. 75–77 Conversely, larger particles that avoid renal filtration may spare the kidney acutely while increasing hepatosplenic burden. 67 , 68 , 75–77 Thus, kidney safety is not determined solely by whether a particle is renally cleared, but by how much material reaches renal microanatomical compartments, how long it remains there, and whether disease-related reductions in glomerular filtration or tubular handling alter its fate. 75–77 For translational assessment, this requires integration of biodistribution, urinalysis, serum chemistry, renal histology, and disease-state pharmacokinetics. 75–77

### Pulmonary Toxicity

The lung is a major safety concern for nanoparticles because it can be exposed both directly, through inhalation or inhaled formulations, and indirectly, through systemic circulation, pulmonary first-pass interactions, immune-cell trafficking, or embolic deposition of unstable aggregates. 78 , 79 Pulmonary toxicology is governed by particle deposition pattern, aerodynamic and hydrodynamic behavior, epithelial interaction, alveolar macrophage uptake, mucociliary clearance, and inflammatory amplification within the delicate gas-exchange architecture. 78 , 79 Recent reviews emphasize that nanoparticle toxicity in the respiratory tract is shaped by particle properties, exposure conditions, and deposition behavior, with oxidative stress and inflammation as recurrent mechanisms. 78

In pulmonary delivery, the lung offers attractive therapeutic opportunities because of its large surface area and accessible epithelial interface, but those same features create vulnerability. 78 , 79 Excessive local deposition, reactive surfaces, or poorly degradable materials can damage alveolar epithelium, activate macrophages, alter surfactant function, and impair respiratory mechanics. 78 , 79 These risks are not limited to environmental nanoparticles; they are directly relevant to inhaled nanomedicines, particularly when formulation stability, aerodynamic sizing, or mucosal interaction is suboptimal. 78 , 79 Reviews of nanoparticle-based inhaled drug delivery highlight the translational promise of respiratory nanomedicine while underscoring the need to control local toxicity, retention, and inflammatory responses. 79

Even for systemically administered nanoparticles, pulmonary safety matters. 78 , 82 Complement-mediated reactions, aggregate trapping, endothelial interaction, and inflammatory cross-talk can produce lung involvement without primary inhalation exposure. 78 , 82 Accordingly, pulmonary safety assessment should not be restricted to inhaled formulations alone. 78 , 79 It should also be considered in intravenous nanomedicine development, particularly for formulations with aggregation liability, strong complement activation potential, or pronounced leukocyte interaction. 78 , 82

### Neurotoxicity and Blood–Brain Barrier Considerations

The central nervous system presents a distinctive safety challenge because the blood–brain barrier, or BBB, strongly restricts entry of most circulating materials, yet some nanoparticles can cross or perturb this barrier depending on size, surface chemistry, ligand decoration, inflammation, or disease-induced BBB disruption. 80 , 81 This has obvious therapeutic importance for CNS drug delivery, but it also raises neurotoxicologic concerns. 80 , 81 Recent reviews note that nanocarriers can cross the BBB and may produce neurotoxic effects through mechanisms including oxidative stress, DNA damage, neuroinflammation, accumulation, and persistence in brain tissue. 80

Neurotoxicity in nanomedicine may arise through several distinct mechanisms. 80 , 81 Nanoparticles may directly enter neural tissue and interact with neurons, astrocytes, microglia, or cerebrovascular endothelium. 80 , 81 They may indirectly compromise CNS homeostasis by disrupting BBB integrity, altering endothelial tight junctions, or provoking systemic inflammatory signals that secondarily affect the brain. 80 , 81 In addition, disease-targeting strategies that intentionally enhance BBB crossing may narrow the margin between therapeutic access and unwanted CNS exposure. 80 , 81 Reviews of BBB-targeting nanoparticles emphasize both the promise of biomaterial engineering for brain delivery and the importance of understanding BBB models, pathological barrier alteration, and nanoparticle permeability determinants. 80 , 81

These issues make BBB-oriented nanomedicine unusually safety-sensitive. 80 , 81 A carrier designed to overcome the BBB is, by definition, designed to reach one of the body’s most protected organs. 80 , 81 Therefore, neurotoxicity assessment should move beyond general cytotoxicity and address BBB integrity, microglial activation, behavioral outcomes where relevant, persistence in CNS compartments, and the long-term fate of materials or degradation products in neural tissue. 80 , 81 This is especially important for chronic neurological indications, repeated dosing, and platforms with uncertain CNS clearance. 80 , 81 The principal strategies for BBB access also carry different safety trade-offs. Receptor-mediated transcytosis can improve endothelial uptake and transcellular transport but may be limited by receptor saturation, ligand density, endosomal routing, and loss of targeting after protein-corona formation. Adsorptive-mediated transport can exploit electrostatic interactions but generally provides less specificity and may increase membrane perturbation. Carrier-mediated strategies rely on endogenous nutrient-transport systems and therefore face competition and capacity constraints, whereas biomimetic or cell-mediated approaches may improve biological recognition at the cost of greater compositional and manufacturing complexity. These approaches should therefore be compared according to transport efficiency, specificity, barrier integrity, intracellular fate, repeat-dose feasibility, and manufacturability rather than by BBB crossing alone. 80 , 81

### Cardiovascular Effects

The cardiovascular system is both the transport network for systemically administered nanoparticles and a direct toxicity target. 68 , 82 Nanoparticles can interact with vascular endothelium, circulating blood cells, coagulation factors, autonomic signaling pathways, and cardiac tissues. 68 , 82 Recent reviews summarize that nanoparticle-associated cardiovascular adverse events include arrhythmia, cardiac hypertrophy, atherosclerosis, thrombosis, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and multiple forms of programmed cell death. 82 These effects are mechanistically plausible because the cardiovascular system experiences immediate nanoparticle exposure after intravenous administration and secondary exposure after redistribution from other routes. 68 , 82

Cardiovascular toxicity may manifest acutely as hemodynamic instability, altered vasoreactivity, complement-mediated cardiopulmonary symptoms, procoagulant activity, endothelial permeability changes, or platelet activation. 68 , 82 It may also emerge subacutely or chronically through vascular inflammation, oxidative injury, atherogenic signaling, myocardial stress, or thrombogenic remodeling. 68 , 82 Importantly, some of these effects may be driven more by surface properties, aggregation, and immune activation than by core chemistry alone. 68 , 82 This means that a nanomedicine with acceptable general tolerability can still carry cardiovascular risk if it perturbs endothelial function or coagulation. 68 , 82

From a translational standpoint, cardiovascular safety deserves special attention in oncology nanomedicine, repeated-dose intravenous regimens, and formulations designed for long circulation. 68 , 82 Many of these products are administered to patients who already have cardiovascular vulnerability due to age, inflammation, prior chemotherapy, or metabolic disease. 68 , 82 Thus, cardiovascular assessment should include not only general blood compatibility but also vascular reactivity, thrombogenicity, endothelial integrity, cardiac biomarkers where appropriate, and interaction with preexisting cardiovascular risk states. 68 , 82

### Reproductive and Developmental Safety Issues

Reproductive and developmental safety is one of the least resolved but most important domains in nanoparticle toxicology. 72–74 Recent reviews emphasize that nanoparticles may affect fertility, gonadal function, endocrine balance, gamete quality, embryonic development, placental biology, and potentially later-life offspring outcomes, although the magnitude and generalizability of these risks remain incompletely defined across nanoparticle classes. 72–74 Recent toxicology reviews conclude that the effects of different nanoparticles on reproductive function are not yet fully determined and that further work is required to clarify reproductive toxicity across in vitro and in vivo systems. 72

Several mechanistic concerns recur in this literature. 72–74 Nanoparticles may cross biological barriers relevant to reproduction, including the blood-testis barrier and, in some settings, the placental interface. 72–74 They may also disrupt reproductive tissues indirectly through oxidative stress, inflammation, endocrine perturbation, mitochondrial dysfunction, or epigenetic alteration. 72–74 The concern is not limited to overt infertility. 72–74 Developmental toxicology also encompasses altered embryo-fetal growth, placental dysfunction, congenital abnormalities, developmental programming, and possible transgenerational effects. 72–74 Reviews on nanoparticle-mediated embryotoxicity underscore the importance of understanding how nanoparticle properties contribute to developmental injury and maternal-fetal exposure risk. 73

For nanomedicine, these issues are especially relevant in chronic indications, products likely to be used in women of reproductive age, and platforms with prolonged systemic persistence. 72–74 They also matter for oncology and inflammatory disease, where treatment may coincide with reproductive vulnerability or pregnancy. 72–74 Reproductive safety assessment should therefore not be treated as an afterthought or a generic toxicology appendix. 72–74 It requires targeted evaluation of gonadal distribution, placental transfer where relevant, endocrine and gamete endpoints, embryo-fetal development, and the possibility that disease states may modify maternal-fetal nanoparticle handling. 72–74

### Integrative Perspective

These organ-specific safety domains are interconnected rather than isolated. 67 , 68 , 72–82 A nanoparticle that avoids renal clearance may increase hepatosplenic retention. 67 , 68 , 75–77 A formulation optimized for BBB crossing may alter cardiovascular or immune safety. 80–82 Pulmonary inflammation may be driven by systemic immune activation rather than only local deposition. 78 , 82 Reproductive risk may depend on the same determinants that shape chronic persistence in liver, spleen, or placenta. 72–74 Organ-specific safety in nanomedicine is therefore best approached as a systems problem linking biodistribution, barrier biology, degradation fate, disease state, and dosing schedule. 67 , 68 , 72–82 This is why organ-resolved toxicokinetics and long-term fate studies are indispensable for clinical translation. 67 , 68 , 72–82

## Major Advances That Have Improved Nanoparticle Safety

The improvement of nanoparticle safety in medicine has not resulted from a single technological breakthrough, but from the progressive convergence of materials science, colloid chemistry, immunology, pharmaceutical engineering, and translational manufacturing. 6 , 42 , 83 Early generations of nanomedicines often focused primarily on payload loading, circulation time, and target accumulation. 6 , 83 Over time, however, it became clear that clinically meaningful progress required deeper control over immune recognition, blood compatibility, degradability, tissue persistence, and product reproducibility. 6 , 24 , 42 , 83–85 This shift has reshaped the field from one centered largely on delivery efficiency toward one increasingly guided by safe-by-design principles. 42 , 83 Contemporary advances that have materially improved nanoparticle safety include stealth strategies such as PEGylation, biomimetic coatings, biodegradable and bioresponsive materials, safer lipid nanoparticle architectures, surface engineering approaches to reduce immunotoxicity, controlled-release and site-specific delivery systems, and cleaner manufacturing approaches that reduce impurities and process-related hazards. 6 , 24 , 43 , 44 , 83–99

### PEGylation and Stealth Strategies

PEGylation was one of the earliest and most influential advances in improving nanoparticle safety because it addressed a central problem in systemic nanomedicine: rapid recognition by proteins and phagocytic cells. 83 , 97 , 98 By grafting poly(ethylene glycol) chains onto nanoparticle surfaces, developers created sterically shielded interfaces that reduce protein adsorption, diminish opsonization, improve colloidal stability, and often prolong circulation time. 83 , 97 , 98 These effects can lower first-pass uptake by the mononuclear phagocyte system and reduce some acute blood-facing interactions, which in turn may improve tolerability and biodistribution for selected products. 83 , 97 , 98 Recent reviews continue to identify PEGylation as a foundational stealth strategy in nanomedicine and a major contributor to the clinical usability of liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, and lipid nanoparticles. 83 , 97 , 98

The safety value of PEGylation lies not merely in longer circulation, but in the fact that prolonged circulation can sometimes be achieved while reducing direct membrane interactions and early immune recognition. 83 , 97 , 98 In practical terms, PEG chains create a hydrated steric barrier that helps prevent aggregation and moderates the immediate protein-layer composition formed in blood. 83 , 97 , 98 This can reduce nonspecific uptake and dampen some forms of acute reactivity. 83 , 97 , 98 For many formulations, PEGylation was therefore a decisive step in moving from highly interactive, rapidly cleared colloids toward more clinically tolerable systemic nanocarriers. 83 , 97 , 98

At the same time, the field has learned that PEGylation is an advance with limitations rather than a universal solution. 83 , 97 , 98 Anti-PEG antibodies, accelerated blood clearance, and PEG-associated hypersensitivity have become well-recognized concerns, particularly under repeated exposure. 83 , 97 , 98 This has not negated the importance of PEGylation, but it has refined its role. 83 , 97 , 98 The major safety advance has been twofold: first, PEGylation itself improved the safety profile of many early nanocarriers; second, recognition of the “PEG dilemma” drove the development of cleavable PEG, alternative stealth polymers, and more nuanced exposure strategies. 83 , 97 , 98

### Biomimetic and Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles

A major conceptual advance beyond classical stealth chemistry has been the emergence of biomimetic nanoparticles, especially cell membrane-coated systems. These platforms use membranes derived from erythrocytes, platelets, leukocytes, cancer cells, stem cells, bacteria, or hybrid membrane sources to cloak synthetic nanoparticle cores with biologically derived surface features. The safety rationale is compelling: instead of merely reducing interaction with the immune system through an inert polymer shell, biomimetic coatings attempt to present a more physiologically recognizable interface that can evade clearance, reduce nonspecific immune activation, and sometimes confer tissue-homing behavior. Recent reviews describe cell membrane-coated nanoparticles as a major frontier in biomimetic delivery precisely because they combine immune-evasive and targeting functions in a single surface design strategy. 43 , 44 , 86 , 87

From a safety perspective, one of the most important advantages of membrane-coated nanoparticles is their capacity to reduce abrupt blood-facing incompatibility. Erythrocyte membrane coatings, for example, may help prolong circulation and mitigate rapid phagocytic clearance, while platelet and leukocyte membrane systems can be designed to exploit native adhesion or inflammatory trafficking pathways without exposing the underlying synthetic core directly to plasma components. This type of camouflage may reduce complement-triggering surface motifs and reshape the protein corona toward a more biologically compatible identity. 43 , 44 , 86 , 87

The major safety advance here is not that biomimetic systems are automatically safe, but that they offer a more sophisticated way to engineer the nano–bio interface. By using natural membrane proteins and lipids, these systems may reduce some of the trade-offs associated with strongly synthetic stealth coatings. At the same time, they introduce new safety considerations such as membrane source selection, pathogen safety, batch variability, membrane integrity, immunologic compatibility, and manufacturing complexity. Thus, biomimetic coating represents an important advance because it shifts safety engineering from steric masking alone toward biologically informed interfacial design. 43 , 44 , 86 , 87

### Biodegradable and Bioresponsive Materials

The move toward biodegradable nanomaterials has been one of the clearest long-term improvements in nanosafety. A major historical concern in nanomedicine has been chronic retention, especially in liver, spleen, and other phagocyte-rich tissues. Biodegradable platforms reduce this risk by allowing nanoparticles to break down into smaller, more excretable or metabolizable components after fulfilling their delivery function. Reviews on biodegradable nanomaterials and biomaterial degradation assessment emphasize that degradability is central to reducing long-term tissue burden and improving translational suitability. 84 , 88

This advance is especially important for polymeric and lipid-based systems. 84 , 88 , 89 Biodegradable polyesters, polypeptides, polycarbonates, natural polymers, and hydrolytically or enzymatically labile linkers have made it increasingly possible to design nanoparticles whose persistence is limited by intent rather than by accident. 84 , 88 In safety terms, this reduces the likelihood that repeated dosing will lead to progressive organ storage, lysosomal overload, or long-term inflammatory signaling. The improvement is not merely theoretical; it changes what regulators and developers can reasonably expect regarding chronic exposure and recovery after treatment cessation. 84 , 88

Bioresponsive materials build on this by coupling degradation or structural change to the disease microenvironment or intracellular conditions. pH-sensitive, redox-sensitive, enzyme-responsive, ROS-responsive, and externally triggered systems can be designed to remain relatively stable during circulation but disassemble or release payload only after reaching a target site or intracellular compartment. The safety benefit is obvious: reducing premature release and minimizing nonspecific exposure can lower systemic toxicity while preserving efficacy. Although bioresponsive systems vary widely in maturity, their key contribution to safety is the replacement of indiscriminate exposure with conditional activation. 88 , 94

### Safer Lipid Nanoparticle Platforms

The recent evolution of lipid nanoparticles has been one of the most important safety advances in all of nanomedicine. 6 , 24 , 89 Modern lipid nanoparticle platforms, particularly those for nucleic acid delivery, differ substantially from earlier cationic liposome systems in that they increasingly rely on ionizable, rather than permanently cationic, lipids. This change has major safety implications. Ionizable lipids can remain close to neutral charge at physiological pH, reducing nonspecific blood and membrane interactions, while becoming protonated in acidic endosomal compartments to support intracellular release. Recent reviews emphasize that this transition has been central to the improved tolerability and clinical viability of LNP-mediated mRNA and siRNA delivery. 24 , 89

In addition to ionizable lipid design, safer LNP platforms have benefited from better control over helper lipid composition, cholesterol content, PEG-lipid type, particle size distribution, biodegradability of lipid tails and linkers, and analytical characterization of potency and reactogenicity. 6 , 24 , 89 These refinements have reduced some of the acute toxicity and inflammatory burden associated with earlier delivery systems while enabling the large-scale clinical success of mRNA vaccines and other nucleic acid medicines. 6 , 24 , 42 , 89 The safety advance here is particularly significant because it demonstrates that rational chemical redesign of a carrier class can turn a historically difficult modality into a clinically deployable one. 24 , 89

Current work on safer LNPs also reflects a broader shift in nanosafety philosophy. Rather than treating toxicity as an unavoidable trade-off of intracellular delivery, developers increasingly optimize lipid chemistry specifically to reduce reactogenicity, improve biodegradation, minimize repeat-dose immune complications, and direct delivery toward desired cell types more selectively. Thus, safer LNP platforms are both a specific technological advance and a model for how safety-guided carrier design can reshape an entire therapeutic class. 24 , 89

### Surface Engineering to Reduce Immunotoxicity

Advanced surface engineering has become one of the most effective ways to reduce nanoparticle immunotoxicity because it directly governs how the material is first interpreted by blood proteins, immune cells, and clearance organs. Recent reviews on surface decoration and surface engineering emphasize improvements in colloidal stability, reduced toxicity, enhanced targeting, and better adaptation to complex biological environments. These strategies include PEGylation, zwitterionic coatings, polysaccharides, ligand-density optimization, charge modulation, biomimetic ligands, protein pre-coating, and hybrid surface architectures. 85 , 90 , 91

The safety benefit of surface engineering lies in its ability to reduce unfavorable early events such as aggregation, complement activation, nonspecific membrane disruption, and uncontrolled protein corona formation. For example, shifting a particle surface from strongly cationic toward near-neutral or zwitterionic character may reduce hemolysis and inflammatory signaling while preserving sufficient delivery function. Likewise, judicious ligand presentation can improve selectivity without exposing highly reactive surface motifs. In many cases, the greatest safety gain is not complete immune invisibility, which is often unrealistic, but a more controlled and less inflammatory pattern of immune engagement. 85 , 90 , 91

This area represents a major advance because it reframes nanoparticle surfaces as programmable biological interfaces rather than passive outer layers. Modern surface engineering seeks not only to enhance delivery, but also to shape the protein corona, reduce innate immune activation, and lower organ-specific off-target burden. In this respect, it has become one of the most powerful operational tools for implementing safe-by-design nanomedicine. 85 , 90 , 91

### Controlled-Release and Site-Specific Delivery Approaches

A major source of nanoparticle-related toxicity is premature or nonspecific exposure of healthy tissues to either the carrier or the payload. Advances in controlled-release and site-specific delivery have improved safety by reducing this unwanted exposure. These approaches include diffusion-controlled matrices, triggerable release systems, stimuli-responsive nanocarriers, prodrug-like nanoconstructs, local depot systems, heat- or pH-triggered carriers, and active-targeting strategies that bias uptake toward particular tissues or cell populations. Reviews on targeted and site-specific nanocarrier systems consistently note that one of their principal safety advantages is the reduction of systemic toxicity through spatiotemporal control of drug exposure. 94–96

Controlled release improves safety because it can flatten harmful peak concentrations, prevent burst release, and keep free drug levels lower outside the intended site of action. Site-specific delivery adds another protective layer by limiting exposure in vulnerable organs. In oncology, for example, nanocarriers that localize drugs more effectively to tumors or release them preferentially within tumor-associated conditions can reduce damage to bone marrow, heart, or gastrointestinal tissues. In inflammatory or infectious disease, localized delivery may similarly decrease the systemic burden of potent agents. 94–96

Importantly, the safety gain from these approaches depends on actual delivery realism. The field has moved beyond simplistic assumptions that all nanoparticles automatically target diseased tissue. The major advance has been the creation of more conditional and mechanistically grounded release strategies, not merely more targeting labels. When successful, these systems reduce the mismatch between where a nanoparticle circulates and where its payload becomes biologically active. 94–96

### Green Synthesis and Cleaner Manufacturing Approaches

Although green synthesis is often discussed mainly in environmental terms, it also has direct relevance to medical nanoparticle safety. Cleaner synthesis and manufacturing approaches aim to reduce toxic solvents, residual reagents, harsh reducing agents, heavy-metal contaminants, and unstable byproducts that can compromise the safety profile of a final nanomedicine. Recent reviews of green nanoparticle synthesis and eco-friendly bio-nanocomposites describe these approaches as environmentally responsible and potentially safer because biologically derived stabilizers and milder process conditions can reduce hazardous residues and improve biocompatibility-related attributes. 92 , 93

In pharmaceutical nanotechnology, the most important safety implication of cleaner manufacturing is not simply that the synthesis is “green,” but that it can produce materials with lower impurity burden, fewer toxic residuals, and potentially more benign surface chemistries. 6 , 92 , 93 This is particularly relevant for metallic and inorganic nanoparticles, where reductants, surfactants, and postsynthetic modifiers can strongly influence toxicity if not adequately removed. 92 , 93 Cleaner manufacturing can therefore support both environmental sustainability and better clinical-grade quality. 6 , 92 , 93

However, this area also illustrates the need for translational discipline. 6 , 92 , 93 Green synthesis does not automatically guarantee batch reproducibility, pharmaceutical purity, or regulatory readiness. The true advance lies in integrating cleaner chemistries with robust process control, scalable purification, and analytical verification. When those conditions are met, greener manufacturing becomes part of a broader movement toward safer nanomedicine production rather than a separate sustainability agenda. 6 , 42 , 92 , 93

### Integrated Perspective

The evidentiary maturity of safety-enhancing strategies is not equivalent. PEGylation and ionizable-lipid formulations have extensive clinical validation but also well-defined liabilities, including anti-PEG immunity, infusion reactions, and repeat-dose effects. Biodegradable materials and controlled-release approaches have platform-specific clinical precedent, whereas cell-membrane coatings, green-synthesis strategies, and highly responsive or transient constructs remain largely preclinical and require stronger comparative toxicology, CMC standardization, and scale-up evidence before generalized claims of improved safety are justified. 6 , 42–44 , 83–99

Taken together, these advances show that nanoparticle safety has improved most when the field has intervened at the interface between material and biology. 6 , 24 , 42–44 , 83–98 PEGylation reduced rapid immune recognition. 83 , 97 , 98 Biomimetic coatings made that interface more physiologic. 43 , 44 , 86 , 87 Biodegradable and bioresponsive materials reduced long-term burden and premature exposure. 84 , 88 , 94 Safer LNP chemistry improved intracellular delivery without requiring permanently aggressive surface charge. 24 , 89 Surface engineering reduced immunotoxicity more broadly. 85 , 90 , 91 Controlled-release and site-specific systems reduced off-target exposure. 94–96 Cleaner manufacturing reduced impurities and process-related hazards. 6 , 42 , 92 , 93 These are not isolated innovations. They are mutually reinforcing developments that have shifted nanomedicine toward more predictable, biologically informed, and clinically defensible design. 6 , 24 , 42–44 , 83–98

The most important lesson is that safety improvements have rarely come from making nanoparticles completely inert. 42 , 83–85 Instead, progress has come from controlling how nanoparticles interact with blood, immune systems, tissues, and manufacturing environments. 6 , 24 , 42–44 , 83–98 In this sense, the major advances described in this section represent the maturation of nanomedicine from formulation ingenuity to translational engineering. 6 , 42 , 83 The major technological and conceptual advances that have improved nanoparticle tolerability and translational safety are outlined in Table 2 . ## Progress in Preclinical Safety Assessment

Preclinical safety assessment in nanomedicine has advanced substantially over the past decade, moving from relatively simple viability assays and gross organ histology toward a more integrated framework that combines physicochemical characterization, mechanistic cell biology, biodistribution analysis, imaging-based tracking, computational modeling, and systems-level toxicology. This evolution reflects a central lesson from translational nanomedicine: conventional toxicology workflows developed for small molecules are often insufficient for nanoparticles because nanoscale materials interact dynamically with proteins, cells, blood components, tissues, and clearance systems in ways that depend on size, surface chemistry, aggregation state, and exposure context. Modern preclinical assessment therefore seeks not only to determine whether a nanoparticle is toxic, but also to understand where it goes, how it transforms, which cells it perturbs, and which molecular pathways link early biological interaction to later adverse outcomes. 71 , 100–102

A second major change is that preclinical safety is increasingly viewed as a tiered evidence system rather than a single experimental domain. In vitro assays remain indispensable for throughput and mechanism discovery, but they are now complemented by 3D cultures, organoids, organ-on-chip systems, advanced in vivo biodistribution studies, physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling, and multi-omics methods that can reveal early molecular signatures of toxicity. The field has therefore progressed not by abandoning traditional methods, but by embedding them within a more mechanistically informed and translationally realistic safety-testing architecture. 68 , 71 , 100–103

### In vitro Models: Strengths and Limitations

Conventional in vitro models remain the foundation of early nanosafety screening because they are rapid, comparatively inexpensive, experimentally controlled, and compatible with systematic variation of nanoparticle properties such as size, charge, coating, and dose. They are especially useful for identifying acute cellular effects including cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, membrane damage, inflammatory signaling, barrier perturbation, endocytic uptake, and assay-specific interactions with blood or immune cells. 71 , 100 Their greatest strength is mechanistic tractability. A well-designed cell-based study can isolate how a specific formulation variable changes cellular uptake, lysosomal burden, mitochondrial function, or cytokine release without the confounding complexity of whole-animal physiology. 71 , 100

The in vitro field has also become more sophisticated in how exposure is modeled. For airborne and inhaled nanomaterials, for example, recent reviews have emphasized the importance of exposure configuration, comparing submerged exposure with air–liquid interface systems and static versus dynamic exposure modes. Jaber et al noted that modern in vitro approaches now encompass primary cells, cell lines, organoids, spheroids, reconstituted tissues, and organ-on-chip systems, together with intermittent, continuous, static, or dynamic exposure methods. 101 This is an important advance because nanoparticle dose delivery to cells is highly sensitive to sedimentation, diffusion, agglomeration, protein content, and exposure geometry. Preclinical assessment has therefore progressed from asking only “what concentration was added?” to asking “what biologically effective dose actually reached the cells?”. 71 , 101

Despite these strengths, the limitations of conventional in vitro models remain substantial. Monocultures often fail to reproduce tissue architecture, multicellular signaling, flow-dependent transport, macrophage surveillance, organ-level metabolism, and long-term fate. Many standard toxicity assays are also vulnerable to nanoparticle interference, particularly optical readouts, dye-binding assays, and colorimetric metabolic assays. Earlier methodological work and subsequent reviews have repeatedly cautioned that nanomaterials may absorb, quench, catalyze, scatter, or otherwise perturb assay reagents, leading to false-positive or false-negative toxicity findings if assay compatibility is not verified. 71 , 100 Furthermore, cellular uptake and toxicity in vitro may not predict in vivo disposition if protein corona formation, tissue barriers, blood interactions, or clearance pathways differ substantially from the cell-culture environment. 71 , 100 , 101

Thus, the progress in this area is not that traditional in vitro systems have become sufficient on their own. Rather, the advance lies in understanding more clearly what they can and cannot answer. They are now used more deliberately for screening, rank-ordering, mechanistic hypothesis generation, and safe-by-design optimization, while more complex models are used to address questions of tissue realism and translational predictivity. 71 , 100 , 101

### 3D Models, Organoids, and Organ-on-Chip Systems

One of the most important developments in preclinical nanosafety assessment has been the expansion of 3D in vitro models, including spheroids, organoids, reconstructed tissues, and organ-on-chip platforms. These systems were developed to address the poor physiological fidelity of standard monolayer cultures. By incorporating multicellular architecture, extracellular matrix, gradients of oxygen and nutrients, disease-relevant microenvironments, and in some cases microfluidic flow, they offer a more realistic framework for evaluating nanoparticle penetration, retention, toxicity, and target selectivity. 101 , 102

The safety significance of these models is considerable. Three-dimensional systems can reveal diffusion limitations, barrier effects, and cell-type-specific toxicities that remain hidden in 2D assays. In tumor spheroids and organoids, for example, nanoparticles may show strong uptake in peripheral cell layers yet poor penetration into the inner tissue, producing very different efficacy–toxicity tradeoffs than those suggested by monolayer culture. Likewise, liver, kidney, placental, gut, lung, and blood–brain barrier organoids can provide more realistic readouts of tissue stress, barrier disruption, and intracellular accumulation than isolated cell lines. Jaber et al explicitly identified organoids, spheroids, reconstituted tissues, and organs-on-chip as part of the modern in vitro toolkit for nanotoxicity characterization. 101

Among advanced in vitro platforms, organ-on-chip systems have generated especially strong interest because they combine tissue architecture with controlled flow and, in some designs, immune, endothelial, or multicompartment interactions. A 2025 review by Sampaio et al concluded that organ-on-chip platforms provide a powerful alternative to traditional in vitro and in vivo models for evaluating nanoparticle toxicity and therapeutic efficacy, helping to identify negative effects and mechanisms of action under more physiologic conditions, while also noting important barriers related to scalability and regulatory integration. 102 This is a meaningful advance for safety science because many nanoparticle toxicities are flow-dependent, barrier-dependent, or multicellular in nature. Endothelialized chips, vascularized liver chips, renal tubule chips, placental chips, and BBB chips can therefore probe safety domains that conventional static cultures capture poorly. 102

Nevertheless, these systems also have limitations. They are more complex, less standardized, lower throughput, and often more difficult to characterize analytically than standard cultures. Their biological relevance depends strongly on cell source, matrix composition, fluid shear, and device architecture, and interlaboratory reproducibility remains a challenge. Regulatory acceptance is still evolving. Thus, the progress here lies not in replacing all other models, but in strategically deploying 3D and microphysiological systems when the safety question specifically depends on barrier transport, multicellular interaction, or tissue architecture. 101 , 102

### In vivo Models and Biodistribution Studies

In vivo studies remain indispensable in nanomedicine safety assessment because only whole-animal models can integrate circulation, protein corona evolution, immune surveillance, organ-level sequestration, metabolism, degradation, repeated-dose adaptation, and long-term clearance. Even the most sophisticated in vitro systems cannot fully reproduce the dynamic redistribution of nanoparticles across liver, spleen, kidney, lung, blood, and target tissues, nor can they capture the full coupling between biodistribution and toxicity. 68 , 103 , 104

A major advance in the past few years has been the more quantitative treatment of in vivo transport and tissue distribution. Xu et al reviewed size-dependent in vivo transport of nanoparticles and emphasized how size influences delivery, targeting, and clearance. 103 Related work on nanoparticle biodistribution coefficients has attempted to quantify tissue distribution across studies and platforms, highlighting how strongly organ exposure depends on formulation variables and how consistently liver and spleen dominate systemic disposition in many intravenous settings. 68 This quantitative turn matters for safety because organ toxicity is fundamentally exposure-driven. Better biodistribution analysis improves the ability to predict which tissues experience the highest cumulative nanoparticle burden and which design changes are most likely to reduce off-target risk. 68 , 103 The scale of the available evidence is increasingly sufficient for cross-platform quantitative synthesis. Kumar et al analyzed 2,018 published pharmacokinetic and biodistribution datasets spanning graphene oxide, lipid, polymeric, silica, iron-oxide, and gold nanoparticles across plasma, tumor, and 13 tissues, demonstrating both strong tissue-dependent partitioning and substantial formulation-dependent variability. 68 Such datasets are valuable because they move nanosafety away from isolated organ-percentage observations toward comparative exposure metrics that can support PBPK modeling, rational dose selection, and identification of organs in which cumulative burden is most likely to become safety-limiting.

Another important development is the closer integration of biodistribution data with pharmacokinetic modeling. A 2024 ACS Pharmacology and Translational Science review highlighted recent advances in physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling for nanoparticles, emphasizing that PBPK frameworks can help simulate absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination for nanomaterials whose disposition differs substantially from that of conventional small molecules. 104 In translational safety terms, PBPK modeling is valuable because it can connect animal biodistribution data, route-specific exposure, and organ kinetics in ways that improve dose selection and interspecies interpretation. 104

At the same time, the limitations of in vivo models remain well recognized. Species differences in protein composition, immune reactivity, phagocyte function, tumor microenvironment, vascular permeability, and clearance pathways can make animal data difficult to extrapolate directly to humans. Rodent models often overestimate delivery performance and may underestimate infusion-related or repeat-dose liabilities. The progress in this domain, therefore, is not that animal studies have become fully predictive, but that they are increasingly interpreted together with quantitative imaging, PBPK modeling, and mechanistic biomarkers rather than as stand-alone evidence. 68 , 103 , 104

### Radiolabeling and Imaging-Based Tracking of Nanoparticles

One of the most consequential advances in preclinical nanosafety has been the use of radiolabeling and imaging-based tracking to determine where nanoparticles go in vivo and how long they persist there. Traditional biodistribution methods based on tissue digestion and elemental analysis remain important, but they provide limited spatial and temporal resolution. By contrast, radiolabeling and multimodal imaging permit longitudinal, often quantitative assessment of nanoparticle localization, clearance, target uptake, and off-target retention. 28 , 105

This progress is especially visible in radionuclide-based nanoparticle studies. Reilly et al described radiation nanomedicines as nanoparticles labeled with radionuclides that emit therapeutic radiation and reviewed the broader landscape of such systems, while also underscoring the need to understand local versus systemic distribution and the safety consequences of radionuclide release or off-target retention. 105 More broadly, recent reviews of radiolabeled nanoparticles for multimodality imaging and theranostic applications emphasize that PET, SPECT, CT, MRI, fluorescence, and hybrid approaches can be used not only to guide therapy but also to resolve key safety questions such as RES uptake, renal clearance, tumor-to-organ ratios, and long-term retention. 28

The safety value of imaging is straightforward but profound. Nanomedicine toxicology depends on exposure, and exposure is difficult to interpret without tracking the intact carrier, not just the released drug or a terminal elemental signal. Imaging-based approaches can reveal whether a formulation remains stable in circulation, whether a label dissociates, whether liver and spleen burden declines over time, and whether repeated administration changes organ uptake patterns. These methods therefore strengthen the causal link between formulation design, biodistribution, and organ-specific safety findings. 28 , 105

Limitations remain. Labels may detach or redistribute independently of the nanoparticle, radiochemistry can alter formulation behavior, and not all imaging modalities quantify the same biological entity with equal fidelity. Nonetheless, radiolabeling and advanced imaging have clearly improved preclinical safety assessment by making nanoparticle fate visible, serially measurable, and more directly linked to toxicologic interpretation. 28 , 105

### Multi-Omics and Mechanistic Toxicology Approaches

A major conceptual advance in nanosafety is the shift from endpoint-only toxicology toward mechanistic toxicology, increasingly supported by transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, and integrated multi-omics analysis. Traditional assays often capture late manifestations of injury such as cell death, enzyme leakage, or histologic damage. Omics approaches, by contrast, can detect early pathway perturbations and reveal coordinated changes in stress response, inflammation, mitochondrial function, metabolism, DNA damage, proteostasis, and immune signaling long before overt toxicity becomes visible. 106–108

A 2023 review in Advanced Drug Delivery Reviews specifically discussed transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, and multi-omics in the assessment of biological responses to nanoparticles, emphasizing their value for characterizing whole-system responses rather than isolated endpoints. 106 More recently, Li et al reviewed omics approaches for assessing toxicity and biological interactions of inorganic nanoparticles, arguing that these methods improve mechanistic understanding and support safer nanoparticle design. 107 Complementing this, a 2024 review on bioinformatics and machine learning in nanotoxicology highlighted how omics data can support grouping, read-across, and mode-of-action analysis for nanomaterials, helping move the field away from one-nanomaterial–one-endpoint logic toward more predictive hazard frameworks. 108

The translational importance of multi-omics lies in its ability to connect formulation properties to biologic mechanisms. For example, two nanoparticles may appear similarly cytotoxic at high dose, yet omics analysis may show that one primarily induces oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction while the other activates inflammatory and DNA-damage pathways. This distinction matters for safe-by-design redesign, chronic-risk prediction, and the interpretation of susceptible populations. Omics also helps bridge in vitro and in vivo toxicology by identifying pathway-level signatures that can be compared across models and, eventually, linked to clinical biomarkers. 106–108

At the same time, multi-omics introduces challenges of data complexity, batch effects, platform comparability, and biological interpretation. Large datasets are only useful if integrated with careful nanoparticle characterization, exposure dosimetry, and orthogonal validation. The field’s progress, therefore, is not simply the accumulation of more molecular data, but the increasing use of omics as part of a mechanistically anchored toxicology strategy. 106–108

### Integrated Perspective

Taken together, progress in preclinical safety assessment has been driven by a move from isolated assays to integrated evidence chains. Conventional in vitro systems remain essential for throughput and hypothesis generation. Three-dimensional models and organ-on-chip systems improve tissue relevance. In vivo studies and PBPK modeling define whole-body exposure. Radiolabeling and imaging visualize nanoparticle fate directly. Multi-omics identifies molecular mechanisms and early hazard signatures. The strongest current preclinical programs are those that connect these layers rather than treating them as substitutes for one another. 28 , 68 , 71 , 100–108

This integrated approach has already improved nanosafety science, but the remaining challenge is standardization and translation. Preclinical models still vary widely in exposure conditions, assay compatibility, imaging strategy, and omics interpretation. Yet the field is clearly moving toward a more rigorous and predictive framework in which mechanistic insight, biodistribution realism, and advanced model systems jointly inform the safety profile of nanoparticle medicines before they enter the clinic. 101 , 102 , 104 , 106–108
