## Analytical and Methodological Challenges

Analytical and methodological limitations remain among the most persistent barriers to reliable nanoparticle safety assessment and, more broadly, to the clinical translation of nanomedicine. 11 , 46 , 71 , 111 , 112 Unlike conventional small-molecule drugs, nanoparticle products are defined not only by chemical identity but also by multivariate physicochemical attributes such as size distribution, shape, surface chemistry, aggregation state, cargo localization, impurity burden, and biological transformation. 46 , 111 As a result, analytical uncertainty does not simply reduce scientific precision; it can change the interpretation of efficacy, toxicity, comparability, and product quality. 46 , 111 , 112 Recent standards-oriented and translational reviews have argued that the absence of harmonized characterization workflows, incomplete reporting of critical quality attributes, and inconsistent experimental design continue to undermine the reliability of the nanomedicine literature. 11 , 46 , 111 , 112

A central consequence of this problem is that apparently similar nanoparticles are often not truly comparable across laboratories, studies, or manufacturing runs. 46 , 54 , 111 , 112 Differences in raw materials, synthesis route, purification, storage, dispersion protocol, protein-containing media, and dose normalization can substantially alter biological behavior. 46 , 54 , 71 , 111 In nanomedicine, therefore, methodological rigor is not a secondary issue. It is part of the safety profile itself, because toxicology findings are only as meaningful as the material definition and exposure conditions on which they are based. 11 , 46 , 71 , 111 , 112

### Lack of Standardized Characterization Protocols

One of the most important challenges in nanosafety is the lack of universally implemented characterization protocols that are sufficiently robust for medical translation. 46 , 111 Nanoparticles are often described using a limited set of measurements, typically mean hydrodynamic diameter, polydispersity index, and zeta potential, but these descriptors rarely capture the full set of properties that govern biological interaction. 46 , 111 Reviews focused on analytical standardization have emphasized that reproducible nanomedicine development requires broader and context-aware characterization, including morphology, composition, aggregation behavior, surface chemistry, protein corona susceptibility, drug loading, release behavior, and stability before, during, and after biological testing. 46 , 111

Recent standardization-focused analyses have argued that the lack of a universal reporting system and decentralized characterization methodologies have contributed to low reliability and reproducibility in the nanomedicine literature, and specifically called for use of existing standards tailored to intended medical use. 111 Similarly, work on critical quality attributes has framed them as essential to therapeutic nanomedicine development, emphasizing that inadequate analytical definition compromises comparability and translation. 46 These observations reflect a broader field-wide transition: characterization is no longer viewed as a descriptive appendix, but as a foundational element of product identity and safety interpretation. 46 , 111

This challenge is amplified by the fact that the “relevant” characterization parameters depend on the product class and test context. For example, the key analytical variables for a radiolabeled liposome, an ionizable lipid nanoparticle, and a mesoporous silica carrier are not identical. Standardization in nanomedicine therefore cannot mean one inflexible assay panel for all products. Instead, it requires harmonized frameworks that define which measurements are essential, how they should be performed, and under which biologically relevant conditions they should be reported. 46 , 111

### Batch-to-Batch Variability

Batch-to-batch variability remains a major obstacle because nanoparticle systems are highly sensitive to small changes in synthesis and processing. Parameters such as precursor purity, mixing rate, solvent removal, temperature, scale-up conditions, and postformulation handling can change size distribution, surface properties, agglomeration tendency, free payload fraction, and impurity levels. These changes may be modest analytically yet significant biologically. 46 , 54 A multicenter study spanning 14 European laboratories and 46 batches of selected nanomaterials highlighted how substantial batch-dependent variation can be even for materials that are nominally the same. 54

From a safety perspective, batch variability is especially problematic because toxicologic effects may be driven by minor subpopulations rather than by the mean formulation. A small increase in large aggregates, free drug, endotoxin contamination, or reactive surface impurities may alter blood compatibility, biodistribution, or inflammatory response without being obvious from a simplified certificate of analysis. This is why batch consistency in nanomedicine is not merely a manufacturing issue. It is a toxicology issue and, ultimately, a clinical safety issue. 46 , 54

The translational literature has increasingly linked batch variability to the need for better control of critical quality attributes and for orthogonal analytical methods capable of detecting subtle but clinically meaningful drift. 46 , 54 , 111 Without such control, safety findings from one batch may not be transferable to later preclinical or clinical material. 46 , 54 In this sense, batch-to-batch variability directly undermines both internal validity and regulatory confidence. 46 , 54 , 111

### Interference of Nanoparticles with Toxicological Assays

Nanoparticle interference with toxicological assays is one of the most widely recognized methodological problems in nanotoxicology. 71 , 109 , 110 Because nanoparticles can absorb, scatter, quench, fluoresce, catalyze redox reactions, bind assay reagents, or sediment onto cells in nonuniform ways, they can distort results from common viability, oxidative stress, fluorescence, enzyme activity, and colorimetric assays. Classical work demonstrated that engineered nanoparticles can interfere with in vitro toxicity assays in concentration-, particle-, and assay-specific ways, while later studies showed that assay interference is widespread enough to threaten the accuracy of nanotoxicity testing more generally. 109 , 110

This challenge has practical consequences. A nanoparticle may appear cytotoxic because it quenches a fluorescent readout, or appear innocuous because it binds or inactivates an assay reagent. Similarly, assay artifacts may vary between formulations that differ only slightly in size or coating, leading investigators to misattribute methodological noise to biologic mechanism. Reviews and commentaries on assay interference have therefore stressed the need for interference controls, orthogonal assays, cell-free control experiments, and validation of readout compatibility before drawing toxicologic conclusions. 109 , 110

This issue also helps explain why apparent contradictions persist across the nanoparticle safety literature. Some inconsistencies likely reflect genuine biological differences, but others arise because different laboratories use different assays, media conditions, dispersion methods, and control structures. Progress in nanosafety therefore depends not only on inventing better assays, but also on recognizing when existing assays are being used outside their reliable operating range for particulate materials. 71 , 109 , 110

### Dose Metrics: Mass, Particle Number, and Surface Area

Dose selection and dose normalization are unusually difficult in nanoparticle toxicology because mass concentration alone often fails to capture the biologically relevant exposure. 71 , 113 , 114 Nanoparticles of the same mass can differ profoundly in particle number, total surface area, and interface reactivity, which means that equivalent mass doses may not correspond to equivalent biological burden. Foundational work argued that surface area is often a more appropriate dose metric than particle mass or particle number for nanoparticle dose–response assessment, and subsequent studies showed that surface area explained acute pulmonary toxicity better than the other common metrics for spherical nanoparticles in the systems analyzed. 113 , 114

This does not mean that surface area is always the correct metric. Rather, the relevant metric depends on mechanism. Surface area may better reflect oxidative or interfacial injury, particle number may be more relevant for certain uptake-driven or fiber-like effects, and mass may remain useful in pharmacologic contexts where payload quantity dominates. The methodological challenge is that many studies still report only mass concentration, making cross-study interpretation difficult and sometimes misleading. 71 , 113 , 114 Reviews on in vitro nanomaterial hazard assessment have specifically recommended the use of comparable and realistic dose metrics and test conditions. 71

This issue becomes even more important when translating between in vitro and in vivo studies. Administered dose, delivered cellular dose, retained tissue dose, and biologically effective dose are not interchangeable. 71 , 113 , 114 Sedimentation, agglomeration, and protein adsorption can all change the actual dose that cells experience. 71 , 109 , 110 As a result, rigorous nanosafety studies increasingly distinguish nominal concentration from effective exposure and justify the selected metric in relation to the hypothesized mechanism of injury. 71 , 113 , 114

### Reproducibility and Comparability Across Studies

Reproducibility remains a field-wide challenge in nanomedicine, extending beyond isolated assay issues to encompass material reporting, experimental design, data analysis, and model selection. 11 , 71 , 111 , 112 In a widely cited perspective, it was argued that transparency and reproducibility are central unresolved issues in nanomedicine and that better reporting, deeper characterization, and clearer justification of biological models are urgently needed. This concern was not merely about academic rigor. It was that weak reproducibility directly impairs downstream translation by making it difficult to distinguish robust platform effects from laboratory-specific artifacts. 112

Comparability across studies is especially difficult because nanomedicine experiments often differ in dispersion protocol, serum content, exposure duration, cell type, endpoint selection, and characterization depth. 11 , 71 , 111 , 112 Even when the same nanoparticle name is used, the tested materials may not be analytically equivalent. 11 , 46 , 54 , 111 , 112 Recent multicenter work on protein corona characterization showed that standardization measurably improved data homogeneity across facilities, illustrating that at least part of the reproducibility problem can be reduced through harmonized methodology. This finding is highly relevant beyond corona research, because it suggests that systematic protocol alignment can improve comparability in other nanosafety domains as well. 11

The broader implication is that reproducibility in nanomedicine is not achieved only by repeating experiments more often. It requires standardized material description, predefined analytical criteria, validated assay controls, appropriate dose metrics, and transparent reporting of all conditions that could alter nano–bio interactions. Without that infrastructure, the literature remains difficult to synthesize, and safety conclusions remain less portable than they need to be for regulatory or clinical use. 11 , 71 , 111 , 112

### Integrated Perspective

The analytical and methodological challenges described in this section are tightly interconnected. 11 , 46 , 54 , 71 , 109–114 Lack of standardized characterization makes batch variability harder to detect. 46 , 54 , 111 Batch variability complicates assay interpretation. 54 , 109 , 110 Assay interference obscures true dose–response relationships. 109 , 110 Inadequate dose metrics hinder comparison across studies. 71 , 113 , 114 All of these factors together erode reproducibility and weaken the evidence base for safe-by-design development. 11 , 71 , 111 , 112

For translational nanomedicine, the central lesson is that methodological rigor is not ancillary to safety. It is part of safety. 11 , 46 , 71 , 111 , 112 A nanoparticle cannot be judged safe, unsafe, or equivalent unless it is sufficiently characterized, reproducibly manufactured, appropriately dosed, and evaluated with assays that the material does not invalidate. 11 , 46 , 54 , 71 , 109–114 The more complex the nanomedicine, the more critical this principle becomes. 11 , 46 , 111 , 112

## Regulatory Progress and Translational Considerations

Regulatory progress in nanomedicine has been substantial, but it has not taken the form of a single unified “nanomedicine law”. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115 Instead, both the United States and the European Union continue to regulate nanomedicines under existing medicinal-product frameworks, supplemented by product-specific guidance, reflection papers, quality expectations, and case-by-case scientific advice. 18 , 19 The FDA guidance for drug products containing nanomaterials explicitly states that the agency does not regard nanomaterial-containing products as inherently benign or harmful; rather, regulation is based on the specific characteristics of the product and its safety and effectiveness for the intended use. 18 In parallel, EMA’s 2025 horizon-scanning report states that there is still no dedicated EU legal framework for nanomedicines, and that these products are regulated under existing medicines legislation, complemented by EMA reflection papers and scientific-regulatory support mechanisms. 19

This regulatory position is important because it reflects both progress and constraint. On the one hand, nanomedicines are no longer treated as regulatory outliers; there is now accumulated experience with liposomes, iron-carbohydrate colloids, albumin-bound nanoparticles, lipid nanoparticle vaccines, micelles, and related complex products. On the other hand, the absence of a globally harmonized, nanomedicine-specific framework means that developers still face uncertainty regarding product classification, critical quality attributes, comparability requirements, and the level of evidence needed to support manufacturing changes or follow-on products. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115 EMA’s recent report identifies quality and manufacturing as key challenge areas, particularly robust characterization of particle properties, critical quality attributes, and control of scale-up, stability, and impurities. 19

### Current Regulatory Expectations for Nanomedicines

Current regulatory expectations increasingly center on a risk-based, product-specific approach. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 The FDA guidance for drug products containing nanomaterials includes specific recommendations spanning pharmaceutical quality/CMC, nonclinical studies, bioanalytical considerations, in vitro tests with human biomaterials, immunogenicity, and postmarket submissions. 18 This is an important sign of progress: nanoparticle-containing products are now expected to be supported by integrated evidence linking material properties, manufacturing controls, biological interaction, and clinical relevance rather than by generic claims of “nanotechnology-enabled” benefit. 6 , 18 , 42

In practical terms, regulators now expect developers to define the nanomaterial within the finished product, justify which physicochemical properties are critical to performance, and show how those properties relate to safety, identity, strength, quality, and purity. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 FDA specifically highlights the need to characterize attributes such as particle size distribution, structural features, surface properties, in vitro release, impurities, sterility, endotoxin levels, and pyrogenicity. 18 This expectation reflects a major maturation of the field: nanoparticle products are no longer viewed simply as formulations with a small size range, but as complex products whose clinically relevant behavior depends on multivariate material attributes. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42

The EU position is broadly similar, though expressed through a combination of legislation, reflection papers, and scientific advice pathways rather than one single nanomedicine guidance document. 19 , 42 EMA’s 2025 report emphasizes that nanomedicines are regulated under existing medicinal product rules, with support available through the Innovation Task Force, Scientific Advice Working Party, Quality Innovation Group, PRIME, and international collaborations such as the IPRP Nanomedicines Working Group. 19 This indicates meaningful institutional progress: although nanomedicine-specific legislation is lacking, regulatory infrastructure for early dialogue and product-specific assessment has clearly expanded. 19 , 42

### Safety-by-Design Approaches

One of the most important translational developments is the growing regulatory relevance of safety-by-design. 18 , 42 , 115 Historically, safety was often treated as a downstream hurdle that followed proof-of-concept efficacy. 42 , 115 In contemporary nanomedicine, this sequence is increasingly viewed as inadequate, because the same properties that drive efficacy also shape blood compatibility, immune recognition, biodistribution, degradation, and chronic retention. 18 , 42 , 115 Recent safe(r)-by-design guidance efforts for the nanotechnology industry reflect this shift by advocating earlier and more systematic incorporation of hazard reduction into material selection, product design, and lifecycle decision-making. 115

Regulatory-science literature in nanomedicine now aligns with this philosophy. 6 , 18 , 42 , 115 The FDA guidance repeatedly ties product quality to safety and effectiveness, while industry-focused reviews emphasize that nanomedicine development requires early identification of critical quality attributes and risk factors that may affect clinical performance. 6 , 18 , 42 In other words, safety-by-design in nanomedicine is no longer just an academic slogan; it is increasingly consistent with what regulators and manufacturers need in order to justify translation. 6 , 18 , 42 , 115

The practical meaning of safety-by-design is not complete elimination of biological interaction, which is often impossible and sometimes undesirable, but rational control of that interaction. This includes selecting degradable materials where long-term retention is a concern, minimizing complement-triggering surfaces, reducing free-drug leakage, designing appropriate release kinetics, and incorporating in vitro and in vivo assays that interrogate likely failure modes early enough to influence formulation decisions. 18 , 42 , 115 That perspective is now central to clinically serious nanomedicine development. 6 , 18 , 42 , 115 Safety-by-design also has practical industrial limits that should be acknowledged. Nanomedicine optimization is intrinsically multi-objective: reducing one liability can worsen another, as illustrated by strategies that prolong circulation but increase immune recognition after repeated exposure, or by cationic designs that improve endosomal escape while increasing membrane toxicity. In addition, formulation changes made during scale-up can shift critical quality attributes enough to invalidate an apparently optimized preclinical safety profile. For industry, safety-by-design is therefore most useful when it is implemented as a risk-based, iterative process linked to manufacturability, analytical comparability, and clinically meaningful performance rather than as an expectation that every theoretical hazard can be eliminated before development advances. 6 , 18 , 42 , 46 , 115

### Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) Challenges

CMC remains one of the most difficult and decisive areas in nanomedicine translation. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115 , 116 The FDA guidance explicitly devotes major sections to nanomaterial quality attributes, structural characterization, physicochemical characterization methods, dissolution or release testing, manufacturing process and in-process controls, excipient function and safety, stability, and postmarket CMC changes. 18 This structure alone reflects how heavily nanomedicine regulation now depends on quality science. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42

The core challenge is that nanomedicine quality is inherently multidimensional. 6 , 18 , 42 FDA notes that nanomaterial-containing products can be highly sensitive to process conditions and production scale, and that robust control strategies and process validation are essential because variability may be unpredictable and scale effects may be unknown. 18 The same guidance also notes that different shape or size distributions can become batch-consistency issues if they affect quality, safety, or efficacy, and that empty carriers or incompletely coated carriers may constitute impurities that need quantification. 18 These are unusually demanding expectations compared with many conventional products, but they are appropriate because nanomedicine performance is often tightly coupled to subtle structural heterogeneity. 6 , 18 , 42

Recent industry and regulatory reviews echo this point. 6 , 42 The 2024 industry perspective in Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences emphasizes the current complexity of nanomedicine drug products and the importance of deep analytical characterization and platform-specific understanding. 6 Similarly, regulatory reviews highlight the complexity of concerns for nanomedicines and gene-vaccine products, including product characterization and quality control. 42 Together, these sources show that CMC is not peripheral to nanomedicine translation; it is one of the principal determinants of whether preclinical and clinical safety evidence remains interpretable across development stages. 6 , 18 , 42

### Scale-up, Sterilization, Storage, and Stability

Scale-up remains a major translational bottleneck because nanoparticle properties are often process-dependent. 6 , 18 , 19 , 116 Mixing rate, shear environment, solvent removal, temperature, filtration, and fill-finish steps can all change size distribution, colloidal stability, surface presentation, free payload fraction, and impurity burden. 6 , 18 , 116 FDA explicitly states that changes in analytical methods, manufacturing process, scale, and manufacturing sites may make bridging from early development lots to commercial-scale lots difficult, and recommends retaining sufficient material from all batches to allow future analysis with updated or complementary methods. 18

Sterilization and microbial control are also unusually important in nanomedicine because the product itself may be sensitive to processes that would be routine for conventional dosage forms. 6 , 18 , 19 FDA specifically identifies sterility, endotoxin levels, and pyrogenicity among relevant quality attributes for nanomaterial-containing drug products. 18 This matters because sterilization methods such as filtration, heat, radiation, or aseptic processing may alter nanoparticle size, aggregation behavior, surface chemistry, or cargo integrity. Thus, for nanomedicines, sterilization is not merely a terminal processing requirement; it is a potential source of product transformation that must be built into formulation and process design. 6 , 18 , 19

Storage and stability are likewise more complex than in conventional small-molecule formulations. 6 , 18 , 19 , 116 FDA states that container closure suitability, storage conditions, shelf life, and in-use conditions must be supported by both chemical and physical stability data, and specifically highlights risks such as changes in size and size distribution, morphology, aggregation, surface charge, release rate, drug leakage, ligand loss, container interactions, and reconstitution behavior. 18 Recent review literature reinforces this point, emphasizing that nanocarrier stability directly affects biocompatibility, targeted delivery, therapeutic efficacy, and shelf life. 6 , 116 The translational implication is clear: stability is not just a logistics issue; it is a safety and performance issue. 6 , 18 , 19 , 116

### Post-Marketing Surveillance Considerations

Post-marketing surveillance is especially important for nanomedicines because pre-approval studies may not fully capture repeat-dose effects, rare immune reactions, long-term organ retention, manufacturing drift, or population-specific responses. 18 , 19 , 117 , 118 FDA’s nanomaterial guidance explicitly includes postmarket submissions within scope, and the agency separately states that postmarketing safety reporting requirements apply to marketed drug and biological products, including serious and unexpected adverse experiences from all sources. 18 , 118 EMA likewise states that monitoring the safety of a medicine once it is on the market is the cornerstone of pharmacovigilance and maintains extensive post-authorisation pharmacovigilance guidance. 19 , 117

For nanomedicine, post-marketing surveillance has several special roles. 18 , 19 , 117 , 118 First, it can detect adverse events that are strongly context-dependent, such as infusion reactions, accelerated blood clearance after repeated exposure, rare complement-mediated events, or long-latency organ effects. 18 , 117 , 118 Second, it can reveal whether real-world manufacturing changes, site transfers, or supply-chain adjustments alter the product’s safety profile over time. 6 , 18 , 19 , 117 Third, it is particularly important for complex or platform-like products, where prior exposure to related excipients or carriers may modify response. 18 , 117 , 118 In this sense, pharmacovigilance for nanomedicine is not only about routine adverse-event collection; it is also about lifecycle control of a complex material system. 18 , 19 , 117 , 118

The broader translational lesson is that nanomedicine regulation increasingly extends beyond approval into lifecycle management. Quality changes, formulation drift, stability problems, and rare safety signals may only become evident after wider clinical use. 6 , 18 , 19 , 117 , 118 Accordingly, post-authorisation pharmacovigilance, CMC comparability management, and real-world safety monitoring should be viewed as integral parts of nanomedicine development rather than as purely downstream obligations. 18 , 19 , 117 , 118

### Integrative Perspective

Regulatory progress in nanomedicine is therefore real but uneven. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115–118 Agencies now recognize that nanomedicines require deeper quality characterization, product-specific nonclinical evaluation, and close attention to process sensitivity, stability, and postmarket change management. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115 Early scientific advice pathways and risk-based evaluation frameworks have expanded. 18 , 19 , 42 At the same time, major challenges remain: no universal legal definition or dedicated framework exists across jurisdictions, CMC burdens are high, scale-up remains difficult, and post-approval surveillance remains especially important because clinically relevant liabilities may emerge only with broader use. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115–118

From a translational standpoint, the most important shift is conceptual. The field has moved away from viewing nanomedicine regulation as a novelty problem and toward treating it as a complex product quality-and-safety problem. That is a major advance. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115 It means the questions regulators now ask are more clinically relevant: Can the product be defined robustly? Can it be manufactured reproducibly? Are the critical attributes linked to safety and performance understood? Can the product remain stable and sterile across its lifecycle? Can postmarketing systems detect safety signals that preapproval studies may miss? These are the right questions for a mature nanomedicine field. 6 , 18 , 19 , 42 , 115–118 Although the FDA and European regulatory systems use different procedural architectures, their scientific expectations converge on the same core principles: product-specific characterization, identification of critical quality attributes, justified nonclinical testing, control of impurities and microbiological risk, stability across the product lifecycle, and evidence that manufacturing changes do not compromise safety or performance. The FDA expresses many of these expectations through dedicated nanomaterial-containing drug guidance, whereas the European framework relies more heavily on existing medicinal-product legislation, product-specific scientific advice, and specialized innovation pathways. This convergence supports international harmonization at the scientific level even in the absence of a single globally uniform legal definition of a nanomedicine. 18 , 19 , 42 Representative clinically established nanomedicines and the safety lessons that emerged from their use are summarized in Table 4 . ## Special Focus: Safety in Oncology and Inflammatory Nanomedicine

Disease context strongly conditions what “safe enough” means for a nanomedicine. A nanoparticle platform that is clinically acceptable in one indication may be unsuitable in another because the relevant exposure pattern, target biology, therapeutic window, and tolerance for adverse effects are different. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123 This principle is especially important in oncology, which has historically dominated nanomedicine development, and in inflammatory disease, which is emerging as another major application space for targeted and stimuli-responsive nanoparticles. 3 , 17 , 28 , 124–128 In both settings, nanoparticles are attractive because they may improve biodistribution, reduce free-drug exposure, and enable combination or image-guided treatment; however, in both settings, the same properties that create therapeutic opportunity can also create disease-specific safety liabilities. For this reason, oncology and inflammation deserve focused consideration as distinct translational ecosystems rather than being treated as generic examples of nanoparticle drug delivery. 3 , 15 , 17 , 28 , 123–128

### Why Oncology Dominates Nanomedicine Development

Oncology has remained the dominant arena for nanomedicine development because cancer therapy presents a convergence of problems that nanoparticles are, at least in principle, well suited to address: poor solubility of cytotoxic drugs, narrow therapeutic windows, severe off-target toxicity, the need for combination therapy, and the biological premium placed on spatial selectivity. 3 , 17 , 28 , 123 Cancer also offers a regulatory and clinical context in which some toxicity is acceptable if it is offset by meaningful gains in efficacy or reductions in severe conventional toxicities. 3 , 17 , 123 These features made oncology the earliest and most persistent proving ground for liposomes, albumin nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, inorganic theranostics, and, more recently, immuno-nanomedicines. 3 , 17 , 28 , 123

This dominance is visible in the clinical landscape. Recent reviews of clinical cancer nanomedicines emphasize that cancer remains the most mature therapeutic area for approved and late-stage nanoparticle products, and that many clinically successful nanomedicines in practice operate by altering pharmacokinetics and biodistribution rather than by achieving exquisitely selective tumor homing. 17 This is an important safety point. The clinical value of cancer nanomedicine has often come from reducing peak normal-tissue exposure, changing tissue partitioning, or enabling formulations that would otherwise be unusable, rather than from absolute elimination of off-target exposure. 3 , 17 , 123 Oncology therefore dominates nanomedicine not only because tumors are biologically interesting targets, but because the clinical need for safer handling of potent drugs is especially acute in cancer. 3 , 17 , 28 , 123

At the same time, oncology has exposed the limits of nanomedicine more clearly than any other field. Because cancer was the major translational test case, it also became the area in which the mismatch between preclinical targeting narratives and clinical delivery reality was most visible. Thus, oncology dominates nanomedicine development both because it offers the strongest rationale for nanoparticle use and because it has provided the clearest evidence that safety and efficacy must be assessed together rather than sequentially. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123

### Tumor Targeting versus Off-Target Toxicity

The core promise of oncology nanomedicine is the possibility of increasing tumor exposure while reducing normal-tissue toxicity. However, this balance is rarely absolute. In practice, most systemically administered nanomedicines still distribute predominantly to clearance organs such as liver and spleen, while tumor deposition is often modest and heterogeneous. Consequently, the relevant safety question is not whether nanoparticles can eliminate off-target exposure, but whether they can improve the therapeutic index enough to justify their complexity and residual organ burden. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123

This issue is particularly important because tumor targeting and off-target toxicity are mechanistically coupled. Features that prolong circulation may increase opportunities for tumor accumulation but also extend exposure of blood-facing immune pathways and clearance organs. Surface chemistries that enhance cellular uptake may promote tumor-cell internalization but can also increase membrane disruption, protein adsorption, and inflammatory signaling in healthy tissues. 3 , 15 , 123 Similarly, active targeting ligands may increase binding to selected tumor-associated receptors, but they can also increase nonspecific uptake in organs expressing related epitopes or intensify immunogenic complexity. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123

Recent translational frameworks emphasize that clinically relevant cancer nanomedicines must be judged by whether the nanoparticle produces a meaningful net safety gain, not by whether it simply reaches tumors more than free drug does in preclinical models. 15 , 17 This distinction is crucial. A tumor-targeting claim is insufficient if the same formulation also produces chronic hepatosplenic burden, infusion-related reactions, or unpredictable repeat-dose clearance. In oncology, where background toxicity of conventional therapy is often already high, nanomedicines are valuable when they reduce the most dose-limiting or life-altering adverse effects without introducing new liabilities that offset the gain. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123

### EPR Effect Limitations and Safety Implications

Few concepts have shaped cancer nanomedicine more deeply than the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect. The EPR framework provided a persuasive mechanistic basis for passive tumor targeting and justified decades of work on long-circulating nanoparticles. However, the contemporary literature is unequivocal that EPR is highly heterogeneous across tumor types, anatomical sites, disease stages, and species, and that its magnitude in human cancers is often overestimated relative to rodent models. 3 , 15 , 123 Reviews on the tumor EPR effect now emphasize its limitations, heterogeneity, and the need for alternatives or patient-selection strategies rather than universal reliance on passive accumulation. 15

This has important safety implications. If tumor accumulation is inconsistent or modest, then the ratio between intended and unintended exposure becomes less favorable. In other words, weak or heterogeneous EPR does not merely reduce efficacy; it can actively worsen the benefit-risk balance by leaving substantial normal-organ exposure in place while failing to generate sufficient tumor benefit. 3 , 17 , 123 A nanomedicine that accumulates mainly in liver and spleen but only minimally in tumor is not simply inefficient. It may represent avoidable off-target burden without commensurate therapeutic value. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123

The limitations of EPR also affect clinical trial design and patient selection. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123 Broad enrollment of heterogeneous tumor populations without regard to vascular phenotype, stromal barrier properties, inflammatory status, or metastatic site may dilute both efficacy and safety signals. 3 , 15 , 123 This is one reason why recent translational perspectives in cancer nanomedicine increasingly advocate imaging-based pharmacology, biomarker-guided stratification, and more realistic definitions of target engagement. 15 , 17 Safety in this context cannot be divorced from delivery realism: a nanoparticle is safer in a clinically meaningful sense when it reduces normal-tissue harm while achieving enough target-site activity to justify exposure. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123 Quantitative interpretation of tumor delivery also illustrates why apparently contradictory nanomedicine findings must be examined carefully. A widely cited analysis of 117 preclinical studies estimated that a median of approximately 0.7% of the injected nanoparticle dose reached solid tumors. 129 A subsequent pharmacokinetic reanalysis showed that conclusions can change when delivery is evaluated using conventional exposure metrics rather than percentage of injected dose alone, emphasizing that absolute tumor deposition, tumor-to-plasma exposure, and pharmacokinetic benefit are related but non-equivalent measures. 130 These studies should not be treated as mutually exclusive; together they demonstrate that low absolute tumor accumulation can coexist with pharmacologically meaningful exposure in selected settings, while also reinforcing that passive targeting is not a universal mechanism of clinical selectivity.

### Combination Nanotherapies and Theranostics in Oncology

Cancer is also the disease area in which combination nanotherapies and theranostic nanomedicines have been pursued most intensively. The rationale is compelling. Tumors are biologically heterogeneous and often require multimodal intervention, whether chemotherapy plus chemosensitization, immunotherapy plus local tumor modulation, or treatment plus real-time imaging. 7 , 17 , 28 , 131 Nanoparticles can, in principle, synchronize pharmacokinetics, co-localize agents that would otherwise distribute differently, and integrate imaging and treatment into a single platform. 7 , 17 , 131

Recent analysis of multi-drug cancer nanomedicine indicates that co-formulated combination nanotherapies can provide therapeutic advantages in preclinical models, particularly when two agents are delivered in the same formulation rather than in separate nanoformulations. 131 From a safety perspective, this can be beneficial because coordinated delivery may reduce the need for higher systemic doses of each agent individually and may flatten unfavorable exposure peaks. 17 , 131 However, combination nanotherapies also increase complexity. They make it harder to control release hierarchy, interpret toxicity attribution, define critical quality attributes, and establish comparability across batches. Thus, while combination nanomedicine may improve efficacy and sometimes safety, it also raises the threshold for robust translational evaluation. 15 , 17 , 131

The same is true for theranostic nanoparticles. Radiolabeled and multimodal nanoparticles can support image-guided treatment, biodistribution monitoring, and patient stratification, all of which may improve safety by identifying poor accumulators early and avoiding futile or harmful exposure. Yet theranostic systems also add material and regulatory complexity, and the imaging component must provide clinically actionable value rather than simply technological appeal. 7 , 17 In oncology, therefore, the safety case for combination and theranostic nanomedicines depends on showing that added complexity produces a real gain in therapeutic precision or toxicity reduction, not merely a richer platform design. 7 , 17 , 131

### Balancing Efficacy and Safety in Cancer Applications

The central challenge in oncology nanomedicine is to balance efficacy and safety under conditions where neither can be considered in isolation. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123 Cancer patients may accept substantial toxicity if benefit is strong, but this does not reduce the need for rigorous nanosafety science. Rather, it increases the importance of identifying which toxicities are acceptable, predictable, and manageable, and which represent avoidable platform liabilities. A clinically meaningful cancer nanomedicine is therefore not one that is “nontoxic,” but one that improves the overall therapeutic index relative to available alternatives. 3 , 17 , 123

This balance is especially delicate in contemporary oncology, where nanomedicines increasingly intersect with immunotherapy, radiotherapy, and precision oncology. 3 , 7 , 17 A carrier that is acceptable in short-course cytotoxic therapy may not be acceptable when repeated chronically as part of immune modulation. Likewise, a formulation with favorable tumor imaging properties may still be problematic if it accumulates persistently in liver or spleen or perturbs innate immune function in ways that compromise combination regimens. 3 , 7 , 15 , 17 , 123 This is why recent translational frameworks emphasize early integration of manufacturability, stability, biodistribution realism, efficacy, and toxicity rather than sequential optimization. 17

The most defensible future direction for oncology nanomedicine is therefore selective ambition. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123 Nanoparticles should be pursued where they solve clinically meaningful problems that conventional formulations do not solve well—such as reducing severe normal-tissue toxicity, enabling otherwise impossible combination regimens, or providing image-guided selection of likely responders. 3 , 7 , 15 , 17 , 123 , 131 When such gains are marginal or uncertain, nanoparticle complexity may not be justified. In oncology more than any other indication, the safety value of nanomedicine must be judged by the degree to which it produces a better clinical bargain, not merely a more sophisticated formulation. 3 , 15 , 17 , 123

### Special Focus: Safety in Inflammatory Nanomedicine

Inflammatory diseases are becoming an increasingly important frontier for nanomedicine because they share several features that favor targeted drug delivery: localized vascular dysfunction, activated immune-cell populations, diseased tissue microenvironments with altered pH or redox state, and major limitations of conventional systemic therapy such as broad immunosuppression, poor tissue selectivity, and cumulative toxicity. 28 , 124–128 Recent reviews emphasize that nanotechnology is opening new possibilities for the treatment and diagnosis of inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disorders, atherosclerosis, and refractory inflammation-related conditions. From a safety perspective, this shift is highly significant because inflammatory disorders often require chronic or recurrent treatment, making long-term tolerability, immune compatibility, and persistence more important than in many short-course oncologic applications. 28 , 124–128

### Why Inflammatory Disease Is an Attractive but Safety-Sensitive Target

Inflammatory disease is attractive for nanomedicine because conventional anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory drugs often have limited site selectivity and substantial systemic adverse effects. Nanoparticles offer the possibility of concentrating therapy at inflamed tissues, improving local bioavailability, protecting fragile payloads, and exploiting disease-associated cues such as reactive oxygen species, enzyme activity, altered mucus layers, or local permeability changes. 28 , 124–128 This is particularly evident in inflammatory bowel disease, where nanoparticle systems have been developed to target inflamed intestinal epithelium, inflammatory immune cells, and locally altered luminal or mucosal microenvironments. 126

However, inflammation is also a uniquely safety-sensitive target because the disease itself modifies the biological environment that nanoparticles encounter. Inflammatory states alter plasma proteins, vascular permeability, macrophage activation, cytokine tone, and tissue barrier properties, all of which can change protein corona formation, immune recognition, cellular uptake, and organ distribution. As a result, a nanoparticle that appears benign in healthy models may behave differently in inflammatory disease because the host biology is altered by the indication itself. 124 , 125 , 127 , 128 This means that safety in inflammatory nanomedicine must be assessed in disease-relevant contexts rather than inferred from healthy systems alone. 28 , 124 , 125 , 127 , 128

### Inflamed-Tissue Targeting versus Off-Target Immunosuppression

The therapeutic logic of inflammatory nanomedicine is to increase local activity while decreasing systemic immunosuppression or organ toxicity. In principle, targeted nanocarriers can deliver corticosteroids, biologics, siRNA, antioxidants, or other immune-modulating agents preferentially to diseased tissues, thereby lowering total systemic exposure. This can be a major safety advantage over conventional formulations, especially in diseases where long-term systemic therapy causes infection risk, metabolic toxicity, endocrine complications, or generalized immune suppression. 28 , 124–128

Yet the same logic creates specific risks. In inflammatory disease, off-target effects do not only mean accumulation in liver or spleen; they also mean unintended modulation of immune function in tissues not meant to be treated. 28 , 124–128 A nanoparticle carrying an anti-inflammatory payload may reduce disease-site inflammation while also suppressing protective host responses elsewhere, or it may alter macrophage and dendritic-cell behavior in ways that change infection susceptibility. 124 , 125 , 127 , 128 Thus, “targeting inflammation” is not automatically equivalent to improving safety. It improves safety only when the formulation materially reduces nonspecific immune perturbation relative to standard therapy. 28 , 124–128

This balance is particularly important in chronic inflammatory disease, where repeated dosing is common. 124 , 126–128 Even a modest amount of unintended immune activation, anti-carrier immunogenicity, or organ retention may become clinically relevant over time. For this reason, inflammatory nanomedicine requires especially careful assessment of repeat-dose tolerance, cytokine perturbation, macrophage interaction, and long-term clearance. 28 , 124–128

### Disease-Associated Permeability in Inflammation: Opportunity and Limitation

Inflamed tissues often exhibit increased vascular permeability, altered epithelial barriers, and local retention phenomena that conceptually resemble, but are not identical to, the EPR effect discussed in oncology. 124 , 126–128 In diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease or inflamed joints, these barrier alterations can be exploited to improve nanoparticle localization. 124 , 126 This creates an important therapeutic opportunity: nanoparticles may accumulate preferentially in diseased tissue even without highly elaborate targeting ligands. 124 , 126 , 128

However, the safety lesson from oncology applies here as well. Disease-associated permeability is heterogeneous, dynamic, and often unpredictable. 124 , 126–128 If inflammatory targeting is weak or variable, then nanoparticles may still distribute primarily to liver, spleen, or other nontarget tissues, leaving patients exposed to both carrier burden and payload-related toxicity without sufficient site-specific benefit. 28 , 124–128 In other words, the existence of an inflamed microenvironment does not guarantee safe or efficient targeting. It simply creates a potential advantage that must be demonstrated under realistic disease conditions. 124 , 126–128

Furthermore, in inflammatory disease, increased permeability may coexist with tissue fragility. 124 , 126–128 A nanoparticle that penetrates inflamed tissue effectively may also aggravate barrier dysfunction, oxidative stress, or local immune-cell activation if its surface chemistry or degradation behavior is unfavorable. 124 , 127 , 128 This is especially relevant in mucosal diseases such as IBD, where a formulation intended to improve local therapy may also interact directly with compromised epithelial barriers and microbiota-associated environments. 126 Thus, disease-associated targeting in inflammation is simultaneously a delivery opportunity and a safety challenge. 28 , 124–128

### Combination Nanotherapies and Theranostics in Inflammation

Combination approaches are also relevant in inflammatory nanomedicine, though they are often less emphasized than in oncology. Chronic inflammatory diseases frequently involve overlapping pathways—oxidative stress, macrophage activation, cytokine dysregulation, endothelial activation, and tissue remodeling—so there is a strong rationale for carriers that deliver more than one therapeutic modality or that integrate treatment with diagnostic readouts. 124 , 125 , 127 , 128 Nanotheranostic strategies for inflammation are being developed to combine imaging of inflammatory lesions with local drug release or responsive treatment activation. 28 , 127

From a safety standpoint, these approaches offer the possibility of better patient selection and response monitoring, which may reduce unnecessary exposure. For example, imaging-guided identification of highly inflamed lesions or nanoprobes that report inflammatory status could help determine when and where a therapeutic nanoparticle is likely to be beneficial. 28 , 127 At the same time, adding imaging or multiple payloads increases formulation complexity and may introduce new sources of immunogenicity, stability problems, or off-target accumulation. As in oncology, the safety benefit of combination and theranostic inflammation nanomedicine therefore depends on whether the added complexity produces actionable precision rather than technological ornamentation. 28 , 127

### Balancing Efficacy and Safety in Inflammatory Applications

The safety calculus in inflammatory nanomedicine differs from oncology because many inflammatory diseases require long-term management rather than short-course intervention. 28 , 124–128 Consequently, tolerability thresholds are often stricter. A formulation that would be acceptable in advanced cancer may not be acceptable in chronic inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or atherosclerosis if it causes persistent organ retention, cumulative immunogenicity, or repeated infusion-related risk. 124 , 126–128 This means that the bar for safety in inflammatory nanomedicine is, in some respects, higher than in oncology even when the payload itself is less intrinsically toxic. 28 , 124–128

For inflammatory diseases, the most promising nanomedicines are likely to be those that combine local or cell-selective delivery with clear advantages in long-term safety—such as reduced systemic steroid burden, less generalized immunosuppression, lower dosing frequency, or better disease-site retention with rapid post-treatment clearance. 124 , 126–128 Recent inflammation-focused reviews also emphasize the importance of designing nanoparticles to minimize unintended inflammatory responses, which is especially relevant when the target indication is itself defined by immune dysregulation. 127 In this context, the best inflammatory nanomedicine is not merely one that reaches an inflamed tissue, but one that does so without amplifying unwanted immune activation or creating chronic carrier burden. 28 , 124–128

### Integrative Perspective

Taken together, oncology and inflammatory disease illustrate two complementary truths about nanomedicine safety. 3 , 7 , 15 , 17 , 28 , 123–128 , 131 In oncology, nanoparticles are justified when they materially improve the therapeutic index of potent therapies, even if some toxicity remains. 3 , 7 , 15 , 17 , 123 , 131 In inflammatory disease, nanoparticles are attractive when they reduce systemic exposure and chronic toxicity relative to long-term conventional treatment, but the tolerability bar is often higher because treatment may be prolonged. 28 , 124–128 In both cases, the central challenge is the same: target-site delivery must be sufficient to justify residual off-target exposure. 3 , 7 , 15 , 17 , 28 , 123–128 , 131

These indications also demonstrate that safety is not a platform-intrinsic label. It is a disease-specific, exposure-specific, and patient-specific outcome. A nanocarrier that is acceptably safe in cancer may be too reactogenic or persistent for chronic inflammatory disease, while a formulation optimized for long-term inflammatory treatment may not deliver sufficient intensity for oncologic use. For this reason, disease-focused nanosafety should become a standard feature of translational nanomedicine development rather than a late interpretive exercise. The future of safer nanomedicine will depend not only on better carriers, but on better alignment between platform behavior and disease-specific safety requirements. 3 , 7 , 15 , 17 , 28 , 123–128 , 131

## Emerging Strategies to Enhance Safety

The next phase of nanosafety is increasingly being shaped by strategies that do not merely mitigate toxicity after formulation, but attempt to predict, personalize, and design out risk earlier in development. This shift reflects a broader maturation of nanomedicine: safety is no longer viewed only as a downstream toxicology requirement, but as a design variable linked to patient heterogeneity, formulation architecture, computational prediction, and lifecycle control. Emerging approaches with particular relevance to safety include personalized nanomedicine and patient stratification, AI-assisted nanomaterial design, predictive toxicology and digital-twin frameworks, safer-by-design methodologies, transient or stimuli-responsive nanoplatforms, and exosome-inspired or other biologically derived nanoparticles. 115 , 132–138

### Personalized Nanomedicine and Patient Stratification

Personalized nanomedicine has emerged from the recognition that nanoparticle behavior is not uniform across patients. Tumor heterogeneity, inflammatory status, vascular permeability, immune tone, organ function, and biomarker expression can all change nanoparticle accumulation, intracellular uptake, and adverse-event profiles. Recent reviews of precision nanomedicine in oncology emphasize that nanoplatforms are increasingly being linked to molecular diagnostics, imaging, and biomarker-informed treatment selection, with the goal of improving efficacy while reducing unnecessary exposure in patients unlikely to benefit. 132 From a safety perspective, this is important because many nanomedicines fail not because the platform is universally unsafe, but because the right patient population has not been identified in advance.

Patient stratification is therefore becoming a safety tool as much as an efficacy tool. If biomarkers, imaging phenotypes, or omics readouts can identify patients with favorable delivery conditions or lower risk of immune and organ-specific toxicity, nanomedicine can move away from empiric “one-platform-for-all” dosing and toward more selective use. This strategy is still early in clinical implementation, but the conceptual shift is already clear: safer nanomedicine will likely depend not only on better materials, but also on better matching of materials to biological subpopulations. 132

### AI-Assisted Nanomaterial Design

Artificial intelligence and machine learning are increasingly being used to optimize nanoparticle composition, size, charge, ligand density, and formulation process parameters. Recent reviews specifically focused on AI and nanomedicine describe this convergence as a way to connect nanoparticle design variables with biological performance, toxicological datasets, and patient-level information. 133 In parallel, work in nanotoxicology has emphasized that AI can help identify patterns in large, heterogeneous datasets that are difficult to resolve through conventional statistical methods alone, thereby improving prediction of biocompatibility and hazard profiles. 135 , 136

The safety relevance of AI-assisted design is substantial. Instead of synthesizing and testing large numbers of candidates experimentally, AI models can help prioritize formulations less likely to aggregate, trigger immune activation, or exhibit undesirable biodistribution. Machine learning models are also being developed specifically for nanoparticle toxicity prediction, using physicochemical descriptors and biological data to estimate cellular or dynamic toxicity outcomes. 134 Although model generalizability remains limited by data quality and standardization, the field is clearly moving toward computational preselection of safer formulation space rather than purely trial-and-error development. 133–136 Current limitations remain substantial, however. Many available datasets are small, heterogeneous, incompletely standardized, and biased toward positive experimental results; descriptors are not always measured under biologically comparable conditions; external validation is uncommon; and models trained on one nanoparticle family may not extrapolate reliably to another. For translational use, predictive performance must therefore be accompanied by transparent feature definition, uncertainty estimation, prospective validation, and experimentally testable mechanistic interpretation. 108 , 133–136

### Predictive Toxicology and Digital Twins

Predictive toxicology is evolving from relatively simple quantitative structure–activity approaches toward multiscale computational frameworks that integrate physicochemical data, mechanistic biology, and exposure modeling. In nanotoxicology, recent analyses argue that AI can reduce dependence on extensive in vitro and in vivo testing by improving pattern recognition, mechanistic inference, and early identification of hazardous nanomaterials. 135 This does not eliminate experimental toxicology, but it can make it more focused and hypothesis-driven.

Digital twins are a more ambitious extension of this logic. In healthcare broadly, digital twins are being developed as virtual, data-updated representations of patients, organs, or disease processes that support prediction and personalization. 137 In nanomedicine, the concept remains largely early-stage and partly aspirational, but recent reviews explicitly identify digital twins as a future route to simulate nanoparticle behavior in patient-specific biological environments, including treatment response and delivery performance. 133 , 135 , 137 For safety, the long-term promise is considerable: digital twins could eventually help forecast organ exposure, repeat-dose behavior, or patient-specific adverse-event risk before actual administration. At present, however, this remains more a strategic direction than a clinically established capability in nanomedicine. 133 , 135 , 137

### Safer-by-Design Frameworks

Safer-by-design has become one of the most influential emerging frameworks because it formalizes the idea that hazard reduction should begin at the earliest design stages. The NanoImpact guidelines developed from the NanoReg2 experience describe safe(r)-by-design as an iterative process that balances functionality, human health and safety, environmental impact, and industrial feasibility from the start of innovation rather than after product definition. 115 The framework is built around three pillars: safer materials and products, safer use and end-of-life, and safer industrial production. 115

For medical nanoparticles, the importance of safer-by-design lies in its operational effect. It encourages developers to treat degradability, immune compatibility, aggregation liability, impurity control, and process safety as core design parameters rather than as downstream validation problems. This approach also aligns with the broader movement in nanotechnology policy toward early integration of safety considerations into research and development strategies. 115 In practice, its success will depend on whether predictive assays, standardized datasets, and translational decision criteria become strong enough to guide real formulation choices. Even so, safer-by-design has already changed the way advanced nanomedicines are conceptually developed. 115 , 135

### Stimuli-Responsive and Transient Nanoplatforms

Stimuli-responsive and transient nanoplatforms are emerging as safety-enhancing strategies because they aim to reduce nonspecific exposure in both space and time. Instead of remaining indefinitely stable or releasing payload constitutively, these systems are designed to respond to endogenous signals such as pH, redox gradients, enzymes, or reactive oxygen species, or to exogenous triggers such as light, ultrasound, heat, or magnetic fields. The safety logic is straightforward: if a nanoparticle remains relatively inert during circulation but disassembles, degrades, or activates only in the target microenvironment, off-target toxicity and long-term retention may be reduced. 138

Recent work on biodegradable, stimuli-responsive silica nanoparticles illustrates this trend clearly. That review emphasizes that poor degradability and nonspecific accumulation have limited broader clinical translation of silica-based systems and argues that multi-stimuli-responsive biodegradable designs can improve in vivo degradation and clearance under pathological conditions. 138 More broadly, transient nanoplatforms represent an important conceptual shift away from persistent multifunctional carriers toward time-limited therapeutic systems whose clinical value depends partly on controlled disappearance after use. 138

### Exosome-Inspired and Biologically Derived Nanoparticles

Biologically derived nanoparticles, especially extracellular vesicles and exosome-inspired systems, have attracted intense interest because they offer an alternative to fully synthetic carriers at the nano–bio interface. Recent high-impact reviews describe exosomes as promising next-generation delivery systems with advantages that may include tissue selectivity, barrier crossing, and favorable safety-related properties compared with some synthetic nanocarriers, while also emphasizing that manufacturing, purity, cargo heterogeneity, and standardization remain major obstacles. 139

Plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles have further expanded this area. A 2024 review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences describes PELNs as membranous vesicles containing proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids, and highlights their abundant sources, high yields, and reportedly low risk of immunogenicity in vivo as reasons for growing biomedical interest. 140 These properties make biologically derived particles attractive as potentially lower-immunogenic and more biodegradable delivery systems, although the field still faces substantial challenges in isolation, characterization, compositional consistency, and mechanism-of-action definition. 139 , 140 Thus, exosome-inspired platforms are promising for safety enhancement, but they are not yet a solved translational problem; their main current value lies in offering a biologically grounded template for the next generation of safer delivery systems. 139 , 140

### Integrative Perspective

Taken together, these emerging strategies indicate that the future of nanoparticle safety will likely depend on integration rather than on any single material innovation. Personalized nanomedicine links safety to patient biology. AI-assisted design and predictive toxicology shift hazard recognition upstream. Digital twins point toward virtual pretesting of patient-specific exposure and response. Safer-by-design embeds risk reduction into innovation itself. Stimuli-responsive and transient platforms reduce unnecessary persistence and premature activity. Biologically derived nanoparticles attempt to solve safety at the interface level by learning from natural vesicle systems. 115 , 132–140

The common direction across all of these approaches is clear: safer nanomedicine will increasingly be predictive, adaptive, and biologically informed. The main challenge now is to convert these emerging strategies from promising conceptual advances into standardized, manufacturable, and clinically validated safety gains.

## Critical Objectives for the Next Decade

If the first generation of nanomedicine was defined by proof-of-concept delivery and the second by early clinical translation, the next decade must be defined by predictability, comparability, and clinical relevance. The principal obstacles to safer nanomedicine are no longer merely conceptual. They are now well recognized: fragmented testing pipelines, incomplete long-term fate data, insufficiently predictive models, limited mechanistic resolution of immunotoxicity, poor reporting consistency, late separation of efficacy from safety, and underdeveloped attention to equity, ethics, and environmental consequences. 9 , 19 , 141 , 142 Recent translational, standards, and nanosafety frameworks increasingly converge on the view that future progress will depend less on inventing ever more complex nanoplatforms and more on building a disciplined evidence infrastructure that can determine which nanomedicines are truly safe, for whom, and under what conditions. 9 , 19 , 141 , 142 The resulting iterative safety-by-design lifecycle is summarized in Figure 4 . ### Harmonized Safety Testing Pipelines

A primary objective for the next decade is the development of harmonized safety testing pipelines that link nanoparticle characterization, exposure definition, in vitro screening, advanced non-animal models, in vivo confirmation where needed, and mechanism-aware data integration. 141–143 Current nanosafety assessment remains too fragmented across laboratories, product classes, and jurisdictions. 141 , 143 Recent standardization-focused reviews explicitly call for global efforts to overcome inconsistency in nanotoxicology workflows, while broader healthcare nanotechnology reviews identify the lack of harmonized safety and risk-assessment frameworks as a continuing translational bottleneck. 141 , 143

What is needed is not a single rigid test battery for all nanomedicines, but a tiered, harmonized logic. 141 , 143 Such pipelines should define which core assays are required for all platforms, which are route- or material-specific, how dose and exposure should be normalized, and what physicochemical descriptors must accompany every safety result. 141 , 143 Harmonization should also include assay interference controls, reference materials where feasible, standardized biological media conditions, and predefined criteria for escalating from simple in vitro testing to more complex models. 141–143 Without this kind of structured pipeline, nanosafety data will remain difficult to compare across studies and difficult to use in regulatory decision-making. 141 , 143

### Better Long-Term Fate and Clearance Studies

A second critical objective is much stronger evidence on long-term fate, degradation, and clearance. Short-term tolerability is not enough for many nanomedicines, especially those intended for repeated dosing, chronic diseases, imaging follow-up, or containing inorganic or slowly degradable components. 19 , 141 Recent healthcare nanotechnology reviews continue to emphasize environmental and biological persistence as major unresolved safety issues, and EMA’s 2025 horizon-scanning report highlights the importance of understanding product quality, biodistribution, and long-term behavior for nanotechnology-based medicinal products. 19 , 141

The field needs longitudinal studies that distinguish the fate of the intact nanoparticle from that of released drug, degradation fragments, dissolved ions, or shed coatings. 19 , 107 , 141 It also needs organ-resolved persistence studies in liver, spleen, kidney, lung, brain, placenta where relevant, and clearance compartments under repeated-dose conditions. 19 , 141 Ideally, these studies should combine imaging, bioanalytical chemistry, histopathology, and mechanistic biomarkers rather than relying on terminal bulk accumulation alone. 19 , 107 , 141 The central goal is to move from static biodistribution snapshots to true fate mapping across clinically relevant timescales. 19 , 141

### Clinically Relevant Animal and Non-Animal Models

A third priority is the development and validation of clinically relevant animal and non-animal models. 19 , 142 , 144 Preclinical nanomedicine has long been constrained by model systems that overestimate delivery success or fail to represent human immune diversity, vascular physiology, barrier function, and chronic disease states. 17 , 142 At the same time, the field is under growing scientific and ethical pressure to reduce unnecessary animal use and adopt more predictive non-animal methodologies. 142 , 144 EFSA’s 2024 review of new approach methodologies for nanomaterials highlights nano-specific frameworks for non-animal testing, while WHO’s draft 3Rs-oriented guidance on phasing out certain animal-derived quality tests reflects a wider movement toward scientifically and ethically improved methods. 142 , 144

The next decade should not frame animal and non-animal approaches as adversarial alternatives. The real objective is a fit-for-purpose model ecosystem. This includes disease-relevant rodent and non-rodent models when whole-body pharmacology is essential, but also barrier chips, immune-competent organoids, microphysiological systems, and exposure-aware 3D platforms for questions involving BBB transport, placental passage, pulmonary deposition, or immune-cell cross-talk. 142 , 144 The highest priority should be given to models that improve human predictivity, not merely experimental convenience. 142 , 144

### Greater Mechanistic Understanding of Immunotoxicity

Among all unresolved safety domains, immunotoxicity remains one of the most urgent. Nanoparticles interact with complement, antibodies, coagulation pathways, macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells, inflammasomes, and innate pattern-recognition systems in ways that are often context-dependent and still incompletely predictable. 9 , 145 , 146 A 2025 review on mechanistic paradigms of nanoparticle immunotoxicity and a 2025 Biochemical Pharmacology article on charting new frontiers in nanoparticle immunotoxicity both underscore that current assessment still relies too heavily on conventional frameworks that were not designed around the distinctive immune interactions of nanoscale materials. 145 , 146 Earlier immunotoxicity reviews similarly emphasize the importance of susceptible populations and disease-state effects. 9

The key objective is not just to catalog immune adverse events, but to build mechanistic maps that link particle attributes to specific immune pathways and then to clinically relevant outcomes such as infusion reactions, accelerated blood clearance, cytokine patterns, macrophage polarization, or chronic inflammatory burden. 9 , 145 , 146 This requires better immune-competent model systems, more standardized complement and cytokine testing, repeated-exposure study designs, and greater use of systems immunology. It also requires recognizing that immunotoxicity is shaped by host biology, including inflammation, prior exposure history, and patient-specific protein corona formation. 9 , 145 , 146

### Standard Reporting Guidelines

A fifth objective is the establishment and enforcement of standard reporting guidelines. The nanomedicine literature still suffers from incomplete reporting of synthesis conditions, physicochemical characterization, biological media composition, dose metrics, assay interference controls, and batch identity. 141 , 143 This undermines reproducibility, meta-analysis, regulatory interpretation, and model building. Standardization-oriented reviews in nanotoxicology explicitly identify this gap, and the broader reproducibility literature in nanomedicine has made the same point repeatedly. 141 , 143

The next decade should produce community-accepted minimum reporting standards covering at least the following: critical material attributes, dispersion protocol, storage and age of material, exposure conditions, dose metric rationale, interference controls, biological model description, statistical treatment, and batch identifiers. 141 , 143 Reporting standards should also accommodate advanced datasets such as omics, imaging, and AI-ready descriptors. 107 , 141 , 143 Without such infrastructure, it will remain difficult to distinguish true biological variability from avoidable methodological noise. 141 , 143

### Integration of Efficacy and Safety Early in Design

Another essential objective is the early integration of efficacy and safety in nanoparticle design. 9 , 17 , 147 Too much nanomedicine development still optimizes payload loading, targeting, or in vitro potency first and then evaluates safety later. 17 , 147 This sequence is often misleading because the very same attributes that increase efficacy may also increase hemolysis, complement activation, off-target accumulation, or chronic organ burden. 9 , 17 , 147 The Nature Nanotechnology “DELIVER” framework emphasizes that manufacturability, stability, release behavior, reproducibility, and therapeutic-index improvement should be assessed early enough to determine whether development should proceed. 17

In the next decade, the field should normalize dual-optimization workflows in which efficacy and safety are treated as co-primary design outcomes. That means designing screening cascades in which biodistribution realism, blood compatibility, degradation fate, and immune compatibility are evaluated alongside potency and target engagement from the earliest stages. 9 , 17 , 147 It also means abandoning platforms whose safety liabilities are not justified by a meaningful clinical advantage, even if they perform well in permissive proof-of-concept models. This is the practical meaning of mature translational nanomedicine. 17 , 147

### Equity, Ethics, and Environmental Considerations

The next decade must also expand the definition of nanosafety beyond individual-patient toxicology to include equity, ethics, and environmental responsibility. 141 , 148–150 The 2024 US National Nanotechnology Initiative EHS research strategy explicitly links nanotechnology research with environmental justice and health equity, and more recent ethical analyses emphasize social justice, public health, data governance, and responsible innovation as integral to nanosafety ecosystems. 148–150

For medical nanoparticles, equity means asking whether safer nanomedicines will be accessible only in highly resourced settings, whether patient stratification tools will work across diverse populations, and whether data used to train AI or predictive models adequately represent the populations who will receive these products. 148–150 Ethics includes informed consent in complex theranostic settings, privacy in data-rich personalized nanomedicine, and responsible communication of benefit versus uncertainty. 148 , 149 Environmental considerations include occupational exposure during manufacturing, lifecycle release of nanomaterials, disposal, persistence, and the broader ecological implications of scaled medical use. 141 , 150 A nanomedicine that is clinically effective but environmentally irresponsible or distributively unjust cannot be considered a fully successful safety achievement. 141 , 148–150

### Integrative Perspective

Taken together, these priorities define a clear agenda for the field. The next decade should aim for harmonized testing pipelines, deeper long-term fate studies, model systems with greater clinical relevance, mechanistically richer immunotoxicity science, enforceable reporting standards, early co-optimization of efficacy and safety, and explicit incorporation of equity, ethics, and environmental stewardship. None of these objectives is peripheral. They are the infrastructure required to turn nanosafety from a reactive screening exercise into a predictive translational discipline. 9 , 17 , 19 , 107 , 141–150

The most important shift is strategic rather than merely technical. Nanomedicine no longer needs only better particles; it needs better systems for deciding which particles deserve to become medicines. That is the central safety objective for the coming decade. 17 , 147
