The design of bioinspired wet adhesives has been largely motivated by marine organisms, such as mussels, sandcastle worms and barnacles, that have evolved effective adhesion strategies in saline, aqueous environments. Mussels secrete MFPs, which form liquid-like coacervates within the narrow secretion ducts of the mussel foot and subsequently undergo gelation into stable underwater adhesive layers in response to environmental cues such as pH, ionic strength, and metal ions [ 27 , 41 ]. For example, the Dopa-modified MFP5-derived polypeptide GK-16* exhibited pH-responsive liquid-to-gel transitions, with an almost 15-fold increase in adhesion force, from 1.64 mN/m (pH = 3) to ∼26 mN/m (pH = 7.4) ( Fig. 8 B) [ 40 ]. Similar principles exist in sandcastle worm cement, where oppositely charged, Dopa-rich proteins undergo complex coacervation to form liquid intermediates that subsequently transition into load-bearing adhesives through Dopa oxidation-mediated crosslinking and divalent metal ion coordination [ 17 , 181 , 206 ]. Traditional electrostatically driven complex coacervates are inherently sensitive to pH and ionic strength, which severely limits their stability and translational potential in complex physiological environments. To overcome this limitation, Yi et al. [ 205 ] constructed a barnacle-inspired simple coacervate system assembled from hydrophobically modified poly(propylene glycol) (PPG) polymers via hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, which remains stable across an extreme pH range (1-14) and under high ionic strength conditions (up to 1 M NaCl). By loading acrylic acid monomers and crosslinkers, the liquid coacervate precursor can undergo rapid in situ photocuring to form a robust adhesive hydrogel, achieving a strong adhesion strength of 479 kPa on porcine skin and enabling effective sealing of gastric perforations in a rat model. In particular, Cui et al. [ 74 ] engineered a fusion protein, TDP43 LC-Mfp5 (TLC-M), which underwent a time-dependent liquid-to-solid transition into dense amyloid nanofiber coatings at 4°C, whereas at 25°C it bypassed the liquid-like coacervate intermediate and assembled directly into sparse nanofibers ( Fig. 8 C). Quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation (QCM-D) measurements demonstrated that the liquid-like coacervate state exhibited lower interfacial energy (reflected by the elevated Δ D /Δ F ) and enhanced wetting on gold surfaces. Consequently, the coatings formed at 4°C achieved an adhesion force of ∼170 mN m −1 and an adhesion energy of ∼18 mJ m −2 , nearly one order of magnitude superior to the sparse coatings formed at 25°C.

Despite these advances, most coacervation-mediated bioinspired adhesives remain at the proof-of-concept stage, with studies primarily focusing on in vitro characterization of environmentally responsive phase transitions (e.g., pH, ionic strength, or temperature) and their associated adhesive and mechanical properties [ 27 , 40 , 41 , 207 ]. Translating these systems into biomedical applications remains challenging because physiological environments are substantially more complex than simplified experimental conditions, requiring precise spatiotemporal regulation of phase transitions while simultaneously maintaining robust wet adhesion, serum stability and biocompatibility.

### Tissue engineering scaffolds

In native tissues, structural integrity is maintained through mechanically resilient extracellular matrix (ECM) networks that provide load-bearing capacity while dynamically remodeling in response to cellular activity [ [208] , [209] , [210] , [211] ]. Elastin, a key structural protein of ECM, exemplifies this principle: its precursor, tropoelastin, undergoes LLPS to form liquid-like coacervates that subsequently transition into gel-like networks through covalent crosslinking, yielding a heterogeneous and cell-adaptable matrix to regulate cell spreading, proliferation, and mechanosensing [ 81 , [212] , [213] , [214] , [215] , [216] ]. Inspired by tropoelastin assembly, Xie et al. [ 142 ] developed a gelatin-based coacervate model with alternating hydrophobic motifs and photo-crosslinking groups. Its propensity for LLPS was enhanced by increasing hydrophobic valency, while light-induced covalent crosslinking enabled a liquid-to-gel transition into heterogeneous dynamic networks with stiff (∼150-200 kPa) and soft (< 50 kPa) domains, thereby promoting stem cell spreading ( Fig. 9 A). ELPs represent a class of genetically engineered polypeptides derived from repeat motifs of LCDs in tropoelastin. Most ELPs consist of pentapeptide repeats (VPGXG), where the guest residue X can be any amino acid except proline, enabling precise tuning of their LCST behavior [ 218 ]. However, ELPs are generally unable to independently form enough stable networks to provide mechanical support, which limits their application in tissue engineering. Therefore, they are typically combined with other motifs to introduce additional physical or chemical crosslinking. For example, by incorporating click-reactive molecules with different hydrophilicities [ 184 ], the LCST could be tuned over a range of 20-37°C, while simultaneously enabling subsequent covalent crosslinking to form hydrogel networks with tunable storage modulus ranging from 100 to 1000 Pa. Another example is provided by a double-hydrophobic ELP system, GPG, which mimics the domain architecture of native tropoelastin by incorporating glycine-rich hydrophobic terminal domains and a proline-rich hydrophobic central domain [ 217 ]. Upon heating to 45°C, the initially formed coacervates gradually transitioned from spherical particles into β-sheet-enriched fibrillar structures with diameters of 20-70 nm ( Fig. 9 B). The self-assembly into nanofibers makes it suitable as a scaffold for regenerative medicine.

Though liquid-like coacervates alone are generally insufficient as load-bearing scaffolds, their low interfacial tension, and wetting properties enable synergistic integration with high-strength reinforcing phases such as cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) [ 187 ] and cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) [ 186 ]. Such hybrid architectures yield bioinspired composite scaffolds that combine strength, stiffness, and toughness, highlighting their potential for applications such as bone tissue engineering [ 219 , 220 ].

Collectively, it is necessary to selectively utilize or coordinate phase-state characteristics according to application-specific functional requirements. For drug delivery, efficient cargo encapsulation, sustained cargo retention, controlled release, and physiological stability are important design considerations. Accordingly, liquid-like coacervates provide dynamic compartmentalization for efficient cargo loading, whereas phase transitions can be introduced to enhance cargo retention and physiological stability. For bioreactors, efficient compartmentalization, reactant enrichment, and sufficient molecular mobility are essential for maintaining catalytic efficiency. Accordingly, liquid-like coacervates provide confined yet dynamic reaction environments that concentrate reactants while permitting molecular diffusion, whereas excessive phase maturation may compromise catalytic activity. For bio-adhesion, interfacial wetting during application together with durable tissue retention is essential for robust adhesion. These functions can be achieved by combining the adaptive spreading of liquid-like coacervates with subsequent liquid-to-gel transitions that provide mechanical support. For tissue engineering, hydrated cell-supportive microenvironments, appropriate degradation, and mechanical support are important for tissue remodeling. Accordingly, gel-like coacervates provide hydrated viscoelastic networks that support cellular activities, whereas localized solid-like reinforcement can be incorporated to improve mechanical robustness when required.

## Summary and outlook

Biomolecular coacervation typically begins with LLPS-driven formation of metastable liquid-like coacervates and may subsequently proceed through post-LLPS phase transitions, including liquid-to-gel and liquid-to-solid transitions, thereby giving rise to gel-like or solid-like states with distinct material properties. Building upon the summarized phase-state characteristics and regulation strategies, we further highlight that the biomedical functions of coacervation-mediated materials can be achieved through the selective utilization or coordinated integration of diverse phase-state characteristics, as exemplified by drug delivery, bioreactors, bioinspired adhesion and tissue engineering scaffolds. Importantly, these phase-state characteristics are not universally advantageous but involve application-dependent trade-offs. For example, liquid-like coacervates provide dynamic molecular mobility, compartmentalization, and adaptive wetting, but generally exhibit limited structural stability and cargo retention. Gelation enhances structural integrity, physiological stability, and tissue retention, although excessive stabilization may compromise injectability and tissue remodeling. Likewise, localized solid-like reinforcement improves long-term mechanical robustness but may reduce degradability and biological compatibility.

Despite the rapid development of coacervation-mediated biomaterials, several challenges remain. 1) Existing molecular design principles—particularly those derived from IDP systems and sticker-spacer concepts—are most effective at predicting whether LLPS occurs, but provide less guidance for programming phase transitions toward gel-like or solid-like states [ 46 , 152 , 221 ]. 2) The mechanistic relationships linking molecular sequence, interaction lifetimes, mesoscale organization and macroscopic material properties remain insufficiently understood, thereby limiting the rational control of stiffness, stress relaxation, toughness and long-term stability required for load-bearing applications. 3) Translational challenges become particularly evident when coacervate materials are exposed to physiological environments and manufacturing constraints. For Dopa-based coacervates—widely explored for wet adhesion—the accelerated autoxidation under neutral-to-basic physiological conditions could lead to premature crosslinking and loss of wet-adhesion capacity, while the competitive adsorption of serum proteins further block DOPA-mediated interfacial binding. For naturally derived protein-based coacervates, concerns center on source-dependent impurities, batch-to-batch variability, and potential immunogenicity, while recombinant protein or polypeptide systems such as ELPs face additional manufacturing challenges associated with recombinant expression, downstream purification, and stringent control of molecular composition and purity. DNA-based coacervates present a distinct safety concern because sequence composition, chemical modification, and intracellular localization may influence innate immune recognition.

Looking forward, several directions deserve particular attention. 1) Molecular design. It will be important to move beyond canonical amino-acid-based design by integrating sequence engineering with residue modification, synthetic side chains and hybrid polymer architectures, thereby expanding the accessible interaction space and enabling more programmable phase behavior. Artificial intelligence and machine learning could further facilitate this process through two promising directions: context-dependent prediction of phase behavior by integrating sequence with environmental variables, and sequence-to-property prediction linking sequence, phase state, and material properties. Recently, Bae et al. developed a condition-aware machine-learning framework LLPSense, which integrates protein sequence features with multiple environmental variables to predict phase-separation propensity, while also enabling model-guided modulation of temperature-dependent phase behavior. However, its predictions deviate from experimental trends under highly concentrated salt conditions and remain insufficient ability to distinguish distinct material states [ 222 ]. Generative artificial intelligence has also been applied to design short condensate-forming sequences without reliance on long repetitive sequences, although their resulting material states and biophysical properties remain to be fully characterized [ 223 ]. 2) Mechanistic understanding. Further efforts are needed to establish predictive relationships linking intermolecular interactions, molecular conformational states, phase evolution and macroscopic material performance. In particular, a clearer understanding of how phase transitions influence interaction network, structural stability and macroscopic mechanical properties will be important for achieving more precise control over coacervate functions. 3) Application-oriented materials design. Future progress may benefit from broader materials-design principles from polymer chemistry and soft matter physics, including block architectures, supramolecular crosslinking, dynamic covalent chemistry and hierarchical assembly. Such approaches may expand the materials-design space of coacervation-mediated systems and enable broader applications.

Scheme 1 Biomolecular coacervation-mediated materials: phase states, phase transitions, and biomedical applications. Biomolecular coacervation initially forms liquid-like coacervates through LLPS, which may subsequently undergo liquid-to-gel or liquid-to-solid phase transitions to generate gel-like or solid-like states. These representative phase states provide distinct material characteristics that can be exploited for different biomedical applications, including drug delivery platforms, bioreactors, bioinspired adhesion, and tissue engineering scaffolds.
Fig. 2 (A) Classification of LLPS. Reproduced under the terms of the CC BY-NC 3.0 license [ 3 ]. Copyright 2021, Royal Society of Chemistry. (B) Molecular driving forces of LLPS.

Fig. 3 Biomolecular coacervate phase evolution. (A) Biomolecular coacervation is a non-equilibrium phase-evolution process driven by multiple weak intermolecular interactions and regulated by intrinsic composition and environmental factors. (B) Typical coacervate phase evolution pathways: from LLPS to liquid-to-gel or liquid-to-solid phase transitions.

Fig. 4 Schematic relative comparisons of liquid-like, gel-like, and solid-like states along a temporal evolution pathway. Liquid-like coacervates are dominated by transient interaction networks and exhibit high molecular mobility, as evidenced by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), together with loss-dominant viscoelastic behavior (G″ > G′) over the entire frequency range. Gel-like coacervates are characterized by a system-spanning (percolated) physical network formed by longer-lived intermolecular interactions. They exhibit reduced but retained molecular mobility, reflected by slow and incomplete FRAP recovery, and frequency-dependent mechanical responses, with G″ > G′ at low frequencies but G′ > G″ at high frequencies. Solid-like coacervates are stabilized by persistent interaction networks, resulting in negligible molecular mobility with little or no FRAP recovery and G′ ≫ G″ over the entire frequency range.

title: Recent Advances in Pathogenesis, Diagnosis and Integrated Traditional Chinese Medicine Therapy for Plasma Cell Mastitis
abstract: Plasma cell mastitis (PCM) is a predominant form of non-lactational mastitis with an increasing incidence worldwide. The condition is characterized by a complex pathogenesis, difficulties in differential diagnosis, and a high rate of recurrence, thereby presenting significant challenges in clinical management. Conventional Western medicine is limited by high postoperative recurrence, difficulty in distinguishing PCM from breast cancer, and unsatisfactory long-term efficacy of single anti-inflammatory or hormone therapy. Against these clinical bottlenecks, Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) shows unique advantages and accumulated extensive clinical experience for the treatment of PCM. This review systematically delineates the epidemiological characteristics and key pathophysiological mechanisms, including activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway, immune cell dysregulation, autoimmune responses, distinctive plasma cell infiltration, and diagnostic methodologies such as imaging techniques, histopathological examination as the diagnostic gold standard, and emerging biomarkers. In addition, the theoretical foundations, contemporary pharmacological mechanisms, and clinical applications of comprehensive TCM therapy for PCM are summarized. Evidence indicates that TCM interventions, guided by syndrome differentiation and targeting liver qi stagnation, phlegm-stasis congealing, and heat-toxin accumulation, exert therapeutic effects by modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, correcting immune dysfunction, and restoring the mammary gland microecological balance. Clinical trials have demonstrated that combining TCM with surgical procedures or western medical treatments significantly improves clinical outcomes, reduces inflammatory mediator levels, and lowers recurrence rates. However, there remains a need for standardization in TCM syndrome differentiation, therapeutic evaluation criteria, and high-quality randomized controlled trials. In summary, integrated TCM therapy constitutes a safe and effective approach for managing PCM, and further rigorous research is warranted to enhance its clinical application and facilitate international recognition of TCM in PCM treatment.

# Recent Advances in Pathogenesis, Diagnosis and Integrated Traditional Chinese Medicine Therapy for Plasma Cell Mastitis

## Abstract
Plasma cell mastitis (PCM) is a predominant form of non-lactational mastitis with an increasing incidence worldwide. The condition is characterized by a complex pathogenesis, difficulties in differential diagnosis, and a high rate of recurrence, thereby presenting significant challenges in clinical management. Conventional Western medicine is limited by high postoperative recurrence, difficulty in distinguishing PCM from breast cancer, and unsatisfactory long-term efficacy of single anti-inflammatory or hormone therapy. Against these clinical bottlenecks, Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) shows unique advantages and accumulated extensive clinical experience for the treatment of PCM. This review systematically delineates the epidemiological characteristics and key pathophysiological mechanisms, including activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway, immune cell dysregulation, autoimmune responses, distinctive plasma cell infiltration, and diagnostic methodologies such as imaging techniques, histopathological examination as the diagnostic gold standard, and emerging biomarkers. In addition, the theoretical foundations, contemporary pharmacological mechanisms, and clinical applications of comprehensive TCM therapy for PCM are summarized. Evidence indicates that TCM interventions, guided by syndrome differentiation and targeting liver qi stagnation, phlegm-stasis congealing, and heat-toxin accumulation, exert therapeutic effects by modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, correcting immune dysfunction, and restoring the mammary gland microecological balance. Clinical trials have demonstrated that combining TCM with surgical procedures or western medical treatments significantly improves clinical outcomes, reduces inflammatory mediator levels, and lowers recurrence rates. However, there remains a need for standardization in TCM syndrome differentiation, therapeutic evaluation criteria, and high-quality randomized controlled trials. In summary, integrated TCM therapy constitutes a safe and effective approach for managing PCM, and further rigorous research is warranted to enhance its clinical application and facilitate international recognition of TCM in PCM treatment.

## Keywords
plasma cell mastitis; traditional Chinese medicine; immune pathogenesis; IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway; integrated therapy

## Introduction

The investigative history of plasma cell mastitis (PCM) dates back to the early twentieth century. However, a comprehensive understanding of its etiology and pathogenesis has evolved gradually over an extended period. Earlier research posited that PCM represents a form of mammary ductal ectasia characterized by ductal dilation accompanied by plasma cell infiltration. 1 In the 1980s, the advent of immunohistochemical methodologies enabled researchers to detect elevated expression levels of inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) within the breast tissue of patients with PCM, implicating immune mechanisms in its pathophysiology. 2 Since the onset of the twenty-first century, advancements in molecular biology and omics technologies have further propelled PCM research, exemplified by the identification of novel transcripts through nanopore sequencing 3 and the investigation of alterations in breast microecology via metabolomic analyses. 4

Therapeutic approaches for PCM have evolved from surgical interventions to more integrative treatment modalities. Initial surgical management primarily involves lesion excision, which is associated with a high recurrence rate. 5 Post-2010, the integration of innovative surgical techniques—such as lesion-based duct resection (LBDR) and nipple correction—with pharmacological therapies, including biological agents and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), has markedly decreased recurrence rates. 5 , 6 Furthermore, advancements in diagnostic imaging technologies, including superb microvascular imaging (SMI) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), have enhanced the precision of differential diagnosis between PCM and breast carcinoma. 7 , 8

Conventional Western medicine encounters prominent bottlenecks in PCM management. As PCM is categorized as a non-bacterial inflammatory disorder, empirical antibiotic treatment achieves limited efficacy and easily triggers bacterial drug resistance. 9 Although immunosuppressants and biological agents can control acute inflammatory responses, they bring obvious adverse reactions, high economic costs, and frequent disease relapse after drug withdrawal. 10 Radical surgical resection can relieve severe lesions yet tends to cause irreversible breast contour deformation and severe psychological distress for patients. 11 PCM features a protracted clinical course and recurrent episodes, often leading to permanent breast disfigurement, anxiety, depression and other mental disorders, which severely impair patients’ physical and mental health and quality of life. 11 There is an urgent clinical demand for a safe and refined therapeutic strategy that achieves disease control while preserving breast morphology.

Within this comprehensive treatment framework, TCM has emerged as a significant component supported by extensive clinical experience and demonstrable therapeutic efficacy. Against the above-mentioned clinical predicaments of Western monotherapy, this review firstly systematically sorts out the epidemiological features, pathological mechanisms and multi-dimensional diagnostic systems of PCM. Afterwards, it elaborates the theoretical connotation, pharmacological mechanism and practical application of TCM comprehensive therapy for PCM. Finally, the limitations of current TCM research and prospective research directions are summarized to provide theoretical reference for standardized integrated Chinese and Western medicine treatment of PCM (see Figure 1 ). ## Epidemiology

PCM, the predominant subtype of non-lactational mastitis (NPM), has exhibited a marked increase in global incidence. However, the absence of standardized diagnostic criteria and comprehensive large-scale epidemiological investigations has resulted in variability in the reported data. The literature indicates that PCM constitutes approximately 1.4% to 5.6% of benign breast diseases, with a notable increase in reported cases in Asian countries, including China and Japan. 12 , 13 A retrospective analysis involving 1,260 pathologically confirmed PCM patients in Chongqing, China, revealed a median patient age of 31 years; 92.8% had a history of childbirth, 67.6% had breastfed for six months or longer, and 44.9% developed the condition within three years postpartum. 12 The study further identified that over 60% of cases occurred in the 30–39-year age group, implicating reproductive and lactational history as significant risk factors. Additionally, socioeconomic determinants, such as psychological stress, reported in 20.5% of patients, and lifestyle modifications may indirectly influence PCM pathogenesis by modulating immune function. 12

Although global prevalence data remain limited, several investigations have suggested that environmental influences, shifts in reproductive behaviors, and advancements in diagnostic methodologies contribute to the rising incidence of PCM. For instance, activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway is prevalent among patients with PCM, with the extent of pathway activation correlating with clinical manifestations such as nipple inversion. 2 This association not only elucidates potential pathogenic mechanisms but also underscores the role of inflammation-related pathways as a biological basis for increasing the incidence of PCM. 2 Moreover, the overall escalation in NPM cases, encompassing PCM and granulomatous lobular mastitis, accentuates the clinical significance of PCM as the principal NPM subtype. 13 Future studies should prioritize multicenter, large-sample epidemiological studies to delineate the global distribution and temporal trends of PCM.

The epidemiological characteristics of PCM vary considerably across populations, particularly age, sex, reproductive history, and clinical presentation. Predominantly affecting non-lactating women of reproductive age, PCM exhibits a median onset age of 31 years, with the highest incidence observed in individuals aged 30–39 years. 12 The aforementioned study of 1,260 patients demonstrated that 92.8% had experienced childbirth, 67.6% had breastfed for over six months, and 44.9% developed PCM within three years postpartum, suggesting that ductal injury during childbirth and lactation may be a critical etiological factor. 12 Clinically, PCM lesions predominantly localize to the central areola (78.9%), present as breast masses in 92.5% of cases (median size 6.8 cm), and exhibit a low bacterial culture positivity rate of 17.2%, reinforcing the nonbacterial inflammatory nature of the disease. 12

Regarding sex differences, PCM is infrequent in males; however, reported cases often involve comorbidities such as obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) and nipple inversion. 14 , 15 For example, a 55-year-old male patient presented with a left subareolar mass classified as BI-RADS 4C/5 on imaging and was pathologically confirmed to have PCM characterized by plasma cell infiltration. 14 This case highlights the necessity of differential diagnosis to exclude breast carcinoma in male PCM and suggests that obesity may contribute to disease pathogenesis via aberrant estrogen metabolism and hypoxia-induced inflammatory processes. 15 Ethnic variations in PCM distribution remain inadequately characterized, with existing studies predominantly focusing on Asian cohorts. Thus, cross-ethnic investigations are warranted to elucidate potential genetic and environmental determinants.

Variations in clinical severity and recurrence risk further reflect the population heterogeneity. Notably, patients exhibiting nipple inversion demonstrated a significantly elevated risk of PCM recurrence compared to those without this feature. Innovative nipple correction techniques, such as single suture or half-pocket suture methods, have been shown to reduce the recurrence risk by 63.7%, 6 indicating that nipple morphology may serve as a prognostic indicator and should be a focal point in clinical management. 16

The multifactorial risk profile of PCM includes nipple inversion, recent breast trauma, and parity as independent risk factors. A case-control study involving 82 patients with PCM and matched controls identified these variables as significant contributors to disease development. 17 , 18 Nipple inversion may facilitate inflammation through ductal obstruction, secretion retention, and bacterial colonization despite low culture positivity, whereas recent trauma may compromise ductal integrity and trigger immune responses. 17 , 18 Additional potential risk factors include obesity (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2 ), which may potentiate immune activation via adipose-derived inflammatory mediators, such as IL-6, and prolonged lactation, which can induce ductal dilation and secretion stasis. 12

Preventive strategies should prioritize early interventions in high-risk populations. For individuals with nipple inversion, corrective procedures during puberty or before pregnancy are recommended to mitigate ductal obstruction risk. 6 The efficacy of novel nipple correction techniques in reducing PCM recurrence underscores the importance of timely intervention. 6 Furthermore, lifestyle modifications aimed at minimizing breast trauma, maintaining hygiene, and alleviating psychological stress, reported in 20.5% of patients, may contribute to morbidity reduction. 12 Enhanced breast examination protocols and health education targeting postpartum women, particularly within three years of delivery, are essential for early symptom recognition, including mass formation and nipple discharge. 12 Prospective interventional studies are necessary to validate these preventive measures and develop biomarker-based risk prediction models incorporating indicators such as IL-6 and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) to facilitate precision prevention. 2 , 19 , 20

## Pathophysiological Mechanisms

### Immunopathological Mechanism

The immunopathological mechanisms underlying PCM are intricate and involve a coordinated interplay between the innate and adaptive immune responses. Central to this process is the activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway and dysregulation of the complement system. Empirical evidence indicates significant upregulation of IL-6 expression in the breast tissue of PCM patients, which correlates positively with phosphorylated STAT3 (p-STAT3) levels. 2 IL-6, a pivotal pro-inflammatory cytokine, not only facilitates the differentiation and survival of plasma cells but also promotes immune cell infiltration through STAT3 pathway activation, thereby establishing a chronic inflammatory microenvironment. 10 , 19 Concurrently, complement system activation, characterized by elevated expression of C3, C5, and their respective receptors, plays a critical role in PCM-associated inflammation. Notably, the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) predominantly localizes to the membranes of mammary ductal epithelial cells, where it exacerbates inflammation by inducing epithelial cell injury and apoptosis. 21

An additional hallmark of PCM immunopathology is dysregulation of immune cell populations. Studies have demonstrated an increased prevalence of M1 macrophages and T helper 17 (Th17) cells within PCM breast tissue, along with a reduction in M2 macrophages and regulatory T (Treg) cells, collectively fostering a proinflammatory milieu. 10 For instance, IL-17 secreted by Th17 cells activates the nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cell (NF-κB) pathway, thereby enhancing the secretion of inflammatory mediators such as IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), which further intensifies the inflammatory response. 10 Moreover, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is instrumental in the fibrotic progression of PCM. The IL-6/JAK/STAT3 axis promotes the transdifferentiation of ductal epithelial cells into mesenchymal phenotypes by upregulating EMT-associated transcription factors, including Snail and TWIST, culminating in fibrosis and structural disruption of the breast tissue. 22 Additionally, exosomes serve as vectors for intercellular communication by transporting chemokines such as CXCL12, which facilitates M1 macrophage polarization and the propagation of inflammation, thereby establishing a self-perpetuating inflammatory cycle. 22

Elucidation of these immunopathological pathways offers promising therapeutic targets for PCM management. Pharmacological agents such as IL-6 inhibitors (eg, tocilizumab) or STAT3 inhibitors may mitigate clinical manifestations by interrupting key inflammatory signaling cascades, whereas complement inhibitors (eg, C5a receptor antagonists) have the potential to reduce epithelial cell damage. 2 , 21 Future research should focus on delineating the interactions among immune cell subsets and spatiotemporal dynamics of signaling pathways to inform the development of more precise immunomodulatory interventions.

### Characteristics of Plasma Cell Infiltration in Breast Tissue

Plasma cell infiltration is a key pathological characteristic of PCM, and its distribution pattern, phenotypic profile, and functional attributes are closely linked to disease progression. In PCM, plasma cells are predominantly localized around dilated mammary ducts, exhibiting either diffuse or focal infiltration, often accompanied by inflammatory cells, such as lymphocytes and macrophages. 2 , 12 Immunohistochemical analyses have demonstrated that plasma cells in PCM express high levels of CD138, a recognized plasma cell marker, and are associated with activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway, with 93.3% of cells testing positive for IL-6. 2 , 23 For instance, in a murine model of PCM, administration of IL-6 induced infiltration of CD138-positive plasma cells within breast tissue, whereas treatment with the JAK inhibitor AG-490 significantly diminished plasma cell numbers, 23 indicating that the IL-6/STAT3 pathway serves as a critical regulator of plasma cell infiltration.

Furthermore, the phenotypic characteristics of plasma cells are correlated with the clinical manifestations of PCM. Notably, IL-6 expression is significantly elevated in PCM patients presenting with inverted nipples compared to those without inversion, concomitant with more pronounced plasma cell infiltration. 2 This finding suggests that nipple morphology may influence plasma cell infiltration by modulating the levels of inflammatory cytokines. Additionally, plasma cells in PCM may secrete autoantibodies, such as anti-ductal epithelial antibodies, which potentially contribute to autoimmune processes. 10 For example, mammary inflammation associated with Sjögren’s syndrome exhibits a plasma cell infiltration pattern analogous to that observed in PCM, characterized by the absence of IgG4-positive plasma cells, implying a shared immunopathological mechanism between these conditions. 24

The functional implications of plasma cell infiltration in PCM warrant further investigation. Current evidence indicates that inflammatory cytokines secreted by plasma cells, including IL-6 and TNF-α, exacerbate ductal epithelial damage and fibrosis, whereas antibodies produced by these cells may participate in immune-mediated clearance of ductal secretions. 2 , 22 Future research employing single-cell sequencing technologies to analyze the clonal diversity and functional status of plasma cells in PCM is essential to elucidate their precise roles in disease pathogenesis and progression.

### Autoimmunity

The autoimmune mechanisms underlying PCM have garnered increasing scholarly interest, with current research supporting the classification of PCM as an autoimmune disorder. First, autoantibodies, including anti-ductal epithelial antibodies, have been identified in the breast tissue of PCM patients. Additionally, an imbalance in immune cell populations, notably an elevated Th17/Treg ratio, aligns with the immunological profiles characteristic of autoimmune diseases. 10 For instance, interleukin-17 (IL-17) secreted by Th17 cells in PCM-affected breast tissues can activate the NF-κB signaling pathway, thereby promoting the secretion of pro-inflammatory mediators. Concurrently, functional impairments in regulatory T (Treg) cells may contribute to the disruption of immune tolerance. 10 Second, activation of the complement system, as evidenced by increased levels of components C3 and C5, may facilitate autoimmune responses through immune complex formation. Elevated concentrations of C3a and C5a have been observed in the breast tissue of patients with PCM, where they mediate inflammatory cell infiltration and epithelial damage via receptor-mediated mechanisms.

The autoimmune hypothesis was further substantiated by clinical correlations observed in PCM. For example, patients presenting with inverted nipples tend to exhibit higher titers of autoantibodies and more pronounced inflammatory responses, 2 suggesting that ductal obstruction may trigger immune activation by exposing autoantigens such as proteins present in ductal secretions. Moreover, the frequent comorbidity of PCM with other autoimmune conditions, including Sjögren’s syndrome, reinforces its autoimmune etiology. 24 Notably, mammary inflammation in individuals with Sjögren’s syndrome is characterized by lymphocytic and plasmacytic infiltration, mirroring the histopathological features observed in PCM. 24

Although preliminary evidence supports the involvement of autoimmune mechanisms in PCM pathogenesis, the precise processes governing autoantigen identification and breakdown of immune tolerance remain to be elucidated. Future research should focus on the identification of PCM-associated autoantigens through proteomic analyses and immunoprecipitation techniques, as well as on elucidating the mechanisms underlying immunomodulatory therapies such as glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants. 25 For example, glucocorticoids may attenuate inflammatory factor release by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway, whereas biological agents, including IL-6 inhibitors, could offer more targeted modulation of autoimmune responses 25 (see Figure 2 ). ### Diagnosis

Although most clinical and mechanistic studies concerning PCM therapeutic targets are currently conducted in Asian populations, the core molecular targets identified in these investigations, including the IL-6 signaling pathway and mammary gland microecological dysregulation, exhibit universal pathophysiological significance and global applicability. Such findings effectively bridge regional clinical observations and international basic research on PCM pathogenesis and diagnosis.

Imaging modalities constitute a critical component in the diagnosis of PCM, with ultrasound, mammography, and MRI each offering distinct advantages. The combined utilization of these techniques markedly enhances the diagnostic accuracy. Ultrasonography is the preferred imaging method for PCM, typically revealing a poorly defined hypoechoic mass within the areolar region, accompanied by ductal dilatation and abscess formation. 7 , 26 In a cohort study involving 111 PCM patients, ultrasound demonstrated a diagnostic accuracy of 82.0% and mammography of 74.8%, and the combined application of both modalities increased the accuracy to 91.9%. 26 Mammographic findings commonly include hyperdense shadows in the areola with ductal dilatation or calcifications; however, the specificity of mammography remains limited. 26

MRI plays a pivotal role in differentiating PCM from breast carcinoma. Characteristic MRI features of PCM include regionally distributed non-mass enhancement, heterogeneous internal enhancement, delayed eccentric diffusion, and associated signs such as nipple inversion, skin thickening, and sinus tract formation. 8 , 27 For instance, comparative MRI analyses of PCM and ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) revealed that PCM exhibits significantly higher rates of regional distribution, internal heterogeneous enhancement, and delayed-phase eccentric diffusion, whereas DCIS more frequently presents with segmental distribution and centripetal diffusion patterns. 27 Furthermore, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequences demonstrate high signal intensity centrally within PCM lesions, with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values exceeding those observed in breast cancer, thereby providing a basis for differential diagnosis. 8 , 27

Emerging ultrasound techniques such as SMI further augment the diagnostic precision of PCM. SMI effectively delineates microvascular architecture within lesions, with resistive index (RI) and pulsatility index (PI) values in PCM being significantly lower than those in malignant lesions. The integration of SMI with conventional ultrasound increases the diagnostic accuracy from 75.59% to 83.16%. 7 Future research should focus on multicenter studies to establish standardized imaging diagnostic criteria for PCM and investigate the potential of artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic models. 28

Histopathological examination remains the definitive diagnostic standard for PCM, which is characterized by ductal ectasia, plasma cell-predominant inflammatory infiltration, and periductal fibrosis. The pathological manifestations of PCM can be categorized into four stages: ductal dilatation, inflammation, abscess formation, and fistula development. 1 During the inflammatory phase, abundant plasma cells and lymphocytes surround the ducts and are accompanied by neutrophils and macrophages. 12 Immunohistochemical analyses have revealed high expression of CD138 in plasma cells, with positive rates of IL-6 and phosphorylated p-STAT3 at 93.3% and 70%, respectively, serving as adjunctive diagnostic markers. 2

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is valuable in diagnosing PCM, particularly in distinguishing it from breast malignancies. For example, in an 85-year-old female presenting with a left breast mass, FNAC identified plasma cell infiltration, which was subsequently confirmed as PCM via postoperative pathology, thereby preventing unnecessary radical mastectomy. 29 FNAC typically reveals numerous plasma cells, lymphocytes, and ductal epithelial cells without malignant cytological features. 21 Additionally, core needle biopsy (CNB) provides larger tissue samples, enhancing the diagnostic accuracy, especially in cases with inconclusive FNAC results. 14

Histopathological assessment also facilitates evaluation of the severity and prognosis of PCM. Patients exhibiting abscess formation tend to have a reduced risk of recurrence, whereas those with nipple inversion display more pronounced inflammatory infiltration. 6 , 30 Future efforts should aim to develop a pathological grading system for PCM, integrate clinical features for prognostic prediction, and explore molecular pathological markers such as IL-6 and complement component C5b-9. 2 , 21

The identification of novel biomarkers offers promising avenues for the early and differential diagnosis of PCM. Among these, IL-6, ICAM-1, complement components, and exosomes have demonstrated significant potential. Serum IL-6 levels, a key inflammatory mediator in PCM, are markedly elevated compared to acute mastitis patients and healthy controls, correlating with nipple inversion. 2 One study reported a median serum IL-6 concentration of 15.2 pg/mL in PCM patients versus 3.1 pg/mL in healthy individuals, with a diagnostic cutoff of 8.5 pg/mL yielding a sensitivity of 82.1% and specificity of 78.3%. 2

ICAM-1 expression is significantly upregulated in the mammary ductal epithelium and endothelial cells of PCM relative to that in normal breast tissue. 19 ICAM-1 contributes to PCM pathogenesis by mediating inflammatory cell adhesion and migration, and its expression levels are positively correlated with inflammation severity. 19 Moreover, complement components C3 and C5 and their active fragments (C3a and C5a) are elevated in the serum and breast tissue of PCM patients, with exosomal levels of C3a and C5a significantly exceeding those in healthy controls. 21 For instance, the median C5a concentration in breast tissue-derived exosomes was 12.3 ng/mL in PCM patients compared to 2.7 ng/mL in healthy subjects, suggesting its utility as a non-invasive diagnostic biomarker. 21

Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses have identified potential biomarkers of PCM. Utilizing nanopore sequencing technology, researchers detected 39,408 novel transcripts in PCM tissues, with significant upregulation of immune-related genes such as IL-6 and CXCL12. 3 Metabolomic studies have revealed aberrations in glycerophospholipid and arachidonic acid metabolism within PCM breast tissue, potentially linked to inflammatory processes. 4 To validate the diagnostic utility of these biomarkers and assess their roles in treatment monitoring and prognostication, large-scale multicenter investigations are warranted 1 (see Figure 3 ). ## Basic Theory of TCM in the Treatment of PCM

PCM is classified within TCM under categories such as “mammary abscess,” “galactorrhea,” and “acne mammary abscess.” Acne mammary abscess. Its etiology and pathogenesis are multifaceted, primarily associated with liver qi stagnation, phlegm and blood stasis, dysfunction of the Chong and Ren meridians, and heat accumulation. According to the TCM theory, the nipple corresponds to the liver, while the breast is linked to the stomach. Emotional disturbances result in stagnation of liver qi, which subsequently leads to blood stasis. Concurrently, abnormalities in the transportation and transformation functions of the spleen and stomach cause endogenous phlegm and dampness, respectively. The intermingling of phlegm and blood stasis within the breast collaterals, combined with progressive heat transformation, culminate in excessive heat that causes tissue necrosis and pus formation, ultimately leading to ulceration and fistula development. Additionally, disorders of the Chong and Ren meridians impair qi and blood circulation, and disrupt the nourishment of milk collaterals, further contributing to disease onset.

Contemporary research has elucidated the connection between TCM pathogenesis and modern pathological mechanisms through network pharmacology and experimental validation. For instance, investigations into Shugan Sanjie Decoction (SGSJD) have demonstrated that its active constituents, such as quercetin and luteolin, target molecules including IL-6 and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and modulate signaling pathways such as JAK-STAT. These findings align with the TCM therapeutic principle of “soothing the liver and regulating qi, dissipating stagnation and detumescence”. 31 Similarly, network pharmacology analyses of Gualou Niubang Decoction (GLNBD) revealed that its bioactive compounds influence pathways such as PI3K-Akt and AGE-RAGE, reflecting the TCM approach of “clearing heat and detoxifying, resolving phlegm and masses”. 32 Clinical observations have identified psychological factors, including anxiety and depression, as significant contributors to PCM pathogenesis (accounting for 20.5%), corroborating the TCM concept of “emotional pathogenesis”. 12 Moreover, the frequent occurrence of inverted nipples in patients with PCM is interpreted in TCM as a manifestation of liver qi dysfunction and obstruction of breast collaterals, further substantiating the role of liver qi stagnation in disease development. 2

The therapeutic mechanisms of TCM in treating PCM include immune modulation, anti-inflammatory effects, regulation of cellular signaling pathways, and maintenance of microecological balance. Network pharmacology studies have identified 47 active components in SGSJD that interact with 20 PCM-related targets, predominantly involving the JAK-STAT, HIF-1, and AGE-RAGE signaling pathways. 31 Experimental data indicate that SGSJD dose-dependently reduced the protein expression levels of phosphorylated JAK2/JAK2, phosphorylated STAT3/STAT3, and IL-6 in PCM murine models, thereby attenuating inflammatory responses. 31 GLNBD contains 164 active compounds that act on 58 targets via PI3K-Akt and oncogenic pathways; key constituents such as quercetin and luteolin exhibit stable binding affinities to albumin (ALB), EGFR, IL-6, and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA). 32 Clinical trials have demonstrated that TCM formulations significantly decrease serum inflammatory markers, including IL-6 and C-reactive protein (CRP), downregulate immunoglobulin IgA and IgG, and enhance immune function in PCM patients. 33 Research on the Yanghe Decoction has shown its capacity to modulate mammary gland microecology by reducing the abundance of Corynebacterium and Rhodococcus species, increasing Staphylococcus populations, and influencing metabolites such as glycerophosphorylcholine and arachidonic acid, suggesting that TCM exerts therapeutic effects by regulating the microbiome and metabolome. 4 Furthermore, TCM components such as sinomenine have been found to inhibit the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway and reduce plasma cell infiltration, contributing to disease amelioration. 34 These mechanistic insights provide a modern biological foundation for TCM interventions in PCM and underscore the holistic regulatory advantages of TCM.

The historical application of TCM in managing breast diseases dates back to Huangdi Neijing, which documents conditions analogous to PCM under the term “mammary abscess.” Eminent ancient physicians, including Sun Simiao, advocated therapeutic principles such as “soothing the liver and regulating qi, clearing heat, and detoxifying” in the Qianjin Yaofang, principles that remain relevant today. With the advancements in modern medicine, TCM approaches to PCM have evolved. Traditional methods primarily involve oral decoctions and topical applications, as exemplified by the Yanghe Decoction and Xianfang Huoming Yin. Recently, the integration of TCM with contemporary technologies, such as ultrasound-guided microwave ablation combined with herbal treatments, has markedly enhanced therapeutic outcomes. 35 Clinical evidence indicates that layered breast defect reconstruction (LBDR) combined with TCM reduces recurrence rates (4.55% versus 45.83%) and improves aesthetic results. 5 Additionally, the application of knowledge-mapping techniques to screen Chinese herbal compounds offers novel strategies for PCM management. 33 Retrospective analyses have reported an efficacy rate of 86.8% for TCM treatments with low recurrence. 35 The increasing incorporation of evidence-based methodologies has fostered a growing body of clinical research; for example, randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that the Yanghe Decoction surpasses conventional Western medicine in symptom relief and immune regulation. 4 Collectively, these developments signify a transition in TCM treatment for PCM from traditional empirical practice toward rigorous scientific validation, thereby providing a more robust foundation for its clinical application (see Figure 4 ). ## Clinical Practice of TCM in the Treatment of PCM

Most existing clinical trials of traditional Chinese medicine for plasma cell mastitis are carried out in Asian populations, but the core therapeutic targets including IL-6 pathway and mammary gland microecology summarized from these trials have universal guiding significance for clinical research and mechanism exploration of PCM worldwide. It is worth noting that the positive clinical efficacy observed in most published TCM randomized controlled trials should be interpreted cautiously, since these studies are mostly single-center trials with limited sample sizes ranging from 30 to 120 participants, and rigorous double-blind design is rarely adopted in trial implementation, which brings certain methodological limitations to evidence grading.

Chunlu et al 36 conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of oral administration of Yiqi Jiedu Sanjie Decoction combined with topical application of Dahu Tincture in treating PCM, as well as its impact on serum levels of procalcitonin (PCT), interleukin-8 (IL-8), and TNF-α. The study enrolled 120 patients diagnosed with PCM at the mass stage and admitted to Hebei Provincial Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine between October 2023 and December 2024. The participants were randomly assigned to either a control group or an observation group, each comprising 60 patients. The control group received standard antibiotic therapy alongside infrared radiation, whereas the observation group was administered Yiqi Jiedu Sanjie Decoction orally in conjunction with external application of Dahu Tincture in addition to the control treatment. Comparative analyses were performed on the clinical outcomes and serum biomarkers, including PCT, IL-8, TNF-α, and immunoglobulins IgA, IgM, and IgG. The findings indicated that the combined treatment significantly improved clinical symptoms, such as breast pain and swelling, attenuated inflammatory responses, and reduced recurrence rates in PCM patients at the lump stage.

Lijing et al 37 designed an RCT to investigate the therapeutic effects of Jiaweiyanghe Decoction on early stage mass PCM, focusing on its modulation of inflammatory responses. The trial included 84 patients with early mass PCM, randomly allocated to two groups of 42 patients each. The control group received conventional Western medical treatment, whereas the observation group was additionally treated with the Jiaweiyanghe Decoction. Post-treatment assessments compared the primary TCM symptom scores, breast mass size via color Doppler ultrasound, and inflammatory markers, including white blood cell (WBC) count, neutrophil (NEU) count, C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and adverse reactions. The results demonstrated that the Jiaweiyanghe Decoction effectively controlled inflammation and alleviated clinical symptoms, thereby exerting a significant therapeutic effect in early mass PCM.

Feng Hao et al 38 conducted an RCT to examine the influence of Shugan Qingre Fang on the Th1/Th2 helper T cell balance in patients with PCM undergoing microwave ablation. Participants were randomized into a control group receiving microwave ablation alone and an experimental group receiving combined treatment with Shugan Qingre Fang and microwave ablation. Clinical efficacy and breast pain, measured using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), were evaluated pre- and posttreatment. The serum levels of immunoglobulins, complement components, and Th1/Th2 cytokines were also quantified. Additionally, an animal model study involved mice allocated to control, PCM, microwave ablation (MWA), Shugan Qingre Decoction (SGQRD), and combined SGQRD + MWA groups, with corresponding treatments administered. Immunological parameters and histopathological changes in the breast tissue were assessed. The study concluded that Shugan Qingre Fang enhanced the therapeutic effect of microwave ablation by modulating the Th1/Th2 cell balance in PCM.

Xu Wei et al 39 performed an RCT to assess the efficacy and safety of combining Chaihu Qinggan Decoction, Haizao Yuhu Decoction, and Sanling Decoction with microwave ablation in treating PCM characterized by liver meridian stagnant heat syndrome. A total of 116 PCM patients were randomly assigned to either a combined treatment group (receiving the three decoctions plus microwave ablation) or a control group (microwave ablation alone). Comparative analyses included therapeutic outcomes, adverse events, total TCM syndrome scores, ultrasonographic parameters, peripheral blood T lymphocyte subsets, serum interleukin-17 (IL-17), and prolactin (PRL) levels measured before and after treatment. A one-year follow-up evaluated PCM recurrence rates. Correlation analyses between the TCM syndrome scores and serum biomarkers were also conducted. The results indicated that the combined treatment was both safe and effective, significantly improving clinical symptoms and quality of life, potentially through the modulation of peripheral T lymphocyte subsets and downregulation of IL-17 and PRL.

Wang et al 40 designed an RCT to evaluate the clinical efficacy of Qingrejiedu Formula in treating cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (CNGM) and to elucidate its mechanism of action via network pharmacology and molecular docking techniques. Thirty CNGM patients received Qingrejiedu Formula for 14 days, followed by a 7-day observation period. Patient demographics and therapeutic outcomes were documented and analyzed. Mechanistic investigations involved screening the active compounds of Qingrejiedu Formula using databases such as TCMSP, BATMAN-TCM, and ETCM, with drug targets identified via UniProt and STITCH. Disease-related target genes for CNGM were extracted from GeneCards and OMIM databases. Overlapping targets between the drug and disease were identified using the Venny online tool. Network construction was performed using the Cytoscape software, and protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were generated using the STRING platform to identify core targets. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses were conducted using the Metascape database. Molecular structures of the active ingredients and core targets were retrieved from PubChem and PDB databases, respectively, and molecular docking was performed using AutoDock Vina software, with visualization using PyMOL. The study concluded that the Qingrejiedu Formula exerts comprehensive regulatory effects on CNGM through multiple active compounds, targets, and signaling pathways, underscoring the advantages of TCM in managing CNGM and highlighting its clinical and research potential (see Figure 5 ). ## Safety and Standardization of TCM in the Treatment of PCM

The safety and efficacy of TCM in the management of PCM remain controversial. Some investigations have demonstrated that TCM formulations can markedly alleviate clinical symptoms and decrease recurrence rates. 4 , 33 Conversely, other studies have highlighted that the multi-component nature of TCM may precipitate adverse effects including hepatic and renal toxicity. 41 Moreover, the absence of standardized criteria for evaluating TCM efficacy, coupled with limitations such as small sample sizes and suboptimal study designs, undermines the reliability of the existing findings. 41 For instance, a systematic review identified significant heterogeneity in both effectiveness and recurrence rates when TCM was combined with Western medicine in PCM treatment. 41 Consequently, there is a pressing need for rigorously designed, high-quality, randomized controlled trials to substantiate the safety and therapeutic benefits of TCM.

The standardization of TCM protocols for PCM faces numerous challenges, including inconsistencies in syndrome differentiation, nonuniform prescription dosages, and variability in efficacy assessment criteria. Currently, TCM syndrome differentiation for PCM predominantly encompasses categories such as liver depression and qi stagnation, phlegm and blood stasis, and heat toxin accumulation; however, no consensus diagnostic criteria have been established. 42 Prescription dosages and treatment durations often vary according to individual practitioner experience, thereby affecting treatment consistency. 41 Furthermore, efficacy evaluations frequently rely on subjective measures, such as symptom improvement and recurrence rates, with a notable lack of objective biomarkers. 4 Therefore, the development of unified standards for syndrome differentiation, prescription formulation, and efficacy evaluation is imperative to advance the standardization of TCM treatments for PCM.

Future research directions in TCM for PCM include: (1) comprehensive elucidation of the underlying mechanisms, such as immunomodulation and microecological regulation; 4 , 42 (2) innovation in TCM formulations, including nanoformulations and targeted delivery systems; 33 , 34 (3) execution of high-quality randomized controlled trials to validate safety and efficacy; 41 (4) establishment of standardized criteria for TCM syndrome differentiation and efficacy assessment specific to PCM; 42 and (5) enhancement of TCM integration with contemporary technologies, including artificial intelligence and advanced imaging modalities. 41 , 42 These endeavors are anticipated to provide a robust foundation for the precise and effective treatment of PCM.

## Future Outlook

Innovative approaches in the TCM treatment of PCM encompass several key areas: (1) the identification of TCM compounds through network pharmacology and molecular biology techniques, including the utilization of knowledge mapping technology; 33 (2) the development and isolation of active TCM constituents, such as quercetin and luteolin; 31 , 32 (3) the integration of TCM with immunotherapy strategies, exemplified by the modulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSCs) function; 43 (4) the regulation of microecological environments, such as the modulation of mammary gland microbiota; 4 and (5) the implementation of personalized treatment protocols based on syndrome differentiation and biomarker analysis. 42 These innovative directions are anticipated to advance the precision and modernization of PCM management within the TCM framework.

Furthermore, international collaboration in the application of TCM for the treatment of PCM has progressively expanded. Notable examples include joint research initiatives between China and countries such as Egypt and Morocco, focusing on classification and therapeutic approaches for chronic mastitis. 44 Additionally, the use of TCM in managing bovine mastitis offers valuable insights applicable to PCM treatment. 45 , 46 Such international partnerships are instrumental in promoting global dissemination and acceptance of TCM. Moving forward, it is imperative to enhance international multi-center clinical trials to rigorously evaluate the efficacy of TCM interventions and facilitate the integration of traditional Chinese and Western medical practices.

## Conclusion

PCM is an intractable non-lactational breast inflammatory disease featured with immune disorder-centered pathogenesis, difficult differential diagnosis and high recurrence rate, which seriously damages patients’ physical and mental health. This review systematically summarizes the research advances in the epidemiology, immune pathogenesis, diagnostic techniques and comprehensive treatment of PCM. Abnormal activation of the IL-6/STAT3 pathway, immune imbalance, autoimmune disturbance and plasma cell infiltration are critical drivers of chronic breast inflammation and tissue injury. The combination of imaging examination, pathological biopsy and novel molecular biomarkers can greatly improve the diagnostic accuracy of PCM. Monotherapy with pure Western medicine has prominent defects for PCM treatment. Empirical antibiotic therapy shows poor efficacy and easily triggers drug resistance, while immunosuppressants and biological agents bring obvious adverse reactions. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) mainly treats PCM by soothing liver-qi stagnation, resolving phlegm and blood stasis, and clearing heat and detoxification via anti-inflammation, immune regulation and breast microecology reconstruction. Integrated TCM and Western medicine therapy can rapidly relieve clinical symptoms, suppress inflammatory response and reduce disease recurrence, so as to remedy the deficiencies of conventional Western medical treatment. Nevertheless, current TCM-related research has obvious limitations. Most clinical trials are single-center studies with small sample sizes without rigorous double-blind design, leading to low level of clinical evidence. Moreover, unified TCM syndrome differentiation criteria and quantitative efficacy evaluation systems for PCM have not yet been formulated. Future research shall carry out high-quality multicenter, large-sample, double-blind randomized controlled trials to verify the efficacy and safety of TCM. Further exploration on the immune regulatory mechanism of TCM and development of innovative Chinese medicinal preparations will facilitate the modernization of integrated Chinese and Western medicine therapy. In conclusion, integrated Chinese and Western medicine serves as a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for refractory PCM, which is worthy of extensive clinical promotion and in-depth research.

figure_captions: Figure 1 Occurrence, progression, and clinical characteristics of plasma cell mastitis (PCM). Risk factors such as nipple inversion, lactation history, breast trauma, obesity, and psychological stress may lead to ductal obstruction, secretion retention, and ductal epithelial injury, thereby inducing chronic inflammation. Disease progression may result in breast masses, pain, abscesses, sinus tracts/fistulas, and a high risk of recurrence. The left panel summarizes high-risk groups and risk factors; the middle panel illustrates localized ductal pathological alterations; the right panel shows clinical manifestations and disease progression.

Figure 2 Immunoinflammatory mechanisms of plasma cell mastitis. PCM is associated with activation of the interleukin-6 (IL-6)/Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) pathway, CD138⁺ plasma cell infiltration, increased M1 macrophages and T helper 17 (Th17) cells, decreased regulatory T (Treg) and M2 cells, and complement activation. These alterations jointly promote ductal epithelial injury, inflammatory amplification, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), periductal fibrosis, abscess formation, and recurrence.

Figure 3 Diagnostic workflow of plasma cell mastitis. Diagnosis of PCM requires integration of clinical presentation, imaging findings, and pathological confirmation. Ultrasonography, mammography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and superb microvascular imaging (SMI) help identify lesions and differentiate PCM from breast cancer, while histopathology remains the diagnostic gold standard. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) and core needle biopsy (CNB) support tissue diagnosis. Immunohistochemical markers (CD138, IL-6, and phosphorylated signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 [p-STAT3]) and auxiliary biomarkers (intercellular adhesion molecule-1 [ICAM-1], complement components C3/C5/C5a, exosomal C3a/C5a, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 [CXCL12], and metabolomic markers) may aid diagnosis. The workflow culminates in confirmation of PCM and differentiation from breast cancer, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), and other non-lactational mastitis.

Figure 4 Correspondence between traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) pathogenesis and modern medical mechanisms in plasma cell mastitis. In TCM theory, PCM is associated with liver Qi stagnation, phlegm-stasis congealing, heat-toxin accumulation, and Chong-Ren disharmony. These patterns correspond to psychological stress and neuroendocrine–immune dysregulation with IL-6-mediated inflammation; ductal obstruction, secretion retention, fibrosis/EMT, and mass formation; nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation with elevated IL-6, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and interleukin-17 (IL-17) leading to abscess and tissue injury; and immune/endocrine imbalance with a tendency toward recurrence, respectively. Representative clinical manifestations (breast mass, pain/swelling, nipple discharge/inversion, sinus/fistula, and abscess) are shown on the left.

Figure 5 Mechanisms and clinical applications of integrated traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) therapy for plasma cell mastitis. Integrated TCM therapy includes oral herbal decoctions—such as Shugan Sanjie Decoction (SGSJD), Gualou Niubang Decoction (GLNBD), Yanghe Decoction, Jiawei Yanghe Decoction, and Shugan Qingre Formula (SGQRF)—external TCM therapies, and combination with Western modalities such as microwave ablation, lesion-based duct resection, nipple correction, and other medical treatments. Proposed mechanisms include anti-inflammatory effects (decreased IL-6, C-reactive protein [CRP], TNF-α, procalcitonin [PCT], and interleukin-8 [IL-8]), immune modulation (T helper 1/T helper 2 [Th1/Th2] balance, Th17/Treg regulation, immunoglobulin A/G [IgA/IgG] modulation, and T-lymphocyte subset regulation), signaling pathway regulation (IL-6/JAK2/STAT3, JAK-STAT, phosphoinositide 3-kinase–protein kinase B [PI3K-Akt], advanced glycation end products–receptor for AGE [AGE-RAGE], and hypoxia-inducible factor-1 [HIF-1] pathways), and modulation of mammary microbiota and lipid metabolism. Clinical benefits include pain and swelling relief, mass-size reduction, lowered inflammatory markers, improved immune function, reduced recurrence, better cosmetic outcomes, and improved quality of life.
