Our structural and lipidomic data suggested significant PUFA-dependent alterations in RPE plasma membrane (Fig. 1 G–I). To directly assess the effects of lipid remodeling on plasma membrane properties, we next isolated plasma membrane fractions and, after confirming their purity (Fig. 3 E, S3 F), characterized their biophysical properties and lipid composition. C-Laurdan, a membrane-phase-sensitive fluorescent dye [ 27 ], analysis demonstrated significantly increased generalized polarization (GP) in ELOVL2-deficient cells, indicating increased membrane order and decreased fluidity (Fig. 3 F). Plasma membrane lipidomics further confirmed enrichment of long-chain ceramides, characteristic for the retina, lysophospholipids and a shift toward MUFA-ceramides with a corresponding decrease in PUFA-ceramides, a pattern similar to the ceramide saturation profile observed in aging eyecups (Fig. 3 G, H, S3 G). Consistently, ceramide accumulation at the cell surface, stained with membrane-binding fluorophore-cysteine-lysine-palmitoyl group (mCLING), was confirmed by immunofluorescence (Fig. 3 I).

### ELOVL2-deficient RPE cells exhibit plasma membrane stress without apoptosis

Given the altered plasma membrane biophysical properties and composition, we next assessed membrane stress in ELOVL2-deficient cells by measuring the loss of lipid bilayer asymmetry. We measured externalized phosphatidylserine (PS), an early marker of membrane stress and apoptosis, using two complementary Annexin V binding assays. ELOVL2 deficiency resulted in increased PS externalization, indicating plasma membrane perturbation (Fig. 3 J, K).

However, this was not accompanied by activation of apoptotic markers, including cleaved caspase-3 or caspase-9 (Fig. 3 L), in contrast to cells treated with H 2 O 2 (6 h) (Fig. S3 J, K). These results indicate that cells maintain viability despite persistent membrane stress.

### Lysosome-mediated plasma membrane repair is activated in response to membrane stress

We next asked how ELOVL2-deficient cells maintain viability under conditions of membrane stress. Live-cell calcium imaging revealed elevated cytosolic Ca 2+ levels in ELOVL2-deficient cells in standard extracellular 2 mM [Ca 2+ ] conditions, consistent with increased plasma membrane permeability (Fig. 4 A, B). Comparing average calcium levels between the 2Ca and 0Ca conditions readily revealed significantly elevated baseline levels in ELOVL2 KD cells compared to control cells (Fig. 4 C, S4 A). Disruption of the calcium gradient across the plasma membrane may promote the mobilization of lysosomes toward the plasma membrane to support membrane repair [ 28 – 30 ]. LAMP1 immunostaining revealed redistribution of lysosomes toward the cell periphery in ELOVL2-deficient cells (Fig. 4 D, S4 B) while no significant changes were observed in lysosomal number or diameter (Fig. S4 C, D). To visualize lysosome dynamics, cells were imaged using 4D adaptive optics lattice light-sheet microscopy (Fig. 4 E). Lysosome positions were tracked and analyzed relative to cell boundaries, and dynamic parameters were calculated from time-lapse image sequences using particle-tracking software [ 31 ]. These results further confirmed increased lysosome accumulation and motility near the plasma membrane (Fig. 4 F), indicating enhanced lysosomal engagement with the cell cortex. Proximity ligation assays, using LAMP2 and ZO-1 antibodies, demonstrated increased lysosome–plasma membrane contact (Fig. 4 G), and surface exposure of LAMP2 confirmed lysosomal fusion at the plasma membrane (Fig. 4 H). Consistently, β-hexosaminidase release into the extracellular medium was significantly increased in ELOVL2-deficient cells, confirming lysosomal exocytosis (Fig. 4 I). These data suggest that ELOVL2 depletion leads to lysosomal exocytosis in response to plasma membrane stress. Because lysosomal trafficking is redistributed to membrane repair, we next examined whether this affects RPE function. In vivo, wild-type animals exhibited robust accumulation of internalized 1D4-positive phagosomes at the earliest time point (ZT1), followed by a progressive decline at later time points (ZT4/ZT8) as phagosomes were cleared (Fig. S4 G). In contrast, Elovl2 C234W mutants displayed significantly fewer internalized phagosomes (ZT1), indicating reduced POS ingestion during the peak of the phagocytic burst (Fig. S4 G). Furthermore, phagosome size was significantly larger in mutants, consistent with delayed processing or stalled lysosomal degradation (Fig. S4 G). In vitro, ELOVL2 knockdown similarly reduced uptake of fluorescently labelled outer segments (Fig. S4 H), indicating impaired phagocytic capacity in both systems. ### ELOVL2 deficiency triggers membrane stress and polarized lysosomal responses in iPSC-RPE

To validate these findings in a human model, we generated ELOVL2 knockout iPSC-derived RPE. Differentiation status was assessed by qPCR, confirming robust expression of canonical RPE markers—including PAX6 , RPE65 , GAS6 , and MFGE8 —while VEGFA and MERTK showed modest reductions in ELOVL2 KO cells, along with a marked decrease in ELOVL2 expression (Fig. S5 A). Similar to previous findings in vivo, morphometric analysis of ELOVL2 KO cells revealed disrupted epithelial morphology (Fig. 5 A). Fatty acid profiling confirmed accumulation of ELOVL2 substrates and depletion of downstream PUFA products (Fig. 5 B), consistent with impaired elongation activity. Next, we examined whether the process of lysosomal exocytosis contributes to plasma membrane remodeling in polarized iPSC-RPE cells by measuring acid sphingomyelinase (ASM) release by basal and apical membranes. First, we found that ASM release was higher in the apical than the basolateral compartment under lipid-rich (FBS) and essential fatty acid only (B27) media conditions. Second, overall ASM secretion was greater in both CTRL and ELOVL2 KO cells in DHA-depleted (B27) medium compared to FBS medium. Third, ELOVL2 KO cells exhibited a selective increase in basolateral ASM release in B27 medium, which was significantly decreased when cells were cultured in a PUFA-rich (FBS) medium (Fig. 5 C), indicating directional lysosomal exocytosis in response to membrane stress. Using a lipidomics-based phagocytosis assay [ 32 ], we found that ELOVL2 KO cells also exhibited decreased internalization of POS (Fig. S5 B). Consistent with broader defects in degradative pathways, ELOVL2 KO iPSC-RPE also exhibited a decreased LC3-II to LC3-I ratio, indicative of reduced autophagosome formation and impaired autophagy [ 33 ] (Fig. S5 C). Finally, in vivo analysis revealed basal redistribution of LAMP1 and increased APOE accumulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface in Elovl2 C234W mice (Fig. 5 D), suggesting coordinated basal membrane remodeling and extracellular deposition.

### ELOVL2-dependent lipid products directly regulate membrane stress and lysosome activity

To test whether restoration of ELOVL2 enzymatic products can reverse membrane stress, we supplemented cells for 4 days with the direct product of ELOVL2, 24:5n-3, and revealed reduced surface exposure of LAMP2 and PS externalization in both control and ELOVL2-deficient cells (Fig. 6 A, B), indicating direct dependence of membrane stress on ELOVL2 activity. Consistent with reduced membrane stress, 24:5n-3 supplementation also altered lysosomal positioning, shifting lysosome distribution in ELOVL2 KD cells from a predominantly peripheral localization to a more perinuclear pattern (Fig. 6 C). In vivo, intravitreal 24:5n-3 supplementation reduced ceramide accumulation and restored lipid balance in aged eyecups (Fig. 6 D, E, F), demonstrating that lipid remodeling is reversible and directly linked to ELOVL2 metabolic output. title: A targeted triple-action redox-modulating hydrogel potentiates fibroblast-mediated repair to accelerate oral wound healing
abstract: Oral mucosal defects cause persistent pain and impair essential orofacial functions, making rapid healing a clinical priority. However, the specific microenvironmental factors that limit mucosal repair are not fully characterized. Using single-cell transcriptomic profiling, we identified oxidative stress-mediated inhibition of fibroblast extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis as a critical barrier to wound healing. To address this, we developed an injectable hydrogel (FA/Zn-KR/Gel) that incorporates ferulic acid (FA) and a Zn 2+ -coordinated Cys-KR-12 complex (Zn-KR) to orchestrate a triple-action redox modulation. The hydrogel attenuates upstream reactive oxygen species (ROS) production via bacterial clearance and macrophage pro-oxidative enzyme suppression, directly scavenges free radicals, and fortifies downstream fibroblast antioxidant capacity through NRF2/HO-1/NQO1 upregulation. # A targeted triple-action redox-modulating hydrogel potentiates fibroblast-mediated repair to accelerate oral wound healing

## Abstract
Oral mucosal defects cause persistent pain and impair essential orofacial functions, making rapid healing a clinical priority. However, the specific microenvironmental factors that limit mucosal repair are not fully characterized. Using single-cell transcriptomic profiling, we identified oxidative stress-mediated inhibition of fibroblast extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis as a critical barrier to wound healing. To address this, we developed an injectable hydrogel (FA/Zn-KR/Gel) that incorporates ferulic acid (FA) and a Zn 2+ -coordinated Cys-KR-12 complex (Zn-KR) to orchestrate a triple-action redox modulation. The hydrogel attenuates upstream reactive oxygen species (ROS) production via bacterial clearance and macrophage pro-oxidative enzyme suppression, directly scavenges free radicals, and fortifies downstream fibroblast antioxidant capacity through NRF2/HO-1/NQO1 upregulation. This integrated redox modulation prevents oxidative stress-induced apoptosis and senescence while rescuing fibroblast proliferation, migration, and ECM synthesis. In a rat oral mucosal defect model, the hydrogel significantly accelerated wound closure and improved tissue maturation. These findings establish a translational pipeline from single-cell mechanistic discovery to targeted, redox-modulating strategies for oral wound healing.

## Keywords
Oral wound healing; Injectable hydrogel; Oxidative stress; Extracellular matrix; Antimicrobial peptide

## Introduction

The oral mucosa serves as a vital barrier against mechanical injury and pathogens [ 1 ]. Defects resulting from trauma, tumor resection, or soft-tissue grafting frequently cause persistent pain and impaired orofacial function [ 2 , 3 ]. Despite the application of growth factors and scaffolds, current clinical interventions often fail to achieve optimal healing [ 4 , 5 ]. These conventional strategies rely on generic principles of tissue repair that are frequently undermined by the unique oral environment characterized by constant salivary flow, microbial colonization, and mechanical strain [ 6 , 7 ]. For oral ulcers, multifunctional materials such as reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive hydrogels, stem-cell lysate hydrogels, and Janus films have been developed to target the inflammatory microenvironment, with some achieving intervention at specific pathways like ferroptosis or pain signaling [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] ]. For mucosal defects, however, despite advances in bioactive factor delivery, antibacterial strategies, and immunomodulation, many approaches remain largely empirical [ [13] , [14] , [15] , [16] , [17] ]. Developing effective therapies therefore requires identifying the specific microenvironmental factors that constrain mucosal healing [ 18 ].

Oral wound healing is a dynamic trajectory shaped by both intrinsic cellular properties and the local microenvironment. Analyses of palatal wounds have documented temporal shifts in gene expression and microbiota during healing [ 19 ], providing tissue-level views of the repair response. By measuring gene expression at single-cell resolution, single-cell transcriptomic profiling resolves distinct cell populations and decomposes tissue-level changes into shifts in cell proportions and transcriptional states [ 20 ]. Previous single-cell studies have mapped the steady-state oral mucosa and identified key signaling pathways involved in mucosal repair [ 21 , 22 ]. However, how the injury microenvironment reshapes the functional states of specific cell populations during healing remains poorly understood.

To identify these constraints, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis of injured oral mucosal tissues. We found that fibroblasts exhibited elevated stress responses and diminished extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, with a negative correlation between ECM synthesis and ROS response. This state of high stress and low synthesis persisted even after the inflammatory response resolved. Since mucosal repair depends on fibroblast-mediated ECM reconstruction [ 23 ], restoring redox homeostasis may provide a critical switch to reactivate fibroblast function and accelerate wound closure. We therefore designed a synergistic redox-regulation strategy combining ROS source reduction, direct radical scavenging, and endogenous antioxidant fortification.

To implement this strategy, we selected ferulic acid (FA) as a core dual-action antioxidant. FA directly scavenges free radicals and activates endogenous antioxidant enzymes, providing an efficient cellular defense mechanism [ [24] , [25] , [26] ]. Unlike many polyphenols, FA resists self-oxidation into H 2 O 2 , reducing the risk of generating toxic hydroxyl radicals via the Fenton reaction in the iron-rich wound environment [ 27 , 28 ]. However, the oral microbiota continuously triggers respiratory bursts in immune cells, creating a persistent source of ROS [ 29 , 30 ]. To address this upstream trigger, we introduced a Zn 2+ -coordinated Cys-KR-12 antimicrobial peptide-metal complex (Zn-KR). KR-12, a core fragment of the oral host-defense peptide LL-37, retains broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and the potential to preserve commensal homeostasis, while exhibiting enhanced stability. Cysteine modification further introduces functional thiol groups [ 31 , 32 ]. Zn 2+ potentiates pathogen clearance through metal-peptide synergy while promoting cell migration and angiogenesis [ 33 , 34 ]. Moreover, both FA and Zn 2+ suppress nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase activation, providing an enzymatic mechanism to reduce ROS production that acts synergistically with bacterial clearance [ 35 , 36 ]. To achieve localized delivery within oral defects, these components were integrated into an injectable hydrogel (FA/Zn-KR/Gel). The hydrogel backbone comprises maleimide-modified gelatin (GelMAL) and thiol-modified hyaluronic acid (HASH), mimicking the native ECM and enabling rapid in situ crosslinking at irregular defect sites [ 37 ].

Here, we show that the FA/Zn-KR/Gel hydrogel addresses the oxidative stress-induced repair impairment through a cascade of effects that encompasses bacterial clearance, pro-oxidative enzyme suppression, direct radical scavenging and NRF2 pathway activation. By restoring the redox microenvironment, the hydrogel protects fibroblasts from apoptosis and senescence under oxidative stress. This intervention rescues their capacity for proliferation, migration, and ECM synthesis, while synergistically promoting angiogenesis. In a rat full-thickness palatal defect model, these coordinated actions translate into accelerated tissue repair ( Scheme 1 ). This work provides an integrated strategy that bridges single-cell mechanistic discovery with targeted redox-modulating intervention for oral wound healing. Scheme 1 Single-cell transcriptomics-informed design and therapeutic mechanism of the triple-action redox-modulating hydrogel for oral wound healing.

## Materials and methods

### scRNA-seq data analysis

scRNA-seq data ( GSE287528 ) were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Downstream analyses were performed using the Seurat package (v5.4.0) in R environment (v4.5.2). Quality control excluded cells with fewer than 200 detected genes or mitochondrial read counts exceeding 20%. Following log-normalization and variable gene selection, datasets were integrated and batch effects were corrected using Harmony (v1.2.0). Principal component analysis was conducted, followed by Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction and graph-based clustering. Cell clusters were manually annotated using SingleR and CellMarker 2.0 as reference databases.

Differential expression analysis was performed using the FindMarkers function in Seurat, and genes were ranked by log 2 fold change. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted using clusterProfiler (v4.18.4) with org.Mm.eg.db (v3.22.0) for Gene Ontology (GO) term annotation, and ReactomePA (v1.54.0) for Reactome pathway analysis. Module scores for ECM synthesis, inflammatory response, and ROS response were calculated via the AddModuleScore function in Seurat. Correlations between module scores were quantified using Spearman's rank correlation, and partial Spearman correlation analysis was performed with the ppcor package (v1.1). For stratified analysis, fibroblasts were divided into tertiles according to their ROS response scores.

### Synthesis and characterization of hydrogel precursors

GelMAL was synthesized using a two-step protocol. Briefly, 3-maleimidopropionic acid (100 mg, Adamas, China) was dissolved in 2 mL of dichloromethane (Adamas), followed by the addition of 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC, 134.8 mg, Adamas) and N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS, 78.6 mg, Adamas). The reaction mixture was centrifuged, and the supernatant was sequentially washed with 2 mL of 10% (w/v) citric acid (Adamas), saturated Na 2 CO 3 (Adamas) and saturated NaCl (Adamas). The organic phase was dried over anhydrous MgSO 4 (Adamas), filtered and concentrated. The resulting 3-(maleimido)propionic acid N-hydroxysuccinimide ester (0.125 g) was dissolved in 1 mL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, Adamas) and added to type A porcine skin gelatin (0.25 g, Sigma, USA) dissolved in a 5:4 (v/v) mixture of deionized water and DMSO at 40 °C. The mixture was dialyzed using a 12 kDa molecular weight cut-off (MWCO) membrane, and lyophilized for storage.

HASH was synthesized via a two-step method. Hyaluronic acid (HA, 1 g, Sigma) and NHS (568.7 mg) were dissolved in 100 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, Adamas). Following the addition of EDC (947.2 mg) and cystamine dihydrochloride (2.2254 g, Adamas) under continuous stirring, the resulting solution was dialyzed and lyophilized. The intermediate was redissolved in 100 mL of PBS and reacted with tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP, 708.1 mg, Adamas) under stirring, after which the pH was adjusted to 4.5. The mixture was dialyzed (2000 Da MWCO) and lyophilized for storage.

The chemical structures of GelMAL and HASH were confirmed by proton nuclear magnetic resonance ( 1 H NMR) spectroscopy. Spectra were recorded on a Quantum-I plus 400 MHz NMR spectrometer (Q.One Instruments, China) using deuterium oxide (D 2 O) as the solvent.

### Preparation and characterization of hydrogels

To prepare the Zn-KR complex, 2 mg mL −1 of Cys-KR-12 peptide (CKRIVKRIKKWLR, Sangon Biotech, China) and 2 mM of ZnCl 2 (Adamas) were dissolved and mixed in deionized water. Complex formation was verified by a JEM-2100 transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL, Japan). Hydrogels were formed by mixing equal volumes of two precursor solutions. Solution A consisted of 10% (w/v) GelMAL in PBS, while Solution B contained 2% (w/v) HASH in PBS supplemented with specific components. Unloaded hydrogels (Gel) were prepared using Solution B without additive. The KR/Gel incorporated Cys-KR-12 alone, whereas the Zn-KR/Gel received the assembled Zn-KR complex. The FA/Zn-KR/Gel was formulated by introducing both FA (Yuanye, China) and the Zn-KR complex. Final concentrations within the hydrogels were 400 μg mL −1 for Cys-KR-12, 400 μM for Zn 2+ , and 2 mM for FA, where applicable. For biological experiments, precursor solutions were passed through 0.22-μm sterile filters before mixing, and other components were sterile-grade.

Hydrogels were characterized by fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy, rheology analysis, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). FT-IR spectra were acquired over a wavenumber range of 4000 to 400 cm −1 on a VERTEX 80V spectrometer (Bruker, Germany). Rheological time sweeps were performed on hydrogels prepared with 5%, 7.5%, and 10% (w/v) GelMAL by adjusting the concentration of Solution A accordingly, using a DHR-2 rheometer (TA Instruments, USA). Storage and loss moduli were recorded at 25 °C under a constant frequency of 10 rad s −1 and a constant strain of 1%. For microstructure imaging, samples were lyophilized, sputter-coated, and imaged via a 6700F SEM (JEOL). Elemental distribution within the FA/Zn-KR/Gel was mapped via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS).

The injectability was evaluated by loading the precursor mixture into a syringe and manually extruding it into predefined shapes on a Petri dish. To facilitate tissue adhesion assays, a trace amount of blue dye was incorporated into the hydrogel for visualization. The adhesive performance was subsequently assessed by applying the hydrogel to a finger joint subjected to repetitive bending, as well as to porcine skin subjected to stretching, bending, and twisting. Lap-shear adhesion was measured using an Instron 5944 universal testing system (ITW, USA) at a crosshead speed of 5 mm min −1 , with the hydrogel placed between two porcine skin surfaces and an overlap area of 4 cm 2 .

### Antioxidant activity assays

The antioxidant capacity of FA/Zn-KR/Gel hydrogels was evaluated across a range of FA loading concentrations from 0.25 to 4 mM. For the KMnO 4 reduction assay, 100 μL of hydrogel was mixed with 2 mL of 30 μg mL −1 KMnO 4 solution (Adamas) and incubated for 30 min. The absorption spectra of the supernatant were recorded across a 400–700 nm wavelength range using a Synergy H1 microplate reader (BioTek, USA). The 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity was quantified using a commercial assay kit (Solarbio, China). 100 μL of hydrogel was added to 2 mL of the DPPH working solution and incubated for 30 min. Absorbance spectra were subsequently recorded across a 300–700 nm range using the microplate reader. The 2,2′-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS) radical cation scavenging activity was measured using a total antioxidant capacity assay kit (Beyotime, China). 100 μL of hydrogel was combined with 2 mL of the prepared ABTS working solution and incubated for 10 min. Optical absorption spectra were recorded across a wavelength range of 400 to 800 nm.

### In vitro antibacterial assays

Staphylococcus aureus ( S. aureus , ATCC 25923) and Escherichia coli ( E. coli , ATCC 25922) were cultured in Luria-Bertani (LB) broth at 37 °C under shaking conditions. For the agar plate assay, bacterial suspensions (1 × 10 6 CFU mL −1 ) were incubated with the respective hydrogels at 37 °C for 24 h. The mixtures were spread onto agar plates, and colonies were quantified after an additional 24 h of incubation. To evaluate biofilm formation, glass coverslips were immersed in a bacterial suspension (1 × 10 8 CFU mL −1 ) containing the respective hydrogels and incubated at 37 °C for 72 h. The resulting biofilms were stained with SYTO 9 and propidium iodide (PI) using a Live/dead Bacterial Double Stain Kit (Maokang, China) prior to confocal microscopy imaging (Nikon, Japan). For morphological analysis, bacteria exposed to the respective hydrogels for 24 h were fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde for 4 h, dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, air-dried, sputter-coated, and examined via SEM.

### Cell culture and treatment conditions

RAW 264.7 macrophages, human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC), and human gingival fibroblasts (HGF) were obtained from the National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures, Chinese Academy of Sciences. RAW 264.7 and HGF were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM, Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Procell, China). HUVEC were cultured in Endothelial Cell Medium (Sciencell, USA) supplemented with 5% FBS and 1% Endothelial Cell Growth Supplement (ECGS, Sciencell). All cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO 2 .

To prepare hydrogel extracts, the hydrogels were immersed in the respective cell culture medium at a ratio of 0.1 g mL −1 , sealed, and incubated under shaking conditions at 37 °C for 24 h. The leachate was collected, centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min, and filtered through a 0.22-μm filter. Extracts were used immediately or stored in the dark at −20 °C for up to 48 h.

For in vitro assays, cells were seeded at a density of 2 × 10 4 cells cm −2 (RAW 264.7) or 1 × 10 4 cells cm −2 (HGF and HUVEC) and cultured overnight unless otherwise stated. RAW 264.7 were subsequently treated with the extracts in combination with 10 μg mL −1 lipopolysaccharide (LPS, Sigma). HGF were treated with the extracts in the presence or absence of 150 μM H 2 O 2 (Sigma), as specified per experiment. HUVEC were treated with extracts alone.

### Cytocompatibility assays

For Live/dead staining, HUVEC and HGF were treated with the extracts for 1, 2, and 3 days, followed by staining with a Calcein/PI Cell Viability Assay Kit (Beyotime). Fluorescence images were acquired using an inverted fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Japan).

For the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay, RAW 264.7 were seeded at 4000 cells per well in 96-well plates, cultured for 24 h, and exposed to the extracts for 24 h. HUVEC and HGF were seeded at 2000 cells per well, cultured for 24 h, and incubated with the extracts for 1, 3, and 5 days. At the indicated time points, the culture medium was replaced with fresh medium containing CCK-8 reagent (Adamas). After 1 h of incubation, absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader.

### Intracellular ROS measurement

After 24 h of the specified treatments, cells were incubated with 5 μM DCFH-DA (MCE, USA) at 37 °C for 30 min, washed, and imaged via fluorescence microscopy. Mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was quantified using ImageJ software (v1.54).

### RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR

RAW 264.7 were stimulated with LPS, and HGF with H 2 O 2 , for 24 h. Total RNA was then extracted using a Cell RNA Purification Kit (Adamas) in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. RNA concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). Complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from total RNA using Hifair® III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (Yeasen, China). Quantitative PCR was performed with Hieff® qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (Yeasen) on a real-time PCR system (Roche, Switzerland). Relative expression was calculated using the 2 −ΔΔCt method. Cybb , Nox1 , and Nos2 were normalized to Gapdh , while HAS2 and XYLT1 were normalized to ACTB . Primer sequences are provided in Table S1 .

### Mitochondrial membrane potential assays

Mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) was assessed via JC-1 staining (MCE) following 24 h of treatment. HGF were incubated with 1 μM JC-1 working solution at 37 °C for 20 min, washed, and imaged using fluorescence microscopy. The MFI of JC-1 aggregates and monomers were quantified in ImageJ.

### Flow cytometric apoptosis assays

Following 24 h of treatment, HGF were harvested using EDTA-free trypsin, washed, and stained with an Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit (Servicebio, China) for 10 min in the dark, following the manufacturer's instructions. Stained cells were analyzed by flow cytometry. Early apoptotic (Annexin V + /PI − ) and late apoptotic (Annexin V + /PI + ) populations were gated, and the total apoptosis rate was calculated as the proportion of apoptotic cells among all cells.

### Senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining

After treatment for 3 days, HGF were fixed, washed, and incubated with SA-β-Gal staining solution (Beyotime) at 37 °C for 24 h according to the manufacturer's protocol. Bright-field images were acquired via an inverted microscope, and the percentage of SA-β-Gal-positive cells was quantified using ImageJ.

### Ki67 proliferation assays

HGF treated with H 2 O 2 and the extracts for 24 h were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA, Servicebio), permeabilized using 0.2% Triton X-100 (Beyotime), and blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA, Beyotime). The cells were then incubated with an anti-Ki67 primary antibody (HA721115, Huabio, China) overnight at 4 °C, followed by a 1 h incubation with a fluorescent secondary antibody (Proteintech, China) at room temperature. F-actin was stained with FITC-phalloidin (Solarbio), and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (Solarbio). Images were acquired using a confocal microscope, and Ki67-positive nuclei were counted in ImageJ.

### Sirius Red and Alcian Blue staining

After 3 days of treatment, HGF were fixed in 4% PFA and stained with Sirius Red stain solution (Solarbio) or Alcian Blue stain solution (pH 1.0, Beyotime) for 1 h. Following removal of unbound dye by washing, bright-field images were acquired on an inverted microscope. Collagen and sulfated glycosaminoglycan (sGAG) deposition were quantified using ImageJ.

### Scratch wound and transwell migration assays

To assess scratch wound healing, a linear scratch was created using a 200 μL pipette tip across confluent HUVEC or HGF monolayers following a 24 h serum starvation period. Detached cells were removed via PBS washing, and the adherent cells were subsequently incubated in the extracts, with or without H 2 O 2 , depending on the experimental condition. Images were captured immediately after scratching (0 h) and at 24 h, and wound area was measured using ImageJ.

Transwell migration was evaluated using 8-μm pore inserts. Cells suspended in serum-free extract were seeded into the upper chamber, while extract supplemented with 2% FBS was added to the lower chamber under the specified conditions. After 24 h, cells were fixed in 4% PFA and stained with crystal violet staining solution (Beyotime). Non-migrated cells on the upper membrane surface were removed using a cotton swab. The migrated cells on the lower surface were imaged via bright-field microscopy and counted using ImageJ.

### Tube formation assays

HUVEC were suspended in the extracts without FBS and ECGS, and seeded at a density of 4 × 10 4 cells per well into 48-well plates pre-coated with Growth Factor Reduced Matrigel (Corning, USA). After 6 h, the resulting tube networks were imaged by bright-field microscopy. The number of junctions and total tube length were quantified using the Angiogenesis Analyzer plugin within ImageJ.

### Western blot analysis

To analyze the NRF2 pathway, cells were treated for 6 h, after which nuclear and total protein were extracted. For apoptosis assessment, cells were treated for 24 h before total protein extraction. To evaluate senescence and ECM-related proteins, cells were treated for 3 days followed by total protein extraction. Total protein was extracted using a RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime) supplemented with a protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Beyotime). Nuclear protein was isolated using a nuclear protein extraction kit (Beyotime). Protein concentrations were determined by a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Epizyme, China). Equal amounts of protein (15 μg per lane) were separated via 10% SDS-PAGE (Yeasen) and subsequently transferred onto 0.45 μm PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA). The membranes were blocked in rapid blocking buffer (Epizyme) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against NRF2 (80593-1-RR ,PTG), HO-1 (10701-1-AP, PTG), BAX (50599-2-Ig, PTG), p53 (10442-1-AP, PTG), p21 (10355-1-AP, PTG), COL1 (14695-1-AP, PTG), FN (15613-1-AP, PTG), β-actin (66009-1-Ig, PTG), NQO1 (bs-2184R, Bioss, China), BCL2 (ET1702-53, Huabio), COL3 (HA720050, Huabio), Histone H3 (A2348, ABclonal, China), and p16 ( R23897 , Zenbio, China). Histone H3 and β-actin served as loading controls for nuclear extracts and total protein, respectively. After incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Proteintech), protein signals were visualized using an ECL detection kit (Proteintech) and quantified with ImageJ.

### Bulk RNA sequencing and transcriptomic analysis

After treatment with FA/Zn-KR/Gel extract for 24 h, total RNA was extracted from HGF using RNAiso Plus (Takara, Japan). Libraries were prepared using the VAHTS Universal V10 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform by OE Biotech. Raw reads were filtered with fastp, aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38) using HISAT2, and read counts were quantified with HTSeq-count. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 with a q-value < 0.05 and an absolute log 2 fold change > 0.585. DEGs were subjected to GO enrichment analysis using clusterProfiler.

### Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation

The crystal structure of the KEAP1 Kelch domain (PDB ID: 4IQK ) and the three-dimensional conformation of FA (PubChem CID: 445858) were obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank and the PubChem database, respectively. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock Vina (v1.2.5), and the binding pose with the lowest binding energy was visualized in PyMOL (v3.1.6). Molecular dynamics simulations were executed in GROMACS (v2022.2) using the Amber99SB-ILDN force field for the protein and GAFF2 with RESP charges for the ligand. The resulting complex was solvated in a cubic TIP3P water box and neutralized with Na + and Cl − ions. Long-range electrostatics were calculated via the Particle Mesh Ewald method, with a 1.2 nm cutoff applied for non-bonded interactions. All bonds were constrained using the LINCS algorithm, enabling a 2-fs integration time step. Following energy minimization, the system was equilibrated for 1 ns under both NVT (300 K) and NPT (1 bar) conditions prior to a 100-ns unrestrained production run. Trajectory analyses, including root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF), and hydrogen bonding, were conducted using GROMACS tools, and a free energy landscape (FEL) was constructed via principal component analysis (PCA).

### Rat oral mucosal wound healing model

All animal procedures were approved by the Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee, School of Basic Medicine, Jilin University (approval number: 2024-545) and conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines. Eight-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rats (250–300 g) were anesthetized via intramuscular injection of Zoletil and xylazine, and subsequently randomized into four groups: PBS, Gel, bFGF (basic Fibroblast Growth Factor, Essex Bio, China), and FA/Zn-KR/Gel, with four rats per group per time point. A full-thickness mucosal defect (6 mm × 2 mm) was surgically created on the hard palate using a sterile scalpel. The defect was oriented along the long axis of the palatine raphe, extending from a transverse line connecting the distal surfaces of the bilateral first maxillary molars anteriorly to encompass the most medial palatine ruga. Treatments were applied topically to the wound bed every other day after defect creation. The rats were euthanized on days 3, 6, and 10 post-surgery. Wounds were photographed in situ before harvesting the wound tissue samples alongside major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney) for downstream analysis. Wound closure areas were subsequently quantified using ImageJ.

### Oxidative stress and bacterial burden analysis

Harvested wound tissues were homogenized in RIPA lysis buffer at a 1:10 (w/v) ratio. Malondialdehyde (MDA) content was measured using a Lipid Peroxidation MDA Assay Kit (Beyotime) according to the manufacturer's protocol and expressed as μmol mg −1 tissue. To assess bacterial burden, wound tissue samples were homogenized in sterile PBS, and the resulting homogenate was cultured in LB broth at 37 °C for 24 h. The bacterial load was then quantified by measuring the optical density at 600 nm using a microplate reader.

### Histology and immunofluorescence staining

Wound tissues and major organs were fixed in 4% PFA, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at a thickness of 5 μm. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, alongside Masson's trichrome staining, were performed according to standard histological protocols. Collagen deposition was quantified from the Masson-stained sections using ImageJ and is expressed as the percentage of the stained area.

For immunofluorescence staining, the sections underwent antigen retrieval in Tris-EDTA buffer (pH 8.0, Servicebio), were blocked with 5% BSA, and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against COL1 (14695-1-AP, Proteintech) or CD31 (GB11063-2, Servicebio). Following a 1 h incubation with fluorescent secondary antibodies (Proteintech) at room temperature, the nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (Solarbio). Fluorescence images were acquired using a confocal laser scanning microscope and subsequently quantified in ImageJ.

### Statistical analysis

The scRNA-seq data were analyzed in R environment using non-parametric statistical methods. These data are expressed as median and interquartile range (IQR), with whiskers extending to 1.5× IQR. Group comparisons were conducted using the pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Bonferroni correction. For all other experiments, statistical analyses were carried out using GraphPad Prism 11. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and were analyzed via one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test. All experiments were performed with at least three independent replicates, with exact replicate numbers detailed in the respective figure legends. Significance levels are denoted as follows: ns , P > 0.05; *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.001.

## Results and discussion

### scRNA-seq analysis identifies oxidative stress as a constraint on oral mucosal repair

To characterize the microenvironment of oral mucosal injury, we reanalyzed publicly available scRNA-seq data ( GSE287528 ) from mouse buccal mucosa (2.5-mm punch biopsy wounds) at baseline (unwounded, UW) and on post-operative day 1 (POD1) and day 2 (POD2) ( Fig. 1 A). Clustering identified distinct populations of fibroblasts, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, neutrophils, and macrophages ( Fig. 1 B and Fig. S1 ). Following injury, neutrophil and macrophage proportions transiently increased at POD1, coinciding with a decline in fibroblasts. By POD2, macrophage populations continued to expand, whereas neutrophils and fibroblasts began returning to baseline. GSEA of the global transcriptome revealed an early transition to a defense state at POD1, enriched for acute inflammatory response, ROS metabolic process, and response to bacterium. Concurrently, tissue reconstruction functions, such as ECM organization and vasculogenesis, were suppressed ( Fig. 1 C). Fig. 1 Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis reveals that oxidative stress constrains fibroblast extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis during oral mucosal repair. (A) Schematic of the analysis workflow and collection time points of the oral mucosal wound scRNA-seq dataset: unwounded (UW), post-operative day 1 (POD1), and day 2 (POD2) ( n = 10 mice per group). (B) Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualization (left) and bar plots (right) showing the clustering and proportional shifts of major cell populations across time points. (C, D) Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of global transcriptional profiles (C) and the fibroblast subpopulation (D) comparing POD1 to UW. (E) Fibroblast module scores for ECM synthesis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) response, and inflammatory response. (F, G) Spearman correlation between ECM synthesis and inflammatory response (F) or ROS response (G) in fibroblasts. Dashed lines indicate linear regression; solid lines and shaded areas represent generalized additive model (GAM) fitting with 95% confidence intervals. (H, I) Stratification of fibroblasts by ROS response levels, showing ECM synthesis capacity (H) and proportional distribution (I). Data are expressed as median and interquartile range (IQR), with whiskers representing 1.5× IQR (E, H). Statistical significance was determined by pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Bonferroni correction. ns, P > 0.05; * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001.

Given that fibroblasts are the primary source of ECM [ 23 ], we investigated their post-injury functional transition. GSEA of the fibroblast subpopulation showed a significant downregulation of ECM organization at POD1, accompanied by the activation of cytokine signaling in immune system and cellular response to chemical stress ( Fig. 1 D). At the gene level, ECM-related genes ( Col1a1 , Col3a1 , Fn1 ) were markedly downregulated at POD1, whereas pro-inflammatory markers ( Il6 , Cxcl1 , Ccl2 ) and oxidative stress-associated genes ( Sod2 , Gpx1 , Gsr ) were upregulated, showing varying degrees of recovery by POD2 ( Fig. S2 ). These suggest that the post-injury suppression of ECM organization stems from both the relative reduction in fibroblast density and the functional transition from ECM synthesis to stress adaptation. Although previous work attributed the reduced expression of COL1A1 and COL3A1 mainly to wound-induced tissue loss [ 19 ], our results demonstrate an additional functional shift that is not readily captured by conventional tissue-level analyses.

To identify the microenvironmental factors that inhibit ECM synthesis, we evaluated three functional modules in individual fibroblasts: ECM synthesis, inflammatory response, and ROS response. At POD1, ECM synthesis reached its nadir, while ROS and inflammatory responses peaked. Notably, by POD2, the inflammatory response had returned to baseline, whereas the ROS response and ECM synthesis recovered only partially ( Fig. 1 E), indicating an asynchronous recovery pattern. Correlation analysis revealed an inverted U-shaped relationship between the inflammatory response and ECM synthesis ( Fig. 1 F), reflecting the well-established dual role of inflammation in tissue repair [ 38 ]. In contrast, the ROS response correlated negatively with ECM synthesis ( Fig. 1 G). This inverse relationship persisted after adjusting for inflammatory response via partial correlation analysis (partial r s = −0.468, P < 0.001). Stratification by the ROS response confirmed this association: the high ROS response subpopulation exhibited the lowest ECM synthesis, and its prevalence increased substantially by POD1, remaining elevated on POD2 ( Fig. 1 H and I).

Together, these findings suggest that elevated ROS response in fibroblasts negatively correlates with ECM synthesis, with recovery lagging behind the resolution of inflammatory response. This accords with prior reports that oxidative stress suppresses ECM synthesis through mechanisms including impaired TGF-β signaling and c-Jun/AP-1 pathway activation [ 39 ]. In the oral cavity, where microbiota-derived H 2 O 2 and host-derived ROS provide continuous oxidative stimuli, this sustained high-ROS state may act as a limiting factor for fibroblast-mediated tissue repair.

Epithelial cells, however, did not show significant post-injury activation of oxidative stress pathways ( Fig. S3 ), likely reflecting their robust endogenous antioxidant capacity [ 40 ]. This divergence suggests that epithelial barrier closure and stromal deposition possess distinct sensitivities to the oxidative microenvironment. Although superficial healing relies primarily on re-epithelialization, repairing full-thickness defects depends heavily on fibroblast-driven ECM deposition [ 41 ]. In wounds requiring substantial matrix remodeling, oxidative stress may represent a weak link that delays healing. Collectively, these findings identify oxidative stress as a major microenvironmental constraint on matrix remodeling, supporting the targeting of redox homeostasis to restore fibroblast function as a promising strategy for oral mucosal repair.

### Synthesis and characterization of FA/Zn-KR/Gel

To restore redox homeostasis in the wound microenvironment, we designed a hydrogel network based on thiol-maleimide click chemistry. This catalyst-free crosslinking proceeds spontaneously at physiological temperature and pH upon precursor mixing, enabling in situ gelation within irregular oral defects without external stimuli [ 42 ]. The resulting network comprises a covalent backbone of GelMAL and HASH, loaded with FA and a Zn-KR metal-peptide complex ( Fig. 2 A). GelMAL was synthesized by reacting the lysine residues of gelatin with a maleimide reagent, providing Michael acceptor sites for covalent crosslinking [ 43 ]. The 1 H NMR spectrum of GelMAL showed attenuation of the lysine ε-methylene peak at 2.93 ppm (-CH 2 NH 2 ) and emergence of a new peak at 3.04 ppm ( Fig. 2 B), which corresponds to the ε-methylene protons adjacent to the newly formed amide linkage, confirming successful maleimide grafting. HASH was synthesized by carbodiimide-mediated coupling of cystamine to HA, followed by reduction, yielding multivalent thiol groups as reactive crosslinking sites [ 44 ]. The 1 H NMR spectrum of HASH exhibited a new peak at 2.55 ppm ( Fig. 2 C), corresponding to the methylene protons adjacent to the thiol group in the grafted cysteamine-derived spacer, confirming successful thiolation [ 45 ].

Upon mixing, GelMAL and HASH underwent rapid gelation to form a composite hydrogel (Gel). FT-IR spectroscopy confirmed successful covalent crosslinking ( Fig. 2 D). Thiol-maleimide Michael addition was evidenced by the diminution of the characteristic maleimide ring vibrations at 831 cm −1 and 698 cm −1 [ 46 , 47 ]. Rheological time sweeps confirmed the formation of an elastic network ( Fig. 2 E). The storage modulus (G′) exceeded the loss modulus (G″) from the onset of measurement, and both moduli increased progressively over time, indicating ongoing network strengthening. SEM revealed a uniform, interconnected porous network ( Fig. 2 F).

Zn 2+ and Cys-KR-12 were pre-assembled into the Zn-KR complex. TEM revealed the formation of an interwoven fibrous architecture ( Fig. 2 G), whereas no ordered structures were observed for Cys-KR-12 alone ( Fig. S4 ). These observations are consistent with Zn 2+ -mediated supramolecular assembly via cysteine thiol coordination [ 34 ]. Metal-peptide assembly enhances peptide structural stability, which supports the retention of biological activity [ 48 ]. The cysteine thiols also provide reactive handles for Michael addition with the maleimide groups of GelMAL, allowing covalent tethering to the hydrogel network and thereby offering a means to mitigate burst release and prolong retention [ 49 , 50 ]. FA and the Zn-KR complex were then incorporated into the precursor solution to form the FA/Zn-KR/Gel hydrogel. EDS elemental mapping demonstrated a uniform distribution of C, N, O, and Zn, without local precipitation ( Fig. 2 H). These findings confirm the homogeneous dispersion of the metal-peptide complex within the hydrogel.

Given the intended oral application, we evaluated the injectability and tissue adhesive properties of the hydrogel. The mixed precursors were readily extruded and cured in situ ( Fig. 2 I). The hydrogel maintained continuous interfacial contact without detachment during repeated bending on a finger joint ( Fig. 2 J) and during stretching, bending, and twisting on porcine skin ( Fig. 2 K). Lap-shear testing further showed an adhesion strength of 6.181 ± 0.566 kPa (mean ± SD, n = 3) between porcine skin surfaces. Collectively, these results support the potential of FA/Zn-KR/Gel for oral application.

### FA/Zn-KR/gel directly scavenges free radicals

FA neutralizes ROS through hydrogen donation, which generates a stable phenoxyl radical ( Fig. 2 L) [ 51 ]. To determine whether FA retains this antioxidant activity after hydrogel incorporation, we assessed its reduction capacity. The hydrogel demonstrated a loading-dependent electron-donating capacity in the KMnO 4 reduction assay ( Fig. 2 M). Subsequent DPPH and ABTS assays confirmed concentration-dependent scavenging of both nitrogen-centered and cation radicals, with the highest FA loading achieving near-complete quenching of ABTS + radicals ( Fig. 2 N and O). These findings indicate that FA confers broad-spectrum antioxidant capacity to the hydrogel. This radical-scavenging performance provides a chemical basis for restoring local redox homeostasis, which may facilitate subsequent fibroblast-mediated repair.

### FA/Zn-KR/gel reduces ROS production via bacterial clearance and macrophage pro-oxidative enzyme suppression

Bacteria constitute a major stimulus of local ROS bursts [ 29 ]. We first assessed the antibacterial performance of the hydrogels against S. aureus and E. coli . Agar plating and quantitative assays demonstrated that while the Gel lacked antibacterial activity, the KR/Gel significantly reduced colony counts. The Zn-KR/Gel and FA/Zn-KR/Gel groups exhibited the highest inhibition rates ( Fig. 3 A and B). Live/dead staining of the biofilms corroborated these findings ( Fig. 3 C). SEM imaging revealed extensive bacterial membrane corrugation, rupture, and cytoplasmic leakage in bacteria treated with FA/Zn-KR/Gel ( Fig. 3 D). This indicates that the hydrogel retains the membrane-lytic properties of Cys-KR-12, a mechanism that is less prone to inducing antimicrobial resistance [ 52 ]. Zn 2+ coordination further enhanced bactericidal efficacy, establishing a robust barrier against bacteria-driven oxidative bursts. Macrophages represent a major source of ROS in wounds [ 53 ]. We evaluated the regulation of cellular ROS production using LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages. Following confirmation of cytocompatibility ( Fig. S5 ), DCFH-DA probe analysis revealed that LPS-induced intracellular ROS accumulation was substantially attenuated by the loaded hydrogels, with FA/Zn-KR/Gel exhibiting the strongest suppressive effect ( Fig. 3 E and F). At the transcriptional level, LPS stimulation significantly upregulated Cybb and Nox1 , which encode core subunits of NADPH oxidase, as well as Nos2 . Consistent with the intracellular ROS observations, FA/Zn-KR/Gel treatment reversed this upregulation more effectively than other groups ( Fig. 3 G–I). Taken together, these results suggest that FA/Zn-KR/Gel reduces ROS production through two distinct actions: eliminating the bacterial stimulus and suppressing macrophage pro-oxidative enzymes.

### FA/Zn-KR/gel promotes angiogenesis and fibroblast migration under non-stressed conditions

Angiogenesis and fibroblast migration are fundamental to granulation tissue formation and drive the repair of the oral mucosa [ 54 ]. Before evaluating the hydrogel under stress conditions, we examined its direct influence on human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) and human gingival fibroblasts (HGF). Live/dead staining and CCK-8 assays confirmed cytocompatibility across all groups, with normal cell morphologies and no detectable cytotoxicity ( Fig. S6 ). Furthermore, Zn-KR/Gel and FA/Zn-KR/Gel significantly enhanced HGF proliferation by days 3 and 5.

To assess angiogenic potential, we measured endothelial cell migration and tube formation. In scratch wound healing and Transwell assays, KR/Gel, Zn-KR/Gel, and FA/Zn-KR/Gel significantly accelerated HUVEC motility ( Fig. 4 A–D). Notably, the Zn-KR-containing groups exhibited stronger chemotactic effects in the Transwell assay than KR/Gel. We then examined vascular network assembly. Whereas control groups formed sparse, fragmented structures, HUVEC treated with Zn-KR/Gel and FA/Zn-KR/Gel assembled into dense, highly interconnected capillary-like networks ( Fig. 4 E). These effects may reflect the established roles of Zn 2+ in cell migration and angiogenesis [ 33 ], along with the supramolecular assembly of the Zn-KR complex. Taken together, the pro-angiogenic and pro-migratory activities of FA/Zn-KR/Gel provide a supportive microenvironment for granulation tissue formation.

### FA/Zn-KR/gel attenuates oxidative stress-induced fibroblast apoptosis and senescence

Excessive ROS can trigger mitochondrial dysfunction, driving apoptosis and senescence cascades that impair wound healing [ 55 ]. To model this oxidative environment, we challenged HGF with 150 μM H 2 O 2 , a concentration previously shown to induce both apoptosis and senescence in human fibroblasts while preserving a viable cell population [ 56 ]. H 2 O 2 exposure significantly reduced cell viability ( Fig. S7 ), confirming the establishment of oxidative stress. Treatment with FA/Zn-KR/Gel effectively rescued the stress-induced decline in cell viability, whereas hydrogels lacking FA offered no protection.

To examine the mechanism underlying this protection, we quantified intracellular ROS using DCFH-DA probes. FA/Zn-KR/Gel significantly suppressed the H 2 O 2 -induced accumulation of intracellular ROS ( Fig. 5 A and B). Given that mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) loss is an early event in oxidative damage [ 55 ], we assessed mitochondrial function using JC-1 staining. H 2 O 2 exposure markedly decreased Δψm, as indicated by a lower ratio of JC-1 aggregates to monomers, and this decrease was reversed by FA/Zn-KR/Gel ( Fig. 5 C and D). To determine whether this mitochondrial preservation inhibited downstream apoptosis, we measured Annexin V-FITC/PI staining using flow cytometry. FA/Zn-KR/Gel significantly suppressed H 2 O 2 -induced apoptosis, whereas the Gel, KR/Gel, and Zn-KR/Gel groups showed no statistical difference compared to the H 2 O 2 group ( Fig. 5 E and F). Western blotting further validated these observations at molecular level. FA/Zn-KR/Gel reversed the H 2 O 2 -mediated upregulation of the pro-apoptotic protein BAX and downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2 ( Fig. 5 G and H). The resulting restoration of the BCL2/BAX ratio indicates that the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway was inhibited.

Oxidative stress also drives cellular senescence. SA-β-Gal staining showed that H 2 O 2 exposure significantly increased the proportion of senescent cells, which exhibited characteristically enlarged morphologies and blue precipitates. FA/Zn-KR/Gel treatment markedly reduced the senescent population and maintained normal cellular morphology ( Fig. 5 I and J). Consistent with this phenotype, FA/Zn-KR/Gel downregulated the core senescence-associated proteins p53, p21, and p16, which had been upregulated by oxidative stress ( Fig. 5 K and L). The simultaneous inhibition of the p53/p21 DNA damage response and p16 cell-cycle arrest pathway indicates that FA/Zn-KR/Gel limits upstream oxidative damage. Taken together, these findings show that FA/Zn-KR/Gel attenuates oxidative stress-induced fibroblast apoptosis and senescence by restoring intracellular ROS levels and mitochondrial membrane potential, highlighting the importance of antioxidants in managing the oxidative microenvironment.

### FA/Zn-KR/gel rescues fibroblast-mediated repair functions under oxidative stress

Fibroblast proliferation, migration, and ECM synthesis are essential for granulation tissue maturation and wound remodeling [ 57 ]. We therefore investigated whether the hydrogel could rescue these core cellular functions under oxidative stress. Ki67 immunofluorescence staining showed that H 2 O 2 stimulation significantly inhibited HGF proliferation, with cells exhibiting an excessively spread, flattened morphology. While the Gel, KR/Gel, and Zn-KR/Gel groups failed to induce significant proliferative recovery, FA/Zn-KR/Gel treatment significantly increased the proportion of Ki67-positive cells and partially restored the spindle-shaped morphology ( Fig. 6 A and B). Scratch wound-healing and Transwell assays yielded consistent results for cellular migration ( Fig. 6 C–F). H 2 O 2 severely impaired both horizontal and vertical migration. The intrinsic pro-migratory activity of Zn-KR observed under non-stress conditions was insufficient to overcome oxidative inhibition, as Zn-KR/Gel showed a statistically non-significant marginal increase. Furthermore, expression of the GAG biosynthetic genes HAS2 and XYLT1 was also rescued by FA/Zn-KR/Gel ( Fig. S8 ). Taken together, these findings indicate that FA/Zn-KR/Gel preserves fibroblast repair functions, supporting its potential to promote wound healing by modulating the oxidative microenvironment.

### FA/Zn-KR/gel potentiates fibroblast endogenous antioxidant defense via NRF2 pathway

To gain insight into the mechanisms underlying these protective effects, we performed RNA sequencing on HGF treated with FA/Zn-KR/Gel. GO analysis revealed significant enrichment in pathways associated with antioxidant activity, oxidoreductase activity, lysosomal lumen, dynein complex, and insulin-like growth factor I binding ( Fig. 7 A). These transcriptomic profiles suggest that alongside direct free radical scavenging, FA/Zn-KR/Gel supports oxidative stress defense by upregulating antioxidant enzymes, autophagic clearance, and pro-survival signaling [ 58 , 59 ]. Guided by these transcriptomic findings, we investigated the KEAP1/NRF2 pathway, a central regulator of cellular oxidative stress. Normally, KEAP1 sequesters NRF2 in the cytoplasm; upon stress, NRF2 translocate to the nucleus to drive the transcription of antioxidant enzymes such as HO-1 and NQO1 [ 60 ]. To determine whether FA interacts with this pathway, we performed molecular docking between FA and the KEAP1 Kelch domain, the primary NRF2 binding site [ 61 ]. The model yielded a binding affinity of −6.7 kcal mol −1 , stabilized by hydrogen bonds between FA and the VAL-606, GLY-367, and ARG-415 residues of KEAP1 ( Fig. 7 B). Since ARG-415 is a critical anchoring residue that binds the ETGE motif of NRF2 [ 62 ], this spatial overlap suggests a structural basis for competitive inhibition. A 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation confirmed the dynamic stability of this interaction. The complex exhibited a steady root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) and low overall root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF), indicating global stability and structural rigidity ( Fig. 7 C and D). A persistent intermolecular hydrogen-bond network maintained throughout the simulation reinforced the binding interface ( Fig. 7 E). Furthermore, the free energy landscape (FEL) converged into a single deep minimum-energy basin, which is consistent with an energetically favorable binding state ( Fig. 7 F). Taken together, these simulations suggest that FA has the structural potential to competitively disrupt the KEAP1–NRF2 interaction, providing a mechanistic rationale for NRF2 nuclear translocation.

To validate this computational prediction, we assessed the expression of nuclear NRF2 and its downstream targets, HO-1 and NQO1. Although H 2 O 2 exposure induced a moderate compensatory upregulation of these proteins across H 2 O 2 , Gel, KR/Gel, and Zn-KR/Gel groups, this antioxidant response was significantly amplified following FA/Zn-KR/Gel treatment ( Fig. 7 G and H). Taken together with our cellular rescue assays, these data suggest that the compensatory activation of the NRF2 pathway is insufficient to prevent oxidative damage. This accords with our scRNA-seq findings of oral mucosal injury, in which fibroblasts exhibited high ROS response alongside suppressed ECM synthesis. In contrast, FA/Zn-KR/Gel treatment significantly upregulates the NRF2/HO-1/NQO1 axis, fortifying the endogenous antioxidant defense. This biological response acts synergistically with direct radical scavenging capacity, ultimately preserving fibroblast viability and repair functions ( Fig. 7 I).

### FA/Zn-KR/gel accelerates oral wound healing in vivo

To validate this biomaterial strategy in a complex physiological environment, we employed a rat model of full-thickness hard-palate mucosal defect. Healing progression was compared across four groups: PBS (negative control), Gel, FA/Zn-KR/Gel, and commercial bFGF gel (positive control). Gross morphological assessment revealed varying degrees of wound closure over time ( Fig. 8 B and C). At day 3, wounds in the PBS and Gel groups exhibited inflammatory exudation and tissue exposure. By contrast, the FA/Zn-KR/Gel and bFGF groups showed active concentric contraction of the wound edges, with closure rates markedly exceeding those of the PBS and Gel groups. By day 6, the wounds treated with FA/Zn-KR/Gel had contracted into narrow lines, achieving a higher closure rate than the bFGF group, and reached near-complete clinical healing by day 10. Notably, the Gel group showed a significantly higher closure rate than the PBS group at day 6, suggesting that the hydrogel provides a fundamental physical barrier against mechanical friction during mastication.

To investigate early microenvironmental remodeling, we analyzed wound tissues on day 3. MDA content, a marker of lipid peroxidation, was significantly lower in the FA/Zn-KR/Gel group than in the other three groups ( Fig. 8 D), indicating an effective attenuation of oxidative stress. Concurrently, wound cultures demonstrated a significantly reduced bacterial burden in the FA/Zn-KR/Gel group relative to all other treatments ( Fig. 8 E). Taken together, these findings suggest that FA/Zn-KR/Gel alleviates the high-ROS state previously identified in our scRNA-seq analysis. By synergistically addressing bacterial infection and oxidative stress, the hydrogel may facilitate the transition from an inflammatory, high-ROS state to a regenerative state permissive for tissue remodeling.

Histological analysis at day 10 corroborated these macroscopic observations. H&E staining revealed persistent tissue defects and discontinuous epithelium in the PBS and Gel groups, accompanied by inflammatory infiltration within the lamina propria at the wound edge. Although the epithelium in the bFGF group was largely continuous, its thickness remained uneven, and residual inflammatory cells were visible. By contrast, FA/Zn-KR/Gel induced a continuous, well-stratified epithelium with resolved inflammation, surpassing the architectural maturity of all other groups ( Fig. 8 F).

Masson's trichrome staining highlighted critical differences in ECM assembly. Collagen fibers were sparse and disorganized at the wound edge in the PBS and Gel groups. Although the bFGF group showed increased collagen density, the FA/Zn-KR/Gel group displayed dense, highly organized collagen bundles filling the defect ( Fig. 8 G). Quantitative analysis confirmed that collagen deposition in the FA/Zn-KR/Gel group was significantly higher than in all other groups ( Fig. 8 H). Further characterization via immunofluorescence revealed markedly higher expression of COL1 in the FA/Zn-KR/Gel group compared to the PBS and Gel groups ( Fig. 8 I and J), consistent with the enhanced ECM synthesis observed via Masson's staining. Additionally, staining for the endothelial marker CD31 showed that the FA/Zn-KR/Gel group achieved the highest blood vessel density ( Fig. 8 K and L), indicating its robust pro-angiogenic activity, which provides the critical nutrient and oxygen transport network required for the high metabolic demands of tissue regeneration.

To assess systemic biosafety, we performed H&E staining on major organs, including heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney. No evidence of cellular necrosis, structural abnormalities, or pathological inflammation was observed in any group ( Fig. S9 ), confirming that FA/Zn-KR/Gel is biocompatible and safe for localized therapeutic use. In summary, FA/Zn-KR/Gel effectively reduced oxidative and bacterial burdens, promoted angiogenesis and ECM deposition, and consequently accelerated wound healing. By outperforming growth-factor therapy, the hydrogel represents a promising strategy for the repair of oral mucosal defects.

## Conclusion

In this study, we identified oxidative stress as a critical barrier to fibroblast-mediated ECM synthesis during oral mucosal repair. Guided by this single-cell transcriptomic insight, we engineered an injectable hydrogel (FA/Zn-KR/Gel) that restores redox homeostasis through ROS source reduction, direct radical scavenging, and NRF2-mediated endogenous fortification. This integrated modulation effectively prevented oxidative stress-induced apoptosis and senescence, rescuing fibroblast repair functions. In a rat model of oral mucosal defects, the hydrogel significantly accelerated wound closure and enhanced tissue maturation relative to growth-factor therapy. These findings offer a promising candidate for oral wound healing and provide a conceptual framework that may inspire the rational design of redox-modulating biomaterials for tissue repair.
