### Toxicity prediction for hit compounds

In early stages of drug discovery, computational toxicity predictions serve as a valuable tool for proactively filtering out compounds that are likely to exhibit clinical failure due to toxicological concerns ( Cavasotto and Scardino, 2022 ). Pharmacological activity prediction using the PASS online server revealed a high probability of antineoplastic activity for the selected hit compounds, as indicated by elevated Pa values and correspondingly low Pi values. Specifically, I1Hit1 exhibited a Pa of 0.792 and Pi of 0.013, I2Hit1 showed a Pa of 0.960 and Pi of 0.004, while PubChem ID 4946 (I1Hit2/I2Hit2) demonstrated a Pa of 0.118 and Pi of 0.058. These results are significantly better than the standard values of Pa = 0.521 and Pi = 0.065, indicating strong potential for anticancer activity. Moreover, the compounds were also found to be inducers of TP53 expression. Pa and Pi values of I1Hit1 were recorded as 0.373 and 0.157 respectively. I2Hit1 showed a Pa of 0.520 and Pi of 0.081, and I1Hit2 & I2Hit2 yielded a Pa of 0.463 and Pi of 0.108. These values significantly exceed the standard values of Pa = 0.291 and Pi = 0.218, indicating a potential role in modulating TP53 expression. Collectively, these findings highlight the therapeutic rationale for the hit compounds as cancer therapeutic agents with combined antineoplastic activity and TP53-enhancing properties. Results of this PASS prediction analysis are summarized in Table 7 . For In silico cytotoxicity prediction, CLC-Pred 2.0, a software tool, was used to predict the cytotoxic activity of chemical compounds on tumour and non-tumour cell lines. The predicted cytotoxicity of the standard and various hit compounds on different brain tumour cell lines has been summarised in Table 8 . Although the hit compounds were variable in their predicted activity (Pa) and inactivity (Pi), they consistently had higher Pa values and lower Pi values compared to those of the standard, indicating enhanced cytotoxic efficacy. Moreover, the invariable accuracy prediction (IAP) of all hit compounds has been predicted to 0.8 to 0.9, indicating extremely reliable and accurate predictions with minimal deviation. Overall, these findings highlight the value of all hit compounds as potential lead structures to target brain tumour cell lines with potent cytotoxic activity. Cardiotoxicity prediction using Pred-hERG 5.0 server for the hit compounds suggested differences in their blockage of hERG channel. In the multiclass prediction, standard compound was classified as a moderate blocker, I1Hit1 as weak blocker, I2Hit1 as a non-blocker, and I1Hit2 and I2Hit2 as moderate blocker. The corresponding confiability scores were 95.10 for the standard, 92.14 for I1Hit1, 99.12 for I2Hit2, and 89.96 for I1Hit2 and I2Hit2. Assessment of the applicability domain (AD) in Pred-hERG 5.0 server also revealed that the standard compound is within it, implying possible prediction precision. In the case of I1Hit1 and I2Hit1, both compounds were known to be outside the AD, whereas I1Hit2 and I2Hit2 (PubChem ID 4946) were categorised in the AD. These results indicate that I1Hit2 and I2Hit2 and the standard compound have comparable predictability in terms of cardiotoxicity, as shown below in Table 9 . The in silico rat acute toxicity evaluation was performed by GUSAR online tool, which provides the prediction of compound toxicities through numerous administrations. Oral administration is currently the most convenient and viable vehicle for drug administration due to its cost-effectiveness and greater patient adherence ( Alqahtani et al., 2021 ). In this context, the standard compound was found to be outside the applicability domain (AD) for intraperitoneal (IP) and oral routes, but within the AD for intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) administration. By contrast, the AD for all active hits were predicted across all administered routes, implying a wider range of potential drug administration. Accordingly, although vorasidenib (Standard) is clinically administered orally, its predicted toxicity was evaluated across all four routes to enable the consistent comparison with the hit compounds. The resulting LD50 values were further classified according to the standard six-class acute toxicity scale, in which lower class numbers denote higher toxicity (Class 1: LD50 ≤5 mg/kg) and higher class numbers denote lower toxicity (Class 6: LD50 > 5000 mg/kg). I1Hit1 and I2Hit1 were predicted to fall within toxicity class 3–5 across all four administration routes, corresponding to LD50 values ranging from approximately 29,390 mg/kg (IV) to 2,459,000 mg/kg (oral) for I1Hit1, and 7,136 mg/kg (IV) 1,600,000 mg/kg (oral) for I2Hit1, indicating generally low predicted acute toxicity and a favourable safety scale relative to the standard. I1Hit2/I2Hit2 was predicted to fall within Class 4 across all routes, consistent with its established clinical safety profile as an approved therapeutic drug. These findings collectively suggest that the identified hit compounds exhibit favourable predicted acute toxicity profiles with reliable applicability domain coverage across all tested routes, supporting their suitability for further experimental safety evaluation. ## Discussion

GBM is the most aggressive primary brain tumour, characterized by therapeutic resistance, high recurrence, leading to poor survival outcomes ( Markov et al., 2023 ) and most frequently observed as metabolic dysregulation caused by IDH enzymes. Beyond its direct enzymatic effects, mutant IDH exerts broader influence on glioma biology through interconnected signaling, immune, and metabolic networks that extend well beyond the IDH active site targeted in this study. The accumulation of 2-HG competitively inhibits α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, including TET methylcytosine dioxygenases and JmjC domain-containing histone demethylases, resulting in a DNA and histone hypermethylation phenotype that epigenetically reprograms the glioma cell transcriptome ( Choate et al., 2024 ). This epigenetic remodelling extends into immune regulation in IDH-mutated low-grade gliomas, interferon signaling undergoes epigenetic silencing that reduces PD-L1 expression and limits T-cell exhaustion, while loss of the epigenetic regulator ATRX has separately been shown to drive PD-L1 production alongside multiple immunosuppressive cytokines, illustrating that IDH and co-occurring epigenetic alteration collectively modulate the immune landscape of glioma ( Wu et al., 2025 ). This immune remodeling occurs amid the highly immunosuppressive and heterogeneous GBM microenvironment, in which myeloid-derived suppressor cells and tumour-associated macrophages dominate the immune infiltrate, neutrophils within this microenvironment express arginase1 (ARG1), reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide synthase in the presence of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), thereby inactivating tumour-infiltrating T cells and reinforcing immune evasion independent of IDH status ( Sun et al., 2024 ). In parallel, IDH-mutant glioma cells exhibit considerable metabolic plasticity, and IDH1-mutant glioma cell lines have been demonstrated to undergo metabolic rewiring in response to glutamine/glutamate pathway inhibition, maintaining 2-HG production through alternative metabolic pathways ( Ruiz-Rodado et al., 2020 ). Collectively, these signaling, immune and metabolic layers indicate that IDH-directed monotherapy, however favourable at the binding level, may be insufficient to overcome the multifactorial resistance mechanisms operating within the GBM microenvironment, underscoring the need for combination therapeutic strategies in future translational work.

In addition, IDH mutations in GBM frequently co-occur with alterations in TP53, ATRX, EGFR, and MGMT, and these co-occurring alterations are not incidental to therapeutic response. IDH1, ATRX, and P53 expression status carry independent clinical and prognostic significance in glioblastoma, MGMT promoter methylation status remains a well-established determinant of response to alkylating chemotherapy, and EGFR, despite being mutationally active in over half of GBM cases, has so far proven difficult to target successfully due to poor tumour penetration and pathway redundancy ( Mansour et al., 2025 ; Weller et al., 2024 ; Ezzati et al., 2024 ). Computational screening approaches, included in this study, assess IDH inhibition in isolation, without capturing this genomic complexity, while actual therapeutic response in genomically heterogeneous GBM population is likely to be further modulated by TP53, ATRX, EGFR and MGMT status.

Recent clinical investigations targeting mutant IDH enzymes have provided important insights into glioma therapy and remain challenging in terms of treatment. IDH inhibitors such as Ivosidenib ( NCT02073994 ) of Phase I trials with a median progression-free survival (mPFS) of 13.6 months and Vorasidenib ( NCT02481154 ) have demonstrated promising activity in IDH-mutant gliomas by reducing the 2-HG level and prolonging progression-free survival in selected patient populations ( Carosi et al., 2024 ). Notably, the phase III INDIGO trial ( NCT04164901 ) showed that Vorasidenib significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma, highlighting the therapeutic potential of mutant IDH inhibition in lower-grade disease ( Carosi et al., 2024 ). Another study reported BAY1436032 ( NCT02746081 ) of a phase I trial to target IDH-mutant low-grade glioma, involving objective response rate (ORR) and PFS of up to 30 months ( Pusch et al., 2017 ). A perioperative Phase I trial ( NCT03343197 ) further reports that combined vorasidenib and ivosidenib treatment reduces 2-HG concentrations by approximately 92%, underscoring the functional on-target activity of IDH inhibition in CNS and Olutasidenib ( NCT03684811 ) achieved a disease control rate of only 48% in relapsed IDH1-mutant solid tumours ( Carosi et al., 2024 ). Beyond IDH-targeted therapies, the broader landscape of GBM clinical trials underscores the profound translational challenges inherent to this disease. Phase II evaluation of BGJ398 (Infigratinib, NCT01975701 ) in recurrent GBM demonstrated only 6 months of PFS ( Lassman et al., 2022 ). Ongoing trials including NEO212 ( NCT06047379 ) targeting IDH-mutant astrocytoma and GBM, Safusidenib ( NCT05303519 , NCT04458272 ) in IDH-mutant grade 2–4 glioma ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Natsume et al., 2023 ), and DS-1001b ( NCT03030066 ) in IDH1-R132 mutations, underscore ongoing efforts to overcome barriers and act as efficient inhibitors ( Natsume et al., 2023 ). Bevacizumab-based combinations ( NCT05201326 ) have similarly yielded limited survival benefit, reflecting the persistent challenge of translating encouraging phase II outcomes into successful phase III trials in GBM. However, despite these advances and the efficacy of IDH inhibitors in high-grade gliomas and GBM, critical limitations include tumour heterogeneity, acquired resistance mechanisms, BBB penetration and the complex immunometabolic landscape of advanced tumours. Such outcomes highlight the translational gap between computational or experimental predictions and clinical efficacy in glioma treatment. These challenges highlight the need for effective therapies capable of crossing the BBB and targeting tumour progression ( Chakravarty et al., 2021 ).

Our study proposes an integrated in silico strategy for glioblastoma therapy in targeting IDH enzymes, involving virtual screening, pharmacokinetic and ADME profiling, toxicity evaluation, molecular docking and MD simulations. Post-simulation analyses, including RMSD, RMSF, Rg, SASA, Hydrogen bonding, PCA, FEL, and MMPBSA, were employed to assess the stability, binding affinity, and dynamic behaviour of candidate compounds. In our study, standard and hit compounds act as better computationally predicted inhibitors with improved binding affinities for both IDH1 and IDH2, with interactions involving key residues such as TRP124, VAL 255, MET259, TYR272, GLN 277, and SER280 against IDH1, TRP164, LEU 298, ASP312 and LEU 320 against IDH2, than the study reported by ( Balaji et al., 2024 ) We compared our results with previously reported IDH1/IDH2 inhibitor studies ( Balaji et al., 2024 ), in which the standard compound Vorasidenib exhibited binding affinities of −5.47 kcal/mol against IDH1 and -6.27 kcal/mol against IDH2, indicating comparatively stronger interaction with IDH2 than IDH1. In contrast, our analysis revealed improved standard binding affinity of −6.17 kcal/mol against both IDH1 and IDH2, with our hit compounds I1Hit1 (−7.57 kcal/mol) and I2Hit1 (−11.23 kcal/mol) exhibiting improved predicted binding affinity relative to the standard. Post-simulation analyses indicated favourable dynamic stability for the lead complexes relative to their respective native proteins, with I1Hit1 and I2Hit1 showing consistently lower RMSF values, narrower and well-defined energy basins in PCA/FEL analysis, and persistent hydrogen bonding, supporting stable and reproducible binding conformations throughout the simulation trajectories. Binding free energy calculations using the MM-PBSA method further distinguished the relative affinities of the compounds. The I1Hit1 displayed strong binding of −20.67 ± 2.32 kcal/mol, whereas I1Hit2 showed −11.77 ± 4.84 kcal/mol with more reliable interactions with the standard (−14.96 ± 4.22 kcal/mol) against IDH1. For IDH2 complexes, I2Hit1 achieved the most favourable binding energy of −28.78 ± 2.67 kcal/mol, compared to I2Hit2 and the standard with binding energies of −8.91 ± 4.74 kcal/mol and −24.87 ± 3.55 kcal/mol, respectively. Collectively, in our study, I1Hit1 and I2Hit1 were identified as promising hit compounds against mutant IDH targets based on integrated in silico analyses. In our study, vorasidenib exhibited binding free energies of −14.96 ± 4.22 kcal/mol against mutant IDH1 and -24.87 ± 3.55 kcal/mol against mutant IDH2. Similar analyses of MM-PBSA were performed with different isoforms of mutant IDH and reported as a separate study examining the mechanistic role of olutasidenib in the selective inhibition of mutated IDH1 with a total binding free energy of −56.82 kcal/mol against mutant IDH1, considerably higher than the corresponding value of −14.48 kcal/mol, against mutant IDH2 ( Salifu et al., 2022 ). Interestingly, I1Hit2 & I2Hit2 (PubChem ID 4946), identified as a potential hit compound in the present study, have been previously reported to inhibit GBM cell proliferation through Notch1 and Hes1 signaling pathway in vitro . While distinct from IDH-mediated mechanisms, this evidence reinforces its potential as a multi-target agent in GBM therapy ( Kim et al., 2021 ). Notably, Propranolol (I1Hit2 & I2Hit2, PubChem ID 4946), a clinically approved cardiovascular beta-blocker that was independently identified as a top computational hit against both mutant IDH1 and IDH2, represents a drug repurposing finding of translational significance. Its established safety profile, oral bioavailability, predicted BBB permeability, and commercial availability make it a promising candidate for further experimental investigation in IDH-mutant GBM, consistent with emerging evidence supporting the anticancer potential of beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists in glioma. Although I1Hit1 has been reported to exert anti-tumour effects through inhibition of tumour angiogenesis and endothelial proliferation ( Ma et al., 2008 ), and I2Hit1 has been reported for diverse biological activities, including cytotoxic and anti-inflammatory properties, their potential role in targeting IDH-driven oncogenic metabolism in glioblastoma remains largely unexplored. In this regard, I1Hit1 (PubChem ID 91457) and I2Hit1 (PubChem ID 71550939) are identified by our docking, molecular dynamics simulation, PCA, and MMPBSA analyses as novel small-molecule inhibitors that may effectively modulate IDH-driven oncogenic metabolism in GBM. Importantly, their predicted pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles further support their efficiency as lead compounds. The present study employed a multi-stage orthogonal computational validation comprising molecular docking, 300 ns of MDS, PCA, MM-PBSA calculations and pharmacophore analysis for a potential drug candidate with high binding affinity and stability to IDH1 and IDH2. Nevertheless, these promising compounds required further experimental validation including, recombinant IDH-R132H and IDH2-R140Q enzymatic inhibition assays, 2-HG quantification and cytotoxicity evaluation in GBM cell lines ( Josephine et al., 2026 ; Schulz et al., 2022 ). Consequently, experimental investigation is crucial for establishing their therapeutic potential and advancing them toward clinical translation.

## Conclusion

This study employed an integrated computational approach to identify potential inhibitors targeting mutant IDH1 and IDH2 enzymes in GBM. PubChem ID 91457 (I1Hit1) against IDH1 and PubChem ID 71550939 (I2Hit1) against IDH2 were identified as individual potential hit compounds following multiple virtual screening, ADMET filtering, and several molecular analyses. These compounds demonstrated better binding affinity, favourable drug-likeness, and enhanced structural stability compared to the standard reference compound. Further, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, PCA, and MMPBSA analyses supported the stability and interaction strength of these complexes, suggesting their potential to inhibit both cytosolic and mitochondrial IDH isoforms. The identified hit compounds may regulate IDH-associated metabolic alterations, including redox imbalance, NADPH depletion, oxidative stress, and epigenetic dysregulation associated with GBM progression. Collectively, these findings highlight I1Hit1 and I2Hit1 as computationally prioritized candidates for IDH-targeted therapy in GBM, and the integrated computational framework outlined in this study provides a replicable platform for advancing novel IDH-targeted inhibitors toward preclinical investigation. As this study is purely computational in scope, future experimental validation, including enzymatic inhibition assays, 2-HG quantification, and cell-based evaluation in IDH-mutant GBM cell lines, is essential to confirm the therapeutic potential of these identified candidates and advance them toward clinical translation.

title: Granular parakeratosis associated with the use of laundry sanitizers containing benzalkonium chloride: a case report
abstract:
### Background

Granular parakeratosis (GP) is a rare benign inflammatory dermatosis that preferentially involves the axillae and other intertriginous, friction-prone skin sites and typically presents with pruritic erythema and scaling. Cases associated with benzalkonium chloride (BAC) exposure have rarely been systematically summarized, and further clinical evidence is needed. Herein, we report a case of generalized GP potentially associated with long-term exposure to a BAC-containing laundry sanitizer, with the aim of expanding the clinical spectrum of cutaneous adverse reactions associated with BAC.

### Case presentation

A 43-year-old Asian man presented with a persistent rash on the trunk and intertriginous areas for more than 1 year. He had a long-standing history of eczema with possible underlying skin-barrier dysfunction but no confirmed diagnosis of atopic dermatitis. He had regularly used a commercial laundry sanitizer containing BAC (0.5 g/L) for clothing disinfection since June 2020, at a frequency of 1–3 times per week. The first rash appeared in July 2021, approximately 13 months after the start of exposure, initially involving the groin and subsequently spreading symmetrically to the neck, axillae, antecubital fossae, lateral waist, back (with sparing of the spinal midline), and undergarment-covered areas. Fungal microscopy and periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining were negative. Histopathology showed epidermal hyperkeratosis with characteristic granular parakeratosis, intracorneal pustule formation, neutrophil aggregation, and superficial dermal perivascular inflammatory infiltrates. Direct immunofluorescence for IgG, IgA, IgM, and C3 was negative. In August 2023, the patient completely discontinued the BAC-containing laundry sanitizer, repeatedly rinsed all garments with clean water, and used topical emollients for skin-barrier repair. The lesions gradually subsided and achieved complete clinical remission in September 2023, approximately 1 month after the intervention. No recurrence was observed during 1 year of follow-up.

### Conclusions

Exposure to BAC-containing laundry sanitizer may be a potential trigger for generalized GP in susceptible individuals. A history of eczema and associated skin-barrier dysfunction may increase susceptibility to irritant exposure. Avoidance of suspected irritants together with skin-barrier repair may be effective in the management of BAC-associated GP. Further prospective studies and confirmatory testing are needed to clarify the causal relationship.

# Granular parakeratosis associated with the use of laundry sanitizers containing benzalkonium chloride: a case report

## Abstract
### Background

The first rash appeared in July 2021, approximately 13 months after the start of exposure, initially involving the groin and subsequently spreading symmetrically to the neck, axillae, antecubital fossae, lateral waist, back (with sparing of the spinal midline), and undergarment-covered areas. Fungal microscopy and periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining were negative. Histopathology showed epidermal hyperkeratosis with characteristic granular parakeratosis, intracorneal pustule formation, neutrophil aggregation, and superficial dermal perivascular inflammatory infiltrates. Direct immunofluorescence for IgG, IgA, IgM, and C3 was negative. In August 2023, the patient completely discontinued the BAC-containing laundry sanitizer, repeatedly rinsed all garments with clean water, and used topical emollients for skin-barrier repair. The lesions gradually subsided and achieved complete clinical remission in September 2023, approximately 1 month after the intervention. No recurrence was observed during 1 year of follow-up.

### Conclusions

Exposure to BAC-containing laundry sanitizer may be a potential trigger for generalized GP in susceptible individuals. A history of eczema and associated skin-barrier dysfunction may increase susceptibility to irritant exposure. Avoidance of suspected irritants together with skin-barrier repair may be effective in the management of BAC-associated GP. Further prospective studies and confirmatory testing are needed to clarify the causal relationship.

## Keywords
benzalkonium chloride; granular parakeratosis; intertriginous areas; laundry sanitizer; skin barrier dysfunction

## Introduction

Granular parakeratosis (GP) is an uncommon benign inflammatory dermatosis characterized histologically by hyperkeratosis with retained keratohyalin granules in the stratum corneum. It mainly affects intertriginous skin, including the axillae, groin, and inframammary areas ( 1 ). Clinically, GP typically manifests as erythematous, scaly, pruritic papules or plaques and may occasionally show pustular features, with exacerbation in hot and humid environments. Its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood and is generally considered to represent a reactive epidermal process associated with occlusion, excessive sweating, maceration, or external irritants ( 2 ).

With the widespread use of disinfectant products, GP associated with exposure to benzalkonium chloride (BAC) has been increasingly recognized ( 5 , 7 ). BAC is a quaternary ammonium compound widely used as a disinfectant and preservative in laundry products, personal-care products, and medical solutions. However, published evidence largely consists of case reports and small case series. Herein, we report a case of generalized GP with a detailed history of exposure to a BAC-containing laundry sanitizer, clinical course, ancillary investigations, and treatment outcome, and discuss the relevant differential diagnoses and potential role of BAC exposure.

## Case presentation

A 43-year-old Asian man presented to our dermatology outpatient department with a more than 1-year history of recurrent and progressive skin lesions. The eruption initially appeared in the groin and gradually extended to the trunk and major intertriginous areas over approximately 6 months. During disease progression, the patient reported intermittent burning pain, local swelling, and mild pruritus. The lesions worsened markedly in summer with heat, sweating, and increased skin moisture, but improved during the cooler and drier autumn and winter months. In hot weather, the lesions were characterized predominantly by bright erythema with numerous pinpoint pustules. During periods of improvement, the erythema faded to brown hyperpigmented patches with thin brown scales.

The patient had a history of eczema, with occasional mild xerosis and pruritus, but had never received a definite diagnosis of atopic dermatitis. He had no other chronic systemic diseases, no history of chemotherapy or long-term use of relevant medications, and no family history of hereditary or autoimmune skin disease. Before presentation, he had intermittently used a topical compound corticosteroid ointment, which temporarily relieved the pruritus and erythema; however, the lesions rapidly recurred after treatment was discontinued. He also reported an unpleasant odor from the affected skin during heavy sweating, which affected his daily life and quality of life. General physical examination revealed no significant abnormalities.

Detailed exposure timeline: The patient began using a commercial laundry sanitizer containing BAC (0.5 g/L) in June 2020, generally 1–3 times per week. The first skin eruption appeared in July 2021, approximately 13 months after the start of exposure, initially involving the groin. Despite persistent and progressive lesions, he continued to use the sanitizer intermittently. In August 2023, he completely discontinued the BAC-containing laundry sanitizer, thoroughly rinsed all garments with clean water multiple times before wearing them, and consistently applied topical emollients for skin-barrier repair. The lesions gradually subsided and achieved complete clinical remission in September 2023, approximately 1 month after the intervention. No recurrence was observed during the 1-year telephone follow-up through September 2024.

Dermatological examination showed symmetrically distributed lesions involving the neck, bilateral axillae, antecubital fossae, lateral waist, paravertebral back (with sparing of the spinal midline), and undergarment-covered areas. The lesions consisted of irregular map-like annular erythema with central hyperpigmentation, superficial leaf-like scaling, and numerous pinpoint pustules on the erythematous base ( Figures 1a–c ).

Fungal microscopic examination was performed on scales scraped from active lesions, and no fungal hyphae or spores were identified. PAS staining of lesional tissue was also negative, providing no evidence of superficial fungal infection. A skin biopsy was obtained from an active erythematopustular lesion in the inguinal region. Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed marked epidermal hyperkeratosis, characteristic granular parakeratosis with retained keratohyalin granules in the stratum corneum, intracorneal pustule formation with prominent neutrophil aggregation, and superficial dermal perivascular inflammatory infiltrates composed predominantly of lymphocytes with scattered neutrophils ( Figures 2a,b ). Direct immunofluorescence showed no deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, or C3 in the epidermis or dermis. Based on the clinical presentation, negative fungal studies, and characteristic histopathological findings, a diagnosis of granular parakeratosis was made.

Following diagnosis, the patient continued strict avoidance of BAC-containing laundry disinfectants, enhanced rinsing of clothing, and regular topical emollient therapy for skin-barrier repair. No systemic medication or topical corticosteroid was used. All lesions resolved completely within approximately 1 month, and no recurrence occurred during the 1-year follow-up.

## Discussion and conclusions

GP is a rare benign skin condition that most commonly affects the axillae and other intertriginous areas and is frequently associated with pruritus. Although its etiology remains uncertain, GP is generally regarded as a reactive epidermal process ( 1 ). Reported precipitating factors include occlusion ( 2 ), warm environments ( 3 ), sweating, obesity, frequent washing ( 4 ), and exposure to external irritants such as antiperspirants, deodorants, and zinc oxide. BAC, a preservative and antimicrobial agent present in numerous products including laundry products, personal-hygiene wipes, and medical solutions, has also been associated with GP ( 5 – 7 ).

Previous studies have suggested that atopic dermatitis may predispose patients to GP because epidermal-barrier dysfunction may facilitate penetration of irritants ( 8 , 9 ). Although the present patient had a long-standing history of eczema rather than confirmed atopic dermatitis, impaired skin-barrier function may have increased susceptibility to repeated irritant exposure. Residual BAC on clothing may have provided repeated cutaneous exposure. As a cationic surfactant, BAC may disrupt epidermal barrier function and interfere with keratinocyte maturation ( 5 , 6 ). Heat, sweating, moisture, and friction may further promote maceration and irritation, potentially accounting for the marked seasonal fluctuation observed in this patient.

Physical factors such as hyperhidrosis, obesity, and friction have also been proposed to contribute to GP by impairing epidermal maturation and barrier function ( 5 , 10 ). The skin microbiome may influence epidermal development and cutaneous immune responses ( 11 , 12 ), and Kumarasinghe et al. proposed that overgrowth of anaerobic flora could contribute to hyperkeratotic flexural eruptions resembling GP ( 13 ). GP has also been reported in association with chemotherapy for ovarian cancer ( 14 ).

Differential diagnosis: The clinical presentation of GP may be confused with several pustular and inflammatory dermatoses ( 1 ). Pustular psoriasis may present with widespread sterile pustules on an erythematous, infiltrated background and, in severe cases, systemic symptoms such as fever. Histopathology typically shows psoriasiform epidermal changes and neutrophilic collections rather than the characteristic granular parakeratosis seen in this case ( 2 ). Superficial fungal infections may present with erythema and scaling and can clinically mimic GP. In superficial fungal infections, direct microscopic examination typically demonstrates fungal hyphae, and PAS staining may reveal fungal elements within the stratum corneum. In the present case, however, repeated fungal microscopic examination showed no hyphae or spores, and PAS staining of lesional tissue was negative, providing no evidence of superficial fungal infection ( 3 ). IgA pemphigus may present with superficial pustules in annular or circinate configurations; direct immunofluorescence typically demonstrates intercellular IgA deposition in the epidermis, which was absent in this case ( 4 ). Subcorneal pustular dermatosis is characterized by recurrent superficial pustules with subcorneal neutrophilic accumulation on histopathology; the presence of characteristic granular parakeratosis supported GP in this patient. Inverse psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, and erythrasma were also considered less likely on the basis of the clinical and ancillary findings.

The prognosis of GP is generally favorable. Removal of suspected irritants and measures to restore the skin barrier may lead to remission, whereas selected persistent cases have been treated with topical or systemic retinoids ( 15 – 17 ). In the present case, complete remission occurred after discontinuation of the BAC-containing sanitizer, repeated rinsing of clothing, and topical emollient therapy. Because these interventions were introduced simultaneously and no confirmatory challenge testing was performed, the clinical response supports an association with irritant avoidance but does not establish BAC as the sole causal agent.

In conclusion, this case highlights BAC-containing laundry sanitizer as a potential trigger of generalized GP. Careful assessment of household product exposure may be useful in patients with GP, particularly when lesions involve flexural or clothing-covered areas. Avoidance of suspected irritants and skin-barrier repair should be considered as practical management measures. Further studies are required to clarify the causal relationship between BAC exposure and GP.

## Limitations

This report has several limitations. First, it describes a single retrospective case and therefore provides limited evidence regarding causality or generalizability. Second, neither patch testing nor a re-challenge test was performed; consequently, BAC should be regarded as a potential trigger rather than a confirmed cause. Third, the commercial laundry sanitizer contained ingredients other than BAC, and a contribution from other components cannot be excluded. Fourth, several interventions—discontinuation of the sanitizer, repeated rinsing of clothing, and topical emollient therapy—were initiated concurrently, making it impossible to determine the independent effect of each measure. Further controlled studies incorporating confirmatory testing are needed to clarify the relationship between BAC-containing laundry products and GP.
conclusions: Exposure to BAC-containing laundry sanitizer may be a potential trigger for generalized GP in susceptible individuals. A history of eczema and associated skin-barrier dysfunction may increase susceptibility to irritant exposure. Avoidance of suspected irritants together with skin-barrier repair may be effective in the management of BAC-associated GP. Further prospective studies and confirmatory testing are needed to clarify the causal relationship.

title: Emerging applications of non-thermal ultrasound technology in functional beverages processing, a comprehensive review
abstract: Non-thermal ultrasonication (US) is emerging as a promising process-intensification technology for producing functional beverages (FB) as the conventional thermal processing and additive-reliant preservation methods often compromise thermolabile nutrients, sensory profile, and clean-label appeal of FB. However, evidence regarding the application of US to the processing and preservation of FB matrices remains limited and fragmented, and clear, reproducible guidelines for process optimization and commercial translation are still lacking. This review critically summarizes recent research on the application of non-thermal US across key FB unit operations, including extraction, fermentation, preservation, and physicochemical structuring, and examines how cavitation-driven mechanisms influence nutritional, functional, sensory, and stability outcomes. A structured literature review was conducted, with studies organized by processing functions and beverage matrix characteristics to identify consistent trends and matrix-dependent variations (including occasional reversals in effects). Overall, US frequently enhances mass transfer and dispersion, improves the recovery and retention of selected bioactive compounds, supports textural and physical stability (e.g., reduced sedimentation or creaming), and aids microbial and enzymatic control, especially when integrated into hurdle strategies (e.g., US combined with mild heating, clean-label antimicrobials, or other non-thermal technologies). Nevertheless, broader translation remains constrained by inconsistent reporting of delivered acoustic energy and temperature profiles, strong dependence on formulation factors (e.g., viscosity, total soluble solids, particulates, and protein–polysaccharide interactions), and a lack of pilot-scale or continuous-flow validation supported by techno-economic assessment. Critically, claims of health relevance of FB are weakly supported because bioaccessibility and bioavailability testing, in vivo animal studies, and human clinical evidence remain largely missing. Collectively, this review provides a function-based framework together with practical research priorities to enable reproducible optimization, scalable processing, and more robust claims regarding the quality and functionality of US-processed FB.

# Emerging applications of non-thermal ultrasound technology in functional beverages processing, a comprehensive review

## Abstract
Non-thermal ultrasonication (US) is emerging as a promising process-intensification technology for producing functional beverages (FB) as the conventional thermal processing and additive-reliant preservation methods often compromise thermolabile nutrients, sensory profile, and clean-label appeal of FB. However, evidence regarding the application of US to the processing and preservation of FB matrices remains limited and fragmented, and clear, reproducible guidelines for process optimization and commercial translation are still lacking. This review critically summarizes recent research on the application of non-thermal US across key FB unit operations, including extraction, fermentation, preservation, and physicochemical structuring, and examines how cavitation-driven mechanisms influence nutritional, functional, sensory, and stability outcomes. A structured literature review was conducted, with studies organized by processing functions and beverage matrix characteristics to identify consistent trends and matrix-dependent variations (including occasional reversals in effects). Overall, US frequently enhances mass transfer and dispersion, improves the recovery and retention of selected bioactive compounds, supports textural and physical stability (e.g., reduced sedimentation or creaming), and aids microbial and enzymatic control, especially when integrated into hurdle strategies (e.g., US combined with mild heating, clean-label antimicrobials, or other non-thermal technologies). Nevertheless, broader translation remains constrained by inconsistent reporting of delivered acoustic energy and temperature profiles, strong dependence on formulation factors (e.g., viscosity, total soluble solids, particulates, and protein–polysaccharide interactions), and a lack of pilot-scale or continuous-flow validation supported by techno-economic assessment. Critically, claims of health relevance of FB are weakly supported because bioaccessibility and bioavailability testing, in vivo animal studies, and human clinical evidence remain largely missing. Collectively, this review provides a function-based framework together with practical research priorities to enable reproducible optimization, scalable processing, and more robust claims regarding the quality and functionality of US-processed FB.

## Keywords
Acoustic cavitation; Clean-label technology; Process intensification; Hurdle technology; Continuous-flow scale-up

## Introduction

The global beverage industry is undergoing a profound paradigm shift, driven by growing consumer awareness of the links between diet, chronic diseases, and long-term wellness [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] . While conventional beverages have traditionally served as convenient sources of hydration, refreshment, and instant energy, they are increasingly associated with a range of health concerns [5] . Beyond their high sugar content, which contributes to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases, many conventional beverages are characterized by high glycemic load, low nutritional density, and the extensive use of artificial colors, flavors, and preservatives [6] , [7] . Even sugar-free formulations often rely on high-intensity artificial sweeteners, which have been reported to alter gut microbiota composition, disrupt metabolic regulation, and raise concerns regarding long-term metabolic health [8] . Energy drinks in particular have been associated with multiple adverse health outcomes, largely attributed to their high caffeine content, excessive sugar levels, and the presence of multiple stimulant additives, highlighting the need for safer and nutritionally balanced beverage alternatives [9] . Moreover, the acidic nature of many carbonated beverages accelerates dental erosion, while added sodium may contribute to hypertension and fluid retention. In response to growing health awareness and evolving lifestyle preferences, consumers are increasingly seeking healthy beverages that combine sensory appeal with genuine nutritional value and functional benefits [10] .

As a result, the global beverage sector is rapidly shifting towards healthy FB. These formulations are enriched with natural, clean-label, and health-enhancing ingredients derived from various sources [5] , [11] . FB are designed to provide specific physiological or health benefits beyond basic hydration and caloric intake, typically by incorporating various BAC, essential nutrients, vitamins, minerals, probiotics, prebiotics, plant extracts, and antioxidants [1] , [12] . FB are formulated to support a wide range of targeted functions, while meeting consumer demand for clean-label, low-sugar, and minimally processed products [3] , [5] , [10] , [13] . FB represent a rapidly expanding sector, with the global market projected to exceed USD 300 billion by 2035, underscoring their growing industrial and consumer relevance [14] . However, despite their strong growth potential, FB face significant technological challenges because they rely on natural and nutrient-rich ingredients; they are highly perishable and exhibit a limited shelf life. This is primarily due to the activity of endogenous enzymes, particularly PPO, POD, PME, and, in some matrices, LOX, together with rapid microbial proliferation [15] . Additional challenges include potential contamination during raw material sourcing, processing, and storage; degradation of nutrients and BAC; pH-related instability; and complex interactions among functional ingredients throughout the supply chain. Collectively, these limitations underscore the urgent need for effective processing and preservation strategies to ensure microbial safety, maintain nutritional and functional quality, and extend the shelf life of FB.

Conventional beverage processing methods can adversely affect the quality, stability, and functionality of these sensitive beverages. During extraction, the use of heat or chemical solvents often degrades thermolabile nutrients and sensitive BAC, thereby reducing the quality of the final product. Traditional fermentation processes tend to be slow, difficult to control, and inconsistent, leading to variability in flavor, microbial balance, and overall product quality [16] . Likewise, conventional homogenization and mixing techniques may cause protein denaturation, reduced solubility, or non-uniform dispersion of functional ingredients. For microbial control, chemical preservatives such as benzoates, sorbates, and sulfites are commonly employed [7] . Although effective in extending shelf life, their excessive or prolonged use has raised health concerns, including allergic reactions, gastrointestinal disturbances, and potential long-term toxicological effects [17] . Furthermore, certain chemical additives may adversely affect sensory attributes, resulting in off-flavors and reduced consumer acceptance. Thermal preservation techniques, such as pasteurization and sterilization, have therefore been widely adopted as alternatives to synthetic preservatives [3] , [18] . Pasteurization effectively reduces pathogenic and spoilage microorganisms while extending shelf life, whereas sterilization achieves more extensive microbial inactivation, including bacterial spores, to ensure long-term stability. However, thermal processing can degrade heat-sensitive functional ingredients, modify delicate sensory attributes, and promote the formation of undesirable compounds in FB [19] . In response to these limitations of conventional processing methods and the growing consumer demand for sustainable, clean-label, minimally processed, and additive-free beverages with fresh-like attributes, the food industry has increasingly turned to non-thermal processing and preservation technologies [15] . These innovative, sustainable, and environmentally friendly approaches provide viable alternatives to traditional methods by enhancing product safety and quality while minimizing losses in nutritional value and sensory attributes [20] , [21] . Several non-thermal processing technologies have gained increasing attention in recent years, including US, high-pressure processing, pulsed electric field, cold plasma, pulsed light, OZ, and irradiation [3] , [18] , [22] . Among them, US has emerged as a particularly promising and cost-effective option due to its versatility across multiple stages of beverage, including extraction, separation, emulsification, homogenization, fermentation, microbial and enzyme inactivation, particle size reduction, nanoencapsulation, mixing, and modification of functional properties [23] , [24] . US operates through the generation of high-frequency sound waves that induce acoustic cavitation, resulting in localized micro-jets, intense shear forces, and transient high–temperature–pressure zones, which enhance mass transfer, disrupt cellular structures, and accelerate desirable physicochemical transformations [25] , [26] , [27] . Furthermore, US contributes to environmental sustainability by reducing energy and water consumption and minimizing reliance on chemical additives, positioning it as an efficient and eco-friendly technology that aligns with both consumer quality expectations and modern sustainability goals in food and beverage processing.

This review critically examines US as a process-intensification platform for producing FB. It integrates current evidence on the application of US in extraction, fermentation, preservation, and quality structuring, while linking cavitation-driven mechanisms to improvements in nutritional, functional, physicochemical, and sensory performance. Although several reviews have discussed US processing, non-thermal technologies, or FB individually, existing reviews generally focus on specific processing operations, particular food matrices, or general food applications rather than providing an integrated assessment of US applications across the major processing stages of FB. The present review adopts a function-based framework that critically synthesizes US-assisted extraction, fermentation, preservation, and physicochemical structuring while emphasizing mechanistic understanding, engineering considerations, scalability, and future research needs. Its novelty also lies in highlighting key engineering and translational gaps that currently limit industrial adoption. These include incomplete reporting of delivered acoustic energy and temperature history, limited pilot/continuous-flow validation, and the weak linkage between processing gains and health substantiation (bioaccessibility, bioavailability, in-vitro digestion, and in-vivo animal or human evidence). In this review, FB are defined as beverage systems formulated or processed to contain elevated levels of bioactives or functional ingredients with potential physiological benefits, while recognizing that many commercial products and research studies still lack direct validation through bioaccessibility, bioavailability, or in-vivo evidence.

## Methodology of review

This review was conducted using a structured and reproducible literature search strategy to evaluate recent research on the application of US in the development of FB. Because US-based processing encompasses a broad range of operating conditions, clear terminology is critical. In this review, non-thermal US refers to the treatments in which the bulk product temperature remains sufficiently low to avoid significant thermal effects, and the observed changes are primarily attributed to acoustic cavitation. Mild thermosonication refers to the intentional combination of US with moderate heating (typically below conventional pasteurization temperatures) to enhance microbial inactivation or processing efficiency through synergistic effects. In contrast, US-assisted thermal extraction involves the application of US together with elevated extraction temperatures, where both cavitation and thermal mechanisms contribute to improved mass transfer and extraction efficiency. Although this review primarily focuses on non-thermal US processing, studies employing mild thermosonication or US-assisted thermal extraction were included when they provided important mechanistic insights or demonstrated practical relevance for FB processing.

Scientific publications were retrieved from three major databases (Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar), yielding 166, 112, and 65 (total: 343) records, respectively, covering the period from 2018 to 2026. The literature search was performed using combinations of keywords related to US processing and FB. Primary search terms included: “ultrasound”, “ultrasonication”, “sonication”, “ultrasound-assisted processing”, “ultrasound assisted extraction”, “ultrasound assisted fermentation”, ultrasound assisted preservation” “thermosonication”, and “ultrasound treatment”. These were combined with beverage-related terms such as “functional beverages”, “functional drinks”, “functional juices”, and “fermented beverages” using Boolean operators (AND and OR) to refine the results. This approach ensured the retrieval of studies specifically addressing the application of US in extraction, fermentation, preservation, and quality improvement of FB systems. To identify thematic structures and research trends within the field, a keyword co-occurrence analysis was performed using Scopus-indexed data. Author keywords were analyzed and visualized using VOSviewer to map the relationships among core research themes, including ultrasonics, ultrasound, functional beverages, extraction, antioxidant activity, physicochemical properties, functional properties, preservation, and pasteurization ( Fig. 1 A) . The time frame (2018–2026) was selected to capture recent advances in the application of US in producing FB, as only limited and fragmented research existed on this topic prior to 2018. The annual publication trend indicates a steady increase in research output from 2018 onward ( Fig. 1 B) . These databases were selected to provide comprehensive coverage of peer-reviewed literature in the field. After importing all records into a reference management system, following duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment based on the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 48 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The studies meeting the following inclusion criteria were retained: (1) ultrasonication, ultrasound, or sonication was directly applied in the extraction or bioprocessing of functional compounds for incorporation into beverages; (2) it improved fermentation efficiency, microbial activity, or functional metabolite production in beverage systems; (3) it was used primarily to extend shelf life or ensure microbial safety while retaining functional constituents; or (4) it contributed to improvements in physicochemical stability, sensory attributes, or uniform distribution of functional ingredients. Moreover, FB primarily comprised non-alcoholic beverages; however, traditional fermented beverage systems with naturally low alcohol contents (e.g., kombucha and Jun tea) were also included when their primary objective was to deliver functional benefits through BAC, probiotics, or fermentation-derived metabolites rather than alcoholic content. Studies focused exclusively on alcoholic beverage production were excluded. Similarly, semi-finished extracts were included only when they were subsequently incorporated into FB formulations. This classification enabled a structured and comparative evaluation of US applications across distinct FB processing and preservation strategies. The selected studies originated predominantly from China, Brazil, Pakistan, Mexico, and India, reflecting the global research activity in this field. Data from these studies were extracted and synthesized narratively to highlight processing mechanisms, functional outcomes, quality attributes, and emerging research trends.

## Overview of FB

The concept of functional foods and beverages is not new, as many traditional diets historically recognized health benefits of certain foods and drinks beyond basic nutrition. With advances in nutritional science in the early twentieth century, researchers began to demonstrate that specific foods could modulate physiological functions, thereby establishing the scientific foundation for functional food research. The modern concept of functional foods was formally institutionalized in Japan during the 1980s with the introduction of the Foods for Specified Health Uses (FOSHU) system, the first regulatory framework permitting health-related claims on foods [4] . From the late 1990s onward, FB emerged as a distinct and rapidly expanding category globally, driven by growing consumer awareness of the links between diet and chronic disease prevention [11] . Recent market analyses indicate continued expansion of the global FB market, reflecting increasing industrial and commercial interest in advanced processing technologies capable of preserving nutritional and functional quality ( Fig. 2 A-D) [14] . FB are designed to support the management and prevention of a broad spectrum of health conditions [11] , [12] while adhering to clean-label, low-sugar, and minimally processed formulation strategies [3] , [22] , [28] . There are different types of FB based on their primary ingredients and intended benefits. Common categories include fortified dairy beverages, prebiotic, probiotic and fermented beverages, functional waters, nutrient-enriched fruit and vegetables juices, beauty and anti-aging beverages, plant-based beverages, phyto-active fortified beverages, sports drinks, energy drinks, herbal and botanical infusions, and psychobiotic drinks [4] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] . Functional dairy beverages are enriched with essential nutrients such as vitamins, minerals, proteins, dietary fiber, omega-3 fatty acids, probiotics, and prebiotics. These components collectively contribute to bone integrity, cardiovascular function, and gut microbiota homeostasis [5] , [12] , [13] , [26] , [29] . Functional dairy beverages encompass a diverse range of products, including probiotic and synbiotic fermented milks (e.g., yogurt drinks and kefir), fortified milks, whey proteein-based functional drinks, other protein-enriched dairy beverages, and dairy-based formulations enriched with prebiotics, antioxidants, or plant-derived functional ingredients [5] , [12] . Probiotic, prebiotic, and fermented FB represent a major segment of the FB industry due to their pronounced effects on gastrointestinal health [4] , [5] , [13] , [27] , [30] . In parallel, functional waters constitute a rapidly expanding category, formulated by enriching water with vitamins, minerals, electrolytes, antioxidants, and other BAC to support hydration and physiological balance. Subcategories include electrolyte-fortified waters for hydration and physical recovery, vitamin-enriched waters targeting immune and metabolic functions, and herbal or adaptogenic waters designed to modulate stress responses and cognitive resilience [12] .

Functional fruit and vegetable juices are fortified with essential micronutrients, prebiotics, probiotics, and BAC [1] , [12] , [28] , [31] . Enrichment with vitamin C, polyphenols, and carotenoids enhances antioxidant capacity and immune functions, while the incorporation of dietary fiber and omega-3 fatty acids supports cardiovascular and digestive health [4] , [32] , [33] . Beauty and anti-aging FB constitute an emerging market segment focused on supporting skin hydration, elasticity, and dermal integrity. Such products commonly incorporate collagen peptides, hyaluronic acid, antioxidants, and botanical extracts, reflecting the growing interest in nutricosmetic approaches that integrate nutritional and cosmetic benefits [34] , [35] . In parallel, phyto-active and plant-based FB, derived from matrices such as oats, almonds, soy, and sea buckthorn, typically offer reduced saturated fat content and moderate energy density compared to conventional dairy-based drinks [28] , [36] . Sports beverages, typically formulated as carbohydrate–electrolyte solutions, are designed to support hydration, energy replenishment, and physical performance [37] , [38] . In contrast, energy drinks aim to enhance alertness and cognitive performance through central nervous system stimulation. They often contain caffeine, amino acids, and herbal extracts [12] , [39] , [40] .

Herbal and botanical infusions deliver plant-derived BAC with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and stress-modulating properties, while psychobiotic beverages represent a rapidly developing category designed to influence gut–brain axis communication by leveraging microbial production of neuroactive compounds, such as γ-aminobutyric acid and serotonin, thereby supporting cognitive and emotional well-being [41] . Overall, FB plays an increasingly important role in modern nutrition by providing targeted physiological support through anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, metabolic, and stress-related pathways. Continued advances in ingredient technology and processing strategies are driving the evolution of this sector toward nutrient-dense, convenient, and scientifically substantiated health-oriented beverage solutions [1] , [11] , [12] . ## Application of US in processing of FB

FB are complex, multi-component systems whose quality, stability, and functionality are strongly influenced by various processing operations, such as the extraction, fermentation, homogenization, emulsification, and preservation. Conventional processing technologies used across these stages, including thermal treatments, mechanical mixing, and chemical-assisted extraction, often suffer from critical limitations, such as low extraction efficiency, prolonged processing times, inconsistent fermentation performance, degradation of heat-sensitive compounds, and undesirable changes in sensory attributes. These challenges are further exacerbated in FB due to their high nutritional density, complex natural composition, and the inherent sensitivity of functional ingredients, necessitating advanced processing approaches that can simultaneously enhance process efficiency while preserving nutritional value and sensory integrity [3] , [22] , [27] , [28] , [42] .

In response to these constraints, a spectrum of non-thermal processing technologies has been explored to enhance processing efficiency and final product quality in FB manufacturing, as summarized in Fig. 4 [4] , [10] . Among these approaches, US has emerged as a particularly versatile platform technology due to its ability to be integrated across multiple processing stages, such as extraction, fermentation intensification, homogenization, degassing, cell disruption and lysis, emulsification, crystallization control, defoaming, microbial and enzymatic inactivation, as well as equipment cleaning and sanitation [24] , [43] . Within FB systems, these capabilities enable enhanced recovery and stability of BAC, improved dispersion and physicochemical stability of complex formulations, modulation of fermentation kinetics, reduction of dissolved gases and foam formation, improved microbial control, and overall preservation of nutritional and sensory quality without reliance on harsh thermal or chemical treatments. US operates through the application of high-frequency sound waves beyond the human audible range (typically 20 kHz–10 MHz), which induce acoustic cavitation [24] . The growth and violent collapse of cavitation bubbles generate localized high-energy microenvironments characterized by extreme temperatures (up to ∼ 5000 K), high pressures (hundreds of atmospheres), intense shear forces, microjets, turbulence, and transient heating. Detailed descriptions of US principles, cavitation dynamics, reactor configurations (bath, probe, plate, and flow-through systems), process parameters, and radical formation mechanisms are provided in our previous reviews on US [16] , [44] . Another significant advantage of US is its energy efficiency and sustainability, as it requires lower energy input and reduced processing time compared to conventional methods, making it a more environmentally sustainable alternative [5] . The application and implementation of US across different stages of FB processing are discussed in detail in the following sections. ### US-assisted extraction

Extraction is a fundamental operation in food processing for isolating target substances from natural matrices using appropriate solvents and processing techniques [16] . Compared with raw or powdered ingredients, extracts are generally preferred due to their enhanced solubility, uniform dispersion, improved bioavailability, and greater consistency in sensory attributes. In the context of FB, efficient extraction is particularly critical, as these products are increasingly formulated with diverse functional ingredients to enhance nutritional quality, physiological functionality, and health-related benefits [45] , [46] . Traditionally, extraction has relied on conventional methods such as maceration, Soxhlet extraction, percolation, reflux extraction, solid–liquid solvent extraction, infusion, decoction, and mechanical pressing. Although widely employed, these techniques are often constrained by long processing times, high solvent consumption, potential degradation of heat-sensitive nutrients, and relatively low extraction yields [44] , [45] , [47] . To overcome these limitations, UAE has emerged as an efficient, sustainable, and clean-label alternative [48] . In contrast to traditional solvent- and heat-intensive methods, UAE employs high-frequency US waves produced using an ultrasonicator (probe or bath type) as shown in Fig. 5 A . The waves generate alternating compression and rarefaction cycles in the extraction medium, leading to acoustic cavitation [44] . The formation, growth, and violent collapse of cavitation microbubbles produce intense shear forces, localized high-energy hotspots, shock waves, microjets, and free radicals, which disrupt plant cell walls, erode matrix surfaces, and induce matrix swelling ( Fig. 5 B and C) [45] . As illustrated by the SEM micrographs in Fig. 5 C , US causes progressive disruption of the plant tissue structure, producing surface erosion, pore formation, and extensive cell wall rupture compared with untreated and solvent-treated samples. These structural changes facilitate solvent penetration and enhance the release of intracellular substances. As a result, UAE markedly improves extraction efficiency and yield while substantially reducing processing time, solvent consumption, energy input, and waste production [27] , [49] . Furthermore, the ability of UAE to operate under mild temperatures minimizes the degradation of heat-sensitive BAC, making it particularly suitable for BAC-rich FB formulations. However, the efficiency of UAE depends on multiple parameters, including US frequency, intensity, duration, solvent type, solid-to-solvent ratio, and temperature. Furthermore, the mode of US application, such as bath, probe, and flow-through reactor, significantly affects energy distribution and scalability, with flow-through systems providing the greatest potential for industrial-scale adoption [45] , [47] . One of the clearest observations emerging from the available literature is that matrix composition is the primary determinant of UAE performance. Plant tissues differ substantially in cell-wall composition, lignification, moisture content, intracellular compartmentalization, and interactions between BAC and structural polymers, resulting in markedly different responses to US cavitation. Consequently, although cavitation-driven cell disruption is the fundamental extraction mechanism in all studies, the processing conditions required to maximize extraction efficiency differ considerably among fruit peels, flowers, seeds, leafy materials, algae, and seaweeds.

Fruit peels represent the most extensively investigated matrices because they constitute abundant agro-industrial by-products rich in phenolic compounds, flavonoids, vitamins, and dietary fiber. Across these matrices, UAE consistently improved the recovery of antioxidant compounds, although the optimum extraction conditions varied according to peel composition and solvent characteristics. Selahvarzi et al. [26] optimized the extraction of phenolics from pomegranate peel and orange peel using response surface methodology and subsequently incorporated the optimized extracts into FB. Under the optimum conditions (70 °C, 40 min, solvent-to-solid ratio 1:40), pomegranate peel produced substantially higher phenolic recovery and antioxidant activity than orange peel, whereas orange peel contributed greater vitamin C and flavonoid enrichment to the final beverage. These findings demonstrate that extraction efficiency alone does not determine beverage functionality; instead, the intrinsic phytochemical composition of each matrix governs which functional attributes are ultimately enhanced. Furthermore, although both extract-based FB experienced gradual reductions in antioxidant compounds during 60 days of refrigerated storage, the beverages retained appreciable antioxidant capacity, suggesting that UAE-derived peel extracts possess acceptable storage stability for beverage applications. Comparable observations were reported for lemon peel polyphenols incorporated into an apple–peach FB [53] . The highest phenolic recovery was achieved using 70% ethanol rather than absolute ethanol or aqueous solvent alone, illustrating that solvent polarity remains one of the dominant factors controlling UAE performance. The superior extraction obtained with aqueous ethanol likely resulted from improved swelling of plant tissues combined with enhanced cavitation-induced solvent penetration into disrupted cellular structures. Importantly, incorporation of the extract obtained through UAE improved physicochemical stability and delayed the decline of phenolic compounds during refrigerated storage, further supporting the suitability of fruit-processing waste as sustainable sources of functional ingredients.

Unlike peel tissues, edible flowers possess relatively delicate cellular structures and generally require less intensive extraction conditions to achieve high BAC recovery. In our recent work investigating Hibiscus rosa-sinensis flowers [54] , UAE was performed at 20 kHz and 40 °C which effectively extracted maximum phenolic compounds while preserving antioxidant activity. Although methanol produced the highest phenolic recovery, the subsequent beverage formulations revealed that maximum extract concentration did not correspond to maximum consumer acceptance. Functional tea containing 75% flower extract exhibited the greatest antioxidant activity, whereas the formulation containing 50% extract received the highest sensory scores. This highlights an important consideration frequently overlooked in extraction optimization studies, that larger concentration of extract does not always maximize beverage quality. Instead, FB development requires balancing extraction efficiency with sensory acceptance, since excessive concentrations of phenolic compounds may intensify bitterness, astringency, or undesirable color changes. Seed matrices generally exhibited even greater dependence on US-induced structural disruption because many compounds remain enclosed within dense, highly organized tissues. Sirichan et al. [27] demonstrated that optimized UAE substantially increased phenolic recovery, flavonoid content, and antioxidant capacity from makiang seeds, with gallic acid identified as the dominant phenolic constituent. When incorporated into orange juice, the extract not only enhanced antioxidant activity but also exhibited antimicrobial activity that extended product shelf life during storage. Compared with flower or peel matrices, the stronger response observed in seeds likely reflects the greater importance of cavitation-induced disruption of rigid cellular barriers that otherwise limit solvent accessibility under conventional extraction conditions. Thus, matrix rigidity appears to influence the magnitude of US benefits, with structurally compact tissues often showing larger improvements following optimized UAE.

Among plant-based matrices, leafy materials exhibit greater compositional complexity because, besides phenolic compounds, they contain substantial quantities of chlorophylls, carotenoids, vitamins, volatile compounds, and organic acids that collectively influence both extraction efficiency and the physicochemical characteristics of the final beverage. Consequently, UAE optimization in leafy matrices must simultaneously maximize the recovery of health-promoting compounds while minimizing pigment degradation and undesirable sensory changes. Demircan et al. [55] optimized UAE of sweet basil leaves using response surface methodology and subsequently developed a sugar-free FB fortified with chlorophyll, riboflavin, and ascorbic acid. Increasing US amplitude and extraction time significantly improved extract yield and phenolic recovery, with the optimum conditions producing approximately 2.5-fold higher extraction yield than the least effective treatment. Besides increasing TPC, the optimized extract also enhanced antioxidant capacity, antidiabetic activity, chlorophyll content, carotenoids, and vitamin C in the beverage formulation. However, these improvements were accompanied by reductions in pH and increases in TSS and TA, illustrating that UAE modifies multiple physicochemical properties simultaneously rather than influencing BAC recovery alone. These observations highlight an important distinction between leafy matrices and fruit waste, where pigments, organic acids, and volatile constituents become equally important quality determinants during beverage formulation.

Algal and cyanobacterial matrices present an even greater extraction challenge because their bioactive constituents are distributed within structurally distinct cellular systems containing proteins, pigments, lipids, and complex polysaccharides. In our recent study, UAE was integrated with NADES to recover BAC simultaneously from Spirulina platensis and orange peel for clean-label FB development [56] . No other studies employing this integrated approach for FB applications were identified during our literature search. Consequently, this strategy represents a promising emerging direction for sustainable extraction and clean-label FB development. Compared with conventional ethanol extraction, NADES alone, and Soxhlet extraction, the combined UAE–NADES system consistently produced superior recovery of extracts. The enhanced extraction efficiency likely resulted from the synergistic interaction between US cavitation and the tailored solvating capacity of NADES, which facilitated both cellular disruption and improved solubilization of chemically diverse compounds. More importantly, these compositional improvements translated directly into beverage quality, as formulations enriched with UAE–NADES extracts exhibited superior nutritional composition, antioxidant capacity, microbial stability, and consumer acceptability. Although this integrated strategy currently represents a single published application in FB, it demonstrates considerable potential for simultaneously addressing sustainability, extraction efficiency, and clean-label formulation requirements. Nevertheless, additional studies across different beverage matrices are required before broader conclusions regarding its industrial applicability can be established.

Marine matrices exhibit a different extraction behavior because their rigid polysaccharide-rich cell walls limit solvent accessibility under conventional extraction conditions. Aung & Eun [57] demonstrated that UAE of Porphyra dentata (laver) substantially improved the release of intracellular constituents prior to kombucha fermentation. Rather than simply increasing phenolic recovery, US pretreatment modified the subsequent fermentation process by promoting higher production of organic acids and enhancing antioxidant activity in the fermented beverage. These findings suggest that, in certain FB, the principal contribution of UAE extends beyond extraction alone and includes indirect modulation of downstream biological processes such as microbial fermentation. Therefore, the functional role of UAE should not always be evaluated solely by extraction yield, but also by its ability to improve substrate availability for subsequent processing operations. Recent developments further indicate that UAE can be successfully integrated with complementary green technologies to improve the stability and applicability of extracted BAC. Gülen et al. [58] combined UAE with microwave-assisted extraction to recover sulforaphane and curcumin from cabbage seeds and turmeric, respectively, followed by spray-drying microencapsulation prior to incorporation into kefir and orange juice. Unlike conventional extract addition, microencapsulation significantly improved the stability of these thermolabile compounds while maintaining acceptable sensory quality. In kefir, incorporation of the encapsulated extracts enhanced antioxidant activity, TPC, and concentrations of curcumin and sulforaphane without adversely affecting lactic acid bacteria viability, whereas orange juice formulations exhibited improved phytochemical enrichment while preserving acceptable color and consumer acceptance. This study illustrates that the success of UAE does not necessarily depend solely on extraction performance; subsequent stabilization strategies may be equally important for preserving bioactivity during beverage processing and storage.
