Collectively, the available evidence demonstrates that the successful translation of UAE-derived extracts into FB depends on considerably more than extraction yield alone. Although nearly all studies reported increased recovery of phenolics and improved antioxidant activity following US treatment, the final beverage performance was determined by the combined effects of extract composition, incorporation level, beverage matrix, storage conditions, and consumer acceptance. Extracts from fruit peels consistently enhanced antioxidant potential and storage stability, seed-derived extracts additionally provided antimicrobial benefits that extended shelf life, flower extracts achieved an effective balance between antioxidant activity and sensory quality, leafy matrices contributed nutritional enrichment through pigments and vitamins, whereas algae and seaweed introduced additional proteins and pigments that improved nutritional functionality. These findings collectively indicate that different raw materials contribute distinct functional advantages, emphasizing that the choice of extraction matrix should ultimately be guided by the intended nutritional and technological objectives of the beverage rather than by extraction efficiency alone.

Despite the generally positive outcomes reported across all studies, several important limitations prevent direct comparison and broad industrial generalization. First, optimization studies frequently identified different combinations of temperature, extraction time, solvent composition, amplitude, and solid-to-liquid ratio as optimal, indicating that no universal UAE processing conditions currently exist. Second, many investigations reported only nominal US power or amplitude while omitting calorimetric power, acoustic intensity, energy density, probe geometry, or energy delivered to the sample, making meaningful comparisons among studies extremely difficult. Third, different substances were quantified using different analytical methods and expressed in inconsistent units, while beverage formulations differed substantially with respect to ingredient composition and extract concentration. Finally, although storage stability was evaluated in several studies, validation periods ranged from approximately one to two months, and almost all investigations were conducted at laboratory scale. Consequently, evidence supporting pilot-scale processing, continuous-flow US systems, long-term commercial storage, and techno-economic feasibility remains extremely limited.

Overall, the current body of evidence provides strong support for UAE as an effective strategy for producing ingredients for FB; however, its benefits are clearly matrix-dependent rather than universal. The most consistent advantages include enhanced recovery, improved antioxidant capacity, and successful incorporation into diverse beverage systems. In contrast, the magnitude of these improvements depends strongly on plant microstructure, solvent properties, US processing conditions, and beverage formulation, while translation toward industrial production continues to be constrained by inconsistent process reporting, limited scale-up studies, and insufficient standardization of extraction and analytical methodologies. Future investigations should therefore prioritize standardized reporting of acoustic energy delivery, evaluate continuous-flow processing systems under industrially relevant conditions, and establish harmonized analytical protocols that enable robust cross-study comparisons and facilitate data-driven optimization of UAE for next-generation FB production. Looking forward, ML and AI offer promising opportunities to accelerate UAE optimization by integrating large experimental datasets and predicting optimal processing conditions across different plant matrices. AI-assisted modeling could facilitate multi-objective optimization by simultaneously considering extraction efficiency, BAC retention, energy consumption, solvent usage, and product quality, thereby reducing the extensive trial-and-error experimentation currently required. As standardized datasets become increasingly available, AI-driven predictive models may also support process scale-up, real-time process control, and digital-twin development for industrial UAE systems.

### US-assisted fermentation

Fermentation serves as a dynamic interface between microbial metabolism and food functionality, transforming raw substrates into nutritionally enriched and biologically active products [62] , [63] . For centuries, this ancient biotechnological approach has been utilized worldwide to produce a diverse array of products. Beyond its traditional roles in food preservation and flavor development, fermentation has emerged as a powerful strategy for enhancing BAC availability, modulating metabolic functionality, and improving health-promoting properties of foods [24] , [64] . Regular consumption of fermented FB has been associated with beneficial effects on gut microbiota composition, immune function, oxidative stress reduction, and a reduced risk of chronic diseases [5] , [65] , [66] . However, maintaining microbial viability and achieving consistent fermentation performance in complex FB matrices remain significant challenges. Conventional fermentation approaches are often constrained by prolonged processing times, high variability in product quality, potential losses of heat-sensitive nutrients, and relatively high energy consumption [66] , [67] . These constraints have stimulated growing interest in integrating emerging non-thermal technologies, such as US, to improve fermentation efficiency and final product quality while minimizing energy requirements [68] . US waves induce acoustic cavitation, generating microstreaming, shear forces, and localized turbulence in the fermentation medium. These physical effects enhance mass transfer, increase microbial cell membrane permeability, stimulate enzyme secretion, improve flavor development, and accelerate overall metabolic activity [62] , [63] , [66] , [67] , [69] . Consequently, US-assisted fermentation can significantly shorten processing time, promote microbial proliferation, and facilitate the release of intracellular compounds, thereby enhancing both the functional and sensory attributes of the final beverages. Compared with other advanced processing technologies, US is relatively cost-effective, energy-efficient, and easily adaptable to existing production lines, making it well-suited for industrial-scale implementation. But it is important to note that the effects of US on fermentation are highly parameter-dependent. Low-intensity or intermittent US can stimulate microbial growth and metabolic activity, whereas excessive power levels or prolonged exposure may induce cellular damage or enzyme inactivation. Overall, US-assisted fermentation represents a promising modern and efficient strategy for process intensification, enabling simultaneous improvements in nutritional quality, functional performance, and sensory characteristics of fermented FB [70] , [71] .

The studies summarized in Table 2 can be separated into four operational categories: US applied to the beverage before microbial inoculation; applied shortly after inoculation or during active fermentation; applied to microbial cells before their addition to the beverage; and applied after fermentation. This distinction is essential because these approaches pursue different technological objectives. Pretreatment of the beverage primarily modifies particle size, macromolecular structure, viscosity, and nutrient availability. US during fermentation is intended to stimulate membrane transport and metabolic activity without causing lethal cellular injury. Treatment of microorganisms before inoculation can attenuate acidification or alter subsequent metabolic behavior, whereas post-fermentation US is generally directed toward physical stabilization, microbial reduction, or modification of sensory and compositional attributes. Combining all four approaches under a single undifferentiated category would obscure the opposing microbial responses reported across the literature. #### Treatment timing determines microbial stimulation and fermentation performance

Among the clearest demonstrations of treatment-dependent microbial responses, Meena et al. [72] investigated the effect of US pre- and post-treatment on the fermentation of a millet-based probiotic FB. US was applied at intensities of 0.53–1.59 W/mm 2 for 5–15 min before inoculation and 0.21–0.35 W/mm 2 for 1–5 min after inoculation at 32 °C. Pre-inoculation treatment was optimized at approximately 0.99 W/mm 2 for 11.09 min, whereas post-inoculation treatment required a substantially lower intensity of 0.29 W/mm 2 for only 2.63 min. Interestingly, US applied after inoculation reduced the fermentation time required to reach pH 4.6 from approximately 9 h in the untreated control to only 3.4 h, representing nearly a 2.6-fold reduction, whereas pretreatment before inoculation produced a comparatively smaller acceleration. This improvement was attributed to cavitation-induced enhancement of membrane permeability, increased nutrient accessibility, reduced particle size, and deagglomeration of suspended particles, all of which facilitated microbial proliferation and substrate utilization. However, the treatment that maximized fermentation kinetics did not simultaneously optimize beverage structure. WHC was highest following pre-inoculation treatment (44.24%), exceeding both the untreated control (37.45%) and post-inoculation treatment (12.10%). Similarly, viscosity varied considerably according to treatment timing and US intensity, reflecting differences in protein unfolding, starch gelatinization, and molecular interactions within the beverage matrix. These observations demonstrate that optimization based solely on fermentation rate may not necessarily yield the most desirable rheological properties. Instead, multiple quality attributes should be considered simultaneously during process optimization.

A similar intensity-dependent response was reported during US-assisted fermentation of ginkgo kernel juice by Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Y2. Chen et al. [74] applied pulsed US (20 kHz) at volumetric intensities of 84.42, 115.50, and 173.88 W/L during fermentation and observed enhanced microbial growth relative to conventional fermentation. After 24 h, viable cell numbers increased by approximately 5.05–5.06% at 115.50 and 173.88 W/L and by 2.19% at 84.42 W/L compared with the untreated samples. SEM further demonstrated that mild US produced transient membrane perforations measuring approximately 50–400 nm without causing irreversible cellular damage, thereby facilitating nutrient transport while maintaining microbial viability. Enhanced microbial metabolism was reflected by accelerated utilization of sugars and proteins together with extensive biotransformation of phenolic compounds, amino acids, and organic acids. Mild-to-moderate US intensities promoted the formation of quinic, shikimic, pyruvic, fumaric, and lactic acids while simultaneously reducing malic and citric acids through enhanced microbial metabolism. Moreover, US significantly increased the degradation of the naturally occurring toxic compound 4′-O-methylpyridoxine, thereby improving the nutritional safety of fermented ginkgo beverages. Nevertheless, the optimum US intensity depended strongly on the selected response variable. Lower intensities favored microbial metabolism and substrate utilization, whereas higher intensity produced greater detoxification efficiency. Likewise, improvements observed in ABTS radical scavenging activity were not always accompanied by proportional increases in FRAP, suggesting that US modifies antioxidant composition through metabolic transformation rather than simply increasing the total concentration of antioxidant compounds. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that microbial stimulation during US-assisted fermentation occurs only within an optimum acoustic window. Mild cavitation enhances substrate transport, membrane permeability, and enzymatic activity, thereby accelerating fermentation. In contrast, excessive acoustic intensity or prolonged exposure shifts the response from reversible physiological stimulation toward irreversible cellular injury and loss of microbial viability.

#### Matrix- and microorganism-dependent responses

The response of FB to US-assisted fermentation varies considerably according to beverage composition and the metabolic characteristics of fermenting microorganisms. Unlike conventional fermentation, where substrate utilization is primarily governed by microbial enzymatic activity, US introduces an additional physical stimulus that modifies substrate accessibility, cellular permeability, and mass transfer. Consequently, the same US treatment may produce markedly different outcomes depending on the chemical composition of the FB, the physiological characteristics of the microbial culture, and the interaction between cavitation-induced mechanical forces and the surrounding fermentation environment. Fruit-based FB generally exhibit the most pronounced improvements in phytochemical composition because their abundant phenolic compounds, organic acids, and soluble carbohydrates provide readily available substrates for microbial biotransformation. Multi-frequency US-assisted fermentation of mulberry and sea buckthorn juices significantly enhanced the production of phenolic compounds, flavonoids, antioxidant metabolites, and desirable aroma compounds while simultaneously modifying juice microstructure and improving sensory quality [71] , [79] . These improvements were attributed not only to enhanced extraction of intracellular phytochemicals but also to increased microbial conversion of phenolic precursors into more bioactive metabolites through cavitation-enhanced mass transfer and enzymatic activity. Similarly, US-assisted fermentation of ginkgo kernel juice promoted the metabolism of sugars, amino acids, phenolic compounds, and organic acids while simultaneously accelerating detoxification through increased degradation of 4′-O-methylpyridoxine, demonstrating that US can simultaneously improve both nutritional quality and product safety [74] . These findings collectively indicate that in fruit-based FB, the primary contribution of US extends beyond accelerating microbial growth to regulating microbial metabolism and facilitating biochemical transformations that enhance overall beverage functionality.

In contrast, cereal- and legume-based FB respond differently because their matrices are dominated by starch, proteins, and dietary fiber rather than soluble phenolics. During fermentation of millet-based probiotic FB, US primarily accelerated fermentation kinetics through improved nutrient diffusion and transient membrane permeabilization of probiotic bacteria rather than through extensive phytochemical modification [72] . Likewise, US-assisted fermentation of chickpea-based FB increased protein extractability, promoted the accumulation of organic acids, and enhanced the release of phytochemicals through disruption of protein-rich cellular structures [63] . Structural characterization using SEM and FTIR demonstrated that cavitation-induced protein unfolding increased substrate accessibility and facilitated microbial metabolism. These observations suggest that in cereal- and legume-based FB, improvements are governed predominantly by structural modification of macromolecules, which subsequently enhances microbial utilization of nutrients rather than directly increasing phytochemical release.

Nut-based FB exhibit another response pattern because their technological challenges are often associated with emulsion instability rather than limited nutrient availability. In fermented almond beverages, US reduced particle size, improved dispersion stability, enhanced antioxidant activity, and promoted probiotic survival during storage and simulated gastrointestinal digestion [77] . These improvements were attributed primarily to cavitation-induced homogenization of suspended particles and stabilization of the beverage matrix rather than accelerated microbial metabolism alone. Consequently, whereas fruit- and cereal-based FB benefit mainly from enhanced microbial biotransformation, nut-based systems derive additional technological advantages from the physical stabilization provided by US. The physiological characteristics of the fermenting microorganisms further influence the effectiveness of US-assisted fermentation. Most available studies have focused on lactic acid bacteria (LAB) [71] , [72] , [74] , [77] , [79] . Although these species generally tolerate mild acoustic cavitation, their responses differ considerably because of strain-specific variations in membrane composition, stress adaptation mechanisms, and metabolic capacity. Studies employing mixed microbial cultures consistently reported greater modifications in metabolite composition and aroma development than monoculture fermentations, suggesting that US may enhance complementary metabolic interactions among different microorganisms [71] , [79] . Nevertheless, these responses should not automatically be interpreted as synergistic because co-cultures also introduce microbial competition, altered substrate partitioning, and interspecies regulation that may independently influence fermentation outcomes. Consequently, optimization of US-assisted fermentation should consider not only the acoustic parameters but also microbial ecology and strain compatibility. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of US-assisted fermentation cannot be generalized across different FB. Instead, beverage composition determines the primary technological response, whereas microbial physiology dictates the magnitude of metabolic stimulation. This explains why identical US parameters often produce different outcomes among fruit, cereal, legume, nut, and tea-based FB, emphasizing that successful industrial application requires matrix-specific optimization rather than universal processing conditions.

#### US modifies microbial metabolism rather than simply accelerating fermentation

Although accelerated fermentation is one of the most frequently reported benefits of US, the available evidence suggests that its principal role is the regulation of microbial metabolism rather than merely increasing microbial growth or shortening fermentation time. Cavitation transiently increases membrane permeability, facilitates substrate diffusion, and improves transport of metabolites across the cell membrane, thereby altering intracellular metabolic fluxes and redirecting biochemical pathways. Consequently, changes observed in fermented FB often reflect qualitative modification of microbial metabolism instead of simple enhancement of microbial proliferation.

Several studies clearly demonstrate that increased microbial activity does not necessarily correspond to proportional increases in all quality attributes. During fermentation of ginkgo kernel juice, enhanced microbial metabolism promoted greater utilization of sugars and proteins together with extensive conversion of phenolic compounds and organic acids [74] . Similarly, multi-frequency US-assisted fermentation of sea buckthorn and mulberry juices substantially altered organic acid profiles, anthocyanin derivatives, volatile compounds, and phenolic metabolites while simultaneously modifying juice microstructure and aroma characteristics [71] , [79] . These observations indicate that US redirects metabolic pathways responsible for secondary metabolite production rather than simply stimulating biomass accumulation. Consequently, improvements in antioxidant activity frequently result from the formation of different bioactive metabolites instead of increases in total phenolic concentration alone. This metabolic regulation also explains many of the apparently contradictory findings reported throughout the literature. For example, fermentation of blueberry–watermelon smoothies followed by US treatment resulted in lower initial phenolic content and antioxidant activity than conventional fermentation, yet significantly improved the bioaccessibility of several individual phenolic compounds after simulated gastrointestinal digestion [70] . Likewise, post-fermentation US reduced viable LAB counts but enhanced microbial safety and increased the intestinal recovery of selected BAC. Rather than representing conflicting observations, these findings demonstrate that US influences the chemical form, molecular interactions, and biological accessibility of phytochemicals, meaning that lower concentrations measured before digestion do not necessarily translate into reduced physiological functionality after consumption.

A similar phenomenon has been observed in sensory-related metabolite production. In kombucha fermentation, low-power US reduced perceived astringency by simultaneously decreasing the concentration of astringent catechins and increasing extracellular polysaccharide production through selective regulation of microbial metabolism [69] . Metagenomic analysis further demonstrated that US altered the microbial community by suppressing Komagataeibacter europaeus while enriching Komagataeibacter saccharivorans , resulting in upregulation of glycolysis, sucrose metabolism, and benzoate degradation pathways. These findings provide direct evidence that US not only modifies microbial growth but also reshapes microbial community structure and metabolic function, thereby regulating flavor development through the microbiome–metabolite–flavor axis. Importantly, this study also illustrates the emerging integration of machine learning with US processing, where neural-network-assisted optimization was successfully employed to identify treatment conditions that simultaneously minimized astringency while maintaining desirable fermentation performance. Such data-driven optimization represents a promising strategy for managing the complex interactions among US parameters, microbial physiology, and beverage quality.

Despite these advantages, microbial stimulation remains highly dependent on the acoustic energy delivered to the fermentation system. Mild cavitation generally induces reversible membrane permeabilization and enhanced nutrient transport, whereas excessive acoustic intensity may cause irreversible membrane disruption, intracellular leakage, oxidative stress, and reduced microbial viability. Consequently, optimum US conditions are not defined by the maximum energy input but by achieving an appropriate balance between microbial stimulation and cellular preservation. This concept of an optimum acoustic window provides a mechanistic explanation for inconsistent responses reported among different studies and emphasizes that successful US-assisted fermentation depends on precise control of acoustic energy according to beverage composition, microbial strain, and fermentation stage rather than application of standardized processing conditions.

#### Functional improvements involve important physicochemical and sensory trade-offs

Although numerous studies have demonstrated that US-assisted fermentation improves the functional quality of FB, the available evidence indicates that these benefits are rarely achieved without accompanying trade-offs. Rather than simultaneously enhancing all quality attributes, US often improves one property at the expense of another, reflecting the complex interaction between cavitation, microbial physiology, and beverage composition. Consequently, optimization of US-assisted fermentation should be based on multiple quality indicators instead of a single response variable such as fermentation time, TPC, or antioxidant activity. One of the most common trade-offs involves the relationship between fermentation kinetics and beverage structure. During fermentation of millet-based probiotic FB, post-inoculation US produced the greatest reduction in fermentation time but simultaneously resulted in the lowest WHC, whereas pre-inoculation treatment generated a more structurally stable beverage despite a comparatively slower fermentation rate [74] . Similarly, viscosity was highly dependent on treatment timing and US intensity because cavitation simultaneously influenced starch gelatinization, protein unfolding, and intermolecular interactions within the beverage matrix [72] . These observations demonstrate that maximizing microbial activity does not necessarily maximize the structural properties required for consumer acceptance or product stability.

A comparable compromise has been reported for sensory quality. During fermentation of chickpea-based FB, US enhanced protein extractability, organic acid production, TPC, total flavonoid content, and carotenoid concentration while simultaneously promoting greater release of volatile compounds associated with acidic and fermented aromas [63] . Although these compositional changes improved nutritional quality, sensory scores were lower than those of the conventionally fermented beverage because increased acidity and intensified flavor reduced overall consumer acceptability. Similar findings were reported in Jun tea, where US improved phenolic release, antioxidant activity, microbial safety, and rheological uniformity but progressively reduced apparent viscosity with prolonged treatment, potentially influencing mouthfeel and beverage texture [73] . Collectively, these studies indicate that excessive structural disruption induced by cavitation may improve the release of BAC while simultaneously altering the sensory characteristics that determine consumer preference.

The relationship between microbial viability and product functionality represents another important trade-off. In blueberry–watermelon probiotic smoothies, post-fermentation US reduced viable LAB populations compared with conventional fermentation, reflecting partial microbial inactivation caused by acoustic cavitation [70] . Nevertheless, the surviving populations remained within levels considered beneficial for probiotic products during portions of simulated gastrointestinal digestion, while the same treatment improved microbial safety by suppressing undesirable microorganisms. Furthermore, despite lower initial TPC and antioxidant activity before digestion, US significantly increased the bioaccessibility of several phenolic compounds after gastrointestinal simulation. These findings demonstrate that reductions in microbial counts or phytochemical concentration measured immediately after processing do not necessarily correspond to lower physiological functionality following consumption.

Trade-offs have also been observed in antioxidant responses. Several studies reported substantial increases in TPC following US-assisted fermentation of fruit-based FB [71] , [73] , [74] , [79] ; however, improvements in one antioxidant assay were not always accompanied by similar responses in others. For example, Chen et al. [74] observed enhanced ABTS radical scavenging activity without proportional increases in FRAP, suggesting that US altered the composition and redox characteristics of antioxidant metabolites rather than simply increasing their overall concentration. Likewise, fermentation of blueberry–watermelon smoothies demonstrated that lower phenolic concentrations before digestion could coexist with higher phenolic bioaccessibility after digestion [70] . Therefore, antioxidant capacity should be interpreted cautiously because different analytical assays quantify distinct antioxidant mechanisms, and higher concentrations of total phenolics do not necessarily translate into greater biological efficacy. Collectively, these studies indicate that US-assisted fermentation should not be evaluated using a single performance indicator. Instead, successful process optimization requires balancing fermentation efficiency, microbial viability, physicochemical stability, nutritional quality, antioxidant functionality, and sensory acceptance. Consequently, multi-response optimization strategies are likely to provide greater industrial relevance than approaches based solely on maximizing fermentation rate or bioactive compound concentration.

#### Emerging evidence for health functionality beyond conventional antioxidant assays

Most studies investigating US-assisted fermentation evaluate product quality using conventional physicochemical indicators, including TPC, TFC, antioxidant activity, organic acid production, and probiotic viability. Although these parameters provide valuable information regarding compositional changes, they do not necessarily reflect the physiological functionality of the final FB after consumption. Consequently, increasing attention has shifted toward evaluating bioaccessibility, digestibility, detoxification, and biological activity, which collectively provide stronger evidence of potential health benefits.

One of the clearest examples is provided by blueberry–watermelon probiotic smoothies, where simulated gastrointestinal digestion demonstrated that US-assisted fermentation substantially increased the bioaccessibility of several individual phenolic compounds despite reducing their initial concentrations before digestion [70] . Improvements in (+)-catechin, gallic acid, chlorogenic acid, and other phenolic metabolites indicate that cavitation not only modifies phytochemical composition but also alters interactions between phenolics and the surrounding food matrix, thereby facilitating their release during digestion. More importantly, digested beverages exhibited pronounced anti-inflammatory activity in macrophage cell models by reducing nitric oxide (NO), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) production while simultaneously increasing anti-inflammatory interleukin-10 (IL-10) secretion [70] . These findings demonstrate that improvements in biological functionality may occur even when conventional antioxidant measurements suggest limited enhancement. Additional evidence of health-related functionality has been reported for ginkgo kernel juice, where US-assisted fermentation accelerated degradation of 4′-O-methylpyridoxine, a naturally occurring neurotoxic compound responsible for ginkgo toxicity [74] . Simultaneously, microbial biotransformation increased the abundance of beneficial organic acids and phenolic metabolites while reducing undesirable constituents, thereby improving both nutritional quality and product safety. These findings illustrate that one important contribution of US-assisted fermentation is the selective modification of metabolite composition rather than simply increasing the concentration of existing phytochemicals.

Protein-rich FB also benefits from structural modifications induced by US. During fermentation of chickpea-based beverages, cavitation promoted protein unfolding, increased nutrient extractability, and enhanced the release of BAC through structural disruption of the plant matrix [63] . Likewise, combined US treatment with enzymatic hydrolysis and gamma irradiation substantially improved protein digestibility by increasing sulfhydryl exposure, reducing ordered secondary structures, and accelerating proteolytic degradation [75] . Although this study evaluated protein ingredients rather than a commercial FB, it provides mechanistic evidence supporting the role of US in improving protein bioavailability through controlled structural modification. Despite these promising findings, the current evidence remains limited because relatively few studies extend beyond conventional compositional analyses. Most investigations rely primarily on chemical antioxidant assays, whereas only a small number evaluate simulated gastrointestinal digestion, cellular bioactivity, metabolomics, or in vivo physiological responses [70] , [74] . Consequently, the biological significance of many reported increases in TPC or antioxidant activity remains uncertain. Future research should therefore integrate multi-omics approaches, metabolomic profiling, simulated digestion, gut microbiome interactions, and animal or clinical studies to establish stronger links between US-induced compositional changes and human health outcomes. Such investigations will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms through which US-assisted fermentation enhances the functionality of FB.

#### Industrial translation, process optimization, and future opportunities

The current body of evidence clearly demonstrates that US-assisted fermentation can improve fermentation efficiency, microbial metabolism, nutritional quality, physicochemical properties, and sensory characteristics of FB. Nevertheless, despite these promising laboratory-scale findings, translation into commercial manufacturing remains limited because several scientific and engineering challenges have yet to be resolved. Most published studies have been conducted using small batch reactors under highly controlled laboratory conditions, with relatively small processing volumes and simplified fermentation systems. Consequently, the scalability of the reported processing conditions remains largely unknown, and direct industrial implementation cannot be assumed without further validation.

One of the major limitations of the existing literature is the inconsistent reporting of acoustic processing parameters. Although studies generally report frequency, nominal power, treatment duration, or amplitude, several important variables that govern cavitation intensity, including acoustic energy density, calorimetric power, reactor geometry, transducer configuration, energy efficiency, and cavitation distribution are frequently omitted. Since cavitation behavior is strongly influenced by reactor design and sample volume, identical nominal US settings may produce substantially different acoustic environments across different processing systems. This lack of standardized reporting makes direct comparison among studies difficult and limits the reproducibility of experimental findings. Future investigations should therefore adopt standardized reporting guidelines that include both acoustic and engineering parameters to facilitate comparison among laboratories and accelerate industrial translation. Another important consideration is that process optimization has traditionally focused on maximizing individual quality attributes, such as TPC, antioxidant activity, or fermentation rate, while overlooking the complex interactions among microbial viability, sensory quality, rheological properties, nutritional composition, and processing efficiency. The evidence presented throughout this section demonstrates that improvements in one characteristic are frequently accompanied by compromises in another. For example, conditions that maximize fermentation kinetics may reduce WHC or viscosity [72] , whereas enhanced release of BAC may coincide with reduced sensory acceptance or probiotic survival [63] , [70] . Consequently, future optimization strategies should employ multi-objective approaches capable of simultaneously balancing microbiological, physicochemical, nutritional, sensory, and economic responses rather than optimizing a single processing parameter.

Recent advances suggest that AI and ML may provide effective tools for addressing this challenge. Unlike conventional trial-and-error optimization, AI-based models can simultaneously evaluate numerous interacting variables and identify processing conditions that maximize multiple quality attributes. For example, low-power US conditions for kombucha fermentation were successfully optimized using an artificial neural network integrated with Bayesian optimization, enabling simultaneous reduction of astringency while improving microbial metabolism and extracellular polysaccharide production through regulation of the microbial community [69] . Although this represents one of the first reported applications of AI-assisted optimization in US-assisted fermentation of FB, it demonstrates the potential of data-driven approaches to improve process precision and reduce experimental complexity. As larger datasets become available, ML algorithms are expected to facilitate prediction of fermentation performance across different beverage matrices, microbial strains, and US processing conditions, thereby supporting more efficient development of industrial fermentation protocols. From an engineering perspective, future research should also focus on continuous-flow US reactors, which offer greater potential for industrial implementation than conventional batch systems. Continuous-flow processing can provide more uniform cavitation distribution, improved energy utilization, enhanced process consistency, and greater compatibility with existing beverage manufacturing lines. However, maintaining homogeneous acoustic energy distribution while preserving microbial viability during continuous processing remains a significant challenge. Further optimization of reactor geometry, flow dynamics, residence time, and transducer placement will therefore be essential for successful scale-up. In addition, comprehensive techno-economic analyses, energy consumption assessments, and life-cycle evaluations are required to determine whether the functional improvements achieved through US-assisted fermentation justify the additional processing costs associated with industrial implementation.

Despite the growing number of studies, several important knowledge gaps remain. Most investigations have evaluated only short-term storage stability, whereas information regarding long-term probiotic survival, metabolite stability, flavor evolution, and consumer acceptance during commercial shelf life remains limited. Furthermore, relatively few studies have integrated metabolomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, or microbiome analyses to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying microbial responses to acoustic cavitation. Such multi-omics approaches would provide a more comprehensive understanding of how US regulates microbial metabolism and could facilitate development of predictive models linking processing conditions with final beverage functionality. Finally, validation through animal studies and well-designed human clinical trials will be necessary to confirm whether the improvements observed in vitro translate into measurable health benefits following consumption.

Overall, future progress in US-assisted fermentation is expected to rely less on increasing acoustic intensity and more on precise regulation of acoustic energy according to beverage composition, microbial physiology, and desired product characteristics. Integrating standardized acoustic reporting, reactor engineering, AI-assisted optimization, and systems-level biological analyses will accelerate the transition of US-assisted fermentation from laboratory research to commercially viable production of high-quality fermented FB. ### US assisted preservation

Traditional heat-based processing has long served as the cornerstone of food preservation, ensuring microbial safety, product stability, and extended shelf life. However, exposure to elevated temperatures often leads to the degradation of thermolabile nutrients and adversely affects key sensory attributes, including flavor, aroma, and color [17] . Consequently, there is growing interest in the development of sustainable non-thermal preservation techniques for nutritionally sensitive FB. These methods aim to maintain microbial safety and shelf life without compromising nutritional, functional, or sensory attributes [28] , [53] , [76] , [77] . US-assisted preservation has emerged as a promising non-thermal processing technology owing to its ability to inactivate microorganisms and deteriorative enzymes primarily through cavitation-induced mechanical and physicochemical effects, while largely preserving thermolabile quality attributes [15] , [77] . During acoustic cavitation, microscopic bubbles undergo rapid expansion and subsequent collapse. This bubble implosion induces intense mechanical shear forces and reactive chemical effects [76] , [81] . As illustrated in Fig. 9 , these cavitation-induced sonochemical reactions lead to oxidative damage and membrane perforation in microbial cells ( A-C ), while microscopic observations further confirm severe structural alterations in bacterial cells, including membrane rupture, intracellular leakage, and morphological deformation ( D-F ). These combined physical and chemical effects play a crucial role in enhancing microbial inactivation and extending the shelf life of FB systems. Based on these mechanistic insights, the following section critically reviews studies on the application of US-assisted processing for the preservation of FB, with particular emphasis on microbial stability, quality retention, and shelf-life extension during storage. Moreover, an overview of US-assisted preservation strategies, key processing parameters, and their effects on the quality and storage stability of FB is summarized in Table 3 . Unlike conventional preservation methods that primarily seek microbial destruction, several studies demonstrated that appropriately optimized US attenuates microbial metabolic activity without substantially reducing viable cell populations. Campaniello et al. [76] reported that all probiotic strains maintained populations exceeding 7 log CFU/mL throughout eight days of refrigerated storage, confirming that US did not compromise probiotic survival. However, post-fermentation acidification differed markedly according to microbial strain, beverage matrix, US intensity, and storage temperature. Soy-based beverages inoculated with Lactobacillus acidophilus LA5 consistently exhibited the lowest acidification, whereas almond beverages inoculated with Bifidobacterium animalis or Lactiplantibacillus plantarum underwent considerably greater pH reductions during storage. Similarly, US at 40% power for 6 min produced significantly lower acidification than treatment at 60% power for 2 min, demonstrating that greater acoustic intensity does not necessarily translate into superior preservation performance. Instead, excessive treatment appears to stimulate microbial metabolism rather than merely attenuate cellular activity. Furthermore, refrigeration proved essential for preserving this attenuation effect because thermal abuse rapidly accelerated acidification regardless of prior US treatment. Collectively, these findings indicate that successful preservation of fermented FB requires simultaneous optimization of microbial strain, beverage composition, US parameters, and storage conditions rather than simply increasing US intensity.

The importance of the beverage matrix became even more evident in probiotic formulations employing encapsulation strategies, where the protective carrier substantially influenced the preservation benefits achieved following US. Lucía et al. [77] demonstrated that US-treated fermented almond beverages containing whey protein or starch phosphate–inulin microcapsules maintained probiotic survival above 93% immediately after processing, whereas rice-starch encapsulation retained less than half of the viable cells. During 28 days of refrigerated storage, free probiotic cells showed gradual viability losses accompanied by pronounced post-acidification, whereas encapsulated formulations effectively moderated acid development while preserving substantially greater cell viability under both storage and simulated gastrointestinal conditions. The starch phosphate–inulin system even exhibited a slight increase in viable populations during storage, suggesting that the encapsulation matrix created a favorable microenvironment for probiotic persistence following US. In addition to microbial protection, US significantly increased antioxidant activity after fermentation through enhanced liberation of phenolic compounds and microbial hydrolysis, while encapsulated systems exhibited superior retention of these functional attributes throughout storage. These observations emphasize that US alone is insufficient to maximize preservation in probiotic beverages; rather, its effectiveness depends strongly on synergistic interactions between cavitation and encapsulation matrices that simultaneously protect probiotic viability, regulate post-acidification, and preserve functional quality. The available evidence demonstrates that preservation mechanisms differ fundamentally among beverage matrices. Fermented and probiotic beverages derive greater benefit from the ability of US to selectively modulate microbial metabolism while maintaining probiotic viability, an effect that is further strengthened by appropriate encapsulation strategies. These findings collectively demonstrate that beverage matrix composition, rather than US treatment alone, is the principal determinant of preservation efficacy, highlighting why processing conditions optimized for one FB category cannot be directly transferred to another. This strong matrix dependence also explains much of the variability reported across preservation studies and underscores the need for matrix-specific optimization rather than universal processing recommendations.

Beyond microbial regulation, several studies have demonstrated that US can substantially improve the retention of BAC during storage, although the magnitude of this benefit depends strongly on beverage composition and the mechanisms governing phytochemical degradation. In polyphenol-rich fruit beverages, preservation is achieved primarily through cavitation-enhanced release and dispersion of antioxidant compounds together with reduced oxidative deterioration during storage. Nawaz et al. [53] demonstrated that UAE of lemon peel polyphenols followed by incorporation into an apple–peach FB significantly improved phenolic stability during 28 days of refrigerated storage. Beverages fortified with 3% lemon peel extract retained considerably higher total phenolic contents than the untreated control while maintaining total soluble solids and exhibiting only moderate increases in TA. Likewise, sensory deterioration progressed more slowly in sonicated beverages, particularly those containing 1% extract, indicating that enhanced phytochemical retention translated into improved product acceptability throughout storage. Similarly, Wang et al. [88] reported that ultraviolet-assisted US applied before probiotic fermentation of mango juice enhanced the stability and gastrointestinal bioaccessibility of phenolics, carotenoids, soluble dietary fiber, and ascorbic acid during 30 days of refrigerated storage while simultaneously maintaining probiotic populations near 7.5 log CFU/mL. The combined pretreatment also improved suspension stability, viscosity, and particle size distribution, suggesting that cavitation-induced disruption of plant tissues increased intracellular compound release while improving the physical integrity of the beverage matrix. These studies collectively indicate that the preservation of phytochemicals depends not only on minimizing degradation during storage but also on maximizing their initial extractability and homogeneous distribution within the beverage, thereby providing greater resistance to subsequent oxidative losses.

Nevertheless, the available evidence also demonstrates that improvements in phytochemical preservation do not necessarily translate into proportional improvements in antioxidant capacity. Although higher phenolic retention was consistently observed after US, several studies reported weak or inconsistent relationships between phenolic concentration and antioxidant assays during storage. For example, Pérez et al. [86] found that sonicated broccoli–carrot beverages contained the highest concentrations of free phenolics, yet antioxidant capacity measured by DPPH and FRAP declined substantially during prolonged storage regardless of treatment. Similar observations have been reported in other fruit-based beverages, suggesting that antioxidant performance is influenced not only by TPC but also by changes in phenolic composition, degradation kinetics, interactions with other phytochemicals, and the analytical methods used for antioxidant evaluation. Consequently, preservation success should not be interpreted solely on the basis of total phenolic retention, but rather through a combination of microbial stability, functional compound preservation, physicochemical integrity, and sensory quality throughout storage. The strongest preservation outcomes were consistently achieved when US was integrated with complementary non-thermal preservation technologies. Rather than functioning as an independent intervention, US served as one component of multi-hurdle preservation systems in which different technologies targeted distinct deterioration mechanisms simultaneously. The authors demonstrated that combining US with HPP produced substantially greater preservation efficacy than either treatment alone during 28 days of refrigerated storage of broccoli and carrot by-product beverages. Compared with thermally processed beverages, the US–HPP combination maintained color changes below the perceptible threshold (ΔE < 4), retained higher concentrations of carotenoids and sulfur-containing phytochemicals, and achieved approximately 6 log CFU/mL microbial reduction by the end of storage while remaining sensorially acceptable beyond 28 days. In contrast, beverages processed with US alone exhibited microbial spoilage after approximately 15 days despite improved phytochemical retention. These findings indicate that US effectively enhances structural and functional quality but may provide insufficient microbial lethality for long-term preservation when used as the sole preservation hurdle in highly perishable beverages.

Comparable synergistic effects were observed when US was combined with OZ. In our own study Chaudhary et al. [87] , we reported that the integrated US–OZ treatment consistently outperformed pasteurization and the corresponding individual non-thermal treatments throughout two months of refrigerated storage of a strawberry–cantaloupe FB enriched with S. platensis and orange peel extracts. The combined treatment achieved the highest retention of total phenolics, flavonoids, carotenoids, antioxidant activity, and ascorbic acid while simultaneously preserving color, cloud stability, viscosity, and overall physical integrity. In addition, US–OZ markedly inhibited polyphenol oxidase, peroxidase, and pectin methylesterase activities, minimized sedimentation and browning, and reduced bacterial and yeast–mold populations to the lowest levels among all treatments. These improvements likely resulted from complementary mechanisms in which cavitation enhanced particle dispersion, mass transfer, and enzyme accessibility, whereas ozone provided rapid oxidative microbial destruction and enzyme inactivation. Consequently, neither technology alone reproduced the comprehensive preservation performance achieved by their combination.

Collectively, these studies identify a robust evidence cluster indicating that hybrid preservation systems consistently outperform US applied as a stand-alone treatment. While US alone effectively improves colloidal stability, enhances phytochemical retention, and moderates microbial metabolism, its preservation capacity becomes increasingly limited as storage duration increases or microbial challenge intensifies Fig. 10 A-B . Integrating US with complementary non-thermal technologies such as HPP, OZ, or ultraviolet irradiation allows multiple deterioration pathways including microbial proliferation, enzymatic activity, oxidation, and physical destabilization to be controlled simultaneously, thereby producing greater overall shelf-life extension than any single technology alone. This convergence of evidence suggests that the future industrial implementation of US in FB preservation is likely to rely on multi-hurdle processing strategies rather than US as an isolated preservation technology, particularly for highly perishable or minimally processed beverage systems.
