Although the collective evidence strongly supports US as an effective non-thermal preservation technology for FB, several important inconsistencies remain that prevent the establishment of universal processing recommendations. The variability reported among studies is largely attributable to differences in beverage matrix composition, physicochemical properties, microbial ecology, storage duration, and US processing parameters. Plant protein emulsions generally benefited most from improvements in colloidal stability through droplet size reduction and enhanced protein functionality, whereas fermented beverages relied primarily on the modulation of microbial metabolism and post-acidification. In contrast, fruit- and vegetable-based beverages derived greater preservation benefits from improved retention of phenolics, carotenoids, vitamins, and antioxidant capacity. These matrix-specific responses explain why identical US conditions frequently produce substantially different preservation outcomes and demonstrate that optimization strategies cannot be generalized across different beverage categories.

Another major source of variation is the considerable diversity of US processing conditions employed throughout the literature. The reviewed studies utilized different frequencies, power outputs, amplitudes, treatment times, temperatures, reactor configurations, and sample volumes, making direct comparison extremely difficult. More importantly, most investigations reported only nominal instrument settings while failing to provide delivered acoustic energy, energy density, calorimetric measurements, acoustic intensity, or cavitation efficiency. Because cavitation is the fundamental mechanism governing microbial inactivation, enzyme inhibition, particle disruption, and physicochemical modifications, the absence of standardized energy reporting substantially limits reproducibility and prevents meaningful comparison among studies. Consequently, many apparently contradictory findings may reflect differences in actual acoustic energy delivered to the beverage rather than genuine differences in US efficacy. Establishing standardized reporting guidelines that include reactor geometry, probe characteristics, sample volume, temperature control, and delivered energy should therefore become a priority for future research to facilitate reliable cross-study comparisons and industrial process optimization.

The available evidence also indicates that preservation efficacy should not be evaluated solely on the basis of microbial reduction or isolated quality parameters. While several studies demonstrated excellent retention of phenolics or antioxidant activity, others showed that improved phytochemical preservation was accompanied by only modest improvements in antioxidant performance or shelf-life extension. Likewise, some beverages maintained excellent physical stability but exhibited limited microbial control during prolonged storage, whereas others achieved effective microbial preservation despite relatively small improvements in physicochemical properties. These observations highlight that successful preservation of FB requires the simultaneous maintenance of microbial safety, physical stability, nutritional quality, sensory acceptability, and functional bioactivity throughout storage rather than optimization of any single quality attribute. Future studies would therefore benefit from integrating microbiological, physicochemical, nutritional, sensory, and bioaccessibility assessments within the same experimental framework to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of preservation performance.

Across the reviewed literature, the strongest and most reproducible evidence was observed for multi-hurdle preservation systems, in which US was integrated with complementary non-thermal technologies such as HPP, OZ, or ultraviolet irradiation. These combined approaches consistently produced greater microbial inactivation, superior enzyme inhibition, improved retention of BAC, enhanced physical stability, and longer sensory shelf life than US alone. The complementary mechanisms operating within these systems suggest that US functions most effectively as a process intensification technology that enhances mass transfer, particle dispersion, and cavitation-mediated structural modifications, while companion preservation technologies provide additional microbial and enzymatic control. Consequently, future industrial preservation strategies are likely to rely increasingly on hybrid processing systems rather than US as an independent preservation treatment.

Despite these promising advances, important research gaps remain before widespread industrial implementation can be achieved. Most published studies have been conducted at laboratory scale using relatively small sample volumes under highly controlled experimental conditions, with limited validation under pilot- or commercial-scale processing environments. Long-term storage studies extending beyond one to two months remain relatively scarce, and comprehensive economic assessments, life-cycle analyses, energy efficiency evaluations, and continuous-flow processing investigations are largely absent. Furthermore, only a limited number of studies have systematically examined the influence of beverage composition, protein source, polysaccharide interactions, lipid content, or packaging conditions on US preservation efficiency. Addressing these knowledge gaps through standardized experimental methodologies, scale-up validation, and techno-economic assessment will be essential for translating laboratory findings into commercially viable preservation systems for FB.

Overall, the available evidence demonstrates that US-assisted preservation represents a highly promising strategy for extending the refrigerated shelf life of FB while maintaining microbial safety, physicochemical stability, sensory quality, and functional attributes. However, its effectiveness is strongly matrix dependent and governed by the interaction between beverage composition, US processing conditions, and storage environment. Current evidence further indicates that the greatest preservation benefits are consistently achieved when US is incorporated into multi-hurdle preservation systems, particularly for highly perishable beverages requiring extended refrigerated storage. Future research should therefore shift from demonstrating the feasibility of US preservation toward establishing standardized processing protocols, quantifying delivered acoustic energy, validating industrial-scale applications, and optimizing integrated non-thermal preservation technologies capable of delivering consistent product quality and commercial scalability. Such advances will be critical for facilitating the broader industrial adoption of US-assisted preservation in the rapidly expanding FB sector. And lastly, the emerging AI and ML approaches also offer considerable potential to accelerate the development and industrial implementation of US-assisted preservation technologies for FB. By integrating large experimental datasets encompassing beverage composition, microbial characteristics, processing parameters, storage conditions, and quality attributes, ML models could predict optimal preservation conditions while simultaneously maximizing microbial inactivation, BAC retention, sensory quality, and energy efficiency. Furthermore, AI-assisted process optimization and digital twin technologies could enable real-time monitoring and adaptive control of continuous-flow US systems, improving process consistency and facilitating industrial scale-up. However, the successful application of AI and ML will require standardized reporting of acoustic energy delivery, harmonized experimental methodologies, and high-quality datasets that accurately capture both processing variables and preservation outcomes across diverse beverage matrices.

### US-assisted process intensification and quality structuring

In addition to its targeted applications in extraction, fermentation, and preservation, US has been extensively employed as a processing aid for FB. In these applications, US is applied as a standalone unit operation to improve product quality and functionality. Rather than primarily aiming to enhance extraction efficiency, modulate microbial activity, or extend shelf life, US induces favorable physicochemical and structural modifications within the beverage matrix [53] , [76] . Specifically, US treatment stabilizes key physicochemical parameters such as particle size distribution and dispersion homogeneity, leading to enhanced beverage uniformity, optical clarity, and short-term physical stability [92] , [94] , [95] , [96] . Collectively, these effects improve freshness perception, visual appeal, and sensory acceptability of FB. From a nutritional perspective, US processing can preserve or, in some cases, enhance the concentration and bioaccessibility of BAC by facilitating their release from food matrices without causing extensive molecular degradation [28] , [86] . Importantly, owing to its largely non-destructive nature, US can maintain the functional integrity of sensitive BAC during processing, thereby supporting their potential health-promoting properties [86] . Within this framework, recent studies have explored US as a process-intensification tool to tailor the physicochemical, structural, and functional attributes of FB, as discussed below.

In fruit- and vegetable-based FB, the most consistent outcome of US-assisted process intensification is an increase in measured phenolic, flavonoid, carotenoid, or antioxidant indices. Nevertheless, these increases do not necessarily indicate synthesis of new bioactive molecules or universal improvement in nutritional value. They more commonly reflect cavitation-induced disruption of suspended tissues, desorption of compounds from cell-wall components, improved solvent–solid contact, deagglomeration of particles, and greater analytical extractability. The response is therefore strongest in beverages retaining appreciable cellular material and weaker in clarified matrices in which accessible phytochemicals are already present in the continuous phase. This distinction is illustrated by the contrast between structured juice blends and prebiotic clarified juices. In an apple–carrot FB sweetened with stevia, treatment at 20 kHz and 60% amplitude for 15 min produced the highest reported TPC, TFC, DPPH, and FRAP values while causing no major alteration in pH, TSS, or TA [98] . The response suggests that moderate US improved phytochemical accessibility without substantially changing the beverage’s bulk composition. However, the benefit was not proportional to amplitude: 60% amplitude performed better than both lower and higher settings, indicating an optimum rather than a monotonic power–response relationship. This is important because reporting only the best treatment could create the misleading impression that increasing acoustic intensity invariably improves functionality. The study instead supports the existence of an intermediate processing window in which release and dispersion exceed oxidative degradation. The absence of reported acoustic power, energy density, reactor geometry, and temperature evolution nevertheless limits transfer of this optimum to other systems. A comparable but more severe treatment was applied to a grape–apple beverage at 20 kHz, 100% amplitude, and 20–40 min [101] . US increased TPC, TFC, and antioxidant indices relative to untreated and pasteurized beverages, while producing only modest changes in pH, TA, and TSS. The results reinforce the ability of US to improve the measurable bioactive profile of fruit matrices, but the much longer treatment time prevents direct comparison with the 15-min stevia beverage process. It also raises an industrial concern: improvements obtained after 20–40 min in a laboratory batch system may not translate into favorable throughput or energy efficiency. Moreover, differences between the two studies may reflect fruit composition, solids content, probe geometry, sample volume, and temperature rise rather than an intrinsic superiority of one treatment. Thus, both studies provide evidence of functional enhancement, but neither establishes a generally applicable acoustic dose.

The influence of matrix composition becomes clearer in more heterogeneous plant systems. In a mango–carrot FB containing turmeric, response-surface optimization identified 21 min, 100% amplitude, and a 0.7-s pulse cycle as the treatment producing increases of 15.5% in TPC, 45.1% in Trolox-equivalent antioxidant capacity, and 15.9% in FRAP [105] . Several individual phenolic acids, curcuminoids, flavonoids, and mangiferin were also present at higher measured concentrations after treatment. The disproportionately larger change in antioxidant capacity than in total phenolics indicates that functional responses cannot be inferred from TPC alone. US may have altered the relative accessibility of compounds with different redox activities, but assay-specific effects and interactions among turmeric, mango, and carrot constituents may also have contributed. Accordingly, simultaneous increases in TPC and antioxidant assays should not automatically be interpreted as proof of improved bioavailability or physiological efficacy. The same optimization principle was evident in a mulberry–pineapple–mango beverage, for which 100% amplitude and 8 min maximized TPC, DPPH, and FRAP, whereas longer treatment reduced the response [104] . This decline beyond the optimum is among the most informative findings in the evidence base because it identifies a negative-effect threshold rather than reporting only a favorable treatment. At extended US, localized heating, oxygen incorporation, and radical-mediated oxidation may outweigh cavitation-assisted release of phytochemicals. The study therefore supports a biphasic response: initial treatment improves extractability and dispersion, but continued energy delivery progressively exposes released compounds to degradation. Such behavior helps reconcile apparently contradictory studies in which US either increased or decreased antioxidant indices. A similar need for careful interpretation applies to sirkencubin, a honey–vinegar syrup with a composition markedly different from fruit-cell suspensions. Treatment at 26 kHz, 60% amplitude, and 2–15 min modified pH, TSS, total sugars, color, phenolic indices, antioxidant activity, microbial counts, and sensory acceptance, with the highest overall liking reported after 8 min [97] . Unlike plant juices, this beverage contains no intact fruit tissue whose disruption could fully explain the increase in phenolic compounds or sugars. The response may instead involve improved dissolution and dispersion of honey-derived constituents, deagglomeration, degassing, and changes in the accessibility of compounds to analytical assays. Statements attributing the results to “cell-wall disruption” or “enzymatic hydrolysis” should therefore be avoided unless directly demonstrated. The sensory benefit at 8 min is technologically relevant, but the decline or lack of further improvement at longer treatments again indicates that maximum exposure is not necessarily optimal. Additionally, because microbial reduction, sensory restructuring, and compositional changes occurred simultaneously, the study spans both preservation and quality-structuring functions rather than representing a purely physicochemical application.

Across these fruit and plant beverage studies, the most robust evidence is therefore not that US universally increases BAC, but that it can shift the balance between compound release and compound degradation. The location of this optimum depends on tissue structure, initial particle size, acidity, solids content, oxygen availability, and acoustic dose. Moderate treatments frequently improve extractability and antioxidant measurements, whereas prolonged treatment or excessive power can reverse these gains. Importantly, most studies evaluated chemical antioxidant assays rather than digestion, absorption, or biological outcomes. Terms such as “bioaccessibility” should consequently be reserved for studies that incorporated simulated digestion or other direct bioaccessibility measurements; increased TPC, DPPH, or FRAP alone demonstrates enhanced analytical recovery or antioxidant potential, not necessarily improved uptake in vivo.

Prebiotic beverages provide a particularly useful test of whether US can intensify processing without compromising functional ingredients. In XOS-enriched orange juice, high-intensity US applied at nominal powers up to 1200 W did not change the chromatographic profile or concentration of XOS, demonstrating strong molecular stability of the prebiotic fraction even under severe processing conditions [107] . This is a robust positive finding because individual XOS species, from xylobiose to xylohexaose, were quantified rather than inferring stability from bulk soluble-solids measurements. Nevertheless, the surrounding juice components were less resistant. Increasing power caused a progressive decline in ascorbic acid, while TPC and FRAP followed a similar adverse trend at high severity. Malic and citric acids initially increased between 300 and 600 W, likely because release or improved analytical recovery exceeded degradation, but decreased as the treatment intensified further. Thus, stability of the targeted prebiotic cannot be generalized to the entire beverage: the functional carbohydrate remained intact while redox-sensitive constituents were compromised. This finding provides direct evidence against describing US as uniformly non-destructive. It also illustrates why evaluation based on a single “functional ingredient” can conceal broader quality losses. A process may be successful for maintaining XOS yet suboptimal for vitamin C and phenolic retention. From an industrial perspective, the optimum should therefore be selected using a multi-response criterion incorporating prebiotic integrity, nutrient retention, microbial safety, sensory quality, and energy demand rather than maximizing nominal power. The behavior of inulin in apple juice further demonstrates that chemical and physical stability are distinct outcomes. Specific energies of 30–300 J/g did not modify the inulin profile, sugar content, TPC, or antioxidant activity, even though treatment temperatures reached approximately 82 °C under the highest-energy condition [99] . Molecular integrity was therefore retained despite combined mechanical, chemical, and thermal stresses. However, untreated and lower-energy samples exhibited inulin precipitation and increased cloudiness after refrigerated storage, whereas 300 J/g suppressed precipitation and produced a more stable appearance.

Together, the plant-based evidence supports three conclusions. First, US is most effective when a specific structural barrier intact tissue, particle aggregation, poor dispersion, or prebiotic precipitation limits product quality. Second, measured increases in phytochemicals primarily indicate improved release or analytical accessibility and should not automatically be equated with enhanced bioavailability. Third, the favorable processing window is strongly matrix dependent: the energy required to stabilize a prebiotic suspension may exceed the threshold at which vitamins and phenolics begin to degrade. Accordingly, future optimization should report delivered acoustic energy, temperature profiles, dissolved oxygen, sample volume, and reactor geometry, and should use multi-objective models that balance structural stability against nutritional and sensory losses rather than selecting conditions from a single maximum response.

In cereal-based probiotic beverages, US-induced quality structuring is complicated by the simultaneous presence of starch granules, proteins, insoluble fiber, phenolic compounds, and living microorganisms. Unlike clarified fruit juices, these matrices respond through several competing mechanisms, including particle fragmentation, starch depolymerization, release of bound phytochemicals, and changes in probiotic metabolism. Consequently, the stage at which US is applied may be as important as amplitude or treatment duration. This is evident in the white finger millet probiotic beverage evaluated by Meena et al. [100] , in which US was applied either before inoculation at 40.11% amplitude for 11.09 min or after inoculation at 41.42% amplitude for 2.63 min. Both treatments reduced particle size relative to the untreated beverage, but the effect was substantially greater when US preceded inoculation: mean particle size decreased from 1271 nm in the control to 599.4 nm, compared with 969.1 nm following post-inoculation treatment. The stronger size reduction under pre-inoculation US was likely driven primarily by its longer exposure and higher acoustic energy density rather than by treatment timing alone. Cavitation-generated shear forces fragmented suspended cereal particles and increased the available interfacial area, potentially improving dispersion uniformity and reducing coarse mouthfeel. However, because sedimentation, rheology, and storage stability were not followed over an extended period, the observed particle-size reduction cannot by itself be taken as evidence of long-term physical stabilization. Treatment timing also produced markedly different compositional and microbial responses. Pre-inoculation US generated the highest reducing-sugar concentration, 1.45 mg/mL, compared with 1.28 mg/mL after inoculation and only 0.11 mg/mL in the control. This response is consistent with disruption of the cereal matrix and increased accessibility of starch to endogenous or microbial enzymes, thereby supplying more readily fermentable substrates. Viable counts consequently increased from 7.77 log CFU/mL in the control to 8.56 and 8.32 log CFU/mL after pre- and post-inoculation treatments, respectively. Nevertheless, attributing this increase solely to direct US stimulation of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus would be premature. Pre-inoculation treatment exposed no cells to acoustic stress and likely acted mainly by restructuring the substrate, whereas post-inoculation treatment directly exposed viable cells but used a considerably lower treatment duration and acoustic density. The experimental design therefore demonstrates that both strategies can support high viability, but it does not isolate whether differences arose from timing, dose, nutrient release, or direct microbial stimulation. The phytochemical results further illustrate why individual quality indicators must be interpreted separately. Pre-inoculation treatment produced the highest antioxidant activity, 22.73%, compared with 17.05% in the control and 14.74% after post-inoculation treatment. TPC was statistically comparable between the pre-inoculation sample and control, at 11.22 and 10.65 mg GAE/100 g, respectively, whereas the post-inoculation sample declined to 5.76 mg GAE/100 g. Conversely, both US treatments increased total flavonoid content to approximately 9–10 mg QE/100 g, compared with 3.64 mg QE/100 g in the control. Thus, the results do not support a uniform increase in all bioactive indices. Instead, they suggest selective release, transformation, or degradation of different compound classes, combined with changes arising during fermentation. The higher antioxidant activity after pre-inoculation treatment may reflect improved accessibility of specific high-activity compounds rather than a large increase in total phenolics. Meanwhile, the decline in TPC and antioxidant activity after post-inoculation US indicates that direct treatment of a fermented system may expose already-solubilized phenolics and microbial metabolites to oxidative cavitation stresses. Accordingly, the finger millet study supports US as a pretreatment for substrate conditioning, rather than establishing post-inoculation US as universally beneficial. US before fermentation reduced particle size, increased available sugars, and supported probiotic growth without directly exposing the cells to prolonged acoustic stress. However, the absence of fermentation kinetics, metabolite profiling, refrigerated-storage validation, and sensory evaluation prevents conclusions regarding whether these immediate compositional gains translate into improved product quality or probiotic stability throughout shelf life.

Smoothies also represent an especially challenging matrix for US-assisted structuring because suspended fruit tissues coexist with milk proteins, starch, soluble and insoluble fibers, seeds, lipids, and added sweeteners. In such systems, a reduction in particle size may improve smoothness and serum stability, but intensive treatment can also alter starch–protein interactions and expose phenolics to oxidation. The functional smoothie studied by Kumar et al. [102] , containing milk, oats, chia seeds, blueberries, and honey, illustrates these trade-offs. Importantly, this investigation should not be described as a comparison between conventional heating and an entirely non-thermal US treatment. The control smoothie was heated at 82 °C for 15 min, and the alternative process involved US-assisted heat treatment using a 750-W, 20-kHz probe system at 60–90% amplitude for 10 min with a 2-s ON/2-s OFF pulse cycle. The product effects therefore arose from combined acoustic, mechanical, and thermal stresses, and the contribution of cavitation cannot be fully separated from heating. Relative to conventional heat treatment, the US-assisted process reduced the particle-size fraction and yielded a more homogeneous, “velvety” structure. The reduction of coarse particles likely improved mouthfeel and limited gravitational separation by decreasing particle settling velocity. Serum separation was lower, and viscosity and sensory properties were more stable during refrigerated storage. These changes are consistent with fragmentation of fruit and cereal particles, improved hydration and distribution of oat and chia polysaccharides, and modification of protein–polysaccharide associations. FTIR spectral changes provided evidence of altered molecular interactions, but they did not establish a single mechanism such as starch gelatinization or protein aggregation. Therefore, the physical improvement should be attributed to a combination of particle-size reduction, hydration, and matrix reorganization rather than to one unverified structural pathway. The nutritional response, however, was less favorable than suggested in the original version of this subsection. Conventionally pasteurized samples retained higher phenolic content and antioxidant activity than the US treatment, even though the latter showed superior physical stability. This finding directly contradicts studies in simpler fruit matrices where moderate US increased measurable TPC and antioxidant capacity. The discrepancy can be explained by the complexity of the smoothie and by the assisted-heat design. Phenolics released from blueberries or other ingredients may have become more vulnerable to oxidation after particle disruption, while oxygen entrainment, radical formation, and treatment-associated heating may have accelerated their degradation. Interactions with milk proteins and polysaccharides could additionally reduce their analytical recovery. Accordingly, improved homogenization and texture did not coincide with maximum bioactive retention. This trade-off is highly relevant to process optimization. Selecting the treatment solely on serum separation or viscosity would favor US-assisted processing, whereas prioritizing phenolic retention might favor conventional heating. A rational process therefore requires multi-objective optimization involving physical stability, sensory quality, microbial safety, bioactive retention, treatment time, and energy use. The study also remained laboratory scale and did not report delivered acoustic power or specific energy, limiting comparison with continuous industrial homogenization. Nonetheless, it provides valuable negative evidence showing that US does not invariably outperform thermal processing across every quality dimension.

Dairy and whey-based FBs provide some of the strongest evidence that US can function as a structural processing operation rather than merely as a preservation tool. These beverages contain proteins, fat droplets, fruit particles, and often hydrocolloids or prebiotic fibers, all of which respond differently to acoustic shear. As a result, US may either increase or decrease viscosity depending on which structural component dominates. Particle disruption and polysaccharide depolymerization generally reduce consistency, whereas protein unfolding, aggregation, hydration, or network formation may increase viscosity. Therefore, viscosity changes should not be interpreted as a universal indicator of successful homogenization. In a pilot-scale blackberry-enriched dairy beverage, Putsakum et al. [103] compared batch US homogenization at an intensity of 10.37 W/cm 2 for 1, 3, and 5 min with conventional rotor–stator homogenization at 10,000 rpm for 1 min. US generated a higher proportion of small particles, and longer treatment progressively reduced the coarse-particle fraction. All US-treated beverages also exhibited greater apparent viscosity than the untreated blackberry–milk mixture. These outcomes suggest that cavitation disrupted blackberry particles while simultaneously promoting interactions among fruit polysaccharides and dairy proteins. The acidic fruit component may have shifted milk proteins toward conditions favoring association or partial aggregation, thereby increasing resistance to flow despite the smaller particle size. However, the original claim that US caused a pH reduction from 5.5 to 4.9 and formed a protein gel should be used cautiously unless those changes were explicitly attributed to US rather than to formulation with blackberry powder. The study mixed blackberry powder with preheated milk, and the acidic fruit ingredient itself would be expected to reduce pH. Moreover, increased viscosity does not independently confirm gel formation. The available evidence supports particle-size reduction and altered rheology, but stronger claims regarding acid-induced aggregation require direct protein-structure or network measurements. US treatment caused only minor color changes, while phenolic content and antioxidant activity were generally comparable with conventional homogenization. The highest values observed at selected treatment durations do not establish a consistent superiority of US because differences were treatment-dependent and not all indices increased monotonically. Rather, the main advantage was structural homogenization with retention of functional compounds, not unequivocal enrichment of BAC. This distinction is important because it places the study correctly within quality structuring rather than extraction. It also represents a stronger scale-up case than most studies in this field because processing was performed in a pilot-scale batch system. Nevertheless, batch operation, treatment of relatively small volumes, and lack of storage validation still limit conclusions regarding commercial throughput and long-term phase stability.

Whey-derived ingredients have become increasingly important in functional foods and beverages because of their excellent nutritional quality, techno-functional properties, and ability to serve as carriers of health-promoting BAC. More recently, whey coproducts such as whey protein phospholipid concentrates (WPPC) have also attracted growing attention owing to their unique combination of high-quality proteins and membrane-derived bioactive lipids, particularly phospholipids and milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) components, which further expand the functional potential of dairy-based beverage systems [122] . In a study, prebiotic soursop whey beverage was sonicated at 0, 200, 400, and 600 W for 3 min [109] . At 600 W, high-intensity US achieved approximately the same reduction in aerobic mesophilic bacteria as high-temperature short-time treatment, despite reaching a lower terminal temperature of 53 °C. More relevant to quality structuring, all sonicated beverages resisted phase separation, whereas the untreated and HTST samples were less kinetically stable. Microscopy and particle-size analysis indicated disruption of larger dispersed structures, while rheological measurements showed a slight viscosity decrease and a significant reduction in consistency. Thus, improved physical stability occurred without an increase in bulk viscosity, demonstrating that suspension stability can result from smaller particles and stronger interparticle interactions rather than thickening alone. The rheological response arose from opposing ingredient-specific effects. Cavitation can fragment fruit-pulp particles, reduce casein-micelle dimensions, and lower the molecular size or organization of polysaccharides, which tends to decrease viscosity. At the same time, partial whey-protein unfolding can expose hydrophobic regions and reactive groups, promoting protein–protein or protein–polysaccharide association. Inulin and gellan gum may also form or reinforce weak networks under high shear. The observed decrease in consistency therefore reflects the net result of these competing processes rather than simple “protein denaturation.” The authors similarly noted that sonicated fruit particles and whey proteins could increase viscosity, whereas polysaccharide and casein disruption could decrease it. Notably, raising nominal power from 200 to 600 W did not further improve phase stability because all sonicated treatments already showed negligible separation. This plateau is an important negative threshold: once a sufficient acoustic dose reduced destabilizing particles and reorganized the continuous phase, additional power provided little structural benefit. Consequently, the highest power may be justified for microbial inactivation but not for homogenization alone. This distinction demonstrates why preservation and structural objectives should be optimized separately. A beverage manufacturer seeking only physical stability could potentially use a lower energy input than one targeting both stability and microbial reduction.

Taken together, the blackberry dairy beverage and prebiotic whey beverage show that US can outperform or complement conventional homogenization by reducing coarse particles and limiting phase separation. Yet their viscosity responses differ: viscosity increased in the blackberry–milk system but decreased slightly in the soursop–whey–inulin system. This apparent contradiction is mechanistically plausible. The blackberry beverage was dominated by acidified milk proteins and fruit solids capable of association and thickening, whereas the prebiotic whey beverage contained a more complex balance of dispersed fruit particles, whey proteins, casein, inulin, and gellan gum, some of which were fragmented or depolymerized. The studies therefore establish matrix composition, not particle-size reduction alone, as the principal determinant of rheological outcome. Beyond physical structuring, high intensity US has been used to modify the nutritional profile of soursop whey beverages. Treatment at 19–20 kHz and powers up to 600 W increased measured phenolic content, antioxidant activity, and ACE-inhibitory potential relative to untreated or HTST-processed beverages [108] . These responses may reflect improved release of fruit phenolics and formation or exposure of bioactive peptide sequences following partial protein unfolding. However, high intensity US also reduced ascorbic acid and selected mineral concentrations and generated changes in volatile compounds. Therefore, the functional gain was selective rather than comprehensive: enhancement of some antioxidant and antihypertensive indices was accompanied by degradation of vitamin C and modification of aroma chemistry. The study itself recognized both beneficial and adverse nutritional changes, which should be retained in the critical synthesis rather than presenting US as uniformly protective. The strongest biological evidence comes from the subsequent in vivo investigation in which healthy Wistar rats consumed high intensity US- or HTST-processed prebiotic soursop whey beverages [106] . The high intensity US beverage was produced at 20 kHz using 520 W nominal power, 20.3 W acoustic power, an energy density of 2.9 kJ/cm 3 , and a 9.5-min treatment for 100 mL, with temperature maintained below 53 °C. This study is notable because it reported delivered acoustic parameters more comprehensively than most beverage investigations and assessed physiological endpoints rather than relying exclusively on chemical antioxidant assays. Consumption of the sonicated beverage was associated with reductions in serum triglycerides, very-low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and alanine aminotransferase, together with changes in antioxidant-enzyme activity and satiety-related outcomes. Nevertheless, the in vivo findings require restrained interpretation. The animals consumed a complex beverage containing whey proteins, soursop compounds, and inulin, so the physiological effects cannot be assigned exclusively to US-induced structural modification. Some outcomes were similar between the high-intensity US and HTST beverage groups, including protection against lipid peroxidation, suggesting that the beverage formulation itself contributed substantially. The authors also proposed that inulin, which retained its primary structure, may have influenced oxidative and metabolic responses independently of processing. Only the high-intensity US group showed significant changes in selected lipid-profile markers, but this isolated animal study does not establish clinical efficacy or direct human-health benefit. It should therefore be presented as preliminary in vivo validation, not confirmation that US enhances health outcomes in consumers.

Overall, the evidence demonstrates that US-assisted quality structuring operates through multiple, sometimes opposing, mechanisms. In cereal systems, treatment before inoculation can condition the substrate by reducing particle size and increasing fermentable-sugar accessibility. In smoothies, improved homogeneity and serum stability may be accompanied by lower phenolic retention than conventional heating. In dairy matrices, US can either increase or decrease viscosity depending on the balance among protein association, particle fragmentation, and polysaccharide disruption, while phase stability may improve in either case. These findings reinforce that process success cannot be defined by a single response such as viscosity, TPC, or particle size. Instead, optimization must integrate microstructure, rheology, physical stability, microbial quality, sensory acceptance, nutrient retention, and energy efficiency. Thermosonication and US-assisted thermal processing broaden the role of US from stand-alone quality structuring to integrated process intensification. These approaches can simultaneously reduce processing time, improve homogenization, modify rheology, suppress enzymatic activity, and enhance microbial control. However, because heat and acoustic cavitation act concurrently, improvements cannot be attributed exclusively to US unless appropriate US-only and thermal controls are included. In an orange juice–whey drink, thermosonication at 70–90 °C produced stronger microbial inactivation and refrigerated stability than conventional high-temperature short-time processing while increasing antioxidant, antihypertensive, and antidiabetic activities [110] . The response was most pronounced at 80–90 °C, indicating that the process relied substantially on thermal–acoustic synergy rather than on a purely non-thermal mechanism. Thermosonication also reduced the consistency index and altered the volatile profile, showing that greater microbial and functional performance may be accompanied by substantial structural and sensory modification. Thus, lower viscosity should not automatically be interpreted as quality loss: in this matrix it may reflect particle disruption and improved flowability, although excessive thinning could be undesirable for products formulated to deliver a full-bodied mouthfeel.

A similar balance between functionality and process severity was observed in pollen-enriched apple juice. Response-surface optimization identified approximately 40.9 °C, 5.63 min, 61.0% amplitude, and 60 mg pollen/100 mL as the optimum conditions. The treatment increased TPC, flavonoids, antioxidant capacity, and several individual phenolic compounds, partially suppressed polyphenol oxidase, and improved sensory scores relative to untreated and pasteurized controls [111] . These results support the use of thermosonication for simultaneous ingredient incorporation and quality structuring. Nevertheless, the observed enhancement resulted from the combined influence of pollen enrichment and processing. Therefore, the nutritional improvement cannot be assigned solely to acoustic treatment, and the optimized condition remains formulation-specific rather than broadly transferable to fruit juices.

US-assisted thermal processing of tejuino further illustrates the importance of balancing microbial safety with preservation of desirable fermentation microbiota. A fixed energy input of 0.5 kJ/mL followed by heating at 45–65 °C decreased aerobic mesophilic bacteria, coliforms, molds, and yeasts in a temperature-dependent manner while retaining substantial lactic acid bacterial populations [112] . Treatments at 45–55 °C preserved total soluble phenols and DPPH- and ABTS-based antioxidant activity more effectively, whereas FRAP values declined above 50 °C. The results therefore identify a clear trade-off: higher temperatures strengthened microbial control but increased the risk of functional-quality losses. This type of threshold information is more valuable for process design than simply reporting an optimum treatment because it defines the transition from beneficial intensification to excessive severity.

In a functional smoothie, US-assisted heating produced smaller particles, lower serum separation, and more stable viscosity and sensory properties than conventional heat treatment, but the thermally treated beverage retained higher phenolic and antioxidant values [102] . This apparently contradictory result reinforces that improved physical structuring does not guarantee superior nutritional retention. In multicomponent beverages, disruption of fruit tissues may release phenolics while simultaneously increasing their exposure to oxygen, radicals, proteins, and metal ions. The net outcome therefore depends on whether release or degradation dominates. For industrial formulation, thermosonication should consequently be optimized using multiple responses rather than a single endpoint such as particle size, microbial count, or TPC. Several investigations used US not merely to process an existing beverage but to facilitate incorporation of functional ingredients into a new matrix. In drinkable yogurt containing ultrasonicated purple cactus pear powder, the treated ingredient increased antioxidant activity and provided a natural source of color and phenolic compounds [113] . However, the yogurt containing non-ultrasonicated powder retained higher ascorbic acid and phenolic content than the formulation containing ultrasonicated powder. This result indicates that ingredient pretreatment may improve some antioxidant responses while simultaneously degrading sensitive compounds. It also demonstrates that stronger analytical antioxidant activity does not necessarily coincide with higher concentrations of every bioactive constituent. Similarly, US treatment of a mango–carrot beverage containing turmeric increased phenolic compounds, carotenoids, and antioxidant indices, while treatment of white finger millet beverage improved reducing-sugar availability, flavonoid content, particle-size distribution, and probiotic counts [100] , [105] . In both systems, the functional response reflected an interaction between processing and formulation: turmeric, cereal carbohydrates, and microbial cultures each influenced the final outcome. These studies support US as a tool for dispersing and activating functional ingredients, but they also illustrate why controls must separate the effects of ingredient addition, sonication, fermentation, and storage.

Taken together, the evidence for US-assisted quality structuring is strongest for three outcomes: particle-size reduction, improved dispersion or phase stability, and increased analytical recovery of selected BAC. These responses have been observed across fruit, cereal, dairy, whey, and prebiotic beverages. Evidence is less consistent for viscosity, antioxidant retention, and sensory improvement because these responses are strongly matrix dependent. Viscosity increased in the blackberry dairy beverage and functional smoothie but decreased in the prebiotic whey system and thermosonicated orange–whey drink. Likewise, moderate treatment frequently increased TPC and antioxidant activity, whereas prolonged treatment, high nominal power, or combined heating caused losses of ascorbic acid, phenolics, organic acids, or antioxidant capacity. The reviewed literature also contains a strong optimization bias. Most studies used response-surface designs or multiple treatment combinations and emphasized the condition that maximized one or more desirable responses. Null treatments, unsuccessful formulations, and negative sensory or storage outcomes were reported less consistently. This creates a risk of publication bias toward apparently successful applications. Furthermore, many studies described improvements using percentages or endpoint values without reporting effect sizes relative to untreated and conventionally processed controls in a standardized format. Cross-study comparison is therefore frequently qualitative rather than quantitative.

Reproducibility remains limited by incomplete acoustic reporting. Although some studies provided acoustic power, intensity, specific energy, or energy density, many reported only nominal power, amplitude, frequency, and time. Reactor geometry, probe diameter, immersion depth, sample volume, duty cycle, temperature history, and calorimetric power were often absent. Nominal settings such as 60% amplitude or 600 W therefore cannot be compared directly across devices. Temperature control is particularly important because several treatments described as non-thermal reached temperatures capable of independently altering proteins, polysaccharides, enzymes, and sensitive nutrients. Industrial validation also remains sparse. Most studies were performed in small laboratory vessels using batch probe systems. The pilot-scale blackberry dairy beverage study provides useful evidence that US homogenization can be transferred beyond analytical volumes, but continuous-flow validation remains uncommon. Scale-up will require control of acoustic-field uniformity, residence-time distribution, equipment erosion, fouling, energy consumption, and localized overheating. High-intensity probe systems may generate strong effects near the horn while leaving less-treated regions elsewhere in the vessel; therefore, laboratory optima cannot be transferred by maintaining amplitude or treatment time alone.

From an industrial perspective, US is most attractive when it replaces or consolidates several operations, such as mixing, particle-size reduction, hydration, deagglomeration, and mild microbial control. Its feasibility is less convincing when equivalent quality improvements require long batch treatments of 20–90 min, because throughput and energy demand may offset the technological benefit. Continuous-flow reactors, recirculating systems, and hybrid technologies may improve processing uniformity, but these approaches need direct comparison with high-pressure homogenization, pulsed electric fields, high-pressure processing, and conventional thermal treatment. Such comparisons should include not only product quality but also energy use, processing capacity, equipment cost, cleaning requirements, and carbon footprint.

Overall, US-assisted process intensification enables the microstructural and functional tailoring of FB through particle disruption, enhanced dispersion, macromolecular reorganization, improved ingredient hydration, and increased release or analytical accessibility of BAC. The most reproducible benefits are obtained when US addresses a defined structural limitation, such as coarse particles, phase separation, poor dispersion, or precipitation of a functional ingredient. However, the relationship between process severity and product quality is generally non-linear. Insufficient energy may fail to produce the desired structural modification, whereas excessive power, prolonged treatment, or uncontrolled temperature rise can accelerate oxidation, degrade vitamins and phenolics, alter volatile profiles, or generate undesirable rheological changes. Accordingly, US should not be presented as universally non-destructive or intrinsically superior to thermal processing. Its success depends on beverage composition, solids content, pH, protein and polysaccharide interactions, oxygen availability, reactor design, and delivered acoustic energy. Future studies should therefore adopt multi-objective optimization, report calorimetric acoustic parameters and complete thermal histories, include positive, null, and negative outcomes, and validate optimized treatments under refrigerated storage and pilot- or continuous-scale conditions. Digestion models, cellular assays, animal studies, and ultimately human trials are also needed to determine whether increases in extractable phenolics or in vitro antioxidant activity translate into meaningful bioaccessibility and health effects. At present, US is best regarded as a versatile but highly matrix-dependent processing aid whose industrial value lies in precisely controlled quality structuring rather than unrestricted increases in acoustic severity. Lastly, AI and ML approaches also provide promising opportunities for advancing US-assisted process intensification in FB. By integrating multidimensional datasets comprising beverage composition, rheological properties, particle size distribution, processing parameters, storage stability, and functional quality attributes, AI-assisted models could predict optimal US conditions while simultaneously maximizing physical stability, bioactive retention, sensory quality, and energy efficiency. Moreover, ML-driven predictive modeling and digital twin technologies may facilitate real-time process monitoring, adaptive control, and scale-up of continuous-flow US systems, thereby reducing empirical optimization and improving process reproducibility. The successful implementation of these approaches will depend on standardized reporting of acoustic energy delivery, harmonized analytical methodologies, and the generation of high-quality datasets encompassing diverse beverage matrices and processing conditions.
