Fifth, benchmark performance indicators: the annotation-transfer reliability score and the quantitative-reproducibility surface defined above, tracked longitudinally on the public scoreboard so that improvement can be demonstrated rather than merely asserted. Defining these targets in advance transforms the profile from an appealing idea into a falsifiable claim: if meta-analysis-ready reporting does not measurably improve these indicators relative to current practice, the proposal will have failed on its own terms.

The living benchmark would do for exposomics meta-analysis what CASP 32 did for protein-structure prediction, what CAMI 33 did for metagenomics, what CASF 34 did for protein-ligand docking, and what various MS proteomics benchmarks have done for that field. It would convert a hortatory reporting standard into a substantive demonstration of cumulative science. The resources required are modest: a small consortium of contributing laboratories, a shared computing infrastructure, and an open governance model. The Pan-ReDU 35 work has already demonstrated that the underlying repositories can support pan-repository reanalysis ( Hosseini et al., 2025 ). The EMLB would build on that infrastructure and transform it from a technical achievement into a community institution.

I deliberately propose the EMLB as a “ living ” benchmark rather than as a one-time exercise. The exposome will not stop changing. New analytical platforms will emerge; new annotation engines will be developed; new cohorts will be added; and new phenotypes will be measured. A static benchmark would freeze the field at a particular moment in time. A living benchmark allows the field to incorporate new tools and cohorts as they arise, maintaining the same baseline reference set for continuity. This is the model of CASP and CAMI, and I see no reason exposomics should adopt anything weaker.

## Regulatory and public health implications, and what to do this year

The argument so far has been methodological. This closing section connects the argument to the broader purpose of exposome science: changing how exposure-related disease is prevented, regulated, and managed in public health. The methodological infrastructure proposed in Sections 6 through 11 is not an end in itself; it is the precondition for using exposome science in regulatory toxicology, cumulative risk assessment, environmental justice, and routine public health practice.

### Regulatory toxicology

Regulatory toxicology has been moving, slowly but visibly, toward the use of omics data in chemical safety assessment, which we refer to as toxicometabolomics ( Bouhifd et al., 2013 ; Ramirez et al., 2013 ). The OECD has produced a Metabolomics Reporting Framework ( OECD, 2023 ) within its Omics Reporting Framework 36 intended to standardize the reporting of metabolomics and transcriptomics data for regulatory submissions ( OECD, 2023 ). MERIT (see text footnote 8) has identified four regulatory use cases for metabolomics: derivation of points of departure via benchmark dosing, discovery of chemical mode of action, chemical grouping and read-across, and cross-species extrapolation ( Viant et al., 2019 ). All four use cases require not just well-performed metabolomics within a single study but also the ability to combine evidence across studies, because regulatory inference relies on the consistency of effects across replicates, doses, species, and laboratories. The four-layer evidence stack and the five-tier quantification scheme are not luxuries for the regulatory pathway; they are necessities. Without them, regulatory acceptance of metabolomics data will remain limited to a handful of well-controlled industry studies, and the broader exposomics literature will not enter regulatory practice at all. With them, the literature becomes machine-readable, machine-poolable, and machine-auditable, which is the condition under which regulators can rely on it.

### Cumulative and mixture risk assessment

The single greatest scientific deficit of current chemical risk assessment is its inability to address mixtures. A regulator who wishes to assess the cumulative risk of a class of chemicals or the combined risk of multiple co-occurring exposures has very few formal tools and little data to support those tools. Exposomics is a natural source of such data because untargeted analysis inherently captures mixtures. However, cumulative risk assessment requires class-level evidence aggregated across studies, with quantitative weights for each member of the class, mechanistic priors from in vitro and in vivo systems, and epidemiologic effect estimates from human cohorts. Each of these components exists; combining them depends on the interoperability profile this article advocates for. A class-level meta-analysis under form D, performed on the EMLB, would constitute a substantive contribution to cumulative risk assessment, particularly if linked to mechanistic priors from adverse outcome pathway frameworks ( Ankley et al., 2010 ) and to in vitro NAM evidence from the Tox21 program and its successors ( Krewski et al., 2020 ).

### Environmental justice and disparities

A second area where meta-analyzable exposomics is important is environmental justice ( Sillé et al., 2026a , b ). Population-level disparities in exposure have been documented for decades for criteria air pollutants, lead, and a small number of specific contaminants. They are largely undocumented for the broader chemical exposome, simply because the data needed to document them do not exist at the relevant scale. Meta-analyses across cohorts with diverse populations, harmonized for residential exposure indices and socioeconomic variables, would produce, for the first time, exposure–disparity estimates across the actual chemical complexity of human exposure. The GA4GH (see text footnote 10) human exposome standards explicitly address external exposure variables alongside internal exposures ( GA4GH Human Exposome Data Standards Study Group, 2024 ), and the federated form of meta-analysis is particularly suited to this question because the participating cohorts often have legal or ethical constraints on data sharing that preclude raw data pooling.

### Global participation and the democratizing logic of the tier system

Untargeted metabolomics at the analytical state of the art described in Section 3 requires high-resolution mass spectrometry, dedicated chromatography, and trained personnel that are currently concentrated in a small number of laboratories in high-income countries. If meta-analysis-ready exposomics is defined as participation only by Tier I and Tier II laboratories, the field will replicate the same geographic concentration that has shaped most of biomedicine. This would be a failure of the Human Exposome Project ( Hartung, 2023 ; Sillé et al., 2026a , b ) before it began, because the populations most at risk from environmental exposure live disproportionately in the Global South and in low-resource settings within high-income countries. The five-tier quantification scheme proposed in Section 7 is, viewed in this light, an explicit democratization mechanism. Laboratories without authentic standards or matrix-matched calibration can still contribute Tier III intensity-ratio data, Tier IV presence/absence detection frequency data, or Tier V recurring-unknown spectral evidence, and those contributions enter the meta-analytic estimator at their appropriate weight rather than being excluded entirely. The Banbury Exposomics Consortium ( Miller and Banbury Exposomics Consortium, 2025 ) and the Global Exposome Forum ( Hartung, 2025 ) have stressed that the public health value of exposomic data is highest where exposure burdens are greatest, which is precisely the population for which Tier IV and Tier V data are most likely to be the only feasible measurements. A meta-analysis-ready profile that treats lower-tier data as legitimate evidence, rather than as data of inferior quality, is the technical infrastructure of an equitable global exposome science. The political infrastructure must follow.

### Evidence-based toxicology

I have argued for two decades that toxicology should adopt the methods of evidence-based medicine, and I have helped build the Evidence-based Toxicology Collaboration to that end ( Hoffmann and Hartung, 2006 ; Hartung, 2009a ; Hartung et al., 2013b ; EFSA and EBTC, 2018 ; Hartung and Tsaioun, 2024 ). Evidence-based medicine works because clinical trials produce harmonized summary statistics that can be combined in systematic reviews. Toxicology does not yet have an equivalent infrastructure, and the absence of one is a primary reason that systematic reviews in toxicology are slow, contentious, and uneven in quality. Exposomics has an opportunity to do better because it is younger and less encumbered by legacy practices. If the field adopts a meta-analysis-ready reporting standard from the start, systematic reviews of exposomic evidence will become routine. If it does not, exposome science risks reproducing the synthesis problems of conventional toxicology at a higher chemical resolution.

### The Human Exposome Project

I argued earlier for a Human Exposome Project ( Hartung, 2023 ) as the natural successor to the Human Genome Project. The methodological agenda of that project rests on the kind of interoperability infrastructure described here. A Human Exposome Project that funds a thousand additional untargeted metabolomics studies without coordinating their reporting will produce a thousand additional islands. A Human Exposome Project that funds the same studies under the four-layer evidence stack will produce a cumulative resource. The political and scientific case for a Human Exposome Project is, in my view, settled; the methodological case is now the limiting factor.

### What to do this year

Big infrastructure proposals tend to drift because no individual laboratory feels the need to act. I want to close by listing concrete actions that any individual exposomics laboratory can take in 2026, without waiting for a coordinated working group to release a final specification. Each of these actions moves the field measurably closer to meta-analyzable exposomics and is feasible within current practice.

First, deposit raw data in mzML format to MetaboLights, Metabolomics Workbench, or GNPS/MassIVE as a standard default, regardless of whether the journal requires it. Second, produce processed results in mzTab-M version 2.0 rather than in laboratory-specific tab-separated files. Third, assign Universal Spectrum Identifiers to at least the annotated features and any recurring unknowns. Fourth, report confidence levels for every annotation under both the MSI and Schymanski schemes, and make the underlying evidence (m/z, retention time, MS/MS spectrum, library match score, in silico score, formula candidate) available for each feature. Fifth, report the quantification tier per feature according to the five-tier scheme. Sixth, export, alongside the feature table, a structured summary-statistics file following the Layer 4 schema, with effect estimates and standard errors for each feature against each pre-specified phenotype. Seventh, register the analytic plan in advance in a public repository before unblinding feature-by-phenotype associations.

None of these seven actions is technically demanding. None requires new infrastructure. Each is at the discretion of the depositing laboratory. The cumulative effect of widespread adoption, even before a finalized profile, would be substantial. If the next thousand untargeted exposomics studies all take these seven steps, the field will have transitioned from an archipelago to a continent by 2030.

## Limitations and what remains to be demonstrated

A proposal of this kind should be explicit about its own limits and which of its claims are evidence-based and which remain hypotheses awaiting demonstration. The central diagnosis—that interoperability rather than analytical capability now limits cumulative exposome science—is well-supported by the existing literature and by the documented fragmentation of standards reviewed in Sections 3 through 5. The individual components of the profile, including mzML, mzTab-M, ISA, the USI, the MSI and Schymanski confidence schemes, and the public repositories, are established and validated in their own right. What remains hypothetical is the profile as an integrated, enforced whole: neither the four-layer evidence stack, the evidence-object representation, the five-tier quantification scheme, nor the Exposomics Meta-Analysis Living Benchmark has yet been implemented, benchmarked, or shown at scale to deliver the cumulative gains claimed for it, so their expected benefits are prospective rather than demonstrated.

Several concrete weaknesses deserve explicit acknowledgment. Metabolite annotation remains incomplete, so a substantial fraction of features will continue to enter meta-analysis only as class-level or recurring-unknown evidence. Laboratory and cohort heterogeneity, along with frequently missing or non-standardized metadata, will limit how many studies can be combined in practice regardless of the profile. Repositories face genuine questions of long-term sustainability and funding. Interoperability between vendor software is still imperfect. Annotation standards and spectral libraries are themselves evolving, so any fixed schema risks obsolescence and must be versioned. Additionally, uncertainty propagation across the four evidence layers—from acquisition through annotation confidence and quantification tier to the final effect estimate—is not yet formalized, so the calibrated uncertainty the profile promises is currently an aspiration rather than a solved problem. These limitations do not undermine the argument; rather, they define the work that a community demonstration such as the EMLB would need to complete before the profile could be considered validated rather than proposed.

## Conclusion

I have argued that untargeted metabolomics-based exposomics has reached the point where its limiting factor is no longer analytical discovery but evidence integration ( Hartung, 2023 ). The discipline is technically mature, but its synthesis is not. The gap is not bridgeable by another checklist. It requires an executable interoperability profile composed of four layers: acquisition comparability, machine-readable reporting, evidence-aware annotation, and meta-analysis-ready summary statistics, which is implemented by the existing standards working groups acting in concert, enforced by repository validators, and demonstrated by a community-scale living benchmark. This is a central challenge for the Global Exposome Forum (see text footnote 4).

The components exist. The mzML format, the mzTab-M format, the Universal Spectrum Identifier, the ISA framework, the RefMet and ChEBI nomenclatures, the GNPS/MassIVE and MetaboLights and Metabolomics Workbench repositories, the SIRIUS and CANOPUS annotation engines, the mQACC and BP4NTA quality control consortia, the MERIT and OECD regulatory frameworks, and the GA4GH human exposome data standards together provide the building blocks. What is missing is the crosswalk, the validator infrastructure, the summary-statistic schema, and the political agreement to require all four layers at deposition. None of these are technical obstacles, especially with the advent of agentic AI easing their implementation.

Three convictions underlie my argument. First, FAIR 37 is not enough. A deposited dataset is not necessarily reusable, a reusable dataset is not necessarily meta-analyzable, and the field's habit of treating “ data shared ” as a synonym for “ data combinable ” has produced a curious situation in which exposomics has more public data than ever before but produces fewer cumulative findings per dataset than ever before. Second, unknowns should not be excluded from meta-analysis. They are first-class evidence and the very point of an untargeted approach. The Universal Spectrum Identifier and spectral similarity-based pan-repository search make it possible to treat recurring unknowns as stable, citable entities, and meta-analysis should do so. Third, annotation confidence and quantification tier should be statistical inputs to meta-analysis, not labels for the methods section. Pooling confirmed compounds with putative annotations under the pretense that they are equivalent evidence is a mistake. Stratifying by confidence and tier is straightforward, scientifically honest, and produces better-calibrated effect estimates.

The exposome is, in Wild's original framing ( Wild, 2005 ), the counterpart of the genome. The Human Genome Project succeeded because it agreed, early and explicitly, on what counted as a deposited human reference sequence and on the formats by which the sequence would be reported. Exposomics has not yet reached its corresponding agreement. The proposal of this article is that the agreement is overdue and that the materials for it are already on the table. I have attempted, in these pages, to lay them out. The work of assembling them is, properly, the responsibility of the standards groups, the repositories, the funders, and the journals. The cost of not doing this work is large and growing, in the form of duplicated discoveries, irreproducible associations, and a steady accumulation of single-study findings that the field does not know how to combine. The cost of doing it is small and front-loaded. The remaining question is one of will.

It is worth separating what can be done immediately from what will take longer. In the near term, individual laboratories can act now, without waiting for consensus, by taking the seven concrete steps listed at the end of Section 12: depositing raw data in mzML, producing mzTab-M outputs, assigning Universal Spectrum Identifiers, reporting dual-scheme confidence with the underlying evidence, recording a quantification tier per feature, exporting structured summary statistics, and pre-registering the analytic plan. In the medium term, the standards working groups, repositories, funders, and journals must produce the three things no single laboratory can: the crosswalk among existing standards, the end-to-end four-layer validator, and the Layer 4 summary-statistics schema. In the longer term, a community-scale demonstration such as the Exposomics Meta-Analysis Living Benchmark, and ultimately a coordinated Human Exposome Project, would convert these components into a durable, cumulative resource. The immediate steps are the ones that make the later ones worthwhile.

I have also argued, in two prior articles ( Sillé et al., 2020 ; Hartung, 2023 ), that the exposome is the natural successor to the genome in the post-genomic era of human health research. The argument of this third article is that the methodological infrastructure to support that succession is now within reach. It requires not new science but new consensus. The opportunity is available. The next study to be published in this field can take the seven concrete steps listed at the end of Section 12, and the cumulative effect of widespread adoption will transform the field within a decade. The whole, in this domain as in Aristotle's, can be more than the sum of its parts. But only if we agree to add it up.

figure_captions: Figure 1 The endo-exo bridge: metabolomics between exposure and phenotype. The metabolome occupies a unique position in human biology, sitting at the intersection of three classes of chemical signals. Exposures and their primary transformation products ( in vivo and microbial) enter from the left. Endogenous biological responses (perturbed metabolic pathways, oxidative stress, inflammation) enter from the right. Intermediate chemistry connecting the two (drug metabolism, conjugates, secondary transformations) sits in between. Untargeted high-resolution mass spectrometry is the only analytical platform that captures all three classes simultaneously in a single biological sample, which is why metabolomics has emerged as the central platform of human exposomics.

Figure 2 The standards landscape map. The exposomics community has produced a rich but fragmented landscape of standards, organized here by their coverage areas. Five vertical columns represent the major coverage areas: quality assurance and quality control (Left) , raw data formats, processed-result formats and identifiers, study and assay metadata, and chemical and spectral identifiers (Right) . Each existing standard or framework is shown as a labeled rectangle within the appropriate column, with arrows indicating where standards reference or extend each other. The figure illustrates the central diagnostic of this article: the ingredients exist; the recipe does not.

Figure 3 Why current studies do not combine: the seven failure modes. Seven failure modes obstruct the cross-study combination of untargeted exposomics data. Each enters the meta-analytic pipeline at a characteristic point: acquisition heterogeneity at the start and governance heterogeneity at the end. The figure traces a generic meta-analytic workflow (left to right: raw data → processed features → annotated features → quantitative estimates → summary statistics → pooled inference) and indicates where each failure mode interrupts the flow. The downstream cost of each failure mode increases as the workflow proceeds, because errors at later stages are harder to remedy without re-acquiring data.

Figure 4 Annotation as evidence object. In conventional practice, an untargeted metabolomics feature is reported as a name (e.g., “carnitine”) and a confidence level (e.g., “MSI Level 2”). This diminishes the information needed for cross-study meta-analysis. The figure shows the alternative: each feature is represented as a structured evidence object carrying all the supporting evidence (m/z, retention time, collision cross-section where available, MS/MS spectrum with USI, formula and structural candidates with probabilities, chemical-class assignment with probability, ontology identifiers, and explicit confidence levels under both MSI and Schymanski schemes). With this representation, downstream meta-analysis can stratify by confidence and integrate features at appropriate levels of certainty.

Figure 5 The five-tier quantification scheme. Untargeted metabolomics intensities vary in how directly they reflect concentration. The figure proposes a five-tier scheme that stratifies features by their quantitative interpretability: Tier I (absolute quantification with authentic standards and matrix-matched calibration); Tier II (semi-quantification with surrogate standards); Tier III (intensity ratio relative to internal standards or pooled QC); Tier IV (presence/absence with detection frequency reporting); Tier V (unknown feature evidence). Each tier supports a different downstream meta-analytic estimator. The figure shows, for each tier, what is reported, the typical uncertainty, the appropriate meta-analytic estimator, and example exposure categories for which the tier is typical.

Figure 6 Five forms of meta-analysis for untargeted exposomics. Meta-analysis of untargeted metabolomics-based exposomics is not a single technique but a portfolio of five (or six) practical forms, each with characteristic strengths, weaknesses, and feasibility under current infrastructure—they are graded by the author's judgment. Form A: Raw data pooled reprocessing (gold-standard pooling of raw spectra under a single pipeline). Form B: Processed-feature harmonization (mapping processed features across studies via m/z, retention time, MS/MS, CCS, and USI). Form C: Metabolite-level summary-statistic meta-analysis (random-effects or Bayesian estimation across per-study effect sizes for harmonized analytes). Form D: Chemical class, pathway, or molecular family meta-analysis (aggregation at the class or network level when compound-level identifications diverge). Form E: Federated meta-analysis (per-cohort local analysis with export of only summary statistics, suitable for governance-constrained cohorts). Form F: Detection frequency meta-analysis (presence/absence aggregation across studies; included here as a primitive but informative special case). Each form is rated along four axes: data-sharing requirement (low to high), feasibility today (immediate to aspirational), statistical strength (qualitative to quantitative effect estimation), and treatment of unknowns (discards them to first-class evidence). The color-coded matrix highlights, at a glance, that no single form dominates and that a mature exposome research program will use several in combination, chosen by question, data, and governance constraint.

Figure 7 The exposome–metabolome evidence stack (central conceptual figure). The exposome–metabolome evidence stack is a four-layer interoperability profile for untargeted exposomics meta-analysis. Layer 1 (acquisition comparability) ensures that differences in instrumentation, chromatography, and ionization are explicitly reported using a controlled vocabulary. Layer 2 (machine-readable reporting) ensures that raw spectra (mzML/mzMLb), processed results (mzTab-M), study metadata (ISA), and spectral provenance (USI) are deposited in open, validatable formats. Layer 3 (evidence-aware annotation) represents each feature as a structured evidence object carrying neutral mass, retention time, MS/MS spectrum, confidence levels, ontology identifiers, and class assignments. Layer 4 (meta-analysis-ready outputs) exports standardized summary statistics (effect estimates, standard errors, model specifications, covariates, quantification tiers) for direct ingestion by downstream meta-analytic software. Each layer is necessary; none is sufficient.

Figure 8 Implementing the interoperability profile: one laboratory's path from an LC-MS run to meta-analysis. A schematic of the worked example: A single untargeted metabolomics study proceeds left to right through four stages, each mapped to the evidence-stack layers by color. In Stage 1, the laboratory acquires data with pooled quality control injections and deposits raw spectra (mzML) and acquisition metadata (ISA) in a public repository (Layers 1–2). In Stage 2, it creates a structured evidence object for every feature (m/z, retention index, adduct, MS/MS spectrum with a Universal Spectrum Identifier, SIRIUS/CANOPUS candidates with probabilities, and MSI and Schymanski confidence levels) in mzTab-M (Layer 3). In Stage 3, it exports, for each feature, an effect estimate, standard error, model specification, covariate set, and quantification tier as a Layer 4 summary-statistics file. In Stage 4, a repository validator checks all four layers and issues a single accession carrying a “ meta-analysis-ready ” badge. A later meta-analyst then queries the badge across comparable cohorts, pools the Layer 4 exports, and stratifies by annotation confidence and quantification tier to obtain a pooled effect estimate. Solid outlines mark tools and standards that exist today; dashed outlines with a “ NEW ” tag mark the three components newly proposed in this article (the Layer 4 export schema, the four-layer validator, and the meta-analysis-ready badge). The figure represents a conceptual workflow, not a validated pipeline.

Figure 9 The Exposomics Meta-Analysis Living Benchmark. The Exposomics Meta-Analysis Living Benchmark (EMLB) is proposed as a community demonstration that meta-analysis-ready exposomics is feasible. A consortium would select 10–20 publicly available untargeted metabolomics studies with overlapping biospecimen types and phenotypic scopes, reprocess them under a common pipeline, and report annotation-transfer reliability, quantitative reproducibility, class-level enrichment, and federated analysis performance against a shared reference set. A public scoreboard would track performance over time as new studies, new pipelines, and new annotation engines are evaluated against the same baseline.

# Ageing in Unani medicine: Conceptual framework and modulatory approaches

## Abstract
In Unani medicine, the sustenance of life and the ageing process are largely attributed to the gradual depletion of Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya (innate moisture), which weakens Ḥarārat Gharīziyya (innate heat), impairs Quwā (all faculties) of the body, and shifts Mizāj (temperament) towards coldness and dryness. These changes lead to impaired digestion, defective Akhlāṭ (humour) formation, increased Taḥallul (wear and tear), and accelerated senescence.

This literature review examines how the balance of these principles, together with A a b Sitta Ḍar u riyya (six essential factors), influences vitality and healthy ageing. It employs a qualitative review of classical Unani texts alongside modern biomedical literature, integrating traditional metabolic concepts with contemporary perspectives on oxidative balance and degeneration.

The findings indicate that Unani medicine advocates a comprehensive, holistic approach, encompassing regimental therapies, dietary modifications, and pharmacological interventions with antioxidant properties, to maintain internal homeostasis and promote healthy ageing and health span. However, the evidence remains largely theoretical, underscoring the need for rigorous mechanistic and clinical studies to facilitate integration into modern geriatric care.

## Keywords
Unani medicine; Ḥararat Ghariziyya; Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya; Ageing; Taḥallul; Geriatric care

## Introduction

Ageing is the process of becoming older, which is a complex and multifactorial process characterised by the progressive accumulation of physiological changes that lead to a decline in bodily functions and ultimately result in death. It is widely recognised as an intrinsic, inevitable, and irreversible phenomenon associated with diminished viability, reduced reproductive capacity, increased vulnerability to diseases, and gradual functional deterioration [ 1 ].

In Unani medicine, ageing is viewed through a holistic framework as a consequence of disruptions in the body's innate equilibrium. Two key life-sustaining principles, i.e. Ḥararat Ghariziyya (innate heat) and Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya (innate moisture), are considered essential for maintaining vitality, metabolism, growth, and organ function. Life is sustained by the harmonious interaction between these forces, Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya (RG) acting as the nourishing substrate and Ḥararat Ghariziyya (HG) as the operative energy [ [2] , [3] , [4] ].

The gradual depletion of RG with age weakens HG, which impairs the vital faculties like Quwwat Tabīʿiyya (natural faculty), Quwwat Ḥaywāniyya (vital faculty), and Quwwat Nafsāniyya (psychic faculty), and shifts the body's Mizāj (temperament) toward Bārid Yābis (coldness and dryness). This results in impaired digestion, faulty humour production, increased Taḥallul (physiological wear and tear), and accelerated senescence [ [5] , [6] , [7] ].

In Unani medicine, HG is considered the primary life-sustaining force of the body. Conceptually, it corresponds to the notion of quality of life, as it governs fundamental physiological functions including sensation and cognition, voluntary and involuntary movements, digestion and assimilation, metabolic activity, and the excretion of waste products. This intrinsic heat enables the performance of vital processes that define living beings and differentiate them from non-living matter [ 8 ].

According to Unani scholars such as Jālīnūs and al-Rāzī, innate heat is generated through the metabolic transformation of the fundamental bodily constituents, referred to as ʿUnṣur-i-Istiḥāla , within the human system. In contrast, Ibn Sīnā described HG as a divinely bestowed life force, emphasising its primordial and sustaining role in human vitality. Although articulated through different philosophical frameworks, these interpretations converge on the understanding of innate heat as the driver of physiological activity. [ 2 , 5 , 9 ]. The gradual decline of Harārat-e-Gharīziyya described in classical Unani texts finds resonance in modern observations of age-related reductions in metabolic rate, mitochondrial efficiency, and cellular energy production [ 10 ].

In Unani medicine, Ruṭūbat-e-Gharīziyya is described as the innate moist medium that sustains and regulates Ḥarārat-e-Gharīziyya by preventing its excessive dissipation. From a conceptual standpoint, its supportive role may be understood, in modern terms, as the cellular biochemical milieu that preserves internal stability, structural integrity, and functional continuity, and provides a foundational framework that maintains molecular organisation, structural coherence, and appropriate physicochemical conditions, thereby allowing metabolic and mitochondrial processes to proceed in a controlled and efficient manner. Progressive deterioration of this supportive framework results in reduced bioenergetic efficiency despite the presence of otherwise intact metabolic machinery [ 11 ].

This study aims to examine the Unani concepts of Ḥarārat Gharīziyya and Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya in the context of ageing, focusing on the two age groups defined in Unani medicine: Sinn-i-Kuhūlat (age of decline) and Sinn-i-Shaykhūkhat (age of superannuation). Unani medicine, therefore, does not primarily aim at prolonging chronological lifespan; rather, its emphasis lies in delaying functional deterioration and preventing premature senescence, a goal that closely aligns with the modern concept of healthspan. Within this framework, preservation of these vital principles through diet, regimens, and drugs, with the regulation of the Asbāb Sitta Ḍarūriyya (six essential factors) being central to maintaining balance, supporting Ṭabīʿat (medicatrix naturae) and delaying degenerative changes.

## Methodology

A structured narrative review was undertaken to critically examine Unani concepts of ageing and healthy ageing and their relevance to contemporary biomedical understanding. The review focused on Ḥarārat Gharīziyya (innate heat), Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya (innate moisture), Taḥallul (physiological wear and tear), Mizāj (temperament), Quwā (faculties), Asbāb Sitta Ḍarūriyya (six essential factors), and Tadābīr-i-Mashāyikh (care of the elderly). Authoritative classical Unani texts, standard translations, and pharmacopoeial literature were reviewed to extract information on the physiology of ageing, age-related changes, preventive principles, dietary and regimental measures, and single and compound drugs.

Contemporary biomedical literature was searched using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect. Relevant combinations of keywords included “ageing,” “healthy ageing,” “gerontology,” “cellular senescence,” “oxidative stress,” “telomere,” “mitochondrial dysfunction,” “autophagy,” “inflammaging,” “diet,” “exercise,” “sleep,” “Unani medicine,” “Ḥarārat Gharīziyya,” “Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya,” and “geriatric care.” Additional searches were conducted for medicinal plants, regimental interventions, and compound formulations discussed in the review. Particular attention was given to descriptions attributed to major Unani authorities, including Hippocrates, Galen, al-Rāzī, Ibn Sīnā, Ismāʿīl Jurjānī, and other recognised classical scholars and standard Unani pharmacopoeial texts.

Relevant original studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and other scholarly publications were considered, with preference given to recent and higher-level evidence, while foundational older literature was retained where appropriate. The retrieved information was organised thematically and narratively synthesised to compare classical Unani principles with contemporary mechanisms of ageing, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, telomere attrition, cellular senescence, autophagy, metabolic dysregulation, and chronic inflammation. These relationships were interpreted as conceptual parallels rather than direct biological equivalence unless supported by experimental evidence.

## Classification of age according to Unani medicine

In Unani Medicine, human life is broadly classified into four distinct stages: Sinn-i-Numū (period of growth), Sinn-i-Shabāb (youth), Sinn-i-Kuhūlat (middle age), and Sinn-i-Shaykhūkhat (old age). Each stage is characterised by a predominant Mizāj and kayfiyāt (qualities), reflecting dynamic changes in HG and RG, the two fundamental physiological forces in Unani philosophy [ 12 , 13 ].

### Sinn-i-Numū (up to 30 years; Mizāj: Ḥārr Ratab )

Also known as Sinn-i-Ḥadāthat (infancy and childhood), this stage represents the period of rapid growth and development. During this phase, the RG is abundant and exceeds the amount required to maintain HG, thus supporting vigorous metabolic activity and the overall anabolic processes essential for bodily development [ 12 , 14 ].

### Sinn-i-Shabāb (30–40 years; Mizāj: Ḥārr Yābis )

This is the stage of full physical maturity. The RG is now optimally balanced, just sufficient to preserve the HG. The organs have reached complete development, and the body possesses maximum vitality. The energy during this period is primarily used for maintaining the structural and functional integrity of fully developed organs and physiological processes [ 14 , 15 ].

### Sinn-i-Kuhūlat (40–60 years; Mizāj: Bārid Yābis )

The RG begins to diminish, making it progressively inadequate to sustain HG. As a result, the body's faculties and metabolic strength weaken. As a result, the body's faculties and metabolic strength weaken. A lighter, more digestible diet with adequate nutrients becomes essential to support weakened digestion and maintain residual energy [ 2 , 15 ].

### Sinn-i-Shaykhūkhat (60 years onward; Mizāj: Bārid Ratab )

This final stage begins after sixty years of age and continues until death. A significant reduction in both RG and HG characterises it. The faculties of the body undergo pronounced dissolution, and the dominance of Burūdat (coldness) and Yubūsat (dryness) surpasses that seen in the previous stage due to the insufficiency of the innate moist and warm qualities [ 2 , 14 , 15 ].

The period of Sinn-i-Kuhūlat marks the onset of physiological decline, characterised by progressive insufficiency of RG to sustain HG. At the same time, Sinn-i-Shaykhūkhat represents a stage of marked depletion of both, resulting in significant weakening of vital functions [ 2 ]. These classical Unani observations are supported by modern research, which demonstrates age-related changes such as reduced basal metabolic rate, diminished body water, and impaired thermoregulation, highlighting the convergence of traditional and contemporary perspectives on ageing [ 1 , 10 ].

## Gerontology

Gerontology is the scientific study of ageing, encompassing the biological, psychological, and sociological aspects of the ageing process [ 1 ]. The Greco-Roman physician Galen made significant contributions to the foundations of gerontology through his concept of Gerocomy, which referred to the care and management of the elderly. He regarded ageing as a natural and inevitable phenomenon rather than a pathological condition [ 16 ].

Modern gerontology identifies telomere length as a biomarker of ageing. As with increasing age, telomere shortening progressively impairs the capacity of cells to divide and maintain genomic stability. When a cell replicates, it loses part of its telomere, ultimately reaching a critically low length. It is then that cells enter replicative senescence, a state in which they continue to be metabolically active but lose the potential for proliferating. This restricts the body's capacity to replace worn-out or damaged cells, causing inefficient tissue regeneration. Concurrently, severely shortened telomeres induce DNA damage responses, genomic instability, and inflammatory signalling, underpinning age-related functional impairment and predisposition to degenerative disease. This finding echoes Unani accounts of the gradual depletion of RG, which is responsible for weakening HG and loss of restorative capacity in late life [ 3 , 17 , 18 ].

## The role of Ḥararat Ghariziyya and Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya in the maintenance of life and the ageing process: [ Fig. 1 ]

According to Unani Medicine, HG and RG are fundamental principles essential for sustaining life, whereas Burūdat (cold) and Yubūsat (dry) are considered antithetical to life, serving as hallmarks of degeneration and death. Many philosophers and physicians believed that HG is the vital life force that drives all physiological processes, acting as the operative energy behind the primary faculties, i.e., Quwwat Tabīʿiyya (natural faculty), Quwwat Ḥaywāniyya (vital faculty), and Quwwat Nafsāniyya (psychic faculty), which regulate and sustain bodily functions [ 19 ]. Any disruption in HG leads to dysfunction, and its severe depletion is ultimately deemed the cause of death. [ 13 ]. Fig. 1 Conceptual framework illustrating the Unani model of ageing.

However, HG depends on RG, which acts as its essential supporting medium. Classical Unani scholars have illustrated this interdependence through the analogy of a lamp, wherein the oil sustains and regulates the flame, ensuring its persistence over time [ 13 ].

Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya is bestowed at the time of conception and constitutes the fundamental moist substrate required for the regulated activity of Ḥarārat Gharīziyya . Classical Unani scholars describe this innate moisture as finite and non-renewable, gradually depleting with advancing age. This depletion is further accelerated by the progressive decline of Ruṭūbat-e-Dammiyya (the moisture component of blood), which plays a crucial supportive role in sustaining Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya . Physiologically, Ruṭūbat-e-Dammiyya attempts to compensate for this loss by supplying moisture generated through proper digestion. However, when dietary intake is inadequate or digestive faculty is weakened due to temperament imbalance or declining Quwā Ṭabīʿiyya, the formation of Ruṭūbat-e-Dammiyya is compromised. As a result, the supportive replenishment of Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya becomes insufficient, leading to unchecked dissipation of Ḥarārat Gharīziyya and acceleration of the ageing process. Thus, impaired nutrition and digestion act as critical factors in hastening senescence by disrupting the delicate equilibrium between innate moisture and innate heat.

As age advances, the quantity and quality of RG gradually diminish. Since HG depends on this moisture for its sustenance, its decline inevitably follows. Classical Unani scholars describe this relationship metaphorically: “ Harārat Gharīziyya is like a flame and Ruṭūbat Gharīziyya like the oil of a lamp.” As the oil diminishes, the flame fades, and with its extinction, life comes to an end [ 2 , 13 , 15 ].

A central concept underlying this decline is Taḥallul , which refers to the continuous physiological wear and tear or gradual dissipation of bodily components resulting from metabolic activity. Under normal conditions, this process is compensated by Ṭabīʿat through HG , which restores tissue loss via digestion and the formation of humours. However, with advancing age and the progressive decline of HG, this compensatory mechanism becomes insufficient, leading to a gradual imbalance between tissue loss and replenishment [ 5 , 12 ].

The weakening of HG impairs Quwā when, particularly, Quwwat-e-Hāḍima (the digestive faculty) weakens, resulting in defective production of Akhlāṭ . These humours are Dam (blood), Balgham (phlegm), Safrā (yellow bile), and Sawdā (black bile). They are essential for nutrition, repair, and maintenance of bodily functions. Under normal physiology, the humours formed through digestion replenish the continuous wear and tear of the body via Badal Mā Yataḥallal (replacement of fluid and energy). However, when the formation of Akhlāṭ becomes defective, this compensatory mechanism is impaired. As a result, the loss caused by Taḥallul is not adequately replenished due to impaired Badal Mā Yataḥallal . Meanwhile, as physiological processes continue, wear and tear persists, leading to a progressive accumulation of loss and thereby accelerating degeneration. Simultaneously, the qualitative shift in Mizāj toward Bārid (cold) and Yābis (dry) becomes prominent. This altered Mizāj not only reflects the depletion of RG but, when altered particularly toward Barūdat (coldness) and Yubūsat (dryness), also predisposes to the formation of Ruṭūbat-e-Gharība (abnormal or morbid moisture) by impairing normal metabolism and humoral balance, which disrupts normal physiological functions. Alongside this, there is a general weakening of Quwā (faculties), affecting the overall vitality of the organism [ 3 , 5 , 20 , 21 ].

Another critical component affected during ageing is Quwwat-e-Mudabbira-e-Badan (medicatrix naturae), the governing and regulatory power of the body. It acts as a regulator, detoxifier, and protector, maintaining the equilibrium of Mizāj and Akhlāt . However, with advancing age, its strength declines. This leads to impaired regulation and inefficient detoxification, resulting in the accumulation of waste products and thereby accelerating degeneration [ 5 , 6 , 22 ].

Thus, the combined effects of diminished RG, reduced HG, defective humour formation, impaired replacement of lost tissues, altered Mizāj , and weakening of regulatory and vital faculties converge to produce the progressive physiological deterioration recognised as ageing.

## The role of Asbāb Sitta Ḍarūriyya (six essential factors) in the maintenance of life and the ageing process

In the Unani system of medicine, preventive care and the promotion of healthy ageing are fundamentally grounded in the regulation of Asbāb Sitta Ḍarūriyya , which governs human health and physiological equilibrium. These include Hawā’-i-Muḥīṭ (environmental air), Makūlāt-o-Mashrūbāt (diet and drink), Ḥarakāt-o-Sukūn Badanī (physical activity and rest), Ḥarakāt-o-Sukūn Nafsānī (mental activity and emotional balance), Nawm-o-Yaqẓa (sleep and wakefulness), and Iḥtibās-o-Istifrāgh (elimination and retention). While ageing is an inevitable biological process, Unani medicine emphasises that healthy ageing is characterised by preservation of functional abilities and physiological resilience. It can be actively pursued through optimal regulation of these factors. Each component directly influences the maintenance of HG, the life-sustaining principles whose balanced interaction is essential for sustaining health, delaying functional decline, and supporting longevity across the lifespan [ 23 , 24 ].

### Hawā’-i-Muḥīṭ (environmental air)

Air plays a crucial role in sustaining life through its functions of Ta'dīl al-Rūḥ (moderation of the spirit) and Tanqiya al-Rīḥ (purification of breath). According to Unani medicine, exposure to polluted or imbalanced air disrupts the body's internal equilibrium, leading to humoral derangement, putrefaction of Akhlāṭ , and premature ageing, whereas fresh and pure air invigorates the Rūḥ , strengthens the humours, and supports optimal physiological function [ 13 , 24 ].

To complement these observations, contemporary research shows that air quality has a key impact on biological ageing: leukocyte telomere length, a proven measure of systemic ageing, declines following prolonged exposure to traffic-related emissions, particulate matter, and occupational toxins, whereas residential greenery and reduced pollution exposure correlate with increased telomeres. As telomeres mirror cumulative oxidative and inflammatory stress, these observations correlate with the Unani system's understanding of polluted air accelerating depletion of HG and RG, leading to quicker physiological decline. Therefore, control of air by staying away from polluted environments, opting for green and temperate surroundings, and proper ventilation can guard against innate heat and moisture, enhance genomic stability, and avert premature oxidative damage. Such regulation delays ageing and promotes longevity by sustaining the body's vital faculties and reducing the cumulative burden of cellular stress [ 25 ].

### Makūlāt-o-Mashrūbāt (food and drinks)

Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna emphasised that a proper diet is central to health maintenance and disease prevention. According to them, nutriment serves to replenish what is lost through the natural process of dissolution in the body. As noted by Maḥmūd Amulī , nutriment not only replenishes bodily substances but also supports growth and sustains metabolic functions. Overeating or consuming incompatible foods burdens Ṭabīʿat , leading to indigestion, formation of Ḥarārat-i-Gharība (abnormal heat), and accelerated tissue deterioration. Conversely, inadequate nutrition depletes RG, weakening organ function and promoting early ageing [ 8 , 26 , 27 ].

Modern studies corroborate these principles: dietary patterns rich in antioxidants, low glycemic index (GI) foods, and high-resistant starch (RS) foods are associated with reduced oxidative stress, lower incidence of coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers, and improved DNA integrity. Polyphenolic antioxidants, in particular, may protect against neurodegenerative diseases and cellular ageing. The available evidence further suggests that the consumption of antioxidant nutrients, fruits and vegetables, and adherence to a Mediterranean diet are primarily associated with longer telomeres. These results are in sync with Unani preference for a diet that keeps HG and RG preserved. They demonstrate that functional foods and nutritionally balanced diets promote healthy ageing and longevity. These principles are molecularly grounded in the hallmark of “deregulated nutrient-sensing,” where overnutrition triggers anabolic sensors like mTORC1 that suppress adaptive stress responses, while the dietary moderation advocated in Unani medicine activates repair-promoting scarcity sensors like SIRT1 and AMPK [ 28 , 29 ].

### Ḥarakāt-o-Sukūn Badanī (physical activity and repose)

According to Unani physicians, physical exercise is essential for stimulating HG and facilitating the excretion of waste products from the body. Movement is regarded as a vital physiological need, as it generates heat, supports the functioning of Ṭabīʿat , and enhances overall health. During digestion, Physis acts upon ingested food, converting it into heat and generating by-products, which must be expelled through movement to prevent harm to both the body and its vital heat. Unani scholars categorise movement based on its intensity and duration, i.e., Shadīd (vigorous), Duʿīf (weak), Qalīl (short duration), and Kathīr (prolonged duration). All types of movements generate heat, but their effects differ: vigorous and brief activity produces intense heat and raises body temperature, while weak or prolonged movement generates moderate heat. However, excessive or unbalanced movement can result in over-dissolution of bodily moisture, leading to suppression of HG and a sensation of cold. Thus, moderation is key [ 15 , 30 ].

Modern studies also support this view, that physical activity causes a hormetic response that favours pro-oxidation and boosts the activity of antioxidant enzymes. Repeated training is protective for lymphocyte DNA, associated with increased antioxidant capacity and reduced DNA strand breaks. It has been reported that oxidative lesions in telomeric DNA are repairable by glycosylases like NEIL1 and NEIL3, thus maintaining telomere integrity. Therefore, exercise not only halts telomere wear but could also extend telomeres, postpone cellular ageing and guard against sarcopenia. This protective effect is further supported by the discovery of exercise-induced mitochondrial microproteins, such as MOTS-c, which decline with age but act as endogenous AMPK agonists to maintain metabolic health and prevent insulin resistance [ 31 ].

### Ḥarakāt-o-Sukūn Nafsānī (mental activity and repose)

In Unani medicine, it is emphasised that just as the body requires a balance between activity and rest, the mind too needs both stimulation and relaxation to maintain well-being. Emotions directly influence the movement of Ḥarārat and Rūḥ (vital spirit and pneuma) within the body; anger and joy drive them outward, while fear and sadness pull them inward. Complex emotions, such as anxiety, shame, combined with anger, or fear mixed with rage, can cause an erratic bidirectional movement of vital heat, disrupting internal balance and affecting overall health [ 3 , 19 , 32 ].

Modern studies offer relevant insights, although the precise mechanisms by which psychological stress relates to cellular ageing are not entirely clear. Current findings suggest that stress-induced premature senescence in humans could be moderated by life stress perceived as chronic or ongoing. Three primary, non-mutually exclusive pathways have been suggestsed: (i) immune dysregulation, in which stress decreases the number of naïve T cells and raises the level of memory T cells, which possess shorter telomeres and lower regenerative potential; (ii) oxidative stress, from chronic autonomic and neuroendocrine activation, most notably through glucocorticoid secretion, which enhances neuronal oxidative damage by raising glutamate and calcium but reducing antioxidant enzymes; and (iii) telomerase activity, where stress is associated with reduced telomerase function, impairing the maintenance of telomere length. Importantly, the exact molecular pathways linking psychological stress to telomere shortening are not well understood, with a role for “unknown pathways” potentially involving cross-talks between stress signalling, mitochondrial function, and cellular senescence [ 33 ].

With these stress-mediated mechanisms, evidence indicates that interventions in mental well-being can reverse these processes. Mental activity regulation and stress management by mindfulness, cognitive behaviour therapy, meditation, and lifestyle interventions have been demonstrated to counteract the harmful effects of chronic stress, decrease cellular ageing markers, and preserve cognitive health. Together, the regulation of diet, movement, and mental well-being forms an integrated strategy that sustains the body's innate faculties, slows biological ageing, and promotes longevity [ 34 ].

### Nawm-o-Yaqẓa (sleep and wakefulness)

Nawm-o-Yaqẓa plays a crucial role in determining an individual's health, vitality, and mental alertness, with a precise balance over 24 h being essential. Jurjānī emphasised that proper sleep benefits all, while its deprivation alters the brain's temperament, impairs digestion and metabolism, and gradually weakens cognition, sensation, and motor function, leading to indecisiveness and mental fatigue. Ibn Rushd observed that humans, being naturally inclined to sleep, cannot function without it, and prolonged sleep deprivation can even be fatal [ 26 ]. Sleep is considered the great restorer, fulfilling key biological roles: conserving energy for optimal daytime performance and restoring neurotransmitters depleted during wakefulness. It also helps clear mental clutter and prepares the brain for new cognitive tasks. Sleep replenishes Buḳhrāt Laṭīfa (subtle vapours), which are continuously lost during wakefulness, by facilitating digestion, concoction, and the restoration of bodily moisture, thus supporting life and delaying senescence [ 35 , 36 ].

Modern research demonstrates that sleep quality is closely linked to biological ageing, with poor sleep characterised by short duration, frequent arousals, insomnia, or sleep apnea, associated with accelerated cellular ageing, as indicated by shortened telomeres. Disrupted sleep increases oxidative stress, inflammation, and impairs cellular repair, processes that contribute to the progression of age-related decline. Age-related changes in sleep architecture, including cortical thinning, white matter degeneration, neurotransmitter alterations, and circadian rhythm disruption, can further reduce restorative sleep and exacerbate functional decline in older adults. Consequently, insufficient or low-quality sleep may accelerate frailty, cognitive decline, cardiovascular risk, and overall deterioration of health in ageing populations. Conversely, maintaining good sleep habits can support physiological restoration, preserve cognitive function, and promote healthier ageing, even in advanced years [ 37 ].

### Iḥtibās-o-Istifrāgh (retention and elimination)

Unani medicine emphasises that health depends on the balance between istifrāgh (elimination) and iḥtibās (retention). Istifrāgh refers to the elimination of waste substances from the body, as their accumulation leads to harmful effects and disrupts the body's internal balance. However, just as the retention of morbid matter is detrimental, the elimination of essential substances that should be retained can also cause pathological conditions [ 3 , 4 ]. Excessive retention of morbid matter increases moisture, suppresses HG, weakens vital functions, and eventually allows Ḥarārat-i-Gharība and Ufūnat (putrefaction) of Akhlāṭ to dominate, thereby accelerating ageing. Therefore, maintaining a balance between elimination and retention is essential for sustaining health and supporting the optimal function of Tabī‘at [ 15 ].

This traditional concept finds support in modern findings on autophagy, the cellular mechanism for clearing out and eliminating damaged proteins, organelles, and metabolic waste. When autophagy declines, waste builds up, cellular balance is disturbed, and senescence progresses, similar to the Unani account of impaired elimination. Modern research now distinguishes “disabled macroautophagy” as a specific hallmark of ageing because it targets entire dysfunctional organelles and non-proteinaceous macromolecules; the failure of this system leads to the accumulation of cellular “waste” that mirrors the Unani concept of Ruṭūbat-e-Gharība (abnormal moisture ). [ 38 ].

Autophagy, on the other hand, can be regulated through lifestyle, dietary, and pharmacological interventions that restore its effectiveness and prevent waste accumulation. Caloric restriction, intermittent fasting, and exercise are potent natural autophagy regulators primarily by mTOR inhibition and AMPK activation, promoting cellular recycling and mitochondrial quality to delay age progression [ 38 ].

## Tadabīr-i-Mashāyikh (geriatric care)

In Unani medicine, Tadabīr-i-Mashāyikh refers to specialised regimens and lifestyle modifications aimed at preserving health and delaying senescence in the elderly. The primary objectives of these regimens are to conserve RG and HG , which are foundational elements of life, as long as possible, thereby sustaining vital functions. Additionally, these measures aim to prevent the formation of Ruṭūbat-i-Gharība and facilitate the elimination of Mawād Fāsida (morbid matter) through natural excretory routes, such as stool, urine, and sweat. Moreover, specialised regimens are employed to strengthen the body's Quwā , especially when natural vitality begins to decline. Through such holistic interventions, Unani medicine emphasises the proactive maintenance of internal balance, resilience, and vitality in later life [ 39 , 40 ].

### Ghizāʼī Tadābīr (dietary therapy)

In Unani medicine, Ghizāʼī Tadābīr plays a central role in the maintenance of health and the prevention of disease, especially in the elderly. According to Jalīnūs , four essential principles should be observed in dietary planning: (1) the timing of meals, (2) the type of food consumed, (3) the quantity of intake, and (4) the quality of food. These principles are particularly significant in geriatric care, where digestive efficiency is naturally reduced due to physiological ageing [ 41 ].

Unani physicians emphasise that the elderly should consume a varied but balanced diet, tailored to their digestive capacity. Meals should be small, light, and given two to three times a day to avoid overburdening the digestive system. Easily digestible and non-flatulent foods are preferred. Heavy foods, especially those that promote the formation of Sawda (black bile) [eg, salted fish, brinjal, and Laḥm Muqaddad (dried meat)], Balgham (phlegm) [eg. watermelon and cucumber], or astringency, are discouraged as they may lead to obstruction, sluggish digestion, and humoral imbalance [ 3 , 42 ].

### ‘Ilāj bi'l Tadbīr (regimental therapies)

#### Riyāḍat (exercise)

Riyāḍat is considered a vital regimen in Unani medicine for promoting health and facilitating the expulsion of Fāsid, Mawād from the body. In the elderly, regular engagement in Muʿtadil Riyāḍat (moderate exercise), such as walking or gentle riding, induces a Musakhkhin (warming) effect, which supports metabolic functions and aids in the elimination of harmful substances without causing undue strain [ 2 , 3 , 42 ].

Studies have consistently shown that exercise in older people brings considerable health advantages. It enhances cardiovascular function by strengthening the heart, improving circulation and vascular elasticity, and decreasing blood pressure and cholesterol levels, which in turn decrease atherosclerosis, coronary heart disease, and cardiovascular mortality. Exercise also stimulates neurogenesis, enhances neuroplasticity, cognition, memory, and executive function, and offers protection against cerebral atrophy. Thus, regular moderate exercise serves as a cornerstone for maintaining physical vitality, cognitive health, and overall well-being during ageing [ 47 ].

#### Dalk (massage)

Dalk is recognised in Unani medicine as a form of passive exercise that facilitates the elimination of toxins, strengthens the body and musculature, and supports overall vitality. In elderly individuals, Muʿtadil dalk (moderate massage) should be performed gently and slowly, using soft hands with minimal pressure to avoid strain [ 15 ]. Depending on the objective and the patient's condition, Dalk may be carried out either without oil, using a coarse cloth to stimulate circulation, or with mildly warming oils ( Hārr in temperament), such as Roghan Zaitūn (olive oil) or Roghan Bādām Shīrīn (sweet almond oil). These oils provide Taskhīn (gentle warmth), support HG, and help retain Ruṭūbat (moisture) in the body. For optimal benefit, Dalk may be performed once or twice daily, as per the individual's constitution and tolerance [ 48 ].

Recent systematic reviews provide convincing evidence that massage therapy is a safe, feasible, and effective non-pharmacological intervention in geriatrics. Massage was always linked with substantial physiological advantages like pain reduction, better mobility, immune function enhancement, and relief of functional constipation, as well as psychological improvements in the form of reduced anxiety, depression, agitation, and behavioural disturbances in vulnerable groups like dementia patients. Hence, Dalk is a vital regimen for sustaining health and vitality in old age [ 49 ].

#### Ḥammām (therapeutic bath)

In Unani medicine, Ḥammām refers to a therapeutic or medicated bath designed to enhance HG, facilitate the excretion of waste materials through the skin, and promote effective Istihāla (metabolic transformation) within the body. It is recommended that elderly individuals undergo Ḥammām therapy regularly, preferably once a week, using fresh lukewarm water, tailored to their physical capacity and health status. Ḥammām therapy provides gentle warmth and moderate moisture, which helps alleviate dryness of the skin, improve its texture, and induce physical relaxation and restful sleep [ 39 ].

Studies on hydrotherapy and balneotherapy show that activities such as warm water immersion, aquatic exercises, and alternating hot and cold baths can enhance physical abilities, joint flexibility, balance, and mental well-being in older adults, while also alleviating pain and reducing stress. Overall, regular Ḥammām therapy serves as a supportive regimen in ageing, maintaining metabolic balance, improving vitality, and enhancing both physical and mental well-being [ 50 ].

### Dawā’-i-Tadbīr (pharmacological regimen)

In the context of geriatric care, Dawā’-i-Tadbīr denotes the prudent application of Unani pharmacotherapy aimed at supporting declining physiological functions associated with ageing. Special emphasis is placed on Adwiya Muqawwī-i-HG ; these drugs help preserve and stimulate the HG, a fundamental force responsible for sustaining life processes and delaying senescence. These drugs help revive metabolic functions, improve digestion, enhance blood circulation, and maintain internal equilibrium, all of which are essential in the management of ageing.

Complementing this approach is the use of general and organ-specific tonics, which play a pivotal role in restoring weakened organ systems and physiological Quwā . This is because ageing is marked by a gradual decline in the functional capacity of organs and Quwā , rendering the body more susceptible to debility and disease. A diverse array of such tonics and restorative agents is well-documented in classical Unani literature. These remedies have been traditionally recognised for their ability to rejuvenate weakened systems, restore physiological balance, and promote overall well-being in the elderly population. Their therapeutic role in enhancing geriatric health is thus both foundational and indispensable within the Unani framework of healthy ageing.

As presented in Table 2 , these Unani formulations are traditionally claimed to promote healthy ageing and potentially extend lifespan when used during old age. This traditional perspective may be supported by emerging pharmacological evidence. Studies on Khamīra Abresham Hakīm Arshad Wala, Majoon Falāsifa, Itrifāl Aftimoon, and Tiryaq Wabā’ī indicate that these formulations possess significant antioxidant properties. Oxidative stress, resulting from the excessive generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), contributes to increased lipid peroxidation and a decline in endogenous antioxidant defence systems, including superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione (GSH), all of which are closely associated with the ageing process [ [51] , [52] , [53] , [54] ].

## Integration of concepts

The normal physiological process of Taḥallul (wear and tear) constitutes the cornerstone of ageing in Unani medicine. Healthy ageing, within this framework, depends on the continuous replenishment of tissues through efficient digestion, balanced humoral formation, and effective tissue repair, all of which are governed by HG. With advancing age, the qualitative and quantitative decline of RG weakens HG, precipitating a cascade of functional deterioration marked by deranged Mizāj , reduced Quwā , compromised digestive and metabolic efficiency, and the production of Akhlāṭ Ghayr Ṭabīʿiyya and Ruṭūbat-e-Gharība , which disrupt internal equilibrium by counteracting HG, thereby accelerating senescence-related decline and eventually leading to Zuʿf al-Aʿḍāʾ (organ debility) [ 5 , 7 ].

This classical understanding of ageing as a gradual decline in vitality and resilience closely parallels contemporary geroscience. The Unani concept of HG, which represents the innate heat responsible for sustaining vitality and all physiological functions, can be correlated with basal metabolic activity and cellular bioenergetics in modern geroscience, particularly ATP generation through mitochondrial function. The decline of HG signifies a reduction in the body's vital energy and functional capacity, which closely parallels Mitochondrial dysfunction, characterised by decreased ATP production, impaired cellular repair, and diminished physiological reserve. The Unani principle of Badal-i-Mā-Yataḥallul , referring to continuous tissue renewal, aligns with modern concepts of cellular turnover, proteostasis, and autophagy; its impairment reflects the accumulation of damaged proteins and defective repair mechanisms. Similarly, the accumulation of Ruṭūbat-e-Gharība (morbid or abnormal substances) corresponds to Oxidative stress, involving reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, and toxic metabolic by-products that lead to DNA damage, protein misfolding, and Cellular senescence [ 10 , 93 ].

Furthermore, the Unani concept of Mizāj, representing the harmonious balance of physiological processes, aligns with systemic metabolic and homeostatic regulation in modern medicine. Its disturbance may be viewed as analogous to metabolic dysregulation and chronic inflammation, both recognised as major contributors to age-related tissue damage. Similarly, Quwwat-e-Mudabbira-e-Badan , the governing force responsible for maintaining coordination among body systems, can be compared to integrated neuroendocrine–immune regulation. Weakening of this governing mechanism results in progressive loss of physiological control and functional decline [ 18 , 94 ].

Moreover, the inherently holistic nature of Unani medicine, which emphasises the interdependence of organs, systems, and environmental influences, also resonates with the contemporary understanding of ageing as a multidimensional and interconnected biological process. Factors such as dysbiosis, metabolic imbalance, and chronic inflammation collectively influence the trajectory of ageing in both paradigms. For instance, the drift toward a unique gut microbiome composition, where the loss of core taxa like Bacteroides is associated with decreased survival, further supports this concept. Thus, both Unani and modern perspectives converge on the view that ageing results from cumulative dysfunction across multiple biological levels, and that maintaining physiological balance through optimisation of metabolism, repair mechanisms, and systemic regulation is essential for healthy ageing [ 10 , 18 ].

This conceptual framework closely aligns with the World Health Organisation definition of healthy ageing, which emphasises the preservation of functional ability and intrinsic capacity rather than mere survival into old age. In this context, HG may be interpreted as a determinant of intrinsic capacity, while RG represents the biological reserve necessary for sustaining physiological resilience. Consequently, the Unani emphasis on preserving functional balance parallels the modern shift from disease-centred geriatric care toward function-oriented healthy ageing strategies [ 95 ].

In accordance with both WHO healthy ageing principles and contemporary geroscience, Unani medicine adopts a preventive and resilience-enhancing approach through the integrated application of ‘Ilāj bi'l Taghdhiya (dietotherapy), ‘Ilāj bi'l Tadbīr (regimental therapy), and ‘Ilāj bi'l Dawā’ (pharmacotherapy). These interventions collectively target key mechanisms associated with ageing, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired tissue repair. Central to this approach is the regulation of Asbāb Sitta Ḍarūriyya , which corresponds closely to modern determinants of healthy ageing such as nutrition, physical activity, sleep, psychosocial well-being, and environmental balance. Proper moderation of these essential factors supports Ṭabīʿat (medicatrix naturae), enhances physiological resilience, and preserves functional ability throughout life [ 3 , 24 , 95 ].

Regimental therapies, including Riyāḍat (exercise), Dalk (massage), and Ḥammām (therapeutic bath), further contribute to the maintenance of intrinsic capacity by improving circulation, enhancing metabolic efficiency, supporting musculoskeletal function, modulating immune responses, and reducing oxidative stress. Contemporary experimental and clinical evidence has demonstrated beneficial effects of these interventions on mitochondrial activity, antioxidant status, vascular health, and neuromuscular performance, all of which are central to delaying functional decline and promoting healthy ageing [ 24 , 95 ].

The review also documents the extensive pharmacological dimension of Unani anti-ageing care, documenting over thirty single drugs and a few Unani formulations traditionally employed to preserve vitality, strengthen Quwā , and retard degenerative changes. These formulations, categorised under Muqawwiyāt and Munā‘iḥa-i-Ḥarārat-e-Gharīziyya. These preparations reflect a multi-targeted approach that addresses the complexity of ageing rather than isolated symptoms, positioning Unani medicine as a historically grounded yet forward-compatible framework for modern global health strategies. Collectively, these principles position Unani medicine as a historically grounded yet forward-compatible framework that resonates strongly with modern geroscience and global healthy ageing strategies.

This literature review serves primarily as a theoretical synthesis drawing upon classical Unani literature. While care was taken to select authoritative classical sources, differences in manuscript versions, translations, and interpretative approaches may influence the understanding of certain concepts. Additionally, the lack of clinical data on Unani interventions in geriatric populations limits the ability to substantiate these concepts quantitatively.

Despite the extensive classical foundations and emerging scientific correlations discussed, further systematic research is warranted to elucidate the precise mechanisms of action underlying Unani anti-ageing interventions. Rigorous experimental and clinical studies are needed to evaluate pharmacodynamics, safety profiles, potential adverse effects, and herb–drug interactions of both single drugs and Unani formulations. Additionally, well-designed longitudinal and age-stratified studies are crucial for developing evidence-based, age-specific guidelines that take into account physiological variability across the lifespan. Such research will be crucial for integrating Unani principles into contemporary healthy ageing frameworks while ensuring efficacy, safety, and standardisation in clinical practice.

## Conclusion

In Unani medicine, ageing is viewed as a modifiable process governed by the balance between Taḥallul and replenishment, regulated by Harārat-e-Gharīziyya and sustained by Ruṭūbat-e-Gharīziyya ; its decline parallels mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. An integrative approach involving diet, regimens and pharmacotherapy to preserve vitality and delay ageing. These principles align with modern healthy ageing concepts, though further mechanistic and clinical research is needed for evidence-based integration.

Key challenges, such as long-term stability, standardization of release studies, scalability, safety assessment, and performance in real formulations, are also discussed, together with future directions for sustainable, application-specific hybrid carrier systems.
