# Intranasal drug delivery to the brain for neurodegenerative diseases: Current efforts and challenges in delivery platforms and modeling

## Abstract
Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD), globally pose a significant challenge with an aging population. Despite the presence of various therapeutic agents, AD and PD treatments with small molecules currently only address the symptoms; certain biologic agents for AD have been approved for their disease-modifying effects, but the risk of intracerebral hemorrhage severely limits their use. Moreover, the bioavailability of orally administered agents in the brain is challenged by the blood-brain barrier, complicating brain-targeted drug development. Extensive efforts are currently underway to develop intranasal platforms with nanoparticles for direct nose-to-brain drug delivery. Additionally, various in vitro designs involving brain organoids, and in vivo models, such as rodents and zebrafish, have been explored to improve the efficiency and accuracy of preclinical models. Efforts to develop sophisticated computational modeling of intranasal drug delivery, including computational fluid dynamics (CFD) deposition and physiologically based pharmacokinetics (PBPK) modeling, also continue to advance the intranasal drug delivery research and potentially improve the feasibility of developing clinically relevant intranasal platforms for neurodegenerative disease.

## Keywords
Neurodegeneration; Intranasal drug delivery; Nose-to-brain; Parkinson’s disease; Alzheimer’s disease; Nanoparticles; Zebrafish; PBPK

## Introduction

Age-associated risk of neurodegenerative disorders poses a significant healthcare burden with aging populations [ 1 ]. In 2019, Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD)—the two most prevalent neurodegenerative disorders—had a global prevalence of 83.6% and 12.3% of all human neurodegenerative diseases, respectively [ 2 ]. According to the 2023 AD report, approximately 6.7 million people aged 65 and older had the disease; the figure is expected to increase to 13.8 million by 2060 [ 3 ]. The prevalence of PD has been growing rapidly, with a significant increase in the age-standardized rate of prevalence by 21.7% from 1990 to 2016, reaching 6.1 million PD patients reported globally in 2016 [ 4 ]. In a more recent study published in 2025, Su et al. [ 5 ] projected that the age-standardized prevalence will further increase from 216 to 267 cases per 100,000 by 2050, corresponding to approximately 25.2 million individuals living with PD globally.

With the greater prevalence observed in recent years, the associated economic burden of neurodegenerative disorders has been increasing rapidly. The total healthcare cost spent on treating patients with AD and dementia was $321 billion in 2022 in the U.S. alone and is projected to exceed $1 trillion by 2050 [ 6 ]. The economic burden of PD—the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disease in the world—was estimated at $51.9 billion in the U.S., accounting for $25.4 billion in direct medical costs and $26.5 billion in indirect non-medical costs; with an increasing elderly population, this figure is expected to rise to $79.1 billion in 2037 [ 7 ].

Neurodegenerative disorders are debilitating conditions in which terminally differentiated neurons lose the ability to repair and renew, impairing crucial brain functions, including motor control, memory, and cognition [ 8 ]. These disorders are characterized by the presence of protein aggregates in various areas of the brain, and these unique protein aggregations are often associated with progressive damage to the central and peripheral nervous systems (CNS and PNS) [ 9 – 11 ]. Significant types of pathology across brain regions related to neurodegeneration include α-synuclein inclusions, tau neurofibrillary tangles, TDP-43 inclusions, neurofibrillary plaques, neuronal loss, angiopathy, and gliosis [ 12 ]. Notably, multiple neurodegenerative disorders present anosmia, loss or reduction of smell, as early symptoms during disease progression [ 13 ]. The human nose is integrated into the CNS through the olfactory and trigeminal nerves, providing connections to the brain. The nose plays a crucial role in filtering inspired air, while serving as a first line of defense against airborne particles and pathogens. The average person inspires between 3 and 4 million liters of air per year, all of which passes through the nasal cavity [ 14 , 15 ]. The filtering function of the nose is particularly relevant when considering the potential impact of environmental factors on neurodegenerative disorders.

The presence of a specific pathological category in a particular CNS region generally defines the type of neurodegeneration. PD displays the degradation of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra [ 16 ]. In AD, structural atrophy often begins in the hippocampus and amygdala and progresses to the middle temporal gyrus and then other parts of the brain [ 17 ]. Classic pathogenesis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) includes a loss of motor neuron cell bodies coupled with damage in corticospinal tracts and lower motor neuron axons [ 18 ].

The observation of unique proteins in different neurodegenerative disorders provides a link to proteinopathy, a group of diseases caused by the abnormal accumulation, misfolding, or aggregation of proteins in specific cells or tissues, leading to dysfunction and damage. The presence of amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregates, α-synuclein accumulation, and cytoplasmic aggregation of TDP-43 are notable characteristics of AD, PD, and ALS, respectively [ 19 , 20 ]. However, some protein aggregates are not truly unique to a single neurodegenerative disorder. For example, α-synuclein aggregation into Lewy bodies is observed in approximately 50% of AD cases, potentially promoting further aggregation of other proteins via interacting with Aβ and Tau [ 21 ]. Moreover, a strong association between α-synuclein levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and progression to dementia and tau levels in CSF was observed in one study that utilized longitudinal data from 331 individuals who did not initially suffer from dementia [ 22 ]. The blurred specificity of protein aggregation types amongst various neurodegenerative disorders poses a challenge in determining biomarkers for these disorders.

Extensive studies have elucidated multiple risk factors that may contribute to the development and progression of neurodegeneration. For AD alone, various genetic mutations in amyloid precursor protein and apolipoprotein E, as well as more than 60 environmental risk factors (e.g., poor air quality, vitamin D deficiency, exposure to aluminum, silicon, selenium, pesticides, etc.) have been identified as being associated with the disease development [ 19 , 23 ]. In a 22-year follow-up study with 6,715 individuals without PD at baseline from the Finnish Mobile Clinic Health Examination Survey to monitor who developed PD over time, Sääksjärvi et al. found that a higher body mass index, non-smoking, and moderate alcohol consumption were associated with a greater risk of developing PD, demonstrating the potential significance of lifestyle parameters in neurodegenerative disorders [ 24 ]. The predominant association with neurodegeneration is observed with age. With increasing age, levels of phosphorylated serine 129 (typically found in Lewy inclusions) and α-synuclein are elevated in the substantia nigra of older primates, confirming a strong association between aging and α-synuclein accumulation, which may increase the risk of developing neurodegenerative disorders [ 25 ]. AD is also considered an age-related condition; in various studies, the age-specific incidence of dementia increased with older AD populations [ 26 – 30 ].

Despite debilitating symptoms that severely affect the patients’ quality of life and the growing economic burden of neurodegenerative disorders, treatment options are still limited and offer only symptomatic relief. For AD, cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists (memantine) are commonly used for symptomatic treatment, while amyloid-targeted therapies (lecanemab and donanemab) are considered disease-modifying treatments that directly target AD pathophysiology [ 31 ]. No disease-modifying agents are available for PD. Levodopa, non-ergot dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, and rotigotine), monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline, and safinamide), amantadine, and anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl and benztropine) are used to provide symptomatic relief to patients [ 32 – 38 ]. These agents are generally associated with debilitating adverse effects, and their therapeutic effects tend to decrease over time, requiring additional medicine in the treatment regimen. For instance, patients on MAO-B inhibitors will likely need other dopaminergic agents within two to three years of therapy [ 32 ]. Due to increased adverse effects, including constipation, urinary retention, and cognitive impairment, anticholinergics are generally avoided in elderly patients [ 39 ].

This unmet clinical need drives the evaluation of alternative drug delivery strategies to improve brain targeting for neurodegenerative disorders. In this review, major neurological disorders, including AD and PD, will be explored from multidisciplinary viewpoints, ranging from pathophysiology to currently available therapeutic agents. Additionally, this review covers current challenges in therapeutic development, including passage across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and the lack of suitable biomarkers for early diagnosis. Current efforts in nanotechnology to deliver drugs to the brain via the nasal route, thereby bypassing the BBB, are also assessed in light of these challenges. Moreover, various computational modeling and in vivo systems are evaluated in this review for their potential to aid therapeutic development.

## Major neurodegenerative disorders and their treatments

### Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)

AD is an age-associated disorder that significantly affects individuals at or over the age of 65 [ 40 ]. It displays various hallmarks of aging, including genomic instability, macromolecular damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction [ 40 , 41 ]. The major features of AD include the aggregation of tau protein and Aβ plaques. Aβ peptides, particularly Aβ40–42 generated through enzymatic cleavage by beta-secretase (BACE1) and gamma-secretase (GS), exhibit a high propensity to aggregate, initially in the neocortex before spreading to subcortical regions [ 42 – 44 ]. These protein aggregates contribute to neuronal dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and progressive cellular damage [ 40 , 45 ]. Increased somatic DNA mutations and impaired DNA repair mechanisms have also been associated with AD progression, further linking tau pathology to neuronal degeneration [ 46 – 48 ]. Genetic mutations, such as APP , PSEN1 , PSEN2 , and APOE e4 , along with chronic microglial activation and astrocyte-mediated inflammation, further exacerbate neuronal damage [ 42 , 49 – 52 ].

Currently available therapies for AD primarily provide symptomatic relief. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine) modestly improve cognitive symptoms but are associated with adverse effects, including insomnia, gastrointestinal issues, hallucinations, and bradycardia [ 31 , 53 ]. Fewer adverse effects and greater tolerability were observed with the transdermal rivastigmine patch compared with the oral form of the drug [ 54 ]. Memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, provides neuroprotective benefits to patients with vascular dementia, but it demonstrates limited clinical benefit despite relatively favorable tolerability [ 31 , 55 ]. More recently, disease-modifying monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab and donanemab) have been approved to reduce Aβ burden; however, their clinical efficacy is modest, while intracerebral hemorrhage has been noted as a major safety concern [ 56 – 58 ]. Table 1 summarizes the U.S. FDA-approved drugs for AD and their clinical characteristics, such as mechanism of action (MOA), recommended doses, and common adverse events (AE) ( Table 1 ).

In addition to amyloid and tau pathology, growing evidence implicates impaired brain glucose metabolism and insulin signaling in AD pathogenesis [ 59 , 60 ]. The concept of “brain insulin resistance” has been proposed as a contributor to synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and cognitive decline [ 61 ]. Insulin plays a critical role in neuron survival, synaptic plasticity, and memory formation; disruption of insulin receptor signaling in the CNS has been linked to reduced glucose utilization and increased accumulation of Aβ and hyperphosphorylated tau [ 60 ]. Intranasal (IN) insulin administration has been investigated in clinical studies; several clinical trials have reported improvements in cognitive performance and memory, including enhanced delayed recall and preservation of functional ability in patients with mild cognitive impairment and early-stage AD [ 62 – 65 ]. These findings highlight the potential relevance of the nose-to-brain (N2B) pathway for both drug delivery and modulation of disease-specific metabolic dysfunction. A comprehensive review of IN insulin delivery for AD by Wong et al. [ 66 ] further explores this topic.

Nevertheless, the clinical benefits of current AD therapies remain limited, and effective drug delivery to the brain is hindered by the BBB, systemic adverse effects, and challenges in achieving therapeutically relevant concentrations at target sites. These limitations point to broader challenges in developing effective therapies for neurodegenerative disorders.

### Parkinson’s Disease (PD)

PD develops with the aggregation of α-synuclein protein (Lewy bodies) in the substantia nigra, and pathology may extend to multiple regions, with some cases overlapping with AD-related features, such as tau aggregation [ 67 – 70 ]. Neurological presentation of AD is frequently observed in synucleinopathies, which are associated with a worse prognosis [ 71 ]. PD exhibits a multifactorial pathophysiology, involving mechanisms such as an increase in SNCA expression and lysosomal dysfunction, as well as mitochondrial impairment associated with mutations in genes ( PRKN , PINK1 , and LRRK2 ) [ 67 , 72 – 74 ]. PD patients often exhibit non-motor symptoms, including constipation and olfactory dysfunction, prior to the onset of motor symptoms [ 75 , 76 ]. The Braak staging hypothesis proposes that α-synuclein pathology progresses from peripheral sites, such as the olfactory and vagal pathways, to the CNS; however, disease progression is heterogeneous, and alternative mechanisms have been suggested based on post-mortem studies [ 77 , 78 ].

Unlike AD, for which disease-modifying agents have been approved, all treatments for PD are limited to symptom management. Levodopa is the gold standard for the initial treatment for early PD due to its motor benefit, but it is associated with adverse effects, such as dyskinesia and neuropsychiatric complications; its efficacy often diminishes over time, as well [ 32 , 79 ]. Alternative treatments, including non-ergot dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, and rotigotine) and MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline, and safinamide), provide modest benefits; however, they are also associated with adverse effects or limited therapeutic efficacy [ 79 , 80 ]. Clinical characteristics of these agents are summarized in Table 1 ( Table 1 ).

As with AD, PD management is still limited to symptomatic therapies, and achieving consistent, therapeutically relevant drug concentrations in the brain remains a significant challenge. These challenges emphasize the need for improved drug delivery approaches that can reliably enhance CNS drug exposure.

## Challenges with developing effective therapies for neurodegenerative disorders

Despite advances in understanding disease pathology and therapeutic development, effectively treating neurodegenerative disorders continues to face obstacles in early diagnosis and targeted drug delivery to the brain. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for neurodegenerative disorders, as targeting underlying pathologies before symptom onset may prevent irreversible neurodegeneration [ 81 ]. Extensive progress has been made in identifying clinical biomarkers for AD and PD. The recently updated diagnostic criteria for AD recognize amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) imaging and p-tau217 as Core 1 biomarkers, whose abnormal results provide sufficient evidence for diagnosing AD without clinical symptoms at the initial stage of the disease [ 82 ]. When compared to CSF biomarkers, p-tau217 immunoassay identified an elevated level of Aβ and tau pathology, leading to an accurate diagnosis of AD [ 83 ]. Biomarkers used in PET, CSF, or blood tend to show lower sensitivity than neuropathologic examination for early/mild AD neuropathologic change; PET or fluid biomarkers often present disease staging different from neuropathological staging [ 82 ]. Currently, no established biochemical biomarker is used for diagnosing PD; however, extensive research on biomarkers collected from body fluids and tissue biopsies is ongoing [ 84 ]. The individual variability in biomarker levels and the limited sensitivity and specificity of the current biomarkers often fail to detect early-stage PD or to distinguish accurately from similar conditions, complicating the establishment of standardized diagnostic thresholds [ 85 ]. Beyond diagnostic challenges, a major barrier to effective treatment lies in the delivery of therapeutic agents to the CNS.

### Blood-brain barrier (BBB)

The BBB poses a significant barrier to developing therapies for neurodegenerative disorders due to its various protective mechanisms against foreign substances. The BBB comprises endothelial cells with tight junctions, pericytes, and astrocytes, thereby limiting drug entry and reducing the targetability of CNS therapeutic agents [ 86 , 87 ]. Moreover, BBB dysfunction, as well as dysregulation of influx and efflux transporters, have been observed in neurodegenerative disorders, including AD [ 86 , 88 ].

Due to the BBB’s high selectivity, drugs must possess specific physicochemical properties to cross the barrier. Small, lipophilic, and nonpolar molecules tend to diffuse through endothelial cell membranes, exhibiting excellent BBB permeability, whereas highly charged or polar compounds display limited entry through the BBB [ 89 ]. Additionally, large molecules, such as recombinant proteins, diffuse poorly across the BBB; bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody used to treat malignant glioma, crosses the BBB only when the BBB is disrupted by external means, such as focused ultrasound [ 90 ].

Various efforts to overcome the BBB have had limited success. Numerous nanoparticle delivery systems have struggled with effective bench-to-bedside translation despite promising in vitro and in vivo outcomes [ 91 ]. The commercial viability of nanoparticles is also an inevitable question that must be addressed; most nano-formulations require intravenous (IV) administration, which limits accessibility, reduces convenience, and may increase drug costs [ 92 ]. Limited translational data on the pharmacokinetics (PK) of nanomedicines also pose a challenge to predicting the safety and efficacy of nanoparticles in patients based on preclinical data [ 91 ]. This is particularly relevant for AD and PD, where chronic administration is required.

### Pathogenesis

Many neurodegenerative disorders are multifactorial and pose a significant challenge to appropriate therapeutic development. These diseases often arise from a complex interplay of factors, including genetic mutations, protein misfolding, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and various epigenetic factors, all of which lead to gradual neurodegeneration over time [ 93 ]. Historically, AD was thought to comprise at least five subgroups that differ by CSF levels of Aβ, tau, and ubiquitin [ 94 ]; today, patient stratification for AD is guided by clinical symptom severity (stages 1–6) and the AT 1 T 2 NISV biomarker framework, which classifies individuals based on amyloid, tau, neurodegeneration, inflammation, α-synuclein, and vascular pathology biomarkers [ 82 ]. This biological variability may contribute to differential drug responses among patients and points to the need for targeted therapeutic approaches.

### Therapeutic limitations

Severe off-target effects, as previously mentioned, and loss of therapeutic sensitivity must also be addressed in developing novel therapies for neurodegenerative disorders. Off-target effects can be particularly detrimental for neurodegenerative patients whose cognition is impaired. Current therapeutic limitations, together with the multifactorial pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disorders, demand more effective platforms to achieve targeted drug delivery to the brain. Because of the BBB’s strict regulation, drug permeability remains limited. Consequently, alternative delivery approaches that can bypass this barrier, such as IN routes, represent a compelling strategy for improving CNS drug exposure. The nasal route offers a non-invasive route to the brain that circumvents systemic circulation, potentially reducing off-target effects and compliance challenges associated with chronic oral or IV administration in neurodegenerative patients.

## Intranasal (IN) delivery: Developing an optimal method for brain targeting

### Advantages and limitations of IN delivery

One way to bypass the BBB involves the IN route of drug administration. Advantages of nasal-brain drug delivery include the local delivery of the therapeutic agent to the brain via the olfactory and trigeminal pathways. Active research is also ongoing on the nasal-brain lymphatic system, which has excellent potential for delivering anticancer medications to the brain [ 95 ]. Though a portion of the administered dose may still be absorbed into the systemic circulation through the nasal epithelium, the noninvasive nature of IN delivery avoids enteric absorption, resulting in a rapid onset of action and the avoidance of first-pass metabolism [ 96 ]. Moreover, despite the small surface area of the olfactory region (approximately 5 cm 2 ), its microvilli comprise around 3,000 cm 2 , providing an extensive network for absorption and distribution [ 97 ].

It has been observed that various intranasally administered substances, such as siRNA, are widely distributed to the olfactory nerve and olfactory bulbs, specifically their glomerular and mitral cell layers; these chemical or biological moieties enter the fila olfactoria as they travel across olfactory neurons and are transported to the olfactory bulb via endocytosis and axonal transport; this route is characterized by delayed delivery due to the multiple layers involved [ 98 , 99 ].

However, current IN delivery to the brain is limited by the small deliverable volume (25–250 μL per nostril), the need to penetrate a mucus layer, potential drug loss via mucociliary clearance, and possible transformation of the compound by nasal enzymatic activity. Nasal illnesses, including nasal irritation, congestion, or lesions, as well as the patient’s administration technique, may pose challenges to IN drug delivery, potentially affecting drug absorption and distribution [ 100 , 101 ]. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, various nanoparticle formulations have been developed, yielding favorable outcomes in in vitro and/or in vivo settings [ 97 ]. Novel therapeutics must address these limitations to ensure reliable patient compliance and maintain therapeutic delivery to the brain.

### Physiology of the Human Olfactory System

The human nasal cavity is approximately 12–15 cm long, with a total surface area of about 150 cm 2 , and it is characterized by having a pH ranging from 5.5 to 6.5 [ 102 ]. The human nasal mucosa comprises vestibular, respiratory, and olfactory regions [ 103 ]. The vestibular region encompasses the nasal entry, covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelial cells [ 104 ]. The vestibular region is not considered an efficient site for N2B delivery due to the small surface area and nasal hair and secretory glands, which protect the body from any xenobiotics [ 103 , 105 ]. For a drug to be delivered to the brain, it needs to travel deeper into the nasal cavity. The largest area in the nasal cavity is the respiratory region, with a surface area of approximately 130 cm 2 , showing a layer of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells [ 103 ]. Its large surface area is due to the ciliated columnar cells with many microvilli [ 103 ]. Trigeminal sensory nerves and blood vessels are found in this region [ 97 ]. The olfactory area at the top of the nasal cavity comprises olfactory, supporting, and basal cells in the epithelial cell layer [ 106 ]. The olfactory cells are bipolar neurons and merge into the olfactory nerve, while interstitial fluid around the olfactory nerve bundle is connected to CSF in the subarachnoid space, connecting the olfactory system to CNS [ 107 – 109 ].

Currently, no clearly defined pathway describes the N2B drug delivery. Four pathways (olfactory nerve pathway, olfactory mucosal epithelial pathway, trigeminal nerve pathway, and systemic pathway) have been identified to explain the IN drug delivery to the brain ( Figure 1 ) [ 108 , 110 ]. The systemic pathway does not allow direct drug delivery from the nose to the brain. It involves systemic circulation after the IN administration of the drug; some low molecular weight lipophilic drugs are absorbed into the blood circulation via a capillary network in the lamina propria of the respiratory region, resulting in the necessity to cross the BBB [ 111 ]. Contrarily, neurophilic viruses, steroid hormones, metal ions, and proteins are proposed to enter the brain via the olfactory nerve pathway; small molecules are presumed to use the olfactory mucosal epithelial pathway or the trigeminal nerve pathway to access the brain [ 108 ]. It is worth noting that the absorption rate differs between these two pathways for the small molecules. The trigeminal nerve pathway shows a prolonged absorption time, about 17–56 hours longer than the olfactory mucosal epithelial pathway, which shows rapid absorption [ 112 , 113 ]. For neurodegenerative disorders, there is currently no U.S. FDA-approved IN drug available on the market despite the ongoing research and the immense potential of IN administration for drug delivery to the brain.

Despite the identification of these transport pathways, their quantitative contributions remain poorly characterized and vary widely across species, molecular properties, and disease states. For example, direct olfactory transport observed in rodent models may be overestimated in humans due to anatomical differences, while physicochemical properties of therapeutic agents can further influence pathway dominance. Consequently, formulation strategies are often derived empirically, and cross-study comparisons remain challenging.

### IN delivery

Despite the limitations of IN delivery, its ability to bypass the BBB remains favorable for drug delivery in neurodegenerative disorders. Beyond the delivery of therapeutic payloads, some nanomaterials also enable diagnosis, serving as “theranostics”; these agents aim to provide personalized treatment regimens and simultaneous disease progression monitoring by the physicians, often with the help of ultrasound [ 114 , 115 ].

Physicochemical properties of nanoparticles are crucial in developing successful IN N2B platforms. In general, a small particle size (below 200 nm) is desirable, as the mucin mesh in the nasal mucus restricts the diffusion of larger particles [ 112 , 116 ]. Polydispersity index (PDI) of less than 0.3 is typically considered acceptable for ensuring uniformity and even distribution of nanoparticles; however, non-spherical nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) often exhibit higher PDI values compared with other IN nanocarriers [ 117 ]. For optimal stability of the formulation, a zeta potential above or below ±30 mV is recommended. Negatively charged particles are often favored because of their lower cytotoxicity, whereas positively charged particles can enhance IN brain delivery by forming electrostatic interactions with negatively charged mucins, thereby prolonging nasal residence time of the nanoparticles [ 96 , 117 ]. Neutral liposomes have been shown to accumulate in the brain more efficiently than charged particles of comparable size and PDI, and PEGylation has been identified to further enhance this accumulation by improving stability and mucosal diffusion [ 118 ]. While these platforms demonstrate potential in preclinical studies, long-term bilayer stability under physiological conditions and maintenance of a physiologically relevant pH range of 4.5–6.5 continue to be immediate challenges to confirming their clinical viability [ 117 ].

Achieving appropriate viscosity is crucial for maintaining adequate residence time in the nasal cavity and ensuring efficient drug absorption. Moderate increases in formulation viscosity have been shown to enhance nasal residence time and drug absorption, whereas excessively high viscosity can reduce drug uptake by limiting diffusion and mucosal penetration [ 119 ]. Importantly, optimal rheological properties depend on the delivery format and devices [ 120 ]. For example, liquid nasal sprays typically require lower viscosities to ensure adequate pumpability, an appropriate droplet size distribution, and uniform deposition [ 121 ]; in situ gels and mucoadhesive systems are designed to increase viscosity upon administration to prolong residence time [ 112 , 117 ]. Powder-based and bidirectional delivery systems introduce additional considerations related to airflow dynamics and particle dispersion. Furthermore, many IN formulations exhibit non-Newtonian behavior, in which viscosity changes under shear during administration. There is an inherent tradeoff between mucoadhesion and mucus penetration [ 97 , 112 ]. Highly viscous or strongly mucoadhesive formulations may prolong retention but can also limit diffusion through the mucus layer, whereas low-viscosity formulations may penetrate more effectively and be cleared rapidly [ 119 ]. Tolerability is an additional consideration, as formulations that are too viscous may cause discomfort or a sensation of nasal obstruction; overly fluid preparations may cause postnasal drip [ 101 ]. For in situ gels, additional parameters, such as the gelation rate and temperature, must be optimized to ensure rapid gel formation upon nasal administration [ 122 , 123 ]. Finally, incorporating mucoadhesive agents into the formulation enhances nanoparticle adhesion to the nasal mucosa, thereby providing sufficient time for absorption and improving overall drug bioavailability.

Examples of novel IN formulation developments and their physicochemical properties, including particle size, PDI, zeta potential, and viscosity, are provided in the accompanying sections and Table 2 . The corresponding in vivo pharmacokinetic study outcomes are also summarized in Supplementary Information (S1) . In preclinical studies, brain exposure following IN administration is often quantified using surrogate pharmacokinetic metrics, such as drug targeting efficiency (DTE), direct transport percentage (DTP), and AUC brain /AUC plasma ratios. While these parameters are useful for comparing relative brain uptake across formulations, they primarily reflect distribution patterns rather than absolute drug concentrations at specific target sites. Consequently, improvements in these metrics do not necessarily translate into clinically meaningful outcomes, including reproducible regional brain delivery, achievable therapeutic dosing within the limited nasal administration volume, or acceptable safety margins in humans. This distinction is critical for avoiding overinterpretation of preclinical success and for realistically assessing the translational potential of IN delivery systems.

Recent advances have expanded the IN delivery landscape beyond conventional nanocarriers to include carrier-free nanosystems formed by self-assembling small molecules [ 124 , 125 ] and surface-functionalized lipid nanoparticles co-targeting multiple AD pathological pathways [ 126 ]. However, given the scope of this review, the following sections will mainly focus on drug delivery platforms for small molecules.

### IN delivery: Liposomes

Liposomes are nanoparticle systems composed of an amphiphilic phospholipid bilayer, which allows them to load both hydrophilic and hydrophobic agents, making them a commonly used vehicle to carry therapeutic agents [ 127 , 128 ]. The wide application of liposomes is attributed to several factors, including their ability to load various drugs, the possibility of surface modifications that can enhance their effectiveness, and their biocompatibility and biodegradability [ 128 ]. After administration, liposomal carriers along with the encapsulated drugs enter the systemic circulation from the respiratory region, from which they enter the brain through the olfactory pathway [ 127 ].

Extensive efforts are underway to develop ideal liposomal platforms for the IN delivery of small molecules for neurodegenerative disorders, notably AD and PD [ 129 – 133 ]. Donepezil HCl-loaded liposomes developed by the ethanol injection method demonstrated an improvement in the PK parameters of the liposome-encapsulated donepezil. The average particle size was 103 ± 6.2 nm with a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.108 ± 0.008 and a favorable entrapment efficiency of 93%; the intranasally applied donepezil-loaded liposome gel displayed a greater permeability across the sheep nasal mucosa and a higher distribution in the brain when compared to IN donepezil HCl gel and oral donepezil HCl solution, respectively [ 129 ]. Utilizing the versatility of the liposomes with various loading molecules, Allegritti’s team developed various IN liposomal formulations with triple agents—levodopa, L-ascorbic acid, and quercetin—for PD. Using saturated phospholipids and the thin film hydration method, L-ascorbic acid and quercetin were co-loaded to prevent levodopa oxidation. The resulting liposomes loaded with the small molecules ranged from 90 to 140 nm in size and displayed positive zeta potential. Although the nasal mucosa permeability was lower with liposome-encapsulated levodopa than with free levodopa, the significantly reduced oxidation of levodopa relative to free levodopa may improve drug stability and potentially support sustained delivery [ 130 ].

Deformable liposomes, transferosomes, that can undergo morphological changes to squeeze through pores, have demonstrated physicochemical properties with a low deformability index and evidence of in vivo N2B delivery. Their deformable nature allows them to squeeze through small pores, making them particularly useful for larger and ionized molecules (MW > 500 Da) [ 134 ]. This property makes transferosomes particularly useful for transdermal administration of therapeutic agents, and this is also applicable for the IN delivery, which requires the nanoparticles to squeeze through the epithelial cells for absorption. Gaynanova et al. developed transferosomes loaded with donepezil and α-tocopherol, which demonstrated favorable physicochemical properties (particle size = 104 ± 1 nm, PDI = 0.067 ± 0.01), as well as measurable brain exposure (C max = 228 ± 21 ng/g), acetylcholinesterase inhibition, and improved cognitive performance in a transgenic AD mice model [ 132 ]. ElShagea’s team reported significant increases in pharmacokinetic outcomes of their rasagiline-loaded transferosome in situ gel, with an absolute brain bioavailability of 131.17%, despite the relatively large size of the carrier without favorable particle uniformity (particle size = 294.85 ± 20.29 nm, PDI = 0.505 ± 0.021) [ 133 ]. It should be noted that absolute bioavailability values exceeding 100% may reflect experimental artifacts or methodological limitations in the reference IV dosing rather than true enhanced systemic exposure and should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Improved in vitro and in vivo parameters, including drug exposure measured in these liposomal IN formulations, demonstrate the therapeutic potential of liposomes for IN delivery in neurodegenerative disorders. These brain-targeting improvements are largely derived from preclinical animal models and, therefore, require further studies that go beyond physicochemical properties and preclinical PK analyses to assess their translational success. Notably, findings such as reduced mucosal permeability of liposome-encapsulated levodopa [ 130 ] and high bioavailability of transferosomes despite poor particle uniformity [ 133 ] show that the performance of liposomal platforms is not always predictable from physicochemical parameters alone.

### IN delivery: Solid lipid nanoparticles

Solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) are lipid-based nanocarriers composed of biocompatible solid lipids that remain solid at both body and room temperatures [ 135 ]. SLNs are produced using 0.1 and 30% (w/v) steroids and glycerides, respectively, and 0.5 to 5% (w/v) surfactants via homogenization, ultrasonication, and various emulsion techniques, yielding particles with diameters of 100 to 300 nm and a hydrophobic core within a single lipid layer [ 105 , 136 ]. Like liposomes, which can encapsulate both hydrophilic and hydrophobic molecules, SLNs can also load both types of molecules within their lipid matrix [ 136 ]. Compared with polymeric nanoparticles, SLNs typically require no organic solvents during production and offer improved stability of encapsulated small molecules, especially lipophilic ones, as well as enhanced targeting with ligands, at lower manufacturing costs [ 137 ]. Moreover, their ability to evade the reticuloendothelial system (RES) may prolong systemic circulation and, consequently, increase the likelihood of CNS distribution, since some intranasally administered particles enter the systemic circulation, from which they must cross the BBB to reach the site of action [ 137 ].

These advantages of SLNs make them excellent candidates for IN delivery platforms for neurodegenerative disorders. Dopamine (DA)-loaded SLNs prepared by the melt homogenization method with Gelucire ® 50/13 yielded SLNs with high encapsulation efficiency (~81%) that exhibited safety in olfactory ensheathing cells (OECs) comparable to DA-loaded liposomes; however, cell uptake by OECs reached 100% within 24 hours with SLNs, whereas liposome cell uptake with OECs was less than 80% [ 138 ]. Piribedil (PBD)-loaded SLNs incorporated into the thermoresponsive methyl cellulose in-situ gel (PBD-SLN-ISG) showed particularly interesting results. Despite a relatively large particle size, the PBD-SLN-ISG formulation, with a particle size of 364.1 ± 16.4 nm at 2–8 °C, demonstrated significantly enhanced brain exposure. Specifically, brain exposure, measured by the area under the curve (AUC) and mean residence time (MRT), was 4.05-fold and 3.14-fold higher, respectively, compared to the PBD suspension. Furthermore, DTE and DTP were also greater with the in-situ gel formulation than with the suspension. This improved performance may be attributed to the delayed mucociliary clearance of the PBD-SLN-ISG particles, facilitated by methyl cellulose, which potentially prolongs the nasal residence time of the formulation [ 139 ]. This outcome further shows that N2B delivery is determined by various factors, rather than a single metric of particle size; it is a fine balance that must be carefully optimized by formulators. While these relative PK metrics seem promising, their therapeutic relevance in actual patients must be studied by assessing the CNS concentrations in clinical settings.

Major drawbacks of SLNs include suppressed crystallization, which may reduce drug payload; polymorphic transitions that may form a dense matrix with unfavorable drug localization; and instability during storage, which can result from particle aggregation or fusion [ 136 ]. As a result, optimizing the manufacturing process to ensure polymorphic stability and payload consistency is vital to the future clinical success of SLNs.

### IN delivery: Nanostructured lipid carriers

To address the limitations of the SLNs, nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), a novel class of lipid-based nanocarriers, have emerged as promising candidates for successful delivery to the brain. The particle size of NLCs generally ranges from 200 nm to 400 nm and is significantly influenced by the amount of surfactants; a particle size of 100 nm is achievable with a higher concentration of surfactants, but this often yields unfavorable safety and stability profiles [ 140 ]. Unlike SLNs, NLCs are composed of solid and liquid lipids, both of which contribute to the higher solubility, stability, and encapsulation efficiency of hydrophobic molecules [ 141 ].

NLCs have emerged as desirable vehicles for drugs targeting the brain. To improve the PK and pharmacodynamic properties of donepezil (DPZ), a common therapeutic agent for AD, Sonawane and Pokharkar [ 142 ] produced NLCs via a melt emulsification high-pressure homogenization process, and an in situ gel was made by adding DPZ-NLC in 10% w/v Lutrol F127 solution, which was then mixed with 0.8% w/v gellan gum solution. The initial particles without gelling compounds showed favorable physicochemical properties, with a mean particle size of 112.5 ± 2.44 nm and zeta potential of −23.2 mV, inferring the good stability, while the final in situ gel demonstrated pH of 5.3 ± 0.31 with an appropriate expansion coefficient of 1.2 ± 0.06 %, which is less than 3%, the value at which the patients may feel discomfort as the gelling process occurs [ 142 ]. When the formulation was tested in male Wistar rats, the in situ gel showed a higher maximum plasma concentration (C max ) (193.41 ± 26.4 ng/mL) and a greater AUC 0–24h (1239 ± 6.7 ng h/mL) in the brain; additionally, the significantly higher DTE, drug targeting potential, and drug targeting index than the DPZ solution (IN and IV) and the oral DPZ-NLC formulation indicated an improved brain-targeting efficiency of the IN DPZ-NLC gel [ 142 ].

NLCs exhibit versatility for simulataneously co-loading multiple agents targeting the brain. A successful IN nanoformulation was developed using NLCs loaded with rivastigmine (RIV) and nilotinib (NIL) to enhance AD treatment [ 143 ]. The RIV-NIL-NLC displayed a particle size of 149.4 ± 8.56 nm with PDI of 0.177 ± 0.048, achieving a desirable uniformity of particles; the zeta potential was close to zero (0.81 ± 0.14 mV) due to the presence of non-ionic surfactants, but only minimal increases in the particle size and PDI were observed during the 90-day stability testing at both room temperature and 40 °C with no evidence of hemolysis [ 143 ]. In an in vivo study with Wistar rats, the RIV-NIL-NLC demonstrated successful N2B delivery of RIV and NIL, with a 2.2 to 2.6-fold increase in plasma C max and significantly higher concentrations in the brain at all time points, as well as greater AUC brain , compared to the RIV and NIL suspensions [ 143 ].

NLCs have been used to improve the PK parameters of Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) Class IV agents, as well. Patel and Wairkar developed the NLC formulation for edaravone (EDR), a BCS Class IV agent, via melt-emulsification probe sonication [ 144 ]. The addition of sodium hyaluronate (SH) as a mucoadhesive agent increased the mucoadhesive strength of EDR-SH NLCs in comparison to the EDR NLCs, and the optimization was achieved through a biphasic method, which employed the Plackett-Burman design for identification of critical process parameters and characteristics at the screening level; the Box-Behnken design was used to achieve final optimization [ 144 ]. The in vivo study conducted in male Sprague-Dawley rats revealed that the EDR-SH NLCs were associated with higher C max and AUC than the EDR nasal suspension, EDR-NLC, and the EDR formulation on the market [ 144 ]. Additionally, EDR-SH NLCs demonstrated significantly higher DTI, DTE, and DTP when compared to EDR nasal suspension [ 144 ].

Due to the improvements in PK and pharmacodynamics, as well as the ease of scalability and optimization, NLCs are widely studied as the brain-targeting carriers [ 145 ]. However, the production of NLCs may be hindered by the instability of their lipid matrix and suboptimal control of drug release compared with SLNs, due to the loss of excess liquid lipids [ 146 ]. The manufacturing challenges unique to NLCs demand careful evaluation of their preclinical outcomes with respect to dose scalability and long-term safety.

### IN delivery: Nanoemulsions

Nanoemulsions (NEs) consist of oil and water phases, which are stabilized by emulsifiers [ 96 ]. Because of their generally small particle size, NEs display efficient transport across the mucosal layer [ 147 ]. The fine particle size enhances the biodistribution and stability of NEs, and the formulation, especially the oil-in-water (o/w) type, has been proposed as a site-specific carrier, owing to its encapsulation of lipophilic drugs and reported ability to cross brain tissues [ 147 ].

The IN NE of resveratrol (RSV), when coated with chitosan, displayed an optimal particle size range (89.2 ± 2.68 nm). The RSV-loaded NE achieved a higher viscosity (3.12 ± 0.46 Pa·s) than the uncoated formulation, possibly due to stronger intermolecular interactions within the system. This may reflect a more structured network and greater interaction between chitosan and the o/w phases of the chitosan-coated RSV NE (CH-RSV-NE) [ 148 ]. In addition to displaying a higher concentration, AUC, and MRT in the brain when compared to the RSV suspension and RSV-NE, the CH-RSV-NE also demonstrated superior ex vivo permeation studies performed with porcine nasal mucosa; the 24-hour permeation was 96.14% and 35% for CH-RSV-NE and RSV suspension, respectively [ 148 ]. These findings demonstrate chitosan’s potential to enhance mucoadhesion and facilitate IN absorption in preclinical models.

Further exploration of IN NEs for brain-targeting therapeutics were conducted as Jiang et al. monitored the possible N2B pathways of these IN NEs in vivo [ 149 ]. The natural product, huperzine A (HupA), and a near-infrared fluorescent probe (P2) were encapsulated in NEs to produce P2-HupA-NE and P2-Lf-HupA-NE; the latter was modified with lactoferrin (Lf), a glycoprotein that binds to Lf receptors in the brain endothelial cells and neurons, to study the pathway [ 149 ]. The NEs without the probes displayed the desirable characteristics of the NEs (particle size < 25 nm) and 3-month stability, while the P2-loaded NEs identified the olfactory nerve as the direct pathway and the blood circulation as the indirect pathway of absorption into the brain for IN NE formulations [ 149 ]. Moreover, peak concentrations in the brain were highest with Lf-HupA-NE compared with HupA-NE and Hup-A solutions, suggesting enhanced brain targeting with the addition of Lf [ 149 ].

Despite their small size, NEs can be decorated with various agents, further improving their permeability and IN delivery to the brain. However, producing NEs generally requires substantial energy and incurs high costs, making scale-up difficult. Although NEs are thermodynamically unstable, they exhibit high kinetic stability; maintaining this over time limits the selection of nonionic surfactants and adds to the challenges of their practical application in developing clinically relevant formulations [ 150 ]. Also, preclinical improvements in brain exposure observed with IN NEs, as indicated by surrogate PK metrics such as elevated AUC, C max , and MRT, are encouraging. Nevertheless, establishing their clinical relevance will require addressing constraints related to NE scalability and thermodynamic instability.

### IN delivery: Polymeric nanoparticles

The ease of the structural modification to improve drug delivery and targeting has expanded the field of polymeric nanoparticles, which have been used in the N2B formulations for neurodegenerative disorders [ 107 ]. The availability of diverse carrier types, such as micelles and dendrimers, facilitates the drug encapsulation of varying therapeutic agents, making polymeric nanoparticles highly versatile. Additionally, numerous structural modifications can directly improve and allow the precise control of drug loading and release [ 151 ]. Using cationic polymers, such as chitosan, can be beneficial for optimizing mucoadhesion and IN absorption, as the positively charged nanoparticles bind to the negatively charged mucin and open epithelial tight junctions [ 107 ].

Polymeric micelles have a hydrophobic core, which is encapsulated by an outer hydrophilic layer. Due to its stealth effect and the prolongation of the half-life of the nanocarriers in the body, polyethylene glycol (PEG) is commonly used to construct the outer shell. Additionally, PEG is easily modified to enhance the carrier’s functionality or targeting capabilities, as shown in the development of rapamycin-loaded PEG-b-PLA micelles for the N2B delivery by Sugandhi et al. [ 152 ]. Developed via a solvent evaporation method, rapamycin-loaded Mixed micelles can also be developed with solubilizing agents, which can lower critical micelle concentration (CMC) and enhance scalability of the formulation; using Soluplus ® and D-α-Tocopherol PEG 1000 succinate, Sipos et al. developed dexamethasone-loaded mixed polymeric micelles with 14-fold increase in solubility, enhancing the IN absorption of the particles for N2B delivery [ 153 ].

Dendrimers are synthetic carriers with extensive branches that make an overall sphere shape. Under a controlled environment, dendrimers with specific and fairly uniform physical and morphological characteristics can be developed, and variable functionalities can be added to the terminal sides of the branches on the surface [ 154 ]. The number of branching cycles determines dendrimer generation (G), with G0 denoting the core and G1 indicating one branching cycle. Higher generations, therefore, are composed of more layers, greater surface area, larger molecular weight, and higher consistency in the globular shape. Commonly used polymers include polypropyleneimine (PPI), polyethylenimine (PEI), and polyamidoamine (PAMAM). Therapeutic agents can be loaded onto the dendrimer in the core, on the surface, or within branches via the covalent interactions [ 155 , 156 ]. PPI G5.0 dendrimers conjugated with oleic acid (OA) encapsulated tacrine (TAC), a cholinesterase inhibitor withdrawn from the market due to hepatotoxicity, for IN delivery to the brain with desirable monodispersity (PDI = 0.187 ± 0.005) and no toxicity concerns in nasal ciliotoxicity and hemolytic toxicity studies [ 155 ]. The IN route may circumvent systemic hepatotoxicity by bypassing first-pass metabolism, offering a potential strategy to repurpose tacrine with an improved liver safety profile.

Nonetheless, polymeric nanoparticles tend to exhibit limited encapsulation efficiency, especially with hydrophobic agents, with an encapsulation efficiency of approximately 1% using a conventional nanoprecipitation method [ 157 ]. Moreover, polymeric nanoparticles are subject to less stability and greater toxicity compared to other nanosystems. Hepatotoxicity is a major concern with polymeric nanoparticles due to the greater hepatic accumulation of polymeric nanoparticles when compared to liposomes and other biological nanoparticles [ 151 , 158 ]. The positive PAMAM dendrimers also tend to exhibit considerable cytotoxicity due to their extensive interaction with cell membranes, and higher generation PAMAM dendrimers (G6 or higher) are generally associated with greater toxicity, as well as higher production costs [ 156 , 159 ].

### IN delivery: Solid dosage forms and film-based technologies

In addition to liquid nanoparticle-based systems, alternative IN delivery platforms have also been explored as potential strategies for N2B drug delivery. Solid dosage forms, including microparticulate powders, are associated with physicochemical advantages (i.e., improved stability and extended shelf life) compared with liquid formulations, and they may reduce reliance on cold-chain storage [ 99 , 160 ]. Such characteristics have contributed to the development of nasal powder systems for N2B delivery, including cyclodextrin-based formulations developed to enhance drug stability and targeting efficiency [ 161 ].

Spray-drying and lyophilization techniques are widely employed to convert liquid nanocarrier dispersions into dry powder formulations, providing a practical strategy to enhance the long-term stability of nanoparticle-based IN delivery systems [ 160 , 162 ]. However, the impact of these processing steps on nanocarrier integrity, drug release behavior, and in vivo performance requires careful evaluation before clinical translation can be considered.

More recently, film-based nasal delivery technologies have been investigated to localize drug deposition within the olfactory region. Papakyriakopoulou et al. developed and optimized polymeric nasal films of donepezil hydrochloride for AD, reporting in vitro and ex vivo permeation profiles through rabbit nasal mucosa [ 163 ]. A 3D-printed Matrix-Piston Nasal Device (MPD) based on human nasal cavity anatomy was designed and evaluated by Menegatou et al.; it served as a proof of concept for olfactory-targeted film delivery in nasal cast models [ 164 ]. Kaikousidis et al. characterized donepezil brain and blood exposures following nasal film administration in mice [ 165 ]. Overall, solid dosage forms and film-based technologies have expanded the IN delivery landscape and may complement nanoparticle-based systems in future therapeutic applications in neurodegenerative disorders. To establish their scalability and clinical relevance, the effects of manufacturing on nanocarrier integrity warrant systematic assessment.

### IN delivery: Comparative analysis of nanoparticle-based platforms

IN nanoparticle-based delivery platforms exhibit distinct advantages and limitations that may affect their translational feasibility. Lipid-based systems, including liposomes, SLNs, and NLCs, generally offer favorable biocompatibility and drug loading. Nanoemulsions are associated with efficient mucosal penetration due to their small size, but they are also often limited by thermodynamic instability and scalability. Polymeric nanoparticles are highly tunable and possess great targeting capabilities; however, they are often associated with toxicity and lower encapsulation efficiency. Across all nanoparticle platforms, brain-targeting efficiency is primarily assessed using preclinical surrogate PK metrics, which are useful for assessing relative brain exposure, but they require further validation and integration with pharmacodynamics and clinical endpoints to support successful translation.
