# Obesity and Cardiovascular Disease: An Obesity Medicine Association (OMA) Clinical Practice Statement (CPS) 2026

## Abstract
### Background

Obesity is a chronic disease that directly contributes to cardiovascular disease (CVD) through biomechanical “fat mass disease” and dysfunction of epicardial adipose tissue, or “sick fat disease.” It also indirectly promotes CVD through adiposopathic immune and endocrine abnormalities that drive type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and thrombosis – all major CVD risk factors. This Clinical Practice Statement (CPS) reviews obesity-related cardiovascular disease pathology and outlines evidence-based strategies for clinical management.

### Methods

This CPS is based on a review of relevant medical literature, interpreted through the clinical expertise of authors specializing in obesity medicine, all members of the Obesity Medicine Association (OMA). Organized into 26 sections, each includes an introduction, essential principles, a “top ten” list of key points, and a summary figure.

### Results

The CPS reviews how obesity intersects with major cardiovascular risk factors, including type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, metabolic syndrome, and thrombosis. Additional metabolic complications such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and chronic kidney disease further elevate CVD risk. The CPS details obesity's impact on cardiac structure and function, including its role in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), atrial fibrillation, and CVD considerations in patients with obstructive sleep apnea, cancer, and psychiatric disease. It also addresses the “obesity paradox,” social determinants of health, pediatric considerations, and disparities by age, sex, and race. Also included are CVD diagnostic challenges and comprehensive management strategies, including medical nutrition therapy, physical activity, behavioral intervention, cardiometabolic medications, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, and bariatric procedures.

### Conclusion

Effective reduction of obesity-related CVD risk requires shifting from treating downstream risk factors to addressing excessive adipose tissue itself, along with improving adipose tissue function. Clinically, this approach is often manifest by a “treat obesity first” approach. Precision diagnostics, lifestyle therapy, obesity medications, and bariatric procedures can modify both adiposopathy (“sick fat disease”) and fat mass disease, improving long-term cardiovascular outcomes.

## Obesity, epidemiology, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 1 ] (See Table 1 and Fig. 1 )

Between 1980 and 2015, the prevalence of obesity doubled in more than 70 countries and continued to increase in most other countries. In 2015, an estimated 603.7 million adults and 107.7 million children worldwide were living with obesity. This surge in increased adiposity is linked to 4.0 million deaths annually, over two-thirds being the result of cardiovascular disease (CVD). In the United States (August 2021–August 2023), the prevalence of obesity was above 40%, with severe obesity in adults at 9.4% (higher in women than men in each age group); overall obesity prevalence has plateaued while severe obesity continues to rise [ 2 ]. Beyond its contribution to risk factors like type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, and dyslipidemia (as well as thrombosis, sleep apnea, and fatty infiltration of body organs – including fat infiltration of the heart) obesity is an independent driver of CVD development and mortality. Childhood and adolescent obesity trends suggest a continued rise in future global CVD risk. Essential principles include: • Obesity increases CVD morbidity and mortality. • Increased visceral adiposity is a body composition pattern associated with increased CVD risk. • Treating obesity and CVD risk requires a comprehensive, equity-focused, system-level, team-based approach. Table 1 Ten things to know about obesity, epidemiology, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 1 ]. Table 1 Key Points References 1. In the past 4 decades, the prevalence of obesity has doubled in more than 70 countries and tripled in the United States (US). In the US (NHANES August 2021–August 2023), obesity prevalence is 40.3% and severe obesity is 9.4%, with severe obesity higher in women than men in each age group. While overall obesity prevalence has plateaued, severe obesity continues to rise. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) accounts for two thirds of deaths attributable to obesity. [ 1 , 2 , 14 ] 2. At a population level, increased body mass index (BMI) is associated with CVD risk. Compared to body mass index (BMI), percent body fat is a better diagnostic assessment of the relative amount of adipose tissue. Visceral adipose tissue accumulation is a better prognostic assessment for CVD risk. [ 1 , 38 ] 3. Obesity is both a direct and indirect contributor to CVD. Obesity is a direct contributor to CVD via biomechanical mechanisms (e.g., increased blood volume and cardiac output, left ventricular hypertrophy from pressure/volume overload, impaired diastolic filling due to pericardial fat, and facilitation of sleep apnea). [ 1 , 3 ] 4. Obesity is also an indirect contributor to CVD and adiposopathic immunopathies and endocrinopathies that lead to the promotion of major CVD risk factors such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and thrombosis, via chronic low-grade inflammation, contribution to insulin resistance, activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, lipotoxicity, and generation of a procoagulant state. [ 1 , 4 , 5 , 7 , 9 ] 5. Regarding types of CVD, increasing body fat contributes to increased risk of CVD such as coronary heart disease, heart failure, cardiac dysrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation), and stroke. [ 1 , 3 ] 6. Obesity and CVD risk is influenced by age, sex, race, income, education, as well as urban versus rural settings. [ 1 , 39 ] 7. Other major contributors to both obesity and CVD are physical inactivity, commercial and environmental factors including ultra-processed foods, food systems, marketing, urbanization, and social determinants of health. [ 1 , 40 ] 8. Childhood obesity increases the risk of adult obesity and CVD. The degree to which obesity contributes to CVD is dependent on lifetime exposure to obesity. [ 1 , 41 ] 9. Sustained weight reduction among individuals with obesity at risk for CVD often improves CVD risk factors and reduces CVD risk. [ 1 , 42 ] 10. Management of obesity and the reduction of cardiovascular disease risk are most effective when delivered through integrated team-based care with equity-focused health strategies, supported by public health interventions that drive population-level change. The World Heart Federation highlights pillars essential to this effort, including strong nutrition and food policy, promotion of physical activity, health-supportive urban design, education and behavioral initiatives, as well as coordinated action across sectors to create environments that enable healthful choices and sustained risk reduction. [ 1 , 12 ] Fig. 1 Obesity, Epidemiology, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Global obesity rates have climbed sharply, doubling in 73 countries since 1980 and contributing to millions of deaths each year—most from cardiovascular disease. In the United States, over 40% of adults have obesity, independently accelerating cardiovascular risk beyond traditional metabolic complications. Commercial, social, and environmental forces are major drivers of this epidemic and its downstream CVD burden. Meaningful reductions in obesity-related cardiovascular disease require a comprehensive, equity-focused, system-level, team-based approach. Sustained weight reduction lowers CVD risk, and the most effective and equitable outcomes arise from coordinated, optimized, multidisciplinary care. Although a higher body mass index (BMI) correlates with cardiovascular risk at the population level, increased visceral adipose tissue accumulation is a more accurate indicator of pathogenic adipose tissue distribution and a stronger predictor of individual cardiometabolic complications and cardiovascular disease risk.

## Obesity, sick fat disease (adiposopathy), fat mass disease, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 3 ] (See Table 2 and Fig. 2 )

Obesity can contribute to CVD via “fat mass disease.” Obesity can also contribute to CVD via adiposopathy or “sick fat disease.” Regarding “fat mass disease,” the biomechanical accumulation of adipose tissue may increase blood volume and cardiac contraction (due to increased adipose tissue blood supply), resulting in increase in heart size (i.e., left ventricular hypertrophy), cardiac dilation, and limitations on post contraction refill (i.e., “diastolic heart failure”), all contributing to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Fat mass disease can also contribute to obstructive sleep apnea, physical inactivity, and arterial vascular compression. Adiposopathy or “sick fat” arises when, unlike healthy adipose tissue that serves as a safe energy reservoir and endocrine/immune regulator, fat cells (adipocytes) undergo excessive enlargement (hypertrophy) with subsequent limitations on further energy storage in peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue, thus resulting in visceral adipose tissue accumulation. The ensuing endocrinopathies, immunopathies, and free fatty acid release promote insulin resistance, high blood glucose, high blood pressure, and elevated atherogenic blood lipids, as well as increased risk of thrombosis. Ultimately, the adiposopathic consequences of obesity may lead to an array of CVD. Essential principles include: • Obesity contributes to CVD in two main ways: through excess fat mass (“fat mass disease”) and through dysfunctional fat biology (“sick fat disease”). • Fat mass disease increases the mechanical burden on the heart and lungs, contributing to conditions like left-ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, sleep apnea, and reduced physical activity. • Sick fat disease occurs when enlarged, dysfunctional fat cells drive hormonal and inflammatory disturbances that raise blood sugar, blood pressure, atherogenic lipids, and clotting risk, ultimately promoting CVD. Table 2 Ten things to know about obesity, sick fat disease (adiposopathy), fat mass disease, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 3 ]. Table 2 Key Points References 1. While the main function of body fat is to store excess energy, adipocytes and adipose tissue are active endocrine and immune tissues whose function and dysfunction have implications regarding cardiovascular disease (CVD). [ 3 , 43 ] 2. Increased adipocyte hypertrophy and visceral adipose tissue accumulation can cause adipose tissue to become “sick” or become diseased or dysfunctional. Adiposopathy is analogous to the “pathies” of other body organs (e.g., myopathy, encephalopathy, ophthalmopathy, retinopathy, enteropathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and dermopathy). [ 3 , 8 ] 3. Cardiomyopathy describes a “disease” wherein pathologic enlargement of heart cells and the heart organ results in anatomic/functional abnormalities leading to adverse clinical consequences. Similarly, adiposopathy describes a “disease” wherein pathogenic enlargement of fat cells and the adipose tissue organ result in anatomic/functional abnormalities leading to adverse clinical consequences. [ 3 , 8 ] 4. “Fat Mass Disease” reflects the biomechanical and structural burden of excess adiposity, driving conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea, diastolic dysfunction, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and venous thrombosis through direct mechanical compromise of airway, cardiac, and vascular function. These complications are further amplified by obesity-related physical inactivity, which worsens cardiopulmonary loading, impairs venous return, and accelerates the adverse downstream consequences of excess fat mass. [ 3 , 8 ] 5. The adverse “sick fat” adiposopathic consequences of obesity often contribute to endocrine and immune dysfunction leading to insulin resistance and development of major cardiovascular risk factors including type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. These pathologic adipose-tissue signals also promote a pro-thrombotic state, further amplifying cardiometabolic risk. [ 3 , 8 ] 6. Illustrative adiposopathic endocrine abnormalities include hypoadiponectinemia, hyperleptinemia, excess circulating free-fatty-acids, and dysregulated adipose-derived renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) activity, which collectively, can drive insulin resistance and major cardiometabolic risk factors (e.g., type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia). These maladaptive hormonal signals may contribute to “ectopic fat deposition,” endothelial dysfunction, and pro-thrombotic adipokine patterns, thereby increasing the risk of CVD. [ 3 , 8 ] 7. Illustrative adiposopathy immune abnormalities include macrophage infiltration of adipose tissue, increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and impaired resolution of inflammation. The increased proinflammatory response coupled with reduced anti-inflammatory response promotes insulin resistance and cardiometabolic dysfunction (e.g., type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia). These immune-mediated disturbances also contribute to endothelial injury and a pro-thrombotic state, accelerating the development of CVD. [ 1 , 3 , 44 ] 8. Treatment of the consequences of obesity must not only reduce adiposity but also improve adiposopathy. [ 3 , 8 ] 9. Obesity-related adiposopathy and the accumulation of adipose tissue in the visceral region, as well as ectopic fat accumulation in organs such as liver, skeletal muscle, pancreas, and kidneys drive insulin resistance, inflammation, lipotoxicity, and metabolic dysfunction, key mechanisms that accelerate the development of cardiovascular disease. These dysfunctional fat depots act not merely as markers of disease but as active contributors to atherogenesis, cardiomyopathy, and vascular injury. [ 3 , 45 ] 10. Adiposopathy can drive inflammation, insulin resistance, and ectopic lipid spillover to other body areas. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is the fat depot in contact with the myocardium. EAT is a potential local mediator of cardiovascular injury. Dysfunctional epicardial adipose tissue releases pro-inflammatory and pro-atherogenic factors that accelerate coronary heart disease and other CVD, making it a mechanistic etiological bridge between systemic and local CVD progression. [ 3 , 46 ] Fig. 2 Obesity, Sick Fat Disease (Adiposopathy), Fat Mass Disease, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Obesity promotes CVD through two complementary mechanisms: the mechanical effects of excess fat mass (“fat mass disease”) and the metabolic–inflammatory dysfunction of adipose tissue (“sick fat disease”). Fat mass disease increases cardiac workload and impairs cardiopulmonary function, contributing to left-ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, sleep apnea, and reduced physical activity. Adiposopathy (“sick fat disease”) arises when hypertrophic, dysfunctional adipocytes trigger hormonal and immune disturbances that elevate glucose, blood pressure, atherogenic lipids, and thrombosis risk, collectively accelerating the risk of CVD.

## Obesity, “ectopic fat” (e.g., visceral, cardiac, hepatic, muscle, pancreas, kidney) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) (See Table 3 and Fig. 3 )

The progression from obesity to adverse health outcomes is best understood not just by an assessment of body weight, but by body composition and the concept of energy overflow and adiposopathy (dysfunctional “sick” adipose tissue). When peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue stores reach their expansion limit or become inflamed, then they fail to safely sequester additional or excess energy. This failure forces an energy metabolic “spillover,” resulting in increased circulating free fatty acids and the pathogenic accumulation of “ectopic fat” in areas other than peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue, such as visceral depots (abdominal and cardiac), the liver, skeletal muscle, pancreas, and kidneys. This ectopic deposition induces organ-specific toxicity (lipotoxicity) and systemic insulin resistance, serving as a driver of atherosclerosis and structural heart changes that increase the risk of CVD. Essential principles include: • Obesity-related increase in CVD risk stems less from body weight alone and more from the functionality or dysfunctionality of adipose tissue, which can be reflected by body composition (i.e., increase in visceral adiposity). • When subcutaneous adipose tissue can no longer expand or becomes resistant to further energy storage (e.g., as might occur with inflammation), then excess energy spills over into the bloodstream in the form of free fatty acids and deposits as “ectopic fat” in the visceral area of the abdomen, and organs like the liver, muscle, heart, pancreas, and kidneys. • Non-adipose organ accumulation of fat can result in “lipotoxicity” leading to insulin resistance, and driving the onset of CVD risk factors, atherosclerosis, and structural heart changes that increase the risk of CVD. Table 3 Ten things to know about obesity, “ectopic fat” (e.g., visceral fat, heart, muscle, liver, pancreas, kidney) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 3 , 4 ]. Table 3 Key Points References 1. Non-adipose tissues help to determine the degree that obesity leads to glucose dysregulation and cardiometabolic disease, including CVD. Ectopic fat delivery to non-adipose tissue can result in either physiological or pathophysiological responses that can either help mitigate or facilitate vascular injury and cardiac dysfunction. [ 3 , 4 , 45 ] 2. Healthy expansion of peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue can buffer excess energy and prevent harmful ectopic fat deposition. By limiting lipid overflow into the heart, vessels, and liver, this protective mechanism reduces cardiovascular disease risk despite increased fat mass. [ 3 , 4 , 45 ] 3. When adipocyte proliferation or differentiation in peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue is impaired, then adipocytes may become enlarged (i.e., hypertrophied) and dysfunctional with limitations in further energy storage. The ensuing energy spillover drives ectopic fat deposition in cardiovascular-relevant organs, promoting inflammation, endothelial injury, and atherosclerosis. [ 3 , 4 , 45 ] 4. Ectopic fat accumulation in the liver and muscle can cause “lipotoxicity,” which can directly impair organ function, resulting in insulin resistance. One illustrative adverse consequence is the accumulation of ceramides, which are sphingolipids that accumulate when tissues are exposed to excess fatty acids. Ceramides can act as key mediators of lipotoxicity by blocking insulin signaling, damaging mitochondria, and promoting inflammation. The end result of lipotoxicity is disruption of the function of the liver, muscle, pancreas, and heart, contributing to insulin resistance and CVD risk factors and CVD. For example, in the cardiovascular system, ectopic fat in epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) can contribute to lipotoxicity, myocardial steatosis, diastolic dysfunction, dysrhythmogenic remodeling, and accelerated atherosclerotic disease. Pancreatic fat can contribute to beta cell dysfunction and diminished insulin secretion, increasing the risk of onset of diabetes mellitus, a major CVD risk factor. Renal fat may activate the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), increasing the risk of onset of hypertension, a major CVD risk factor. [ 3 , 4 , 47 ] 5. Prediabetes, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia arise from multi-organ insulin resistance, which is worsened when ectopic fat infiltrates organs such as the liver, muscle and pancreas. Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia are CVD risk factors. [ 3 , 4 , 48 ] 6. Age, sex, race, genetics, medications, and comorbidities may potentially influence whether excess energy (caloric intake beyond energy absorbed and expended) is stored safely in adipose tissue or diverted into ectopic depots. These same factors therefore shape susceptibility to CVD driven by ectopic fat. For example, aging compromises the storage capacity of peripheral adipose tissue, contributing to a ‘lipid spillover’ effect that shifts fat accumulation toward visceral and ectopic sites. Compared to White individuals and males, Black individuals and females tend to sequester excess energy in subcutaneous adipose tissue, resulting in lower visceral fat mass for any given body mass index. Individuals of Asian descent typically exhibit a limited capacity for subcutaneous adipose tissue expansion, causing excess lipid to overflow into visceral adipose tissue depots at a lower Body Mass Index (BMI) compared to other populations. Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) activate PPAR-gamma which promotes the creation of a “metabolic sink” where energy storage is enhanced via the proliferation and differentiation of more healthy, insulin-sensitive subcutaneous adipose tissue - which in turn - helps mitigate the otherwise harmful ectopic fat deposition such as energy spillover into visceral adipose tissue depots. [ 3 , 4 , 45 ] 7. During weight-reduction interventions, peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue (by far the largest fat depot) typically shows the greatest absolute reduction, increasing the potential for energy storage, which helps reduce lipid spillover. The greater capacity for energy storage via weight reduction reduces the substrate available for ectopic fat deposition, thereby lowering CVD risk. [ 3 , 4 , 40 ] 8. Weight reduction improves the function of multiple organs, but the degree of improvement varies widely among individuals. These variable responses influence how effectively ectopic fat is cleared from organs, thereby modifying CVD risk. [ 3 , 4 , 49 ] 9. Adipose-tissue and hepatic insulin sensitivity often improve with modest weight reduction, reducing systemic lipid spillover to other body organs and reducing hepatic secretion of atherogenic triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, both which may slow progression of CVD. [ 3 , 4 , 48 ] 10. Obesity promotes ectopic fat deposition within epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), creating a metabolically active reservoir that releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, free fatty acids, and oxidative stress mediators that directly injure adjacent coronary vessels and myocardium. This inflammatory and lipotoxic microenvironment accelerates atherosclerosis, impairs vascular function, and increases the overall risk of CVD. [ 3 , 4 , 46 ] Fig. 3 Obesity, “Ectopic Fat” (e.g., Visceral, Cardiac, Hepatic, Muscle, Pancreas, Kidney) and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Obesity leads to CVD not simply through excess body weight, but through limits in adipose tissue expandability in peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), triggering both adiposopathy (i.e., resulting in adipocyte and adipose tissue endocrinopathies and immunopathies/inflammation) and energy overflow. During limitations in SAT energy storage, free fatty acids spill into the circulation and deposit as ectopic fat in visceral adipose tissue depots and within organs such as the liver, muscle, heart, and pancreas. In addition to adiposopathic immunopathies and endocrinopathies, the “ectopic fat” infiltrations of non-adipose tissue organs may result in lipotoxicity, insulin resistance, worsening cardiometabolic risk factors, and ultimately, CVD (i.e., atherosclerosis and myocardial damage).

## Obesity, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 4 ] (See Table 4 and Fig. 4 )

“Sick fat” (i.e., adiposopathy) is a common pathophysiological link between obesity, T2DM, and CVD. Adipocyte hypertrophy and visceral adipose tissue accumulation reflect an anatomic manifestation of global adipose tissue dysfunction leading to immunopathies, endocrinopathies, and lipotoxicity that impair the function of non-adipose organs (such as the liver, muscle, and pancreas), ultimately driving insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction. Addressing the adiposopathic consequences of increased body fat is one of the rationales for the “treating obesity first” paradigm, where clinically meaningful weight reduction can potentially lead to T2DM remission and improved cardiometabolic outcomes. Weight reduction can also improve fat mass disease, which has implications regarding glycemic control. Among patients with overweight or obesity, alleviating conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea through weight reduction may help improve hyperglycemia otherwise driven by hypoxia, sympathetic activation, and insulin resistance. Weight reduction strategies include evidence-based healthful nutrition, routine physical activity, behavior modification, and the use of pharmacotherapy [specifically incretin mimetics such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA), as well as sodium-glucose linked co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors] or bariatric procedures - that all collectively treat excessive body weight, type 2 diabetes mellitus, CVD risk and CVD. Essential principles include: • “Sick fat” (adiposopathy) links obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease through dysfunctional adipose tissue that drives inflammation, hormonal disruption, and lipotoxicity leading to insulin resistance and beta-cell stress. • Clinically meaningful weight reduction can help treat adiposopathic consequences, improve obstructive sleep apnea–related metabolic stress, and even enable diabetes remission with better cardiometabolic outcomes. • Effective management of obesity and type 2 diabetes includes healthful nutrition, regular physical activity, and evidence-based therapies such as GLP-1 RA, SGLT2 inhibitors, or bariatric procedures to reduce adiposity and cardiometabolic risk. Table 4 Ten things to know about obesity, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 4 ]. Table 4 Key Points References 1. Excess adiposity is a dose-dependent risk factor for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), raising the risk roughly three-fold for those who are overweight and sevenfold or more among those with obesity. T2DM is a major cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factor. Higher body weight further increases both these risks. For most non-pregnant adults with T2DM, a hemoglobin A1c goal is <7.0%, with an even lower goal of <6.5% among select patients with diabetes mellitus and obesity who can achieve it safely through evidence-based weight reduction interventions (e.g., healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavior modification, obesity medications, and/or bariatric procedures). [ 4 , 50 , 51 ] 2. About 40% of US adults have obesity; over 70% of US adults have overweight or obesity; about 25% of patients with obesity have T2DM; about 80–90% of adults with T2DM have overweight or obesity. [ 4 , 52 ] 3. The adiposopathic effects of increased body fat are not the only causes of hyperglycemia. Other potential causes of hyperglycemia include hemochromatosis, hypercortisolism, excessive growth hormone, pancreatic insufficiency due to pancreatitis or surgical excision, side effects of concomitant therapies, genetic syndromes of insulin resistance, and genetic syndromes of limited pancreatic insulin secretion. [ 3 , 4 ] 4. Adipocyte hypertrophy and visceral adipose tissue accumulation is reflective of an anatomic body composition pattern that results in endocrinopathies and immunopathies that directly contribute to glycemic-related CVD and indirectly contribute to CVD risk factors such as insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and hyperglycemia. [ 3 , 4 ] 5. Both obesity and T2DM are CVD risk factors that contribute to atherosclerotic coronary heart disease, endothelial dysfunction, microvascular disease, and left ventricular dysfunction (i.e., heart failure with preserved ejection fraction). An important unifying pathogenic mechanism among many patients with overweight or obesity is insulin resistance, which often leads to compensatory hyperinsulinemia. In addition to being a metabolic hormone, insulin has growth factor activities such that hyperinsulinemia promotes cardiovascular disease through pathway-selective resistance. While the metabolic signaling pathway (Phosphoinositide 3-Kinase or PI3K) is impaired with hyperinsulinemia - causing endothelial dysfunction and reduced nitric oxide - the growth-promoting pathway (Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase or MAPK) remains sensitive to the high insulin levels. Consequently, hyperinsulinemia drives excessive anabolic signaling via MAPK, triggering inflammation and pathological cardiac hypertrophy, effectively acting as a potent, independent risk factor for heart and vascular disease. [ 4 , 53 ] 6. Hyperglycemia develops when pancreatic beta-cell hyperinsulinemia can no longer compensate for insulin resistance. Hyperglycemia itself can drive cardiovascular disease through mitochondrial superoxide overproduction that activates four major injurious pathways: increased flux through the polyol pathway with depletion of antioxidant defenses, heightened hexosamine pathway activity, accelerated formation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), and activation of protein kinase C (PKC). Together, these mechanisms produce endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, vasoconstriction, impaired nitric oxide signaling, and a pro-thrombotic state that promotes adverse CVD consequences such as atherosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, microvascular dysfunction, and even autonomic cardiac dysregulation potentially resulting in resting tachycardia, silent ischemia, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias. [ 4 , 54 ] 7. While from a population standpoint, central obesity (increased waist circumference) is associated with both increased risk of T2DM and CVD, from an individual standpoint, an increase in waist circumference has variable correlation to an increase in visceral adiposity, especially upon consideration of age (i.e., older individuals have increased visceral adiposity), sex (i.e., females have less visceral adiposity than males), and race (i.e., Black individuals generally have decreased visceral adiposity while those of Asian descent may have increased visceral adiposity). [ 4 , 55 ] 8. Hyperglycemia is one component of the metabolic syndrome (MetSyn), with MetSyn being a constellation of CVD risk factors. MetSyn includes central adiposity (as the only anatomic physical exam component), as well as high blood sugar, high blood pressure, and abnormal blood lipids. [ 4 , 8 ] 9. In individuals with obesity and T2DM, weight reduction not only lowers CVD risk but is also the most reliable predictor of diabetes remission, whether achieved through dietary intervention, obesity medications, or bariatric procedures. [ 4 , 56 ] 10. While some diabetes medications potentially worsen obesity (e.g., sulfonylureas, insulin), medications whose mechanisms reduce both blood glucose and body weight have among the strongest degree of evidence of reducing the risk of CVD (e.g., incretin mimetics such as glucagon-like peptide – 1 receptor agonist based therapies and sodium glucose transporter - 2 inhibitors). [ 4 , 57 ] Fig. 4 Obesity, Diabetes Mellitus, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) . “Sick fat” (adiposopathy) is anatomically manifest by adipocyte hypertrophy and visceral adipose tissue accumulation. The accumulation of visceral adiposity can be considered a marker of global fat dysfunction and immune/endocrine dysregulation. The resultant insulin resistance and beta cell dysfunction can lead to hyperglycemia, with type 2 diabetes mellitus being a major CVD risk factor. Clinically meaningful weight reduction can reverse aspects of adiposopathy, improve conditions like obstructive sleep apnea that worsen glycemic control, and in some cases even facilitate diabetes remission. Effective treatment of patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus combines healthful nutrition, regular physical activity, behavioral strategies, and evidence-based therapies (e.g., obesity medications and bariatric procedures) to reduce excess body fat and lower cardiometabolic risk.

## Obesity, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 5 ] (See Table 5 and Fig. 5 )

Increased body fat is the leading modifiable contributor to hypertension, with population-attributable estimates of approximately 78% in men and 65% in women. This strong correlation is driven by “fat mass disease,” where pathogenic physical forces - such as the compression of kidneys by visceral adipose tissue - increase intrarenal pressure and stimulate the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to sodium retention and volume expansion. Additionally, “sick fat disease” (adiposopathy) contributes to hypertension through metabolic dysfunctions, including the secretion of angiotensinogen by adipose tissue which upregulates RAAS, as well as hyperleptinemia and insulin resistance which increase sympathetic nervous system activity. Ensuring an accurate assessment of blood pressure requires consistent measurement techniques to control for variables such as cuff size and white-coat hypertension. Clinical management of obesity-related hypertension prioritizes weight reduction through healthful nutrition (e.g., the “Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension” or DASH diet), other healthful eating plans that reduce blood pressure (e.g., low carbohydrate dietary intake) [ 6 ], routine physical activity, bariatric procedures, and obesity medications like GLP-1 RA. Among patients with obesity-related hypertension, the degree of blood pressure reduction generally correlates with the magnitude of weight reduction. Essential principles include: • Increased body fat is the leading contributor to hypertension. • Accurate blood pressure assessment requires consistent technique, including proper cuff size and attention to white-coat effects. • Treatment of high blood pressure in patients with obesity focuses on weight reduction through evidence-based healthful nutrition, physical activity, obesity medications, and bariatric procedures, with blood pressure improvements generally proportional to the amount of weight lost. Table 5 Ten things to know about obesity, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 5 ]. Table 5 Key Points References 1. Hypertension increases the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) such as coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, peripheral artery disease, and aortic aneurysm. The 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association blood pressure goal for nonpregnant adults is <130/80 mmHg, with encouragement to achieve a systolic blood pressure <120 mmHg (when it can be safely attained) for potential additional health benefits. The lower optimal blood pressure goal is relevant for patients with obesity who can achieve it safely through evidence-based weight reduction interventions (e.g., healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavior modification, obesity medications, and/or bariatric procedures). [ 5 , 58 ] 2. The adiposopathic effects of increased body fat are not the only causes of hypertension. Other potential causes of high blood pressure include pheochromocytoma, primary hyperaldosteronism, hypercortisolism, hyperthyroidism, renal artery stenosis, kidney diseases, side effects of concomitant therapies, and familial or genetic syndromes. [ 5 , 58 ] 3. The relationship between body fat and blood pressure is approximately linear on a population level. Obesity-related hypertension arises partly from “fat mass disease,” in which visceral adipose tissue mechanically compresses the kidneys - activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Expanded adipose tissue increases total blood volume, cardiac output, and results in venous compression. Unlike the kidney, arteries are not confined within a rigid capsule, so perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) does not raise blood pressure by physically squeezing them; arterial pressure far exceeds the pressure of surrounding soft fat, and healthy PVAT even acts as a buttress that stabilizes the vessel. Instead, dysfunctional, obesity-associated PVAT drives hypertension through an “outside-in” process: inflammation and fibrosis stiffen the adipose tissue into a rigid scaffold that limits arterial expansion, loss of normal PVAT stress-relaxation keeps vessels under higher tension, and paracrine signaling promotes collagen deposition within the arterial wall, collectively increasing arterial stiffness and promoting hypertension. [ 5 , 59 ] 4. Increased fat mass contributes to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which promotes hypertension through activation of the sympathetic pathways and the RAAS, leading to increased blood pressure. Treating obesity and OSA - through weight reduction (e.g., including the use of tirzepatide) or continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) - reduces blood pressure and improves other CVD risk factors. [ 5 , 58 ] 5. Adiposopathic “sick fat” contributors to hypertension include hyperinsulinemia and hyperleptinemia, which increase sympathetic nervous system activity; increase angiotensinogen, mineralocorticoids, RAAS activity, and sodium reabsorption; increase the adiposopathic release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-6) that impair endothelial function; and reduce anti-inflammatory adiponectin release. [ 3 , 5 ] 6. Ensuring an accurate diagnosis of hypertension requires consistent measurement techniques tailored for patients with obesity. Improper cuff size can significantly distort readings, sometimes (depending on the cited reference) by as much as ∼5–20 mmHg. Given the bias and discrimination against those with obesity, and/or fear of potential bias and discrimination (even within the healthcare setting), standardized measurements are necessary to control for “white coat syndrome,” which better allows for clinicians to distinguish true hypertension from stress-related elevations and avoid misdiagnosis. [ 5 , 58 , 60 , 61 ] 7. Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) uses individualized nutrition assessment, education, and behavioral counseling to help patients modify dietary patterns in ways that improve obesity and hypertension. MNT emphasizes calorie-appropriate, nutrient-dense eating patterns such as reducing sodium and saturated fat while increasing fruits, vegetables, and whole grains to support weight reduction and improve blood pressure control. Illustrative examples of recommended, healthful eating pattern to help manage obesity and hypertension include the “Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension” or DASH diet or Mediterranean Diet. [ 5 , 62 ] 8. Among patients with obesity and hypertension, regular physical activity includes routine non-exercise activity thermogenesis (i.e., NEAT), dynamic training, beginning at a minimum of 5000 steps per day and potentially progressing toward 10,000 steps per day or more and resistance training, all which may help support weight reduction management, improve blood pressure, enhance functional capacity, and reduce cardiometabolic risk. Health risks of physical exercise are generally low but may include musculoskeletal strain, overexertion, or transient blood-pressure elevations, underscoring the importance of medical supervision, gradual progression, and individualized guidance (such as through an exercise prescription), especially in those with obesity-related complications, such as CVD. [ 5 , 63 ] 9. Optimal choice of antihypertensive agent is essential because different drug classes have different side-effect profiles [e.g., edema with some calcium-channel blockers, electrolyte disturbances with thiazide diuretics, weight gain with some older beta-blockers (e.g., atenolol and metoprolol) and risks like hypotension or syncope]. Patient-centered antihypertensive therapy better allows clinicians to balance efficacy with safety by anticipating these potential complications and tailoring treatment to each patient's comorbidities, risk factors, and physiological vulnerabilities. For example, in patients with obesity who have increased RAAS activity, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone) may be effective. [ 5 , 64 ] 10. Among patients with obesity and hypertension, weight reduction through healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavior modification, obesity medications, or bariatric procedures, may all lower blood pressure – depending on the degree the evidence-based interventions are implemented. Substantial weight reduction can even lead to hypertension “remission” or a reduced need for antihypertensive medications, highlighting the importance of weight-focused and blood pressure treatments as adjunct to traditional blood-pressure management. While obesity medications such as orlistat do not generally alter heart rate, and while weight reduction among patients with obesity generally decreases blood pressure, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists may mildly increase heart rate by 2–3 beats per minute. Phentermine/topiramate, phentermine monotherapy, and naltrexone/bupropion may have a higher heart rate at the end of studies compared to placebo, but many have the same heart rate or lower than baseline. [ 5 , 63 ] Fig. 5 Obesity, Hypertension, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Increased body fat is the leading contributor to high blood pressure, driven both by the physical effects of excess body fat (e.g., compression of the kidneys and sleep apnea) which activate the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, and by dysfunctional adipose tissue that increases hormone and immune activity. Among the adiposopathic consequences of obesity leading to hypertension include increased sympathetic nervous system activity because of insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and hyperleptinemia. Accurate measurement of blood pressure requires consistent technique, including proper cuff size and awareness of “white-coat syndrome” elevation. Treatment of obesity and hypertension is best focused on weight reduction through healthful nutrition such as the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension and Mediterranean eating patterns, regular physical activity, behavior modification, obesity medications, and bariatric procedures, with improvements in blood pressure generally proportional to the degree of weight reduction.

## Obesity, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 7 ] (See Table 6 and Fig. 6 )

Obesity is defined as a chronic, relapsing disease characterized by “adiposopathy” (adipose tissue dysfunction), wherein excess adiposity both directly and indirectly contributes to increased risk of CVD. “Adiposopathic dyslipidemia” is a lipid pattern often found in patients with obesity, distinguished by elevated triglycerides, reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and increased atherogenic particles such as increased small dense LDL concentration and increased apolipoprotein B (apoB) levels, even when LDL cholesterol levels are only modestly elevated. Pathophysiologically, this state is driven by adipocyte hypertrophy, inflammation, and impaired lipolysis, which increase circulating free fatty acids. Weight reduction therapies such as healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavior modification, obesity medications, and bariatric procedures can often improve the patient's lipid profile (particularly triglycerides and HDL-C) and reduce adverse CVD outcomes. This underscores the benefits of an “all of the above” approach when treating excess adiposity and atherogenic cholesterol levels. Essential principles include: • Obesity is a chronic, relapsing disease marked by adipose-tissue dysfunction that increases cardiometabolic risk, at least partially through generation of “adiposopathic dyslipidemia.” • “Adiposopathic dyslipidemia” is characterized by high triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, and often, an increase in non-HDL cholesterol and apoB-containing particles. • While weight-reduction strategies can often improve triglyceride and HDL cholesterol levels, optimal control of LDL cholesterol often requires specific cholesterol lowering therapies such as statins. Table 6 Ten things to know about obesity, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 7 ]. Table 6 Key Points References 1. Obesity is often associated with an “adiposopathic dyslipidemia” which includes increased triglycerides and reduced high density lipoprotein cholesterol. Most medical organizations recommend the following goals among patients at high CVD risk, which may include many patients with obesity having other CVD risk factors: Low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol <70 mg/dL, non-high density lipoprotein (non-HDL) cholesterol goal <100 mg/dL, and apolipoprotein B goal <80 mg/dL. Patients with obesity at higher CVD risk have even lower, more aggressive lipid goals. [ 7 , 65 ] 2. Particularly when accompanied by insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus, the obesity-driven “adiposopathic dyslipidemia” may include increased atherogenic particles such as increased number of circulating small dense low density lipoproteins (LDL) and increased apolipoprotein B, even when LDL cholesterol levels are only modestly elevated. Small, dense LDL particles are more likely to penetrate arterial walls and contribute to atherosclerosis. [ 7 , 66 ] 3. The adiposopathic effects of increased body fat are not the only causes of dyslipidemia. Other potential causes of increased circulating atherogenic lipids include inadequately controlled hypothyroidism or diabetes mellitus, liver disease, kidney disease, side effects of concomitant therapies, and genetic dyslipidemias. [ 7 , 65 ] 4. Impaired storage of triglycerides in adipose tissue may lead to increased circulating free fatty acids, increased delivery of fatty acids to the liver, increased hepatic very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) cholesterol secretion (which carry triglycerides) and thus increased circulating triglyceride levels. [ 7 , 45 ] 5. Increased triglyceride rich lipoprotein production may contribute to enzymatic exchanges of lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides, resulting in reduced levels of high density lipoprotein cholesterol, which is a hallmark of “adiposopathic dyslipidemia.” [ 7 , 66 ] 6. Typically, obesity only results in modest increases in LDL cholesterol levels. However, an LDL cholesterol level alone may underestimate the number of atherogenic lipoprotein particles. Better lipid measures include non-HDL-cholesterol, which is a measure of cholesterol carried by all atherogenic lipoproteins (i.e., inclusive of atherogenic triglyceride rich lipoproteins, and not just LDL). A perhaps even better measure is apoB, which is a direct measure of atherogenic particles number and a proven CVD risk factor. [ 7 , 65 ] 7. Increased visceral adiposity strongly correlates with elevated apolipoprotein B (apoB) levels, which is a structural protein found on the surface of all atherogenic (plaque-forming) lipoproteins. ApoB is thus a measure of the number of all circulating atherogenic lipoproteins. [ 7 , 40 ] 8. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined CVD risk factor not meaningfully affected by nutrition, physical activity or weight reduction in patients with obesity. Especially in patients at high CVD risk, it is often recommended that Lp(a) be measured at least once in a lifetime. [ 7 , 67 ] 9. Among patients with obesity, healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavior modification, and obesity medications may somewhat improve dyslipidemia, mainly via lowering triglycerides and raising HDL-cholesterol. Unless substantial weight reduction is achieved via highly effective obesity medication and bariatric procedures, LDL cholesterol is often only marginally improved. That said, especially with lower dietary fat intake, HDL cholesterol may transiently decrease during weight reduction. [ 7 , 68 , 69 ] 10. Statin therapy remains a cornerstone treatment for patients with obesity at increased risk for CVD – a recommended treatment unlikely to change with the modest improvement in LDL cholesterol most often found in most clinical treatments of obesity. [ 7 , 65 ] Fig. 6 Obesity, Dyslipidemia, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Obesity is a chronic, relapsing disease that in addition to adverse fat mass consequences, may result in dysfunctional adipose tissue, which in turn, promotes a harmful lipid pattern known as “adiposopathic dyslipidemia.” This pattern features high triglycerides, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and increased atherogenic particles such as small dense low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and apolipoprotein B. While weight-reduction strategies improve triglycerides and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, achieving optimal low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) control often requires substantial weight reduction coupled with evidence-based cholesterol-lowering therapies such as statins.

## Obesity, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 8 ] (See Table 7 and Fig. 7 )

The relationship between obesity, metabolic syndrome, and CVD can be attributable to “adiposopathy” or “sick fat,” which can be defined as adipose tissue dysfunction resulting from positive caloric balance and sedentary lifestyle in susceptible individuals. Rather than obesity being merely an accumulation of inert mass, this “sick fat” acts as an active endocrine and immune organ that drives the cluster of CVD risk factors associated with metabolic syndrome - such as high glucose, high blood pressure, and high atherogenic lipids. Beyond genetic influences, in many patients, adiposopathy represents the single, primary cause of this constellation of CVD risk factors. Essential principles include: Table 7 Ten things to know about obesity, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 8 ]. Table 7 Key Points References 1. Those of Asian descent may have different metabolic syndrome cutoff points regarding waist circumference: men ≥35.4 inches or ≥90 cm and women ≥31.5 inches or ≥80 cm. [ 8 , 19 , 20 ] 2. The presence of metabolic syndrome is associated with a 2–3 × higher risk of cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke). The presence of metabolic syndrome is associated with a 2 × higher risk of cardiovascular mortality. [ 8 , 70 ] 3. Metabolic syndrome (utilizing Adult Treatment Panel III criteria) has a >90% specificity for insulin resistance (albeit <50% sensitivity). [ 8 , [71] , [72] , [73] ] 4. The presence of metabolic syndrome is associated with 5 × higher risk of developing T2DM, which is a major CVD risk factor. [ 8 , 74 ] 5. Increased waist circumference (abdominal obesity) is the only anthropometric physical exam/phenotypic component of the metabolic syndrome. [ 8 , [75] , [76] , [77] ] 6. Body mass index (BMI) is sometimes substituted for waist circumference in some definitions of metabolic syndrome. BMI definition for overweight is commonly 25–29.9 kg/m 2 and for obesity is commonly ≥30 kg/m 2 . In the case of those of Asian descent, the cutoff points are more commonly BMI 23–24.9 kg/m 2 for overweight and ≥25 kg/m 2 for obesity. [ 8 , 78 ] 7. Increased low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is not a component of the metabolic syndrome; however, those with metabolic syndrome (especially those with obesity, T2DM, and increased triglyceride levels) may have an increased number of atherogenic lipoproteins, including an increase in small, dense LDL particles. [ 8 , 69 ] 8. In addition to the defined diagnostic components, metabolic syndrome is also often a state of insulin resistance and chronic low grade inflammation, as can be measured by high-sensitivity C-Reactive Protein. Adiposopathic increases in circulating insulin levels are often considered a contributor to metabolic syndrome; other contributors may be genetic predisposition, physical inactivity, and aging. [ 8 , 76 ] 9. The presence of the metabolic syndrome may be associated with other systemic disorders, such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS; formerly polycystic ovary syndrome or PCOS), gout, and acanthosis nigricans. [ 8 , 79 ] 10. Among patients with obesity and metabolic syndrome, treatment includes evidence-based weight reduction interventions as well as treatment of individual components (e.g., treatment of T2DM, hypertriglyceridemia). [ 8 , 80 ] Fig. 7 Obesity, Metabolic Syndrome, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Adiposopathy, or “sick fat,” explains how obesity leads to metabolic syndrome and CVD by transforming adipose tissue into a dysfunctional endocrine and immune organ that drives high glucose, high blood pressure, and atherogenic lipid abnormalities. In many individuals, this adipose-tissue dysfunction—not genetics alone—is the primary cause of the clustered risk factors that define metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when three or more are present: abdominal obesity, elevated fasting glucose, elevated blood pressure, high triglycerides, or reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Increased low density lipoprotein cholesterol is not a diagnostic component of the metabolic syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome diagnosis includes the presence of 3 or more of the following 5 risk factors : 1. Abdominal Obesity: Waist circumference ≥102 cm (40 in) for men, ≥88 cm (35 in) for women. 2. Elevated Fasting Glucose: ≥100 mg/dL (or on drug therapy for hyperglycemia). 3. Elevated Blood Pressure: Systolic ≥130 mmHg and/or Diastolic ≥85 mmHg (or on antihypertensive drug therapy). 4. Elevated Triglycerides: ≥150 mg/dL (or on drug therapy for hypertriglyceridemia). 5. Reduced HDL Cholesterol: <40 mg/dL in men, <50 mg/dL in women (or on drug therapy for reduced HDL cholesterol).

## Obesity, thrombosis, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 9 ] (See Table 8 and Fig. 8 )

Obesity contributes to a prothrombotic state through “fat mass disease,” where adipose tissue exerts pathogenic physical forces causing vascular compression and venous stasis. Obesity can also promote thrombosis through “sick fat disease” (adiposopathy), which promotes inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and hypercoagulability. In addition to managing deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and chronic venous insufficiency, clinicians sometimes encounter obesity-related lymphedema and the distinct familial disorder of lipedema (i.e., chronic accumulation of adipose tissue, primarily in the legs, that often causes pain, tenderness, easy bruising) [ 10 ]. Regarding treatment of thrombosis, some anti-thrombotic medications are weight based. This is important because while weight reduction strategies such as healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavior modification, and bariatric procedures have their role, weight reduction alone among patients with obesity is often not sufficient for all venous, lymphatic, or lipedemic disorders. Essential principles include: • Obesity contributes to venous and lymphatic disorders through both “fat mass disease,” which causes mechanical compression and stasis, and “sick fat disease,” which drives inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and hypercoagulability. • In addition to deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and chronic venous insufficiency, clinicians may also encounter obesity-related lymphedema and the distinct familial condition of lipedema. • Although weight-reduction strategies are valuable, they are often insufficient on their own to fully address venous, lymphatic, or lipedemic disorders in patients with obesity. Table 8 Ten things to know about obesity, thrombosis, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 9 ]. Table 8 Key Points References 1. Obesity creates a chronic pro-thrombotic state, through mechanical, metabolic, and inflammatory pathways. [ 9 , 81 ] 2. Adiposopathic pathways that increase the risk of thrombosis among patients with obesity include increased coagulation factors, platelet activation, thrombin generation, and inflammation via inflammatory cytokines that contribute to plaque instability (i.e., vulnerable atherosclerotic plaques have a thin fibrous cap that are prone to rupture). [ 9 , 81 ] 3. Among patients with obesity and adiposopathy, fibrinolytic activity is downregulated. [ 9 , 82 ] 4. Obesity contributes to endothelial dysfunction which may promote platelet adhesion. [ 9 , 83 ] 5. Obesity leading to adiposopathic “sick fat disease” and biomechanical “fat mass disease” may create a pathogenic environment with all components of Virchow's Triad (i.e., endothelial dysfunction, hypercoagulability, and venous stasis). [ 9 , 84 ] 6. Venous stasis in obesity increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary emboli. Specifically regarding DVT, patients with obesity are at increased risk for post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), with greater challenges in recanalizing (clearing) the vein after a clot, and thus potentially leading to chronic venous insufficiency, ulcers, and permanent swelling that is distinct from lymphedema (see below). [ 9 , 85 ] 7. The risk of thrombosis varies among patients with obesity, and is dependent on other risk factors such as age, sex, comorbidities, concomitant medications, socioeconomic status, and mobility status. In many, if not most cases, thrombosis among patients with obesity represents a “two-hit” phenomenon, such as obesity and prothrombotic states such as pregnancy, estrogen therapy, or cancer. Obesity itself can complicate diagnosis of thrombosis in limbs, resulting in under-recognition; similarly, obesity stigma can obscure clinical risk, reduce patient engagement, and lead to underdiagnosis of thrombotic conditions. [ 9 , 84 ] 8. Anticoagulation management is more complex in patients with obesity, sometimes presenting challenges regarding optimal dosing, monitoring, and drug selection, especially for direct oral anticoagulants or DOACs (e.g., direct thrombin inhibitors like dabigatran and factor Xa inhibitors like apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban). Optimal treatment is patient centered. [ 9 , 86 ] 9. Lymphedema (i.e., lymphatic accumulation causing persistent swelling of the arms or legs) is typically asymmetrical and can sometimes present diagnostic challenges in patients with obesity; delayed recognition can potentially lead to irreversible lymphatic damage and more severe swelling. Early diagnosis of lymphedema enables more timely therapeutic interventions, such as compression therapy, weight management, and infection prevention, which can reduce complications and improve long-term outcomes. [ 9 , 87 ] 10. Lipedema (i.e., abnormal, painful fat accumulation in the hips, thighs, legs, and sometimes the arms) is typically symmetrical and can sometimes present diagnostic challenges in patients with obesity, with physical findings sometimes perceived as due to simple weight gain. Treatments such as compression therapy, lymphatic support, and when appropriate, surgical intervention can reduce pain, improve mobility, and limit additional fat accumulation. [ 9 , 88 ] Fig. 8 Obesity, Thrombosis, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Obesity promotes a prothrombotic state through the mechanical effects of excess fat (“fat mass disease”), which cause vascular compression and venous stasis. Obesity may also facilitate thrombosis through the metabolic–inflammatory effects of dysfunctional adipose tissue (“sick fat disease”), which may lead to increased inflammation, endothelial injury, and increased tendency for blood clotting. In addition to deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and chronic venous insufficiency, clinicians may also encounter obesity-related lymphedema and the distinct familial condition of lipedema. Although weight-reduction strategies are beneficial, they are often not sufficient to fully address venous, lymphatic, or lipedemic disorders.

## Obesity, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 11 ] (See Table 9 , Figs. 9a and 9b )

Obesity is a primary contributor to sleep-disordered breathing. An example would be adverse anatomical changes such as pharyngeal airway narrowing and increased tongue fat deposition which play mechanistic roles in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA may occur in up to 70% of patients with obesity. The relationship is bidirectional: pharyngeal fat narrows the airway contributing to OSA, while sleep fragmentation from OSA increases ghrelin and decreases leptin, resulting in increased appetite and a vicious cycle of weight gain and worsening sleep dysfunction. Untreated OSA leads to sympathetic overactivity, resistant hypertension, and dysrhythmias like atrial fibrillation, as well as increased risks for T2DM and hypertension (two major CVD risk factors), as well as stroke, heart failure, and sudden death. Treatment includes weight reduction through healthful nutrition, physical activity, and behavior modification. Obesity medications (e.g., tirzepatide) and bariatric procedures can also improve OSA. Essential principles include: • Obesity contributes to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) through anatomical changes such as pharyngeal airway narrowing and increased tongue fat, and up to 70% of people with obesity may develop OSA. • The relationship is bidirectional, as OSA worsens appetite-regulating hormones and promotes weight gain, creating a cycle of worsening sleep and metabolic dysfunction. • Untreated OSA increases cardiovascular and metabolic risks, while weight-related treatments such as weight reduction, lifestyle changes, obesity medications (e.g., tirzepatide), and bariatric procedures can improve OSA Table 9 Ten things to know about obesity, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 11 ]. Table 9 Key Points References 1. Approximately 70% of patients with obesity may have OSA. In community-based cohorts, roughly 30–40% of adults with OSA have obesity, rising to ∼50% among those with severe OSA; clinic-referred populations report substantially higher proportions. [ 11 , 89 ] 2. Obesity contributes to airway obstruction, leading to hypoxia, sympathetic surges, physiological vascular stress, and hypertension. Intermittent hypoxemia and sleep fragmentation trigger sympathetic activation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and insulin resistance – all potentially contributing to increase CVD risk. [ 11 , 90 ] 3. The relationship between obesity and OSA is bidirectional. Excess body weight increases the likelihood of obstructive sleep apnea because adipose tissue deposition around the neck and upper airway makes the airway more prone to collapse during sleep. In turn, poor-quality sleep from untreated obstructive sleep apnea can disrupt hormones that regulate appetite and metabolism, making weight gain and obesity more likely over time. [ 11 , 91 ] 4. OSA contributes to T2DM and hypertension (two major CVD risk factors), as well as stroke, heart failure (e.g., left ventricular dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension/right sided heart failure), cardiac dysrhythmias (e.g., bradycardia, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular tachycardia), and sudden death. OSA is a leading cause of “resistant hypertension”, defined as blood pressure above goal despite three or more antihypertensive medications of different classes at maximally tolerated doses, one of which is a diuretic. [ 11 , 92 ] 5. Estimates suggest that up to 70% of patients hospitalized with coronary artery disease have OSA. Severe untreated OSA doubles the risk of future myocardial infarction. [ 11 , 92 ] 6. OSA is diagnosed by objective sleep testing, most commonly an overnight polysomnogram that measures breathing, oxygen levels, and sleep stages. In selected patients, a simplified home sleep apnea test may be used to detect breathing pauses and oxygen drops during sleep. During these sleep studies, the apnea–hypopnea index (AHI) is the average number of apneas (complete breathing pauses) and hypopneas (partial obstructions with reduced airflow and oxygen drops) that occur per hour of sleep, measured during a sleep study. Mild OSA is defined as 5–14 events per hour, moderate OSA as 15–29, and severe OSA as 30 or more events per hour. [ 11 , 93 ] 7. The STOP-Bang questionnaire is an eight-item screening tool for obstructive sleep apnea that combines four symptom questions (snoring, tiredness, observed apneas, and high blood pressure) with four objective measures: body mass index (BMI), age, neck circumference, and gender. Its cutoff points assign one risk point each for BMI >35 kg/m 2 , age >50 years, neck circumference >40 cm, and male sex, helping stratify patients into low-, intermediate-, or high-risk categories for OSA. [ 11 , 94 ] 8. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy delivers a stream of pressurized air through a mask to keep the upper airway open during sleep, preventing the repeated oxygen delivery pauses that characterize obstructive sleep apnea. This form of positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment is the most effective non-invasive option for reducing nighttime oxygen drops of OSA, improving daytime alertness, and lowering long-term health risks associated with untreated sleep apnea. Other treatments include mandibular advancement devices, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, and positional therapy. Finally, other interventions include avoidance of alcohol and sedative-hypnotics (like benzodiazepines), which relax the upper airway muscles and worsen OSA and nighttime hypoxia. [ 11 , 93 ] 9. Some obesity medications can improve OSA because even modest reductions in body weight decrease upper-airway collapsibility and reduce the frequency of oxygen delivery interruptions during sleep. More effective obesity medications have shown the ability to lower apnea severity and enhance overall sleep quality when used alongside standard sleep apnea treatments. Tirzepatide is illustrative of an obesity medication that has an FDA indication to treat moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity. Weight reduction via bariatric procedures can improve obstructive sleep apnea via reduced upper-airway collapse and decreased number of breathing interruptions during sleep. While many patients experience meaningful reductions in apnea severity after bariatric surgery, some may still require ongoing sleep-focused evaluation and treatment to achieve full symptom control. [ 11 , [95] , [96] , [97] ] 10. Addressing the dual burden of obesity and OSA significantly reduces cardiovascular strain by lowering chronic systemic inflammation and decreasing sympathetic nervous system overactivity. Effective treatment of OSA leads to clinically meaningful improvements in blood pressure control, often resolving resistant hypertension, and significantly reduces the risk of dysrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation. Ultimately, managing these interconnected conditions improves heart structure and metabolic health, providing a robust defense against long-term complications such as heart failure, myocardial infarction, and stroke. ## Obesity and cardiovascular structural changes [ 12 ] (See Table 10 and Fig. 10 )

With obesity, cardiovascular pathology is driven by the specific anatomical location of adipose tissue and its subsequent structural impact on the heart and vasculature. Epicardial Adipose Tissue (EAT) lies within the pericardial sac directly contacting the myocardium, and without a separating fascia, can direct “outside-to-inside” diffusion of inflammatory cytokines, fatty acids, and lipotoxic intermediates (e.g., ceramides, diacylglycerols) into coronary arteries and heart muscle. This local toxicity, combined with systemic volume overload, systemic inflammation, RAAS activation, and metabolic dysregulation, can contribute to left ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial steatosis (intracellular lipotoxicity), and interstitial fibrosis that stiffens the heart and disrupts electrical pathways. In addition to “outside-to-inside” damage that stimulates vascular smooth muscle hypertrophy, resulting in generalized arterial stiffness and accelerated atherosclerosis, coronary arteries may suffer a dual assault via “inside-to-outside” damage from intraluminal proinflammatory factors and atherogenic lipids that generate inflammation and plaque and result in adverse metabolic consequences such as the uncoupling of endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Thus, both the “outside-to-inside” pathogenic effects from EAT and “inside-to-outside” from atherogenic promoting circulating factors within the vascular lumen to vessel wall increase the risk for CVD. Essential principles include: • Obesity affects the heart and blood vessels not just by excess weight, but by where adipose tissue is located and how it interacts with nearby tissues. • Epicardial and perivascular adipose tissue release inflammatory signals and toxic lipids directly into the heart and coronary arteries (“outside-to-inside”), promoting cardiac hypertrophy, steatosis, and fibrosis. • In addition to potential adiposopathic effects on all arteries in patients with obesity, coronary arteries can also be damaged from the systemic complications of obesity, resulting in “inside-to-outside” pathogenic effects where inflammatory factors and atherogenic lipoproteins within the lumen of coronary arteries cross from inside the arterial lumen into the respective endothelia, leading to stiffness and accelerated atherosclerosis. Table 10 Ten things to know about obesity and cardiovascular structural changes [ 12 ]. Table 10 Key Points References 1. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) lies directly between the myocardium and visceral pericardium, with no fascial barrier. Its shared microcirculation with the coronary arteries places it in intimate structural continuity with the heart. EAT thickness is often measured via echocardiography (parasternal long axis), while volumetric quantification is done via cardiac computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. This is relevant because EAT volume is an independent predictor of coronary events, separate from body mass index. [ 12 , 98 ] 2. Paracardial adipose tissue resides outside the parietal pericardium, is supplied by non-coronary vessels, and is anatomically separated from the myocardium, preventing the direct paracrine diffusion of inflammatory or lipotoxic mediators that characterizes EAT. Both depots expand in obesity and are often grouped under the umbrella term “pericardial fat,” and their structural differences determine their distinct cardiovascular effects. EAT drives injury through two separate tracks — direct paracrine/vasocrine vascular toxicity (via shared microcirculation) and mechanical restraint on diastolic filling (via its location inside the pericardial sac). Paracardial fat, lacking shared circulation and lying outside the sac, contributes mainly as a systemic visceral-adiposity marker rather than through either of those local mechanisms. [ 12 , 99 , 100 ] 3. EAT and visceral abdominal adipose tissue arise from the same mesodermal embryonic origin, with EAT representing the visceral adipose tissue depot of the heart. These two adipose tissue depots expand in parallel, and both correlate to a higher risk of CVD. Both EAT and visceral abdominal adipose tissue are also associated with greater coronary artery calcification, underscoring their shared contribution to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. Thus, during an evaluation of body composition, an increase in visceral adipose tissue may suggest an increase in EAT. That said, unlike the white adipose tissue found in the abdomen, EAT expresses Uncoupling Protein-1 (UCP-1), giving it characteristics of brown or “beige” adipose tissue making it more metabolically active than paracardial or subcutaneous adipose tissue. The loss of this “brown” phenotype during obesity (whitening of fat cells) is a key driver of dysfunction. [ 12 , 100 ] 4. In obesity, EAT undergoes hypertrophy and becomes metabolically inflamed which may result in structurally disruptive, pro-inflammatory tissue. [ 12 , 46 ] 5. EAT can serve as the origin of inflammatory cytokines and free fatty acids that can diffuse directly into the coronary adventitia. This structural pathway accelerates atherosclerosis, endothelial dysfunction, and dysrhythmogenic remodeling. [ 12 , 100 ] 6. Obesity increases total adipose mass requiring perfusion, creating chronic volume overload. This drives left ventricular dilation and eccentric hypertrophy as the heart adapts to increased circulatory demand. [ 12 , 101 ] 7. When obesity causes hypertension, the cardiac left ventricular remodeling pattern shifts toward concentric hypertrophy. This structural change of the heart reflects the combined effects of increased pressure and volume overload. [ 12 , 102 ] 8. Excess circulating free fatty acids in obesity accumulate within cardiomyocytes, producing myocardial steatosis. This lipid infiltration and accumulation of pathogenic lipids such as ceramides (“lipotoxicity”) impairs contractile architecture and contributes to diastolic dysfunction. [ 12 , 103 ] 9. Adiposopathy is characterized by a shift toward a pro-inflammatory local and systemic immune environment, with increased inflammatory macrophages, T-lymphocytes, and mast cells. Increased adiposopathic adipokines and fewer vasculoprotective adipokines create an imbalance that promotes cardiovascular injury and increases the risk of CVD. [ 3 , 12 ] 10. Obesity cardiomyopathy reflects the combined impact of EAT, lipotoxicity, inflammatory signaling, and chronic hemodynamic load. These processes drive structural and functional myocardial changes that manifest as impaired cardiac performance, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), atherosclerotic coronary disease, cardiac dysrhythmias, and increased coronary calcium. In the development of dysrhythmias specifically, EAT can infiltrate the myocardium, separate cardiomyocytes, and create fibro-fatty disruption that interferes with electrical conduction and promotes micro-reentry circuits. Additionally, because EAT houses cardiac autonomic ganglia, local inflammation can heighten autonomic activity, further predisposing the heart to dysrhythmogenesis. [ 12 , 46 ] Fig. 10 Obesity and Cardiovascular Structural Changes. Obesity contributes to CVD not only through excess body fat but also through the specific location of adipose tissue and its direct structural effects on the heart and blood vessels. Epicardial and perivascular adipose tissue can release inflammatory signals and toxic lipids directly into the heart and coronary arteries, promoting hypertrophy, steatosis, and fibrosis through an “outside-to-inside” mechanism. At the same time, circulating inflammatory factors and atherogenic lipoproteins can injure coronary arteries from the lumen outward, creating an “inside-to-outside” assault that accelerates arterial stiffness and atherosclerosis.

## Obesity and heart failure [ 13 ] (See Table 11 and Fig. 11 )

Obesity increases cardiac output because expanded adipose mass increases whole-body metabolic demand, prompting the cardiovascular system to enlarge blood volume, boost preload and stroke volume, and activate sympathetic pathways. Although individual adipose tissue depots develop microvascular rarefaction and higher local resistance, the early systemic cardiovascular phenotype is a high-output, low-resistance state driven by metabolic demand, vasodilatory adipokines, hyperinsulinemia, and compensatory vasodilation in non-adipose vascular beds. However, over time, progressive sympathetic activation and arterial stiffening elevate systemic vascular resistance, creating a combined pressure-and-volume load that drives left ventricular hypertrophy and forms a central mechanistic link to HFpEF – with these systemic hemodynamic burdens representing a first “hit.” Excess epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) then delivers the second “hit” by mechanically constraining the heart within the pericardial space and infiltrating the myocardium with fat, impairing diastolic relaxation and amplifying the hemodynamic injury initiated by obesity. Essential principles include: • Obesity initially creates a high-output, low-resistance circulatory state because increased adipose mass raises metabolic demand, prompting expanded blood volume, greater preload, and sympathetic activation. • Chronically elevated cardiac output drives left ventricular hypertrophy and establishes a key hemodynamic link to HFpEF. • Excess epicardial adipose tissue further worsens HFpEF by mechanically constraining the heart and promoting myocardial fatty infiltration, both of which impair diastolic filling.
