Obesity raises cardiac output because the enlarged mass of adipose tissue increases the body's metabolic needs. Meeting these needs requires a greater volume of circulating blood. [ 13 , 101 , [104] , [105] , [106] ] 2. In heart failure, expanded total blood volume increases the amount of blood returning to the heart, boosts the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat, and heightens sympathetic nervous system activity. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] , [107] ] 3. A sustained increase in cardiac output creates structural strain on the heart, even at rest, to maintain adequate tissue perfusion. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] , 108 ] 4. The “first hit” in obesity-related hemodynamic change is a high-output state: expansion of both fat and lean mass increases metabolic demand and plasma volume, so cardiac output rises - largely via increased stroke volume - while systemic vascular resistance falls to normal or subnormal levels. Superimposed early is neurohormonal volume retention, with sympathetic activation and renal sodium retention driven by leptin signaling, hyperinsulinemia, obstructive sleep apnea, physical compression of the kidney by visceral and perirenal fat, and RAAS/mineralocorticoid activation. Sustained preload elevation from this chronic volume overload produces ventricular dilation with eccentric remodeling and left atrial enlargement. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] ] 5. A “second hit” arises when adipose tissue expands faster than its vascular supply, producing local hypoxia, capillary rarefaction, and a shift in secretory profile toward pro-inflammatory adipokines and away from protective ones such as adiponectin. Analogous capillary rarefaction and endothelial dysfunction are described in skeletal muscle, kidney, and myocardium, contributing to coronary microvascular dysfunction, while arterial stiffening progresses in parallel. Superimposed on pre-existing volume overload, these afterload- and fibrosis-promoting influences can shift remodeling away from a purely eccentric pattern toward a mixed or concentric geometry. The net effect is accelerated progression to diastolic dysfunction and heart failure over years to decades. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] , 109 ] 6. The persistent elevation in cardiac output often leads to thickening of the left ventricular wall. This structural change reflects the chronic hemodynamic burden placed on the heart. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] , 110 ] 7. An increase in hemodynamic burden on the heart helps explain the strong association between obesity and Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF). Additionally, accumulation of EAT around the heart restricts cardiac motion and promotes fatty infiltration of the heart muscle, impairing its ability to relax and fill properly. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] , 111 ] 8. In a ∼2 year randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 731 adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity (SUMMIT), tirzepatide significantly reduced the combined risk of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure and substantially lowered the rate of heart-failure–related events. Although cardiovascular death alone did not differ meaningfully between groups, tirzepatide overall improved clinical outcomes and patient-reported health status compared with placebo. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] , 112 ] 9. In a 52-week, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 529 adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity (STEP-HFpEF), once-weekly semaglutide produced greater improvements in symptoms, physical function, and inflammation, including larger gains in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores, 6-min walk distance, and reductions in C-reactive protein. It also led to substantially greater weight reduction than placebo, with a mean reduction of 13.3% compared with 2.6%. [ 13 , [104] , [105] , [106] , 113 ] 10. Obesity initially creates a high-output state with normal-to-low vascular resistance: the expanded fat mass raises metabolic demand, which increases blood volume, preload, and sympathetic activity. Over time, sustained sympathetic tone and arterial stiffening raise afterload, so the combined volume and pressure load produces left-ventricular hypertrophy and a central pathway to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Excess epicardial adipose tissue adds a second injury by restraining the heart within the pericardium and infiltrating the myocardium with inflammatory and fibrotic signaling, further impairing diastolic filling and worsening HFpEF.

## Obesity and cardiac dysrhythmias [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] (See Table 12 and Fig. 12 )

Obesity contributes to a wide spectrum of cardiac rhythm disturbances through its effects on cardiac structure, electrical signaling, and systemic metabolic stress. Structural and electrical remodeling in obesity creates a substrate for atrial fibrillation. Fatty infiltration of the atrial myocardium and fibrosis disrupt conduction pathways, promoting erratic electrical activity and increasing the likelihood of sustained rhythm disturbances. Atrial fibrillation risk increases progressively with increasing body mass index, reflecting the cumulative impact of excess adiposity on atrial size, pressure, inflammation, and cellular architecture. Weight reduction and incretin mimetics (e.g., GLP-1 RA based therapies) have shown promise in reversing atrial remodeling and reducing the incidence and burden of atrial fibrillation, underscoring the importance of comprehensive metabolic management in preventing obesity-related cardiac dysrhythmias. Essential principles include: • Obesity promotes a range of cardiac rhythm disturbances by altering cardiac structure, electrical signaling, and metabolic homeostasis. • Obesity-related pathogenic changes such as atrial enlargement, fatty infiltration, and fibrosis, create a potent substrate for atrial fibrillation, with risk rising steadily as BMI increases. • Among patients with obesity, weight reduction and GLP-1 RA can improve atrial remodeling and reduce atrial fibrillation burden, highlighting the value of comprehensive metabolic management in preventing obesity-related dysrhythmias. Table 12 Ten things to know about obesity and cardiac dysrhythmias [ 1 , 14 , 15 ]. Table 12 Key Points References 1. Increasing adiposity alters cardiac structure, autonomic tone, and metabolic milieu in ways that collectively favor the development and maintenance of cardiac dysrhythmias. Beyond its association with hypertension, diabetes, and sleep apnea, obesity is an independent risk factor for both atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias, as well as sudden cardiac death. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 2. Excess adiposity leads to left atrial enlargement, increased wall stress, and cellular changes that create a vulnerable substrate for atrial fibrillation. Structural and electrical remodeling in obesity creates a substrate for atrial fibrillation, with atrial dilation, myocyte hypertrophy, and altered ion channel expression all contributing to dysrhythmia susceptibility. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 3. Fatty infiltration of the atrial myocardium and fibrosis disrupt conduction pathways, creating regions of slow and heterogeneous conduction that promote reentry. Expansion of epicardial adipose tissue adjacent to atrial tissue is strongly linked to atrial fibrillation burden, likely through local inflammatory and fibrotic signaling. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 4. Atrial fibrillation risk increases progressively with body mass index, with higher classes of obesity associated with a markedly greater incidence of atrial fibrillation. This gradient suggests that both total adiposity and central adipose tissue distribution contribute to atrial electrical instability, making weight management a key upstream prevention strategy. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 5. Obesity is also associated with increased risk of ventricular dysrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, potentially mediated by left ventricular hypertrophy, fibrosis, and ischemia. Prolongation of repolarization, altered autonomic balance, and sleep apnea- related hypoxia may further destabilize ventricular electrophysiology in people with obesity. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 6. Weight reduction reduces the incidence and burden of atrial fibrillation, partly by reversing atrial enlargement and improving hemodynamics. Sustained reductions in adiposity also improve blood pressure, glycemic control, and sleep apnea, which collectively lower the overall pro-dysrhythmic load. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 7. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) increase heart rate primarily by enhancing sympathetic activity and reducing parasympathetic (vagal) tone at the sinus node, leading to modest sinus tachycardia in many patients. Despite this chronotropic effect, emerging data suggest that GLP-1 RAs may lower atrial fibrillation- related events in people with obesity, likely through weight reduction, reduced inflammation, and favorable atrial remodeling. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 8. Real-world and observational data in populations with obesity and atrial fibrillation indicate fewer atrial fibrillation–related hospitalizations, cardioversions, and ablation procedures among GLP-1 RA users, supporting a net antidysrhythmic effect despite a small increase in resting heart rate. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 9. Sympathomimetic agents such as phentermine can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and they may increase the risk of palpitations, sinus tachycardia, and, in susceptible patients, atrial or ventricular dysrhythmias. In contrast, agents without direct sympathomimetic effects, such as orlistat, are generally considered to have a neutral or favorable profile regarding cardiac rhythm, with dysrhythmia risk largely mediated indirectly through weight reduction and metabolic improvement. [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] 10. As previously noted above, GLP-1 RA can modestly increase heart rate, but generally decrease blood pressure. Similarly, naltrexone/bupropion and phentermine/topiramate may also modestly increase heart rate. Because weight reduction typically lowers blood pressure and heart rate compared to baseline in both treatment and placebo groups, the net, placebo-adjusted signal is the meaningful metric when interpreting cardiovascular effects of obesity medications. Thus, in patients with atrial fibrillation or elevated dysrhythmia risk, obesity medication choice should balance the data on the potential for dysrhythmia and prescribing information cautions, balanced against the potential cardiometabolic benefits of sustained weight reduction, improved hemodynamics, and better control of cardiometabolic disease. Obesity increases the risk of cardiac rhythm disturbances by altering heart structure, disrupting electrical signaling, and creating metabolic stress that destabilizes normal conduction. These changes—including atrial enlargement, fatty infiltration, and fibrosis—form a potent substrate for atrial fibrillation, with risk rising steadily as body mass increases. Weight reduction and therapies such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists can reverse aspects of atrial remodeling and reduce atrial fibrillation burden, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive metabolic management.

## Obesity paradox and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 8 ] (See Table 13 and Fig. 13 )

An apparent “obesity paradox” arises when individuals with higher body weight appear to experience better health outcomes than those with lower body weight. However, this pattern becomes less paradoxical when the clinical context and physiological role of body fat are considered. Many people at low body weight have serious underlying conditions (e.g., cancer, chronic infections, advanced pulmonary disease, malnutrition, or severe cardiovascular disease) that drive unintentional weight reduction. Behaviors like cigarette smoking can also reduce body weight. It is expected, and not “paradoxical,” that individuals who are underweight due to life-threatening illness or cigarette smoking have poorer outcomes than individuals with overweight or obesity who do not have these chronic illnesses. Even in the absence of chronic disease, elevated mortality among the lowest-weight individuals may stem from frailty, sarcopenia, and reduced metabolic reserves. Higher-weight individuals may possess greater nutritional and energy stores, which can be beneficial during episodes of acute severe illness. Because body mass index (BMI) cannot distinguish between fat mass and lean mass, those classified as having “normal” weight may actually have sarcopenia, which is a high health-risk state marked by a substantial loss of muscle mass, potentially accompanied by loss of muscle function. In this case, any apparent survival advantage attributed to obesity may better reflect the increased mortality associated with low muscle mass in leaner patients, rather than a true protective effect of excess adiposity. Essential principles include: • The so called “obesity paradox” largely reflects the poor health outcomes in individuals with low body weight due to underlying illness, smoking, frailty, or sarcopenia rather than any true protective effect of excess adiposity. This creates selection bias leading to the illusion of an effect if not appropriately accounted for in the statistical methods [ [16] , [17] , [18] ]. • Higher-weight individuals often have greater metabolic and nutritional reserves, which can be advantageous during acute illness, while BMI fails to distinguish between healthy lean mass and high-risk muscle loss in people labeled as “normal weight.” • Individuals with obesity who are physically fit generally have better prognoses than unfit individuals of normal weight, indicating that degree of physical fitness, rather than the amount of body fat, is the primary driver of survival. Table 13 Ten things to know about the obesity paradox and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 8 ]. Table 13 Key Points References 1. Anatomic Obesity Paradox: Peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) can be metabolically “protective” via healthy adipocyte proliferation during times of excess energy (i.e., when caloric gastrointestinal absorption from food exceeds energy expenditure). SAT can become pathogenic when the ability to expand is limited (i.e., via genetics or concomitant medications), resulting in adipocyte hypertrophy, energy overflow, and ectopic fat deposition, as reflected by the increase in visceral adiposity and epicardial adipose tissue and fatty infiltration of other body organs. [ 8 , 45 ] 2. Physiologic Obesity Paradox: Individuals with obesity vary in their susceptibility to the development of cardiometabolic disease and CVD risk factors, giving rise to phenotypes such as “obesity without complications,” which has many other analogous terms. The prevalence of obesity without complication is directly dependent on the intensity of the diagnosis of complications and whether diagnoses are inclusive of all “sick fat disease” (adiposopathic) and “fat mass disease” complications. Conversely, individuals without obesity or overweight may exhibit cardiometabolic disease due to adiposopathy or dysfunction in other organ systems. [ 8 , 116 ] 3. Demographic Paradox (Age, Sex, and Race) : Age, sex, and race influence body fat distribution and cardiometabolic risk, creating paradoxical patterns where similar BMI values do not translate to similar cardiometabolic outcomes. For example, among those with overweight or obesity, women, and Black individuals may have lower visceral adipose tissue, while older individuals and those of Asian descent may have higher visceral adipose tissue for comparable body weight. [ 8 , 55 ] 4. Therapeutic Obesity Paradox: Although increase in body fat generally promotes type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), thiazolidinediones represent a drug treatment for T2DM that increases the proliferation and differentiation of functional fat cells. This “paradoxically” increases adipocyte number and increases fat mass despite better achieving improved glucose control. Conversely, some drugs associated with reduced fat mass, such as some human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antiretroviral regimens (e.g., older protease inhibitors including indinavir, lopinavir, ritonavir), may worsen metabolic disease by impairing adipocyte function, generating relative loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue, and increasing the relative proportion of visceral adipose tissue. [ 8 , 117 , 118 ] 5. Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) Outcomes Obesity Paradox: Patients with overweight or obesity may demonstrate better survival after cardiovascular events, potentially due to greater metabolic reserve, earlier diagnosis due to management of cardiovascular disease risk factors, or more aggressive preventive therapy. Additionally, evidence suggests that the CVD outcome paradox is largely explained by cardiorespiratory fitness, as the apparent survival advantage of higher body mass index often disappears when studies adjust for aerobic capacity. This suggests that individuals with obesity who are physically fit generally have better prognoses than unfit individuals of normal weight, indicating that degree of fitness, rather than the amount of body fat, is the primary driver of survival. [ 8 , 119 ] 6. Stroke Obesity Paradox: Although obesity increases stroke risk, individuals with higher body weight may experience better post-stroke outcomes due to greater nutritional reserve and fewer catabolic comorbidities. Patients who are at low weight may have poorer outcomes because of frailty, chronic illness, or smoking-related diseases, with cigarette smoking contributing to both reduced body weight and poorer outcomes from stroke. [ 8 , 120 ] 7. Acute Respiratory Distress and Critical Illness Obesity Paradox: Patients with obesity may have improved survival in acute respiratory distress syndromes and critical illness, possibly due to enhanced energy reserves. In contrast, underweight individuals often have chronic lung disease, malnutrition, or other chronic conditions that worsen respiratory and health outcomes after an acute illness. [ 8 , 121 ] 8. Kidney Disease Obesity Paradox: In chronic kidney disease, higher BMI is associated with lower mortality. This may reflect better nutritional status, improved hemodynamic stability, or sequestration of uremic toxins within adipose tissue. [ 8 , 122 ] 9. Therapeutic Approach Obesity Paradox: It is usually not productive, and may be counterproductive, to assign “blame” to patients with adverse health outcomes as the result of obesity. As such, some might believe it “paradoxical” that accountability is a mainstay component of most behavior modification interventions. However, blame focuses on fault and shame, while accountability focuses on metrics to achieve better health and without judgment. Effective obesity management requires balancing accountability with empathy, avoiding blame while encouraging shared decision-making and behavior tracking. Overemphasizing guilt undermines engagement, whereas structured accountability supports sustainable change. [ 8 , 123 ] 10. Cardiovascular Frequency and Severity Obesity Paradox : Cigarette smoking is disproportionately represented among ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) relative to non-STEMI presentations, reflecting acute thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery. Smoking is also associated with worse risk-adjusted long-term mortality after myocardial infarction (MI). Smokers tend to have lower BMI than non-smokers and leaner MI cohorts are therefore enriched for smoking-driven STEMI with intrinsically worse prognosis. Thus, while obesity may increase the risk of both STEMI and NSTEMI, the confounding of infarct type and etiology by adiposity means the apparently more favorable outcomes in patients with obesity cannot be attributed to increased body fat itself. [ 8 , 124 ] Fig. 13 Obesity, “Obesity Paradox,” and Cardiovascular Disease. The so-called “obesity paradox” is largely explained by the poor outcomes seen in people with low body weight due to underlying illness, smoking, frailty, or loss of muscle mass, rather than any true protective effect of excess body fat. Higher-weight individuals may fare better during acute illness because they often have greater metabolic and nutritional reserves, while body mass index cannot distinguish between healthy lean mass and high-risk sarcopenia in those labeled as “normal weight.” Overall, physical fitness—not body fat—is the strongest predictor of survival, with fit individuals who have obesity generally experiencing better outcomes than unfit individuals of lower weight.

## Obesity, age, sex, race, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ [19] , [20] , [21] , [22] , [23] ] (See Table 14 and Fig. 14 )

Across the lifespan, cardiometabolic and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk is shaped by how excess adiposity interacts with biology, sex-specific physiology, and social determinants of health: older adults face sarcopenic obesity and the cumulative effects of long-standing adiposopathic endocrine and immune dysfunction; central “apple-shaped” body fat distribution, more common in males, promotes visceral-driven insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, whereas “pear-shaped” gluteofemoral body fat deposition is less pathogenic. Female-specific conditions - including polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), gestational diabetes, and the menopausal decline in estrogen - intensify insulin resistance, increased visceral adiposity, vascular dysfunction, and ultimately CVD risk. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) disproportionately affects women, especially postmenopausal women with obesity-related inflammation. Racial and ethnic differences further modify risk. Beyond obesity, Black individuals experience higher burdens of hypertension, arterial stiffness, and chronic stress-related neurohormonal activation. Those of Asian descent, particularly South Asians, often develop increased visceral adiposity and metabolic disease at lower BMI thresholds. Finally, many minority populations face structural inequities that heighten exposure to obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Together, these factors illustrate how adiposity, metabolic vulnerability, sex-specific physiology, and social context converge to drive disparities in CVD outcomes. Essential principles include: • Excess adiposity influences cardiometabolic and cardiovascular risk differently across the lifespan, shaped by age-related changes such as sarcopenic obesity, sex-specific physiology, and fat-distribution patterns that drive varying degrees of metabolic dysfunction. • Women face additional risk from PMOS, gestational diabetes, menopause-related estrogen loss, and a heightened susceptibility to HFpEF, while racial and ethnic groups experience distinct vulnerabilities, including higher hypertension and arterial stiffness in Black individuals and increased visceral adiposity at lower BMI thresholds in many Asian populations. • Structural inequities further amplify these risks, demonstrating how biology, sex, adiposity, and social context intersect to produce disparities in cardiovascular outcomes. ## Obesity and cardiovascular diagnostic procedures (See Table 15 , Fig. 15 , and Chart 1 )

Obesity can complicate cardiovascular evaluation and requires specific adjustments in risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and procedural planning. Many standard risk calculators do not account for increased adiposity, perhaps making Body Mass Index (BMI) inclusive tools such as the Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular disease EVENTS (PREVENT) model or QResearch (QRISK) algorithms more appropriate. Basic diagnostic cardiovascular tests are also vulnerable to error, including blood pressure cuff-size error from incorrect cuff sizing and electrocardiogram (ECG) voltage attenuation. Excess soft tissue can degrade image quality on echocardiogram (potentially requiring ultrasound enhancing agents) or Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT). Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography (CCTA), and coronary angiography frequently require higher radiation doses during imaging. Obesity may also suppress B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) levels, masking acute heart failure. Finally, anatomical challenges in obesity often favor transradial over transfemoral catheterization to reduce the heightened bleeding risk associated with femoral access. Essential principles include: • Obesity complicates cardiovascular evaluation by requiring adjustments to risk assessment tools, physical examination techniques, and imaging strategies. • Excess adiposity can distort blood pressure readings, attenuate ECG signals, degrade SPECT and echocardiographic image quality, and suppress BNP levels. • Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography (CCTA), and coronary angiography frequently require higher radiation doses during imaging of patients with obesity. • Procedurally, anatomical considerations often make transradial catheterization safer than transfemoral access due to the increased bleeding risk associated with femoral approaches in individuals with obesity. Table 15 Ten things to know about obesity and cardiovascular diagnostic procedures [ 125 ]. Table 15 Key Points References 1. Most standard cardiovascular risk calculators do not incorporate body mass index (BMI) or body composition, despite the well-established cardiometabolic impact of excess adiposity. The non-laboratory version of Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular disease EVENTS (PREVENT), QResearch (QRISK2, QRISK3, and QRISK-lifetime calculator), and the non-lipid version of the Framingham Risk Score (where BMI is used instead of total cholesterol and high density lipoprotein cholesterol) are exceptions that include BMI to better reflect obesity-related CVD risk. [ [125] , [126] , [127] ] 2. Incorrect cuff selection is the most frequent blood pressure-related diagnostic error in people with obesity. Using a standard-sized cuff on a large arm produces cuff size error, which depending on the cited reference/source, may result in spuriously high readings that can exceed the true value by (depending on the reference) as much as ∼5–20 mmHg. This can lead to false diagnoses of hypertension and unnecessary treatment. Additionally, the conical arm shape common in severe obesity can prevent oscillometric devices from obtaining reliable measurements. These challenges underscore the importance of proper cuff sizing and, when non-invasive methods remain inaccurate, consideration of invasive arterial monitoring. [ 58 , 60 , 61 , 125 , 128 ] 3. Obesity can alter electrocardiographic electrical signals through increased chest wall mass, axis shifts, and low-voltage patterns (e.g., left axis deviation, T-wave flattening, low QRS voltage, prolonged QTc interval, ST depression, and false-positive criteria for inferior myocardial infarction). Obesity most commonly causes false-negative ECG detection of left ventricular hypertrophy via voltage attenuation (worsened, not offset, by an accompanying leftward axis shift), and separately reduces the accuracy of ECG-based coronary artery disease testing through mechanisms like limited exercise tolerance and baseline ST-T abnormalities rather than the same voltage/axis effect. [ 1 , 125 , 129 ] 4. Excessive body weight often limits a patient's ability to perform exercise stress testing due to early fatigue, breathlessness, and mechanical constraints, requiring pharmacologic stress testing instead. Common pharmacologic stress testing agents include regadenoson, adenosine, dipyridamole, or dobutamine, which are typically paired with nuclear myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) or cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). However, Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) often performes poorly in obesity because soft-tissue attenuation - particularly from breast or diaphragmatic fat – can obscure the signal. This artifact often produces apparent ‘fixed defects’ that mimic prior infarction or ischemia, prompting avoidable invasive angiography. For this reason, many diagnostic pathways favor PET or coronary CT angiography (CCTA) in individuals with obesity, as these modalities offer superior attenuation correction and more reliable image quality. [ 1 , 86 , 125 ] 5. Excess body weight can exceed the table or gantry limits of common imaging modalities, including dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which often cap at 350–450 pounds, depending on the scanner. Although newer systems may accommodate higher weights, image quality can still be compromised by increased tissue thickness. Obesity is also closely associated with atrial fibrillation and elevated resting heart rates. Because coronary CT angiography (CCTA) and cardiac MRI rely on electrocardiographic (ECG) gating to capture motion-free images, dysrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation or tachycardia significantly hinder image acquisition. Achieving adequate image quality may require aggressive beta-blockade for rate control, which introduces additional risk in patients with reactive airway disease - a condition frequently seen alongside obesity. [ 86 , 125 ] 6. Increased soft-tissue mass in obesity attenuates ultrasound waves, making cardiac structures harder to visualize and reducing the reliability of echocardiographic evaluation, especially for valvular assessment and diastolic function. Ultrasound Enhancing Agents (UEAs), such as perflutren lipid microspheres or sulfur hexafluoride lipid-type A microspheres, are guideline-recommended for patients with obesity who have suboptimal acoustic windows to improve endocardial border definition. The threshold for using UEAs should be low, as they are often essential for rescuing non-diagnostic studies and ensuring accurate measurement of left ventricular ejection fraction. [ 125 , 130 ] 7. Perivascular Fat Attenuation Index (FAI) provides a noninvasive CT-based biomarker of coronary inflammation. In many clinical practices, Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) scoring is a more common CT-based assessment that correlates not only with coronary plaque burden but also is associated with epicardial adipose tissue volume. Increased abdominal visceral adiposity similarly tracks with higher CAC scores, reflecting shared pathophysiologic pathways (e.g., adiposopathy, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, as well as immunopathies and endocrinopathies such as systemic inflammation and oxidative stress). CAC is reported in Agatston scores that quantify calcified plaque in heart arteries: • 0: No calcified plaque, unless accompanied by diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking, or strong family history of cardiovascular disease, suggests very low risk for major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) for the subsequent 5 or more years • 1 – 10: Minimal plaque, low MACE risk • 11 – 100: Mild plaque, moderate MACE risk • 101 – 400: Moderate plaque, moderately high risk for MACE • Over 400: Extensive plaque, high risk for MACE If only evaluated with traditional CVD risk factors via common CVD risk assessment tools, the risk for atherosclerotic CVD may be underestimated. Additionally, increased CAC scores correlate better with increased visceral adiposity, rather than BMI. Once statin therapy is initiated, CAC scores may worsen in some patients such that the value of serial CAC scores in patients with elevated CAC scores at baseline treated with statins is uncertain. [ 125 , 131 , 132 ] 8. CT coronary angiography and calcium scoring often require higher radiation doses in individuals with larger BMI to maintain adequate image quality. Increased adipose tissue can also necessitate higher contrast volumes. [ 1 , 125 , 133 ] 9. Obesity can make vascular access, catheter navigation, and fluoroscopic imaging more difficult, often lengthening procedures and raising the likelihood of complications. In patients with increased adiposity, transradial access (TRA) is favored over transfemoral access (TFA) because femoral access carries a significantly higher risk of retroperitoneal bleeding and hematoma. The femoral head - an essential anatomical landmark - is harder to palpate or visualize under fluoroscopy in patients with obesity, and achieving adequate post-procedural compression is more challenging. For these reasons, TRA is generally considered the safer and more dependable approach in individuals with obesity. [ 125 , 134 ] 10. Obesity lowers circulating levels of B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) and N-terminal pro–B-type Natriuretic Peptide (NT-proBNP) through a combination of increased clearance and reduced myocardial secretion. This suppression can mask even acute heart failure (HF), leading clinicians to miss the diagnosis when relying on standard BNP cut-points. Since BNP remains a central biomarker for identifying HF, diagnostic strategies in patients with obesity should consider lower BNP thresholds to avoid false reassurance and delayed recognition of cardiac decompensation. [ 125 , 135 , 136 ] Fig. 15 Obesity and Cardiovascular Diagnostic Procedures. Obesity complicates cardiovascular evaluation by requiring adjustments to risk-prediction tools, physical examination techniques, and imaging approaches. Excess adiposity can distort blood pressure readings, reduce electrocardiogram signal strength, impair the quality of nuclear and ultrasound imaging, suppress natriuretic peptide levels, and necessitate higher radiation doses or alternative modalities such as positron emission tomography or coronary computed tomography angiography. Procedurally, anatomical considerations often make transradial catheterization safer than transfemoral access because obesity increases bleeding risk with femoral approaches. Chart 1 Cardiac Diagnostic Testing. Cardiac diagnostic testing in patients with obesity often reveals sinus tachycardia, left ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, myocardial perfusion abnormalities, and increased coronary calcification. Across electrocardiogram, echocardiography, ambulatory monitoring, nuclear imaging, computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), and catheterization, excess adiposity contributes to technical challenges such as poor acoustic windows, soft-tissue attenuation, motion artifact, vascular access difficulty, and machine weight or gantry limits. Despite these constraints, advanced modalities like positron emission tomography (PET) and CMR maintain high accuracy, though they frequently require pharmacologic stress agents and careful consideration of equipment limitations. ## Obesity, nutrition therapy, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 24 ] (See Table 16 , Figs. 16a , 16b , and Chart 2 )

Medical nutrition therapy is most effective when it provides clear, evidence-based guidance that patients can sustain long term. Multiple dietary patterns have demonstrated benefits for obesity and CVD risk reduction. Structured low-calorie and very low-calorie diets can produce clinically meaningful short-term improvements in weight and cardiometabolic markers, while fat-restricted and low-carbohydrate approaches - when focused on nutrient-dense, minimally processed foods - also improve key CVD risk factors. Robust trials support the cardioprotective effects of the Mediterranean diet, the “Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension” (DASH), and plant-based vegetarian and vegan patterns similarly reduce atherogenic lipids and improve metabolic health. Chart 2 provides an overview of some sentinel dietary patterns and their effects on CVD. Core principles for patients with obesity emphasize limiting ultra-processed, energy-dense foods and prioritizing whole, fiber-rich, nutrient-dense options. For individuals treated with GLP-1 RA, the nutritional focus shifts from further caloric restriction to ensuring adequate hydration, sufficient micronutrient and macronutrient intake, and adequate protein to help preserve lean body mass. Guidance regarding adequate hydration is also critical, given that reduced food intake, nausea, vomiting, and diminished thirst may increase the risk of dehydration and acute kidney injury. Essential principles include: • Medical nutrition therapy is most effective when it offers sustainable, evidence-based dietary guidance, with multiple eating patterns ranging from low-calorie plans to Mediterranean, DASH, and plant-based diets demonstrating benefits for weight and cardiovascular risk reduction. • Core principles emphasize limiting ultra-processed, energy-dense foods while prioritizing whole, fiber-rich, nutrient-dense options that improve cardiometabolic health. • For individuals using GLP-1 RA, the focus shifts toward maintaining adequate hydration, ensuring sufficient macro- and micronutrient intake, and consuming enough protein to preserve lean mass, given their increased vulnerability to dehydration and related complications. Table 16 Ten things to know about obesity, nutrition therapy, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 24 ]. Table 16 Key Points References 1. Medical nutrition therapy is most effective when dietary interventions are grounded in evidence and delivered with clear quantitative and qualitative guidance. Approaches that support long-term adherence consistently yield better outcomes in obesity and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk reduction. [ 24 , 137 ] 2. Low-calorie diets, typically providing 1200–1800 kcal per day, offer a structured reduction in energy intake to support clinically meaningful weight reduction. Very low-calorie diets (VLCDs), generally defined as <800 kcal per day, require close medical supervision due to their intensity but have demonstrated short-term improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors. Among adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, VLCD therapy can produce short-term and rapid reductions in body weight, blood glucose, blood pressure, and blood atherogenic lipids. [ 24 , 138 ] 3. Fat-restricted dietary patterns, which typically limit fat intake to 10–30% of total daily calories, can facilitate weight reduction and improve cardiometabolic risk when paired with nutrient-dense food choices. A comprehensive umbrella review of randomized trials found that reducing saturated fat intake - an essential component of fat-restricted approaches - significantly lowered CVD events. [ 24 , 139 ] 4. Low-carbohydrate dietary patterns generally limit carbohydrate intake to 50–150 g per day, with very low-carbohydrate diets restricting intake to <50 g per day. In a meta-analysis of 21 randomized controlled trials involving adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, low-carbohydrate ketogenic diets produced significantly greater improvements in key cardiovascular risk factors than non-ketogenic comparators, including reductions in body weight, body mass index, waist circumference, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and triglyceride levels, alongside increases in high density lipoprotein cholesterol levels. These diets emphasize minimizing refined and ultra-processed foods, high-glycemic carbohydrates, and trans fats. For some individuals, nutritional ketosis may also reduce hunger and facilitate sustained caloric reduction. [ 24 , 141 ] 5. The Mediterranean dietary pattern emphasizes extra-virgin olive oil, vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds, seafood, fermented dairy, poultry, and eggs. It limits red and processed meats as well as ultra-processed carbohydrates, fostering a nutrient-dense, cardioprotective eating pattern. In the Prevención con Dieta Mediterránea (PREDIMED) randomized controlled trial, adherence to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with either extra-virgin olive oil or nuts significantly reduced major cardiovascular events compared with a low-fat control diet, establishing this approach as one of the most robustly supported dietary strategies for CVD prevention. Of note, PREDIMED was retracted and republished in 2018 following identification of randomization irregularities, with the primary finding preserved. [ 24 , 142 , 148 ] 6. The DASH dietary pattern emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, lean proteins, nuts, seeds, legumes, and foods naturally rich in potassium, calcium, and magnesium. It limits high-sodium foods, excessive total fat, cholesterol-dense items, red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, and added sugars. In a secondary analysis of the DASH-Sodium randomized controlled trial, the DASH diet significantly lowered estimated 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk compared with a typical American diet, with even greater reductions when combined with sodium restriction. [ 24 , 143 ] 7. Vegetarian dietary patterns center on plant-based foods - including vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, seeds, and nuts - while limiting or excluding meat. Vegan diets extend this approach by eliminating all animal products and relying entirely on plant-derived nutrition. In a meta-analysis of 20 randomized clinical trials, vegetarian diets produced significant improvements in major cardiometabolic risk factors among adults with or at high risk for cardiovascular disease, including reductions in LDL cholesterol, hemoglobin A1c, and body weight. These findings support the cardioprotective potential of vegetarian eating patterns. A caveat is that beyond the absence of meat, it is the nutritional quality of the diet that most contributes to reduced CVD risk, a benefit negated if the diet consists of calorie dense, ultra-processed foods, high in refined starch and sugar, and resulting in obesity and major CVD risk factors such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. [ 24 , 144 ] 8. Both ultra-processed carbohydrates and saturated fats increase cardiovascular disease risk when consumed in excess. Exchanging one for the other on an isocaloric basis does not meaningfully improve cardiovascular outcomes. [ 24 , 145 ] 9. Dietary principles of healthful nutrition in patients with obesity include limiting ultra-processed, energy-dense, and low-nutrient foods such as sugary drinks, ultra-processed meats, trans fats, excess sodium, alcohol, and simple sugars. Nutrient rich options are encouraged and include minimally processed foods and marine oily fish, nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains, high-fiber carbohydrates, and no-sugar-added dairy, with a focus on foods that support cardiometabolic health. [ 24 , 146 ] 10. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) are indicated for weight reduction, and in some cases, to reduce CVD events. In most patients with obesity who are treated with GLP-1 RA, the primary goal of nutritional therapy shifts away from guidance regarding weight reduction through additional caloric restriction. Instead, the emphasis switches to healthful nutritional intake of nutrient-dense foods that provide sufficient vitamins, minerals, and macronutrients. Adequate protein consumption helps preserve lean body mass, including skeletal muscle. As importantly, adequate hydration is necessary to support overall metabolic and renal health because reduced food intake can significantly decrease water consumption from food sources. This, combined with common side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and diminished thirst, may increase the risk of dehydration and acute kidney injury in patients treated with GLP-1 RA. ## Obesity, physical activity, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 24 ] (See Table 17 and Fig. 17 )

Regular physical activity improves cardiovascular health through several interconnected mechanisms: it reduces total body fat and visceral adipose tissue while preserving lean muscle, improves harmful endocrine and immune disturbances associated with excess adiposity, and strengthens metabolic, musculoskeletal, heart, lung, cognitive, mental, and sexual health. These whole-body benefits enhance functional capacity and resilience against cardiometabolic disease, and higher levels of cardiorespiratory fitness are strongly associated with lower mortality even when body weight does not change. Physical activity also helps prevent weight gain and weight regain, while resistance training preserves muscle mass, muscle function, and resting metabolic rate, all which protect against insulin resistance and unhealthy blood lipid patterns. Because prolonged sitting and inactivity independently increase cardiovascular risk, increasing total daily movement and interrupting long periods of inactivity through leisure activity and everyday movement is essential. Sustainable exercise programs follow principles that address frequency, intensity, duration, type, and enjoyment, and individuals with excess adiposity or existing cardiovascular risk should undergo appropriate medical evaluation before beginning a demanding exercise plan. Tracking activity through logs, wearable devices, or periodic body composition measurements supports adherence and highlights early improvements relevant to cardiovascular prevention. Professional guidelines recommend 150–300 min of moderate-intensity dynamic activity per week or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week, along with resistance training at least twice weekly, and they also encourage step goals beginning at a minimum of 5000 steps per day and progressing toward 10,000 or more steps per day to promote accessible and scalable cardiovascular protection. Essential principles include: • Regular physical activity improves cardiovascular health by reducing excess adiposity, preserving lean mass, correcting endocrine and immune disturbances, and strengthening metabolic, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, pulmonary, and cognitive systems. • Physical exercise benefits include enhanced functional capacity and reduced cardiometabolic risk, with higher cardiorespiratory fitness linked to lower mortality regardless of weight change, while minimizing sedentary time and incorporating resistance training further protect against insulin resistance and adverse lipid patterns. • Sustainable programs emphasize individualized frequency, intensity, duration, and enjoyment, supported by activity tracking, and align with guidelines recommending 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous aerobic activity weekly, plus twice-weekly resistance training, with an alternative of step goals progressing from 5000 toward 10,000 or more per day. Routine physical activity may improve body composition by reducing overall adiposity, reducing visceral adiposity, and preserving lean mass. These improvements directly support cardiovascular health by lowering cardiometabolic risk factors that drive atherosclerotic disease. [ 24 , 167 ] 2. Routine physical activity may improve adiposopathic endocrine and immune body processes, reducing inflammatory and hormonal disturbances associated with obesity. This reduction in adiposopathy is critical for cardiovascular disease prevention because chronic inflammation accelerates vascular injury. Routine physical activity may also favorably affect adipose tissue and muscle interactions and crosstalk (i.e., adipo-myokine profile). [ 24 , 168 ] 3. Physical activity supports metabolic, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, pulmonary, mental, sexual, and cognitive health. Together, these multisystem benefits lessen cardiovascular disease burden by enhancing functional capacity and strengthening cardiometabolic resilience. Moreover, higher cardiorespiratory fitness independently predicts lower mortality, often irrespective of weight change. Therefore, when regular physical activity improves a patient's fitness, it confers meaningful health benefits even in the absence of weight reduction – which can be an important patient motivator. [ 24 , 169 ] 4. While dynamic training may promote weight reduction, physical exercise is especially beneficial in preventing weight gain or weight regain. Stabilizing weight trajectories is essential for cardiovascular disease prevention because progressive increased adiposity worsens cardiometabolic risk. [ 24 , 101 ] 5. Resistance training may improve body composition, prevent muscle loss during weight reduction, and increase resting energy expenditure. Preserving muscle mass and function contributes to cardiovascular health because sarcopenia and reduced metabolic rate contribute to insulin resistance and dyslipidemia. [ 24 , 170 ] 6. Prolonged physical inactivity is an independent risk factor for CVD. In addition to structured and scheduled physical exercise, increased energy expenditure can be achieved via increased leisure-time physical activity and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). Higher total daily movement and breaking up prolonged periods of physical inactivity reduces CVD risk. [ 24 , 171 ] 7. A common physical exercise prescription (FITTE) includes frequency, intensity, time, type, and enjoyment. Using FITTE principles ensures sustainable activity patterns that meaningfully reduce cardiovascular disease risk over time. Prior to implementing any rigorous physical exercise program, individuals with obesity and existing CVD risk factors, should undergo an evaluation of overall health and potential risk, especially from a cardiopulmonary and musculoskeletal standpoint. [ 24 , 172 ] 8. Tracking physical activity can be done through activity logs, wearable devices, and periodic body composition measurements using reliable techniques. Monitoring progress reinforces adherence and allows early identification of cardiometabolic improvements relevant to cardiovascular disease prevention. [ 24 , 173 ] 9. The Obesity Medicine Association (OMA) recommends 150–300 min or more of moderate-intensity dynamic activity per week or 75–150 min or more of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week, plus resistance training at least twice weekly. These targets align with cardiovascular disease prevention guidelines and ensure adequate stimulus for cardiometabolic benefit. Where the OMA differs is the specified inclusion of at least 5000 steps per day, progressing toward 10,000 or more steps per day to meet dynamic training goals. Step-based targets are particularly valuable for cardiovascular disease prevention because they increase daily movement in accessible, scalable ways. [ 24 , 174 ] 10. Obesity and physical inactivity act synergistically to worsen insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and systemic inflammation, amplifying the risk of cardiovascular disease. Regular physical activity—whether structured exercise, NEAT, or step-based movement—improves endothelial function, autonomic balance, and myocardial efficiency, thereby enhancing vascular health and reducing cardiac workload. Because these physiologic adaptations accumulate over time, sustained long-term adherence to physical activity is one of the strongest predictors of reduced cardiovascular disease morbidity and mortality. ## Obesity, behavioral modification, eating disorders, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 25 ] (See Table 18 and Fig. 18 )

Eating and activity patterns in individuals with overweight or obesity arise from a complex interplay of genetic, physiologic, psychological, sensory, and environmental forces that strongly promote weight gain, weakly defend against weight reduction, and accelerate cardiovascular disease (CVD) through both fat-mass related cardiac strain and adiposopathic cardiometabolic risk. Sensory cues, stress, sleep loss, stigma, emotions, socioeconomic barriers, medications, psychiatric conditions, and reward pathways can intensify overeating and undermine adherence to heart-healthy nutrition, while eating disorders further worsen metabolic parameters relevant to CVD prevention and treatment. Physical inactivity, driven by medical conditions, immobility, fatigue, disinterest, or sedentary environments, exacerbates CVD by impairing fitness, worsening cardiometabolic risk factors, and promoting increased visceral adiposity. Behavioral contributors to weight gain, including perceived time scarcity and inherited tendencies toward higher energy intake or lower expenditure, can derail CVD management unless addressed through tailored, supportive interventions. Effective behavior therapy relies on structured strategies such as education, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, goal setting, self-monitoring, and social support, and may be enhanced by pharmacotherapy or metabolic treatments that reduce intrusive food thoughts. While technologies and supportive environments can help motivated patients adopt healthier behaviors, meaningful CVD risk reduction ultimately requires readiness for change and sustained engagement with evidence-based treatments, reinforced through ongoing monitoring, clinical follow-up, and social reinforcement. Essential principles include: • Eating and activity patterns in individuals with overweight or obesity reflect a complex mix of biological, psychological, and environmental forces that promote weight gain, hinder attainment of healthy body weight, and heighten CVD risk through both excess fat mass and adiposopathic metabolic dysfunction. • Stressors such as sensory cues, sleep loss, stigma, psychiatric conditions, medications, socioeconomic barriers, and physical inactivity further intensify overeating, impair fitness, worsen cardiometabolic markers, and contribute to increased visceral adiposity. • Effective CVD risk reduction requires tailored behavioral strategies—education, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, goal setting, self-monitoring, and social support—potentially augmented by pharmacotherapy, along with sustained readiness for change and ongoing clinical reinforcement. Eating behavior in individuals with overweight or obesity often reflects an imbalance of genetic, physiologic, psychologic, and environmental forces that strongly promote weight gain and weakly resist weight reduction - an imbalance analogous to the strong physiologic symptoms (e.g., tachycardia, diaphoresis, diminished mental status) of hypoglycemia versus the often weak or absent signals of hyperglycemia. These same biologic pressures contribute to excess adiposity that accelerates CVD through both adverse biomechanical “fat mass disease” (cardiac effects) and adverse adiposopathic “sick fat disease” (generation of cardiometabolic risk factors). [ 25 , 175 ] 2. Because eating behavior is shaped by sight, smell, hearing, taste, and tactile cues, individuals living with obesity may experience intensified sensory-driven eating that promotes caloric excess. In the context of cardiovascular disease, these sensory triggers can perpetuate unhealthful dietary patterns high in sodium, saturated fat, and refined carbohydrates, thereby worsening cardiometabolic risk. [ 25 , 176 ] 3. Genetic predisposition, chronic sleep deprivation, mental stress, experiences of weight stigma, emotions, habitual time cues, environmental exposures (including socioeconomic barriers and food insecurity), weight-promoting medications, information gaps, reward pathways, and psychiatric disease all influence eating behavior. These factors can compound CVD risk by reinforcing maladaptive dietary patterns and limiting adherence to heart-healthy nutrition strategies and options. [ 25 , 146 , 177 ] 4. Eating disorders (e.g., binge-eating disorder, bulimia nervosa, night-eating syndrome, and sleep-related eating disorder) can significantly disrupt energy balance and metabolic health. When present in patients with CVD or at CVD risk, these conditions may worsen insulin resistance, blood glucose, blood pressure, and atherogenic blood lipids, complicating both CVD prevention and treatment. [ 25 , 178 ] 5. Physical inactivity may stem from musculoskeletal, neurologic, pulmonary (including obstructive sleep apnea), cardiac, and other health disorders, as well as fatigue, disinterest, or unhealthful environments that promote sedentary behavior. Reduced physical activity directly contributes to CVD progression by impairing cardiorespiratory fitness, adversely affecting cardiometabolic risk factors (insulin resistance, high blood glucose, high blood pressure, high atherogenic blood lipids), impairing endothelial function, increasing systemic inflammation and thrombosis, and facilitating a body composition associated with increased CVD risk (i.e., increased visceral adiposity). [ 25 , 171 ] 6. Behaviors contributing to weight gain or regain often reflect personal and physiologic priority imbalances - such as perceived “lack of time” - that can disrupt nutritional intake and energy expenditure. These imbalances can undermine CVD management by limiting engagement in heart-healthy eating and regular physical activity. [ 25 , 179 ] 7. Eating habits and physical activity behaviors may be substantially influenced by genetic predisposition, shaping an individual's baseline tendencies toward energy intake and expenditure. In CVD, these inherited behavioral patterns can amplify risk trajectories unless addressed through tailored, supportive interventions. [ 25 , 180 ] 8. Optimal behavior therapies are feasible, efficacious, measurable, and promote self-ownership, with enhanced outcomes achieved through frequent professional encounters, education, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, goal setting, self-monitoring, behavioral contracting, and social support. For patients with CVD, combining these behavioral approaches with appropriate pharmacotherapy or metabolic interventions can suppress intrusive food thoughts (‘food noise’), allowing patients to meaningfully improve dietary quality, physical activity, and long-term CVD risk reduction. [ 25 , 181 ] 9. For patients ready for change, weight-management technologies, access to healthful food environments, and availability of physical activity resources can support improved nutrition and exercise behaviors that reduce CVD risk. However, in individuals not yet ready for change, simply providing these resources rarely produces meaningful or sustained cardiometabolic benefit. Clinically meaningful change in CVD risk requires clinically meaningful changes in behavior and willingness to accept and adhere to evidence-based treatments. [ 25 , 182 ] 10. Healthful behavior change is more effective and consistent when supported by self-monitoring, record-keeping, education, routine clinical assessment, and social reinforcement. In CVD care, these strategies help patients maintain adherence to nutrition, activity, and medication plans that are essential for long-term risk reduction. ## Obesity and cardiovascular disease medications [ 26 ] (See Table 19 and Fig. 19 )

In patients with obesity, choice of pharmacologic management of cardiovascular and metabolic disease should consider drug-specific metabolic effects, fluid balance, and altered pharmacokinetics. Older β-blockers such as propranolol, atenolol, and metoprolol can promote weight gain by lowering metabolic rate, reducing energy expenditure, and decreasing lipolysis through blocking beta-adrenergic receptors; carvedilol and nebivolol are generally weight-neutral. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers often cause edema from precapillary vasodilation, which is more pronounced in obesity. Choosing a weight-neutral agent can help avoid worsening cardiometabolic risk in individuals with obesity and cardiovascular disease (CVD). [ 26 , 86 , 184 ] 2. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine and amlodipine frequently cause peripheral edema, which increases body weight through fluid retention rather than adipose tissue accumulation. This edema results from precapillary vasodilation and increases hydrostatic pressure. In individuals with obesity, the edema can be more pronounced and complicate assessment of true volume status. [ 26 , 185 ] 3. Insulins, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones (e.g., TZDs such as pioglitazone), and meglitinides (e.g., nateglinide and repaglinide) can all contribute to weight gain, either by enhancing insulin signaling or by causing fluid retention. Notably, TZDs are contraindicated in patients with NYHA Class III or IV heart failure. [ 26 , 186 ] 4. Diabetes medications such as metformin, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), SGLT2 inhibitors, α-glucosidase inhibitors, and amylin analogs promote weight reduction. Semaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide are examples of diabetes medications that also produce clinically meaningful weight reduction. Among patients with diabetes, semaglutide, liraglutide, and SGLT2 inhibitors have cardiovascular outcomes trials demonstrating reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) such as "Semaglutide Unabated Sustainability in Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes" or SUSTAIN-6, "Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcome Results" or LEADER, and for SGLT2 inhibitors, the "SGLT2i Meta-Analysis Cardio-Renal Trialists Consortium" or SMART-C meta-analysis. A cohort study also links tirzepatide to reduced all-cause mortality, MACE, and kidney events compared with GLP-1 receptor agonists. [ 26 , 27 , 187 ] 5. Obesity increases intra-abdominal pressure, impairs renal venous return, and diminishes the effectiveness of loop diuretics. As a result, clinicians may need higher doses or sequential nephron blockade with agents like metolazone to maintain fluid balance, although this approach raises the risk of electrolyte abnormalities and kidney injury. Obesity also promotes elevated aldosterone levels, making spironolactone a consideration in cases of resistant hypertension, albeit one that requires careful monitoring for hyperkalemia, especially in patients taking renin-angiotensin system inhibitors or those with obesity-related chronic kidney disease (CKD). Finerenone is indicated for adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (CKD) to slow renal decline and reduce cardiovascular events. Finerenone is also indicated for patients with heart failure with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥ 40%. As a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (nsMRA), it offers high selectivity for the mineralocorticoid receptor with minimal affinity for androgen and progesterone receptors, leading to a lower risk of gynecomastia compared to spironolactone. Finally, obesity suppresses circulating B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels because adipose tissue increases natriuretic peptide clearance and expresses receptors that degrade them, which can lead to “normal” or only mildly elevated BNP values in patients with obesity and acute heart failure, contributing to under-recognition of congestion. Some evidence suggests obesity may reduce production of BNP. These BNP imbalances further support the use of ARNIs such as sacubitril/valsartan, which inhibit neprilysin and help restore effective natriuretic peptide activity. [ 26 , 188 , 189 ] 6. Antithrombotic therapy in individuals with obesity requires careful adjustment to account for altered pharmacokinetics. Among direct oral anticoagulants, apixaban and rivaroxaban are preferred in patients with very high BMI (>40 kg/m 2 or weight >120 kg), because standard dosing is supported by stronger evidence, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban are generally avoided due to less predictable drug handling and limited data in this population. In patients with a BMI above 50 kg/m 2 or those who have undergone bariatric surgery, absorption becomes increasingly variable, prompting the use of drug-specific peak and trough anti-Xa monitoring to confirm therapeutic levels. Similar concerns apply to antiplatelet therapy: standard low-dose aspirin (81 mg) may provide inadequate platelet inhibition in individuals with higher body weight because of increased esterase activity and a larger volume of distribution. Although not currently in established guidelines, some evidence indicates that patients weighing more than 70–90 kg may require higher or more frequent dosing - such as 325 mg or twice-daily regimens - to achieve sufficient antiplatelet effect; however, such adjustments may increase bleeding risk and should be framed as pharmacokinetic considerations or areas of ongoing debate rather than established guideline standards. [ 9 , 26 , 86 ] 7. Highly lipophilic drugs such as amiodarone have a substantially increased volume of distribution in obesity, as expanded adipose tissue acts as a reservoir that prolongs their elimination half-life (a process less pronounced for moderately lipophilic drugs like lidocaine). While loading doses for lipophilic drugs often require scaling toward total body weight to achieve therapeutic concentrations, amiodarone loading is typically capped or calculated using ideal or adjusted body weight to prevent toxicity. Maintenance dosing requires caution and should be based primarily on metabolic clearance rather than total body weight. Hydrophilic agents like digoxin and sotalol distribute chiefly into lean tissue and body water rather than fat, so their volume of distribution rises little with excess adiposity and dosing is more accurately based on ideal or lean body weight. Statins vary in their lipophilicity, with lipophilic agents entering cells by passive diffusion and hydrophilic agents relying on transporters. Both moderate intensity and high intensity statins are sometimes associated with small increases in body weight, and high-intensity statins (e.g., lipophilic atorvastatin and the hydrophilic agent rosuvastatin) are sometimes associated with small increases in fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c, occasionally contributing to type 2 diabetes. That said, the cardiovascular benefits of statins overwhelmingly outweigh these potential adverse metabolic effects. Pravastatin and pitavastatin appear to have the least influence on glycemic parameters. The fact that rosuvastatin, despite being hydrophilic, still carries a risk of glycemic worsening underscores that statin intensity, rather than solubility characteristics, is the principal determinant of new-onset diabetes risk. [ 26 , 86 , 190 , 191 ] 8. Using total body weight in the Cockcroft–Gault equation overestimates creatinine clearance in individuals with morbid obesity, increasing the risk of overdosing renally cleared medications. In contrast, the CKD-EPI equation is less biased by body size and is the most widely used method for estimating glomerular filtration rate; its accuracy for drug dosing can be improved by de-indexing, which converts the laboratory-reported eGFR (normalized to 1.73 m 2 ) to an absolute GFR (mL/min) based on the patient's actual body surface area. De-indexed CKD-EPI is particularly relevant for medications whose pharmacokinetics depend on true renal clearance, including metabolic and endocrine agents such as metformin, renally cleared GLP-1 RA (e.g., exenatide, lixisenatide), insulin, and most DPP-4 inhibitors (except linagliptin), as well as cardiovascular and heart-failure therapies such as SGLT2 inhibitors, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, sacubitril/valsartan, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, loop and thiazide-type diuretics, renally cleared beta-blockers (atenolol, nadolol, sotalol); direct oral anticoagulant dosing are based on the Cockcroft-Gault equation. [ 26 , 192 ] 9. Sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors reduce the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events; empagliflozin and dapagliflozin markedly reduce hospitalizations for heart failure (especially heart failure with preserved ejection fraction) among individuals with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Emerging evidence indicates that people with obesity may derive even greater cardiovascular benefit than those with lower body weight. This pattern underscores the substantial cardiometabolic value of this drug class in a high-risk population, likely due to improved myocardial energy utilization, reduced inflammation, enhanced autophagy, and favorable influences on blood pressure, arterial stiffness, and reduction in body weight. Collectively, these pathways promote healthier cardiac structure and function and may also lessen the risk of myocardial infarction, dysrhythmias, and vascular dysfunction. [ 26 , 193 ] 10. Pharmacological management of CVD in patients with obesity requires a strategic shift from treating isolated complications of obesity to prioritizing agents that synergistically treat both the cause (i.e., obesity) and the adverse consequences (e.g., type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia). For example, for treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, clinicians should preferentially select medications that substantially reduce body weight (e.g., GLP-1 RA) or therapies that modestly reduce body weight or that are weight neutral (e.g., SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, alpha glucosidase inhibitors, amylin) while avoiding weight-promoting agents (e.g., sulfonylureas, insulin, thiazolidinediones, meglitinides) whenever possible. Furthermore, standard dosing regimens must be rigorously adjusted to account for obesity-altered pharmacokinetics to ensure therapeutic efficacy and safety. Finally, beyond cardiometabolic drug treatment, bariatric surgeries such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass may impair gastrointestinal absorption of extended-release formulations and should often be replaced with immediate-release alternatives. Pharmacologic management in individuals with obesity must account for drug-specific metabolic effects, fluid balance, and altered pharmacokinetics, since several medications—including older beta-blockers, certain calcium channel blockers, and multiple glucose-lowering agents—can promote weight gain or edema, whereas metformin, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors support weight reduction and improve cardiovascular outcomes. Obesity also alters drug handling by reducing loop-diuretic effectiveness, increasing aldosterone-driven hypertension, suppressing natriuretic peptide levels, modifying antithrombotic pharmacokinetics, and changing dosing requirements for lipophilic and hydrophilic drugs, with renal dosing requiring adjusted body weight, or more accurately, deindexed Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI); extended-release formulations may be unreliable after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Overall, optimal cardiovascular therapy emphasizes weight-neutral or weight-reducing medications and careful dose adjustment to accommodate obesity-related changes in drug distribution, metabolism, and clearance.

Several glucose-lowering agents [(e.g., insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones (TZD), and meglitinides)] also contribute to weight gain, with TZDs contraindicated in advanced heart failure. In contrast, metformin, GLP-1 RA, SGLT2 inhibitors, α-glucosidase inhibitors, and amylin analogs promote weight reduction and improve cardiovascular risk factors, with semaglutide and SGLT2 inhibitors [ 27 ] demonstrating reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and tirzepatide undergoing CVD outcome clinical trials in patients with obesity. Obesity also reduces loop diuretic effectiveness, increases aldosterone-driven resistant hypertension, and suppresses B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels, supporting the use of spironolactone, finerenone, and angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) such as sacubitril/valsartan.

Antithrombotic therapy must account for altered drug pharmacokinetics, with apixaban and rivaroxaban preferred at very high BMI and aspirin potentially requiring higher or more frequent dosing due to pharmacokinetic dilution. Lipophilic drugs like amiodarone and lidocaine require higher loading doses, while hydrophilic agents such as digoxin and sotalol should be dosed using ideal or lean body weight. High-intensity statins may modestly worsen glycemia (and potentially increase appetite), though the CVD benefits outweigh risks. Renal dosing must avoid overestimation of creatinine clearance by using adjusted body weight, or more accurately by deindexed Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI); extended-release formulations may be unreliable after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.

SGLT2 inhibitors provide broad cardiovascular protection - particularly in individuals with obesity - through mechanisms including improved myocardial energetics, reduced inflammation, and favorable hemodynamic effects. Overall, optimal concomitant CVD therapy emphasizes weight-neutral or weight-reducing agents and precise dose adjustment to accommodate obesity-related changes in drug distribution, metabolism, and clearance. Essential principles include: • Pharmacologic management in individuals with obesity requires attention to drug-specific metabolic effects and altered pharmacokinetics, as several agents - including older β-blockers, certain calcium channel blockers, and multiple glucose-lowering drugs - can promote weight gain or fluid retention, where metformin, GLP-1 RA, SGLT2 inhibitors, and related agents support weight reduction and improve cardiovascular outcomes. • Obesity also affects drug handling by reducing loop diuretic effectiveness, increasing aldosterone-driven hypertension, suppressing BNP levels, altering antithrombotic pharmacokinetics, and changing dosing needs for lipophilic and hydrophilic medications, with renal dosing requiring adjusted body weight and extended-release formulations becoming unreliable after gastric bypass. • Optimal therapy prioritizes weight-neutral or weight-reducing medications and precise dose adjustments that account for obesity-related changes in drug distribution, metabolism, and clearance.

## Obesity medications and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 28 ] (See Table 20 , Figs. 20a and 20b )

Among patients with obesity, modest weight reduction of 5%–10% via evidence-based interventions can reduce cardiometabolic risk factors. Greater weight reduction is usually required (>10%) for more consistent and demonstrable reduction in CVD events. In the Look AHEAD (Action for Health in Diabetes) Lifestyle study, mostly lifestyle-only interventions did not reduce CVD events despite 3–8% weight reduction at various points during the ∼10 years of follow-up. However, a post hoc analysis of participants in Look AHEAD who reduced at least 10% of their body weight in the first year had a 21% lower risk of the primary outcome (heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death) compared to those who had stable weight or gained weight. Thus, among patients with obesity, a >10% reduction of body weight may be considered a clinical threshold for improvement in CVD.
