Among patients with obesity, modest weight reduction (e.g., 5%–10% of total body weight) is often sufficient to improve cardiometabolic risk factors, including blood glucose, blood pressure, and blood lipid levels (i.e., decreases triglyceride levels and increases in high density lipoprotein cholesterol levels). Larger reductions in body weight (>10%) more reliably reduce CVD events and mortality. [ 1 , 28 , 175 , 194 , 195 ] 2. Tirzepatide is an unimolecular glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) that at a maximum dose of 15 mg injectable once a week is approved for chronic weight management in adults with obesity or overweight. Tirzepatide not only reduces body weight, but also improves cardiometabolic risk factors such as blood glucose, blood pressure, and atherogenic blood lipids. In the SUMMIT trial [Study of Tirzepatide in Participants With Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF) and Obesity], tirzepatide produced substantial weight reduction and a significant reduction in the composite risk of heart-failure events and cardiovascular death. Tirzepatide has undergone and continues to undergo clinical trials to evaluate obesity and weight management (SURMOUNT), as well as diabetes mellitus (Study of Tirzepatide in Participants with Type 2 Diabetes or SURPASS). The SURMOUNT Morbidity and Mortality Outcomes (MMO) trial will assess CVD events, with an estimated study completion date of October 2027. [ 28 , 78 , 112 , 194 ] 3. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 RA with robust evidence for cardiovascular protection. In the landmark SELECT trial, semaglutide at a maximum dose of 2.4 mg injectable weekly reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) such as heart attack and stroke by 20% in adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease and without diabetes mellitus. In 2024, semaglutide was the first obesity medication to achieve an FDA indication to reduce cardiovascular death, heart-attack, and stroke risk. Beyond MACE reduction, semaglutide has demonstrated meaningful benefits across other high-risk cardiometabolic conditions. As assessed by the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) and 6-min walk distance, the “Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with Obesity (STEP) – HFpEF” trial showed significant improvements in symptoms, functional capacity, and quality of life in patients with HFpEF and obesity. Regarding patients with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus, the FLOW trial was stopped early for efficacy after achieving a 24% reduction in the primary endpoint of a composite that included: onset of kidney failure, a ≥50% reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate, and death from kidney or cardiovascular causes. [ 28 , 194 , [196] , [197] , [198] ] 4. Liraglutide is a GLP-1 RA approved at lower doses (1.8 mg injectable per day) for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and at higher doses (3.0 mg injectable per day) for the treatment of obesity. While liraglutide improves cardiometabolic parameters including blood glucose, blood pressure, and atherogenic lipid levels, clinical evidence for cardiovascular risk reduction is currently limited to the diabetes population. Specifically, in the “Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcome Results (LEADER)” trial, the drug significantly reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and cardiovascular death in patients with type 2 diabetes using the 1.8 mg per day dose. However, unlike semaglutide, liraglutide does not carry an FDA indication for cardiovascular risk reduction in individuals with obesity but without diabetes, as no trial analogous to the SELECT study has been conducted to evaluate outcomes in this population. That said, liraglutide is approved for the treatment of obesity and is available as a generic formulation. [ 28 , 78 , 194 ] 5. Cardiovascular outcome trials suggest that GLP-1 RA deliver cardiovascular benefits prior to clinically meaningful weight reduction, with event-curve separation apparent within the first year. Acute negative caloric balance contributes to rapid improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors (glucose, BP, lipids). While speculative and yet to be proven, some authors suggest that early CVD benefit may also be driven by direct vascular and anti-inflammatory actions independent of weight reduction. These include reduced vascular inflammation, improved endothelial function, enhanced endothelial-dependent vasodilation, decreased arterial stiffness, renal protection, and enhanced atherosclerotic plaque stability. Finally, while GLP-1 RA therapies generally lower blood pressure, they can modestly increase resting heart rate, a well-recognized class effect. [ 28 , 194 , [199] , [200] , [201] ] 6. While much needs to be confirmed in humans, rodent studies suggest that GLP-1 RA can favorably affect “sick fat.” Adiposopathy describes hypertrophic, hypoxic, fibrotic adipose tissue infiltrated by pro-inflammatory immune cells that release cytokines and maladaptive adipokines which results in adipocyte and adipose tissue dysfunction, insulin resistance, ectopic lipid deposition, and elevated cardiometabolic and CVD risk. GLP-1 receptors are found in the beta cells of the pancreas, brain, gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidneys, and heart, as well as adipose tissue. Human adipocytes express fewer GLP-1 receptors compared with the pancreas and brain; thus, the effects of GLP-1 RA on adipocytes likely reflect both direct effect as well as indirect effects via sympathetic pathways. Direct effects of GLP-1 RA may include cellular signaling, reduced adipose inflammation and relief of adipocyte endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Facilitated by weight reduction, as adipose tissue function normalizes, insulin sensitivity improves, peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue can store energy appropriately, visceral adipose tissue declines, and ectopic fat is reduced. By correcting adiposopathic endocrine and immune signaling, GLP-1 RAs improve cardiometabolic risk factors, enhance vascular function, and lower CVD risk. Additionally, GLP-1 RA may remodel adipose tissue, shifting it from energy storage toward energy expenditure and stimulating lipolysis, suppressing de novo lipogenesis, shrinking adipocyte size, and promoting browning of white fat to increase thermogenesis. Thus, beyond reducing fat mass, GLP-1 RA may improve adipose function by decreasing chronic inflammation and increasing glucose uptake via glucose transporter 4 translocation, producing smaller, more insulin-sensitive, less toxic, and more thermogenic adipocytes. [ 28 , 194 , 202 , 203 ] 7. Phentermine is a sympathomimetic amine that suppresses appetite and is FDA-approved only for short-term use - typically up to 12 weeks - for the treatment of obesity. Because it increases norepinephrine release, phentermine can raise both heart rate and blood pressure, requiring caution in individuals with uncontrolled hypertension or established cardiovascular disease. No prospective, randomized, long-term cardiovascular outcome trial has shown that phentermine monotherapy reduces major adverse CVD events. [ 28 , 194 , 204 , 205 ] 8. The combination of phentermine and topiramate in an extended-release formulation is approved for chronic weight management and typically achieves greater weight reduction than either agent alone. It has been associated with improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors, including blood glucose, blood pressure and atherogenic blood lipid levels; however, the phentermine component can produce a modest rise in heart rate, warranting routine monitoring. Although observational studies support its overall safety, no prospective, randomized cardiovascular outcome trial has yet demonstrated that this combination reduces cardiovascular morbidity or mortality. [ 28 , 194 ] 9. The naltrexone/bupropion combination works centrally to reduce appetite and food cravings, producing modest weight loss in many patients. Its cardiovascular safety was evaluated in the “Light” trial, but the study was stopped early, leaving the long-term cardiovascular benefits or risks inconclusive. While it has the potential for several drug interactions, naltrexone/bupropion can improve cardiometabolic risk factors. That said, the bupropion component can cause transient increases in blood pressure and is contraindicated in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. [ 28 , 194 ] 10. Orlistat is a reversible gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor that inhibits the absorption of dietary fats, resulting in modest weight reduction and modest improvements in blood pressure. Orlistat may lower low density lipoprotein cholesterol beyond what weight reduction alone would predict, likely due to reduced intestinal lipid absorption. No large-scale cardiovascular outcome trial has demonstrated that orlistat reduces major CVD such as myocardial infarction or stroke. In the SUMMIT trial, tirzepatide produced substantial weight reduction and significantly reduced the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or worsening heart-failure events in patients with obesity-related HFpEF. The composite benefit was driven mainly by fewer worsening heart-failure events, with no significant difference in cardiovascular death alone. In the “Semaglutide Effects on Heart Disease and Stroke in Patients with Overweight or Obesity” (SELECT) trial, semaglutide demonstrated a 20% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). In the “Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with Obesity (STEP) – HFpEF”, semaglutide improved HFpEF symptoms. Finally, in the Evaluate Renal Function with Semaglutide Once Weekly (FLOW) trial, semaglutide provided renal protection. Prior obesity medications such as phentermine, phentermine/topiramate, naltrexone/bupropion, and orlistat can support modest weight reduction and improve select risk factors, but none have demonstrated definitive reductions in MACE. Essential principles include: • Among patients with obesity, modest weight reduction of 5%–10% with healthful evidence-based interventions improve key cardiometabolic risk factors. However, weight reduction of >10% is more consistently associated with reduced CVD events. • Tirzepatide and semaglutide have demonstrated substantial weight reduction along with significant reductions in heart failure events, cardiovascular death, and major adverse cardiovascular events, with additional renal benefits. • While older agents can produce modest weight reduction and improve select risk factors, none have shown definitive CVD event reduction.

## Obesity, bariatric procedures, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 29 ] (See Table 21 and Fig. 21 )

Examples of bariatric interventions include bariatric surgeries such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy, along with other procedural options such as intragastric balloon therapy, transoral gastric volume-reduction techniques (e.g., endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty), and emerging ablation-based technologies. Among operative approaches, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy have the most consistent and compelling evidence for long-term cardiovascular benefit. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass provides the most extensive longitudinal data and demonstrates superior remission rates for type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia, while sleeve gastrectomy achieves comparable metabolic improvements with a more favorable safety profile. Surgical interventions such as the Duodenal Switch remain important options for individuals with extreme obesity or pronounced metabolic resistance. Most of the documented reduction in cardiovascular disease risk with bariatric surgery comes from studies of gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy. These procedures reliably produce substantial and durable weight reduction accompanied by broad cardiometabolic improvements, including reduced weight regain, lower blood glucose, improved blood pressure, decreased concentrations of atherogenic lipids, reduced systemic inflammation, and lower long-term risks of myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease progression, and all-cause mortality. By decreasing total fat mass and correcting dysfunctional adipose-tissue biology, bariatric surgery promotes remission of type 2 diabetes and improves hypertension control. Current clinical guidelines recommend bariatric surgery for individuals with severe obesity and for selected individuals with obesity defined by a body mass index of 30–34.9 kg per square meter who have uncontrolled metabolic disease, with expanded eligibility under the 2022 American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery and International Federation for the Surgery of Obesity and Metabolic Disorders criteria. For the individual patient with obesity, the potential adverse complications of bariatric surgery should be weighed against the potential reduction in CVD events. Essential principles include: • Bariatric surgeries such as gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy produce substantial and lasting weight reduction that leads to meaningful improvements in major cardiovascular risk factors such as improving blood glucose, blood pressure, lipid levels, and systemic inflammation. • Gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy lower long-term risks of heart attack, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease progression, and cardiovascular-related death. • For the individual patient with obesity, the potential cardiovascular benefit must be balanced against the surgical risks and long-term complications of bariatric procedures. Bariatric surgeries such as gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy are the most durable intervention for achieving and maintaining substantial weight reduction, with metabolic and anti-inflammatory effects that translate into cardiovascular benefit. By limiting the weight regain common with lifestyle or obesity medications alone, bariatric surgery preserves improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors and meaningfully reduces long-term cardiovascular risk. Specifically, bariatric procedures can facilitate remission of type 2 diabetes mellitus, with less durable remission of hypertension (although control of both are more easily achieved with fewer medications). By shrinking adipose depots and restoring healthier endocrine and inflammatory signaling, bariatric surgeries produce metabolic and immunologic improvements that contribute to broad cardiometabolic benefits. [ 29 , [208] , [209] , [210] ] 3. Specifically, bariatric surgery lowers long-term myocardial infarction risk and stroke by improving the atherosclerotic environment. Early improvements in glycemic control, blood pressure, and atherogenic lipids, along with sharp reductions in systemic inflammation (as evidenced by rapid declines in highly sensitive C-reactive protein and interleukin 6) reflect decreased adipose-tissue inflammation and healthier metabolic signaling, collectively mitigating the atherosclerotic process. [ 29 , 211 ] 4. Longitudinal studies demonstrate that bariatric surgery patients outperform matched non-surgical cohorts in weight trajectories, metabolic parameters, and cardiovascular outcomes, with advantages that endure for ten years or more. [ 29 , 212 ] 5. Bariatric procedures can sometimes be used in combination with obesity medications. Obesity medications prior to bariatric surgery can reduce surgical risk (e.g., hepatomegaly). Obesity medications after bariatric procedures can improve the weight reduction and maintenance of weight reduction. Either way, the combined use of obesity medications with bariatric procedures can help maintain weight reduction and persistence in improved CVD risk factors. [ 29 , 213 ] 6. Long-term evidence consistently demonstrates that bariatric surgery is associated with substantial reductions in all-cause mortality, driven in part by significant decreases in cardiovascular, metabolic, and cancer-related deaths. Because obesity accelerates both atherosclerosis and chronic kidney disease, the renal improvements seen after surgery - such as slower progression of albuminuria and a reduced risk of end-stage renal disease - add to its cardiovascular benefits and underscore its value as a comprehensive cardiometabolic intervention. Specifically, regarding the heart, bariatric surgery improves heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, reduces the risk of new onset atrial fibrillation, and improves the success rate of cardiac ablation procedures. [ 29 , 175 , 214 ] 7. Current clinical guidelines support bariatric surgery for individuals with severe obesity, particularly when cardiovascular risk is increased by conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, or obstructive sleep apnea. Surgery may also be considered for people with Class I obesity, defined as a body mass index of 30–34.9 kg/m 2 , when metabolic disease remains insufficiently controlled. The 2022 guidelines from the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery and the International Federation for the Surgery of Obesity and Metabolic Disorders broadened eligibility by recommending surgery for all individuals with a body mass index of 35 kg/m 2 or higher, regardless of accompanying medical conditions, and by considering surgery for those with a body mass index of 30 kg/m 2 or higher when cardiometabolic disease is present. [ 29 , 215 ] 8. Although bariatric surgeries are generally safe and deliver substantial cardiovascular benefit, they are associated with distinct long-term risks. Nutritional deficiencies are common - particularly of vitamin D, vitamin A, vitamin B1 (thiamine), vitamin B9 (folate), vitamin B12 (cobalamin), as well as minerals and trace elements such as calcium, magnesium, iron and zinc - often requiring lifelong supplementation and monitoring. Patients also face an elevated risk of bone fractures and, in some cases, may require reoperation for complications or anatomical issues that arise over time. Procedure selection must be aligned with broader cardiometabolic management. For example, the presence of gastroesophageal reflux disease is a key determinant: Sleeve Gastrectomy can worsen reflux symptoms, whereas Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass often leads to meaningful improvement. [ 29 , 97 , 216 , 217 ] 9. Long-term cardiovascular benefits of bariatric procedures depend on structured follow-up that ensures nutritional monitoring, behavioral support, and ongoing management of cardiometabolic comorbidities. Sustained engagement with a multidisciplinary team is essential to preserve these gains. [ 29 , 218 ] 10. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy lead to substantial and durable reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events, with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass supported by the most extensive long-term data showing marked decreases in myocardial infarction, heart failure, and all-cause mortality. Sleeve gastrectomy - now the most performed procedure - achieves comparable cardiometabolic improvements with a more favorable safety profile, although Roux-en-Y gastric bypass often yields superior long-term remission of type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia. Hypoabsorptive procedures such as the Duodenal Switch, while used less frequently, remain important options for patients with super-obesity or marked metabolic resistance. Bariatric procedures - particularly gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy - produce durable weight reduction that drives broad improvements in cardiovascular risk profiles. These cardiometabolic benefits include enhanced glycemic control, lower blood pressure, improved lipid patterns, and reduced systemic inflammation, collectively mitigating the cardiometabolic burden of obesity. Long-term evidence shows that gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy substantially decrease the incidence of myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease progression, and cardiovascular mortality. For each patient with obesity, however, these cardiovascular gains must be weighed against the procedural risks and the potential for long-term surgical complications.

## Obesity, cancer, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 30 ] (See Table 22 and Fig. 22 )

Obesity is a leading preventable cause of cancer and a dominant driver of cardiovascular disease, acting through intertwined metabolic, inflammatory, hormonal, and hemodynamic pathways that elevate risk for gastrointestinal and hormonally driven cancers as well as lifelong CVD. Excess adiposity contributes to 5% of cancers in US men and 11% in women, parallels rising early-onset cancer and cardiometabolic disease in younger adults, and fuels carcinogenesis and vascular injury through cytokine excess, oxidative stress, hypoxia, hormonal dysregulation, and hyperinsulinemia. These same mechanisms worsen endothelial dysfunction, atherosclerosis, arterial stiffness, and vulnerability to chemotherapy-related cardiotoxicity, particularly in phenotypes such as sarcopenic obesity. While GLP-1 RA now reduce cardiovascular events in people with obesity, no therapy is yet indicated to simultaneously treat obesity and prevent cancer, even as emerging obesity medications show promise across both domains. Diets high in processed meats, sugars, and pro-oxidative exposures amplify cancer and CVD risk, whereas nutrition rich in fiber, antioxidants, and phytochemicals, along with sustained weight reduction and physical activity, reduces inflammation, improves cardiometabolic health, and lowers both cancer incidence and recurrence—positioning lifestyle and weight management as shared, foundational prevention strategies. Essential principles include: • Obesity is a leading preventable cause of both cancer and cardiovascular disease, driven by shared metabolic, inflammatory, hormonal, and oxidative mechanisms. • These pathways accelerate carcinogenesis, atherosclerosis, cardiotoxicity vulnerability, and early-onset disease, while lifestyle and dietary factors can either worsen or mitigate risk. • Weight reduction, improved nutrition, physical activity, and emerging obesity medications provide overlapping protection across cancer and cardiovascular outcomes. ## Obesity, psychiatric disease, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 31 ] (See Table 23 and Fig. 23 )

Obesity, chronic mental stress, and psychiatric illness form a tightly interwoven network of physiological, behavioral, and social forces that accelerate cardiovascular disease (CVD). This relationship is driven by shared biological pathways: obesity increases sympathetic tone and metabolic strain, while chronic stress drives adiposopathic endocrine dysfunction and meta-inflammation that degrade endothelial health. Stress-induced limbic dysregulation alters hunger and reward pathways, promoting high-caloric intake and insulin resistance. Meanwhile, mood disorders and Serious Mental Illness (SMI) independently raise CVD risk through autonomic imbalance and intrinsic metabolic disturbances - contributing to a 10–25 year reduction in life expectancy for patients with SMI. These cycles are compounded by iatrogenic effects from psychotropic medications, sleep fragmentation, and obstructive sleep apnea, which introduces intermittent hypoxia that drives resistant hypertension and dysrhythmias. Rooted in upstream drivers like adverse childhood experiences, genetic pleiotropy, and socioeconomic adversity, these vulnerabilities are often exacerbated by weight stigma and healthcare avoidance. Consequently, effective management requires dismantling these self-reinforcing cycles through coordinated psychiatric, behavioral, and cardiometabolic intervention. Essential principles include: • Obesity, stress, and psychiatric illness heighten sympathetic activation, systemic inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction via overlapping pathways. • Early-life trauma, genetic overlaps, and socioeconomic adversity embed biological vulnerability, creating self-reinforcing cycles of weight gain, mood disturbance, and cardiometabolic decline. • The compounding force of these factors accelerates atherosclerosis and shortens life expectancy, necessitating integrated care that addresses metabolic and mental health simultaneously. Obesity acts as a chronic physiologic stressor that heightens sympathetic tone, elevates blood pressure, and increases cardiometabolic workload. Chronic stress induces adiposopathic endocrine and immune dysfunction—such as hypercortisolemia and persistent low-grade inflammation that worsens glucose regulation, raises blood pressure, increases inflammatory burden, and may disrupt the microbiome. These stress-driven abnormalities impair endothelial function and accelerate atherosclerotic plaque development, thereby promoting cardiovascular disease progression. [ 31 , 229 ] 3. Stress-related limbic dysregulation disrupts appetite control and reward processing, fostering a preference for hyper-palatable, calorie-dense foods that drive weight gain, increased visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Mood and anxiety disorders add further autonomic and inflammatory strain, and when layered onto obesity, these behavioral and biologic disturbances compound to markedly elevate cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Obesity and depression reinforce one another—obesity increases depression through inflammatory and psychosocial pathways, while depression promotes obesity through inactivity and neuroendocrine disruption. This bidirectional cycle amplifies inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and physical inactivity, creating a self-perpetuating decline that independently heightens the risk for CVD. [ 31 , 230 ] 5. Serious mental illness - particularly schizophrenia and bipolar disorder - carries intrinsic metabolic vulnerability even before psychotropic medications are introduced, predisposing patients to obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. These metabolic disturbances contribute to the well-documented 10–25-year mortality gap, driven predominantly by accelerated cardiovascular disease rather than suicide. [ 31 , 231 ] 6. Many psychiatric medications - especially second-generation antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, and some anti-depressants - can promote weight gain, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Even agents considered “weight-neutral” may have variable and unexpected weight and metabolic effects in individual patients. Yet untreated psychiatric illness itself increases cardiovascular risk, making a careful risk–benefit assessment and proactive metabolic monitoring essential for patients with or at risk for CVD. [ 31 , 231 , 232 ] 7. Binge Eating Disorder and Night Eating Syndrome are common but often underrecognized conditions that drive excess caloric intake and significant metabolic dysregulation, worsening obesity-related cardiovascular risk. Their impact typically exceeds what standard dietary counseling can address, requiring integrated psychiatric and metabolic treatment. This may include targeted behavioral therapies or obesity medications such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist based agents to prevent further cardiometabolic deterioration. [ 31 , 178 ] 8. Chronic stress and psychiatric illness disrupt sleep and undermine core health behaviors, driving dysregulated appetite, impaired glucose metabolism, elevated blood pressure, and progressive weight gain. As obesity develops or worsens, it further amplifies psychological stress and contributes to obstructive sleep apnea, where intermittent hypoxia becomes a powerful physiological stressor that promotes resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, systemic inflammation, and worsening mood and cognitive symptoms. These mutually reinforcing pathways create a cycle of metabolic, psychological, and cardiovascular deterioration that requires coordinated cardiometabolic, psychiatric, and behavioral intervention. [ 31 , 231 ] 9. Early-life trauma and Adverse Childhood Experiences create lasting neuroendocrine dysregulation that “biologically embeds” vulnerability to obesity, mood disorders, and early-onset cardiovascular disease. These early insults interact with stigma-related stress and maladaptive coping to accelerate cardiometabolic decline across the lifespan. Genetic pleiotropy further reinforces this clustering: the same variants that influence synaptic plasticity also regulate appetite and metabolic function, predisposing some individuals to obesity, depression, and schizophrenia independent of behavior. Socioeconomic conditions then shape the broader environment, amplifying or buffering these inherited and trauma-related risks. [ 31 , 233 , 234 ] 10. Weight stigma and mental health discrimination act as potent toxic stressors that elevate allostatic load in individuals with obesity, particularly those with co-occurring psychiatric illness. These social pressures reduce engagement with preventive cardiology and contribute to delayed diagnosis and worse cardiovascular outcomes. At the same time, chronic stress fosters maladaptive coping behaviors such as smoking and alcohol use, which further amplify obesity-related insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, compounding overall CVD risk. This convergence of biological, behavioral, and medication-related factors accelerates cardiometabolic deterioration and heightens long-term cardiovascular disease risk, underscoring the need for integrated psychiatric and metabolic management. Additionally, weight stigma and mental health discrimination act as chronic toxic stressors that elevate allostatic load and reduce engagement with preventive cardiology, leading to delayed detection and worsening of cardiovascular disease. These social pressures also drive maladaptive coping behaviors—such as smoking and alcohol use—that compound obesity-related hypertension, dyslipidemia, and metabolic dysfunction. Together, these forces create a self-reinforcing pathway that accelerates cardiometabolic deterioration and heightens long-term CVD risk.

## Obesity, pediatrics, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) (See Table 24 and Fig. 24 )

Increased childhood CVD risk emerges from a complex interplay of early biological programming (e.g., genetics, epigenetics), metabolic disease, social adversity, and behavioral factors. Excessive maternal adiposity in fetal life accelerates atherosclerosis through inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and metabolic derangements, while rapid infant weight gain and persistent obesity in childhood can amplify CVD risk via adiposopathic consequences such as insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), sleep apnea, and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). That said, as part of the differential diagnosis, it is important to note that pediatric cardiovascular diseases arise independently of obesity. Examples include congenital heart disease, cardiac dysrhythmias, myocarditis, cardiomyopathies, Kawasaki disease sequelae, rheumatic heart disease, chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity, familial hypercholesterolemia, congenital coronary anomalies, autoimmune conditions, and substance-related injury. Both the potential for obesity dependent and obesity independent CVD underscores the need for universal and routine screening (including targeted physical exam evaluation) for CVD risk factors. Traditional screening tools such as body mass index trajectory, blood glucose, blood pressure, and blood lipid panel can help assess early CVD risk. However, CVD risk factors such as these are often inadequate in fully predicting CVD risk, prompting interest in other assessments in select cases, such as inflammatory biomarkers and advanced imaging. Complicating CVD risk is that weight stigma itself acts as a toxic stressor that raises cortisol and inflammation. Excessive screen time, poor sleep, food insecurity, neighborhood disadvantage, adverse childhood experiences, mental health disorders, and the metabolic effects of some medications (e.g., atypical antipsychotics) may further elevate CVD vulnerability. In many cases, reduction of body mass index to normal range in childhood and adolescence in individuals with obesity can lower cardiometabolic risk in adulthood similar to that of an adult who never had obesity [ 32 ]. Treatment with healthful nutrition, physical activity, and behavior modification are foundational. In addition, use of evidence-based obesity medications and, in select adolescents, metabolic surgery can meaningfully reverse risk trajectories and improve long-term CVD outcomes. Essential principles include: • Childhood CVD risk develops through early biological programming, persistent obesity, and clustering conditions such as insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, often associated with MASLD, sleep apnea, and PMOS, all which accelerate vascular aging. • Many pediatric cardiovascular diseases are independent of obesity, highlighting the need for universal CVD risk screening, with earlier testing in individuals with family history of premature CVD, along with a targeted physical examination. • Social determinants, weight stigma, mental health conditions, excessive screen time, poor sleep, and the metabolic effects of atypical antipsychotics further amplify cardiometabolic vulnerability, while early lifestyle therapy, evidence-based pharmacotherapy, and selective metabolic surgery can meaningfully reverse long-term cardiovascular risk trajectories. Early intervention is recommended because the longer the exposure to obesity, then the longer the individual is exposed to adiposopathic endocrinopathies and immunopathies, which often leads to insulin resistance, vascular aging, and end-organ injury. Early identification and treatment in childhood can meaningfully alter this trajectory, preventing the cumulative burden of complications that otherwise accelerate across adolescence and adulthood. ## Obesity, social determinants of health, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ [33] , [34] , [35] ] (See Table 25 and Fig. 25 )

Obesity is a chronic, biologically mediated disease involving disrupted appetite regulation, altered energy balance, and dysfunctional adipose tissue, but its expression is profoundly shaped by social conditions such as access to nutritious foods, safe activity spaces, and stable housing. Lower-income communities face disproportionate exposure to ultra-processed “food swamps,” food insecurity, and feast-or-famine cycles that promote fat storage and insulin resistance. These inequities begin early: maternal stress, inadequate nutrition, environmental exposures, and epigenetic programming heighten lifelong susceptibility to obesity and CVD, compounded by genetic–environment mismatches like the “thrifty gene” hypothesis. Minority youth are targeted with marketing of sugar-sweetened beverages and ultra-processed foods, while structural racism shapes neighborhood conditions, healthcare access, and chronic stress, contributing to disparities such as markedly higher hypertension and maternal mortality among Black adults and women. Adverse Childhood Experiences further embed biologic risk through chronic stress pathways that drive dopamine resistance, cortisol dysregulation, increased visceral adiposity, and elevated heart disease risk. Limited access to preventive care and advanced therapies, along with weight stigma in healthcare, allows metabolic dysfunction to progress in underserved populations. Environmental stressors include noise, light pollution, shift work, and poor sleep that disrupts circadian rhythms, as well as impoverished communities that face additional barriers such as food deserts, provider shortages, and higher preventable CVD mortality. Structural constraints on physical activity and disproportionate exposure to obesogens (i.e., chemicals, often called “endocrine disruptors,” that disrupt normal metabolic, endocrine, or developmental processes in ways that increase the risk of excess adiposity) and environmental toxins add inflammatory and endothelial injury burdens that cannot be overcome by individual behavior alone. Coordinated clinical, community, and policy interventions addressing obesity, social determinants, and CVD together offer far greater impact than treating each in isolation. Essential principles include: • Obesity and cardiovascular disease share deep biological roots, but their expression is powerfully shaped by structural forces, from lack of promotion and/or access to healthful foods and environmental exposures to chronic stress, racism, and limited access to overall medical care. • The adverse consequences of unhealthful social determinants of health begin early in life, are reinforced by targeted commercial influences and neighborhood environments, and are amplified when advanced treatments and preventive services are inaccessible. • Meaningful progress requires addressing biology and social determinants together, because no single intervention can overcome the cumulative, lifelong pressures that drive cardiometabolic disparities. These forces elevate allostatic load, which represents the cumulative physiologic stress that raises cortisol, blood pressure, and metabolic dysfunction - driving higher rates of both obesity and cardiovascular disease. Black Americans ages 35–64, for example, are about 50% more likely to have hypertension than White Americans, reflecting the cumulative physiologic burden of structural stressors, differences in health-care access, and social and economic conditions. Pregnancy also functions as a metabolic “stress test,” and complications such as gestational diabetes and preeclampsia independently predict future CVD. Health disparities often originate before birth and in early childhood, when maternal stress, unhealthful nutrition, and environmental exposures shape lifelong metabolic vulnerability. Epigenetic changes arising during these periods can “program” increased susceptibility to obesity and cardiovascular disease, helping explain why equalizing healthcare access in adulthood does not immediately erase disparities. The “thrifty gene” hypothesis adds important context: some populations carry genetic traits that historically promoted efficient fat storage - a survival advantage in environments marked by scarcity. In calorie-dense, highly processed food environment, those same traits can become liabilities. At the same time, many underserved communities face environmental stressors such as noise, light pollution, and the demands of shift work - that disrupt circadian rhythms and worsen insulin resistance. Poor sleep and chronic stress can reinforce one another, creating a metabolic feedback loop that accelerates both obesity and CVD. When coupled with the disproportionate environment of “food deserts,” “food insecurity,” and “food swamps,” all these social determinants translate into measurable disparities. CDC data show obesity prevalence is substantially higher in rural counties (34.2%) than in metropolitan areas (28.7%), with rural residents experiencing a 40% higher rate of preventable CVD deaths compared with their urban counterparts. [ [33] , [34] , [35] ] 9. Communities without sidewalks, parks, or safe transportation options are effectively forced into sedentary patterns, limiting energy expenditure regardless of individual motivation. This constrained physical activity accelerates obesity progression and erodes cardiovascular resilience. Beyond the absence of supportive infrastructure, many lower-income and minoritized neighborhoods face an added burden: environmental toxicity. These communities are disproportionately located near highways, factories, and industrial zones, where exposure to obesogens and endocrine disruptors [e.g., bisphenols (BPA, BPS, BPF), phthalates, certain pesticides (atrazine, DDT), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), and organotins] trigger insulin resistance, systemic inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction, which increase the risk of CVD. [ [33] , [34] , [35] ] 10. Addressing obesity, social determinants of health and CVD together yields greater impact than treating each in isolation. Effective strategies require moving beyond individual “advice” toward coordinated clinical, community, and policy interventions. Such multilevel approaches can meaningfully reduce disparities and improve cardiometabolic health. ## Obesity, future directions, paradigm shift, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 36 , 37 ] (See Table 26 , Figs. 26a and 26b )

Obesity is a generational disease. Optimal management of obesity should begin no later than during the prenatal period, extending through childhood, and continued into adulthood. Given that CVD risk is shaped by epigenetic and generational influences, then one might argue that “optimal” obesity management might best begin with grandparents or earlier. In the past, adipose tissue was considered as little more than an energy storage organ. However, adipose tissue is now recognized as an active endocrine and immune organ. Additionally, since adipose tissue is like other organs (such as the heart) where anatomy often reflects function, this reinforces the diagnostic need to move beyond body mass index alone towards a more detailed assessment of body composition. Evidence acquired over decades supports some anthropometric measurements as being superior to BMI in assessing CVD risk. While BMI is sufficient in population studies, it may lack precision in the individual. For example, an increase in BMI can be due to increased muscle mass and not necessarily fat mass. A normal BMI may be misleading in a patient with sarcopenic obesity. Thus, percent body fat is a better diagnostic measure than BMI. That said, among the most validated prognostic anatomic measure for CVD risk is the accumulation of visceral (and epicardial) adipose tissue, which is an anatomical reflection of global adipose tissue dysfunction. It is the combination of both “fat mass disease” and “sick fat disease” that are the most common contributors to the most common cardiometabolic complications encountered by clinicians. Obesity commonly leads to fat mass and adiposopathic multisystem adverse consequences, such as multiple CVD complications (e.g., atherosclerotic coronary artery disease, heart failure, cardiac dysrhythmias, and stroke), MASLD, as well as Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) Syndrome. Because most of the increase in CVD risk due to obesity is due to the adverse consequences of obesity itself, and because obesity-related adverse consequences are modifiable (at least early in the disease process), then this often supports the “treat obesity first” paradigm. Comprehensive obesity management integrates the control of blood glucose, blood pressure, and blood atherogenic lipids, as well as sleep apnea. Optimal care depends on coordinated, multidisciplinary teams and expanded access to evidence-based obesity therapies that include access to, and education regarding healthful nutrition, routine physical activity, behavior modification, obesity medications and bariatric procedures. Essential principles include: • Optimal obesity management begins early and is best maintained lifelong. • CVD risk in patients with obesity is often modifiable, especially when treatment is initiated early in life; when appropriate, treating obesity first with evidence-based strategies has the greatest likelihood to produce successful long-term improvement in CVD risk reduction. • Precision tools, individualized approaches, integrated management of all cardiometabolic factors (including sleep apnea), and coordinated multidisciplinary care collectively strengthen outcomes and might best reduce overall CVD risk. Early intervention, beginning prenatally and extending through childhood, can alter cardiometabolic trajectories before the complications of the disease of obesity become irreversible. Epigenetic and generational influences underscore the need for preventive strategies that start before conception. [ 36 , 37 ] 2. Adipose tissue is an active endocrine and immune organ whose dysfunction fuels inflammation, insulin resistance, and atherogenesis. This understanding underscores the need to move beyond a simplistic “fat-mass” framework and toward true body-composition assessment for more accurate risk stratification and targeted treatment. Some guidances emphasize anthropometric assessments such as waist circumference (previously discussed in metabolic syndrome section), waist-to-hip ratio of ≥0.9 for men and ≥0.85 for women, waist to height ratio ≥0.5, and direct measures of body composition (i.e., percent body fat and visceral adipose tissue assessment), rather than body mass index (BMI) alone. A sole focus on BMI may overestimate the degree of adiposity in muscular individuals, underestimate the cardiometabolic risk in many Asian populations, and underestimate the amount of body fat in patients with sarcopenic obesity. [ 36 , 37 , 247 ] 3. Obesity affects multiple interdependent organ systems, leading to not only CVD and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but also chronic kidney disease and cardiometabolic risk factors (i.e., Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) Syndrome framework). One of the more compelling developments within this framework is the emerging recognition of the obesity – heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) connection – which disproportionately affects females, and like obesity, illustrates how a single measure (i.e., BMI in obesity and ejection fraction with HFpEF) is often inadequate in clinical assessments. [ 36 , 37 ] 4. Among those with obesity, CVD risk assessment has value because, especially when due to obesity, cardiometabolic complications such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia can be improved with evidence-based weight reduction – which in some cases – can result in remission of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and clinically meaningful CVD risk reduction. [ 36 , 37 ] 5. Confronting obesity early and decisively reshapes the trajectory of CVD by targeting the upstream metabolic disturbances that drive cardiometabolic risk. Making obesity treatment the first therapeutic priority (“treat obesity first”) reframes it as the foundational intervention- one that strengthens and amplifies every downstream component of CVD management rather than functioning as an optional add-on. (See Fig. 26b ) [ 36 , 37 ] 6. With rare exception, treatment of obesity requires sustained, lifelong management comparable to treatment of other chronic conditions like diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Recognizing its relapsing course enables clinicians and patients to adopt care strategies that are durable, compassionate, and grounded in evidence. Describing obesity medications as disease-modifying agents - much like statins – more accurately reflects an evolution in priorities, with the goal being improvements in health (and not just weight), which may help mitigate a key conceptual gap that treatment of obesity is mainly for cosmetic purposes. [ 36 , 37 ] 7. Emerging biomarkers (e.g., inflammatory markers, metabolic signatures, and genetic indicators) have the potential to refine cardiovascular risk prediction in individuals with obesity. Incorporating these tools supports a precision-medicine approach with tailored therapy to biological phenotype rather than population averages. [ 36 , 37 ] 8. Obesity and CVD risk manifest differently across racial, ethnic, socioeconomic, and biological groups, requiring individualized assessment and therapy. Tailored approaches improve equity, relevance, and clinical effectiveness. [ 36 , 37 ] 9. Treatment of obesity must integrate the management of blood glucose, blood pressure, and blood atherogenic lipids, as well as healthful nutrition and routine physical activity, which may have health benefits beyond weight reduction. Assessment and management of other obesity complications, such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), are key in reducing CVD risk (especially atrial fibrillation and resistant hypertension), making sleep hygiene and routine OSA screening essential components of any truly comprehensive approach. [ 36 , 37 ] 10. Optimal care for obesity-related cardiovascular disease relies on a coordinated, multidisciplinary team including clinicians, nurses, dietitians, behavioral specialists, exercise physiologists, psychologists, pharmacists, obesity medicine experts and often bariatric surgeons, all working together to deliver patient-centered treatment. This collaborative model improves adherence, enhances outcomes, and minimizes fragmented care. Expanding access to evidence-based obesity medications further supports this approach by helping improve cardiometabolic risk factors and lowering overall CVD risk. [ 36 , 37 ] Fig. 26a Future Directions of Obesity, Paradigm Shift, and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Early, lifelong obesity management is emerging as a cornerstone of future cardiometabolic care, reflecting a paradigm shift toward intervening before CVD risk becomes entrenched. Treating obesity first - using evidence-based, disease-modifying strategies - positions clinicians to meaningfully reduce long-term cardiovascular risk, especially when initiated early in life. Accurate body composition analyses, precision tools, individualized phenotyping, integrated Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) - aligned management, and coordinated multidisciplinary care represent the next generation of CVD prevention, strengthening outcomes by targeting the full spectrum of cardiometabolic drivers, including sleep apnea. Fig. 26b Treat obesity first. Treatment priorities for patients with co-occurring obesity and complications such as type 2 diabetes (and other cardiometabolic diseases) may best be based on the severity and immediacy of the cardiometabolic abnormality. For patients without acute disease, the primary goal is treating obesity, preferably with evidence-based treatment known to improve glucose and other cardiometabolic risk factors. For patients presenting severe acute illnesses like very high blood glucose, blood pressure, or triglycerides, the immediate priority shifts to stabilizing the acute condition, preferably while also addressing obesity.

## Conclusion (See Fig. 27 )

This Obesity Medicine Association Clinical Practice Statement characterizes obesity as a primary driver of cardiovascular disease (CVD) operating through two distinct but complementary mechanisms. First, “fat mass disease” refers to the direct mechanical effects of excess adipose tissue, which impose biomechanical stress and contribute to conditions such as heart failure and sleep apnea. Second, “sick fat disease” (adiposopathy) reflects dysfunction of adipose tissue, which indirectly elevates CVD risk by promoting major risk factors such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, and directly increases CVD risk through the adverse immune and endocrine activity of epicardial adipose tissue. The overall risk of CVD is strongly influenced by age, race, and sex, as well as by social determinants of health. For many individuals with excess adiposity, a rational clinical approach follows a “treat obesity first” paradigm, which includes healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavioral modification, and evidence-based medical and surgical interventions. Fig. 27 Overall Summary of Obesity and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD). Obesity drives cardiovascular disease through two primary pathways: “fat mass disease” causing biomechanical stress and “sick fat disease” (adiposopathy) leading to endocrinopathies and immunopathies. Determining CVD risk among patients with obesity goes beyond simple body mass index to include factors like body composition, racial, sex and age differences, assessing obesity complications (e.g., insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, chronic kidney disease), and social determinants of health. Finally, optimal CVD risk reduction includes the engagement of a team approach, whose collective goal is to integrate healthful nutrition, physical activity, behavioral modification, evidence-based obesity medications, and bariatric surgery to improve the health of patients, and reduce CVD risk.

### Takeaway messages

• Obesity promotes CVD through “fat mass disease” (biomechanical forces) and “sick fat disease” (adiposopathic endocrine and immune dysfunction). • CVD risk stratification best involves assessment of body composition, while accounting for racial, sex, and age influences, as well as social determinants of health. • The standard of care for obesity has evolved to include healthful nutrition, routine physical activity, behavior modification, and highly effective obesity medications and metabolic surgery as treatment strategies that reduce CVD risk.

## Disclaimer and limitations

This Clinical Practice Statement is not a Guideline, in that it does not provide graded clinical recommendations. Instead, this expert review was developed by the Obesity Medicine Association members to assist clinicians in providing care for patients living with obesity, drawing upon the best available evidence. In areas where scientific data were inconclusive or insufficient, then the authors applied their professional judgment, and portions of this Statement necessarily reflect their expert interpretation of the evidence. This Clinical Practice Statement represents the state of obesity medicine at the time of publication and should not be considered a substitute for ongoing review of emerging research. Decisions by practitioners to apply the principles outlined herein are best made by considering local resources, individual patient circumstances, patient preferences, and applicable federal, state, and local laws and guidance.

conclusions: Effective reduction of obesity-related CVD risk requires shifting from treating downstream risk factors to addressing excessive adipose tissue itself, along with improving adipose tissue function.
