Phosphoinositides (PIPs) are a family of phosphorylated derivatives of phosphatidylinositol (PI) that play essential roles in regulating membrane dynamics, intracellular trafficking, and signal transduction [ 1 , 2 ]. These lipids are tightly regulated by a network of specific kinases and phosphatases, allowing for spatial and temporal control of signaling at distinct membrane compartments. Through their interactions with a wide range of effector proteins, PIPs help define membrane identity and mediate diverse cellular functions.

Viruses, as obligate intracellular parasites, have evolved sophisticated strategies to exploit host cellular machinery, including lipid signaling pathways, to support their replication [ 3 , 4 , 5 ]. Evidence indicates that many viruses manipulate PIP metabolism to facilitate critical steps in their life cycle, such as entry, replication organelle (RO) formation, assembly, and egress [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. In addition to their role in viral replication, PIPs are increasingly recognized as key regulators of innate immune responses. Indeed, several components of antiviral‐signaling pathways, including Toll‐like receptors (TLRs), retinoic acid‐inducible gene I (RIG‐I)‐like receptors (RLRs), and the cyclic‐GMP‐AMP synthase (cGAS)‐stimulator of interferon genes (STING) axis, are influenced by PIP levels and localization [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ]. This dual role of PIPs, supporting both viral replication and antiviral immunity, underscores their central position at the host–virus interface. Given their functional importance, PIP‐related pathways have emerged as attractive targets for antiviral strategy. Approaches include the modulation of PIP metabolism, targeting specific lipid kinases, or interfering with lipid‐transfer proteins, such as oxysterol‐binding protein (OSBP).

This review aimed to provide an overview of the role of PIPs in viral infection. We first examine how they are co‐opted during the viral life cycle, including entry, replication, and egress. Next, we explore how PIPs contribute to antiviral immune signaling through key innate immune pathways. Finally, we highlight emerging strategies for the development of host‐directed antiviral therapies, focusing on targeting PIP kinases or proteins involved in PIP transport as promising broad‐spectrum antiviral approaches.

## Phosphoinositides in viral replication

Many viruses are dependent on host cell metabolic machineries to survive and replicate, and there is substantial evidence that PIPs play a role in regulating many steps in the life cycle of various viruses, such as their attachment and entry into host cells, by remodeling cellular membranes to generate sites of viral replication, and finally for facilitating their assembly and egress.

### Virus entry and endocytosis

PIPs are well‐known regulators of membrane trafficking, cytoskeletal dynamics, and endocytosis, all of which are processes exploited by viruses to enter host cells. Notably, phosphatidylinositol‐4,5‐bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P 2 ] is a critical lipid scaffold that nucleates clathrin‐mediated endocytosis by recruiting the AP‐2 complex, clathrin, and scission factors, a common pathway for the entry of many viruses, including influenza A virus (IAV) and dengue virus (DENV) [ 13 , 14 ]. In the case of human immunodeficiency virus‐1 (HIV‐1), viral entry involves the formation of a fusion pore, which is initiated by the clustering of the T‐cell surface glycoprotein CD4 receptor and chemokine coreceptors [C‐X‐C chemokine receptor type 4 (CXCR4) and C‐C chemokine receptor type 5 (CCR5)] [ 15 ]. This clustering event induces the activation of the kinase phosphatidylinositol 4‐phosphate 5‐kinase type‐1 alpha (PIP5K‐Iα), which produces PI(4,5)P 2 . In parallel, the HIV‐1 glycoprotein gp120 also triggers PIP5K‐Iα activity during viral contact with the host cell, thereby increasing PI(4,5)P 2 levels [ 16 ]. PIPs are also critical regulators of Ebola virus (EBOV) entry into host cells [ 17 , 18 ]. The lipid phosphatidylinositol 3,5‐bisphosphate [PI(3,5)P 2 ], produced by the kinase 1‐phosphatidylinositol 3‐phosphate 5‐kinase (PIKfyve), is essential for endosome maturation and the delivery of EBOV to late endosomes containing the Niemann‐Pick C1 (NPC1; also known as NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 1) receptor, a key step for viral fusion [ 18 ].

### Formation and maintenance of replication organelles

PIPs, especially phosphatidylinositol‐4‐phosphate (PI4P), play a central role in the formation and maintenance of viral replication compartments. These compartments, also referred to as ROs, are specialized membrane structures that many positive‐strand RNA (+RNA) viruses rely on for efficient genome replication. ROs vary in morphology and complexity according to their viral origin; for example, double‐membrane vesicles (DMVs) are produced during hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection (Fig. 1A ), whereas vesicle packets (VPs) originating from endoplasmic reticulum (ER) invagination are induced by orthoflaviviruses, such as DENV or Zika virus (ZIKV) [ 19 , 20 , 21 ].

The virus‐induced remodeling of host cell membranes to create these replication platforms involves both structural rearrangements and the recruitment of specific host lipid signaling pathways, notably those involving PI4P. For example, DMVs formed during HCV infection contain significantly elevated levels of PI4P. This lipid enrichment is achieved through the hijacking of host phosphatidylinositol 4‐kinase‐IIIα (PI4KIIIα/PI4KA), which is recruited and activated by HCV nonstructural protein 5A (NS5A) (Fig. 1B ) [ 22 , 23 ], and PI4KIIIβ/PI4KB [ 24 , 25 ]. Picornaviruses, such as coxsackievirus, poliovirus (PV), and rhinovirus, also use viral proteins to recruit PI4KB to their ROs in order to produce PI4P and support replication [ 26 , 27 , 28 ]. One of the main roles of PI4P in this context is to facilitate key lipid exchange processes through the recruitment of lipid‐transfer proteins, such as OSBP. OSBP mediates the transfer of cholesterol from the ER to the Golgi or viral ROs in exchange for PI4P [ 26 , 29 , 30 , 31 ]. In noninfected cells, this counter‐transport system operates at membrane contact sites (MCS), where the ER comes into close proximity with other organelles and enables the transport of cholesterol against its concentration gradient [ 32 , 33 ]. By generating PI4P at ROs, viruses enhance OSBP recruitment, thereby promoting the influx of cholesterol, a critical lipid component for membrane rigidity, curvature, and viral replication (Fig. 1B ) [ 34 ]. Inhibition of either PI4KB or OSBP disrupts this lipid transport pathway, leading to reduced viral RNA synthesis and disorganization of the RO structure [ 6 , 35 ]. In the case of rhinovirus infection, each protein involved in the OSBP cholesterol/PI4P exchange cycle, including the ER‐receptor VAMP‐associated protein (VAP), the PI4P phosphatase Sac1, and the PI‐transfer protein‐β (PITPβ), contributes to viral replication [ 26 ]. PITPβ is important for transporting PI, regenerated through Sac1‐mediated hydrolysis of PI4P, to ROs, where it helps replenish PI4P levels and sustains the OSBP cycle. Similarly, another PITP called Pyk2 N‐terminal domain‐interacting receptor 2 (NIR2; also known as membrane‐associated phosphatidylinositol transfer protein 1) was shown to support HCV replication by replenishing ROs with PI (Fig. 1B ) [ 36 ].

In addition to OSBP, other PI4P‐binding proteins play important roles in the function of ROs. One such protein is four‐phosphate adaptor protein 2 (FAPP2; also known as pleckstrin homology domain‐containing family A member 8), which localizes to the Golgi apparatus and is involved in glycosphingolipid transport [ 37 ]. FAPP2 is implicated in HCV replication, and its depletion significantly disrupts viral RNA replication. Another key player is ceramide transfer protein (CERT), which is essential for the transport of ceramide, the precursor of sphingomyelin (SM), a lipid that is critical for the structure and function of DMVs during HCV infection (Fig. 1B ) [ 38 ].

Note that some viruses also exploit the endocytic system to acquire the cholesterol necessary for replication. For example, PI4K not only generates PI4P but also participates in trafficking functions by interacting with Ras‐related protein Rab11, a small GTPase associated with recycling endosomes [ 39 ]. Rab11‐positive endosomes can be recruited to ROs to facilitate lipid delivery. Furthermore, several late‐endosomal sterol‐binding proteins, including StAR‐related lipid‐transfer protein 3 (STARD3) and NPC1, transfer low‐density lipoprotein (LDL)‐derived sterols into viral ROs and have been identified as essential for efficient HCV replication [ 40 , 41 ].

In summary, PI4P is instrumental in the viral strategy of reprogramming host lipid metabolism to form and sustain replication compartments. Viruses stimulate PI4K activity to generate PI4P at their replication sites, which in turn drives the recruitment of lipid‐transfer proteins, such as OSBP and FAPP2, and establishes contact sites with other compartments. This interconnected network supplies lipids, such as cholesterol, required for the construction and function of ROs. By co‐opting this machinery, viruses create a protected environment that supports high levels of genome replication while evading host immune detection.

Surprisingly, although replication of flaviviruses, such as DENV or ZIKV, relies heavily on ER lipid remodeling and takes advantage of host lipid pathways, proteins of the OSBP cycle, including VAP, Sac1, and PITPs, as well as PI4Ks, have not been prominently implicated to date [ 42 , 43 , 44 ]. Nevertheless, pharmacological studies showed that OSBP inhibitors block DENV and ZIKV replication [ 45 , 46 , 47 ], suggesting that OSBP may play some role, but further mechanistic evidence is lacking. Moreover, an unbiased proteomics screen placed OSBP‐related proteins ORP9 and ORP11 among Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) and ZIKV‐NS5 interactors, suggesting that they are recruited during Orthoflavivirus infection [ 48 ]. A recent report indicates that ORP9 and ORP11 form a heterodimer at ER– trans ‐Golgi network (TGN) contact sites that counter‐exchanges phosphatidylserine (PS) for PI4P [ 49 ]. Interestingly, the resulting PS buildup in the Golgi apparatus promotes the synthesis of SM, an essential lipid for the flavivirus lifecycle [ 50 , 51 ]. Finally, PI4P itself could play a role in ZIKV infection by facilitating RO formation: a study shows that nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) has a high affinity for PI4P and that this interaction promotes NS1‐induced ER remodeling. Downregulating PI4P levels impairs NS1‐induced ER remodeling and attenuates ZIKV replication [ 52 ].

### Virus assembly and egress

PIPs take central stage during viral particle assembly and egress across very different viruses, including HIV‐1 and EBOV. In the case of HIV‐1, which assembles and buds at the plasma membrane (PM) of infected cells, PI(4,5)P 2 plays a dual role, both as a PM‐targeting signal and as a functional component of the viral assembly platform. First, PI(4,5)P 2 directs the Gag polyprotein to the PM via specific binding to its matrix (MA) domain [ 53 ]. Then, Gag multimerization reorganizes the lipid environment, trapping PI(4,5)P 2 and cholesterol into rigid membrane nanodomains, which facilitate virus budding [ 54 ]. Finally, Gag‐driven local lipid remodeling selectively enriches PI(4,5)P 2 in the viral envelope during assembly [ 55 ]. These processes highlight a reciprocal relationship in which PI(4,5)P 2 recruits Gag to the membrane, and Gag reshapes PI(4,5)P 2 distribution, forming a nanodomain essential for HIV‐1 particle formation.

In the case of EBOV, the matrix protein VP40 binds directly to PI(4,5)P 2 as well as PS via two basic, lysine‐rich regions located on its C‐terminal domain (CTD) [ 56 , 57 ]. Specifically, PS primarily interacts with CTD region 1, facilitating the initial association of VP40 with the PM and inducing conformational changes necessary for oligomerization. However, the stability of these oligomers is limited when only PS is present. PI(4,5)P 2 interacts more strongly with CTD region 2, leading to much greater stabilization of VP40 oligomers and dimers. PI(4,5)P 2 binding results in highly stable oligomeric structures, which are critical for efficient virus‐like particle formation and budding. Notably, decreasing PI(4,5)P 2 levels or preventing VP40–PI(4,5)P 2 binding impairs filamentous virion formation [ 56 ].

PIPs also play a key role in coordinating the last stages of the viral cycle of IAV, a segmented negative‐stranded RNA virus. Upon nucleus exit, IAV viral ribonucleoproteins (vRNPs) must travel to the PM. Recent studies indicate that vRNPs are transported through the cytoplasm by first associating with a remodeled ER, then being loaded onto irregularly coated vesicles that bud from the ER. These vesicles, which rely on the host factor RAB11A, ferry the vRNPs to the PM [ 58 , 59 ]. Interestingly, IAV co‐opts the host protein autophagy‐related protein 16‐1 (ATG16L1) at ER subdomains, where it likely acts as a scaffold or regulator, facilitating the local synthesis of PI4P by interacting with Hyccin (FAM126A; a subunit of the PI4KA complex) and inositol polyphosphate 5‐phosphatase K (INPP5K; a 5‐P phosphatase that generates PI4P) [ 60 ]. This PI4P enrichment creates specialized membrane platforms that recruit RAB11A and its effectors, driving membrane remodeling and the formation of vRNP‐coated transport vesicles. Of note, RAB11A also regulates PI4P turnover and distribution, suggesting that this coordinated action ensures efficient trafficking of viral components to the PM [ 60 ]. At the PM, PI(4,5)P 2 ‐rich nanodomains facilitate the recruitment and clustering of IAV matrix (M1) and hemagglutinin (HA) proteins, promoting coordinated membrane curvature and budding. Super‐resolution studies showed that PI(4,5)P 2 not only marks assembly sites but also contributes to membrane reorganization during virion scission [ 61 ].

Similarly, nonsegmented negative‐strand RNA viruses from the Paramyxoviridae family, which includes measles and Nipah virus, use PI(4,5)P 2 to coordinate their budding from the PM of infected cells [ 62 ]. In this case, PI(4,5)P 2 acts as a crucial membrane anchor and regulator of the viral matrix (M) proteins. At assembly sites beneath the PM, M proteins form a paracrystalline lattice that bridges viral glycoproteins with the ribonucleocapsid complex, driving virion formation. It was shown that M binds specifically to PI(4,5)P 2 , and depletion or inhibition of this lipid reduces M PM localization, virus‐like particle production, and virus replication. Moreover, PI(4,5)P 2 binding induces conformational rearrangements in M dimers that expose a basic patch, enhancing contacts with PM lipids, such as PS. Functionally, PI(4,5)P 2 is indispensable for M‐driven membrane deformation and for M oligomerization into lattices on the membrane [ 62 ]. Taken together, these examples show how viral components interact closely with the host PIP signaling pathway to help viral assembly and exit.

PIPs such as PI4P and PI3P are also exploited during the complex egress process of the Poxiviridae vaccinia virus (VACV). Following initial assembly in cytoplasmic factories, VACV virions are wrapped in crescent‐shaped membrane bilayers derived from the ER, forming spherical immature virus (IV) upon closure. These IVs are subsequently enveloped with membrane cisternae derived from the Golgi or endosomal compartments, giving rise to mature virus (MV) [ 63 ]. A set of conserved viral proteins called virus membrane‐associated proteins (VMAPs) is actively involved in this process and is essential for viral membrane biogenesis and the generation of infectious progeny. Studies have shown that MVs are enriched in PIPs and that several PI3Ks are involved in VACV morphogenesis [ 64 , 65 ], including the IV‐to‐MV transition, likely by enriching these membranes with PI3P. Interestingly, the VMAP H7 possesses a putative PX domain involved in binding PI3P and PI4P [ 66 ]. This interaction is essential for the formation of IV and the infectious brick‐shaped MV, as H7 drives proper formation of hexamers of the scaffold protein D13, which shapes the newly assembled viral membrane into a sphere by organizing a honeycomb‐like lattice [ 67 ]. Thus, PI3P, and possibly PI4P, act as key spatial and functional signals that facilitate the proper envelopment and egress of VACV.

During HCV infection, rewired PI4P also plays an essential role in Golgi phosphoprotein 3 (GOLPH3)‐mediated viral secretion: PI4P generated by PI4KB at the TGN recruits GOLPH3, which in turn interacts with unconventional myosin‐XVIIIa (MYO18A) to exert a tensile force on budding vesicles. Disrupting PI4KB, GOLPH3, or MYO18A impaired the trafficking of HCV particles through the Golgi without affecting viral RNA replication, indicating that this PI4P–GOLPH3–MYO18A axis specifically supports HCV assembly and egress [ 68 ].

## Phosphoinositides as mediators of antiviral immunity

Cellular innate immune processes are responsible for the detection of viruses and participate in the activation of adaptive immune responses. One crucial step allowing the initiation of the pathways involved in these processes is the recognition of viral components by host receptors and the induction of signaling cascades. This leads to the production and secretion of type‐I interferon (IFN) and cytokines displaying broad antiviral activities. As in other signaling pathways, PIPs often serve key roles in sensing and regulatory processes that control cellular responses [ 2 ]. The antiviral response begins when innate immunity receptors from the pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) superfamily, including TLRs, RLRs, and cGAS, detect conserved viral molecular motifs known as pathogen‐associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). PAMPs consist of virus‐derived structures, such as glycoproteins, single‐stranded RNA (ssRNA), double‐stranded RNA (dsRNA), double‐stranded DNA (dsDNA), and unmethylated CpG‐containing DNA. Upon activation, PRRs initiate signaling cascades that lead to the activation of downstream effectors, such as TANK‐binding kinase 1 (TBK1; also known as serine/threonine‐protein kinase TBK1), through post‐translational modifications, ultimately resulting in the nuclear translocation of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF‐3) or nuclear factor kappa B (NF‐κB) to drive the expression of antiviral genes [ 69 ].

### PIPs control of toll‐like receptor pathways

TLRs are type‐I transmembrane proteins encompassing N‐terminal extracellular/luminal leucine‐rich repeats (LRRs) and a C‐terminal cytosolic Toll/interleukin‐1 receptor (TIR) domain (Fig. 2A ). PAMPs such as viral glycoproteins can be recognized by LRRs of TLR2 and TLR4 at the PM, whereas within endolysosomal compartments, TLR3 detects dsRNA, TLR7 and TLR8 sense ssRNA, and TLR9 responds to unmethylated CpG DNA [ 70 ]. For example, TLR4 is activated by glycoproteins from several RNA viruses, such as DENV, SARS‐CoV‐2, EBOV, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) [ 71 ]. Some PIPs help regulate the spatial localization of TLRs, thereby controlling the fate of downstream signaling cascades (Fig. 2A ). Upon sensing, TLR dimerization activates signaling pathways that originate from the interaction between TIR domains and adaptor proteins, such as TIR domain‐containing adaptor protein (TIRAP) at the PM or TRIF‐related adapter molecule (TRAM) at endosomes: TIRAP recruits myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88), triggering NF‐κB and mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways, whereas TRAM is required for the engagement of TIR domain‐containing adapter‐inducing IFN‐β [TRIF; also known as TIR domain‐containing adapter molecule 1 (TICAM1)], promoting type‐I IFN signaling [ 72 ]. Of note, TIRAP encompasses an N‐terminal PI(4,5)P 2 ‐binding site, which enables its recruitment to the PM and is necessary to induce proper cytokine production following TLR4 activation [ 73 ]. PIP5Kα appears to provide the PI(4,5)P 2 needed for this process, as its knockdown or inactivation in microglial cells blocked TLR4 signaling. Furthermore, degradation of PI(4,5)P 2 by 1‐phosphatidylinositol 4,5‐bisphosphate phosphodiesterase gamma‐2 (PLCγ2) has been proposed to act as a molecular switch in the transition from the TLR4–TIRAP–MyD88 complex at the PM to the MyD88‐independent pathway involving the TLR4–TRAM–TRIF complex at the endosomes, after internalization of TLR4 through clathrin‐ and dynamin‐mediated endocytosis [ 9 ].

In addition to its role at the PM, TIRAP has also been proposed to mediate TLR7 and TLR9 signaling: in cells lacking TIRAP, responses to TLR7 and TLR9 ligands were impaired, unless the ligands were present at very high concentrations [ 74 ]. To facilitate proper bridging of MyD88 to endosomal TLR9, TIRAP was shown to preferentially bind lipids, such as PI3P, PS, and likely PI(3,5)P 2 , rather than PI(4,5)P 2 , highlighting the diverse roles of PIPs in shaping distinct TLR signaling pathways [ 74 ].

### PIP signaling in modulating the RIG ‐I pathway

Another way for the host cell to sense dsRNA is through the RLR. Recent studies have revealed an important role for PIPs in regulating RIG‐I signaling at endosomes. Upon RNA recognition, RIG‐I translocates to endosomes/lysosomes, where it undergoes lysine 63 (K63)‐linked ubiquitination by the E3‐ligase tripartite motif‐containing protein 25 (TRIM25; also known as E3 ubiquitin/ISG15 ligase TRIM25), a process that depends on the adaptor protein TBK1‐associated protein in endolysosomes (TAPE; also known as coiled‐coil and C2 domain‐containing protein 1A) (Fig. 2B ). TAPE binds strongly to PI4P‐ or PI3P‐rich membranes, enabling its endosomal attachment, and links RIG‐I to TRIM25. TAPE also associates with mitochondrial antiviral‐signaling protein [MAVS; also known as interferon beta promoter stimulator protein 1 (IPS‐1)], a mitochondria transmembrane protein [ 75 ]. Upon ubiquitination, RIG‐I oligomerizes and binds to MAVS, triggering MAVS oligomerization (Fig. 2B ). These MAVS filaments on the mitochondrial surface serve as scaffolds for recruiting downstream signaling proteins, including TBK1. Disrupting endosomal function or TAPE expression impairs ubiquitination of RIG‐I and dampens antiviral responses, highlighting the importance of PIP‐rich endosomal domains in supporting RIG‐I signaling [ 76 ].

Interestingly, IAV induces RIG‐I‐dependent PI3K signaling, ensuring proper activation of downstream pathways and expression of type‐I IFN. PI3K activation is reported to be necessary for complete IRF‐3 phosphorylation, and inhibiting either PI3K or PIP3 signaling in IAV‐infected cells resulted in reduced TBK1 and IRF3 activities [ 77 ]. Notably, IAV viral RNA (vRNA)‐induced PI3K activation is abolished when RIG‐I , TRIM25 , and MAVS are silenced, supporting the idea that IAV vRNA serves as a stimulus for the RIG‐I–MAVS axis, mediating the activation of PI3K. Inhibition of PI3K with LY29400 also decreases downstream IRF3 activation and IFNB mRNA expression following vRNA stimulation, suggesting the importance of RIG‐I‐dependent activation of PI3K signaling in immune response [ 78 ]. Another study further supported a role for PI3K, along with Akt, in the regulation of IRF3 activation and IFNB expression in RIG‐I–MAVS signaling upon polyinosinic‐polycytidylic acid [poly(I:C)] stimulation or Sendai virus infection [ 79 ]. Moreover, co‐immunoprecipitation experiments showed that both the Akt pleckstrin homology (PH) domain and PI3K regulatory subunit p85β bind to the MAVS caspase activation and recruitment (CARD) domain. PI3K and Akt were hence suggested to associate with MAVS upon viral infection, providing a signaling platform for activation of downstream immune events. In a parallel pathway, the IAV NS1 protein directly interacts with the p85β subunit of PI3K, leading to PI3K activation and contributing to a delay in virus‐induced apoptosis [ 80 ].

Overall, although the involvement of PIPs is suggested by their downstream enhancement of IRF3 activation and type‐I IFN production, their precise roles in modulating RIG‐I–MAVS complexes remain unclear. Similarly, the contribution of the PI3K signaling network to antiviral innate immunity requires further elucidation. Given its broad involvement in diverse cellular processes, the downstream pathways and biological effects of PI3K activation are likely to vary in a spatiotemporal and context‐dependent manner. Additional limitations include the potential off‐target effects of PI3K inhibitors used in these studies, as well as possible virus‐ and cell‐type‐specific differences in how PI3K is engaged during RIG‐I signaling.

### PI4P turnover in the cGAS – STING pathway

The cGAS–STING pathway is activated when cGAS detects cytosolic viral or self‐derived dsDNA in the cytosol, leading to the production of the second messenger 2′,3′‐cyclic‐GMP‐AMP (cGAMP) (Fig. 3A ). Then, the binding of cGAMP to STING, an ER‐resident transmembrane protein, triggers STING activation and induces its transport to the Golgi apparatus, where it binds luminal sulfated glycosaminoglycans (sGAGs) through electrostatic interactions, promoting its polymerization [ 81 ]. Thereafter, polymerized STING recruits and activates the kinase TBK1, thereby leading to the nuclear translocation of IRF3 or NF‐κB (Fig. 3B ). Of note, cGAS is sequestered at the PM in its inactive state through interaction with PI(4,5)P 2 , a localization shown to be crucial for preventing inappropriate activation by self‐DNA while still allowing effective detection of viral DNA [ 10 ]. Evidence suggests that STING also plays a role in immune responses during infection with several RNA viruses, such as DENV, ZIKV, HCV, SARS‐CoV‐2, and IAV [ 82 , 83 ].

Recent work has shed light on the critical role of lipid homeostasis, especially of PI4P and cholesterol, in regulating STING localization and activation (Fig. 3C ). Fang et al . [ 11 ] showed that PI4KB and PI4P are essential for STING downstream signaling, with armadillo‐like helical domain‐containing protein 3 (ARMH3; C10orf76/DGARM) acting as an important mediator. ARMH3, an ADP‐ribosylation factor‐like protein 5 (ARL5) effector localized to the distal Golgi/TGN, recruits PI4KB, enhances PI4KB‐dependent PI4P synthesis, and was found to interact with STING [ 84 , 85 ]. The interaction between ARMH3 and PI4KB was found to be crucial for promoting STING polymerization, and, notably, only the catalytically active form of PI4KB supported STING puncta formation and downstream signaling [ 11 ]. Moreover, the depletion of PI4P by directing Sac1 phosphatase to the TGN suppressed STING puncta formation and type‐I IFN induction, emphasizing the essential role of PI4P in this pathway. Mechanistically, PI4P is thought to: (a) facilitate anterograde transport of STING from the TGN to endosomes by recruiting PI4P‐binding clathrin adaptors, such as the AP‐1 complex or Golgi‐localized γ ear‐containing ARF‐binding protein 2 (GGA2), and (b) promote cholesterol and SM enrichment at the TGN by recruiting lipid‐transfer proteins, thereby creating a lipid environment favorable for STING activation (Fig. 3C ). The post‐Golgi trafficking of STING is important for sustaining and amplifying STING activation, likely because its interaction with sGAGs is enhanced in the acidic environment of endosomes. Moreover, lipid‐transfer proteins that bind PI4P, including CERT, OSBP and various OSBP‐related proteins (ORP1, ORP6, ORP9, and ORP11), were found to be critical for STING activation [ 11 ]. Indeed, the inhibition of CERT by HPA‐12 or by deleting SM synthetase 1 (which converts ceramide to SM) significantly impaired STING signaling, highlighting that SM, rather than ceramide, is important for STING activation [ 11 ]. Similarly, blocking OSBP using itraconazole (ITZ), or interfering with cholesterol trafficking using methyl‐β‐cyclodextrin, disrupted STING activation, indicating that cholesterol homeostasis also accounts for STING function. Furthermore, evidence suggests that STING clustering, which strengthens its association with TBK1, depends on both its palmitoylation and the ordered lipid environment of the Golgi membrane, defined by cholesterol accumulation [ 86 , 87 ]. Notably, blocking STING palmitoylation significantly impairs TBK1 phosphorylation. Interestingly, STING activation also induces the expression of cholesterol 25‐hydroxylase (CH25H), which produces 25‐hydroxycholesterol (25‐HC), a natural inhibitor of OSBP. By blocking OSBP, 25‐HC acts as a negative regulator of STING, revealing a cholesterol‐dependent feedback loop [ 86 ]. Finally, the Golgi adaptor protein acyl‐coenzyme A binding domain‐containing protein 3 (ACBD3; also known as Golgi resident protein GCP60), known to recruit PI4KB to the TGN and increase its activity [ 88 ], was found to be another key player in STING activation during innate immune responses [ 12 ]. ACBD3 and STING were found to colocalize in Golgi clusters and, upon ACBD3 depletion or knockout, STING remained at the ER. However, in this study, inhibition of PI4KB and OSBP had opposite effects on STING signaling: ITZ, which inhibits OSBP and thereby increases PI4P levels at the TGN, was shown to enhance STING activation. OSBP inhibition via ITZ also induced a significant decrease in STING degradation, up to 20 h after its activation [ 12 ].

Thus, STING emerges as a key player in antiviral immunity, with its activity and spatial regulation tightly controlled by the lipid environment, most notably through PI4P accumulation at the distal Golgi, which appears to be a dominant factor in its activation (Fig. 3C ). However, these observations were established essentially upon DNA stimulation and not upon RNA or poly(I:C) stimulation, which mimic RNA virus infection. Still, STING's noncanonical involvement in viral replication was recently described for some RNA viruses, either through enhancement of their replication, such as during human rhinovirus, enterovirus D68, and SARS‐CoV‐2 infections, in which STING localizes to PI4P‐rich replication organelles [ 89 , 90 ], or its impairment, in the case of human coronavirus OC43 (HCoV‐OC43), in which STING seems to disrupt the interaction between nonstructural proteins Nsp4 and Nsp6 [ 91 ]. In addition, the involvement of STING in the life cycle of RNA viruses of concern, notably through immune activation or evasion strategies employed by these viruses to thrive, has been discussed previously [ 82 , 92 ].

Overall, PIPs are more than membrane‐organizing lipids; they can act as gatekeepers of compartmentalized immune signaling, having an active role in defining spatial localization and activation of key antiviral effectors, such as TLRs, RIG‐I, cGAS, or STING.

## Phosphoinositides in the development of antivirals

### Antiviral properties of PI in pulmonary surfactant

Pulmonary surfactant, primarily known for reducing surface tension in the alveoli to prevent lung collapse, also plays important immunological and antiviral roles [ 93 ]. PI, a minor lipid component of pulmonary surfactant, as well as phosphatidylglycerol (PG), has been increasingly recognized for their direct antiviral properties [ 94 ]. Notably, they play a significant role in inhibiting viral entry and endocytosis, particularly during infection by RSV, a leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections in children. PI and palmitoyl‐oleoyl‐PG (POPG) bind RSV with high affinity and strongly disrupt its attachment to epithelial cells [ 95 ], thereby blocking viral entry and subsequent infection. Other lipids do not demonstrate the same inhibitory action on viral attachment, highlighting the unique role of PI and PG in preventing viral spreading at the earliest stage of infection. In addition, PI and POPG liposomes can inhibit RSV infection in vivo when administered to mice intranasally simultaneously or as a prophylactic treatment [ 95 ]. The slower turnover of PI compared with PG in mice lungs may provide longer protection. Beyond its antiviral properties, surfactant PI also antagonizes TLR activation, particularly TLR4, which contributes to the pathogenesis of several respiratory viral infections, including IAV and SARS‐CoV‐2 infections [ 93 ]. By interfering with the recognition of PAMPs by TLR coreceptors, PI prevents the initiation of pro‐inflammatory signaling cascades. Thus, PI provides a two‐layer defense: it prevents pathogens from entering cells and limits harmful inflammation.

### Antivirals targeting PI3 ‐kinases and PIKfyve

PI3Ks are lipid kinases that regulate cell growth, survival, metabolism, and vesicular trafficking. Many viruses exploit the PI3K–Akt pathway to facilitate entry, vesicle trafficking, replication, and to prevent premature apoptosis of host cells. This has prompted interest in PI3K inhibitors as antiviral agents [ 96 ]. However, PI3Ks also play roles in antiviral host defenses, including IFN signaling [ 78 ]. Unlike PI4Ks, which are exploited predominantly by positive‐sense single‐stranded RNA [(+)ssRNA] viruses, PI3Ks are hijacked by a broader range of viruses, including both positive‐ and negative‐sense RNA viruses. A key example is IAV, which recruits type‐I PI3K at multiple stages (entry, replication, and inhibition of apoptosis) via its NS1 viral protein [ 77 , 80 ].

Among the most studied PI3K inhibitors are wortmannin and LY294002. Wortmannin irreversibly inhibits PI3K with high potency, whereas LY294002 is a reversible, less potent but more stable compound. Both prevent PIP3 production and downstream Akt activation, and have shown antiviral effects against IAV, arenaviruses, orthoflaviviruses, and HCV [ 97 , 98 , 99 , 100 , 101 ]. In JEV and DENV infections, early PI3K–Akt activation protects infected cells from caspase‐dependent apoptosis. Inhibitor treatment restores apoptotic signaling and cell death, thereby limiting viral spread without affecting viral protein synthesis or RNA replication [ 98 ]. However, DENV can bypass PI3K inhibition by switching to cap‐independent translation during stress, showing its adaptability [ 102 ]. Wortmannin also reduces ZIKV infection by blocking early stages of autophagy, and subsequently decreasing lipid droplets and cholesterol availability, disrupting the maintenance of infection [ 103 ]. However, in neural stem cells, ZIKV suppresses PI3K–Akt via its NS4A and NS4B proteins to induce autophagy and support replication, a process normally inhibited by wortmannin [ 104 ]. In some contexts, PI3K inhibition can be proviral. For example, LY294002 enhances West Nile virus (WNV) replication in macrophages by impairing IRF7‐dependent IFN responses, especially via PI3K p110δ [ 105 ], underscoring the context‐ and cell‐type‐specific effects.

More recently, C20 ( PWT33597 ), a dual PI3K/Akt inhibitor, displayed broad activity against β‐coronaviruses, such as SARS‐CoV‐2 and HCoV‐OC43, along with immunomodulatory properties [ 106 ]. Indeed, beyond roles in autophagy and survival during viral infection, PI3K inhibitors can modulate adverse outcomes of viral infection, such as immune response and associated inflammation. For example, the PI3Kγ inhibitor AS605240 significantly lowered ZIKV replication and neuronal damage in vitro and in vivo , limiting viral pathology in mice [ 107 ].

Targeting phosphatidylinositol 3‐kinase VPS34, the sole type‐III PI3K, is also a promising antiviral approach. VPS34 produces PI3P, a precursor of PI(3,5)P 2 , via the downstream kinase PIKfyve. VPS34 inhibitors, such as SAR405 or PIK‐III impair the replication of viruses, such as SARS‐CoV‐2, but also Enterovirus 71 (EV71), for which VPS34 was shown to contribute to RO biogenesis [ 108 ]. SAR405 inhibits SARS‐CoV‐2 replication and spike protein levels in a dose‐dependent manner. Cell pretreatment up to 24 h prior to infection enhances this effect by reducing endocytic uptake and decreasing the availability of apically localized angiotensin‐converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors, which are critical for viral entry [ 109 ]. Similarly, VPS34‐IN1 (a highly selective and potent inhibitor of VPS34) and PIK‐III reduce SARS‐CoV‐2 replication, likely acting on viral entry and a later stage of the viral cycle [ 110 ].

PIKfyve, which converts PI3P to PI(3,5)P 2 , is essential for endolysosomal membrane dynamics. Viruses such as EBOV, Marburg, and SARS‐CoV‐2 depend on this pathway for entry [ 18 , 111 , 112 ]. PIKfyve inhibitors such as apilimod and YM201636 block viral entry by preventing virion trafficking to compartments where membrane fusion occurs [ 112 ]. Furthermore, dual‐targeting approaches seem promising: for instance, UNI418 (a dual PIKfyve/PIP5K1 inhibitor) is active against SARS‐CoV‐2 [ 113 ]. Combining inhibition of PIKfyve and TMPRSS2, a serine protease involved in SARS‐CoV‐2 spike protein priming, using apilimod in conjunction with camostat mesylate or nafamostat mesylate produces synergistic entry blockade [ 114 ]. Apilimod has nanomolar efficacy against SARS‐CoV‐2 in vitro and has reached phase II trials, although it may worsen immune dysfunction [ 115 ].

### Antivirals targeting PI4 ‐kinases

Mammalian PI4Ks are divided into type‐II PI4Ks, including PI4KIIα and PI4KIIβ, and type‐III PI4Ks, comprising PI4KA and PI4KB [ 1 ]. Among these, type‐III PI4Ks have been the most extensively studied in the context of viral infections. PI4KA is primarily localized at the PM, whereas PI4KB is enriched at the Golgi and TGN. Both enzymes contribute to maintaining PI4P homeostasis and regulating lipid composition at specific subcellular membranes (Fig. 1B ).

PI4KA plays a key role in the replication of some (+)ssRNA viruses, including HCV and encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) [ 116 ]. These viruses recruit PI4KA to their ROs, generating PI4P‐ and cholesterol‐rich membranes that support replication, making PI4KA a potential antiviral target. Various compounds have been studied for this purpose (Table 1 ). Tyrphostin AG1478, originally an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitor, also inhibits PI4KA directly [ 117 ]. Other selective inhibitors, such as 4‐anilinoquinazoline derivatives (e.g., AL‐9 and quinazolinone 28), have shown anti‐HCV activity in vitro [ 118 , 119 ]. More recently, GSK‐A1, a derivative of quinazolinone 28, was shown to impair vRNP trafficking and viral progeny production in IAV‐infected A549 cells [ 60 ]. However, amid promising in vitro results, in vivo PI4KA inhibition has proven highly toxic. One study reported that both pharmacological inhibition and genetic inactivation of PI4KA in adult mice were lethal, although through distinct mechanisms [ 133 ]. Thus, although the pivotal role of PI4KA is clear, its targeting remains limited by severe toxicity concerns.

PI4KB is essential for the replication of many Picornaviridae viruses, including PV, coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3), Aichi virus (AiV), and enteroviruses 68 and 71 (EV‐D68, EV‐A71) [ 134 ]. These viruses encode the nonstructural protein 3A, which hijacks ACBD3 to recruit PI4KB, promoting PI4P‐enriched membrane formation at replication sites [ 135 ]. Given the demonstrated proviral effect of PI4KB across several (+)ssRNA viruses, multiple PI4KB‐targeting antivirals have been developed (Table 1 ), some reaching clinical trials.

PIK93, a potent and relatively selective PI4KB inhibitor, has been widely used to study enterovirus replication [ 24 ]. It also showed effects on HCV replication [ 24 , 25 , 120 ], although siRNA experiments later highlighted PI4KA as the primary kinase involved [ 23 ]. Despite its potency, off‐target effects of PIK93 on type‐I and type‐III PI3Ks limit its specificity [ 136 ]. To improve this, selective analogs, such as PI4KIIIβ‐IN‐9 (IN‐9) and PI4KIIIβ‐IN‐10 (IN‐10), were developed, showing antiviral activity against HCV and ZIKV, although data remain limited [ 121 ].

Enviroxime, a benzimidazole derivative discovered in the 1970s [ 137 ], was one of the first antivirals found to target PI4KB, although its mechanism remained unclear for decades. It blocks RO formation by disrupting the PI4KB–3A viral protein axis, a mechanism conserved across picornaviruses [ 122 , 123 ]. Resistance mutations in 3A confirmed its role as the functional target of enviroxime and related enviroxime‐like compounds [ 27 , 138 ]. Although enviroxime and the enviroxime‐like compound BF738735 also showed activity against HCV, this was later linked to PI3K inhibition rather than PI4KB [ 139 ]. Due to poor pharmacokinetics, side effects, and limited efficacy in vivo , clinical development of enviroxime was discontinued [ 124 , 125 ]. However, it inspired the development of more potent and selective PI4KB inhibitors, including the enviroxime‐like compound T‐00127‐HEV1 [ 27 ], GSK3923868, CUR‐N399, and KR‐26549. Among these, CUR‐N399 demonstrated strong in vitro activity and a favorable safety profile in preclinical models [ 140 ]. GSK3923868 entered clinical trials (2020–2024) primarily targeting respiratory conditions, such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which are frequently exacerbated by viral respiratory infections, providing groundwork for their antiviral use [ 121 ].

Most PI4KB inhibitors show efficacy mainly against picornaviruses, but some studies explored their role during Orthoflavivirus infection, as these vector‐borne pathogens pose a growing public health threat linked to their strong reemergence potential and lack of efficient treatment. Results are mixed: PIK93 did not affect WNV or Usutu virus (USUV) replication [ 44 ], and IN‐10 failed to inhibit ZIKV in some models [ 43 ], although IN‐9 did reduce ZIKV replication at higher doses [ 52 ]. Bithiazole‐based PI4KB inhibitors have emerged as promising broad‐spectrum antiviral candidates, showing activity not only against viruses from the Picornaviridae but also Flaviviridae and Coronaviridae families [ 141 ]. The bithiazole core is essential for antiviral activity, and further functionalization has led to compounds, such as MR340, which inhibits human rhinoviruses (hRV2 and hRV14), ZIKV, and SARS‐CoV‐2 at low micromolar concentrations. Newer derivatives (e.g., MR373 and MR370) demonstrated potent, selective PI4KB inhibition and broad antiviral activity, supporting their potential for further preclinical development [ 126 ]. Of note, only five out of 10 of the newly designed compounds were active against ZIKV, whereas none were effective against WNV. The observed effects on ZIKV could be attributed to their action on PI4KB but also on additional unknown targets, suggesting that targeting solely PI4KB seems insufficient to tackle Orthoflavivirus infection [ 126 ].

Finally, a recent study reported that, in A549 cells treated with T‐00127‐HEV1, PV replication was inhibited, although that of orthoflaviviruses remained largely unaffected, with the exception of WNV, which exhibited modest sensitivity [ 127 ]. These mixed results emphasize the need for caution when generalizing the role of PI4Ks and the use of PIPs across orthoflaviviruses, which may employ distinct lipid‐modifying strategies, as highlighted by recent lipidomics studies [ 142 ]. Overall, although many PI4KB inhibitors show high potency, off‐target effects on PI4KA and PI3Ks remain a concern, contributing to cytotoxicity and limiting therapeutic use.

The ability of PIP kinases to participate in diverse viral processes, ranging from entry to replication, underscores the therapeutic potential of modulating such lipid pathways. However, the central role of PIP kinases in fundamental cellular processes, such as membrane dynamics, endocytosis, and immune signaling, poses a major limitation, raising concerns about toxicity and off‐target effects. Future antiviral strategies will need to focus on achieving selectivity, context‐dependent targeting, and minimizing disruption of essential host functions.

### Targeting host lipid‐transfer protein OSBP

OSBP has emerged as a critical host factor in viral replication, particularly for HCV and picornaviruses, through its role in cholesterol trafficking and membranous web integrity. OSBP interacts directly with the HCV protein NS5A (Fig. 1B ), and its intracellular levels influence both replication and viral particle release [ 29 , 143 ]. Similarly, OSBP supports replication of several picornaviruses, including AiV, PV, CVB3, rhinovirus, and EMCV [ 26 , 116 , 144 , 145 ]. For this reason, although OSBP inhibitors were initially studied for their anticancer potential [ 146 ], OSBP has since gained attention as a promising target for host‐directed antiviral strategies (Table 1 ).

Various structurally diverse small molecules inhibit OSBP, with antiviral effects. Minor enviroxime‐like compounds showing anti‐PV activity, such as T‐00127‐HEV2 and AN‐12‐H5, target OSBP and interfere with PI4P turnover at the Golgi, similarly to 25‐HC, a natural OSBP ligand [ 30 ]. TTP‐8307, another identified OSBP inhibitor, inhibits replication of CVB3, EMCV, and HCV, likely by binding the OSBP‐related ligand‐binding domain (ORD) [ 128 ]. Among approved drugs, the antifungal ITZ inhibits OSBP‐mediated cholesterol/PI4P exchange, showing broad activity against enteroviruses and HCV [ 31 ]. ITZ also targets OSBP‐related protein 4 (ORP4; also known as oxysterol‐binding protein 2). Over the years, the role of OSBP in the replication of viruses beyond picornaviruses and HCV has started to emerge through both pharmacological inhibition and gene‐silencing approaches. Posaconazole (POS), a structural analog of ITZ, blocks DENV and ZIKV replication by impairing viral RNA synthesis. Knockdown and rescue studies confirmed OSBP, but not ORP4, as the principal target, although ORP2, ORP11, and possibly ORP4 may also contribute to replication [ 45 ].

In addition to triazoles, ORPphilins, natural products first recognized for their anticancer properties and their ability to modulate OSBP function [ 146 , 147 , 148 ], have demonstrated potent antiviral activity. OSW‐1 (also known as Orsaponin), the most studied ORPphilin, inhibits the replication of a large panel of enteroviruses, DENV, and coronaviruses, such as SARS‐CoV‐2 and human coronavirus HCoV‐229E [ 28 , 29 , 31 , 45 ]. Interestingly, transient, low‐dose OSW‐1 treatment induces prolonged OSBP depletion via an unknown mechanism, resulting in multigenerational inhibition of enterovirus replication [ 129 ]. Studies also demonstrated efficient inhibition of SARS‐CoV‐2 and HCoV‐229E upon treatment with OSW‐1 at concentrations ranging from n m to μ m [ 130 , 131 ]. Electron microscopy revealed that OSW‐1 disrupts DMV formation and downstream viral morphogenesis during SARS‐CoV‐2 infection [ 130 ], with Nsp3, Nsp4, and Nsp6 likely implicated in both OSBP and vesicle‐associated membrane protein‐associated protein B (VAPB) recruitment. ZJ‐1, a simplified OSW‐1 analog, also reduces OSBP levels and inhibits coronaviruses at nanomolar doses [ 132 ]. Additionally, the function of OSBP in SARS‐CoV‐2 infection appears not only to be limited to DMV formation, as OSW‐1 treatment upregulates type‐I and ‐III IFN‐stimulated genes (ISGs) in airway epithelial cells [ 131 ]. Nevertheless, OSW‐1 cytotoxicity and limited selectivity have restricted its therapeutic use. A promising alternative is macarangin B, a newly identified ORPphilin with a minimalist structure and lower cytotoxicity across multiple cell lines [ 46 ]. It potently inhibits ZIKV RNA replication and progeny production. Both enantiomers of macarangin B effectively reduced ZIKV RNA even at nanomolar concentrations and demonstrated higher selectivity for OSBP over ORP4, in contrast to OSW‐1.

Current studies strongly suggest a proviral role for OSBP during viral infection, highlighting the need for further investigation to determine its exact function throughout the viral life cycle and the potential involvement of other partners or ORPs in these processes. These findings also underscore the promising potential of OSBP inhibitors as antiviral agents, provided they exhibit low cytotoxicity, minimal off‐target effects, and suitable bioavailability.

## Conclusion and perspectives

The role of PIPs has long been studied during HCV and picornaviruses infections, laying the groundwork for investigating their involvement in other viral infections. While an increasing number of studies are now focusing on various emerging and re‐emerging viruses of concern, data on the specific functions of PIPs in their life cycles remain limited and, currently, strategies to combat these viruses are often inadequate. A notable example is arboviruses (arthropod‐borne viruses), including members from the Orthoflavivirus genus among others. These viruses, once largely restricted to tropical endemic regions, are now spreading into temperate zones. Climate‐related hazards and globalization can exacerbate the spread and impact of these diseases [ 149 , 150 ], treatment for which often only relies on management of the symptoms, urging the need for novel antiviral strategies.

Since the approval of the very first antiviral, idoxuridine, in 1963, about 100 antiviral treatments have been approved by regulatory health agencies worldwide; however, these primarily target a limited set of pathogens, including HIV, HCV, hepatitis B virus, herpesvirus, human cytomegalovirus, RSV, and, more recently, SARS‐CoV‐2, among others [ 151 ]. Most of these drugs are direct‐acting antiviral agents (DAAs) that inhibit viral enzymes, such as proteases, polymerases, or integrases to block viral genome replication and polyprotein processing. Despite their success in improving clinical outcomes, DAAs have intrinsic limitations, including a narrow spectrum of activity and the rapid development of resistance, particularly among RNA viruses with high mutation rates. These limitations have intensified efforts to identify host‐targeted antiviral (HTA) strategies that exploit cellular pathways essential for viral replication. By targeting host functions, such strategies promise broad‐spectrum efficacy and a higher genetic barrier to resistance. Their limitations include the need to minimize toxicity and identify an appropriate therapeutic window, particularly in the context of acute infections.

Given the central role of lipid metabolism in various stages of the viral life cycle, from membrane fusion and replication complex formation to virion assembly, this cellular pathway has emerged as a promising target for novel antiviral strategies, particularly against viruses of rising concern for which often no vaccines or specific treatments currently exist. Mirroring the surge of drug repurposing efforts seen during the COVID‐19 pandemic [ 152 ], cholesterol‐lowering drugs, such as statins, for instance, have been evaluated for their ability to modulate lipid pathways involved in viral replication, including cholesterol biosynthesis and lipid droplet dynamics [ 153 , 154 ]. Beyond neutral lipid metabolism, PIP metabolism, involving minor but dynamic phospholipids with multiple roles in viral infection, has been and continues to be studied for its potential for novel antiviral strategies. However, it should be noted that the use of compounds targeting PIP metabolism requires a finely tuned strategy, since this pathway is essential for normal cellular function. Such an approach may narrow the therapeutic window but could also offer a dual benefit by simultaneously inhibiting the viral life cycle and enhancing antiviral defenses.

figure_captions: Fig. 1 Model for lipids exchange at ER‐DMV contact sites. (A) During infection, some +ssRNA viruses induce protrusion‐type ROs, generally consisting of DMVs. They act as a platform to enable proper viral replication but also as a means to escape from the cytosolic antiviral response. DMVs, generated for instance by HCV, originate primarily from the ER. The replication complex faces the cytoplasmic leaflet of the ER within DMVs, which release the newly formed viral genome into the cytosol for subsequent virion assembly. (B) Molecular details corresponding to the black square in (A). PI4KA and PI4KB are both recruited to DMVs, the first one specifically through HCV NS5A, to promote PI4P synthesis. PI4P triggers the recruitment of several lipid‐transfer proteins, such as OSBP, CERT, NIR2, and FAPP2. NS5A interacts directly with OSBP as well (dotted arrow). OSBP promotes cholesterol influx to DMVs thanks to the counter‐transport of PI4P, whereas CERT imports ceramide, which will be converted into SM. NIR2 replenishes the DMVs with PI, originating from PI4P hydrolysis by Sac1 phosphatase at the ER. This PI will serve as a substrate for PI4KA or PI4KB to produce more PI4P at the DMVs. Finally, FAPP2 enables the transport of glucosylceramide (GlcCer), which is the precursor of glycosphingolipids. The figure was created using Canvas X Draw. Fig. 2 Model for PIPs contribution to the TLR and RIG‐I pathways. (A) Upon recognition of a ligand, TLR4 activates and dimerizes. The TIRAP adaptor is recruited to activated TLR4, specifically through PI(4,5)P 2 binding at the PM, enabling the proper recruitment of MyD88 adaptor and subsequent activation of NF‐κB, ultimately leading to cytokine production. In the MyD88‐independent pathway, TLR4 is relocated to endosomes through the generation of diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5‐trisphosphate (IP3), along with Ca2+ release, by PLCγ2. TRAM and TRIF adaptors are then recruited to enable a downstream cascade leading to type‐I IFN production. Of note, the TLR4–TRAM–TRIF axis was elucidated in the context of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), from Gram (−) bacteria, binding to TLR4. Upon recognition of CpG DNA by endosomal TLR9, the TIRAP adaptor is recruited to the endosome through its affinity with PI(3,5)P2, PI3P and PS, thereby ensuring downstream IRF3 and NF‐κB translocation along with appropriate immune responses. (B) RIG‐I changes its conformation upon sensing vRNA released following virus–endosome fusion, exposing its CARD domains, and is proposed to relocalize to the endosomal surface. The TAPE adaptor is recruited to endolysosome membranes via binding of its C2 domain to PI4P. This enables the recruitment of TRIM25, which ubiquitinates RIG‐I, allowing its oligomerization. Then, RIG‐I oligomers trigger MAVS oligomerization and activation at mitochondria. TAPE also interacts with MAVS, but whether TAPE enables endosome–mitochondria MCS is unclear. The MAVS oligomer serves as a scaffold for proper TBK1 recruitment and activation, triggering the downstream cascade leading to type‐I IFN signaling. The figure was created using Canvas X Draw. Fig. 3 Model for PIPs as modulators of the cGAS–STING pathway. (A) In its inactive state, cGAS localizes to the PM by binding to PI(4,5)P 2 . Upon sensing viral or self‐derived dsDNA, sometimes triggered by RNA viruses, cGAS translocates to the cytosol, where it dimerizes and synthesizes the second messenger 2′,3′‐cGAMP. This cyclic dinucleotide then binds to ER‐resident STING homodimers, inducing conformational changes and promoting their oligomerization. (B) STING recruits TBK1 and is transported through the Golgi apparatus, where it encounters luminal sGAGs that facilitate the oligomerization and activation of the complex. As the STING/TBK1 oligomers move to acidic endosomes, their interaction with sGAGs is strengthened, further stabilizing the oligomers and enhancing their activity. (C) PI4KB is recruited by both ACDB3 and ARMH3 to generate PI4P at the TGN. Accumulation of PI4P at the TGN leads to the recruitment of MCS lipid‐transfer proteins, such as OSBP and CERT, promoting cholesterol/SM enrichment at the TGN. Such a lipid‐ordered membrane environment promotes STING palmitoylation, which in turn favors STING clustering and oligomer stability. This ensures stable binding and phosphorylation of TBK1, with subsequent IRF3 activation. PI4P enrichment at the TGN also contributes to the proper trafficking of STING to endosomes by recruiting PI4P‐binding clathrin adaptors AP1 or GGA. title: Skin Relevant Biomaterials from Wound Healing, Medical Aesthetics, Flexible Electronics to Artificial Intelligence and Beyond
abstract: Recent advancements in biomaterials have profoundly transformed the fields of dermatology and tissue engineering, etc., offering innovative solutions that markedly improve skin treatment outcomes. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the latest developments in natural, synthetic, and composite biomaterials tailored for skin treatments and skin‐related medical devices, including wound healing, tissue engineering, drug delivery, dermatological therapies, medical aesthetics, e‐skin, and skin‐related surgery‐assistant devices. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into biomaterial design has facilitated the development of adaptive and predictive systems capable of responding dynamically to the skin's physiological needs. Moreover, an in‐depth understanding of the interactions between biomaterials and cells, as well as the activation of biological pathways and regulation of cellular processes is pivotal for enhancing skin health and function. Looking forward, the main efforts toward future in this field are suggested as follows: 1) Development of novel materials remains central; 2) Responsive biomaterials enable precise therapy; 3) Integration with cell therapy is pivotal in regenerative medicine; 4) In‐depth investigations into material‐driven biological mechanisms are critical for innovative design of skin‐related materials; 5) Interdisciplinary collaboration is vital for the rapid evolution of biomaterials; 6) Enhanced applications of AI is driving the development of adaptive and predictive biomaterials.

title: Revolutionizing diabetic foot ulcer treatment: phage therapy as a next-generation antimicrobial approach- a review on breaking the cycle of resistance
abstract:
### Background

Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a major complication of diabetes, impacting approximately one-third of diabetic patients worldwide. Treating DFUs has become increasingly difficult due to the rise of multidrug-resistant bacteria like Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa . These pathogens often form biofilms, which protect them from both antibiotics and the immune system, making infections harder to eliminate. As a result, new treatment approaches are urgently needed to overcome the limitations of traditional antibiotic therapies. This integrative review investigates the potential of bacteriophage (phage) therapy as an alternative treatment for DFUs. A thorough analysis of recent scientific literature was conducted to explore the underlying mechanisms of DFUs, the impact of antibiotic resistance and biofilms, and the biological properties of bacteriophages that make them effective against resistant infections. Key phage components—such as structural proteins, tail fibers, endolysins, and enzymes that degrade bacterial capsules—were examined for their therapeutic relevance.

### Results

Evidence from laboratory studies, animal models, and early clinical research shows that phage therapy is effective in targeting drug-resistant bacteria involved in DFUs. Phages offer several advantages, including their ability to specifically target harmful bacteria, break down biofilms, and multiply at infection sites. These characteristics make them a promising tool for treating chronic, non-healing wounds.

### Conclusion

Bacteriophage therapy represents a cutting-edge strategy for managing DFUs, particularly in cases where conventional antibiotics fail. By utilizing the natural antibacterial properties of phages, this approach could lead to more personalized and precise wound care, potentially transforming the way chronic diabetic ulcers are treated.

title: Emerging lipid nanoparticle systems capable of efficient intramuscular RNA delivery
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) enable RNA delivery, primarily via intramuscular (IM) injection, catalyzing breakthroughs like the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines. LNPs encapsulate RNA, using ionizable lipids for endosomal escape and PEG-lipids for stability. IM administration leverages muscle tissue’s immune-rich environment, enabling localized antigen production, reduced systemic toxicity, and scalability. Challenges include cold-chain dependence, RNA instability, and immunogenicity from PEG/lipids. Future advancements, driven by AI (e.g. AGILE platform), hybrid lipid-polymer systems, and stimuli-responsive formulations, aim to enhance controlled release and stability. Innovations like thermostable lyophilized LNPs and biodegradable materials promise improved accessibility and safety. Beyond pandemics, LNPs hold potential for accelerating vaccines against HIV and malaria, and advancing personalized medicine through CRISPR therapies and cancer neoantigen vaccines. Interdisciplinary efforts in chemistry, immunology, and AI are poised to expand RNA therapeutics for genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and precision oncology. Evolving from emergency tools to mainstream platforms, LNPs herald a paradigm shift toward equitable access and tailored treatments for unmet clinical needs.

Future advancements, driven by AI (e.g. AGILE platform), hybrid lipid-polymer systems, and stimuli-responsive formulations, aim to enhance controlled release and stability. Innovations like thermostable lyophilized LNPs and biodegradable materials promise improved accessibility and safety. Beyond pandemics, LNPs hold potential for accelerating vaccines against HIV and malaria, and advancing personalized medicine through CRISPR therapies and cancer neoantigen vaccines. Interdisciplinary efforts in chemistry, immunology, and AI are poised to expand RNA therapeutics for genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and precision oncology. Evolving from emergency tools to mainstream platforms, LNPs herald a paradigm shift toward equitable access and tailored treatments for unmet clinical needs.

## Keywords
Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs); RNA delivery; mRNA vaccines; intramuscular administration; personalized medicine

The cGAS–STING pathway, a pivotal component of the innate immune system, plays a crucial role in the pathological processes of various neurological diseases and injuries. In neuroinflammatory diseases and neural injuries, aberrant activation of the cGAS–STING pathway amplifies neuroinflammation, type I interferon responses, and cell death. Inhibition of cGAS–STING-related genes holds promise for promoting neural regeneration following disease recovery and defect regeneration. Future research must apply advanced omics technologies to further delineate the exact functions of the cGAS–STING pathway in neural regeneration. # cGAS–STING pathway modulation: A new hope for neural regeneration

## Abstract
In recent decades, the limitations of therapeutic interventions have elevated neurological disorders and injuries to a prominent position in academic research. Existing neurotherapeutic methodologies have demonstrated insufficient efficacy in fostering neural regeneration. The current integration of precision medicine technologies and innovative tissue engineering methods holds significant promise for attaining neural regeneration. The cGAS–STING pathway, a pivotal component of the innate immune system, plays a crucial role in the pathological processes of various neurological diseases and injuries. In neuroinflammatory diseases and neural injuries, aberrant activation of the cGAS–STING pathway amplifies neuroinflammation, type I interferon responses, and cell death. Inhibition of cGAS–STING-related genes holds promise for promoting neural regeneration following disease recovery and defect regeneration. In this review, the foundational pathophysiological mechanisms underlying cGAS–STING-related gene regulation in neurological disorders and injuries are elucidated with a special emphasis on its implications in nerve-related cells. In this review, we highlight the advances in tissue engineering technologies that integrate cGAS–STING pathway modulators, highlighting their potential therapeutic efficacy in modulating neural regeneration. Nevertheless, the role of the cGAS–STING pathway in neural regeneration remains relatively limited. Bibliometric analysis demonstrates a significant correlation of cGAS–STING pathway activation with various neuropathological processes. Studies have progressively focused on the critical role of this pathway in neurological diseases and injuries. As it stands, the effectiveness of tissue engineering technologies involving cGAS–STING-related gene modulators in achieving neural regeneration remains unfulfilled in its potential. Future research must apply advanced omics technologies to further delineate the exact functions of the cGAS–STING pathway in neural regeneration. Integration of these results with precision medicine approaches will be necessary for creating tissue engineering biomaterials with capabilities for precise delivery and targeted controlled release of cGAS–STING-related genes in neural regeneration-related cells, towards functional recovery from neurological injury and diseases.

## Keywords
biomaterials; cGAS–STING; nerve injury; neural regeneration; neurodegeneration; neuroinflammation; precision medicine; tissue engineering

## Introduction

The cGAS–STING pathway is a crucial regulator of innate immune signaling and is heavily involved in many neurological disorders and injuries (Xu et al., 2024b; Huang et al., 2025a). cGAS, the primary cytosolic sensor for DNA, is able to detect both exogenous pathogen DNA and endogenous DNA that is liberated from cellular damage. This detection triggers STING, which subsequently activates type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling and the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Yang et al., 2024c), which act to neutralize pathogens and coordinate immune responses. The cGAS–STING pathway has been identified as an important mechanism for the pathogenesis of neurological diseases and injuries (Wang et al., 2024e).

The nervous system is a precisely regulated and complex ecosystem where precise regulation of immune responses is crucial to maximize neuronal recovery of function and permit neural regeneration (Enamorado et al., 2023). Hyperactivation of the cGAS–STING pathway leads to increased neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration, which promotes disease progression and impedes neural regeneration (Gulen et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025c). Recent reports have demonstrated the presence and functional significance of cGAS–STING signaling in various cell types of the nervous system, including resident immune cells, neurons, and glial cells (Verma et al., 2024). Currently, therapeutic reagents against the cGAS–STING pathway have been developed for the therapy of neural injuries and neuroinflammatory diseases to alleviate neuroinflammation and promote the restoration of neurological function (Huang et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2025b). However, there is no systematic review that synthesizes the cGAS–STING pathway mechanisms and its applicable targeted therapeutic material in neurological diseases and injuries.

This review summarizes the current research status and treatment methods including the cGAS–STING pathway in neurological diseases and injuries, indicating their limitations and suggesting directions for future research on mechanisms and the establishment of treatment methods. Through bibliometric analysis, we have extracted the research hotspots and key events in this field, highlighting the most important role played by genes associated with cGAS–STING in neurological injuries and diseases. It also hopes to give directions for future studies of the mechanisms involved in and therapeutic strategy design with cGAS–STING in these disorders. By conducting the clarification of the role of cGAS–STING in neurological disorders and injury, we hope to encourage future studies on related mechanisms and propose new directions of research on the application of tissue engineering technologies in the treatment of neurological diseases and injuries.

## Overview of the cGAS–STING Pathway

cGAS–STING pathway, a quintessential component of innate immunity, perceives cytosolic DNA to induce the activation of inflammatory cytokines and IFN-Is to promote immunity. It is also crucial for intercellular communication and cellular perturbation sensing, contributing significantly to various pathophysiological processes.

### The components of the cGAS–STING pathway

The cGAS–STING pathway provides a critical connection between DNA detection and the innate immune system (Kirchhoff et al., 2025). This pathway involves genes such as cGAS, STING, nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), IFNs, Janus Kinases (JAK), and signal transducers and activators of transcription (STAT) ( Figure 1 ), which play pivotal roles in neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and neuroimmune functions (Hou et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2025b). Above all, the cGAS–STING pathway acts on immune cells and activates inflammatory cytokine secretion that aggravates neuroinflammation (Shi et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024d; Zhou et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025c). In addition to influencing immune cells, activation of the cGAS–STING pathway is also observed in non-immune cells such as neurons and glial cells, where it regulates their cellular processes (Jiang et al., 2023a).

cGAS functions as a DNA sensor through the recognition of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) in the cytoplasm and the catalysis of production of the second messenger cyclic GMP-AMP (cGAMP) from ATP and GTP (Zhang et al., 2023b). The cytoplasmic DNA may be of exogenous or endogenous origin. Exogenous origin includes pieces of microbial pathogens, and endogenous origin includes genomic DNA damage and mitochondrial breakage (Cao et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2023c). The cGAMP synthesized binds to the adapter protein STING, which is anchored in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This binding causes STING to be relocated from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where it phosphorylates TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) and IκB kinase (Wang et al., 2025). TBK1 subsequently phosphorylates interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), leading to its dimerization and nuclear translocation, which subsequently activates the production of IFN-Is, along with other inflammatory mediators, pro-apoptotic genes, and chemokines (Lam et al., 2021). In addition, IFNs also induce the production of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) via the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, which creates a positive feedback loop, thereby activating the cGAS and STING activation (Shaikh et al., 2025). Ultimately, whether localized within the autophagosome or sourced from the Golgi apparatus, STING is transported to the lysosome for degradation (Sliter et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2025c; Yang et al., 2025a).

### Intercellular cGAMP signaling networks

Existing research has revealed that cGAMP is a critical intercellular signaling molecule, playing a key function in intercellular communication and enhancement of immune responses (He et al., 2025). cGAMP transmits intercellularly through two primary pathways: gap junctions and non-specific transmembrane carriers ( Figure 1 ). Gap junctions are not only formed between homotypic cell types but also between heterogeneous populations of cells participating in physiological immune responses (Decout et al., 2021; Ge et al., 2025; Tishchenko et al., 2025). Amplification of cGAS–STING activation signals between neurons and between non-neuronal cells and neurons is facilitated by gap junctions, thereby increasing neuroinflammation and immune responses (Elzinga et al., 2022; Ullah et al., 2022). The modulation of cGAS–STING signaling in bystander cells is obtained through inter-neuronal gap junctions, resulting in enhanced neuronal apoptosis (Tan et al., 2022). cGAMP was also discovered to be passed from neurons to microglia, passing neuroinflammatory signals (Ge et al., 2025). Interestingly, gap junction inhibition has the ability to significantly inhibit cGAS–STING-linked gene-mediated neuroinflammation in the brain (Elzinga et al., 2022). Moreover, intercellular cGAMP signaling gap junction-dependently takes place among the cancer cells and plays a critical role in tumor destruction and immune evasion (Yi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b).

Non-selective transmembrane carriers, or transporters, channels, and pores such as SLC19A1, SLC46A2, P2X7, ABCC1, and volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs), are vital for extruding cGAMP into the extracellular milieu and bringing it into cells (Decout et al., 2021; Blest et al., 2024). Some viruses have been found to target the downregulation of SLC46A2, P2X7, and the VRAC subunits LRRC8A and LRRC8C, thereby limiting innate immune response through decreased intercellular communication mediated by cGAMP (Blest et al., 2024). Ablation of the volume-regulated anion channel LRRC8/VRAC by genetics or chemical inhibition results in impaired cGAMP transfer between tumor-associated macrophages and fibroblasts, decreasing STING-dependent interferon response (Wang et al., 2024a). Furthermore, cGAMP importation by LRRC8C and subsequent STING-p53 activation represents a novel inhibitory mechanism in adaptive immunity and T cells (Concepcion et al., 2022). Some cells possess members of the ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase family that catabolize cGAMP and thus inhibit cGAMP-mediated intercellular communication (Mardjuki et al., 2024).

Vesicles in atypical autophagosomes with activated STING in Rafeesomes are released as R-EVs (RAB22A-induced extracellular vesicles). R-EVs activate the IFNβ pathway in acceptor cells of the tumor microenvironment and thereby enhance anti-tumor immunity (Gao et al., 2022). The transport routes of these new targets must be investigated in future studies on neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases related to the cGAS–STING pathway to elucidate aberrant intercellular communication and identify new targets for activation.

### Detecting cellular perturbations via the cGAS–STING pathway

The cGAS–STING pathway not only works as a typical pattern recognition receptor but also as a central mediator of danger detection for sensing non-environmentally linked self-DNA (Lei et al., 2023; Zecchini et al., 2023). Intracellular DNA stability can be disturbed by different pathological processes, thereby activating the cGAS–STING pathway (Huang et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024b; Figure 1 ).

Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is vulnerable to damage induced by reactive oxygen species generated by the electron transport chain in the process of respiration due to its proximity to the electron transport chain complexes (Chen et al., 2007; Green et al., 2008). In contrast to the robust repair machinery that safeguards nuclear DNA, repair pathways for mtDNA are comparatively inefficient, making it more vulnerable to damage (Marx et al., 2025). mtDNA damage is also linked to various neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases (Gulen et al., 2023; Zong et al., 2024). Within mitochondria, mitochondrial transcription factor A plays a role in stabilizing mtDNA by forming nucleosomes, which is essential for mtDNA stress prevention and blocking the abnormal activation of cGAS (Xie et al., 2024a). Numerous stress signals can induce mitochondrial dysfunction, potentially leading to apoptosis in severe cases, which facilitates the loss of mtDNA compartmentalization (Carloni et al., 2024). Under stress, mtDNA can be expelled through the inner mitochondrial membrane and subsequently released through BAX/BAK or via pores generated by the voltage-dependent anion channel on the outer mitochondrial membrane (Victorelli et al., 2023). The mitochondrial permeability transition pore may provide an alternative route for mtDNA to traverse the inner mitochondrial membrane (Yang et al., 2024a). mtDNA entry into the cytosol activates the cGAS–STING pathway, promoting the upregulated expression of ISGs and the downstream inflammatory and immune responses (Du et al., 2025).

Nuclear DNA can be accessed by cytosolic cGAS through three distinct mechanisms (Peng et al., 2025). The first mechanism is the derepression of retrotransposon elements, specifically long interspersed nuclear element 1 (LINE1). This derepression leads to increased LINE1 transcription and the accumulation of LINE1 cDNA, which activates the cGAS–STING pathway, resulting in the secretion of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype and subsequent cellular senescence (Tang et al., 2024). The second mechanism involves DNA damage or replication stress, which can cause the direct leakage of nuclear DNA into the cytosol (Haase et al., 2022). Furthermore, during senescence, chromatin protrusions may emerge from the primary nucleus, leading to the accumulation of cytosolic chromatin fragments (Dasgupta et al., 2024). In situations of genomic instability, nuclear DNA may be encapsulated into micronuclei during mitosis and later released into the cytoplasm (Zannini et al., 2024). All these mechanisms of cytosolic DNA recognition originating from the nucleus are effectively inhibited by the exonuclease TREX1 (Yang et al., 2025c). Within the cellualr nucleus, nucleosomes and structural chromatin proteins, including histone H1 and the barrier-to-autointegration factor, collaboratively restrict aberrant cGAS activity (Broussard et al., 2023). Notably, these various activation modes are not mutually exclusive; they may redundantly and synergistically trigger cGAS activity in different contexts.

### cGAS–STING pathway and cell death

Cell death is crucial for tissue and organ development, as well as for removing infected, damaged, or transformed cells to maintain tissue homeostasis (Tsvetkov et al., 2022). Multiple forms of cell death, such as apoptosis, ferroptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, autophagy, and immunogenic cell death (Huang et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025a; Zha et al., 2025), are vital in neurological disorders and injuries (Li et al., 2022c; Wang et al., 2022b). Recently, evidence has shown that there is crosstalk between the cGAS–STING pathway and various types of cell death, which in turn affects neuronal survival ( Figure 2 ).

#### Autophagy

Autophagy is a crucial cellular process in eukaryotes that entails the sequestration of cytosolic components within double-membraned autophagosomes, which then fuse with endosomal or lysosomal vesicles to facilitate the degradation and recycling of the sequestered substrates (Zhao et al., 2025a). This process consists of five key steps: initiation, nucleation, elongation, autophagosome formation, and degradation (Murthy et al., 2020).

STING contains a domain that interacts with the classical autophagy protein LC3 (Xun et al., 2024). p62 is a member of a broad family of ubiquitin-binding autophagy receptors that link ubiquitin to autophagy through its ubiquitin-binding domain and light chain 3 (LC3)-interaction region. In the initial phase of autophagy, STING dissociates from the ER and is transported to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment after binding to cGAMP, which supplies membranes for LC3 lipidation and autophagosome formation (Gui et al., 2019). STING is then incorporated into autophagosomes and sorted into lysosomes (Xun et al., 2024). Herein, p62, autophagy protein 5 (ATG5), and WIPI2 are necessary for canonical autophagosome formation stimulated by STING (Wan et al., 2023), while the UNC-51-like autophagy-activating kinase 1 (ULK1) complex and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase catalytic subunit type 3 (PIK3C3/VPS34) complex are dispensable (Gui et al., 2019).
